I give it a "meh". I recommend it only because I really enjoyed the story. Often when I was getting through cutscenes I would be bummed out that I would have to get back to gameplay because I was engaged in the story.
A lot of collectibles in the game. Some people like that sort of stuff but I only collected the things if they were nearby to me. Music was good but the problem I had was that it would repeat probably the same ten or so songs (I realize later that only certain songs played in certain areas during certain times, etc.) but it did get annoying.
Gameplay? It was okay, I guess. Very repetitive. Kill a group of guys, interrogate some guys. Go from point A to point B then go back to point A to kill a boss and then go to point B again then go back to point A to kill the actual boss. Repeat, repeat.
Dialogue was good and fun. I didn't feel like a mafia boss, though. I couldn't really collect cars and I was just kinda running around like a super soldier occasionally calling some contacts.
As for bugs, oh there's a lot of them. At least for me. My character clipped through the ground and fell out of the map a few times, their clothes would get glitched, things would happen in cutscenes (had a couple NPCs get hit by cars during cutscenes so it was unable to trigger a necessary event, etc). There's typos, you name it. Sometimes my screen would flicker and become unstable if things were being loaded or spawned.
The driving is abysmal. I mean it doesn't need to be racing game quality but damn it really says something when the NPCs can't even drive the cars. The damn chick that picked up my money hit me with her car every time I called her, and I would often have cutscenes calling in reinforcements or something and just laugh as the cars are hitting and running over each other.
If you're gonna play it, don't get it for $40. Get it when it's much cheaper or on sale. The story is engaging enough to keep your attention (well for me it was) but that's about it.

This is very much a First Impressions sort of review.
After three hours, I'm loving this game. First, let me say it runs smoothly on Vista (some of us are still in the Dark Ages...). It does "chop" a bit every time the day ticks over, which it does often, but I got used to it fairly quickly. This is something the studio's other grand strategy games do as well, if I'm not mistaken, it's simply more noticeable here because of the real-time movement and the like.
I've read the dev diaries on this game so I know I haven't even scratched the surface of what's here. What I've got access to right now is fun to play around with. The universe I've been generated into - home to 600 star systems - is brimming with possibility to the point that I'm actually feeling giddy. It's a complex game, make no mistake; but the basics are easy to process once you've taken some time to absorb the visual information in front of you when you first appear in the game world.
There's simply too much in the way of features to note very much here; for those, I suggest Googling "Stellaris dev diaries" or looking for a more in-depth review. I'm instead going to give you the short version:
If you like space, you will definitely enjoy this game.
If you like grand strategy, you will most likely enjoy this game.
If you like 4X-style games, there's a good chance you'll like this game.
If you like the studio's other grand strategy titles, you'll probably like Stellaris.
If you like the studio's other grand strategy titles AND you like space, you will want to wed this game like a French princess with a 78 year-old father and no living brothers.
In essence, the game is Europa Universalis in space. If that phrase gets you excited, you should buy this right now.
BONUS REVIEW: Civilization creation. Creation is an aspect of ANY game I personally enjoy, so I'd like to make specific notes about this. The creation mechanic is astounding; far beyond anything I've seen in another strategy game that allows you to customize your civilization. Everything from the name and appearance of your first leader to demonym to the insignia that represents you is customizable (all with very nice options, might I add). Further, the way you're allowed to customize your civilization's ethos and traits really make it come alive. Each choice has a tangible effect on gameplay in a number of ways, not all of them statistical. You even get to choose what type of weapons your ships can use from the start (mass drivers such as autocannons, missiles, or laser weaponry.) I had a ton of fun just making my civilization.
The gameplay is so repetitive that I got bored before finishing it.

First thing first: the game works flawlessly on Linux.
The graphics are beautiful, and the game runs smooth even on my laptop which has an Intel graphic card (using the open source Intel driver).
Second, this is Paradox game with the best tutorial I've ever seen.
It also helps that the UI design is way, way better than their other titles.
Also last but not least, the gameplay. Oh man, it was ridiculously addictive, and deep! Playing for just 2 hours I ran into all kinds of anomalies while exploring the galaxy, making the task of sending a ship to explore unknown stars feel like an episode of Star Treks. From space whales to long lost civilizations. And we haven't even got to other factions yet.
In short, think MoO2, but with all the goodies you expected from Paradox grand strategy game. Each government has its own unique mechanics, each ship is commanded by a captain that has attributes (a la CK2 lite), hell even your goverment is run by a politician who also has attributes and gained experiences, Each planet has pops that works factories or labs, and these pops would also influence how your government is run. Hell, This game is basically the culmination of Paradox grand strategy games, and a very refined one at that.
I'd write more, but I need to get back to my empire. I feel like I barely scratch the surface of what this game has to offer. So, tl;dr is game is good, really, REALLY good. From the gameplay to graphics to sounds. Paradox really hit the homerun with this one

This game is by far better than it's reviews! I played MAFIA I & II and didn't expect much of part III 'cause of all the bad reviews. I got surprised a lot.
-TLDR: I had a ton of fun in ~40h playtime.
-Tech stuff:
In 2017 I had no technical problems as far as i remember. The performance could be optimized but it was quite OK on an i5 with an R9 380. The ingame graphic seems a little outdated for a relatively new game, but it still looks good overall. The cutscenes tho are just AMAZING, especially the face expressions.
-Story, Gameplay:
The game draws a really nice picture of the 70s and the ongoing Vietnam war. One of the greatest things in the game is the SOUNDTRACK. You will listen to the hits of that time, from Rolling Stones to Steppenwolf, which adds HUGE flair.
The 'revenge' main storyline isn't too inventive but you really get connected with some characters. It's true that during the main missions a lot of gameplay is repetitive (taking over racks and districts mainly always works the same way), but for me it never really got boring, the game also doesn't force you to do all available tasks, just a certain amount. The character development throughout the game is superb, especially meeting Vito again was a pleasure. Only the side missions which raise your income are in fact quite lengthy and boring, but you really don't need them to finish the game. But if you do, the game will give you a lot of background infos about the side characters, which round the picture of MAFIA III's world.
One point of critique is that the open world is in fact crowded, but seems kinda 'dead' anyways - it can't compete with GTA V for example. Driving around is still fun since the car mechanics work quite well and the game devs did a nice job designing the different areas of the city, imo.

This game is so much better than I expected, and I'm so glad I picked up the developer bundle. LiEat was the first game from Miwashiba that I'd ever played, and I was absolutely amazed.
First off, the soundtrack is gorgeous. It makes the story feel more alive than it already is. Each chapter has its own music too, it's not just one soundtrack being filled into every storyline. As the game advertises the OST comes with the game, which makes it all the more worth it. Not just the sound, but the art style is gorgeous as well. Not so much as the main world, but the CGs during certain cutscenes. Some of them you can see above, in the game's featured videos/screenshots. I absolutely love the art style and how well it fits into the game.
But besides the soundtrack, the story is downright amazing. The game is split into three distinct chapters. The storylines don't fully connect, as they take place in completely different locations, but they do tie together and are told chronologically, so I would highly recommend playing them in order. Each chapter takes about an hour and a half to two hours to complete, depending on how fast of a reader you are, or if you read the content at all.
The entire storyline focuses around Efina, the Lie-Eating Dragon and her "papa", who goes by Leo/Hal/Sid in the three chapters. Along they way they solve three separate mysteries, while learning about Efina and her power, and where she came from. There's a heavy emphasis on the story's tales of dragons, along with liars and how they relate to the world. There's a large portion of the story that's either downright adorable, or so intense that you feel strongly for what is going on. For a cute game, it also has it's serious points, mostly to do with liars and caring for loved ones. It's charming in a way that works, even for a simple and short RPG.
The only thing I would even remotely have against this game is how small the world is. There's only one area and a couple side areas to explore. I feel like this game makes it work rather well. All the story is in one spot, which makes it straight forward and you aren't getting lost or turned around often. For the story requiring you to do things in a certain order, I feel like this is more of a good thing than a bad thing, but if you enjoy exploring a massive world, you may not enjoy how small the map is.
For you achievement hunters out there, some of them are more difficult to find as they require you to interact with the world. Reading the info on the achievement should give you a straight-forward idea of how to get them all, though they're all chapter specific, so you have to know where to look for what. In my first runs of each chapter I got probably half of them, or a little over half.
This game is one of my new favorites, and I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys RPGs and fantasy. This game deserves so much more attention than it's getting.

Just finished The Witcher 2 and I got to admit it's like it tries to be both a RPG and a VN, yet fails (as I see it) to be either. I guess that's just because I like my RPGs to be action RPGs and my VN be no action (in the sense of text and choiced only, nothing else). Yet I will recommend it for I suppose it's not that the game is bad, it's that I wanted not the things this game has to offer me and it's kind of my fault for not having thought this through.
The fights are either too short (too few enemies) or either too hard (too strong enemies) the only fun being those fought when approaching the Harpies nests and on the Vergen's walls. Oh! And no experience for you, level up via the quests only, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (well, you technically can gain 2-3 levels by fighting during the game, but you have to fight loads of monsters, more than the game actually gives you. And you will not get the exp for them after some time, so no grinding for ya). The loot is poor and you are poor as the Price/Sell ratio is like x5, more for better items (buy for 2500, sell for 100, yeah, right. Or the crafting! Buy a recipe for 100 gold, buy ingridients for 150 gold + pay 20 gold to craft a subart... which you can buy for like 25 gold. Why, again?). Do I have to mention the horribly sluggish system of potions, alchemy, crafting, trading and menus in general? I had to ggole how to switch off the mouse smoothening (there is not a single PC player happy with mouse acceleration/deceleration)

Apart from some early Bioware titles, i have never been quite so hooked to a game series as i have been to the first two Witcher titles.
Immersion is what gives this series, in my humble opinion, the edge over its contemporaries.
By not being open world, the Assassins of Kings can focus primarily on its compelling central story line. Open worlds provide you with 'options' but risk not being able to make you care enough about any one thing. The most recent Elder Scrolls for example have had pretty lacklustre main storylines. Other games such as Kingdom of Amalur fall into the trap of giving the player too many, and repetitive tasks.
In other words the Witcher 2 plays a very nice balance between freedom and narrative.
The world and its lore is incredible and worth immersing yourself in, BUT, if you don't read the Sapkowski novels or play the previous game you risk becoming bewildered quickly.
Crafting, levelling, gear accumulation, are all satisfying and add a lot to the depth.
There are alternative story paths you will only get to see by playing multiple times, meaning there is great replay value in this; you get to see the result of your choices, either from the first game, or in an early chapter of this game, in what happens later on. for the RPG fan this is very satisfying.
No environments are recycled a la Dragon Age 2.
So, any caveats with this game?
Yes, Combat. it's not such a black and white case of poor combat in the way that Dragon Age 2 was, but, it can be very frustrating. A lot of the time what you really crave is a good duel, one on one (or one versus two) swordfight. Ocasionally, you will have extremely satisfying and rewarding fights with parrying, dodging, the whole shebang. But most of the time especially in the early game it's hard to survive without spamming the 'roll' key, the result being that Geralt launches himself to and fro like a lunatic. With parrying fairly ineffectual before you level up damage reduction and with many enemies invulnerable from the front, you will be reduced to rolling behind them and slashing he/she/they/it from behind. It can feel disappointing when the game forces you to win by these unsatisfying means.
However, combat can still look a treat, like the rest of the game, and this is no reason not to buy such a well executed game

PROS: simple, casual gameplay
"easy to pick up hard to master" sorta thing, but in the sense of building your character and synergising different abilities
Finds a way to make anything and everything useful to some degree, and you'll find yourself digging into several stats at once to make a build that holds its own
Super intelligent UI and menu management, something essentially nonexistant in the modern era
NEUTRAL: Isometric
CONS: definetly a dated game, not in the way Half-Life was the revolutionary FPS game but more of the "old gem that's outshadowed by other games, yet retaining really cool features that modern games have lost"
Less-that-helpful tutorial system, it teaches you the very basics but unless you're willing to look at all the niches of all the stats and find out information for yourself in the dungeon, you'll miss out. Seriously, it took me until floor 8 to realize that I could run away from a strike and have it miss my hitbox.
OVERALL: 82/100, has charm and is endless fun but is relatively simple. Some shortcomings here and there, but most are overshadowed by good excecution by the developers.
do note that this does hold a nostalgic place in my heart, but not enough to keep me playing if I didn't enjoy it. Even non-fans on RPGs will like it, and 2 hours (steam's max refund playtime) is more than enough to grasp a general feel of the game.

Little Inferno is an enjoyable little game whose story is more compelling than the gameplay. Its feature is burning stuff and doing so in various combonations to earn the right to progress further into the game. The thrill of burning things, itself, is limited. By the time you unlock the second or third catalog of items to burn, you've got the idea and experienced pretty much the extent of it.
Little Inferno's story -- told through letters delivered on a regular basis -- is what keeps you burning things and searching for the right pairings of items to match the list of combos it offers you. While the story is compelling, it is not necessarily ultimately satisfying.
After about three hours, you'll have completed the game and consumed its somewhat cryptic story and not-so-cryptic parable (yes, there is a life lesson that it's trying to convey to you).
I can't advise this game for someone looking for a solid puzzle game. There's just not enough content to last long. If you're interested in a fairly clever little story told through interesting  means, then it's definitely worth trying. Regardless of what you're looking to get out of it, I don't know that it can quite justify its full price.

Blood is one of the finest classic 2.5D shooters ever made.
You play as Caleb, an undead gunslinger that used to worship the dark god Tchernobog but for some reason gets betrayed and killed off along with his cultist friends and many years later has risen from his grave seeking revenge against his old master, simple enough.
What really sets Blood apart from other shooters is its creative weapons, great level design and plenty of gore.
The weapons that you use are incredibly varied and ranges from a Pitchfork and Tommy Gun to Dynamite and a Tesla Gun which all include alternate firing modes letting you destroy your opponents in tons of different ways.
These range from setting enemies on fire, to electrocuting them and even peeling their skin off with a voodoo doll.
Levels in Blood run the gamut, ranging from Cathedrals and Carnivals, to Haunted Hotels and Train Stations. You even journey through the stomach of a living being at one point.
All the levels feature plenty of secrets full of goodies and feature lots of humorous references to horror novels and movies, they're also fairly lenghty and sometimes require you to collect up to 6 keys to complete which can make the levels confusing to navigate at times.
While the graphics are certainly dated, their still more than playable even if some of the colours used can be repetitive. The music is fantastic and fits into the game perfectly and the voice of the main character adds plenty of personality to the gameplay.
Overall Blood is a fantastic game and in my opinion is the best BUILD engine game, with over 40 levels there is lots of replay value as well.

For folks looking for space exploration and empire builders, the 4X crowd, this is your holy grail.
Early game focuses on exploration, charting, and colonization with strong barriers blocking the normal early-game colony rush.  Science and discovery is as important as raw resource might in this phase and adds endless charm and uniqueness to each game.
Mid game transitions into one of diplomacy and early warfare as you and your neighbors establish a pecking order.  Exploration still occurs but the sites are dwindling by this point.
Late game moves into vast empires and federations staking claims and rearranging neighborhoods all over slights big and small.
Add to this late game crises (extra-dimensional invaders for example), relic ancient empires vastly beyond your starting capacity, nascent and emerging low-tech races, and a rewarding tech system you have a game that breathes fun and freshness in every play through.
Personally, this is what I've been waiting for nearly 20 years.
It was worth the wait.  And even more so now with the post-release improvements!

Blood, in case you are not familiar, is 1997 black comedy/horror shooter from renowned Monolith Software. Made in the same vein as Duke Nukem 3D and Shadow Warrior, Blood is one of those games in which character helped to create and solidify its cult-like status. Oh, and gore. Lotsa-lotsa gore, BLOOD, dismemberment and blatant disregard for any kind of moral boundaries.
Plot may be considered sub-par by today's standarts (Fahrenheit, Mass Effect and others come to mind), but back then simply HAVING plot could be considered a reason to give the title of GOTY. But, jokes aside, the story does get into you and push you forward, it keeps you playing. And it's also pretty gory.
Movement ontrols may be considered slippery, you may accidentally slide off a cliff and plummet into chunky salsa, however, in everything combat related, I would dare say it's near perfect. Even slippery movement can help you slither between enemies, with enough skill.
Graphics? Do I even need to talk about them? This game is made in 1997, expect sprites and voxels for some reason. All the sprites are nicely detailed, though. They're also easily recognizable from a distance, and tend to explode in pink mist at any good reason.
Atmosphere keeps nice balance between "creepy" and "hilarious" in a way that yes, those piles of meat may well be human bodies carved up for cooking, but it becomes hard to consider it a tragedy when Caleb utters "leftovers" and immediately unloads double barrels of lead into anything he didn't like, all while humming "Strangers in the Night".

Just finished The Witcher 2 and I got to admit it's like it tries to be both a RPG and a VN, yet fails (as I see it) to be either. I guess that's just because I like my RPGs to be action RPGs and my VN be no action (in the sense of text and choiced only, nothing else). Yet I will recommend it for I suppose it's not that the game is bad, it's that I wanted not the things this game has to offer me and it's kind of my fault for not having thought this through.
The fights are either too short (too few enemies) or either too hard (too strong enemies) the only fun being those fought when approaching the Harpies nests and on the Vergen's walls. Oh! And no experience for you, level up via the quests only, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (well, you technically can gain 2-3 levels by fighting during the game, but you have to fight loads of monsters, more than the game actually gives you. And you will not get the exp for them after some time, so no grinding for ya). The loot is poor and you are poor as the Price/Sell ratio is like x5, more for better items (buy for 2500, sell for 100, yeah, right. Or the crafting! Buy a recipe for 100 gold, buy ingridients for 150 gold + pay 20 gold to craft a subart... which you can buy for like 25 gold. Why, again?). Do I have to mention the horribly sluggish system of potions, alchemy, crafting, trading and menus in general? I had to ggole how to switch off the mouse smoothening (there is not a single PC player happy with mouse acceleration/deceleration)
The "VN" element is... well it's not bad in and of itself, yet the differences in the endings are minute and the dialogue is diluted by the need to fight - or just run around - in between. So I won't be playing it through again, not in the nearest half a year, at least, I see no reason to. Fun is heavily diluted. For me at least.
What an irony, but for the aforementioned combination the game might have been actually fun for me. Like if the action RPG elements were to be enhanced and stripped off of all the dialogue nonsense OR if the VN elements (well it's kind of R part of the RPG, so you should give them credit for that) were to be enhanced with meaningful differencies in endings and without the need to have to fight 2-3 enemies in between (come on, 500 enemies slain only after playing for good 30 hours?)
But I assume all the modern "story rich" RPGs are in some way like that (ME, DE, whatever else). Or am I mistaken and the fighting system and other "action" elements of an RPG in those are fine?
All in all I suppose personally I should have picked the Skyrim instead. Or Diablo 3, still haven't played but for its Demo.

Apart from some early Bioware titles, i have never been quite so hooked to a game series as i have been to the first two Witcher titles.
Immersion is what gives this series, in my humble opinion, the edge over its contemporaries.
By not being open world, the Assassins of Kings can focus primarily on its compelling central story line. Open worlds provide you with 'options' but risk not being able to make you care enough about any one thing. The most recent Elder Scrolls for example have had pretty lacklustre main storylines. Other games such as Kingdom of Amalur fall into the trap of giving the player too many, and repetitive tasks.
In other words the Witcher 2 plays a very nice balance between freedom and narrative.
The world and its lore is incredible and worth immersing yourself in, BUT, if you don't read the Sapkowski novels or play the previous game you risk becoming bewildered quickly.
Crafting, levelling, gear accumulation, are all satisfying and add a lot to the depth.
There are alternative story paths you will only get to see by playing multiple times, meaning there is great replay value in this; you get to see the result of your choices, either from the first game, or in an early chapter of this game, in what happens later on. for the RPG fan this is very satisfying.
No environments are recycled a la Dragon Age 2.
So, any caveats with this game?
Yes, Combat. it's not such a black and white case of poor combat in the way that Dragon Age 2 was, but, it can be very frustrating. A lot of the time what you really crave is a good duel, one on one (or one versus two) swordfight. Ocasionally, you will have extremely satisfying and rewarding fights with parrying, dodging, the whole shebang. But most of the time especially in the early game it's hard to survive without spamming the 'roll' key, the result being that Geralt launches himself to and fro like a lunatic. With parrying fairly ineffectual before you level up damage reduction and with many enemies invulnerable from the front, you will be reduced to rolling behind them and slashing he/she/they/it from behind. It can feel disappointing when the game forces you to win by these unsatisfying means.
However, combat can still look a treat, like the rest of the game, and this is no reason not to buy such a well executed game

Kopanito is a fast paced arcade football game where standard football rules do not apply. On a match level the games are 5v5 with no referee, no offsides, no fouls and crazy mechanics. Tackles are brutal but harmless. There's next to no dribbling and occasional power-ups spice up the games. And above all it's simply fun to play.
The controls feel simple but in fact provide quite a few possibilities. On a basic level you've got shoot and pass buttons. But holding them longer results in a long pass, or a more powerful shot. Additionally when near the opponents goal charging the shot slows time and you're able to bend the shot. The amount of power charged defines as well how high the ball goes. This can result in quite spectacular goals. If you combine this with the cross ins and spectacular kick flip goals - well enough to say that the goals are really satisfying and fun to watch.
Addition of power ups adds another layer to the game strategy and the fact that they're not abundant and you get just 2 or 3 per game makes them a good addition.
Graphics are cartoon like with a distinct style. Really nice looking and fitting the game perfectly.
The only complaints I have with this one is that it gets boring playing by yourself. There's a lot to unlock - teams and arenas, but they don't add anything to the game really. The teams are always of same skill level - and same as arenas are only decoration. The multiplayer while being there at the time of me playing had around 10 players at the same time and all games I was able to play online were laggy to the point of not being fun.
I can see this game being fun playing with your friends locally with a beer or during a party. But as a single player experience - I clocked in 8 hours in it and have no desire to play it any longer. Even the hardest difficulty while challenging at first can be mastered and there is little challenge after that.
Still a fun game worth picking up.

Geralt, The Witcher, hunter and slayer of monsters, is once again stuck in some game developer's Game of Thrones homage. Sighing, head-shaking and face-palming ensue.
~~~
* First game provided choices that affected overall plot. However, developer had to cement a specific path as canon to develop the plot for the new game. What this does is essentially ruin a lot of gamer's choices from the first game.
EG: I played a decent Geralt that got the non-humans to side with the king to overthrow the mutiny. Everyone was pardoned, and all was well. I told the king I wasn't his lackey. I also spurned Triss Merrigold (a powerful sorceress ally) by taking a young kid with magic powers to someone else instead of her. This not only ticked her off, but prevented her from being a love interest.
In starts W2 ... the King has turned into a royal jerk, treating non-humans like trash. (!?) They revolt, and he quells them with a wholesale slaughter. (?!??!) Geralt has turned into the king's body guard. (you're a monster hunter, not a body guard!), and I'm waking up next to a naked Triss as if we're long lost lovers that never had a spat. (ugh)
Essentially, every choice I made in the first game is tossed out the window, because the path the developers chose to lay the ground work for W2 didn't mesh with the choices I made in W1.
Making me feel special, guys.
~~~
* W1 was about moral choices & philosophy. W2 is just about choices. Most folks are scumbags, and you have to choose which one you become an errand boy for. After a while you realize there is no moral dilemma in this game. It's just a matter of being presented "choices", and not having enough information to determine what impact each choice would have.
So, you don't feel like you're making conscious choices to evolve the story in a specific direction. Instead, you're grasping at straws and feel helpless as you make choices and watch yourself become a victim of circumstances you didn't foresee or got forced upon you.
In the end, you realize these "choices" are just contrivances to give Geralt a "reason" to be involved. The plot's going to happen whether you like it or not. But, why are you there? Answers, vengeance, what? They let you decide ... but you're going along whether you want to or not. Some choices impact plot direction, but it all turns out tragic regardless. They have a clear idea of how the third game is going to start. The second game just offers multiple paths to get to the same point. So, again, "choices" are just contrived and pointless.
~~~
* Sometimes dialogues don't flag the "final" topic, or make it clear that the ones you have to choose from are actually forks in a road where there's no going back. This sucks.
EG1: 4 topics to talk about. Pick one ... show a cut-scene we're moving on. Wait! I wanted to ask about the other topics! Nope, sorry, the one you picked was to move on with the story.
EG2: You ask a question. 4 topics show up to choose from. Pick one. That's all you get. You can't ask about the others. Know why? Because this was an "I will answer only one question" scenario that you didn't realize until it's over. Didn't ask the right questions? Sorry, sucks to be you.
It doesn't help that the verbiage for each topic doesn't match what Geralt actually ends up saying. You read it thinking it's neutral or hostile or whatever, then Geralt goes off in a different direction and you're like "whoa, I didn't know I was going to act like that!... or get that reaction!" (usually in a bad way)
~~~
* This is a nitpick, but you have to set your gfx and control options OUTSIDE the game in the launcher. It's the 21st century, and a AAA title is doing this? Wow...
~~~
* The fonts are all over the place. They're extremely tiny while walking around looking at peoples' names or looking through your inventory / character screens. Then you get to fist-fighting, and the key references for the quick-time-events use such a huge font it truncates the key reference if you chose something unusual.
EG: I mapped WASD to numpad. So, instead of "W" or "A" in the fight-scenes I see "NU" and "NU". What flipping key is it?! I cn't tell, b/c the huge font truncates the key name. You can't alt-tab out of the game to look at game guides. So, I get to watch Geralt get beat like a wuss, then have to exit out  and look up how to have a fist-fight in this game.
~~~
Speaking of mini-games, dice poker is back. But this time the computer seems to cheat less. However, you can't wager very much. And... you can literally throw your dice off the board (or sometimes one or two will bounce off it). Those dice don't count then, leaving you screwed. And the hand hovers over the board making it hard to tell where you're going to toss them. Why did they change it? The original worked so well.
~~~
* The plot is all over the place. Thankfully there is more monster hunting actually worked into it this time instead of just used as side-quest garbage. But, the over-arching Game of Thrones plot still weighs upon this heavy and bogs things down.
There are layers upon layers of intrigue as you find out someone that acts one way is doing decent / scummy stuff on the side then you find out later that they are not merely a local rabble but actually part of the grander scheme of things.
You've been making choices based on what you know about these people at the time of the choices, but as you learn more and more about them your choices may change to support or deny them. This just puts you in a huge, hodge-podge mess where none of your choices seem to support each other or direct the plot with any sense. Eventually you will think to yourself "how did I get here? why are things happening like this?"
Basically, this game teaches you that trying to make a difference one way can end up causing the very things you were trying to avoid. Likewise, you're not making the best choices, you're choosing the lesser of two evils. And that's all subjective, so utterly pointless, too.
Great.
~~~
* The inconsistency in Geralt in his game is face-palming. He starts out as a King's paid lackey, but then reminds other folks through-out the game that he is no lackey for hire. Wut? Then he takes payment to go do some job, just re-affirming that he's a lackey for hire.
Likewise, Geralt is a monster hunter, but you will literally spend the first hours of the game doing nothing more than trudging through political drama, fighting humans, watching cut-scenes about humans, etc, etc.
Eventually you get to parts where you're doing some serious monster hunting, but it feels thrown in, like they decided to use it as an easily-contrived plot device, and it could have just as simply been replaced with some non-monster thing if the game didn't revolve around Geralt.
Other than plot-related monster hunting, the rest is just side-quest contracts a la W1. It's just filler, and it's insulting.
And that's my main concern. Why start your game series starring a monster hunter by dumping him  in the middle of a political drama? The first game should have let us play during their glory days. Days when a Witcher was all about monster hunting, and being welcomed with open-arms by a grateful populace. Days when Geralt was first going through the trials to become a Witcher, and eventually had to set out on his own?
Instead you're dumped in games where the "Age of the Witcher" is over, everyone hates them (for no reason other than a propoganda pamphlet and "ZOMG, Mutation!" even though they still provide a valuable service everyone wants), and they're tied up in political drama.
What's worse is depending on how you play him, Geralt is more noble then the nobles and knights he comes across.
W1 & W2 are decent games trying to get through, but the Game of Thrones junk seems like a really bad use of IP. Like "Duke Nukem Forever" bad. Can't recommend.

ORION: Prelude is a game based around working solo or in co-op mode to survive a horde of dinosaurs. Dinosaurs range from small raptors to large T-rex's, Stegasauri, and other large dinosaurs as well as other players (in Deathmatch modes). That's basically the game in a nutshell.
ORION: Prelude is built around a modified Source Engine and although it doesn't have realistic visuals, it has enormous potential for modification by the community. With that said, the environments are still very large and offer a unique weather system that rains, snows, and fogs as the days pass in a match. At times, the visuals stutter against certain tall environments like rocks or mountains and seem broken or choppy, but this doesn't take away from enjoying the game.
The game's controls are quite solid and offers a solid controller support for those wishing to play from a distance or on a larger screen. Action is fast-paced when a wave starts and there's very little time to stand around unless you want to be killed by a dinosaur. The maps offer a variety of vehicles to use in a match hoowever, at times it feels like they are useless since dinosaurs rarely chase any players around the map.
ORION: Prelude offers some decent visuals and solid gameplay to last a while however, I'd recommend playing with a friend or two because solo is not all that fun. If you're interested in a PVP/PVE dino-hunting game, then ORION: Prelude may be worth your $1 and if you've got friends, get the 4-pack for just $3.

This game unearths the pyromaniac in all of us, which is somewhat unsettling, but one doesn’t linger long on that thought. It’s easy—almost, too easy—to become engrossed by glow of the raging inferno, regardless of what may be squirming and squealing while coming to its fiery end.
The player begins with a single ‘catalog’ (American spelling, ew) of items to purchase and thereafter throw into their Little Inferno Entertainment Fireplace. Burning these items yields money to purchase more toys and miscellaneous doodads for imminent incineration, as well as tokens to express ship purchases. Money and tokens are plentiful, so there’s no need to be frugal with their usage. Moreover, it’s encouraged that you splurge at all times, and keep your Little Inferno red-hot.
New catalogs are unlocked by burning through the range of wares in the current catalog, but the hook of this title is not to scorch as much as possible as quickly as possible—rather, there are ninety-nine COMBOS to unlock when two or three specific items are burned together (COMBOS are limited to the number of catalogs unlocked). The name of each COMBO serves as a riddle to discern; some virtually tell you what items are needed, while others aren’t immediately apparent, and require some thought.
Although slightly morbid, Little Inferno has a great sense of humour. The writing is excellent, especially where item names and descriptions are concerned. Finished the game and I gotta say that I enjoyed it. For the most part. In short, Mafia 3 is a good game but a bad PC port that lacks optimization and polish. It's a damn shame that the game is plagued with technical issues because other than that there's really not much wrong with it, despite the negative reviews.

Mafia 3 certainly has its charms, some elements of the game can easily rival that of GTA 5. The music and the soundtrack is phenomenal and it plays a massive role with all the driving around, it's literally the soul of the game. Voice acting is also top drawer stuff, as you would expect from a AAA game of this size, with so many colorful heavy accents (southern, French, Italian, Irish). New Bordeaux (basically New Orleans) is pretty big and the city itself along with its surroundings looks fantastic, the attention to detail is incredible. The whole southern setting is bang on, with the bayou and the alligators, the rednecks and their southern accents and the uncensored racism, it's all there. Everything is spot on and the open ended game world is alive and very believable. The core gameplay mechanics like driving, gunplay and stealth are fun enough with just enough variety so that it doesn't get too stale. There are some weapons and items that are really fun to use, for me those were throwing knives and silenced pistols, it was very satisfying to silently headshot a whole row of enemies in slow motion. Same goes for cars, some of them handle beautifully and driving them everywhere can be pure joy (Traviata and Nightcrawer). Most of the characters along with their personalities are really well made, some of them are stereotypes, some of them are hilarious (Donovan) and some of them are just plain awesome (Vito Scaletta). All 3 of the main DLCs are actually pretty good and add much needed variety to the gameplay. Faster Baby is a trollfest where you drive around the countryside doing crazy stunts just to mess with the sheriff's department, it's definitely the most fun DLC. In Stones Unturned you team up with your bestie Donovan for some top secret jungle CIA save-the-world type of stuff. Sign of the Times is a very serious and spooky story with horror elements involving a deadly cult, but you can avoid it if you're scared easily. I also really liked the ability to choose my own ending to the whole story, the endings drastically vary from one another.

Most of the issues that the game has are technical in nature. Game was released with a 30 FPS cap so everyone left a negative review because of that reason alone. It was a disaster but they quickly fixed it so keep that in mind. However, it doesn't help too much because the game is poorly optimized in general so FPS drops will sometimes happen, it's not super smooth all the time but it's playable. It also has a few annoying bugs but luckily nothing game breaking. The story itself is actually pretty good but the narration is all over the place. It's pretty hard to immerse yourself and to keep track of everything with so many characters and names being thrown around at the start. By far the biggest issue with the game lies in its grindy design that most people don't like (in the style of Mad Max and Shadow of Mordor). Basically, the city is divided into a number of districts and in order to progress with the story you need to conquer them one by one, eliminating districts and their bosses until you eventually reach the big boss. Which is fine, except you conquer every district in pretty much the same way so it can easily get repetitive, there are many identical missions but in different locations to go through and that can quickly get tiresome and boring for players who need a good degree of variety in their gameplay. So that's the biggest

Like I already said, the game is a poorly optimized PC port so it suffers from weird technical issues, this is a fix for one of those issues. Sometimes the game "lagged" like crazy for me until somebody told me (apparently others had this issue as well) that I needed to change the game's priority process from high to normal in the Windows Task Manager, pretty annoying but it had to be done every time I played to avoid the laggy fps drops.
For me the good easily outweighs the bad and I can absolutely recommend Mafia 3 to fans of the genre who don't mind a bit of grind in their gameplay.

A little more so that it was easily understandable would have pushed the game from the 9 I'm giving it into a 10/10. My other complaint is that I don't quite understand the hitboxes of the mines. My first playthrough, I only hit one. Second, I struck about seven of them, but I didn't seem to be closer to them than I was on my first run. So, that was a little offputting.
Oh: and when the game says a controller is strongly recommended? They aren't kidding. I can't imagine playing this with a keyboard and mouse. The controls are going to be a little erratic for you the first time you play because the camera, character direction, and character movement are all separate. "I live again!"
This is what Caleb, the protagonist says, then he opens the grave in which he was buried. And this is where you take control of him and go on a rampage to punish your master for getting rid of you. It makes sense, right? :)
The game follows in the footsteps of Doom and Duke Nukem 3D:
1) You eliminate hordes of enemies
2) Once you encounter the boss you get rid of it
3) Many weapons are at your disposal with which you can do a great massacre
Rinse and repeat! Oh, and not only does it look similar than above-mentioned gems from the '90s, but Blood is equally hard. F*cking hard at times.
Notice how outdated this game is! Well, this is the Build engine at works which was at the time considered 2.5 dimension instead of 3. Why? Because the game only made us feel the height but rooms were always adjacent to one another (there were actually no rooms on top of another). This game is from a time where we hardly used the mouse for aiming and shooting and the movement keys were not bound to WASD.
At the time the game was a bit outdated (I believe Quake had already been released) but people needed time to get used to those. Blood, therefore, was a refreshing experience mainly because it introduced fun to the genre. It did in a different way than Duke did: while the protagonist had great one-liners he also had "clever" guns. In Blood your flamethrower is an aerosol spray and lighter combined and one of the most powerful weapon is a voodoo doll. Oh, and your only (the genre-typical and mandatory) melee weapon is not a fist or knife or a crowbar but a pitchfork.
I played the Steam version a bit and it seems to be running just fine thanks to the emulator used. The game has two expansion packs with two more chapters to the already great 4 chapters. If you liked Blood back in the day grab this one quickly. If you loved all those games using the Build Engine (Duke Nukem, Shadow Warrior, Redneck Rampage, Nam etc.) but skipped this one make sure you have one of the best in the genre in your library. :)

Overall 8.5/10. I played the previous version, GalCiv2, and enjoyed it as well. The graphics and complexity hae come along way in the intervening decade or so.
But in a strategy game, what counts, at least for me, is the ability of the game to have you make choices, with consequences, to present you with a fuild and dynamic environment that forces you to adapt to changes in technology, other civilizations, and random events. This game has that in spades. You control planets, ships, starbases, fleets, economic manufacturing and research policies, engage in space battles, cultural conversions, have an enormous tech tree with branching choices that you'll likely never complete in a normal game, can customise a faction not only interms of looks, but actual traits and gameplay, and have a ship designer which is almost a mini-gmae in itself given the nigh infinite combinations of parts allowing you to create any ship you've seen or can imagine. You can even form alliances and trade.
As much as I enjoy this latest offering from Stardock, I dislike it being only available on steam. I also noticed a couple of minor annoying, but not game breaking, graphical glitches on my second sandbox game, but as this is only patch 1.1, I'm sure they will get sorted quickly. My biggest complaint, and this can be said of any 4x strategy game, is the lack luster AI, and a relative dearth of reference information about some aspects of the game. Without going into too much detail, certain choices like technologies or colonization events, don't tell you everything that you need to know to make an informed decision, and as the game is new and semi-niche, there isn't a massive wiki or other reference site available yet to make those decisions any easier.
The AI, while occasionally crafty, and definitely distinict and focused, couldn't fight it's way out of a wet paper bag. It made repeated tactical and strategic blunders. In fact the mighty Dregin empire, with 12 planets, the warrior scoruge of the galaxy, spent over 100 turns trying to assault ONE minor race planet, and was ultimately unsuccessful. Basically all you need to be successful in fighting the AI isn't  a competitive number of ships, or defensive points, or nebula ambushes, just draw a straight line from their nearest planet to your nearest planet/starbase, counter their weapon of choice, chose a weapon they haven't, and station some ships on that line. You will win even if hilariously outnumbered and outteched. First Impression:
When I first got this game I was met with horrible performance issues on an Alienware computer of all things. Not exactly what you would expect from a game that was apparently designed with Alienware tech in mind (The game links with the keyboard lights and changes them when in combat). I was able to fix them by turning things down some, and the game was still beautiful, but it was still a slight disappointment.
Combat:
Then came the combat. Clunky, slow, unintuitive, and with little guidance for the player resulted in a nightmare for anything more impressive than an imp. Sword play relies on 2 things: Blocking/parrying and dodge rolling. While you can block right off the bat, you have to put points into a skill to be able to parry. Similiarly, the roll exists, but it has such short range you often still get hit even after rolling until you double, then triple the distance with more precious skill points. See, the game's max level is 35, and you only get 1 skill point per level. And before you can put ANY points into the important trees, you have to first spend 6 of those valuable points in the bloody training tree. Which is largely worthless. Probably the most valuable skill in it is the ability to throw knives. So for the first 6 levels of game play (which is a fair bit, as leveling is painfully slow) you're on death's door in just about any fight, especially if there's more than one enemy. Then there's magic, which is a great concept, but they ♥♥♥♥ed it up. You magic is painfully weaker than everyone else's in the game, even after fully filling out the magic tree. Not only this, but most enemies that you really need to use that magic on are highly resistant to it. Furthermore, selecting your sign in the middle of a fight may as well be the death of you. That has got to be my main complaint for the magic. If they simply implemented a pause button like in the first game, that would never be a problem. Next up on the list is alchemy, and how it's so close to useless while being utterly necessary it's mind boggling. There are at least a dozen different potions you can use. Unfortunately, without pumping skill points into the alchemy tree they barely make a difference. Care to guess what 20% of 20 is? It's 4. Congratulations, this potion now lets you do an additional 4 damage. Woopty ♥♥♥♥ing doo. I literally only ever use 3 potions, with cat being an exception and really I only ever needed to use it once in a cave filled with torches that strangely don't give off light. Those 3 are Gadwall, which gives a big bonus to health regen (compared to base stats and other potions) at the cost of damage, Rook, which balances out that lost damage, and Swallow, for extra health regen. This set actually allows me to regenerate my ♥♥♥♥ing health when the game decides I'm in combat (which generally is anytime there is an enemy within 50 yards of you). Magical damage boosting potions are laughable, as Aard barely does any damage, Yrden only damages enemies after putting points into it, and the same with Quen. Igni is literally the only sign that ends up benefitting from it, and with limited casts in the form of endurance that slowly regenerates and taxes how much damage you deal when it's low, you're better off throwing down a Yrden sign and hoping it stuns whatever's trying to tear your throat out at the moment so you can backstab it. While I'm on the subject, Axii is borderline broken. I could count the number of occasions I had the chance to use it and managed to make it work. Some enemies just shrug it off without any good reason. Otherwise it takes too long to cast so by the time you're about to catch someone with it, their buddy has slapped you in the face with fist/claw/sword etc and breaks the cast. Again, better off just using a sword. back to the alchemy now. Throwables and traps sound great right? Well they aren't. Throwables take even longer to toss than casting an Aard and often are less effective than the Aard (which is even more pitiful after I just ripped into magic). Traps are only effective if you know what's coming, and generally, the things you need to use them on only show up once and don't give you any warning what so ever. Hope you don't mind spoilers if you're a trapper.
Mutagens:
These really just♥♥♥♥♥♥me off. In order to use mutagens, you have to have a point in a skill that's mutatable. You also need a mutagen. And if you don't know what you're doing, since they're irreversable and the game doesn't tell you this, you'll have a tendency to ♥♥♥♥ yourself over. Mutagens are rare in the first place. And the only ones worth using are the Greater versions, which are even more rare. Actually, let me simplify this. There's only ONE mutagen that's worth it, and that's the critical effects mutagen. And it's broken. It works, but in a stupid way. With both points put in the perk that boosts the power of mutators by 35%, the critical effect mutagen boosts all critical effect chances by 5%. That's incineration, freezing, stunning, etc. Sounds helpful but not game breaking right? Well for some stupid reason as soon as you put those chances above 0% a simple steel sword will suddenly start setting people on fire, among the other effects. Makes perfect sense right? [Insert sarcasm here] Furthermore, there's an exploit to get all 13 of the mutatable skills without hacking in extra skill points. So basically, you can let yourself set people on fire with a normal sword every other hit. Welcome to making the game so stupidly easy it isn't worth playing.
Difficulty:
So my gripe with this is highly opinionated from my perspective on how games should operate. There's Easy, Normal, Hard, Dark, and Insane. Insane, by the way, is a no death campaign or all your saves get deleted. I'm currently playing on Dark for this reason: You don't get access to everything the game has to offer unless you play on Dark and up. If you get why this is annoying then you get it, if you don't get it you won't get it cause you're not that sort of person. Anyways, the difficulty on Dark is so blitheringly unbalanced its infuriating. I previously played it on Normal up to the third chapter where I simply lost interest, so I have some comparison material. On Dark difficulty Geralt is an anemic without an immune system. You get hit twice by a normal guy with a sword, expect to be dead. You get set on fire or poisoned at full health, you're ♥♥♥♥ing dead. This lessens as the game goes on and your health pool expands and you get access to better armor, but new enemies show up just to make it awful all over again. You can't save in the middle of a fight, quicksave or no, and even during 'fight events' where you're not necessarily in a fight at the moment and you can pick things up and intereact with objects, but you still can't save because more fighting is just around the corner. So if you're going to fight, better do it all perfectly the first time if you don't want the imersion to be obliterated by Geralt slowly dying and the game slowly fading to a load last save screen. Death is handled so poorly you can't help but feel you're never supposed to die in the first place, and it leaves a bad taste in your mouth when you do since it goes so slowly about it, practically waving it in your face. So yes, Dark is hard as hell when it comes to staying alive. You always have to be defensive, even on small enemies when they're in groups. If you get surrounded you're dead. If you get knocked down you're dead, since you take 5 hours to stand up and they can just keep hitting you while you do so. Now, this is where the irritating part comes in. On normal mode, the big boss in chapter 2 must have killed me a dozen times before I adopted a strategy defensive enough I was able to whittle him down to nothing. Want to take a wild guess what happened on Dark?

I'm changing my review. After an initially positive review where I noted that I've planyed this game quite a bit, I've got an ongoing issue with this game that others might want to be aware of. This won't apply to everyone, but if you've ever restarted your game because you looked at your starting conditions and realized that you didn't want to put as much time as a game takes into something so dismally inadequate, you'll feel my pain. I've been trying to get a game started now for almost 2 hours. I cannot seem to get more than 2-3 planets to colonize for every 10-12 planets surveyed. This is extremely frustrating. I've even gone as far as 15 planets at a time but come up with only 2-3, and sometimes those planets were junk. I reluctantly changed the game settings to make the planet frequency "common," and I am still seeing 9-12 star systems without a single colonizable planet. If I'm going to play this game it would be nice to be able to find some colonizable planets, otherwise "what kind of space empire is this?" A one planet space empire makes for a pretty boring, and ultimately a losing, game. Two hours of restarting the game over and over again, but not getting enough planets to make it a real game is very frustrating. If this keeps up I will likely become so frustrated with this game that I will have to stop trying to play it. If that happens I will come back and change my recommendation on this game. Though I reviewed it well initially trying to get a game started has been the biggest challenge. I have spent waaay too much time not actually playing - while hunting for a game that has a chance of turning out to be an enjoyable experience.
One last thing for anyone aware of the reality that habitable planets IRL are virtually NIL as far as we can tell, my comments are about the game itself. If we're going to be trying to build a space empire (that will stand the test of time?) then we're going to need planets to do this on.

I am going to go against the grain here and say that this game is not that great. It's not that it is bad either. It's just mediocre. The main probelm is that The Witcher 2 does not stand out in any particular aspect. Everything is derivation of something that has been done better in some other game. Overall it's just a boring game.
The story, which I've seen stated as being the most outstanding part of the game, is convoluted and disjointed. It tries to be Game of Thrones but it falls short. There are plenty of political intrigue but it fails to draw your interest. 17 hours in the game I don't really fully understand what's going on and neither do I care. The writing is aiming to be very dark but it comes off a bit adolesent. Everyone is just being a racist ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to everyone else. It all becomes a bit tiresome. Also, any conversation between a male and a female character is filled with sexual innuendos. Some are just cringe worthy. During a part where one female character is healing another female character from poisoning, a male character says "Now that's my favorite kind of magic - lesbomancy!" Enough said.
The combat is clunky as hell. Very little control of where Geralt (your character) is going to strike next. The combat doesn't really evolve through out the game. Your character becomes stronger but there is no skill or new combat elements to try to overcome. You always apply the same stratagey to all your foes. Click till they die. I would say combat is the weakest part of the game.
The inerface is another element that is very clunky. Somethings can only be done from a partcular menu and not from the other. For example, character skill screen can be accessed by pressing c. So this would seem like a logical place to level up but it's not. You level up from  meditation screen which brings you to the scren that looks identical to character screen. And only there you can level up. Why? No good reason. If I have to google how to level up in an RPG, I think it's safe to say that the interface needs some improvment. There are many elements throught out Witcher 2 that are just unecessary complicated. The epitome of this is the fact that Geralt has 2 swords. One silver sword for fighting monsters. One steel sword for fighting humans. This doesn't add to gameplay at all. Both swords work in exactly the same way except of course that one doesn't do any damage to the creature it's not meant for. Why did they make this design decision? I think because it looks cool.
So overall I would give this a 7/10

Buyer beware - PVP online only.
A fun little strategy game.  It's fairly simplistic but enjoyable.  It's online player verus player only, with no skirmish mode, and I hate that.  Buying it on steam gives you access to two teams, the humans and the Team Fortress 2 team, but there are three others.  Just pray you don't get matched against someone who's paid to unlock the dark elves, you'll lose.
That's part of the problem with the game, the racial abilities for some teams are radically overpowered.  Teamfortress2 team has the ability to gain an extra move every time they 'kill' a unit by stomping.  Since each round has 5 moves, adding a 6th is pretty huge.   But the dark elves ability to heal EVERY TIME THEY DO DAMAGE is ridiculously overpowered.  I have played over 30 games so far and I haven't been able to beat the dark elves even once.
For $5, if you like strategy games like this, it's definitly fun.  Maybe if you buy the 2 pack and play with a friend, it would be better.

A hidden treasure for sure. I never heard of this game before. Until I ran across it here on steam.
The game is older and the graphics are not going to pretty enough for certain types of people.  The game definitly is unique. It's a more strategy oriented RTS with limited armies and supplies.  The game is still very playable and entertaining. The value of the game is definitly worth it.  I would say it is a very refreshing game compared to new games coming out.  The game is based upon towns and their provinces. Some are of greater value than others and some are just rare.  This makes for a great strategy themed game.
The downside of the game. Its a pure vanilla game with no additional add ons or expansions. The game concept is great. It is a shame that no sequals were created or even an expansion. The game is lacking in variety of units. But that said, the game is still very fun. This is one of those great games that fell to the side and was never finished being polished to its full glory.

Abzû strives to strike true where Journey once did while inverting the setting from an arid desert to an underwater labyrinth, but it misses the bullseye. For every dolphin leap from the water, every new species of aquatic life discovered, every deep-sea dive with a sperm whale, there are inconsistencies such as there being no indication as to the purpose of having more than one mechanical companion, or that the story aims for ambiguousness but succeeds vagueness. Ominous mines flicker violently as the Avatar closes in proximity to them, but even when they are set off, the Avatar is visibly in pain, but survives even a chain reaction of several. Why do these mines even exist? Why is this Avatar seemingly invulnerable? What are some things that I can take away from experiencing Abzû that will help me remember it years from now besides the fact that I swim for approximately two hours (and about three if looking for hidden items and fish)? I cannot answer any of these questions, so I can only conclude that this game is a bold experiment that is missing the polish that I have come to expect even from indie developers such as Giant Squid.

A "virtual fireplace" that is so much more than just the sum of its parts.
Very interesting game with a minimalist approach to gameplay, and a pretty deep message for those who get it (it's rather thinly veiled, so no Nobel prize needed).
The world is freezing, and it's getting colder every day. Sit at home, burn all your toys, and stay warm.
[ NOTE: I tried to make this as spoiler-free as possible. DO NOT spoil the experience for yourself by reading full reviews before playing it. I almost ruined my experience by doing that.]
> Sandbox-ish gameplay mixed with simple shop/buying elements.
> No real goals. No score. No penalties. Just you and your trusty fireplace...
> Burn your toys. Gain money. Enjoy the fire. Order more toys. Burn them too.
> Really more of an "experience", rather than a game. But a brilliant one IMHO.
Pro:
+ Highly polished presentation
+ Beautiful visuals and sound
+ Burning stuff is fun
+ Great dark/quirky humor
+ Great narrative
+ Lots of charm.
+ Stuff happens, and you won't be expecting it
+ Awesome soundtrack. Like, really, REALLY good.
+ Lots of different things to burn, many with special properties and effects.
+ "Combo" system keeps you busy throughout the game
Con:
- Really short (2-4 hours for a playthrough)
- Not necessarily great replay value (but I will play through it again with pleasure)
- High-ish price for the game's length
- Not much of a "challenge" to beat, gaming-wise
- Pacing can be a bit slow at times due to long toy delivery times.
- Many combos are either painfully obvious or really obtuse.

I am going to go against the grain here and say that this game is not that great. It's not that it is bad either. It's just mediocre. The main probelm is that The Witcher 2 does not stand out in any particular aspect. Everything is derivation of something that has been done better in some other game. Overall it's just a boring game.
The story, which I've seen stated as being the most outstanding part of the game, is convoluted and disjointed. It tries to be Game of Thrones but it falls short. There are plenty of political intrigue but it fails to draw your interest. 17 hours in the game I don't really fully understand what's going on and neither do I care. The writing is aiming to be very dark but it comes off a bit adolesent. Everyone is just being a racist ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to everyone else. It all becomes a bit tiresome. Also, any conversation between a male and a female character is filled with sexual innuendos. Some are just cringe worthy. During a part where one female character is healing another female character from poisoning, a male character says "Now that's my favorite kind of magic - lesbomancy!" Enough said.
The combat is clunky as hell. Very little control of where Geralt (your character) is going to strike next. The combat doesn't really evolve through out the game. Your character becomes stronger but there is no skill or new combat elements to try to overcome. You always apply the same stratagey to all your foes. Click till they die. I would say combat is the weakest part of the game.
The inerface is another element that is very clunky. Somethings can only be done from a partcular menu and not from the other. For example, character skill screen can be accessed by pressing c. So this would seem like a logical place to level up but it's not. You level up from  meditation screen which brings you to the scren that looks identical to character screen. And only there you can level up. Why? No good reason. If I have to google how to level up in an RPG, I think it's safe to say that the interface needs some improvment. There are many elements throught out Witcher 2 that are just unecessary complicated. The epitome of this is the fact that Geralt has 2 swords. One silver sword for fighting monsters. One steel sword for fighting humans. This doesn't add to gameplay at all. Both swords work in exactly the same way except of course that one doesn't do any damage to the creature it's not meant for. Why did they make this design decision? I think because it looks cool.
So overall I would give this a 7/10

I was a bit skeptical of this one at first because the rest of my library just doesn't feature many furries. Or any. At all. But I quickly became enchanted by the story, lovely animation, and addictive combat. The controls aren't very deep and only take a few hours to master, but once you know all the combos and are able to chain them together it's easy to feel like an elite squirrel-person warrior. My favorite part of Dust was the item and levelling systems. There are TONS of items with various stat boosts that are fun and challenging to collect, and I found myself really pushing for XP so that I get use my next talent point. Again, all very addictive gameplay elements.
As for the cons I only have a few. The voice acting is a little cheeseballs. But it fits the story and art style so I can't be too judgemental. And there's not a ton of replay value outside of the combat being fun, and making a few differnent choices with NPCs along the way, none of which actually affect the story in general.
TL;DR: Fun combat, item and leveling systems. Beautifully animated. Kind of cheesey. Little replay value. Worth playing even if you don't have any other games featuring furries. 7/10

I played an endless amount of GCII in high school and it distracted me from many problems and helped create interest in different fields for me. I took that interest and have worked to translate it into a career. Stardock is one of my favorite developers and I am proud to support and continue to support them. Accordingly, I bought a founder pack the day it was announced.
And I am so disappointed in this game. The core gameplay is strong, but it's strong because it is iterative. But that isn't enough, because if you are going to produce a sequel to a great game and only iterate on it, you need to include core features from the prior game.
Let's talk about things from GCII that GCIII does not have:
Espionage (even basic espionage as it appeared in Dread Lords)
Super Abilities (an expansion feature)
Heavily differentiated tech trees (also an expansion feature)
Outstanding AI (perhaps this is an opinion but I am terribly disappointed that the game has not lived up to the standards and promises set early in its development)
So three and a half out of four of these were features added by Dark Avatar and Twilight of the Arnor that built on Dread Lords' foundation. And GCIII doesn't have them. And that is not okay. I talked early about iteration, and what I'm observing is that GCIII iterates on Dread Lords: not DA or ToA. We're playing a new game that lacks major features that its predecessor (ToA is GCIII's predecessor, not Dread Lords). Why play it? What does it bring that's new?
Adjacency on the planet screen? Starbases that are marginally easier to manage? More complex combat that is still not interactive at all (something that was on the drawing table when the game was announced but never came to pass). An easier early game? Very marginal graphical improvements? None of these things are significant changes and none of them are worth the loss of the features I mentioned earlier.
We do have multiplayer but...there are 1500 people in-game and one lobby up in the multiplayer browser, so that's a big success.
We have a few new features, too.
An poorly designed UI that manages to obscure information and make the player work harder to manage their empire. I'll quote what I said in this thread (with some additions).
The UI is slow and lags when doing things like clearing notifications. Meanwhile, I have to click all of my ships to know where they are going. In GC II I could see their paths on the minimap and had highlighted spots on the main view to identify spots ships were heading, while telling me how long they would take to get there. Also worth mentioning is that there are still spots where text doesn't physically fit and the game continues to be filled with glaring spelling and grammar issues (just like GC II -- I guess some things never change). And let's say I want to move from shipyard to shipyard to change rally points. Nothing tells me, unless I move into the govern screen, which rallypoint a shipyard is set to. Indeed, if I move to select a rallypoint, the existing one isn't highlighted.
If you look at your fleets, you'll see that the fleet management options have been incredibly limited. Some examples: there's no auto-retreat, and there's no upgrade-all command. The details window doesn't provide any additional information. Well...that's not entirely true. It tells me the crew size and the combined mass of the fleet. Very useful. This screen is a lost opportunity considering that the game has added a lot of additional functional customization options for ships.
Ships also auto-join fleets they share a hex with (this can't be turned off) and when ships arrive at a fleet, the fleet's prior commanders are overriden and you end up with more "idle ship buttons." If a basic fighter arrives to join a major fleet, the fleet should not to ask for new orders. A "go-to ship/fleet" command would be nice, too.

Not played Stellaris for that long I must admit but these are my initial views.
The game is absolutely fantastic and I do love the early game decisions and issues you will come across. You will face issues such as hostile aliens that will try to destroy your research and mining stations and you will have to use your initially pitiful fleet to defeat them.
The game has a great technology tree as it composes of Engineering, Physics and Social trees. You will initially be given 3-4 options on a technology choice for each section and these will affect the game in multiple ways, for example you could get the tech that allows you to build colony ships early on, or a tech that gives you more food buildings.
Stellaris allows you a lot of flexibility when it comes to running your nation/government. For example, migration; you get the options of "prohibited" where none of your population can migrate, "primary-species" where only your starting species can migrate or "allowed" where all your citizens can migrate freely.
Sorry for the short-ish review, haven't played the game for that long so far. As for the bugs that i've encountered the game has run flawlessly and it has been completely fine.
In conclusion I would definetly recommend Stellaris to any strategy games player and even if you are completely new to strategy games, the game has a fantastic tutorial.

Galactic Civ 3 is clearly a game made by gamers for gamers. The game utilizes a solid well-designed engine that provides strategic and tactical turned based game play. Players build a space empire from among 100's of worlds in galaxies that can contain 1000's of star systems and expand their empire as the game progresses. There are many game options when beginning game such as custom factions, custtomizable galaxies, customizable rules and the player can select the number and difficulty of the AI factions. Multi-player play has been implemented for the 1st time in Galactic Civ history and though there are still some bugs to be worked out with multi-player play, overall, it is relatively solid. The size of the galaxy is chosen be the player and this can lead to short games of only a few hours to long games lasting weeks or even months. One relatively unique feature of Galactic Civ 3 is that the games development team is very active and very concerned with the success of the game and the enjoyment of the players. Unlike nearly any other game out there, this DEV Team cares about your experience and they want this game to be the best that it can be. They have steadily patched every issue that has been brought to their attention and they actively pursue and new bugs that may arise.
Overall I would give GC3 a rating of 9 out of 10 for its game play and the quality of the technical support and development team.  When they get the AI working at par and iron out the last few major bugs, GC3 may supplant Masters of Orion 2 as the definitive Space Empire game of all time.

-resources system, those can make a big difference in early and mid game, so if you controll lots of resources but your enemy is way stronger then you are, just build few enchaced ships and they will win war for you.

So small ships with kinetic weapons (and thrusters to get quicker on long range ships) are able to counter rocket-ships. Thrusters are uselss now, so in next patches you could give them possibilty to increase miss rate by 5% up to 30% so that rockets have 80% miss rate on tiny ships. Also give ships not only role (support, escort, capital, etc) but main range of weapons, so if you build a ship with mixed weapon types you can say it to stay at long range (6000km rocket range) or move in to kinetic range. Battle should then start at range of 8000 and at this range support ships should stay. This is just a porposition which would make battles more interesting and make you place for tactics even without dirrect controll of the battle.

Really good game, and they're not lying about it being skill based. See this gif of a goal I scored, partly by accident - its what made me realise this game allows for some serious skill to be developed:
I've been trying to replicate that goal ever since. You can further develop skills as well - even the AI will tend to pass the ball into space and then sprint onto it, but I kept finding that when I tried doing that against professional (i.e. hard) AI they could still slide into where you put the ball, so I started turning around quickly soon after picking up the ball again after sprinting onto it and it often means I evade their slide tackle attempt and I'm gifted a glorious chance on goal. Speaking of which, scoring is an absolute delight in this game, as it should be in any football game, especially when you get just the right amount of curve on the ball that it beats the keeper. I wish airshots were a bit more complex - its nothing more than just holding down the shoot button, but then again it does require some skill with lobbing and corners before you get a prime opportunity to airshot the ball into the net.
Gameplay is VERY fast on higher difficulty, the ball will travel a lot an utmost attention is required to keep up. The game certainly provides ample challenge for players and, as mentioned, the AI will start to show off their skill too (which I didn't expect, the hard AI in Rocket League is terrible, so I had lower standards for the AI in Kopanito).
My only issues are: no custom-made teams, the online play doesn't seem to be working (although you can still play against people on your Steam friends list, which is enough for me), there's no in-game chat, the keyboard sometimes adds itself as another player, and your friend can't personally choose their own team. Also I wish the crowds were animated (it's like playing at the Emirates Stadium) and that there were people on the subs bench - minor details that would add some nice touches. Being able to choose what colour Player 1, 2, 3, etc, is would also be really helpful - I played locally with a friend on the same team and I had pink and he had red so it was a bit confusing.
Overall I definitely recommend this game, I was already happy with my purchase only a few hours in.
