This game was basically my childhood, and is still fun and addictive. There are many, many hours of varied gameplay available and the graphics aren't even that bad for today (Just... don't expect much out of it. It's no Diablo III). It plays like a dungeon crawler should - very variably - and is NOT a walk in the park. Overall, here's what I'd say are the pros and cons.
Pros:
+Varied monsters
+Varied weapons
+Good graphics for the time period
+Large amount of content
+Difficulty scales well (Easy is actually easy, while hard is actually very hard)
+No overpowered items or spells
+A nice cartoony look
+Very, very easy to mod with a little knowledge of Javascript and Photoshop or Gimp
Cons:
-Faces look kinda messed up, limited character appearance customization
-Less than stellar translations (From what I hear... I do not speak French or Spanish fluently enough to try Fate in either)
-Occasionally annoying sounds (I'm definitely talking about the cat or dog. I'd recommend getting a fish to permanently transform them as quickly as possible)
-Point and click style can get boring
-Some... creative names can come up for bosses and for items (Like "Zulgthar's Holy Bec de Corbin of Spite" or "Og the Facesmasher").
-Lack of interesting spells (They're the pretty cut and dry "Fireball" spells, "Summon ______" spells, and "Raise defense" spells typical of this genre. The only really interesting ones are the meteor one and the one that turns enemies to your side.)
-Not for everyone. There are free trials for this game - use them. Decide if you like it or not before buying. It is dated, after all.
-No online multiplayer of any kind
-Not many in-game settings options
-A bit of a confusing fame system. (You get skill points to spend for becoming more famous)
-Some logical fallacies (Fishing in lava)
Overall, even though numerically there are more negatives, the positives far outweigh the negatives for this game. If you haven't given this classic a try, go ahead and get the demo then buy the full game if you like it. I know I did, and I know that I've sunken hundreds of thousands of hours into this immersive fantasy dungeon-crawler. (I just got it for Steam, though)

There are many games which combine very quirky game mechanics or ideas that would not seem to logically fit together, and sadly many of them fail because the ideas, in practice as well as concept, don't work well togehter. However, I am certainly glad that the developers of Crypt of the Necrodancer went for it anyway, because their decision to combine dungeon crawling and rhythm mechanics has created one of the best indie games I've ever played, competing with both the giants such as FTL and The Binding of Isaac and the gems such as Gunpoint and Battleblock Theater.
The concept is simple: It's a dungeon crawler where you must move, attack, cast spells, loot chests, and kick♥♥♥♥♥to the beat of a wonderful soundtrack composed by Danny Branowsky, composer of the soundtrack to other great games such as The Binding of Isaac, Super Meat Boy, and Desktop Dungeons. As you advance through the increasingly dificult levels, slashing skeletons and slaying slimes, you acquire better and better magical loot with which you must battle the final boss of each floor; one of four randomly selected music-themed bosses (all of whom are walking puns). Once you beat the Necrodancer himself, you unlock new characters to do it all again!
I personally have not tried out the Co-op mode myself, but it also looks very fun.
Overall, it is a great game with beautiful art, amazing music, and just enough difficulty and satisfaction to make it fun game after game.
EDIT: Fair warning: it does get pretty hard toward the end. The difficulty curve is not unbalanced per se, but zone 4 is just very, VERY hard, and the boss fights that follow zone 4 are also very difficult, meaning that they'll kill you quite a lot, meaning that you'll have to start all over from the beginning of the zone. Again, it's not an unfair difficulty curve by any means, but it is extremely challenging. That being said, the challenge adds a wonderful degree of satisfaction to finally slaying the Necrodancer, so if I could redesign the game I wouldn't change a thing.
EDIT: Forget everything I said about the difficulty. Even if you've played hard games, you don't know difficulty until you've tried to beat zone 4 as Aria. To this day I've only ever gotten to the boss fight at the end of the zone once. Dios mio, those devs are EVIL. I can't even imagine trying to play Coda.

This is basically a prettier and less complicated version of the Europa Universalis games. The mechanisms are more transparent compared to that series, and the game feels more limited, less open-ended. This can be both a good and a bad thing, depending on your preferences.
Trade plays a relatively important role, because you have to have access to trade goods in order to gain kingdom advantages, and you probably can't produce all of these trade goods yourself unless you conquer a lot of territories.
Military and combat are straightforward. Waging extensive wars is complicated by two factors: one, you can only have a limited number of armies at any time; and two, rebels regularly appear in recently conquered territories, so you have to garrison some of your armies in the new territories for a rather long time to defeat the rebels.
The limit on the number of armies is due to a clever idea that I don't remember having seen in any other similar strategy game: You have a set number of slots to which nobles from your kingdom can be assigned, and you also assign a specific role to each noble. One such role is the general (marshal), which is important because every army must be led by one. Second, a noble can be assigned the trader role; traders are sent to other kingdoms either to earn money or to gain access to goods that you don't produce yourself. Third, there is the cleric who can convert your provinces to your state religion. And fourth, a noble can serve as a spy either to intercept other spies sent by foreign powers or to be sent to other powers by you in order to gather information and carry out covert attacks.
Having played through one game, it is obvious that Knights of Honor is far too easy on default settings. I played as the kingdom of Hungary and was able to conquer the whole eastern half of Europe and part of Anatolia during the rule of my first 6 kings or so (which seems the only way to measure time in this game, since the current calendar year is not shown anywhere as far as I can tell). Given the fact that Hungary was at best an intermediate regional power during this time span and most definitely did not have the resources to carry out such conquests, it is safe to say that you can forget about Knights of Honor if you want to play something that resembles a historical simulation. (For example, when I tried to pull the same stunt in EU III, I was duly wiped out by the Turkish.)
The winning conditions are a point that is more problematic than historical accuracy (which is not really that important for a game). One way to win the game is to collect all of the kingdom advantages. This is easy to achieve, you basically have to have access to 5 sea ports and money, both of which are easy to come by. The second way is to be elected the emperor of Europe, for which it is necessary to have the support of the five most powerful kingdoms. This seems rather difficult to achieve. Being the most powerful kingdom yourself is easy, but to get the support of the others you would also have to have perfect relations with them. This wouldn't be that difficult per se either, since everybody else is more than happy to ally themselves with you if you are the most powerful kingdom. However, if you are already allied with one power, this excludes an alliance with powers that are enemies of your ally. So not only is it necessary for you to be on good terms with other kindoms, you should also guarantee that your friends are friends with each other as well. This is quite impossible to achieve given the mechanisms provided by Knights of Honor.
Logically, diplomacy should be the way to do this, but the diplomacy system in this game is quite useless. You can only ask your allies to attack some other kingdom, but there is no option available to ask (or order) them to make peace with one another and leave each other alone, or else. This, of course, is not surprising but rather seems to be the norm in these games, but it is still a completely stupid omission that basically renders the whole diplomacy system completely useless.
Beside the fact that the emperor victory condition is unrealistically and artificially difficult to achieve, another major problem with the game is the AI. They don't seem to be interested in the victory conditions. Coastal powers should presumably have it easy to attain the kingdom advantages victory, since all they need for that is ports, but apparently no AI power does that. As for the emperor condition, in the emperor elections no kingdom ever got any votes, which suggests that the AI isn't even trying to win that sort of victory. The AI also tends to do stupid things. For example, tiny, one-territory kingdoms constantly declare war on my kingdom, being by far the most powerful empire in Europe, with the explanation that they need land. It apparently does not occur to them that they should rather try to expand toward their similarly tiny neighbors, which might not destroy them instantly.
To sum it up, Knights of Honor is a rather one-sided affair. You either win a trade victory relatively early on, or you try to win the diplomatic victory, which takes unreasonably long, and the computer players do not really represent any serious challenge to this. The only thing they are somewhat good at is the military challenge, which is especially present in the early game. Later on you become so powerful that even this part becomes too easy.
Despite these serious problems, I'll give Knights of Honor a recommendation since there are good ideas in it, and the early game is relatively good. The fact that the late game becomes very unbalanced is rather annoying, but this is unfortunately the case for lots of strategy games (even otherwise ingenious games like the Civilization series).

You know those "alchemy" type games on your phone, where you combine different stuff and see if it reacts together? Well, this is it, only with fire.
Lots of fire.
You buy stuff, place it into your Little Inferno Entertainment Fireplace and burn it. Many items react together as they burn, unlocking combos and giving you more stuff to burn.
Yeah, there's a lot of burning stuff involved in this game.
It's not really a GAME per se, it's more of a clever satire of contemporary timewaster "casual" games (complete with clicking on coins to pick them up), with hilarious item descriptions (which are sometimes razor-sharp remarks, satire and irony). It's a sandbox thing with a very, VERY nice fire simulation where you burn stuff to see what happens when you do it.
Oh, it also has a story. Which is told in a similar manner to the World of Goo story, through seemingly weird and random letters you get periodically.
All in all, this is probably NOT worth the full price, but wait until it gets cheaper and do get it, especially if you are fascinated with burning stuff :)

What can I say about The Binding of Isaac that hasn't already been said? It's a rogue-like, procedurally generated game wherein you take control of Isaac the game's protagonist in his quest to evade his mother's murderous intent. As you collect powerups (and powerdowns), coins and hearts to replenish your HP you will travel through rooms and eventually fight a boss to proceed to the lower level. For me at least, the game is incredibly deep and even the buggy Flash platform upon which the game was built adds a layer of strategy to how you tackle the rooms in the game. The enemies are very varied, forcing you to think on the fly evading projectiles, explosives and using the room's elements to your advantage. As you progress through the game you will unlock more characters and more items each of which adds another layer to how you progress through the game. No 2 runs are ever the same, sometimes you'll curse the RNG gods when you keep finding crappy items. Other times you'll breeze through rooms and bosses. There are also times when progression feels so right you won't believe that this game is made on Flash.
That said this game does have some downsides to it. Namely, the Flash platform will make even top-end PCs and Macs struggle to put out acceptable frame rates. The game is also prone to game-breaking bugs and sudden crashes. The religious subject matter will also offend some and it is the reason why the game never got ported to Nintendo's ecosystem.
Overall however, this game is an amazing rogue-like made by the same guy that brought you Super Meat Boy and is just as hard. I highly reccomend this game, the hours will just fly by especially when you unlock the insanse end-game bosses. Also the remake is coming soon!!

Dust does a lot by keeping it simple. The story is engaging and the entire 'world' is successfully created with the use of detailed backgrounds and characters. This game is truly beautiful and witty.
Visuals: A fun art style that is unique and backgrounds that are breathtaking. I often caught myself going back through areas just to really see all of the details. My personal favorite location is Archer's Pass.

Story: Engaging and interesting. Luckily, Dust doesn't try to do too much. Everything really adds to the story. And I felt a sense of sincerity with the story which allowed me truly immerse myself into the story. I could just react to what was happening instead of trying to predict what was going to happen. Combat: Easy to pick up, fast paced and really addicting. I loved how one could 'fly' through combat. A good variety of enemies that required a bit of strategy and always kept with the theme of the area.

Side quests/notes: Simple notes brought an extra challenge and allowed you discover more of the stage.
Overall, a lot of fun and easy to get into! :)

TLDR: If you tried to like the original The Witcher, but failed like I did, get The Witcher 2. If you liked the original The Witcher, definitely get this one.
I found the original The Witcher an intriguing but very confusing mess of a game. Even with the release of the Eanhanced Edition of the original I could not get into it because nothing in the game made eny sense to me.
Enter The Witcher 2 (:Assassins and all that stuff I'm too lazy to type out each time). Here is a game that throws you into the deep end of a non-conventional RPG mechanic, as well as a lore-rich story that will most likely be very unfamiliar and quite foreign to most players. And yet the game presents itself in a way that draws you into the story and lore, and teaches you just enough about its game mechanics to get you confortably started, but lets out enough detail to make you feel like you're getting better at it as you start to fine-tune your approach to the game.
Even though the story and lore can be seen as very standard fare fantasy at a glance, I advise any player to take the time to read up in the Journal to learn more about the characters, events, locations and monsters. You'll quickly see that this is not just another Middle-Earth clone, and the quality of the lore leans much more heavily towards the Game of Thrones class of fantasy world. People are driven my human desires, and no-one in the game is an idealistic representation of virute. In this world, no-one is perfect.
Then you get to the gameplay anr RPG mechanics. Yes, you have skill trees you advance through to earn new and better skills and abilities. But the game leans heavilty toward strategic planning for each fight you're going to face. Drink potions and apply temporary enhancements to your equipment to give you the edge you'll need to survive. You're not playing a standard RPG here where your character is basically a demi-god able to wade through armies of enemy troops at a whim. You may be a mutant bred for slaying monsters, but you're still very much human, and very much mortal, so you better put some thought into what the world is going to throw at you so that you can meet it prepared.
When combat erupts, things hardly go exactly according to plan though, which forces you to improvise within the general planning you had laid down. You have a wide selection of Signs (spells) and items at your disposal to help keep the odds in your favour. Drop  some traps during a fight to snare up your enemies, trow bombs to stun and damage as you hack away, and even use mind control to tun an enemy against his mates and tip the scales.
One of the things I found hardest to comprehent in the original The Witcher was the combat system. I can beilieve that it was a brilliant system, but I just never felt comfortable with it. In The Witcher 2, the combat is redone completely, feels much more action-packed and impressive than the original.
The game also forces you to go through certain choices that influence the game as you progress. And unlike other "morality-based" games, there is never a clear-cut definition of which choice is the "good" and which is the "bad". You need to make up your own mind, because the the world of The Witcher 2, things work in shades of grey, and nothing is Black & White (see what I did there?)
All in all, I highly recomment this game. I bought it on special during the Holiday 2014 Sale, because I wasn't too impressed with the original, but after playing it for a few hours I'd gladly pay full price for it.

The star of this game is the combat, which needs only one word to describe it: fun. Right there,
nails the cardinal rule of gamemaking: make it
. And it is. Early on, you obtain the bulk of your magical-talking-sword-fighting mechanics with a whirling dervish sword attack called the Dust Storm and magical projectiles from your cheerfully snarky companion, Fidget, which combined make it possible to let loose ridiculous combos on your opponents, by combining a few staple sword moves with the two aforementioned special moves and the fact that Dust Storm will launch you into the air so you can endlessly slash at monsters all the way across the screen, high up into the air and back down again with nary a pause in the combat 'til they're all dead. Again: fun. Simple, uncomplicated fun. There's a lot of combat across 10+ areas, and if you backtrack (which you will if you want to track down the secrets/collectibles which include a lot of fun little nods to other indie darlings) it does unfortunately get a little tiny bit old because the earlier enemies do not level with you, but it's such a small gripe because it's still just plain
to tear the crap out of them with the incredibly responsive swordplay. If I had any
about the combat it would be to advise you to play the game on a harder difficulty than normal; I more or less suck at twitch combat and I found myself breezing through the majority of it on normal. So, just a thought.
My enjoyment of the combat in
far outshined anything else during my time with the game, which is great because -- and here's where I have to be a little bit of a jerk -- my first impressions were less than sparkling. I picked up
in a Humble Bundle, and probably would not have bought it by itself because it is marketed exactly as how I described it in the beginning of this review: it heavily features anthropomorphized animals in the Disney tradition and the story and voiceacting has a distinctly "anime" feel to it, and to be completely honest, neither of those are what I look for in games. Or anywhere else for that matter. I'll leave it at that; suffice to say, I was not expecting to be wowed by
from the first few minutes of the game. Having played through it, I would have to say that
hits the sweet spot of having great appeal to its core audience and at the same time having enough artistic chops to satisfy the rest of us who aren't perhaps into the same thing. There's a lot of comic relief in the banter between the main character and his companion, and a few touching moments in the story, an otherwise plain "who the hell am I" plot. It's not as bad as it could be, though some of the voiceacting really borders on laughable and/or unlistenable at times. This is all just my opinion, of course, so don't hit me or anything; fact of the matter is that this will appeal to some people and not others. If you can get past the trappings of the story, there is an awesome game waiting underneath, it's just a question of how much eye-rolling you're willing to put up with.
And here's another reason you should just suck it up: the art in this game is freaking gorgeous. Every new level is hand-painted and lovingly animated, with special mention for the waterfalls in the underground levels. Just pure eye-candy, and it looks even better while you're kicking tail all over the place. It is clear that the development of
was very much a labor of love, because I repeat, the art is beautiful!
It's a very fun game, it's an amazing achievement for such a small studio, and it serves as a good reminder not to judge a book by its cover.

The game is terribly sterile.
I think I have isolated the problem, and it is how colonies are presented. They are just a set of hand drawn tiles. When I click on my mars colony it does not look any different from another planet. Zero immersion, because paradox went for the quick and cheap low production value "paint some hand drawn images and let that work".
They should have at the very least have a 3d representation of the colony with little ships landing and taking off. And some weather or atmospheric lighting. Like on an arid place without an atmosphere, there should be harsh lights like in the appollo landing photos. On Mars, some red tinted fog.
It is the same like in CK2. The provinces never felt like real places, just a sheet with numbers on it. In the total war games, each province town would represent its size. Same for CIV or any other games that have colonies or cities. Even the very first civ game had an option to see the city and it would show a new screen with the city. Having an actual representation of the place on the game map does so much to drive the immersion home.
So I ask, why do paradox games have to be the ♥♥♥♥ing text adventures of strategy games? I am sure ck2 sold enough copies to afford some 3d graphics.
Paradox had countless opportunities to recreate little 3d scenes for the different planet types. ANd I am sure they had the $ from previous games to afford it.

well, what can I say... the basic idea and premise of this game is great, the execution not so much.
its a good 4x game, no doubt, but after playing one or two playthrough you are basically done.
research is mostly broken - your ships will be outdated before they are even done building.
the tech tree has a few "must haves" (logistics etc) so you will basically research the same in every game.
there is only a tiny selection of maps that offer little variety so you will mostly be playing on the same map (of course you can buy more maps in their rip off of a DLC).
The biggest issue this game has is the AI. Its is quite simply dumb as bread and will pose no challenge whatsoever. There are countless ways to exploit the AI through the broken trade system (for example feed them with useless tech, sell them resources noone needs cause they already have 10 of them etc).
Due to how combat works (you form fleets and if your fleets log count is largr than the enemies you win 99%) the AI is completeley incapable of attacking or defending in any strategic manner. the AI will build huge amounts of tiny ships, leave them in small fleets and watch them get shot into pieces by your larger fleets. THat means to counter an enemy with say 100 ships all you need is a fleet ot 10 larger ships.
so make this short: nice game in theory, poor execution, abysmal AI which breaks the game and destroys replayability.

I didn't think I would like this game, it looks a bit like the kingdoms of a childrens story and sounds like it's narrated by Morgan freeman. But you can get use to the art design and the gameplay is actually what I was looking for.
If you thought "Total War" has been missing the mark recntly with grand strategy as I have, then this game is perfect for you. Sure you're not going to have much in the way of Epic battles but the strategy part is there. Both the campaign map and battles are in Real Time, and there is not time pausing as far as I can tell. The game requires you to think on your feet, busy marching your armies north? well you just missed the enemy swing around and invaded you from the east.
This game also simulates one thing "Total War" does not; Campaigning. For instance if you want to take the fight in enemy territory you have to plan, you only get a base 100 food in your cart (Can be upgraded with buildings or leader abilities) if you run low half way to your target you have to plunder a farm to get more which is time comsuming. Also the Longer your on the march the more your men's morale will drop, you'll have to Camp your Armies to keep morale up or plunder villiages wich give you gold.
There is no prisoners of war like later "Total War" titles however if you decimate an army without killing it's leader (Member of enemy royal court) you capture him and can ransom him off let him go or execute him.
The game also gives your Great historical infomation with 3 playable start times all with a diffrent mix of nations to choose from, and a lengthy introduction to each one.
To summarize, if your looking for a grand strategy game that is just that, one that you can prepare your armies and plan massive operations, buy this 10 dollar game, you won't regret adding it to your library.

This game left an impact on me like no other game has before. I know a lot of people will compare this to Journey, but it felt even more impactful or real and I am not sure why. It could be because all the creatures I were seeing were REAL wildlife that felt, acted, interacted, like I would expect them to do in real life. It could be that the music or the art set even more of an emotional tone, or that I felt more immersed in this game than I have ever felt before, even in a VR experience.
It has done what many interactive experiences fall short, taking me to a place where I feel like I am really there. That makes my physically feel affected, emotionally affected, spiritually affected.
I cannot believe that I was able to identify so many of the species so easily and that it really helped me understand what it feels like swimming next to these creatures. I will never in my life swim next to a blue whale, but after this game, I feel like I have a basic understanding of what that is like. I will never know what it is like to swim in a circling school of fish being attacked by predators, but I have a cusp of what that feels like now.
There were so many moments where I had to simply stop swimming and just be in absolute AWE of what I was seeing which gave me sense of both happy and sad feelings. Happy in the sense of just an absolute delight in seeing this and playing the game, but sadness in the fact that I will never see something like this in my life. It really put an impact on doing what we can to save our oceans and sea life and to preserve what we have so that maybe I can see something like this or my children can or anyone else's children in the future.
This wasn't a game to me. It really was a spiritual experience. And when it was over, I had to reflect on what I just went through and it hasn't left my mind at all. I was depressed when it was over, and I am sad that when I replay it, though I will still enjoy it and find new things I missed, it won't be the same as the first time you experience something wonderful. That first play through will be a one time thing that will really be unique to you.
I wish there were more games like this. And for a game that isn't in VR to have successfully made me feel so immersed, I cannot wait to see how a game like this can  be translated to VR.
I give huge congrats and thanks to Giant Squid for making this. Not only have you given me such a wonderful memory, you've also re-ignited the desire to enjoy our beautiful world and do what I can to help preserve it and doing all this without no dialogue, words, missions, or real depth. Just simply wonderful visuals, top-notch audio, beautiful orchestra music, and a simple desire of discovery. Thank you. You guys deserve all the praise.

Ok, I was really doubting this game. I thought it wasn't going to be as all the fanboys says it would be. "OH MAH GAWD THIS IS BEST GAME EBER" basically that. So I played alittle and I'm like, it's alright. But let's say a year later, a really good youtube channel (The Completionists') were doing a special on FF7. Since I saw that, I'm like, "Hey! Why not finish this game so I don't get any spoilers from the video!" It jurastically changed from that. I couldn't stop playing. It's like it was sucking me into this game. Although if it weren't for the PS1 music patch for this game, I wouldn't be here and playing this version, because I would be playing on the PS1 (but if I would have, it would take years because I never get on my PS1 on a daily basis). The graphics are a step up, and if you see a side-by-side comparison of the original vs this one, you only see that the character models are more high-def, and the pre-rendered graphics are displayed in a better resolution. Other than that, there is no difference gameplay-wise, except for the SUPER-OP character booster. What it does is that it makes any 3 of your characters in your party right now have 9999 hp and 999 mp (I'm not sure on the gil, it wasn't 99,999 but it was like 60,000 or something like that) other than that, it doesn't give you status buffs, nothing else. Just that (preety weird if you ask me, but you know, Square Enix will make anything worse *Puts on sunglasses*). It will also feel weird the first times using the keyboard, and I have found some mini-games unplayable when using my layout (A is OK, B is CANCEL, D is MENU, Space for START, Shift for SWITCH, Page Up and Down for left and right bumpers 'PS1 controller') and it is real nice that you can use an XBOX 360 controller even though I don't have one, I just use my PS3 controller and have some software to emulate the 360 (I'm not going in-depth about that). You can also use a PS2 controller, but you need an adapter (the best way to play if you ask me, but again, I don't have an adapter). In conclusion, it is the best Final Fantasy I've ever played, but not the best game I ever played.

A typical control scheme supports passes, shots, and slide tackles; shots can be manually shaped. As an arcade sports title, games have a fast pace, with powerful slide tackles the primary means to catch up and steal the ball. In addition, randomized super moves (a ball magnet, teleportation, super shot, and wind-driven goal defense) increase scoring. The AI opponents play well at a range of difficulty settings, though friendly players don’t push up the field enough (making cooperative play much more desirable). Kopanito All-Stars Soccer is an enjoyable, accessible arcade sports title.

Overall, I think that FFVII is one of the best FF games (right up there with IX) and should not be missed.

A gem from the original Doom, Duke Nukem and Heretic era (so expect old school play here)
As I played through the first episode, I remembered everything I loved about the game.  The use of alternate fire modes which was pretty much unheard of in it's day, a few weapon types that are comletely unique to the game, set to a protaganist who's dark humour makes you smile while feeling oddly disturbed at the same time.
The game is hard - as I said, we're talking old school here.  The game doesn't hand hold you one bit.  But if you can figure the weapons out along with their alternate fires, the gameplay is very satisfying.
And finally, the 8 bit music.  Hard to believe, but this stuff is actually pretty good.  They hit that sweet spot where it sets the mood nicely and at times is deeply disturbing.  Rarely repetive or annoying.
It's a steal at 5 bucks.

This game is probably the best game I've played in a while. This game shines in it's own unique way while still adding an obvious nod to it's inspiration, The Legend of Zelda. As a Zelda fan myself, I found this very charming, as it didn't copy/paste Zelda into the game, but it had little details that said "Hey! Listen! We like Zelda, too!"
It's addicting, rage-inducing (but in a good way), and has enemies that are neither too easy nor too hard. There is always a way to defeat enemies, even if it isn't too obvious at first. Strategy is a big part of the game. If you choose the wrong room at the wrong time, you lose and have to start all over. Each time you start over, you start back at the beginning, but nothing is as it was before. Your first boss may or may not be the first boss you encounter in your next playthrough. This adds a level of unpredictibility that you rarely get with other games in this genre. There is no "Save" button, which may be a huge turn-off to some people. When I first saw that lack of savability, I thought I was going to rage-quit and never play the game again. However, now that I've played it for a while, I realize that permanent death is what really makes this game amazing. It makes you want to strategize better, play better, and focus better. The only downside I could find to this game is that it is too addicting and you may lose track of time while playing it!
You have been warned!

After reading so many positive reviews for this game I thought I'd love it as I gained an entertaining and heartfelt insight into the struggle of creating something in such a difficult and heavily scrutinised medium. Instead, what I got was a slow, trudging mini-game collection that seemed more concerned with poking fun at others rather than contributing anything worthwhile of its own.
Warren is a game dev who's lost all the data for his current project the day before it's to be uploaded to the app store. Not wanting to be empty-handed, he raids the computers of all the other devs who live in the same building and hacks their roms to claim them as his own. What follows is half an hour of plodding around an apartment complex to gain access to mini-games satirising various trends in the industry. That in itself could have made for some astute and hilarious commentary as it lambasted some of the worst aspects of gaming (like shoddy business practices from certain publishers or DLC and pre-order culture or overly sensitive gamers who'll tear apart anything and anyone they even remotely disapprove of for the slightest, pettiest of reasons), but rather than take aim at some of the biggest offenders, it comes across more as somewhat small-minded as it reinforces some of those very issues and berates anything that doesn't fit into its narrow view of being acceptable.
I've no particular love for "bronies" or "otakus" or the likes of David Cage and Phil Fish, but I don't feel any particular need to sh*t all over them either and belittle their work or contributions, or anyone who praises them, either. Meanwhile, this game seems to revel in doing just that. I wouldn't say it comes across as bitter or "sour grapes" at all, more like someone being childish as they point and laugh at something they don't like rather than address any of the important issues that really deserve being held up and ridiculed.
As much as it tried to be funny, given how poorly it decides to choose its targets, I just couldn't get into it and its material at all (or even any of the not very good mini-games, for that matter). They could have made some really great, biting points about the shortcomings of the video game industry had they turned their focus there, but given that they seem way more interested in admonishing the works of others while making tons of tired references to better games and the pop culture that surrounds it, this really feels like part of the problem more than anything else.
For achievement hunters looking for a free and easy 100%, this is probably 30 minute's worth of content you could put up with. For everyone else, I really wouldn't bother.

Oh FATE... It was one of the first, if not the first aRPG I've ever played! I used to love this game... After replaying it, I can tell i'm not impressed, there are many things done wrong, there are many bugs in this version and the translation is utterly terrible!
Here's the list of issues with the game.
1. Language locked to your System Language.
Since I don't have Windows 7 Ultimate, it's impossible for me to change my game to english... I'm forced to play in French, which, I dislike to do, first of all. Also if you try to modify the language of the game by playing with files, you will most likely break it at some point and the game will just crash. The names of the monsters or items are hilarious to look at, because they all look like "Hammer of of fire of the the great Tahl bat" and the likes...
3. The voice acting is poor. (French)
The english voice acting is fine, but the laughs and the quotes from the narrator in french are really cringe...
4. Bugs.
Well, first of all, if you launch the game and click anywhere during it's loading, it crashes your computer! It did that on 3 of my computers, all desktops. Pretty much, the game gets stuck with the in-game cursor + the computer mouse at the same time, everything you click does nothing and CTRL+ALT+DLT doesn't alt-tab you. Items names are very hard to click on and they stack on top of each other, You always have your inventory clustered with junk you did not even want to loot because of that.
7. Game Balance.
Griffons dies in 2 hit, they're huge! However, rats summoned by a same level Vampire will tank more hits, what?
Also, Yeti deals insane damage and are relatively tanky. Where some mobs deals less damage and dies in 2-3 hits.
Melee + Shield is somewhat weak. You have to split your skill points in 1 type of weapon (for example swords), points in block and points in critical strike. For example, summoners or rangers, only have to put their points in 1 or 2 of them, so they're alot better in that aspect. And even for stat points! If you're a summoner, all into Vitality (and enough magic to cast your favorite summon), because nothing else is worth it. Ranger and melee though, you need 3 to 4 stats! You hit very rarely with melee or range unless you have lots of Dexterity and Attack(accuracy) on gear. Mages always hit, how fair.
Also with melee, or range, you're stuck with mostly the same type of damage (slashing, piercing etc), since you have to spec into a certain kind of weapon. So if a monster resists 100% of it, good luck! But if you're a mage, no problem. Summoners have every types of summons and caster mages have Fire, Ice, Poison, Lightning spells with 0 penalty for using every elements, because all you need is "Attack magic!".
8. Frame Rate issues.
The Steam version has horrible frame rate issues! I've played FATE on multiple computers before and it always ran fluently, even on my Pentium III and on my cheap i5. But my gaming PC with an i5 that maxes out almost any games, lags as soon as there are 4-5 mobs on the screen... Were talking about 10-15 fps drops. So, scratch playing a summoner if you're unlucky enough to get this Frame Rate bug i'm having. I tried a few fixes, but nothing seemed to help.
9. Gambling.
Gambling in this game is... Poor. First of all, you get tons of stuff that you cannot even use, because they have very high requirements or requires alot of fame. Then you get bases that are still very weak later in the game. Also, the price sometimes doesn't seem to matter at all. I've bought items at 10,000 gold that were good and were cyan (the best before unique items) and I've bought items at 800,000 gold tags that were pruple (the worst kind of magic items) with an horrible stat (even negative stats!). It's like it's 100% random when you roll your item. You could pay 1 million gold and end up with an item that gives you -19% life and nothing else.
I understand it's gambling, but this looks like a true random item generator.
Overall, I like the game, but compared to Torchlight or pretty much any other aRPG, it's just a bit too unbalanced to be enjoyable. It's got broken achievements and bugs too. Looting is wonky and if you're computer is not in english, you just can't set the game to english, if you try to modify files, you will most likely break the game at some point.

It was some time around 2008. I was in Elementary School still. (4th grade I think). I didn't drink enough water on a daily basis, so my bladder got infected. It felt good to pick up that game, and put it into the cart. My mom even let me get some candy on the way out. (Some sour candy. I LOVE sour candy). Of course, I couldn't play it right as I got home. I live on a farm, btw.)
I rushed home soon, and heard that sweet sound the bank software makes when you log out; A really crunchy CHA-CHING!!! So, I sat down and put the disk into the computer. Like I said earleir, it was a long time ago and computers were super slow back in the day. So, I had to wait until the game finished installing.

The game is called Fate, you know that. You're a young adventurer with your Animal Companion (Dog or cat. You can change it later...). You arrive in the town of Grove, where the entrence to a large dungeon stand, beckoning the daring adventurers in.
You start off basic. You don't have any armor, but you do have a hachet. (Axe). I'm going to do a walkthrough on my YouTube channel, so you can get the jist of the starting.
You  can fish, too! So I recommend that you buy a fishing rod and fish to your heart's content. You can sell those fish or feed them to your pet. Each fish has different effects. Let's say you feed your pet a fish, and it turns them into a spider!! All the fish you get can turn your animal companion into a Dungeon Creature, but it will stay loyal to you and fight for you.
You can chose what kind of skill you want to use. Personally I use the sword and shield the most, but I've used magic and bows too.
It's good because you can use Magic and be a swordsman, or use magic and be an archer.  Magic, magic, magic.
You can get quests from certain people around town. I strongly suggest you take the quests, because they pay off well.
The main goal of the game is to find the boss of the Dungeon (It tells you at the beginning. It's always randomized too), and get rich!
I haven't actually gotten that far, but I've been to floor 100 and beyond. Which is almost as good I guess.
I STRONGLY recommend this game. It's a steal for $7.99 . I hope you liked this review of it, and be sure to find my channel on YouTube so you can watch gameplay of it, if you're not sure about it. Thanks for reading.

I'm glad to see this game come to PC, since I don't own any consoles and I've heard my friends say for years how great of a game it was.  As a result, when it became available for a remarkably good price of four USD I picked it up.
That said, they could have done a much better job on porting this game.  By the numbers:
1.  The controls are permanently set, and if you don't own a gamepad you're permanently saddled with the most non-intuitive control scheme I've ever seen, where the binds make little to no sense and are scattered all over the keyboard.
2.  The client is inherently unstable, to a point where I suffered from 4(!) crashes by the time I had finished the first battle.  I'm talking complete crash to desktop restarts here.
3.  In addition to this glaring problem, the client hangs severely even when next to no load is being placed on the system.  The first fight, as mentioned earlier, while not overly complicated and only requiring a total of 4 attacks including the ones against the player character took me over five minutes to complete.  Now I know that I don't have the best computer in the world, especially when I'm playing on my laptop like I am, but this system has no difficulty handling modern games.  It should be taking FFVII and bending it over the table, but instead it hangs... especially in the CGI sequences where I had to use CTRL+ALT+DEL to force close the client a few times because the video had picked a spot and froze while the TERRIBLE 8 bit sounding music was on a 2 second loop that would make the most patient man in the world go insane.
To sum up, while I was very interested in playing this game, and I am sure that if it is patched to a playable state it will be excellent and enjoyable, I simply cannot recommend it to anyone in its current condition.  Ya let me down Square Enix.

This is one of those games that you'd play in elementary school when your class would go to the computer lab once a week, except now it's being sold as an actual product. This game is a disaster.
As soon as you launch SAMOLIOTIK, you get blasted with an extremely loud, old-school, 8-bit style song. Naturally, as any sane person would do, I immediately muted the game for the rest of eternity.
Silencing the game didn't help make the rest of the trashheap better, though. It feels like one of the cheapest games you'll ever play. You control this plane which follows your exact mouse movements. Pressing the left mouse button shoots these painfully slow bullets that could be compared to the sluggishness of shooting in Namco's Galaxian. On-screen are a bunch of other planes, some of which are darker grey than the rest, which are the ones that actually hurt you. So basically, try not to pay attention to any of the lighter enemies, because if you do, you'll just get dizzy and die.
In order to "progress" from level to level, you have to earn points. Like you'd expect, you get points from gunning down enemies. However, the different enemy types don't net you more points. The whole system is poorly executed since you can rely solely on killing the slowest and easiest enemies of the bunch. Occasionally a boss appears and takes up a huge chunk of the screen. It won't attack you at all, but touching it means death. It's also worth mentioning that enemies still pass through the boss for some reason, and you can't see them until they're two inches in front of you. Unless, of course, you were paying attention to the top of the screen where they first appear, but I strongly suggest against trying to micro-manage the enemies in this game for fear of getting nauseous. When the boss dies, it falls to the bottom of the screen where you're positioned shooting (since you can only shoot up). If the falling boss manages to touch you, you're instantly dead, even though the boss is already defeated. This would probably be fine if they weren't as big as half of the screen.
The game overall is horribly boring. The only challenge comes from trying hard to avoid getting miserably bored. You'll start trying to entertain yourself and probably get yourself killed. Death completely restarts the game over again which is similar to classic arcade games.
This game is a test of patience, a test which I obviously failed. But honestly, there's no point to this game. It's good for about thirty seconds of fun before you think "is this all there is?" The answer is yes.

This game left an impact on me like no other game has before. I know a lot of people will compare this to Journey, but it felt even more impactful or real and I am not sure why. It could be because all the creatures I were seeing were REAL wildlife that felt, acted, interacted, like I would expect them to do in real life. It could be that the music or the art set even more of an emotional tone, or that I felt more immersed in this game than I have ever felt before, even in a VR experience.
It has done what many interactive experiences fall short, taking me to a place where I feel like I am really there. That makes my physically feel affected, emotionally affected, spiritually affected.
I cannot believe that I was able to identify so many of the species so easily and that it really helped me understand what it feels like swimming next to these creatures. I will never in my life swim next to a blue whale, but after this game, I feel like I have a basic understanding of what that is like. I will never know what it is like to swim in a circling school of fish being attacked by predators, but I have a cusp of what that feels like now.
There were so many moments where I had to simply stop swimming and just be in absolute AWE of what I was seeing which gave me sense of both happy and sad feelings. Happy in the sense of just an absolute delight in seeing this and playing the game, but sadness in the fact that I will never see something like this in my life. It really put an impact on doing what we can to save our oceans and sea life and to preserve what we have so that maybe I can see something like this or my children can or anyone else's children in the future.
This wasn't a game to me. It really was a spiritual experience. And when it was over, I had to reflect on what I just went through and it hasn't left my mind at all. I was depressed when it was over, and I am sad that when I replay it, though I will still enjoy it and find new things I missed, it won't be the same as the first time you experience something wonderful. That first play through will be a one time thing that will really be unique to you.
I wish there were more games like this. And for a game that isn't in VR to have successfully made me feel so immersed, I cannot wait to see how a game like this can  be translated to VR.
I give huge congrats and thanks to Giant Squid for making this. Not only have you given me such a wonderful memory, you've also re-ignited the desire to enjoy our beautiful world and do what I can to help preserve it and doing all this without no dialogue, words, missions, or real depth. Just simply wonderful visuals, top-notch audio, beautiful orchestra music, and a simple desire of discovery. Thank you. You guys deserve all the praise.

For what it is worth. It's a Mafia game. But the main reason why it simply can't live up to the previous titles of the series are a few but very critical pieces.
Let's start this off with something positive. The gunplay and action parts are satisfying. You work mostly alone and if by chance your AI friends pop in it's not really much of helping you. But the action parts are still good. The main reason is that the combat is very fluid and if you decide to go stealth, well it's OP becuase you do one hit everything and the AI won't be smart enough to find you.
Lincoln was after all in the Vietnam war as a special forces guy. They focus alot of the combat around this. For me they actually do that too much. The combat may feel good and the guns feel what you expect. But even on harder difficulties it feels like you being a trained spec ops is simply too much. Back in the 2nd game Vito is a combat vet but he was just a standard infantry. But it was enough to make him a better shooter than those untrained.
Lincolns ability to skillfully and masterfully use every single pistol, smg, assault rifle and heavy weaponry makes it feel a bit like Tom Clancy's The Division. Over-simplified combat controls for the sake of great combat feeling but not so much complex and satisfying combat. The Division tried to counter that by blending in RPG elements such as various skills and various abilities, but they should have skipped RPG level scaling. But as I've said before. They made the combat feel good so it's not an issue as long as you don't overthink it.
My first big issue with this game is within both the gameplay and storyline. Mafia and Mafia 2 has always for me been about chapter based singleplayer storytelling. Strong tale of "from rags to riches" and the exploraton of using subtle ways to complete missions. When things get hot, hot as if burning alcohol and wood is sorounding you levels of hot, it was always down to your trusty pistol and any decent gun picked up. You used your head to succeed and if it failed or was scripted to fail you had to be both gutsy and clever to seek any advantage.
The storylines in both the first and the second game are incredible. Both start off with you being at the lower end of your poor life but you are given a chance. A chance to prove your worth to the people that actually has any power. Whilst Thomas got super lucky during a normal night shift. Well luck is maybe not the right word and you know what I mean if you've played the first. The second game learned what good storytelling was from the first and built upon that. You get a really good "from rags to riches" story. Vito has to learn the hard way how the criminal world works. He constantly sees betrayal from all sides and this turns him into being commited to the one thing he believes in, Loyalty and Family.
The flow of how you get better in the second game is heavily tied in with the story. IT does something the first never did. Blending mechanics into a great storytelling. You don't just know how to do♥♥♥♥♥♥just becuase "the player has done it before" but becuase Vito actually learns stuff. Lincoln however in this game, well he does not really learn new things. You get to do more with more stuff becuase you build up trust to unlock new stuff. This game focus too hard on how it wants you to feel that you're playing a spec ops soldier and not a gangster.
There were quite a few times I felt that the story was dumb becuase some decisions made by the characters did not add up to them being so high ranking within the enemy factions. Sure everyone can make a mistake but it does not explain why someone suddenly decides to make themselves vulnerable just beuase you had a good shootout with thier goons. The game also tries way too hard to be a game with an open world like GTA V but sort of remembers it's not supposed to be a GTA game halfway in on every plan. It just ends up being a game with a decent story and a map with incredible boring repeatable quests and lackluster AI fights.
That's my third point, AI. The AI can be so stupid and so incredibly weird at times. Throughout the game, the enemies would happily waltz in line into my line of sight and letting me take a simple headshot. Other times they run around like a headless chicken trying to find cover. If they find a dead body they spend so much time searching places you would not be hiding at. A few times I've caught a gaurd staring into the wall thinking that I could be seen from there. The Pathfinding for the AI can also be utter♥♥♥♥♥♥ This game let's you call a car or for weapons and even some back up. But the delivery can actually go to a different area, something like up to 250 meters away. No the game simply feels like a threeway crossbreeding of The Division, a bad version of GTA V and bits and pieces of the previous Mafia games.
But everything is not bad and here's a good point it gets from me which simply is the music. Man did the 60's have good rock. It's always a blast when you hop in your favorite set of wheels only to hear a song such as Bad Moon Rising or I fought the Law. These are great songs to just enjoy while your cruise around town in your car. It makes the game and it's world feel so much richer actually. Among the parts that would go under "attention for detail" is the hard work they put in making the world feel like the 60's of southern US. Racism is very strong in both the fancy parts of the town and along the Bayou and rural areas controlled by either white supremacists or Dixies. There are certain shops with signs telling you that colored are not allowed in there and the shopkeeper of that place is even going to try to force you to leave if you enter. You will hear a lot of racist slurs being thrown around, not just towards black people but to pretty much anyone that is not a non-italian, non-white person. Altough most of it is focused towards the colored population. It's a good reflection on a bygone time. It's terrible that it happened. But it was important to add these elements of hate to make the game more believable. Just for the sake of suspending the disbelief that I'm NOT in a game but actually there.
This is a Mafia game, so how could I not bring up the cars. They move a bit better than the other games. But as they mostly tend to do they don't feel very good. It's not going to need race car genre standards but at least give it some small love like Rockstar gave it's games. The cars of the GTA series has always felt great and responsive.
The Mafia games has always made it feel like a bunch of clunky and hard to control vehicles. Which is ok becuase they often emphasise on the realism of how old cars can feel. However they have made some improvements on how the carplay should feel for this title.
Truth be told the driving is not♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's just not great or superb either. But the cars feel good to use but I don't like the silly ramming mechanic. It never felt good and it sort of feels just as dumb as the Assassins creed game with ramming horse carriage. Altough that made even less sense.
The final point is about the games ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ttery of how easy it is to beat the game. Just use silenced weapons in this game. You can't fail if you are a patient and plan to hide bodies.
In the end I think the developers simply got lost during the planning phase and forgot what was really good about the Mafia games. Instead opting for a chance at the big cash piles while sacrificing the overall quality.
The game simply hides it's bad parts by luring people in on what made the previous games good. Still the game got some 70+ hours out of me so it's worth during sales.

Equipment exists only as linear upgrades with minor flavour text acquired just by rummaging through (mostly the inhabited) rooms/areas of the game.
No replayablity beyond the necessity to fail to get all the achievements.
The game lacks some details too, there are no names during dialogue, no alerts for the consumables given during conversation and doors are poorly indicated when not above your character (this was a minor issue during the second chapter when I did not immediately realize there were side rooms).
Redeeming qualities are the cute characters with decent designs and fairly enjoyable dialogue/interactions. Sprites are good, profiles lack clarity and don't show much facial detail due to their scope but are otherwise good and the animated clips/cgs are done well enough but for some reason the animated bits look like they're being played in 240p

I was not gonna recommend it, but after playing the 3rd game, I changed my mind.
LiEat is 3 mini-RPGs where you control 2 characters, a guy who uses knives and a small dragon girl who has a unique power, eating lies. The game consists in going through a town (which is not very big, consist in 1 to ~5 screens and houses/rooms), talking to people and eat the lies that materialize around them to uncover the truth.
I did not like this game much, but it has its charm. Mostly, I didn't like the game's direction. It had great potential, good artistic skills, and great musical skills.
The art is very confusing. It's close to impossible to tell which character is a guy or a girl, and it's hard to identify their dialogue-sprite with their in-game sprite, the sprites just don't have enough detail. Also, there is a weird drawing around the dialogue-sprite which is confusing, and at the beginning, I thought it was part of the sprite where the character had some weird wings or something.
As for the music, there are sudden changes between dead silence and cheery music in a dark atmosphere. Most of the time the music did not feel quite right.
The thing I liked the most from the game, is the battle theme. At first, you fight small lies which take seconds to defeat, but later in the game, you face a big deformed lie, which takes some time, and that was when for the first time I heard the whole battle theme, and woah, it's a masterpiece. The piano is fantastic, it really gets you pumped up to fight.
I said this game had a lot of potential, mostly because of the following reasons:
Bad directing, too short, and boring gameplay.
The combat is really easy, it's almost impossible to get a game over. You always equip the same items in all 3 games, and there is 0 strategy. I know the game tries to focus mainly on the story, but a more challenging combat would have been nice too.
Something that surprised me, was that the game had animated cutscenes, which look nice, but too short.
As for the story... it was ok, it's a matter of taste, really. I liked the "couple" Efi and Leo, but I wish there was a bit more interaction between them. Leo always seemed way too distant from Efi, which made me kind of sad. I would have enjoyed a bit more "romanticism" or affection between them.
The 3rd game has the best story, in my opinion, that is why I decided to give a recommended vote instead of a non-recommended.
It's very cheap, but I'd suggest to put it on your wishlist and wait for a sale. I'd also suggest to not listen to the soundtrack before you play it (especially the battle theme) since it's great and it's better to hear it while you're inside the story.

A great rhythm based roguelike. You move and attack along to the beat, pick up equipment that increase damage, defense, view radius and movement buffs, and items that heal, explode cast spells, etc. Enemies follow certain pattern of movement, but don't let that fool you into thinking it'll turn easy. Just because you know their movement pattern doesn't mean you'll be able to dodge and attack his when you have 3 other enemies nearby, all with different movement patterns. And when the moves/turns are set to a rhythm, you often don't have time to calculate all their patterns and move in an efficient way. Of course, you have to get yourself into those situations. There's a lot of strategy involved in this game.
And if you don't want to be forced to play to a rhythm, you can change you character to Bard, who can move whenever and all enemies move after you. There's other characters with different abilities and/or starting items, but I'll let you find them.
If you like rhythm based games and roguelikes, you'll love this.

9.25/10
Gameplay:
Possibly The most fun I’ve had in a dungeon crawler. Everything moves around the crypt landscape to the rhythm of the music. This happens in quick, quarter note long turns that have both you and your enemy acting at the same time. The aim is to learn the enemies’ movements and fight without getting in their way. Striking and dodging to the beat is extremely satisfying, especially when in quick succession. Though be warned, things can get really difficult.  I consider myself pretty good, and have come to accept that I will never 100% this game. NecroDancer also features a mode to play on a dance pad, as well as local co-op. Despite how there isn’t much reason to replay characters that you’ve already completed, I could see this having great replay value simply for the fun of it.
Story:
The Plot is surprisingly enthralling despite most of it being told through ten second cut scenes. It makes your journey actually have purpose and drive, where they could have easily coasted on the gameplay alone. It’s all pretty emotionally charged too. Though with the blend of music and gameplay, it mostly comes off as totally badass. The characters are likable and have some handicaps that really mix up gameplay.
Music:
NecroDancer has not one, but three amazing soundtracks, so any stage you play will have 3 different versions of its music. Add this to the fact that every stage and boss has unique tracks; it piles up to be roughly 70 songs. And honestly, I haven’t found one that I didn’t like. I’ve even danced to the OST while alone in the dark cause I was getting so into it. Thankfully, the Soundtracks are also available on Steam. And if it’s not your thing, you can even import music from your own library. My personal recommendation is to go into options, and set all character soundtracks to random. This way, you will get the most variety out of your experience right away as you’re still learning the game.
Art:
As much as I don’t care for the pixel style in general, they do a great job with it. Every character moves smoothly to the rhythm, bending knees, bobbing heads and whatnot. The cut scenes are basically just a moving slideshow with dialogue, but they’re still very nice to look at. Each boss also has a little intro splash screen that I just love.
Tip:
If you're having trouble starting, switch to the character named Bard, he is not constrained by the songs rhythm so you can really take your time.
All in all amazing. I would recommend it to anyone, on sale or not.

I cannot say enough good things about this game. The concept is ingenious- stylishly blend rythm elements into a turn pseudo turn-based dungeon crawler, complete with adorable dancing monsters and one of the most enjoyable soundtracks I have heard from a video game.
Combat and movement works really well with the rythm based system- especially since there is a little more leway than in most rythm based games. The game impliments a roughly 60% accuracy threshhold for staying on beat, meaning the game doesnt penalize you for being slightly off the beat. This is somewhat necessary: because the game throws so much at you (especially in the later levels), managing the traps, monsters and staying on beat at the same time would be too much for new players.
The levels are procedurally generated, which means that you will never play the same map twice (any dungeon crawler that doesnt include this feature should be uninstalled immediately)
The monsters and environments are really vibrant and unique- The boss battles really feel epic and stand apart from one another (Its not just a bigger or more powerful version of monsters you have already faced)
The sheer number of items in the game bring meaningful variety to how you approach different enemies, and keep the game fresh.
Overall, this has quickly become one of my favorite games and I just cant stop telling people about it.

A hidden gem of grand strategy. If you like CK and EU, you'll dig the heck out of this. I found myself losing hours and hours and hours I couldn't afford to waste.
There are short-term problems and long-term problems in this game. After a little bit of time you will know how to solve all of them, so even a problem that wrecks a whole lifetime in your kingdom will be only a little obstacle for you. You'll find yourself accepting when bad things happen, because you will know that if you slowly work toward reversing your losses, you'll come out way ahead. I find this to be tremendous in comparison to EU4, where after many hours of play the game will constantly set out to screw you and you can't stop it, and you will not be able to recover.
I wish there was a sequel or an expansion that made provinces smaller, allowing for slower conquest of the continent. For example Scotland is just two provinces with only one or two trade goods available - if the game were expanded and Scotland were made into more provinces, and more of its RL trade goods implemented in each, then I feel like starting as Scotland and slowly taking over the island would be less annoying. But, I did it anyway. Scotland now rules most of Europe, having started from like 2 guys with swords and a salt mine. Though the HRE is aligned against me, its most powerful members being arab sultanates from the middle east...? Alt history fun.

On top of that, the design of this game is remarkable. Sure you don't have a billion polygon just like a typical Call of Duty game, but you have a gorgeous well-animated undersea level where you will be inspired to draw a fanart over and over again.

I recommend everyone to play this game to experience the beauty of the underwater world.

This game is absolutely fantastic. I've always had a knack for playing RPGs ever since I was young with a controller in my hand. There is something about the magic in them that cannot be explained. I'm sure I'm just reiterating what everyone thinks, but FF7 is a masterpiece. I never got the chance to play it before, but when I saw a friend playing it on Steam, I was filled with ecstasy. The happiness continued through playing it. I judge fantastic game from fantastic game by the goosebumps it gives me. And FF7 truly fulfilled my desire for that. However, I must say I was a bit disappointed by the lack of instruction and the faulty PC controls. Call it ignorance, but I don't care. I feel like I understand battle mechanics at a very basic level, and it feels awkward when I'm in a tight spot. Perhaps it's just the Steam rendition of the game. Still, that doesn't stop this game from defining what it means to "play a game". And one other thing. I've always been "100% perfection guy-play perfectly first time through". Thus I quite struggled through the giant universe of FF7. Of course, this doesn't even matter to the well-being of this picture perfect journey, as it is completely on me. And then again, no one is gonna ever see this, and my opinion won't matter in the grand scheme of things. :P Anyways, in conclusion, Final Fantasty 7 is one of the best games you'll ever play. So, for my sake, just buy it and play it. You won't disagree.

Quick introduction to the game -
Stellaris is a very noob friendly grand strategy game that lets you manage a galactic empire, grow your fleet and conquer many planets that may or may not have foreign life (that you can enslave or not).
After 30 hours of it, I still don't know certain aspects of the game, especially the relationship between empires when allied, rivaled and others and I'm looking forward to growing my nation and conquering the galaxy!
Military is a bit too focused because sometimes you don't have a choice other than go to war with someone who annoys you. I personally like to play a pacifist and then simply pacify everyone around me, one way or another. You can approach the game in a few different ways of course but wars are easiest and most fun, which is perhaps a pity if you wanted to attempt a playthrough without military. It is actually impossible because there are pirates and random alien ships scattered across the systems that you need to clear to be able to survey and inhabit them.
It definitely consumes you once you start and you keep thinking about it the entire day, which is exactly what you should do, being a glorious empire overlord!

Graphics wise the game has it's moments, sometimes the skyline of New Bordeaux can be very nice (still not beautiful) to look at but most of the times it just looks washed out during the day. Nighttime is when the engine really shows some beauty, the lighting is very nice to see in the centre during nighttime and in the outskirts it's darker like it has to be.
Combat is also very enjoyable but during the game there is so much combat that you get used to it and it becomes not very spectacular anymore. In the beginning the combat is more easy but during endgame the fights get mone difficult.
It was a nice adventure but I wouldn't replay the game because of the boring part between the beginning and end of the game. If you have patience and maybe like the gameplay more than I do or maybe want to pick it up once in a while, this is a buy

It's so hard to believe that this beautiful game was constructed from the ground up by the hand of a single individual over the course of nearly five years of his life as a passion project. Smooth animation, amazing sound quality, beautiful artwork style and music tracks, responsive controls, and brilliant gameplay. This game is the shining example of what the indie community is capable of doing.
This game in indie game standards is nearly 100% perfect. The voice acting in the game is not as bad as people may claim it to be. Granted at some times during cutscenes, some voices are a little hard to listen to at times, meaning its not the best but its not bad by any means. The art style choice of the game may give some thick-skulled individuals on the internet a bad first impression. People should look at the art design as NOT being a nod to the furry community, but rather look at it as what the art choice was for some early Disney films like Robin Hood or Lion King. This game caters to several game genres including RPGs, Metroidvanias, hack & slash or beat em' ups, platformers, and even puzzle games.
There is no reason why anyone should have to miss out on this incredible expierence. Whether its on sale or at full price, this game will show you that its worth every last penny. There is only one complaint I can honestly say about this game. Though it has several difficulty settings, if you are familiar and well-aquainted with Beat em up side scroller games than this game can be very easy for some of you. The only time the game can be honestly challenging to everyone is on the hardest difficulty setting. Other than that one complaint, the game is sheer perfection. If you buy this game, you will not regret it.

Blood is a classic, nothing else needs to be said about that.  You loved it for good reason back in 1998.  The religious horror setting really helped it to stand out among Duke Nukem and Shadow Warrior, two other games developed in the same engine.  It was obvious that with the porting of Duke Nukem and Shadow Warrior that retro FPS fans would be excited for a port of Blood.
However, this is not a good port, it is just a lazy dosbox emulation.
The game doesn't even let you play all of it's episodes that it comes with until you edit configuration files.  You also have to edit and mod just to get mouse look to work, to get the game to not suffer performance issues, to restore the music to its original format and prevent t from bugging out and looping, to get the Steam overlay to work, among other things.
The worst part is that nobody can get the rights from Monolith to do anything with this property ever since they were bought out and gutted from the inside by Warner Bros, so we will probably never get an enhanced port that offers the basic modern features we have adjusted to, or at least one that doesn't have problems out the gate.
I have spent several hours just trying to get this game set up the way I want and it won't work out for me, I'm done trying.  You shouldn't have to put in hours of work just to get a game to run the way you want it.
It's like I took five dollars and burned it because I wanted to experience Blood again.
Don't do what I or anyone else did, you might as well pirate the game and dump it into an emulator/engine that will actually let do what you want with ease.  The pain and effort to get to play this game might technically be worth it, but there is simply not enough that you can do to make this playable.
And honestly, does anybody look back at the days of using your mouse to move and the arrow keys to turn fondly?

Pros
- Has most of the good things about Diablo and Diablo II, though it's quite an obvious protege.
- Gold is automatically picked up, yay.
- Nice mindless game to play through if you're not looking for much variety.
Neutral
- Not too crazy about the art style, but it's not bad either.
Cons
- Generic dungeon crawling with quests on about every level. Kill this, retrieve item, return to town, repeat. There's no originality here.
- The skill tree isn't very interesting, and isn't really a tree at all.
- Dungeons are often needlessly filled with many dead ends, requiring a looottt of time to backtrack overall.
- It's needlessly difficult to heal at the beginning for some reason; you generate not even one single hit point when out of combat and health potions aren't always easy to come by or buy early on.
- The voice acting for when traps are sprung, etc. is a bit annoying, as well as low quality.
- This game requires a lot of grinding to be able to defeat monsters; the yeti on levels 10 and 11 is way overpowered compared to the rest of the monsters leading up to that point, and the ogres starting on level 12 are sudden, too.
- Magic casting is ridiculously slow at the beginning, almost comically so.
- Incredibly repetitive content; the quests are for randomly generated items or to kill random beasts, and always just for a formulaic reward in experience, fame, and gold.
- The sound effects are also very redundant; every single attack by an enemy has only their one designated sound effect, so enemies that attack quickly sound super annoying. The game is also too loud and ear-piercing even on a low sound effects volume.
- There are many miscellaneous bugs with the game, such as my dog sometimes appearing over gaps where he cannot walk such as ascending and descending stairs, and the hitboxes for picking up items are some of the worst I've ever seen.
Basically, I recommend this game only as a mindless bit of entertainment to play through. There's nothing very defining or special about it.

Ultimately, I'm recommending this because it is very good looking. It does a lot of things right visually. The gameplay however is fighting with the overall game.
There are a lot of throwbacks to Journey, from the goal to shot for shot scenes. Journey really wanted the player to enjoy traveling and going between levels. Abzu, thematically, wants you to stay still and enjoy each level to the fullest. However, Abzu takes many aspects of Journey that push the player to go through levels quickly. The result is that there is a weird mixed message from Abzu, where it wants you to stay still but get through it quickly.
For most of the game, I spent my time comparing it to Journey. Many of the things that made Journey so memorable, from the way it handled environmental storytelling to multiplayer, feel either copied with little thought or emulated with little thought in Abzu. Overall, Abzu fights to live up to Journey rather than being its own independent piece, and the game suffers for it.
It's immensely fun and satisfying (after You get used to the gameplay), especially co-op. : )
