Eh, It’s not too shabby.
I dragged my boyfriend into playing this with me, as it looked like a decent game that would be an easy 100% and I read that it’s easier to complete in co-op rather than on your own.
So with that said this review is based purely on my co-op experience.
First of all, the game generally came across kind of low budget. The graphics are okay but it’s the animation that gives it that feeling I think. Expression can be hard to read sometimes seeing as your character has no mouth (his eyes just kind of roll around in their sockets and you kind of wonder to yourself “Why is there no character to this character?” and “Dude where’s your mouth though seriously?”). It’s noticeable but it doesn’t exactly ruin the game.
The story is kind of weird. I’m not even entirely sure I know what was going on but I guess you can get a general kind of idea from what they give you. There is no voice acting in the game (excluding sound effects, I think) and with what I said above about expression, it can be difficult sometimes to feel totally in sync with what it’s trying to tell you.
Despite the above negativities, the gameplay itself was quite fun. There were some clever little mechanics with the use of the shadow and although the game wasn’t all that challenging (despite it having it’s moments towards the end) it was still an enjoyable game to play.
We played this for around 4 hours, with one or two breaks in-between and we managed to 100% it in that time. It was getting quite late towards the end of the game and I think we both (more so my poor boyfriend) just wanted to finish it and get it over with. The very last part of the game when you confront the main antagonist had our jimmies rustling in the cold night wind that little bit but hey hoe it was still fun.
I would definitely suggest playing this game co-op (only because I can’t imagine playing it solo) if you wanted to give it a try. I think it’s worth a playthrough. It’s nothing amazing but it’s a decent little game.
TL;DR : A fairly short but decent little game that I would recommend you to play with a friend. It has some decent mechanics and is fun to play despite it not being all that challenging.
I don't know why, but I keep coming back to this game from time to time. Something about the experience just keeps calling me back for more.

Duck Game is basically the opposite of competitive Smash: No fighting moves, 1 shot kills, (most the time) and almost entirely based around items and maps. For whatever reason, it works very well. The seemingly chaotic mayhem that usually occurs is actually quite a balanced fighting game. The skill cap is tremendous, but easy enough to pick up that even afk players can sometimes win matches. The hats, quacks, and other mechanics, such as rag-dolling and instruments, make the game so silly that I would find it very hard to ever get frustrated even from losing several matches in a row. Even when game breaking glitches occur, or you find yourself getting trolled by a talented group of friends in random matches online, it's almost impossible not to find joy at any moment. The only real downside I can see, is that it's very hard to learn how to do techniques some high skill players use online. I also had a very hard time finding any resources to help improve. 10/10 for best quacks.

Love this game. Card game similar to familiar names as Magic The Gathering and Heartstone, but with enough unique aspects to keep me returning to this game every single day.
Some examples of the unique features:
Instead of one resource (mana/lands) you have two (supply and energy).
You have three abilities available per game (where Hearthstone has one).
Each hero has more than one unique ability to choose from.
Interesting card abilities, such as Link (synergy with certain types of cards if they are adjacent), Soak (absorb one or two damage per hit) and Mutate (apply certain buff).
While Hearthstone is a very fun game to play, Star Crusade seems to offer more depth.
I like this game. I recommend it. What else?

It'd be perfect were it not for the fact that you have to get a Square Enix account in order to play it. That's... annoying, to say the least.
However, this is one of the greatest games ever made. It'd have to be a hell of a lot worse if something like a little unecessary DRM could spoil it. It's a pure classic, and the best JRPG I've played; the battle system is perfectly well-paced, Materia customisation is intuitive, characters are well-formed and interesting - and the evironments, while looking slightly dated nowadays, retain the aesthetic greatness that made the game look so imaginative and vibrant all those years ago. This is coming from someone who never played the PS1 version, and never really liked RPGs up until playing this version of Final Fantasy VII - so if it can convert me from a dyed-in-the-wool arcade gamer to a JRPG nut, it *has* to be worth something.
It's not perfect, though; the mini-games (namely snowboarding and chocobo racing/raising) are lame, some of the most iconic (and best) bits of the game happen before you even reach the world map, and it's occasionally quite unclear where you actually need to go to advance through the story. Characters mention names of destinations and mission objectives once in text-heavy cutscenes and then don't mention them again if you lose your way - and it's at times like this that I'd suggest looking up your next location in a walkthrough, To be honest, I think that the whole game would have been far slicker had the world map been a simple menu/selection screen (as in Dust: An Elysian Tail) as opposed to a trawl of random encounters, or if at the very least it had some waypoint markers - but these niggles are only occasioanlly irritating, as largely, the game's pacing is excellent.
There seems to be something strangely compelling and addictive about Final Fantasy VII; something that makes the flaws forgivable and the game itself an enduring symbol of RPG excellence. If you have even a passing interest in RPGs, Square Enix or the Final Fantasy games, then I'd recommend it entirely - but if you're new to the genre (as I was), or if you don't think that an RPG could ever interest you (as I didn't), then this is a *very* good place to start; you might even find yourself pleasently surprised. Oh, and the soundtrack is absolutely glorious.

Mafia III is a linear, open world, third-person shooter rpg.  There is an over-arching storyline which must eventually be satisfied, but you have the freedom to pursue that end goal however you deem appropriate.  It has a "territory takeover" component that reminds me of GTA San Andres and Godfather II, as you attempt to completely take over the city.  The game allows you to play however you prefer: guns blazing or stealthy.  There are tons of collectibles and optional side missions that can really prolong the storyline and gameplay experience.  Ultimately, however, you will have nothing left to do other than kill the final enemy, at which point the game basically ends and the credits role.   End-game is truly the end of the game.
The storyline is rich and immersive, combining Mafioso elements with those of a highly racially-charged American South.  Playing as a black man in a fictionalized Louisiana in the 60's, there are many points of conflict that Lincoln Clay must endure.  What I love about the game is that in the end, it feels like you've made a difference.  Is he a rampaging murderer? Yes.  But is he stopping injustice in a completely flawed system?  Also yes.
The game offers you the power of choice constantly, and it asks you "Who do you want this man to be?"  Are you hell-bent on revenge, or are you trying to change the status quo?  Most enemies and informants you come across, you can choose to either kill or spare them, and eventually you can potentially turn on your greatest allies if you so choose to.  With so many choices to be made, and the number of side missions available, a full and immersive play-through could easily last 50 hours (with the DLC included).
I am currently on my second play-through after devoting my first game to killing everyone.  This time around, I'm taking my time, learning about these characters' lives, and truly trying to live out a genuine experience.  I liked the game as a fast-paced action shooter, but I'm loving the game as a slower-paced, introspective RPG with shooting elements to it.
While the game has some repetitive elements to it, overall I highly recommend this game for those who enjoy a good story!

The cult classic, and for my money the best thing ever produced for the Build engine, lives again, again.
Even after all these years, I'm happy to say it holds up remarkably well; apart from some minor sensitivity issues with mouselook, the transition to DOSBox is largely painless (e: for me, anyway), although as some clever person already mentioned, you're going to want to jettison the "improved" soundtrack files ASAP. Fortunately, while the engine may be a bit creaky, the weapon selection remains one of the most entertaining and bizarre collections of kill-a-majigs ever assembled in a game.
It's extremely telling that Blood's designers make sure the player learns the joys of the pitchfork, flare-gun, and Dynamite well before they pick up anything as mundane as a shotgun. This is a game with more interesting things on its mind, like the Tesla Gun, the Napalm Launcher, and in one of many, many hat-tips to the game's influences, the humble-yet-devastating Aerosol and Lighter combo pack. And yet, while all of these weapons have their charms, as far as this game is concerned, Danny Dynamite is practically a second character.
Provided in ACME-approved, bright red bundle fashion, Dynamite is a constant source of spontaneous comedy as well as giblets, as it is handed out in positively
quantities, and actively encouraged in its use. Our zombified hero hits hard, but withers quickly under gunfire, prompting a strategic approach to clearing out baddies that was remarkable for its time, especially combined with the designers' love of elaborate environments, and stashing inconvenient murderers behind newly-opened doors and false walls.
Ultimately, what makes Blood special is the moments where all these pieces come together; hunting around for a spare zombie-head to kick into the carnival game, dropping a napalm bomb right smack in the center of a horde of shrieking cultists, and perhaps most of all, the sight of a lit fuse slowly burning down in your twice-dead hands as your killers linger stupidly beside your corpse.
TL/DR: If horror, black comedy, and clever design get your... ugh,
flowing, then you'll probably enjoy this.

"Lies are just a messy way of covering up for your past."
LiEat is a simple, turn-based JRPG centered around a traveling conman of many names and his faithful "sidekick", Efina. However Efina is not your average young girl...she instead is a dragon, blessed with the power to see and devour the lies of others. An interesting premise for sure, especially considering her choice in a traveling partner. I wasn't expecting much out of LiEat, but I was pleasantly surprised.
The game is broken down into three acts (LiEat I, LiEat II, and Lieat III). Each act involves the conman main character taking on a different name and getting involved in a few messy situations in different locations, from a sleepy town to a fancy resort. In the process of doing so, the conman's unfortunate past is slowly revealed and Efina grows from a naive newborn dragon into a capable young girl (although she's still pretty naive). LiEat I and II are really just build-up for the finale in the third act, in which you can get a bad, neutral, or good ending depending on your choices during the third act. The story, while simple, is still interesting enough and is able to resolve itself happily in the end (or tragically, if you got the neutral ending). Each act takes around an hour to complete, and it's one of the most entertaining games I've played that takes under five hours to complete.
The combat is in a simple turn-based format. I'm not sure how the turn order entirely works, as it seems like the enemies almost always took the first turn, which was mildly annoying as healing items do not take priority. Each character has a few different skills to use, most of them dealing single-target or AoE damage. The format is extremely simple and does not take long to pick up on. Throughout the games, if you are diligent in searching around the world, you can find some nice new gear, including legendary weapons which allow you to one-shot most enemies and make boss fights absolutely trivial. However, without a guide, these weapons are rather difficult to find. Quite frankly, they break the game, so it might be better not to hunt for them.
The OST, while nothing special, does what it needs to do to evoke certain emotions in certain scenes. In particular, the final boss fight for the first act is something that stands out as one of the better tracks in the game. It's nothing to write home about, but certainly above-average for a cheap Steam JRPG.
LiEat is a game that ends up being a lot better than it first lets on, and if it goes on sale, I would recommend picking it up. It certainly makes for an interesting evening, if absolutely nothing else, and...come on. Efina is adorable. How can you say no to that face?
Doing much more than suggesting you buy it and play it to the end would spoil it. It's fun.

Ultimately, I'm recommending this because it is very good looking. It does a lot of things right visually. The gameplay however is fighting with the overall game.
There are a lot of throwbacks to Journey, from the goal to shot for shot scenes. Journey really wanted the player to enjoy traveling and going between levels. Abzu, thematically, wants you to stay still and enjoy each level to the fullest. However, Abzu takes many aspects of Journey that push the player to go through levels quickly. The result is that there is a weird mixed message from Abzu, where it wants you to stay still but get through it quickly.
For most of the game, I spent my time comparing it to Journey. Many of the things that made Journey so memorable, from the way it handled environmental storytelling to multiplayer, feel either copied with little thought or emulated with little thought in Abzu. Overall, Abzu fights to live up to Journey rather than being its own independent piece, and the game suffers for it.

I love playing cooperative videogames. They let you test your teamwork and communication skills. Its great way to pass the time with friends and family. Its not very often a co-op game really catches my attention and as online gaming continues to grow local co-op is becoming limited. So when me and my sister played through Shadow Puppeteer over the last couple weeks I was extremely impressed. This is a great, stand-out, co-op experience and developers should be taking notes.
In shadow puppeteer your character becomes aware of a man stealing everyone's shadows. He fails to capture your shadow but he does manage to separate it from your body. Now you and your shadow must help each other traverse different obstacles as you chase down the shadow puppeteer.
The first thing you'll notice about Shadow Puppeteer is the asymmetrical game-play. The boy lives in three dimensions where as the shadow lives on a 2D plane. The shadow needs to keep on top of other shadows to keep from falling out of the world. The boy has to help move objects around to help the shadow navigate. The shadow also can help out since he has the ability to reach places the boy can't.
You and your partner really need to cooperate if you want to progress. Both characters share an equal load of the work. This isn't the kind of game where one player can just compensate for the other. There are challenging situations that requires both players to be in sync and they often take several tries to complete. Its feels extremely rewarding when you finally succeed together.
The game is not perfect. The physics are touchy and aren't very predictable. Also the game isn't particularly long. This all being said it was a very fulfilling experience. If you're looking for co-op games for PC and have a couple 360 controllers I highly recommend it. This is what co-op games are all about. I really hope we continue to see more games like it.

It's the kind of game that you'll only launch to do something while another game updates, and an hour later you've completley forgotten about the updating game. Let me start by saying I bash on Hearthstone a bit in this review. I don't hate it. In fact I played it quite a bit. It's just not what it COULD be. Let me also say that steam only shows me on this game for a few minutes. I have the game on my phone and have been playing it for a few months now. So, on to the review.
Most of the reviews for this game that I've seen are pretty...well...just WRONG, lol. I'll start by addressing some of the negative concerns I've seen posted that simply aren't true.
'It's a hearthstone clone.' : Saying it's a hearthstone clone implies the game was built around the same mechanics that Hearthstone was, which it isn't. Not only do Star Crusade "Commanders" (your chosen hero) get several interchangable abilities, but the cards and abilities are all played using two different sources of currency. One currency that builds per turn and one currency that is earned through various conditions such as destroying enemy cards or damaging the enemy Commander. Those things alone make it vastly mechanically different than Hearthstone, which only uses a single currency automatically applied each turn.  Also, lets face it, If we really want to be realistic most games of this type are "clones" of Magic The Gathering or Pokemon anyway, lol. Yeah, the concept of it being a battle-card game is the same, but it's FAR from being a clone in its execution.
'It's pay to win.' : Again, not accurate at all. People have lost track of what "pay to win" means. Pay to win means that there are things in the game available to purchase with real currency that are not available to players that choose not to spend real currency, thereby giving paying players an edge or advantage. So, most of the time that people say pay to win, what they really mean is "pay to save time". That's the case with Star Crusade. There is not one single thing in Star Crusade that you can purchase with money that can't be gained just by playing the game. There is no edge to be gained by spending money, only time to be saved by spending money. Therefore, it's NOT pay to win.
Now that those two big lies are out of the way, on to the game itself. It's great. As i stated previously, each commander has it's own unqiue method of play, just like heroes or factions in other card games. BUT, in Star Crusade, each Commander also has an interchangable trio of abilities to choose from or to synergize with their decks. Which means that there is far more variation in play styles even when two people are using the same commanders. This is an amazing mechanic not found in simpler card games....like Hearthstone.
The atmosphere of the game is very Sci Fi and it doesn't have the same shine and personality as more developed games....like Hearthstone. That doesn't mean it's not an amazing game, it simply doesn't pull players in with it's appearance. It's one of those games you have to just PLAY and give it a fair chance. Once you start putting together a deck of your own you'll quickly realise the potential of the game and the potential of all the deck ideas that will go swarming into your head. Highly recommended if you're a fan of MTG, Eternal....sigh, Hearthstone...or any card game of similar styles.

Blood is a 90s old school shooter and is also the most underrated and under looked shooter of all time.
The story is that you play as Caleb who is a gunslinger who’s friends are killed and he is buried alive and he wants revenge… that’s it… that’s the story… if you were expecting more you are playing this the wrong way since this is an old school shooter and the story matters the least and is forgotten during gameplay. The theme of the game is horror, the kind of satanic and supposedly dark and disturbing horror but this game isn’t meant to be taken seriously at all.
The gameplay is basically the same as Duke Nukem 3d but much better, nearly everything that was in Duke 3d is in blood and used better and made to fit the theme and doesn’t suffer from any of the problems found in Duke 3d, those being: blowing yourself up too much with the rocket launcher and the tedious level design and key hunts that will have you aimlessly wondering around a level when you’ve killed everyone.
Blood is also the most violent game of the 90s, and it’s really fun to group up some enemies and blow them to pieces or blow their skin off by using the napalm rocket launcher or a bundle of dynamite and have Caleb laughing like a sadistic madman.
The weapons you get consists of a pitchfork, a flair gun, a sawn off shotgun, a tommy gun, a napalm rocket launcher, three different variations of dynamite, spray cans, a telsa gun, a voodoo doll and a staff. The majority of these weapons have alternate fire, with the flair gun you can either fire one flair or fire a huge fire ball, with the shotgun you can either fire one barrel at a time or both at once, with the tommy gun you can either just plain fire it or you can fire it so it sways to the left and right which is good for a wide group of enemies, with the napalm launcher you can either fire it like a rocket launcher or a grenade launcher, with the spray cans you can either use it as a flamethrower or you can fire bomb enemies with it.
Why this game is underrated and under looked:
At the time of its release people would rather play quake 2 because it has a fully 3d engine when blood is 2.5D and the game almost became forgotten which is quite pathetic because this is a massively better game than quake 2.
There aren’t really any problems with the game itself but there are a few very small irritations with the difficulty and that being that all of the enemies with guns are pixel pin point accurate and do not miss a single shot and have really quick reactions where sometimes you’ll open a door and you get killed immediately, and with enemies that use projectiles they tent to fire to the left and right hitting you every single time since your natural reaction is to strafe left and right.
If you like old school shooters definitely get this game without a doubt it’s always fun to play.

Blood is a cult (literally) classic old-school FPS created by Monolith Software around the Doom / Duke3D era. It features fantastic graphics from the era, multiple (and sometimes comedic) references to music, poetry, books, movies, and even other videogames, a plethora of fun and unique weapons each with two different attacks (except the pitchfork), a strong line up of memorable levels like the Carnival and the Hedgemaze spanning 5 chapters, engaging and exciting enemies, and great midi music with modern (2004) remakes of each.
For old-school FPS gamers who remember playing this back in 1998, this is a warm welcome.
Unfortunately, Blood has to run through DOSBox. Don't let this dissuade you, it works fantastically, but there are a number of .cfg tweaks to get it to run completely properly.
My two biggest and only gripes I have involve the music.
1. From the untweaked version, the default music is the (in my opinion) inferior 2004 remakes of the original midi music.
----1a. This is easily fixed by deleting the blood0#.ogg files in the main folder. This fix reverts the music back to the original midis.
2. The music's volume cannot be lowered or turned off through BLOOD.CFG or the ingame options menu. Now if you enjoy the music, this shouldn't be a problem, but if you want your game to be a bit more quiet, you'd have to adjust the volume in Windows Volume control and raise the Sound Effects volume in game.
Blood has been one of my favorite old-school FPSes for a very long time and I'm glad to see it and it's sequel finally land on Steam. While a couple of tweaks and fixes are neccessary, they should not sway your purchase negatively. Blood still runs flawlessly and contains hours and hours of fun. Now we just wait for Redneck Rampage to be added to Steam.

The Trinity of Ken Silverman's Build Engine is finally complete with BLOOD.
Where as Duke Nukem 3D is a throwback to 80's action movies and Shadow Warrior is a parody of kung-fu movies, Blood is a tribute to horror movies.
The game's levels are moody and dark, and well crafted. Your arsenal includes weapons such as flare guns, tommy guns, dynamite, voodoo dolls and sawn off shotguns.
The game's protagonist is Caleb, once the supreme commander of a cult called "The Cabal", worshippers of the forgotten god Tchernobog. Caleb is slain by Tchernobog in betrayel and rises from his grave one faithful night to seek vengence.
There are many references to horror movies, such as Nightmare on Elm's Street, Friday the 13th, The Shining, Psycho and more. The game is quite possibly the best Build engine game in my opinion.
Unlike the re-ports of Duke Nukem 3D and Shadow Warrior, Monolith never released the source code for Blood, and thus source ports were never made. This is pretty much the
version, which runs on DosBox, which runs just fine on my Windows 7 64-bit.

Used to love this game alot then stopped cannot remember why, saw it on sale immediately picked it up, excited to play it booted up and went in and remembered why I stopped playing.
Pros-
1. Alot of unit variety
2. Alot of "factions"/countries
3. Nice blend of combat and managing of country and family/court
4. Loads of different builds for cities/provinces depending on resources and needs
5. Diplomacy seems better than some games where every AI does not immediately declare war
Cons-
1. Combat is really really stale and way too fast, archers are really good for killing own units, tactics vary little.
2. AI constantly recruits peasants but yet said peasants always manage to kill alot of my own better trained ones like spearmen/swordsmen
3. Unit variety does not really help when certain units arent even good at what they are supposed to be for, eg. light cavalry charged head on into 2 tightened formation of spearmen, managed to wipe my spearmen out easily by kiting them.
4. AI really kind of cheats, I burned down his coastal village, imprisoned 2 of his marshalls, sacked and pillaged most outlying villages producing money and yet he manages to dig out 6500 coins each to rescue both marshalls, instantly recruit full stacks of swordsman and come back at me with 3 marshalls when I have yet to even earn 1000 coin to buy a new unit. Supposed his traders were simply floating off or teleporting to the other nations to trade with them
5. Hardware/outdated software issues. Game runs in 1024 x 768 max causing borders and stretching on pretty much current industry standards of widescreens. Scrolling is either too slow, too fast or very "jerking" in a sense probably due to aforementioned stretching. Unable to zoom in/out makes decision making and planning tough.
Probably some other pros/cons slipped off my mind but this should be enough for now.
Conclusion: Buy if PC is dated and cannot play any new strategy games/runs in 1024x768 resolution. A good game back then but unfortunately just cannot keep up now.

Brothers : Tales of two sons comes to mind for its obvious inspiration. However that game is designed so well that playing both characters as one person is not only easy its required. Sudden juts of shadow will force the shadow character into strange places making jumping difficult to judge. There are numerous “move this box”, “hold this thing there” for other character to make a jump sequences. The only problem is its not always clear what you can jump on as its a side scrolling camera in a 3D space (but only for the human character). There is also some double minecart riding while being chased action.
Not to mention the UI for such things requires the player to stand in a very specific spot to interact with the object. Making a confusing puzzle that much more frustrating. I should also mention there is zero indication of the fact you must press a separate button for interaction with the minecart on the shadows behalf.

If this game hadn't been abandoned, then it could’ve ended up becoming one of the best (and manliest) off-roading sims on Steam. Fortunately, the support from the community has ensured that there's no shortage of extra vehicles to download on the Workshop, and even with the lack of official updates, this is more than worthwhile if you're at all interested in off-roading (or just keen on driving colossal manly Russian trucks).
I occasionally take my own 4x4 off the beaten track in Scotland, so I was instantly hooked on Spintires at the time of its release. Your objectives are pretty simple - fetch logs, deliver, repeat, get stuck in mud a lot. I can see this being a turnoff for some people, but it's somewhat akin to the appeal with MS Flight Simulator or Euro Truck Simulator - there's just something inherently joyful in completing simple practical tasks mixed in with a realistic physics system. And the physics in Spintires are phenomenal - mud convincingly churns around your tyres, ruts are gouged into the terrain as you lumber onward, and bow waves sweep forward as you ford the rivers. Even if the graphics aren’t especially advanced (though the attention-to-detail is impressive), the way the terrain changes and moulds as you cross it makes for some of the best soft-body physics you’ll likely see in a game.
The main downside to the general gameplay is the camera, which swings about wildly like the truck driver downed one too many vodkas the night before. You eventually get used to it, but it is a shame that the devs never really sorted this particular nitpick.
There’s not really much else to say in this review that others haven’t covered already - if you want a game that lets you drive Russian behemoths through the misty forests of Siberia, then Spintires is your game, though I’d recommend waiting for a sale first.

Dust has a beautiful background and badly drawn characters. The characters are also vaguely to highly annoying. Luckily, the main character isn't bad, but your "companion" is almost as annoying as Navi. If you're lucky, you can read fast and skip over the voice acting/bad dialogue writing. The story is also subpar and fairly predictable.
But, then you may wonder why I've played this game for 14 hours (as of writing this review.) Well, that's because the game play is just fun. It's not quite a beat 'em up but there are small hoardes of weak characters with some stronger ones thrown in (not counting the bosses.) There is a hit-combo tracker in the top corner of your screen and a minor quest, plus the steam achievements drive you to really try to continuously hit as many times as possible. It's not simple. It also contains moves that are done using certain button pressing and joystick controls in a row or in combination. Beyond that, it contains "metroid-vania" skills that give you access to new areas, further parts of the story, and treasure you missed when first going through areas. There are side quests and the ability to buy or make armor/rings/weapon-improving items.
There are definitely some things that I just would rather not deal with with this game, but it's all in the cut scenes/story which is not a huge part of the actual gameplay which is good, because the game play is fun and continuously makes me want to move forward in the game. (Except for the very beginning which I played maybe a half hour of, and then didn't pick up the game for several months.)
I'd recommend getting it if it is on sale for cheap because it's fun, but it's not really all that original, and it's not all that polished.
Additional note: I cannot speak to how the game plays with a keyboard&mouse or just a keyboard (both options). I played this game using an Xbox remote as it seemed to be easier on my fingers since there is a lot of action-button pressing and thumbs do that better than fingers.

How to make the controls better:
A few things you will probably want to do to make the game more playable is to set up the controls like a modern FPS game i.e. WASD keys for movement instead of directional keys and enabling mouse control.
You can change keyboard binding inside the actual game menu. So your going to want to change strafe left and right to 'A' and 'D'; 'E' or 'F' or whater to use action and so on. Change space to jump probably, Ctrl or C or whatever to crouch. If you repeatedly bind an action to a key I think it will clear unwanted controls (if you are using the in game menu). For example repeatedly binding space to jump will clear the 'A' key from jump so that you aren't jumping everytime time you strafe left. There doesn't seem to be a proper way to just unbind keys in the in game menu.
You can also change keybindings in the setup program which is also the only way that I could see to change the mouse button binding which you will probably want to change. So to get in the  setup program for Blood. Find the One Unit Whole Blood folder in the steam/steamapps/common folder or wherever. Then drag setup.exe into the dosbox.exe icon. This will launch  the setup program which probably won't work if you try run without the dosbox emulator. In the setup program I rebound the right click to secondary (special attack or whatever it's called) instead of move forward, turned the the sensitivity and inverted mouse control. Just keep pressing escape when you are done to exit the setup and make sure you save by pressing 'y' when you are prompted. Launching the game from setup.exe might not work. Just restart the from steam after closing the setup and saving your changes.
Okay so the game a few flaws which I will just warn you about. Actually I can only think one now other than the default controls, maybe I'll add more later. Sometime projectiles from your weapons will clip in objects when they should clearly go straight to your target. Basically I was firing at a Zombie point blank over a cash register but I hitting the cash register. You just have work around this sort of stuff.

Kopanito All-Stars Soccer is a fast-paced action soccer game that has been in development by Merixgame since September 2015. Throughout this development timeline they have continued to make regular updates to the game. They have also, at all times, communicated openly and quickly with their fans.
In fact, because of their consistent development and their great communication with their community it wouldn’t be out of place to consider them an Early Access role model. I honestly believe that indie developers would do well to look at the way in which they have gone through the early access pipeline.
The developers have openly claimed to have been inspired by some of the greatest soccer games in gaming history. These include Kick Off, Sensible Soccer and Nintendo World Cup. These games provided gamers around the world thousands of hours of entertainment. I believe that Kopanito fits that niche rather nicely.
The gameplay has been designed so that it is easy for gamers to jump into and play immediately. However, it is frenetic and challenging enough that it is a beast to master. There have been numerous times throughout the time that I have cursed at missed opportunities and even more when I’ve learned a new tactic or strategy that was previously unknown to me.
This is perhaps the biggest surprise to me. The game appears to be very simple. Players don’t need to worry about the general rules of soccer. There are no offside calls, fouls, etc. Yet the depth of the game to include strategy is deeper than it first appears to be.
There are 16 different tournaments to play in. Some of them need to be unlocked by winning certain tournaments in various game modes. A nice feature of tournaments is that each game of the tournament can be played with up to five players and it isn’t dependent upon the number of players you began the tournament with. Therefore, if you have friends or family members come to your house and you’d like them to join you they can easily do so.
There is also an option for players to create their own tournament.
There are a whopping 114 teams within the game. These represent countries from around the world.
I do have two minor sticking points with these teams. Firstly, I don’t believe that players have unique modifiers or attributes. If they are there then they are not necessarily clear. Each team plays the same as any other. While this ensures a level playing field with games determined purely by skill it doesn’t provide any point of difference on any of the teams. You’re not going to pick a South American team (e.g. Brazil) and expect to be able to play with more floor and pizazz.
Secondly, do not expect to be able to play as your favourite countries right away. The majority of the major countries are locked. They unlock when you complete a set task. For example, to unlock my native Australia I need to win the Oceania Cup on professional difficulty. To unlock England, you need to win the World League on Professional difficulty. This is intended to be motivating but when every team seemingly plays the same as any other the primary motivation may not be as high as anticipated.
A significant part of the game’s enjoyment comes in the is the ‘super-moves’ feature. There are a number of super-moves. You gain one super-move for filling up the super bar. To fill up the super bar players have to do successful things in the field of play (e.g. a successful tackle, pass, score, etc.). These Super-moves can often prove to be match winners on both ends of the field.
I was playing a tournament game as Tonga against New Zealand and was 2-1 up late in the game. I unlocked a super-move which turned out to be a wind move. New Zealand had the ball late in the game and my last defender had unsuccessfully slide tackled the Kiwi striker. I quickly used my super-move just as he was about to slot the game-tying goal. The ball proceeded to be blown back out of the penalty area. New Zealand pounced on the ball and passed it back to the striker who again was met with the wind. My super-move saved the game for me.
Conversely, in the final against Australia I was tied late in the game when I unleashed my power shot super-move. The keeper deflected it but it dazed him which opened up the goal completely for my rebounding striker who slotted in the game winner.
My word is this game Steamified. There are over 200 achievements. They unlock frequently enough that you’ll want to continue playing more and more. Yet there are enough achievements that are a challenge to unlock that perfect game does not feel cheap. It will take even the most skilled players many hours of play before they unlock every achievement.
The game also has a set of six trading cards. The developers are working on implementing Steam Workshop features into the game. Players can already create stadiums, balls and teams for modding. This should prove
If you’re looking for a casual soccer experience that provides entertainment and challenge, then look no further than Kopanito All-Star Soccer. It’s as enjoyable as any casual soccer game has been in years.

Even though this game is in Early Access, there are really few mentionable flaws that could restrain someone from buying it in this phase of game development, like the fact that online mode is still in its early stage, or some AI flaws still persisting when it comes to picking up a passed ball.
Anyway, the game is very fun and playable, with an easy start in the Beginner AI modes and becoming very challenging when climbing the skill ladder. The developers look closely to comments and involve and let participate the KAS community in selecting the next enhancements to where the game should be developed to.
What I especially like about Kopanito is the simplicity of controls compared to other high class (AAA) football games like the FIFA (tm) series e.g.. In Kopanito, one does not need a long learning curve to become familiar with the controls and can start playing at an instant. Still one can do some really nice (trick-)shots, and especially playing local multiplayer gains a lot of Schadenfreude, e.g. when kicking the ball with an overhead kick into the opponent's goal (including their goalkeeper), or smashing the forward just before the shot with the goalie and a defender in synchronicity...
Keeping away no-fun rules (like offsides, yellow and red cards) and plainly focusing on game flow, Kopanito reminds me on the goody old times when a friend of mine and I played Sensible Soccer on the Amiga for hours and hours (he won most of the time ;-) ).
Taking into account the absolutely fair game price, I believe that no one will make a mistake in buying this game who likes casual sports games that suddenly evolve into a family affair... :-)

I tell myself I'm playing this to learn user interfaces... yah... uh huh...
The interface is a little convoluted.  There are buildings you can build which won't have ANY USE WHATSOEVER because your nation isn't able to build specific units related to the building.  For example a plate armourer builds his shop in your city.  He builds magnificent armor - but all the people just walk by... they can't figure out what to do with the stuff.  So you just wasted resources to build a building that has no use for your kingdom, but would have use if you happened to be the next country over.  That's a bit silly and annoying - those buildings should be greyed out if they can never be used.
Still the gameplay is very compelling, not for the sake of the graphics, but for the learning curve and immediate challenge with some difficult economics.  The buildings have interdependencies, i.e. you can't build some buildings before you build a lower tiered building first.
The various technology trees:  Building interdependencies, Ruler designations, Resources and trade, Advantages (bonuses to groups of resources acquired), maybe 1 or 2 more as I'm just getting started.
Oh yeah... "when are they going to have some babies?"  In that way this is a "be the pestering mother-in-law simulator".
I play most of the tactical battles in auto-resolve, which is still a slow animation that is interesting and fun to watch, but my guess is the tactical battles will eventually become a requirement at higher difficulties.
The Pope keeps issuing annoying crusades calls, which if you refuse other nations relations will deteriorate, but if you take, you'll lose a marshall at least for the duration of the crusade, or permanently if you generate a vassal nation from the crusade conquering.
Lastly the voice acting is not bad overall, and pretty good in many places.
10/10 I have already got more than my $1.99 and probably easily more than the regular price.  It's a no brainer can't stop playing.

This game has a few serious flaws:
- no full-screen mode, not even stretched. Horrible.
- no zoom-in/out over the map: difficult to estimate the size of a nearby kingdom, difficult to navigate your own kingdom and cities, difficult to get a sense of what is going on
- every diplomatic agreement among any other country appears on the notification area, however you receive absolutely *no warning whatsoever* when a kingdom *declares war* on you: if they just immediately on an outpost that has no defensive walls, you are screwed. Now, how does this game qualify as *real time strategy* when it gives you no time to plan and enact a strategy to counter the computer's moves?
- apparently, the time can not be paused while still being able to interact with the map to get a better understanding of what is going on in the nearby cities.
- the tutorial goes to great distances to explain trivial stuff like 'click here and there to show this and that' - thank you Captain Obvious, I can learn that myself - but it doesn't spend a single word on the most crucial aspects of the game, that is how stats affect other stats. Basically, you've got to do a lot of trial and error the first dozen of matches before you are able to design a sensible strategy and not waste your gold.
- at times, armies just sit there doing nothing despite of being given an order repeatedly
Positive aspect
- The overall idea of the game is great, but the technical implementation of these ideas is horrific and it is not worth a single penny.

This game is an absolute blessing. After the disappointment of No Man's Sky I was worried we wouldn't get an interesting game about exploration and what not, This is where Abzu comes in, being the breakout star of summer games. What is Abzu exactly? It's a game that carries the spirit of "Journey" that was released exclusively for the PS3 but the setting is underwater. It's a fantasic adventure in the long run with story that's about as deep as the depths of the ocean you explore (maybe not that deep). When I first started Abzu, I was immediately stunned by the first area you venture into.
It's beautiful, it's bright and very alien in a sense. This is a game that allows you to experience the ocean in all its glory. Do you remember Ecco the Dolphin or Jaws Unleashed? Throw those bad memories out the window because Abzu will be the only underwater adventure game you'll want to remember. The music will you pull you in and the visuals will trap you until the ride is over, it's a short and sweet adventure that you'll love from start to finish.
Is it worth $20 for a 4 hour long adventure?
If you want to escape reality for that long and just enjoy the Ocean then yes, please buy this game.

Shadow Puppeteer is a good game to play local co-op with your daughter.  If you don't have a daughter, I really suggest investing in one, as they are really useful to have around.  I've seen some criticism of Shadow Puppeteer as not being a good single player game, and that may be completely true, but my recommendation is based entirely on the co-op experience.
First thing to do here is get the obvious comparison out of the way.  Shadow Puppeteer gets compared to Contrast, but that seems to be based on the general premise.  Shadow Puppeteer is no Contrast.  If you want a really good single player game and don't have Contrast, get that.  It is very cool.  But if you want a good local co-op game to play with your daughter, and I'm assuming you have acquired one by this point based on my previous suggestion, get Lara Croft and the Guardian of Light.  After you have finished that, get Shadow Puppeteer.

"Damn, Otter"  I hear you say, "This sounds like rather faint praise."  I understand it might sound like I'm not even recommending this game, but all I'm really saying is that while Shadow Puppeteer isn't the best co-op experience out there, it's certainly worth playing.  Just, you know, after you've played the games that are better.  Look at it this way.  If your cat throws up on the rug, do you immediately get rid of the cat?  Of course not.  Cats are just inherently evil animals that seek ways to cause trouble for their owners.  They cover up their evil  by being cute, so that no matter what they do, your daughter will say "Aw, she's so adorable, she didn't mean it!"  This leaves you with the difficult choice of either putting up with the cat which is intent on destroying your home and all that you own, or sending the cat on its merry way, thereby alienating the daughter that you rely on to play co-op games.

It's not always easy maintaining a balance between video games and daughters and cats, so here are a few qualifying questions to help sort it out.
Of cats, video games, and daughters, which have you had to drive for medical care in the middle of the night?

Which are you worried might get pregnant?

Which have given you hours upon hours of fun?

Which have made you proud?

Which have you spent the most money on?

Which would you not want to live without?

I know that for myself, these answers are obvious, and it may also be as obvious that I've written this review for Kira, my love, who certainly places above the cat on the list, and without whom I could not play local co-op games at all.  Oh, and Shadow Puppeteer is fun.  If you have someone to play with.

This game has a cute idea, but fails badly on execution. The basic premise is that you control a little boy and his shadow, who are chasing after a man who has stolen everyone else's shadows. There's no dialogue in the cutscenes, but it's pretty simple and easy to follow the very thin plot. The core of the game is the platforming, and this is where it has trouble. The boy moves through a 3D environment, and the shadow moves across the wall or floor in a 2D environment. This provides for some cool ways to twist the traditional platforming concepts, as he must stay on shadows, and they can be manipulated in interesting ways.
Right off the bat, you get the feeling the game is unpolished, as the boy's legs don't consistently animate. He just glides around for a while, then his legs will sometimes start moving. The jumping sequences are sometimes pretty frustrating, but what makes them worse is that sometimes you will encounter weird clipping glitches where the boy will pass through ostensibly solid surfaces. Sometimes this helps, like when you can move through a wall and get past a tough spot, but sometimes he'll just fall through the floor into the abyss. There was one spot in the game where I got stuck in a loop where the boy would die for no reason, and immediately respawn, only to die again. There was no way to get out of this other than to restart the level. And that was about halfway through relatively long level, so I lost a good amount of progress.
There are also some bad design choices, like the energy line connecting the boy and the shadow. If they get too far apart, they apparently die and you have to start over at the last checkpoint. This is annoying enough as something to constantly worry about, but in one leve, where the surfaces the shadow is standing on are moving great distances side to side, it's just about game breaking, because it's extremely tough to keep the boy and the shadow close enough together to avoid insta-death and having to go back to the last checkpoint yet again.
So in summary, neat idea marred by bad design and sloppy execution. There's no way this is worth the price they're asking. Give it a miss.

Note: There are numerous reviews for this game which compare it to Overwatch, although a valid comparison it serves against the game if you were to rate it upon it's own accord, so I shall do both.
NON OVERWATCH REVIEW
This game is fun, plain and simple. Each champion has abilities to make it so a one on one fight is entertaining between any two characters in the game, as well as make team fights engaging. That in mind this game is by no means perfect and there is a list of pros and cons, just like any game.
Pros:
It's free: Even if you find the game to not be for you, there is little lost, perhaps an hour of your time at worst.
Combat is fluid: Every character has either a movement ability, a sustain tool, or an applyable debuff to turn a fight in their favor and to make a fight more entertaining and engaging than holding down the m1 button.
The developers proactively make updates: Although these updates may not contain exactly what you wanted, a developer that outputs a sizeable update every two weeks or so, is impressive. Keep in mind this game is in beta; updates are likely to slow upon it's full release
The game can run on a potato: This game works with unreal engine 3, which is incredibly old by this point, so even a computer with not the greatest specs can run this game with decent frame rates. Additionally, the game does look quite nice if you have a computer that can support the higher end settings.
Queue times aren't horrible: I can't recall waiting for a match to be ready for more than one minute at a time, and steam statistics show the playerbase to range from about 8,000 to 30,000, which is decent.
Characters are enjoyable: Whether it be for their design, gameplay, voice acting, or overall feel, it's obvious a lot of work went into perfecting the characters, and they are enjoyable because of it. Also, the way the game was stylized, every character sort of pops out in the enviornment, perhaps I'm old fashioned for finding this stylization enjoyable, but hey, it's worth noting.
Cons:
Bugs: This game is in beta, so they are to be expected, but oh my goodness. There are a lot of bugs, and not just funny ignoreable bugs like bodies occasionally ragdolling in entertaining ways, which exists, but game breaking bugs that can make you mad. Occassionally bullets will just, go through a shiled, sometimes defending a payload push won't award your team with a point for the round, sometimes you will purchase a card and put it into a loadout only to find you don't have the card anymore the next day. It's to be noted.
Balance: You will notice while playing this game that there are some characters that are just noticeably better than others, maybe it means I'm playing some characters incorrectly, but I there are some characters with which I find underpowered compared to others. I can tell you about it, but you likely wont really understand until you find out for yourself.
Loot Boxes and skins: There are two levels of loot box, one which costs gold, and one which costs the hard to obtain gems (if you log in every day, you can probably get one of these boxes a week), take a guess which one contains all the cool loot. Admittedly you will be getting the cheaper loot box with quite some frequency for free which sort of makes up for the crappy loot, but it's still annoying. Loot Boxes don't only give you cosmetic loot however, mostly they are used for obtaining cards (special things that allow you to tune a characters play style to your liking), but rarely legendary cards. Legendary cards are a single card you can select before a match that will dramatically change up how the character plays. You get one for free for every character, but there are two others that will cost a lot to obtain if you want them.
Character unlock: You wont be getting every single character when you start up the game, but they aren't hard to obtain. If you play actively, and log in every day, you can buy a new character every week. If you play more periodically, it will take about two or so. You could avoid this hastle with a $20 purchase that unlocks all characters as well as provide exclusive skins and a lot of loot chests. This is a generous amount of content for a fairly low price, but if the game being free was of interest to you, then this con would be of great importance.
OVERWATCH REVIEW:
I have played Overwatch on ps4 for a generous amount of hours, likewise for this PC version of Paladins, so having 50+ hours in each game I feel grants me some level of credibility whilst comparing the two in review.
Firstly, if you compare this game to Overwatch, it wont be a fair comparison, Overwatch has a level of polish one would expect from a $60 AAA title with over year of development by Blizzard that would vastly out match that of a game that's still in a beta made by a moderately sized gaming company. Because Paladins claimed fame as being an Overwatch clone, it's a necesarry comparison, so if you are going into this game having played Overwatch, there are a few things to keep in mind.
A lot of the characters have similar playstyles to an Overwatch counterpart. Take for instance Androxus, this is your Mcree. He has a revolver with a m1 and m2 you'd expect, but completely different abilities. Although they are akin to that of other Overwatch characters (Genji's reflect and Tracers dash in this instance) the combination makes for some interesting results that will make each character feel unique in it's own right.
The game modes are exactly the same to that of Overwatch. Capture an objective, push a payload, it's the exact same, although there is no king of the hill game mode. Having noticed both the gamemodes and the characters are undeniably similar, if you have pumped inumerable hours into Overwatch, this game will not feel like a unique experience for you.
Ranked sucks. The only real difference that this game mode has from casual play is longer match queues and people that think they are better. Honestly, if you are looking for the competative experience found in Overwatch ranked mode, don't look here.
Lastly and most importantly. If you have played Overwatch before, keep in mind that this game is a different game and a fun one at that. I guarentee the only way you wont in some way find joy out of the experience is if you are trying not to enjoy it.

An EXTREMELY unique and good game. It should be noted that it does require half life two as well as its episodes, and CS:GO if you want to make full use of the game to its best extent. You can Play it with just Half life 2 and Garry's mod, however it will not have as many props or items, and quite a few addons require at least one of those to function properly.
Although it is well worth it being as Garry's mod is essentially several dozen games in one. Want to build a helicopter out of an old bathtub and some wooden planks? The game won't just allow you to build it, using the tools it gives you you can make the thing fly, turn, and emit sparks because why the hell not? Want to just fight a bunch of enemies or watch them fight each other? You can do that as well. Want to roleplay as a citizen in a world filled with insane weirdo's? You can do that in Darkrp. (There are also serious RP servers but I find those less fun.)
How about be a part of a murder mystery where someone or some people are killing you all off and you don't know who?... Maybe be the one that is the killer and having to deflect the blame onto others? The gamemodes "Murder" and "Trouble in terrorist town" are for you. Want to play hide and seek on a derelict space station? There is a gamemode literally called that and multiple maps that fit that description.
There is also prophunt where one team is disguised as ordinary objects and must hide from the other team trying to kill them. Kind of like a harder variety of hide and seek. (You can also do that on a derelict space station if you want.) Want to run a literal death maze filled with all manner of trap? Then Deathrun is for you! Parkour game modes, zombie survival, horror maps, team deathmatch, capture the flag, racing. There is most likely a Gamemode for it, or at the very least a map.
You can also download all manner of maps, weapons, Npc's, vehicles, player models, posable ragdolls, and items, You can run around as a Knight, a soviet soldier, a random guy, an imperial stormtrooper, or a character from your favorite movie. There are maps meant to represent anything from a flat area to build things, to a castle on floating islands, or even the Mushroom kingdom from Mario. It is probably the only game that exist where you can run around as a medieval Knight beating soviet conscripts to death with a crowbar on Mars.

Crypt of the Necrodancer could have easily been a gimmick. It's not. The rhythm-based mechanics aren't just tacked on to the well-tread genre of roguelikes; they form the core pillar of the game, through which all other aspects are bolstered.
The game truly feels like dancing. The core learning mechanisms are a combination of memorizing the patterns (much like dances) of enemies, predicting what they'll do next, and reacting quickly and gracefully to everything happening around you.
When you pull off a full clear of a room without taking damage or missing a beat, it feels like you've just completed a flawless dance routine. It's exhilerating in a way that roguelikes--often focused primarily on a slow, calculated approach--almost never are.
Oh, and the music is Danny Baranowsky's best work.

This is a beautiful example of how to make a game when you don't have a Bethesda-class budget to play with.  The devs didn't try to go head-to-head with the latest hyper-realistic FPS or amazingly vast open world.  Instead, they took a very old, tried-and-true genre (the Metroidvania action platformer) and did it really well.
The animation is smooth, and the sound is pleasant.  The storytelling allows itself some indulgent moments with overdramatic tropes, but then lightens up again with fourth-wall breaking, winking references to other games, and comedically petty sidequests for NPCs, rather than continually wallowing in melodrama.
The style of gameplay is dated, and Dust can't compete on technical merits with big-studio offerings, but what makes this a pleasant experience is the degree of polish.  The devs put a lot of attention into this game, and it shows.

I'm giving this a thumbs up with some reservations.
PROS:
1. The strategy level you can achieve is awesome. Nothing works best like driving the opponents into a choke point or moving your conquering fleets from civilization to civilization.
2. Race customization is amazing. There is great balance when choosing an skill or perk. You can litteraly create a super race of dinosaurs, cyborgs or a technological advance otter race. What ever comes to mind.
3. The ability to actually manufacture your own designs puts the game at a different level. You can create your own Borg Cube, Star Destroyer, Starcraft Battle Crusier...etc etc etc.
4. Good Story telling and some funny dialogues.
5. Great ambient music.
6. Awesome cutscenes. Nothing tops the fun of having your supper carrier PACMAN face ship shooting lasers from their eyeballs...(not so great camera views tho)
7. Interesting Factions and Lore. Just the dive into the galactic civilizations wiki and metaverse already.
8. Map customization is also great, you can pretty much modify every variable on the map.
CONS:
1. The learning curve of this game is hard, tutorials are not good and any "let's play"/"walkthroughs" on youtube is probably outdated. Plus the common joe wont invest 6-8+ hours of their lives to actually learn everything.
2. The AI is really dumb. This needs a lot of work, you'll have to play the game (once you get the hang of it) at suicidal level to actually feel some challenge. And yes the Ai cheats, but again you won't really notice it because you'll know how to exploit things. However this helps with the learning curve, you can choose a begginers difficulty and after a few matches you'll grab a sense of the game.
3. The game requires a better way to macro-manage your civilization. You'll feel this once you have more than 15 planets under your control. Every turn will feel like an eternity because you'll have to micromanage everything and once a few turns have passed you'll have to check each planet to recall what's actually happening and why you choose to build a particular building. This needs to be adrees urgently.
4. There are so many ways to exploit the game once you know how things work. Pls stardock I really have a problem with people being able to put colony modules on tiny ships. You can practically launch a colony ship every turn within the first 5 turns...
5. NOW this one really bothers me. There are NO Stargates in this game. The game allows you to choose a gigantic map but there is no mechanic or late-technology that allows you to fast-travel from point A of the Galaxy to point B. A simple solution would be to create a technology for late game that allows you to jump between one starbase to another. Why is this important? Imagine you have conquered half of the galaxy, you have 50+ planets under your control and your fleet is at east wing of the map, suddenly the second most strong civ drops war on yours from the west side. You won't be able to use your ships. You'll have to go block by block watching how the enemy conquers your worlds. If the game is gonna allow players to use gigantic maps then there should be ways to navigate through.
6. Regular Bugs. Planetary destrucion is bugged, jumping between the galaxy view and the tech tree view creates a bug.
I trust Stardock will look into this and other things and all in all the pros supersedes the cons after you get a sense of the game.

Preface: I’ve only played through Chapter 1 completely but if my opinion of the game as whole changes, I’ll change my review to reflect that.
Overview:
Visuals: 10/10
Gameplay: 8/10
Sounds: 8/10
Story: 7/10
Overall: 9/10
Lieat is one of the most refreshing indie rpgs I’ve had the pleasure of experiencing. The first area where this game succeeds in its world building. The world and its structure are reasonable and creative. Basically, there are humans and monsters, most monsters are uncommon and/or urban legend but dragons are the exceptions given that they’re born near humans (each dragon, born with their own unique power). Our heroine is a dragon that was born with the ability to sense and eat lies. Our hero (if you can call him that, he’s kind of a jerk), Is a human that is something of an information broker which we can assume is a popular trade in this world, given that at least ⅓ of the characters you meet in the first chapter are information brokers too. In chapter 1, the narrative comes off headstrong in that it does a weak job of immersing the player into this world and suffers from an issue that plagues most ametuer narratives; world building is eagerly thrown at the player left and right without pacing or tact. Between each plot point are moments that seem purposely designated for combat.
The combat doesn’t do much to break from a traditional turn-based system but it doesn’t do anything to fail that tradition either. The combat never drags on, the enemies are diverse enough, and the battle system is simple: attack, skill, item. This makes it easy to keep fighting  I wish there was a “defend” option for the player because sometimes the quantity of enemies is overwhelming (and the enemies can defend) but I can understand leaving it out because every turn spent defending is one that you could’ve spent doing something offensive and that’s what this game’s combat is about: supplementing the story through quick and simple turn based mechanics. This is executed perfectly, better than the turn-based combat in a lot of big budget titles. Combat is coupled with satisfactory animation and great music.
Prior to finishing the first chapter, I was ready to dismiss the game’s audio as satisfactory at best but the post chapter ‘theater room’ (my term, not theirs) was an excellent way to emphasize the quality art and music this game had to offer. In the center of the room is a music box-esque system that lets you play the tracks from throughout the chapter with a twist. Each track can be sped up or slowed down using on screen sliders. Every track sounds just as good at any speed and there are plenty of tracks to play around with. I would have been satisfied with this but the theater room has a far wall with different art from the chapter.
This is a great opportunity to appreciate the well crafted aesthetic of the game. The chibi anime art style is complemented with a mix of pixel-vintage-theatre visuals which serve to reflect the narrative of the game perfectly and contributes further to the fantasy theme. The theater room was so impressive and well done, it made me wish every rpg had something like it. Opportunities to reflect on what a game does well (in this case, the art and music) leave the player with a more memorable experience overall.
It might seem from my review that Lieat is an average game that hits a few good points but it’s execution confirms the opposite. It’s rare that a game does simple things the right way with satisfying results like Lieat. In a time where the rpg genre is oversaturated with lengthy cutscenes, over-the-top combat that tries to reinvent the wheel, long/drawn out narratives, Lieat is a breath of fresh air that I recommend to any fan of the genre.

LiEat is a beautiful game, the first location you visit has a very eerie atmosphere to it. The small town slowly becomes darker and darker as night approaches. I especially love that they give new character portraits when you are playing later chapters, you can see some characters have grown, indicating time has passed. Short little animations and CG scenes also play out during parts of the game, a very nice touch to give the game some life out of pixel rpg sprites.
The music has a really gentle tone, but it is also used to build a sense of unease during certain events. It's not used carelessly either, sometimes no music plays and you can feel something bad happened. It's good stuff, I don't usually complement the music in reviews but I really should for this one.
The writing... The characters are often times are very humourous, I liked almost all the main and supporting characters. I can't put into words how much I enjoy the dialogue in this game. Talking to a NPC multiple times sometimes trigger dialogue that is both interesting and adds to the lore of this game. My favourite characters have to be the Captain of the force and the main character Efina, both dragons with interesting abilities. Conversations between them give some context to the captain's backstory and even a possible reason why Dragons with unique abilities are born.
Buying LiEat gives you 3 games, I highly recommend finishing each of the games in a single sitting. As stopping midway during one of the games can be immersion breaking and ruin the atmosphere. They aren't very long, about 1-3 hours for each game. I do not regret this purchase and I urge anyone who wants a great time to give it a shot.

Witcher 2 is my favorite game. It is a solid RPG with a lot of action and a brilliant story. It is very mature in a lot of its themes and situations. This game is based on novels written by a Polish authornamed  Andrzej Sapkowski. You play as Geralt, a Witcher, or a genetically enhanced monster hunter. They have been described as a kind of warrior monk. Geralt drinks special potions that let him far exceed the abilities of normal humans. These potions are needed to battle the various beasts of the realms. Witchers also have a very limited understanding of magical energy called Witcher's Signs. Basically the Signs are spells, like a fireball and a paralysis trap spell and a few others. Geralt is an interesting character because he is not quite human but hes not a monster either. Due to their methods and abilities, however, many in the world see Witchers as freaks and monsters. Which is really what the game's ideology is all about; the greyness in everyone, not the clear cut black and white. Which to me, is a welcome change from the usual: 1) "hey I'm a good guy I will help you"  2) "Not my problem Kachinsky" 3) F*** YOU F*** FACE," that many other game are notorious for.  Geralt is often put in positions of just making a choice, not good or evil, just difficult decisions that have a lot of positives and negatives to them. The story is top notch, and eerily real in many of the stuggles of the world.
Geralt has a set of skill trees (sword, magic, alchemy) that the player can advance in any way. All into one or spliced between the three. Sword fighting is a core mechanic though, so no matter how you play, Geralt will always have two swords. A silver sword for monsters, and a normal sword for humans. There are a few other weapons too but mostly its swords. Depending on the player preference combat can be a bit like the Batman games, or the Assassins Creed games. In some ways it can be like Chivalry: Medieval Warfare. Weapons and armor play a big part as well and can effect all of the skill trees. Making the game very balanced between gear and character tree choices. Not to the crazy levels of a Diablo game but enough to make for a very quality rpg.
Mostly though, Witcher 2 is a lot like skyrim. I do not want to bash on skyrim here, it is also a great game that a lot of people absolutely love. I feel, however, that Witcher is far better than skyrim and think the people that love skyrim should try the Witcher. Both games have the northern lore and feel. Witcher 2 is no where near as large or open as skyrim. Witcher is much more linear but the story and combat and the world just feel so much better in every way to me. The enemies and the different races were better portrayed during the game. When I came to a new town in skyrim I did not get that feeling of truly new. Just another town and another barbarian guy leading it. Witcher was totally different, you get the feeling of racial tensions and social tensions in every part. The powers that be are very different and each very developed and very human. As it plays out you really see how the choices alter the world, instead of it coming down to "OK I'm a good guy so I will save good guy town." A lot of games try to get that feeling across of the characters true M.O. and demeanor but fail. Witcher acomplishes this very well. Triple AAA quality. Superb graphics, superb voice acting. I enjoyed every character. There were a few times, of course, where some tones were a bit off but that happens in every game. Overall amazing game. When I learned that this game was made by a small studio in Poland I was shocked.
As someone who never read any of the books and did not play the first game, I found that after a second playthrough the story and everyhting started to click and I realised how well done everything really was. The way the game is, one would want to play it at least twice to see both sides of what is going on.
It seems as though more than a few people found the game to be really difficult. It can be, but now there are plenty of guides and discussions about it. The game has a kind of reverse curve for the difficulty. It is much harder in the beginning due to a lack of points in the skill tree and low grade weapons and armor. By the end though, Geralt is pretty much on par with jezuz. I like games of this nature, because being really stong at the end makes it feel like you really acomplished something.
This game also has subtitles in many languages so I found it made a great gift for steam friends who are not natural to the english language.
I would reccommend this game to anyone. Especially anyone who likes Skyrim, Assassin's Creed, Batman, Chivalry, Darksouls, Lord of the Rings or any games like them.

Mafia 3 is an open world sandbox game which is set in 1968 in the city of New Bordeaux, which is a fictional creation of New Orleans.
The game ran at around 45 to 50 fps at 1920x1080 with custom graphics settings which were around the medium preset on my 1050ti and i7 7700hq. I didnot encounter any bugs apart from the game game crashing on me twice. The game has this filter which gives this orangish hue and the colors seem washed out. Reflections are horrible and some low res textures are seen. Even then the game does manage to look gorgeous at times. The facial animations for the cutscenes are some of the best ive seen (ahem andromeda)  and help make the story even more authentic. You can see the love and care put into the game when free roaming the city, listening to the radio the effort to make this game as true to the time period shows.
The game starts out with Lincoln Clay returning from Vietnam to meet his uncle Sammy after which things take a turn for the worse for Linoln.I must say that the opening 5 hours are really gripping and action packed and had me completely involved in the story. Its after this when you need to collect the underbosses the game gets into a repetitive rythm of doing these missions where you either have to destroy certain supplies, kill or interrogate the enforcer. These missions can be a real grind but the underlying shooting mechanics and the sticky cover system and the option to play stealthy is what kept me going through the game. But when the story missions came boy they were good, taking down each area boss felt satisfying and the missions were in varied areas with different settings and circumstances. A mission in an abandoned theme park and one on a sinking ship are especially memorable. The underboss system where you assign districts to one of the three underbosses feels like a missed opportunity and they could have done more with that mechanic. It is towards the end where things start to pick up storywise and the story although predictable but the journey through it all and learning more about these characters and their motivations really makes you want to finish it to the end.
The season pass with the three stories are great and offer something different from the main game. The DLCs have been integrated well into the main game and can be played at anypoint throughout the main story. Id recommend playing them when the grind gets too much and for a change of pace.
Id recommend Mafia III. Why? Its a game meant to played at leisure and if you are remotely interested in the setting I promise youll be hooked.
