Do you like to be a part in a grand adventure?
Do you enjoy a good novel?
Do you take thrills in making meaningful choices that will impact entire kingdom?
If your answer was yes to any one of those question, I HIGHLY urge you to go and get this flawed masterpiece right away. This is a gem that i will forever be proud to have in my catalog of games. I bet some people will ask the question "do i need to play the first game to fully grasp the story of Witcher 2?" and i honestly have to say, not really. But, if you're a returning player from the first game, no doubt that you'll get more enjoyment out of the game, but new player can rest assure because this is an entire new journey and much different from the first game. Since the intro is now done lets move on and talk about the story.
The Witcher has always been one of my favorite franchise for many reasons. For me it's the mature, greedy, and novel like story that CD Project Red was able to craft for this amazing game. The story will treat you like an adult as it force you into ridiculous choices that will not only make you sit there and question your moral values, but to also teaches us that in a cruel society there is no such things as right or wrong, there is only choices and their consequences. The story that will be unfolding in this game and the painstaking choices that you'll be making in this game will never simply be black or white, it will always be grey. That is the best way I can describe this story without spoiling it. In short, if you're tired of games telling you "This is the good choice. This is the bad choice" but want to come to the conclusion for yourself, I think you'll be very happy with what Witcher 2 can offer.
There has also been quite a drastic improvement from the first game to the second game. Combat is no longer clunky, awkward, and slow. Instead, it is  now much more fluid, simpler, faster, more responsive, and much harder than the previous installment. This is a change that I very much welcome because I feel the combat that was in the first Witcher was rather dull. If you're somebody that played the first game and find the combat quite unpleasant I highly suggest you give this game a change. Did I forgot to mention that this game has huge replay ability? Since this is a game where you constantly affect the story with your choices, you can easily lose more than 100 hours into this game figuring out the different kind of ending that you missed and answering all the "what if" question you had during the game.
I think I have said quite enough about the game in this short review. The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is nothing short of an epic adventure. The visual and graphic fidelity stand toe to toe with some of the highest triple A titles today, and the story rival with some of the best story telling in video game history. I could praise this game all day, but in the end it is still just my humble opinion. It is now up to you to take my review into consideration and make that last and final decision. I hope this short but honest review has given you some information and help you clear some doubt about this game.

Crypt of the Necrodancer is a refreshing indie game to hit the market and is defintely worth every penny spent. It is a rhythm rougue like bolstering a unique gameplay. Every enemy including you moves according to the beat of the music and the faster the music, the harder the level is. There is 4 zones for each character, each showcasing it's unique enemies with interesting attack patterns as well.
Although people may say that 4 zones may be little for a game but there are multiple characters to test your skills in the 4 zones. This game looks easy but is no joke. It's a tough rhythm rougue like challenging your fast thinking and reaction time. Many characters change the gameplay such as:
1. Die in a single beat, only dagger as a weapon.
2. 2x Speed of music
3. Jump 2 spaces instead of one all the time.
4. Cannot pick up money.
5. Cannot kill anything.
6. Can only use bombs to attack.
7. etc.
It also includes a character that the developers say that is almost impossible to complete (he is extremely difficult) but one person on youtube has already. This game offers so much enjoyment and the Original Sountrack by Danny Baranowsky, A-Rival and FamilyJules7x all offer a good accompaniment. Even after you get tired of the original soundtrack, custom music from your own libraries are also supported in this game.
If you are tired of the keyboard, get a dancepad and get onto your feet. This game has support for dancepads and even have official ones just for this game and if you're game for it, go get it and try!
Overall, this game offers a full package and experience as an indie game and was a refreshing entry to the indie game scene and if you are looking for something unique yet really enjoyable to play, this game is for you!

This is a great game. It's a weird mix of Europa Universalis (real time strategy map, faction events such as rebels) and Total War (tactical battles, faction/location unique units and province improvements). And it works wonderfully.
Pros:
A quicker yet deeper Total War-like game. The strategic map is real-time, so the game flows better than Total War's turn-based strategic map. It remains manageable because you have a limited set of knights (who can be generals, merchants, priests, etc).
Europa Universalis-like events, like rebels, nations rising, crusades. It makes the strategic game really fluid, with factions moving across the map, overextending, and collapsing to rebels or nations rising. Even large nations are not immune, so there isn't an invincible, immovable big blob (except for you if you play things right).
Cons:
The game is 2D only. While the art style is ok, the low resolution (1024x768) makes playing both the strategy map and tactical battles cumbersome. An HD remake that allows you to zoom out would be awesome. See Majesty HD for reference.
Can get repetitive towards the end of the game once you become dominant.
AI is a easy once you get over the hump at the start of a new game. AI factions don't often concentrate their forces, and builds way too many low quality units. Even worse, AI alliances don't support each other's armies, which leads to them being defeated separately.

Note: There are minor spoilers in the paragraphs preceded with a *. These are unavoidable as I explain my frustrations with the game but, in case you want to avoid them, the note is there.
Nothing frustrates me more than a game than a game with a good idea that doesn't use it to its fullest or, possibly, manages to make the entire idea frustrating in execution. Shadow Puppeteer is one of those games. I'm getting ahead of myself, though. Let me explain what the game is all about.
In Shadow Puppeteer, you are separated from your shadow by the titular shadow puppeteer. He plays his creepy little song and split - there goes your shadow, disconnected from you. However, for some reason or other, he fails to capture your shadow and now you must go on an adventure, chasing after him, to get your shadow reconnected to you.
On the surface, it's a game not unlike Contrast, where you are constantly manipulating both a character in the 3D world and the 2D shadow world. The big difference is that, unlike Contrast, you're controlling them both at the same time. Now, I played the game with Kat in co-op for its entirety and I can't even begin to describe how frustrating the single-player setup seems like it would be. Just having looked at it, it looked nightmarish, controlling one character with each joystick and using buttons on the same side of the controller as the joystick, except for one button which is placed on the opposite side of the controller for the boy. It doesn't look fun. The game was clearly built for co-op. Which, by the way, the game doesn't even fully explain its controls. It gives you instructional videos on how to play - without the controls attached. I had to read an external guide to figure some of the controls out, mostly just figuring them out by frantically pressing buttons until something happened. Oh, and for the shadow, there's a dedicated "hold on to/let go of mine cart" button.
Playing as the boy is pretty simple. You walk around, you manipulate objects, you jump across the occasional rooftop. The boy's playing experience is exponentially simpler than the shadow's despite having an extra dimension. There are numerous times that his role is relegated to handing the shadow different objects that are collected over the course of the game. The shadow, however, is required to manipulate all sorts of objects using only their shadows, has a lot more platforming, and, generally, gets more puzzles, as well as being the one in mortal danger during boss fights.
These puzzles are rather clever at times. Some of them get a bit repetitive, almost all of the game's puzzles making use of the same four or five objects, with those that aren't being very simple, but there are some in there that are very clever. There are even those that aren't clever that will make you "ooo" and "aaah" at the uniqueness of it and the fact that they got it working at all. I was pleasantly surprised with a number of them. I was equally disappointed with repetitiveness.
Some of the puzzles get extremely frustrating, though. About halfway through the game, the shadow gains a new set piece - circular lights. For some reason or other, the shadow can only jump on shadows...unless it's a circular light source, which should burn him up but, instead, suddenly gains the ability to orbit around them. These circular lights are incredibly finicky, sometimes requiring several jumps in the exact same spot to get the game to trigger the switch to another light. Other times, these lights caused weird issues with gravity that shot the shadow upwards, into some part of the level or other, triggering instant death. In general, these lights were a major nuisance.
Those weren't the only nuisance, though. Despite having a simpler play experience, the boy can be very difficult to maneuver due to poor viewing angles. I can't tell you how many times I fell off a cliff because the viewing angle threw my depth perception off. There were even times that the game obscured gaps in fences with the viewing angle, making it look like they were connected when they weren't, and I went off the edge.
I also was largely disappointed in level design as a whole. The sections of the game that I could really consider to be clever were all too brief. The levels that they were part of lasted a significantly smaller amount of time than those that rehashed old design ideas. The levels themselves were also significantly smaller than the levels providing rehashes, usually being just large enough to cover the unique puzzle whereas the rehashed segments would have lots of extra running room.
But that isn't even the most frustrating part. The game focuses even more on its most frustrating parts than it does on rehashes. The longest segments of the game are the seemingly inevitable chase scenes, this one frustratingly long mine segment, and the final boss battle. The chase scenes lasted longer than any one puzzle did and I really did despise that fact. They're all frustrating mine cart segments that are a bit temperamental at times.
The mine segment I had issues with was this segment that required the player to jump from one elevator of sorts to another when they came into close proximity of each other. It required you to do this for nigh on ten different elevators in a row, requiring both characters to cross. It lasted way too long for what it required you to do and, often, the slightest mistake in timing could spell doom, forcing a restart.
*The final boss battle was, by far, the worst. It's an awkwardly designed battle that requires the shadow to repeatedly stay on circular shadows while being affected by a source of gravity not unlike a planet, only the circular shadows aren't the ones manipulating the gravity; the object in between them is. When the gravity combined with the slippery nature of the circular objects are working against you - I cannot tell you how many times it took to get the shadow to make a jump onto one of these objects that he clearly could make because he kept slipping off - it makes even the simplest tasks difficult. But then you also have to make use of the bomb powerup, which...isn't affected by the same gravity that you are, as if that makes even the slightest amount of sense. This leads to frustrating situations if you drop the bomb just the wrong way, trying to stay on the circular platform while dropping it off, instead getting it stuck on the platform you're on and stuck choosing between death by explosion and death by being sucked into the gravity's center. And then these circular platforms start moving.
*But the battle doesn't end there. It has another entire segment where the boss now shoots projectiles at you; projectiles that are twice your size and lock onto your position. Oh, and the shadow regularly has to climb up circular lights. Combine this with collision detection issues that the shadow has while on lights, occasionally dying when these projectiles hit the other side of them, and the depth perception issues that the boy has and you have one incredibly frustrating boss fight that already outstayed its welcome with the first half.
So, if you're looking for a unique co-op experience and don't mind a lot of minor frustrations that build into a larger amount of frustration, you might consider Shadow Puppeteer. If you're not looking for a co-op experience, I wouldn't even slightly recommend it at all. We had enough issues in co-op and I don't even want to begin to fathom how they would be in single-player. And ultimately, that's the thing. The game is frustrating. There are bad design decisions and minor issues all over the place that cause this frustration. This game is an absolute blessing. After the disappointment of No Man's Sky I was worried we wouldn't get an interesting game about exploration and what not, This is where Abzu comes in, being the breakout star of summer games. What is Abzu exactly? It's a game that carries the spirit of "Journey" that was released exclusively for the PS3 but the setting is underwater. It's a fantasic adventure in the long run with story that's about as deep as the depths of the ocean you explore (maybe not that deep). When I first started Abzu, I was immediately stunned by the first area you venture into.
It's beautiful, it's bright and very alien in a sense. This is a game that allows you to experience the ocean in all its glory. Do you remember Ecco the Dolphin or Jaws Unleashed? Throw those bad memories out the window because Abzu will be the only underwater adventure game you'll want to remember. The music will you pull you in and the visuals will trap you until the ride is over, it's a short and sweet adventure that you'll love from start to finish.
Is it worth $20 for a 4 hour long adventure?
If you want to escape reality for that long and just enjoy the Ocean then yes, please buy this game.

This game is awesome. I play a lot of card games both online and in real life and this one stands out among many. Lots of players compare this game to Hearthstone and I will have to do the same. The free to play model for this game is suprisingly good, I have only been playing for about a day and have already opened somewhere around 15 packs, Hearthstone player Trump made a video on it and you can get 3 packs from his code. LiEat is not a game for people who are looking for a challanging RPG game -- it is by no means difficult or try to focus in that department...
But only because it doesn't have to.
All three LiEat games are mostly exploration and story focused, being rather heavy on dialouge and story. All three games are proper sequels to the previous(well, there WERE a few towns skipped but that's because nothing really important happened there).
The story is of a man who's present is riddled to the brim with lies and a dragon girl born from his wishes, who can eat lies. The games sum the story up, as if you were watching an anime: it keeps it short, semi-well detailed yet entertaining. Personally, I enjoyed the twists the stories had each time, with new, unfamiliar faces with each of their own backgrounds and reasons for their actions.
The sprite work is pretty fancy and smooth to the eyes, yet sometimes very very distracting(for example the alley way in 1, that took some time to find!), but over all pretty pleasurable to look at. Character design focuses very heavily on making every character look as adorable as they could possibly make them.
...Thing is, that's where LiEat begins to fall short.
The gameplay is rather dull, as there's not much thinking to be done during combat. The moves are very straight forward and often you just need to spam them to win basically any battle. Exploration is often limited or pointless, and it's very easy to get confused. There aren't many places to explore and there aren't anything worthwile to find.
Pros:
+Endearing spritework, pleasurable to look at
+Story is indeed, pretty good and the world keeps it as consistent as it could.
+Efi. That's all.
+The price is rather low for such an experience.
Mixed:
+/- It doesn't focus on music too well. Sure, it gets the job fairly done, but it is, still, just midis.
+/- Characters often don't return, some for good, some for bad.
Cons:
-Combat isn't exciting, rather dull and repetitive.
-Exploration is stuck to a maximum of 9 maps, very few things to find.
-The games aren't really that difficult, as they serve little to no challenge.
-All three games combined are really really short, summing up to 4 hours.
Over all, I do recommend LiEat. Why? It aims to be a story telling RPG game, and it does that job well, and I absolutely adore that. The world is pretty well built together, makes you wonder on and on about what could, what would and what is in that universe. Characters are memorable and adorable and the spritework does it's best to reflect that.
If you did like LiEat(especially part 3), I'd reccomend you check out DSP(Deep Sea Prisoner)'s works. They being The Gray Garden, Mogeko Castle and Wadanohara and the Great Blue Sea. These are all story driven games with fun characters where the story does end up getting really eerie near the end. Funnily enough, vgperson is the very same person that translated their works and LiEat! While I do recommend these, be vary DSP's works have an intense amount of gore, controversial subjects and other triggering events to some.
While I do recommend these, I still do recommend you to check out LiEat first if you want something way less eerie, cute and memorable.

It took little more than fifty years for me to establish galactic supremacy as the Igarian Galactic Assembly. A military republic of religious, long-living felines, it was my manifest destiny to hold political and military sway over the other space-faring peoples. True, I may have shared technology with underdeveloped civilizations with the sole intent of having them as march-states against other, growing empires; and my sprawling web of vassals was mostly the fruit of military intervention, rather than voluntary co-operation; but as a xenophile I never enslaved or exterminated an alien species, even when they were little more than over-sized, rebellious ants, and when the Gold Concordat threatened to expand into my circle of influence I, instead of crushing them, joined their alliance and, as its strongest member, pushed a vote to transform it into the Bright Concord, a pan-species federation where all those willing to work had a place.
To those acquainted with Paradox's Grand Strategy games, the emergent gameplay described above is a common element, a trademark of their complex games - and, for the most part, a consequence of said complexity and depth. This element is also well present in Stellaris, a hybrid between 4X and Grand Strategy that eschews some of the depth of the latter's genre by borrowing some of the former's streamlined, simpler mechanics. While Stellaris is a step closer to Endless Legend and Civilization than it is to Distant Worlds, that doesn't mean it's not as much of a sandbox game as Crusader Kings and Europa Universalis: without the turn-based constrictions and with open-ended goals and objectives, your empire's future is yours to shape.
Which brings us to the first feature of the game, and one of my favorites: empire creation. If you're not content with the eight pre-made options the base game comes with, you can instead choose to create your own empire and species (or have one randomized for you). With a visual diversity that's in line with the game's strong characterization, you'll be able to choose from six classes, such as arthropods and avians, each with several different animated portraits and appearances, and then pick the species' traits, homeworld type, government form and ethics, among other things. The galaxy is a vast and varied place, and you'll have situations where a scientific directory comprised of octopodes is vying for power side-by-side with a monarchy of militarily-inclined eagle-looking creatures.
Aside from the AI empires and you, the galaxy is home to societies of varying technological level: from planets where the dominant species are still ruled by kings and swords to others where nuclear fission and initial space exploration are already well known. In a way that reminded me of Star Trek's Federation, you can opt to either observe these civilizations from afar, actively intervene in their society, aid them in the development of FTL space-travel or genetically modify members of your species to covertly invade and substitute the political class with your own, effectively becoming the planet's ruler.
These scattered civilizations, along with the various roaming aliens - from gentle space cows to hostile crystalline entities - and the games' events add a touch of flavor and flair that space games often lack. Discovering anomalies, surveying planets and exploring different systems can yield events and questlines where you'll often have to make decisions or perform multiple tasks to earn certain rewards. On one of my playthroughs as the technocrat Gwesibor Foundation I happened upon a heavily-guarded Tree of Life, and once I'd harvested its sap I could either focus its regenerative power on my leaders, increasing their lifespan, or spread it among the population, diluting its effects but increasing their happiness. Whereas space games often feel bland and empty, Stellaris' beautiful visual presentation and plethora of interactions keep it clear from the spreadsheet and user interface pit that many games in the genre fall into.
The game borrows frequently from common 4X features, and these mechanics are tactile and intuitive: planets are divided into tiles, upon which your populations grow and where you can create buildings to generate resources, further your research or attain other specific benefits. The research part of the game is equally intuitive, with three separate categories that you're constantly researching in order to either improve your current options or make available new ones. A few of these research options can change the way you play entirely, introducing robot workers that you can build instead of grow or genetic splicing that you can use to uplift base animals into sentient-hood. An even smaller amount of them are labelled as dangerous, such as Artificial Intelligence, and if you're not careful they can lead to disastrous end-game events...
The 4X elements and small start (you always begin with a single planet and a handful of ships) are accompanied by an exceptionally well-implemented tutorial that's only as intrusive as it needs to be. I say exceptional because there aren't many strategy games that you can pick up and play for the first time without failing horridly, and while there are plenty of details and advanced features that you'll only uncover as you play, the tutorial does a perfect job of conveying what needs to be known to get things flowing. For those that want things on a grander scale, as the game progresses and your empire grows you'll find that the smaller aspects of 4X management give way to the more indirect, delegating nature of grand strategy games.
There are a few mechanics that stood out as particularly interesting and novel, however. Your government type and traits dictate how certain policies are initially applied, such as migration, slavery, voting rights and war economy - and populations react differently to said policies. Your individualist, freedom-loving human of The Fourth Great and Bountiful Human Empire might think your prohibition of slavery is great, but that collectivist race of insectoids you integrated might think otherwise. Even your own species' populations gain particular quirks as your empire grows, due to something called ethics divergence: that faraway sector might with time shun your empire's pacifism and become jingoist warmongers, radically opposing your lack of military intervention in surrounding empires. Let a population become too unhappy, and it'll start joining factions: it might want you to release or return a planet to its former owner; stage a coup to place a pretender or even create a separate empire from that sector that you foolishly let grow too big. The sector system is also an effective way at minimizing micro-managing: you can designate systems and planets to a sector, which will then rule over that region in a semi-autonomous way, granting you taxes and research but with autonomy to construct buildings as it wishes.

A few of us the other day found ourselves trying to come up with words to explain to others what Stellaris felt like and we settled on: "Civ 5 meets EU4, but in space and a lot cooler!" Yeah, that works. *nods*
Like Europa Universalis 4, Stellaris is a grand strategy 4X game: explore, expand, exploit, exterminate. Unlike EU4, if you've never played this type of game before you probably won't need a bottle of wine, 2 spa days, and vacation to relax after trying to learn it. (Okay, I exaggerate and confess I only needed a couple of glasses of wine and one long weekend to recover from my first (delighted, dazed, and confused) hours in EU4.)
Grand strategy indeed; you will be exploring space, managing resources and influence, keeping your people happy, colonizing and building, deciding ethical matters, terraforming, pushing the boundaries of science, making or breaking alliances, building ships and armies, waging wars or trying not to, and spreading your own special brand of All The Things across the glittering universe.
However....you've probably already heard, "Stellaris is accessible". Yes, it is! The tutorial behaves like a proper host and shows you around the place with kindness and interesting explanations and a welcoming attitude. The game starts slow and easy; you'll have lots of time to click on buttons, read well written explanations, and poke around the place. The learning curve meanders gently into the game and gives you lots of time to breathe and don't worry be happy. And little flashy bits up top warn you of the things you really need to pay attention to anyway.
What could possibly go wrong?
Then of course, being a Paradox Interactive grand strategy game you will land on your backside (repeatedly I expect) with a resounding thump, be surprised by things you didn't seen coming, delighted with new lore that hadn't come up before, and stunned by the variety of ways in which you can get it wrong, get it right, win all the things today, or go out in high drama and ranging storms tomorrow.
As you expand and there are endless details to take care of you create 'sectors' and tuck some things aside to manage themselves (under your orders) and supply you with lootz while you make friends and influence people and wage war in the neighborhood. But, if you just love micromanaging all the things, you can do that too.
And then there is modding; this game is as customizable as you want to deal with. Off to the Workshop with you!
If you like space games this is my favorite of the last 20 years (I was addicted to Sierra's Outpost back in the olden days, bugs and all).
If you like character creation, this alone could be worth buying the game. Seriously, it's awesome fun! :D
If you love EU4 (or are terrified of it but secretly always wanted to try) you're going to love Stellaris.
If you've never considered playing grand strategy 4X games Stellaris may be the open door, with the welcoming host, that changes your gaming life forever.

(Excerpt of my review here:
"With only a ”mere” 20 or so hours with the game, I have barely begun to scratch the surface in Stellaris. If I know Paradox (and I think I do) there are many, many more hours of entertainment to be had because of the dynamically generated gameplay, where every universe you create is unique.
In my opinion, Stellaris brings a much needed breath of fresh air to an otherwise stagnated 4X strategy genre, where almost every game is in part inspired by either Civilization or the Master of Orion series. It’s done with a finish rarely seen outside of big budget, big studio productions – with a very small team. Stellaris has an excellent combination of freedom of design and deep political system that we don’t see nearly enough of in my opinion.

The pace of the game is great for the most part, starting out with a complete hands on control of the empire early on, while slowly handing off more and more power to local governors that can administrate entire regions of systems for you, in exchange for more autonomy and a reduced tax rate. Your neighbors react in a very realistic manner to your world views – which can very easily lead to war. I can say from personal experience that being pro-slavery is not easy when you’re surrounded by pacifist hippies – who suddenly seem less interested in peace, and much more focused on plotting your inevitable demise and raising war fleets to accomplish that.

I’ve really enjoyed my time with Stellaris, and I’m sure I’ll be having many more late nights of playing it over the coming years. I have minor gripes with how automation of ships work (or the lack thereof), where I definitely think it should have been an option. Information about mechanics and choices is also a little on the light side at times. With all of that in mind, I’ve come to a final score for Stellaris of 9 (and a half...appendage). It falls just shy of a full 10 at current, but knowing Paradox’s DLC model, they will easily make it there in time…and maybe more."

Before we begin, I'd like to point out that although I bought this game a while ago, I never bothered to play it until now due to it's very negative reviews at launch.  Since they've repeatedly patched the game since and have apparently fixed most of the bugs, reviews have improved enough to compel me to give it a shot.  This means that my review is based off of the game as it is currently, rather than how much it's been improved.  After all, how the hell should I know how it's improved?
THE GOOD:
First of all, this game has some great pacing!  It has exactly the kind of frantic, pulse-pounding action that you'd expect from an online/co-op FPS.  I mainly played Survival mode, which is basically a horde mode; you and your team are trying to survive as many waves of dinosaurs as possible and it does not disappoint.  Even the weakest of dinosaurs can take quite a beating, making the experience of taking them out a very satisfying one.  You definitely feel a sense of accomplishment when you take one out.
The stronger and larger dinosaurs act as boss battles that occur throughout each round (similar to the Tank in the Left 4 Dead series).  When I refer to certain dinosaurs as being "larger" I'm not kidding!  The sense of scale is very impressive as the larger dinosaurs tower over you to the point where you will constantly have to tilt your aim upwards to get a decent view of them.  In some cases, though, the scale of the "bosses" can be kind of ridiculous (the Stegosaurus is roughly the size of a small office building, when in reality they were supposed to be approximately the size of a bus), but hey-- you're shooting dinosaurs with futuristic weaponry so who cares about minor details like that?  While headshots on any dinosaurs don't have the same effect that most games would (instant death), they significantly increase the amount of damage you deal out, so expect to spend a lot of time running and gunning on each target.
THE BAD:
Although most of the launch bugs were apparently fixed in later patches, there are still quite a number of bugs and perplexing gameplay choices.  I, almost immediately found a bug where if I found myself pinned into a corner by a minor dinosaur, they would clip into me and couldn't harm me, although I could still kill them.  Movement can be kind of buggy, as you can get stuck in doorways temporarily and the screen will start stuttering until you back away from the doorway.  I can see this causing a lot of frustration in more intense matches.
THE "SLIGHTLY ANNOYING"
I also couldn't figure out how to swap my default weapon (pistol) for something automatic until my game was almost over, you have to approach one of the two blue computers located back at base, press the action button ("e" by default) and then select my new guns from the menu.  The reason why this was a problem was because the game never explained that to me and the computers can kind of blend in with the other vaguely computer-like objects that have no interaction and are only intended for design.  Even having an on-screen prompt while standing near the computer would've been enough, but there's literally nothing to suggest that it was even interactive, like you're just expected to know this stuff already.
I'm sure the game has far more decent qualities and a lot more bugs, but I actually haven't played much of it at all.  This is just based off of my inital reaction.
8/10  There's still room for improvement, but it's also a very solid game as it is now.
Always a classic to play!

Stellaris is a beautiful mix of visuals and mechanics that allows for a very deep 4x  Experience, with a much more accessible game compared to other paradox titles, while retaining the complexity we love.
Full review:
Textual summary:
As always - watch the full review for the best possible impression, a few paragraphs of text can do this game no justice.
Based on the 4 cornerstones of a 4x, the first is exploration.
Using multiple ways to do FTL Travel and a variety of exploration options it allows for interesting exploration. It also ties in very nicely into expansion / exploitation that allows for figuring out unique locations, lore, resources and research ideas. It allows for a good mix of civilian and military exploration as well as a nice mix of possible dangers and risks associated with that.
Expansion is also very nicely done. Expanding your empire requires outposts, orbital facilities, habitable words, population and their management and growth, a variety of variables to manage and allow for control over them.
Which brings us to exploitation : The balance between colonies (and limits) mining facilities, defensive structures, upkeep and everything in between provides a nice experience, that while not very deep (multi use orbitals / global economy) is still in depth enough to provide a interesting challenge and need careful planning.
Lastly, extermination is the weakest part of the game, with combat feeling very bland. The various military aspects have quite a bit of planning and management, but most of that is based in the way you design, research and build ships as well as your diplomatic activities, rather than the combat mechanics in and of themselves.
The major drawback i feel is the PC Options & Help menu that are very lazy and subpar, compared to the rest of the game. The help menu opens a in-game browser that loads a public Wikipedia page.
I especially applaud the active helper that provides a fully voiced over tutorial for many of the mechanics in the game, as well as the stellar performance of the title.
My final issue is with the overall very well executed research system: it also tell you very little what to expect and doesn't allow for a lot of planning of activities moving forward, while it does have that very depth you want. a true shame.
So overall I can wholeheartedly recommend the title as a very solid 4x. Not perfect, but pretty damn good.

For those new to Grand Strategy games and/or cautious of Europa Universalis:
Stellaris offers a nice entry to the genre if you haven't played one before. If you'd like, comparing to Civilisation, it is similar in concept in that you are managing your ever growing empire, maintaining relations with other empires, gathering resources and waging wars, but the system is somewhat more deep and complex in a number of ways. You must manage ‘leaders’ which includes balancing your investment in Science, Military and Government for example. There are various caps which mean that you cannot do everything at once and so must think about short term as well as long term goals in that regard. For those used to managing ‘population’ in Civ-like games this will not be too much of a step up.
There are other aspects to the game as well such as exploration, missions, research projects and events – should you use the in game tutorial this can help guide you through some of these as and when they appear.
The next thing to talk about is the level of customisation this game offers. To a new comer to the genre this will be very intimidating. I loaded up my first game having seen the huge numbers of different traits, policies etc for a given race only to find further customisation such as individual spaceship specifications and leader characteristics – it’ll be quite a challenge to try to learn these all at once so don’t try and just take it as it comes. I cannot say how it compares to games like EU4 and Crusader Kings in terms of level of customisation however as I have not played those games.
The gameplay itself is reasonably placed, there was never really a time during my time playing that I have felt like I have nothing to do. The only down time I did have was when I myself couldn’t pick a strategy I wanted to pursue – to try and explore more for potential research events, to try and get trade deals with my neighbours, to clear out nearby star systems of hostile space creatures, to colonise more systems or even to wage war to capture a system in order to preserve my borders and corridor of travel between outposts.... the list goes on.
Overall I felt that as a new comer I haven’t been as overwhelmed as I thought I would be. Having said that, while the tutorial pop-ups are helpful, they are few and far between after you get the very superficial basics down and the in game help is ‘currently’ non-existent in any meaningful capacity. Instead of having a comprehensive Civolopedia or sorts the help button takes you to a Wiki which at present is bare bones and not helpful in the slightest. I spent ages trying to figure out ways to increase my influence and having narrowed it down to a building upgrade I couldn't then find anything about how I can get to a stage where that building is available to me. No doubt this Wiki will be fleshed out over time however.
Final points – the sound track is stellar *wink* and the gameplay is relaxing, reasonably paced and relaxing with the ability to ‘pause’ time while you manage your empire as it grows so that you do not miss anything important. During my time streaming in advance of release it certainly seems as though the community that this game will have will likely be helpful and welcoming as I had many enter my stream and point me in the right direction and clarify any questions I had regarding aspects of the game.
Lastly the game certainly has that “Just a little longer.....” vibe and I found myself wanting to keep playing after midnight, and there is a certain satisfaction upon seeing your borders expand and your navy winning glorious victories.
Stellaris gets a firm recommendation from me to players unfamiliar with the Grand Strategy and 4eX genres.

It was a groggy morning when I was on steam browsing around for upcoming games to see if any of them caught my attention. I suddenly stumbled across this title ‘Stellaris’ which instantly grabbed me by the font of the text upon a very abstract image. Upon closer inspection my cravings and demands for a space exploration game suddenly peaked as soon as my eyes browsed the pictures and videos behind Stellaris.
I have never before been interested in tactical space games, this was all new to me. Just like the whole idea behind the game. Starting on a planet and then exploring space. The fear of the unknown, the fear of not knowing what is next. I was very scared because I am new to the whole Space Genre and 4X. Before I knew it, twenty hours had passed on this game. Here is what I liked and disliked about the game.
– The tutorial on this game comes in three options. Full, tips and none. I am so grateful for the fact that this tutorial really does help, without it I would’ve still been left swimming with the fishes. It’s completely voiced over by an AI robot (Your assistant) who is eager to help you with every menu click and move you make. Once you feel you know the ropes of the game you can happily turn him off in menu and he will disappear into the void.
– The graphics of this game, the universe are indeed beautiful to look at. From the Sun in the centre of the solar system to the swirling dust clouds on the surface of each planet, I want to be instantly shot into space to the beautiful colors that surround me. Some systems which you explore have Black Holes, Yellow Dwarves and other vortexes which are really stunning to look at.
– With a Galaxy size ranging from 100 stars to 1000 stars and with up to 39 AI Empires, the whole galaxy really feels alive and the game suddenly becomes life with the amount of interaction and size. I have yet to scratch the surface of a 1000 star scenario and I’ve been playing for around 15 hours on that one save.
– The customisation for each empire is crazy. From the character portraits to their traits, names, visions and planet names you can really have a heavily customised empire. You can also go and edit the preset empires to slightly change them too.
– The magic m’s are definitely on this game. Multiplayer is a really really good experience. It plays very similar to single player, the only difference is that only the host can pause and move the time. A really great super feature is that you can also save games online and then come back to them later. The other magic M is mod support, the game has extensive support for mods and they said “every aspect of the game is moddable”.
– I swear it was only an hour. At least it felt that. Before you know it, your day has disappeared. The game has a special talent of taking away that time you have.
– The fact time flies when playing this game means you will need a lot of spare time. This game requires a lot of time investment and could easily cost you your job or family. Okay... maybe not that bad... but it still does suck your life away.
– There is no easy difficulty on the game. Just Normal and upwards. For newbies to the genre like me starting from normal is almost suicidal. Even with 20+ hours invested in the game I have not got to a point yet of seeing if I can actually take over the AI so I cannot comment so much on that but I believe they won’t be a push over. The several jousts me and the AI have had with the combat had ended in me losing mostly although it was not by much and pretty fair.
– The settings in the game are pretty minimum and there are in fact no graphic settings. I would’ve loved to have options for low, medium, high and ultra but the game seems to have only one setting. The game still runs fine for me however but I believe people who have a lower specified computer will have more issues trying to play the game with no options of lowering quality for playability. Which brings me on to my next point.
– With the maximum stars and 36 empires all playing in one game, the game gets slightly jumpy. The game remains playable however and is still enjoyable. I won’t talk too much about my specifications or in detail but it’s an average PC. (2GB VRAM) and according to the steam stats page it’s better than half the peoples PC’s out there. I know it’s not the best and you can get much better but for the people who may not have that then the game falls into a grey area for running bigger scenarios.
– I feel a story mode or scenarios which puts you into situations like being outnumbered or two massive Alliances with a back story fighting each other would’ve been really good. The game does have some story in the situation log however but I feel a more dedicated story mode would’ve been perfect for this game.
I came into Stellaris as a novice and was very scared of being unable to handle it. I was delighted however to be able to easily grasp the basics and progress to a point where I did not want to sleep and continue playing all night long. I played a single player game and a multiplayer game in the time I spent playing Stellaris and even though I spent a chunk of time playing the game I did not progress too much into a point of conquering enemies. In fact I only went to war with one of the thirty seven nations and only made contact with 8 in the whole time of me playing the single player game.
The game is real fun and addictive however, so much that I highly recommend it to all my friends, family and viewers. Paradox have really blown my mind with this game and how much I can get lost in the galaxy and far beyond. I would avoid this game however if you wanted to spare your life... but then again... go for it! It’s definitely worth experiencing and I highly recommend this game.

Sending a spy to infilitrate an opposing faction and watching him seize their lands for you, only to find out he has claimed the lands for himself and has usurped you, is just a taste of the possibilities the campaign gives you. Highly recommended and I would love to see features from this game introduced and evolved in future TW titles.

I dont know what this ridiculous notion of "p2w" is in regards to collectiable card games because since the dawn of Magic the Gathering CCGs were always expensive as heck. That said, there is a bunch to unpack about this game:
You definitely don't feel that you need highly expensive cards to win. While some cards feel very powerful, this isn't something constrained to Paragon tier cards, there are very common or even basic cards which are very powerful (I got two ranks on ladder just playing the base Terran Deck).
The Raid mode is a draft mode where you can choose multiple paths. There aren't any in-game explanations for this but apparently the point is that you can choose to go for bonus matches to gain higher rewards. The game doesnt bother to explain you a lot so eh. At least its kinda fun and you're guranteed to at least gain 3 random cards, so you never feel like you wasted time.
That said, there are a couple of things of which I don't know how impactful they are but they leave me concerned. First, unless you shell out a lot of money, you see a lot of Elite and higher Chests you unlock get discarded. I don't seem to be able to throw out common chests out of my collection (not even in advance), so I think this is something to try to trick the player into dropping cash to "save" a coveted Paragon Chest. Since I only saw Cosmetics in chests so far however, this might not even be very significant.
Second, crafting cards. In general, it feels significantly more effiicent to buy packs than bothering to disenchant cards. You have a loss ratio of 1:10 (!), so you need to disenchant 10 cards to get another card of the same rarity. Unless you have like a million excess cards, this is mostly just wasting cards.
To wrap this up, The game is a lot of fun and the module system in particular allows for a lot of gameplay choices. There are questionable aspects in regards to Pay content which is further amplified by a lack of explanations in game. Ultimately, I will recommend this because its worth checking out and heard good things about the devs. I would advise caution before putting money in here because it feels like there are a lot of money sinks with little return.

Replay value, this game is all about replay value.
Granted, Binding of Isaac is part of the rogue-like genre, but it is still refreshing to find a game that can achieve that "fresh" feeling everytime you play it. You never truly know what is going to come next, since the maps are randomly generated, and the difficulty of each playthrough can vary greatly depending on the items you find.
Another plus is the artwork, this is an Edmund McMillen game, so you can expect a lot of cohesion between artwork, gameplay and thematic.
Twisted, grim and cute, it's a game that delivers what it promises: Fun and challenging gameplay, with hundreds of hours of replay value.

Some people might be wondering why I am reviewing a free game when I could be reviewing one that costs something more than free. After all, a free game is one you can try and decide if you like it or not, and all you lose is a few minutes, compared to the money you could have spent buying a particularly tasty pack of gum. I counter this argument by saying... ...nothing, really. I just felt like reviewing this since I blindstreamed it yesterday for some friends and had a grand time with it.
Let's talk about the positives first, which highly outweigh the negatives. First of all, it's pretty funny. I got a kick out of it. Some people might counter this claim by saying that many other people have made fun of typical game genres/My Little Pony lovers/car tow-people (I'm sure there's a few out there). I counter this counter by saying it's still fairly amusing. Heck, I love visual novels/anime and I enjoy My Little Pony: Friendship is Magic. That doesn't mean I protest the tongue-in-cheek representations of them. I laughed, my friends thought it was funny, that's good enough for me.
So what about those other pesky things, such as graphics, music, and, oh, I don't know, gameplay? The graphics are fairly minimalistic, but they work. I was rather endeared to the legless protagonist I controlled, Warren, and his faithful companion, Everlasting Cigarette (which my significant other suggesting he gets the same brand Snake has). Sure, he's a dirty thief, but after the garbage he goes through, I can offer some sympathy. Other than him and the minimalistic world (which really doesn't need anything beyond what it has), the graphics in the minigames vary wildly, and the ones that look like they are out of MS Paint look like that to make a point. It's a joke about how bad some games do look that are made by indie developers. The "better" ones have nicer graphics. Props for the cute cat girl.
Music is... well, I didn't notice it much. My computer was being a piece of junk last night and lagging thanks to my capture device. The music actually cut out in the last minigame and the credits. Before that, I wouldn't call any of it special. None of it was offensive to the ears, so there you go, neutral opinion is neutral.
The gameplay is, overall, pretty good. As Warren, it goes smoothly, with only a few keys being needed to get around. The minigames are fine too. Other than the afformentioned lag, which was not the game's fault at all (I tried it off-camera and it worked without a hitch), I had no problems with the controls. It does what it needs to do, and that works for me.
There is little to mention about the plot, other than that it connects a bunch of jokes in a straightforward fashion. The minigames it leads to give achievements, and they are all reasonable to get. You can actually skip the minigames, which is a plus in my book. I mean, no, I didn't skip any, because I'm an extremely stubborn person who insists on doing everything... and to me, they were fun anyway. But to have that option certainly doesn't hurt. I particularly enjoyed the three-pony game, which evidently is based off a game I have never heard of. IOW, I need to check that game out too.
Oh, and it has interactive credits. Yay interactive credits. (I mean that sincerely, interactive credits are neato.)
So, negatives. There aren't many. The main one I have is about the last minigame. It's a long haul and there are no checkpoints. My initial thought was that you got checkpoints at every percentage met (25%, 50%, 75%). Nope, if you die, you start at the beginning. That got annoying. Since the obstacle course looks pretty much the same in each portion, I kept forgetting where certain traps were and would fall for them multiple times. Partially my fault, partially the game's for not having many significant cues to remember, and it would have overall been nice to have checkpoints, like the other minigames did.
Other than that, there's the lack of proofreading. Don't get me wrong, the game is fine in terms of understanding it. I was never left questioning what something met because of errors in grammar and the like. But there were words spelled incorrectly, and there was a constant lack of capitalizing names, periods where appropriate, and the dreaded "your/you're" and "lets/let's" sprinkled about. Never hurts to have a proofreader check for that sort of thing.
There is also no way to save. I do have to ding it for that, but it isn't as bad as usual. Without the lag and camera problems I had, I probably would have finished it in an hour and a half, and that's mainly because I try to find/examine everything possible. My guess is most people could finish it in an hour. It's not hard to set aside an hour to run through it in one go. The lack of frustrating areas also means you're unlikely to get annoyed and want to exit out for a bit. Still, a save feature would have been nice.
For the low price of free, this game is definitely worth it. Even if it cost something along the lines of $2-$3, I would still recommend it. It's a fun experience and a nice break from long/srsbusiness games (I played this after some Downfall, so... yeah, talk about mood whiplash). Give it a go! At best, you get to be amused. At worst, you lost ten minutes deciding you hated it and can never get said ten minutes back. A tragedy, to be sure.

Do you like good things? Then you will llike this game.
The Witcher 2 is a mature RPG set in a believable fantasy world. Let me put that to you another way: this game is the characters from Game Of Thrones set in the world of Lord Of The Rings... and I don't say that lightly.
The highpoint of this game is its believable storytelling. You can be an adult and still become engrossed in the story without being asked to suspend your belief in the characters. That's because the story of The Witcher is based of off a Polish novel series of the same name.
But the believable world and characters are just the beginning of what's to like about this game. It also has amazing graphics that are still good compared to today's AAA games even though they're 3 years old, a difficult combat system that accurately simulates what it must feel like to be a real swordsmen, and a branching storyline with realistic consequences for your actions and choices that will challenge you.
In a way, this game is really the worst game you will ever play. Not because it's bad, but because every other game you will play in the future will seem bad by comparison. Seriously, I just beat Dragon Age Inquistion and this game still does things that other AAA RPGs have yet to learn from.
If you like good things, buy this game. If you're a masochist, then don't.

(Excerpt of my review here:
"With only a ”mere” 20 or so hours with the game, I have barely begun to scratch the surface in Stellaris. If I know Paradox (and I think I do) there are many, many more hours of entertainment to be had because of the dynamically generated gameplay, where every universe you create is unique.
In my opinion, Stellaris brings a much needed breath of fresh air to an otherwise stagnated 4X strategy genre, where almost every game is in part inspired by either Civilization or the Master of Orion series. It’s done with a finish rarely seen outside of big budget, big studio productions – with a very small team. Stellaris has an excellent combination of freedom of design and deep political system that we don’t see nearly enough of in my opinion.

The pace of the game is great for the most part, starting out with a complete hands on control of the empire early on, while slowly handing off more and more power to local governors that can administrate entire regions of systems for you, in exchange for more autonomy and a reduced tax rate. Your neighbors react in a very realistic manner to your world views – which can very easily lead to war. I can say from personal experience that being pro-slavery is not easy when you’re surrounded by pacifist hippies – who suddenly seem less interested in peace, and much more focused on plotting your inevitable demise and raising war fleets to accomplish that.

I’ve really enjoyed my time with Stellaris, and I’m sure I’ll be having many more late nights of playing it over the coming years. I have minor gripes with how automation of ships work (or the lack thereof), where I definitely think it should have been an option. Information about mechanics and choices is also a little on the light side at times. With all of that in mind, I’ve come to a final score for Stellaris of 9 (and a half...appendage). It falls just shy of a full 10 at current, but knowing Paradox’s DLC model, they will easily make it there in time…and maybe more."

Stellaris is a beautiful mix of visuals and mechanics that allows for a very deep 4x  Experience, with a much more accessible game compared to other paradox titles, while retaining the complexity we love.
Full review:
Textual summary:
As always - watch the full review for the best possible impression, a few paragraphs of text can do this game no justice.
Based on the 4 cornerstones of a 4x, the first is exploration.
Using multiple ways to do FTL Travel and a variety of exploration options it allows for interesting exploration. It also ties in very nicely into expansion / exploitation that allows for figuring out unique locations, lore, resources and research ideas. It allows for a good mix of civilian and military exploration as well as a nice mix of possible dangers and risks associated with that.
Expansion is also very nicely done. Expanding your empire requires outposts, orbital facilities, habitable words, population and their management and growth, a variety of variables to manage and allow for control over them.
Which brings us to exploitation : The balance between colonies (and limits) mining facilities, defensive structures, upkeep and everything in between provides a nice experience, that while not very deep (multi use orbitals / global economy) is still in depth enough to provide a interesting challenge and need careful planning.
Lastly, extermination is the weakest part of the game, with combat feeling very bland. The various military aspects have quite a bit of planning and management, but most of that is based in the way you design, research and build ships as well as your diplomatic activities, rather than the combat mechanics in and of themselves.
The major drawback i feel is the PC Options & Help menu that are very lazy and subpar, compared to the rest of the game. The help menu opens a in-game browser that loads a public Wikipedia page.
I especially applaud the active helper that provides a fully voiced over tutorial for many of the mechanics in the game, as well as the stellar performance of the title.
My final issue is with the overall very well executed research system: it also tell you very little what to expect and doesn't allow for a lot of planning of activities moving forward, while it does have that very depth you want. a true shame.
So overall I can wholeheartedly recommend the title as a very solid 4x. Not perfect, but pretty damn good.

For those new to Grand Strategy games and/or cautious of Europa Universalis:
Stellaris offers a nice entry to the genre if you haven't played one before. If you'd like, comparing to Civilisation, it is similar in concept in that you are managing your ever growing empire, maintaining relations with other empires, gathering resources and waging wars, but the system is somewhat more deep and complex in a number of ways. You must manage ‘leaders’ which includes balancing your investment in Science, Military and Government for example. There are various caps which mean that you cannot do everything at once and so must think about short term as well as long term goals in that regard. For those used to managing ‘population’ in Civ-like games this will not be too much of a step up.
There are other aspects to the game as well such as exploration, missions, research projects and events – should you use the in game tutorial this can help guide you through some of these as and when they appear.
The next thing to talk about is the level of customisation this game offers. To a new comer to the genre this will be very intimidating. I loaded up my first game having seen the huge numbers of different traits, policies etc for a given race only to find further customisation such as individual spaceship specifications and leader characteristics – it’ll be quite a challenge to try to learn these all at once so don’t try and just take it as it comes. I cannot say how it compares to games like EU4 and Crusader Kings in terms of level of customisation however as I have not played those games.
The gameplay itself is reasonably placed, there was never really a time during my time playing that I have felt like I have nothing to do. The only down time I did have was when I myself couldn’t pick a strategy I wanted to pursue – to try and explore more for potential research events, to try and get trade deals with my neighbours, to clear out nearby star systems of hostile space creatures, to colonise more systems or even to wage war to capture a system in order to preserve my borders and corridor of travel between outposts.... the list goes on.
Overall I felt that as a new comer I haven’t been as overwhelmed as I thought I would be. Having said that, while the tutorial pop-ups are helpful, they are few and far between after you get the very superficial basics down and the in game help is ‘currently’ non-existent in any meaningful capacity. Instead of having a comprehensive Civolopedia or sorts the help button takes you to a Wiki which at present is bare bones and not helpful in the slightest. I spent ages trying to figure out ways to increase my influence and having narrowed it down to a building upgrade I couldn't then find anything about how I can get to a stage where that building is available to me. No doubt this Wiki will be fleshed out over time however.
Final points – the sound track is stellar *wink* and the gameplay is relaxing, reasonably paced and relaxing with the ability to ‘pause’ time while you manage your empire as it grows so that you do not miss anything important. During my time streaming in advance of release it certainly seems as though the community that this game will have will likely be helpful and welcoming as I had many enter my stream and point me in the right direction and clarify any questions I had regarding aspects of the game.
Lastly the game certainly has that “Just a little longer.....” vibe and I found myself wanting to keep playing after midnight, and there is a certain satisfaction upon seeing your borders expand and your navy winning glorious victories.

Why would this be fun?

It was a groggy morning when I was on steam browsing around for upcoming games to see if any of them caught my attention. I suddenly stumbled across this title ‘Stellaris’ which instantly grabbed me by the font of the text upon a very abstract image. Upon closer inspection my cravings and demands for a space exploration game suddenly peaked as soon as my eyes browsed the pictures and videos behind Stellaris.
I have never before been interested in tactical space games, this was all new to me. Just like the whole idea behind the game. Starting on a planet and then exploring space. The fear of the unknown, the fear of not knowing what is next. I was very scared because I am new to the whole Space Genre and 4X. Before I knew it, twenty hours had passed on this game. Here is what I liked and disliked about the game.
– The tutorial on this game comes in three options. Full, tips and none. I am so grateful for the fact that this tutorial really does help, without it I would’ve still been left swimming with the fishes. It’s completely voiced over by an AI robot (Your assistant) who is eager to help you with every menu click and move you make. Once you feel you know the ropes of the game you can happily turn him off in menu and he will disappear into the void.
– The graphics of this game, the universe are indeed beautiful to look at. From the Sun in the centre of the solar system to the swirling dust clouds on the surface of each planet, I want to be instantly shot into space to the beautiful colors that surround me. Some systems which you explore have Black Holes, Yellow Dwarves and other vortexes which are really stunning to look at.
– With a Galaxy size ranging from 100 stars to 1000 stars and with up to 39 AI Empires, the whole galaxy really feels alive and the game suddenly becomes life with the amount of interaction and size. I have yet to scratch the surface of a 1000 star scenario and I’ve been playing for around 15 hours on that one save.
– The customisation for each empire is crazy. From the character portraits to their traits, names, visions and planet names you can really have a heavily customised empire. You can also go and edit the preset empires to slightly change them too.
– The magic m’s are definitely on this game. Multiplayer is a really really good experience. It plays very similar to single player, the only difference is that only the host can pause and move the time. A really great super feature is that you can also save games online and then come back to them later. The other magic M is mod support, the game has extensive support for mods and they said “every aspect of the game is moddable”.
– I swear it was only an hour. At least it felt that. Before you know it, your day has disappeared. The game has a special talent of taking away that time you have.
– The fact time flies when playing this game means you will need a lot of spare time. This game requires a lot of time investment and could easily cost you your job or family. Okay... maybe not that bad... but it still does suck your life away.
– There is no easy difficulty on the game. Just Normal and upwards. For newbies to the genre like me starting from normal is almost suicidal. Even with 20+ hours invested in the game I have not got to a point yet of seeing if I can actually take over the AI so I cannot comment so much on that but I believe they won’t be a push over. The several jousts me and the AI have had with the combat had ended in me losing mostly although it was not by much and pretty fair.
– The settings in the game are pretty minimum and there are in fact no graphic settings. I would’ve loved to have options for low, medium, high and ultra but the game seems to have only one setting. The game still runs fine for me however but I believe people who have a lower specified computer will have more issues trying to play the game with no options of lowering quality for playability. Which brings me on to my next point.
– With the maximum stars and 36 empires all playing in one game, the game gets slightly jumpy. The game remains playable however and is still enjoyable. I won’t talk too much about my specifications or in detail but it’s an average PC. (2GB VRAM) and according to the steam stats page it’s better than half the peoples PC’s out there. I know it’s not the best and you can get much better but for the people who may not have that then the game falls into a grey area for running bigger scenarios.
– I feel a story mode or scenarios which puts you into situations like being outnumbered or two massive Alliances with a back story fighting each other would’ve been really good. The game does have some story in the situation log however but I feel a more dedicated story mode would’ve been perfect for this game.
I came into Stellaris as a novice and was very scared of being unable to handle it. I was delighted however to be able to easily grasp the basics and progress to a point where I did not want to sleep and continue playing all night long. I played a single player game and a multiplayer game in the time I spent playing Stellaris and even though I spent a chunk of time playing the game I did not progress too much into a point of conquering enemies. In fact I only went to war with one of the thirty seven nations and only made contact with 8 in the whole time of me playing the single player game.
The game is real fun and addictive however, so much that I highly recommend it to all my friends, family and viewers. Paradox have really blown my mind with this game and how much I can get lost in the galaxy and far beyond. I would avoid this game however if you wanted to spare your life... but then again... go for it! It’s definitely worth experiencing and I highly recommend this game.

Honestly this game is a lot better than I initially thought.
What first was a 2 dollar steam sale purchase I thought i'd spend 1-2 hours with has now become one of my most beloved rts games so far. If you like the total war series or crusader kings and are looking for a fine mixture of managing and actually controlling armies and empires this is the right game for you.
Pros:
-It offers 3 (dark , middle and late medieval age) periods and a huge map (Extended map of europe) letting you play as almost all nations that were present at that time.
-New factions can emerge when certain provinces are captured (uniting england , ireland and such)
-It offers a interesting kingdom power system that encourages you to act with honor. Breaking agreements and treaties will result in a loss of reputation, leading to civil unrest.
-Royal families, their offspring and marriages can be managed as well as knights you can employ in different positions such as generals , spies , priests and merchants.
-Battles can be fought automatically or you can take direct control yourself
-Still has working multiplayer support due to direct connections via lan or tcp/ip
-Game can be quite difficult if you want it to be but the learning curve isnt so bad. It didnt take me long in order to do well and build a small empire.
Cons:
-The units are a bit hard to get into formation when directly leading your battles and it has some minor flaws. Its not bad but dont expect it to live up to total war battles.
-The steam version is not updated to patch 1.05 , its 1.03 instead so manual patching is required.
-Widescreens and windows 8 arent properly supported but there are some people that have been able to get it to work. I do recommend to check the forums on that.

If you have Windows 8, don't worry.
Try running the game, if it crashes then try this:
If you have created a desktop icon then skip part one.
1. Go to where the game installed on your computer, which is most likely:
PC/C:/Program Files(x86)/Steam/steamapps/common/Knights of Honor
2. Right click on the KoH icon(The icon with the tiny helmet)
Windows will automatically know if the game crashed.
4. And select the troubleshoot option, at this point windows will automatically recommend it to run in a compability mode.
5. Windows will give you a message that gives you the option to test the compability mode and you shouldn't have a problem again.
*This should also work with any other old game. I've had this work with Stronghold Crusader as well.

TL;DR version: a cute bite-sized set of JRPG vignettes. While extremely easy and containing a weirdly-written finale in its third vignette, it's worth sitting through in an afternoon.
[Actual Review]
LiEat is a series of three short JRPGs made by Miwashiba on WOLF RPG Editor, originally released in 2004. It follows a dragon by the name of Efina -- who has the ability to eat lies -- and her conman "papa". Each tale brings them to a new location on a different job, usually where supernatural circumstances are at play.
The story of LiEat is very easy to condense down into what happens within these three chapters as well as the loose worldbuilding connective tissue between each one. Playing each episode in close succession allows these threads to all come through, even if some of the characters end up being filler. The main problems I personally had with the stories as a whole included the shoehorned bad/neutral ends. At best, they came out of nowhere (one of them I actually had to look up a guide to get, simply because you have to go out of your way for it). At worst, they contain questionable writing choices (particularly in the third story in the set). The entire third game feels like a series of padding decisions after a little while, and it all feels like it's a rush job to a neat-on-paper character arc resolution. I still like it, but it definitely felt rushed. What I enjoyed about the story the most, however, was the nature of why people lie, and how that is addressed. The reasons people lie, the consequences when found out, and how one lives with themselves when they tell nothing but lies for a living. It's worth looking at even for that alone, along with the different powers that dragons possess in terms of standard fantasy worldbuilding.
Aesthetically, this game has a distinctive style to it that I greatly appreciate. It feels like a NIS game's typical art style combined with GBA Castlevania in a sense, thrown into WOLF and garbled a bit. It feels like I should be playing it in either 240p or on a handheld, which is not a knock against it. There's a lot of imagination to the character designs in general, even when playing with anime archetypes in design. It's a nod to the good bits of subtle worldbuilding in LiEat, not being afriad to differentiate between what is and is not human.  The soundtrack is pretty alright, too, with some standout variations on the battle theme throughtout and some musical progressions that bring to mind European folk villages; there's a lot of good, tense additions to the atmosphere in the score that I really appreciated.
The gameplay is standard turn-based RPG format. You wander around a standard map, interact with things (you don't have to do moving "puzzles" of any sort until LiEat 3), and then get into battles that spawn on the map (no random encounters here). Battles are the typical Attack/Skill/Item/Nothing system, but I appreciated how quickly it flowed. Every episode has strong weapons you can find on the map, and it makes battles a major breeze to get through. Not much strategy, but given how quickly each game unfolds, it's nice. The exploration in LiEat 3, as explained with the general story of that game, feels like padding more often than not, but it still includes a lot of streamlined elements within battle to make that a lot easier.
Overall, LiEat is an easy but interesting experience. The nature of the release is benefitted by how streamlined it all is, and for as cheap as it often is and how quick of a play it is, it's a worthwhile investment if you enjoy JRPGs.

One of the most beautiful games I've ever played. The parallels to Journey are many and obvious, but ABZU stands on its own as a love song to all things aquatic.
The creators' passion for sea life shines through on so many levels. They clearly did their research on the numerous creatures you encounter, including many that don't often get the spotlight in popular media. The swimming mechanics are integral to the experience, not just a more cumbersome form of walking or perfectly weightless flying like in most games with underwater segments. You'll be spending about 99% of your time underwater, so it's vital that the sensation feels as authentic as possible.
The controls take some getting used to, but once you get the hang of them, it feels natural and walking on dry land becomes the alienating experience. Fair warning: it is possible to develop motion sickness after playing for long stretches, but unless you're determined to see and find absolutely everything on your first playthrough, you should be able to finish the game in 1-3 hours. The shortness shouldn't be seen as a negative point: when it comes to game length, the important thing is that the experience feels satisfying and ABZU absolutely does.
If I have one criticism, it is that if you have played Flower and Journey, the narrative beats and game mechanics of ABZU will feel very familiar indeed. Free some cute creatures from underground prisons and pull a few levers to advance to the next area, that's all. If they wanted to avoid the inevitable comparisons to similar games that have come before, they should have focused on making the progression system different. Having some actual puzzles to solve instead of simply pressing buttons could have already made a difference.
On the whole it's the perfect game for when you just want to relax, ride on the backs of sea creatures and marvel at the sights.

The visuals are great for the time, the soundtrack was and still is absolute dynamite, and it is rich full of culture (seriously, go read the actual wikipedia page on 'Sephiroth').
But bottom line, this game has not aged well at all. Majority of enemy encounters can be dispatched by holding down the O button.  You can't strategically use your Limit breaks in combat as you're forced to use them whenever they happen to pop up.  And 90% of the time, characters are all functionally identical besides "melee or ranged".
Materia was criminally undercooked, there's not a lot to it. Something as simple as making Cloud levels materia faster, but will cause it to be weaker in the long run, would have helped.  Or some kind of mechanic where like: Tifa adds extra Agility stats to a materia as it levels up, so that can be swapped onto other characters to help out their stats.  Something to make me think about my party, how it's growing, what lineup I'm running, and how often.
It's not always clear where I'm supposed to go, or what I'm supposed to do.  Seriously, how was I supposed to know I had to be looking for a battery for that lift thing, or that I'm supposed to pick some (seemingly) unrelated text option for that guard to unlock the next zone.  Trial-and-error, or just wondering around talking to everyone hoping they tell you something useful does not make for good game design.  I wont fault the story's execution as it was standard for the time, but the endless text-dumps aren't helping.
I don't hate this game, and I'm not being deliberately provocative.  This game is just not nearly as amazing as people would have you believe, it could have been so much more.  I acknowledge that this game is totally a part of history, and deserves all the recognition for being groundbreaking (it was).  But this is not the greatest game ever made, it's not even the greatest Final Fantasy, not by a longshot.
