First of all,I'd like to say there is no good or bad game really.It all depends on your personal preferences.One may find a certain game fun while the other might not.Anyway,I'm actually a bit half-half on this game when it comes to recommending and I'll tell you why.
-FF7 has a really GREAT storyline to it(that's what I love about Final Fantasy).It's not your typical predictable story.It just pulls you in.PLUS POINTS FOR THAT.
-When it comes to gameplay,it's not your typical hack-n-slash style or fps.It involves characters taking turns to make their moves and you select and action for the character to take for example attack/magic/defend etc etc.(If you don't understand what I'm saying,you can always search for a video on youtube on final fantasy 7 battles).Personally I like this system.It's fun and unique:} In case there are people out there who are worried it may be confusing,don't worry,it's not:)PLUS POINTS!
-Brilliant cutscenes.For a game that has somewhat "oldish" looking graphics (no offence it's a fact),it has some pretty neat looking cutscenes.I was amazed when I saw the first few cutscenes(and the later ones afterwards).I really enjoyed watching every one of it.PLUS POINTS AGAIN!
-As you play the main character,you're not alone.You have friends together on your journey:3 Hurray! So,these other characters that join your main character are interesting,fascinating and unique.Having their own rich personality as well and their own stories.PLUS POINTS.
Now for the negative part..
For some reason,I feel that the amount of damage you can deal is pretty "suckish" even if you level up pretty high.Either that or the enemies are superbly strong.Or it could be both.I say that because from my experience from another Final Fantasy game,FFX to be exact,I levelled up my characters to a pretty decent level(not all the way to 99) and I could still win and complete the game)Some enemies can just easily land you one-hit kills.ONE-HIT and you're dead.This pretty much means that it's kinda tricky to take down enemies.It can be really frustrating sometimes.I remember when I was stuck near the final stages of the game where I had to beat the enemy boss.He was so difficult to take down even after 30 mins.I've seen several people on youtube who posts videos of their ff7 gameplays on beating this boss and they successfully did it but I realised something.I've seen people who levelled up their characters all the way to lvl 99,acquired special items from side quests,special moves etc(basially it's like they've gone through almost everthing in the game) and yet,it still takes some time to beat the boss.So it's still a little bit tricky but it's possible.And to get to lvl 99 and acquire all those special items and moves is a whole different story.You will need A LOT OF PATIENCE AND PERSEVERANCE with this game.That is like the key to this game.If you have that,then this negative part of the review should not be a problem for you~
p.s This review is a personal view and opinion.I understand that not everyone will agree with me as they have their opinions as well.I can respect that.Also,everyone's gonna have their own different and unique experiences from the game.Oh and one more thing I need to admit.Remember I said you need a lot of patience with this game?Yeah...I don't have that.So I'm actually stuck at the final boss.Yup.I do NOT have the time and patience to do all the side missions and battle for hours and hours just to get to lvl 99 all just to beat that one freaking♥♥♥♥♥boss.I find that it's not worth my time.But if you feel otherwise,by all means go ahead~ There's an amazing cutscene after that and well,not forgetting the sense of satisfaction and achievement it bringsTvT
All in all,it's best to have your own experience of the game:)

Final Fantasy VII,  if you haven't heard its name by now, either by someone you know who has played it or from other game sites, you would be well adviced to take a step or two out of that cave of yours and see some sunlight.  It's THE jRPG classic, it pretty much single handedly put PS1 on top of the charts, and changed the jRPG genre for the better.  Now, it is still evolving to this day, but FFVII made the standards, it's what we are looking for in other jRPGs, great writing, character development and entertaining mini games and great cutscenes.
Square did it right with this game, that doesn't mean it comes without flaws.  It wasn't a graphical masterpiece when it came out, and I dare say it hasn't aged well.  That doesn't mean it's not enjoyable, it's just something you either have to ignore, or if you are willing can mod the damn out of it to make it look more appealing.
The game doesn't have any voice acting, though, back in the day that was not exactly the standard anyway, it does have great musical score and it sort of sets the feel for characters and situations which voice acting rarely does in some situation in newer games.
The battle system while there are random battles present, it does feel fast paced and doesn't include long cutscenes ( excluding the summons, but you probably won't be using them a lot anyway ).  It's a simple mechanig if you are used to jrpgs, and it does help to read up about it, it isn't necassary thing to do.
I would suggest this game to any fan of the genre, even newcomers, however be adviced, the game does take time to get you in to the story, which in my opinion is a good thing, for others less patient, give it at least 4 hours or so before deciding to play further or not.

The Witcher 2 is an excellent RPG that manages to be both better and worse than its predecessor. It tells a much tighter, more personal story with much better narrative reactivity (to the point where an entire third of the game will occur in a different location--with different characters, quests and stories--depending on player choices--at the expense of some of the "witching charm" of the first game. One of the best elements of the first Witcher game were all the sidequests, typically involving interesting monsters, interesting dialog, and interesting characters.... those are all gone. In Witcher 2 you spend very little time being a witcher, and most of the quests are simple fetch quests.
But on the other hand, combat is a lot more fun.
The environments are also MUCH smaller in Witcher 2 than Witcher 1, and more linear--you won't be spending much time exploring... anywhere. But the improved action combat, stellar writing and narrative reactivity more than make up for these deficits, and easily propel Witcher 2 to "classic" status. It's no exaggeration to call this one of the very best CRPGs of all time, right up there with Baldur's Gate II, Planescape Torment, Ultima VII, and so on.
Keep in mind, however, that the game is rather poorly optimized, so expect framerate and texture issues on anything less than a top-of-the-line machine.

Crypt of the Necrodancer is an amazing take on the Dungeon Crawler genre while also putting in a spice of rhythm making the game enjoyable and better to listen to. Every rhythm game needs a decent soundtrack to succeed. Not only did Danny B. (Also known for his music in BoI and Super Meat Boy) fill this quota but Rival (known for his Electro Dubstep type music) and FamilyJules (Creator of several Metal Covers on OSTs.) made this game's soundtrack amazing. Not only that, but the characters are rememberable and make you actually feel for them, giving you different gameplay for each character, which is where Crypt of the Necrodancer gets it's replayability. These are the reasons why I still come back every day to this game. The art looks fresh and actually makes you wanna stop and see how your character moves to the beat of the music. This game also supports Steam Workshop, giving you the ability to play as a jiggling piece of bread if you wanted to. All of this for the decent price of $14.99 makes me believe that ANYONE, whether you enjoy Roguelike Dungeon Crawlers or the Music Lover that listens to game soundtracks in their daily lives can enjoy Crypt of the Necrodancer.

Great follow-up to TW1. It's bigger and better in every way. Combat is much more refined and not so much a point-and-click combat system. QTEs are present, but only on the big boss fights spliced in between normal combat and are actually challenging.
I have been on steam for a long time and have a lot of games. The Witcher series is in my top 10 GOAT for all PC games. In terms of RPGs I consider it as high quality as KOTOR1/2, even though the gameplay and style is dramatically different.
Setting is medieval European fantasy (Polish developers and based on novels by a Polish author). There are monsters, spectres, and in general paranormal and fantastical beings in addition to traditional human enemies.
CDProjektRed is an awesome developer. This game is worth full price as it is long and the developers are great. They listen to the community and supported TW1 and 2 well after most AAA devs would have stopped. They released free zero-day DLC for TW2 and released Director's Cut for TW1 and Enhanced Edition for TW2 free of charge to all owners. EE includes the free DLC as well as hundreds of GUI, combat, and story improvements as well as additional voice work. Yes, they actually brought back their voice actors to add additional lines. This is not cheap, and they didn't charge a dime more.
Highly recommended if you enjoy RPGs in general, but especially if you:
-like action RPGs
-love story-heavy games
-don't mind mature themes and even nudity

I think you are better off just buying the soundtrack (which is just absolutely amazing) and leaving this game alone.The whole randomized levels thing isn't very well implemented. You start with the same items on every level you often end up severely lacking in some resource, be it a weapon, healing items, armour, shovel etc. It also leads to a lot of shenanigans such as: Starting off right next to the miniboss (all of which have a near global aggro range btw) and a bunch of tought to kill cronies, teleporting into 5+ mobs most likely leading to death because the monsters stepped onto the floor switch but haven't moved off the destination spot, and the ole classic "Shopkeeper's on fire". The whole beat gameplay thing is fun for a while, and it is, but late game enough you are better off ignoring it since you get plenty of gold without needlessly putting yourself at risk. I think it's kind hilarious that a lot of the monsters will move/attack to the beat as well, sometimes putting you in a bad spot as long as you are playing the game the way it's meant to be played. That makes it seem near discouraged. This may sounds a bit mean, but the cutscenes are quite poorly made, I would even go as far as compare them to Zelda CDI games. Of course they don't stoop to that level but the resemblance is very strong. I don't expect something insane from a 15 dollar indie game, but there are other ways of adding story content without excess animation, take the old school dialogue box scenes they used a lot in RPGs in them good ole days. Voice acting is pretty odd, I'm currently playing as the protagonist (the game does feature a variety of playable characters), female character Cadence and her voice seems to change during battle, certain spells and hits from certain attacks will cause her to sounds like a deep voiced bloke. Peace.

I wasn't too fond of Sword of Asumi even though I liked the premise and Kaori, but I wanted to give Dharker Studio another shot and, well, this was in a bundle once upon a time. It's just that it's somehow worse. To the novel's credit we still get our lovable character - this time in the guise of childhood friend Taka Shinobi so if there is any ending I'm happy to have achieved it's her ending, even if the protagonist really doesn't deserve her.
And that's about it. The premise is blatant wish fulfilment of a typical unlucky in love guy who has two demi-goddesses turn up out of nowhere, declare him an incarnation of a god and literally fight over him to see who gets to marry him. And they're absolutely psycho, to the point that the protag has to actively talk them out of straight up murdering other potential love interests. Then we have a girl who manipulates you into a relationship (to the point that my first ending was with her completely by accident despite actively pursuing someone else) and another girl who decides she wants her two potential suitors to physically fight over her. With the exception of Taka I really don't know how I'm supposed to be interested in any of them and equally perplexed about how a protagonist can go from hopeless in love to having every pursuable girl literally throwing themselves at him, done in a completely serious tone. There's just no attempt to develop the characters beyond what we're immediately presented with.
The choice system is improved from Sword of Asumi's. It's not without its blind faith moments, like the aforementioned girl who you'd only end up on her route by accident, but at least I was able to figure out the right moments to respond to some of the other girls, and some of the bad endings are clearly "too dumb to live" moments you'd have to actively try to get. Multiple save slots help players to work through all the routes to endings as well.
That voice acting though. The good feeling of seeing it fully voiced in English (sans protag) was quickly demolished by actually listening to it. The quality varies greatly, with Taka being the better of the performances, but the ones for Yui and Ryn are terrible. I think Yui's trying to be sultry but it comes off as bore inducing and Ryn sounds like she's just reading from a script with no emotional context. Sadly more performances linger around the terrible end of the scale that I genuinely would have felt the effort would have been better spent with a voiceless script with more depth afforded to each girl.

TL;DR version: a cute bite-sized set of JRPG vignettes. While extremely easy and containing a weirdly-written finale in its third vignette, it's worth sitting through in an afternoon.
[Actual Review]
LiEat is a series of three short JRPGs made by Miwashiba on WOLF RPG Editor, originally released in 2004. It follows a dragon by the name of Efina -- who has the ability to eat lies -- and her conman "papa". Each tale brings them to a new location on a different job, usually where supernatural circumstances are at play.
The story of LiEat is very easy to condense down into what happens within these three chapters as well as the loose worldbuilding connective tissue between each one. Playing each episode in close succession allows these threads to all come through, even if some of the characters end up being filler. The main problems I personally had with the stories as a whole included the shoehorned bad/neutral ends. At best, they came out of nowhere (one of them I actually had to look up a guide to get, simply because you have to go out of your way for it). At worst, they contain questionable writing choices (particularly in the third story in the set). The entire third game feels like a series of padding decisions after a little while, and it all feels like it's a rush job to a neat-on-paper character arc resolution. I still like it, but it definitely felt rushed. What I enjoyed about the story the most, however, was the nature of why people lie, and how that is addressed. The reasons people lie, the consequences when found out, and how one lives with themselves when they tell nothing but lies for a living. It's worth looking at even for that alone, along with the different powers that dragons possess in terms of standard fantasy worldbuilding.
Aesthetically, this game has a distinctive style to it that I greatly appreciate. It feels like a NIS game's typical art style combined with GBA Castlevania in a sense, thrown into WOLF and garbled a bit. It feels like I should be playing it in either 240p or on a handheld, which is not a knock against it. There's a lot of imagination to the character designs in general, even when playing with anime archetypes in design. It's a nod to the good bits of subtle worldbuilding in LiEat, not being afriad to differentiate between what is and is not human.  The soundtrack is pretty alright, too, with some standout variations on the battle theme throughtout and some musical progressions that bring to mind European folk villages; there's a lot of good, tense additions to the atmosphere in the score that I really appreciated.
The gameplay is standard turn-based RPG format. You wander around a standard map, interact with things (you don't have to do moving "puzzles" of any sort until LiEat 3), and then get into battles that spawn on the map (no random encounters here). Battles are the typical Attack/Skill/Item/Nothing system, but I appreciated how quickly it flowed. Every episode has strong weapons you can find on the map, and it makes battles a major breeze to get through. Not much strategy, but given how quickly each game unfolds, it's nice. The exploration in LiEat 3, as explained with the general story of that game, feels like padding more often than not, but it still includes a lot of streamlined elements within battle to make that a lot easier.
Overall, LiEat is an easy but interesting experience. The nature of the release is benefitted by how streamlined it all is, and for as cheap as it often is and how quick of a play it is, it's a worthwhile investment if you enjoy JRPGs.

LiEat is a turn-based indie RPG that follows a cast of characters across three episodes, each with their own self-contained plot. The gameplay is pretty typical for these sorts of RPGs developed with software like RPG Maker with simplistic but quickly paced combat. On top of that, the difficulty is more or less nonexistent — in fact, the only times I got KO'd by any enemy encounters (including bosses) were done willingly in order to get the achievements for getting the bad ends of each episode.
Instead, what makes LiEat stand out amongst the crowd of these sorts of games is just about everything aside from the gameplay: interesting characters, fun and witty dialogue which occassionally tugs at the heartstrings, detailed pixel art with a strong sense of color, and an emphasis on mystery, moral ambiguity, and, to a lesser extent, horror (if only in an atmospheric sense).
Each episode takes about an hour to complete, maybe closer to an hour and a half for the third, but the plots for each are fulfilling in their own right. Each episode presents a new mystery to be solved as well as characters with a variety of ideological beliefs around a common theme of lies and deception whilst further elaborating on the backstories and hidden depths of recurring characters. Every plot-important character gets an impressive amount of depth and development considering the overall brevity of each episode. If nothing else, LiEat managed to completely endear its two main characters to me in just under five hours.
Aside from the simplicity of combat, there's not many other complaints I have about LiEat, and the ones I do have are nitpicky at best. For example, each new episode completely resets the two main characters' levels, stats, and equipment to the starting points. Since the episodes are so short and it's fairly quick to level up and get back to where you ended off in the previous episode, it's not a huge deal, but I would have preferred to have all of my previous stats and skills and instead face against progressively stronger enemies as the game went on.
Overall, it's evident that this game cares more about telling its story than it does about providing anything all that special in terms of gameplay. The point I'm trying to get across is that whether or not you'd enjoy LiEat depends on how much you care about story and characters in video games versus how much gameplay matters to you. For me personally, it varies on the genre; with turn-based RPGs, I tend to expect underwhelming gameplay but a rich and memorable story, and that's exactly what I got from LiEat, so I can't say I'm disappointed.
tl;dr - LiEat is a short but satisfying experience for fans of plot-heavy games that's well worth the low price, especially if you get it on sale, but those who prioritize gameplay over everything should look elsewhere.

A short but sweet "lite" RPG about the power of lies.
The gameplay is simple and the RPG aspects are very forgiving (in fact, to lose key fights and collect bad endings, you might have to unequip your gear!) but the story is the clear focus of this title.  Separated into three acts, the story presents brief snapshots of an endearing relationship across the period of a year.  It's touching, but not tearbait; the developer isn't out to make you cry!  Most impressively, in the short time I played this title, (around four hours total for one hundred percent completion) I came away with a strong sense of who each of the primary actors are and how they relate to a larger narrative that exists only in subtext.  It's rare for "RPG Maker" type small-team projects to develop a world and characters this well, and even rarer for the characters to arrive intact when translated into English.  The icing on the cake is the original spritework and Visual Novel-style animations which add a lot of personality to the simple visual aesthetic.

Final Fantasy VII,  if you haven't heard its name by now, either by someone you know who has played it or from other game sites, you would be well adviced to take a step or two out of that cave of yours and see some sunlight.  It's THE jRPG classic, it pretty much single handedly put PS1 on top of the charts, and changed the jRPG genre for the better.  Now, it is still evolving to this day, but FFVII made the standards, it's what we are looking for in other jRPGs, great writing, character development and entertaining mini games and great cutscenes.
Square did it right with this game, that doesn't mean it comes without flaws.  It wasn't a graphical masterpiece when it came out, and I dare say it hasn't aged well.  That doesn't mean it's not enjoyable, it's just something you either have to ignore, or if you are willing can mod the damn out of it to make it look more appealing.
The game doesn't have any voice acting, though, back in the day that was not exactly the standard anyway, it does have great musical score and it sort of sets the feel for characters and situations which voice acting rarely does in some situation in newer games.
The battle system while there are random battles present, it does feel fast paced and doesn't include long cutscenes ( excluding the summons, but you probably won't be using them a lot anyway ).  It's a simple mechanig if you are used to jrpgs, and it does help to read up about it, it isn't necassary thing to do.
I would suggest this game to any fan of the genre, even newcomers, however be adviced, the game does take time to get you in to the story, which in my opinion is a good thing, for others less patient, give it at least 4 hours or so before deciding to play further or not.

Overall The Binding of Isaac is a must try for all gamers alike, especially if you enjoy a challenge

If you are looking to be immersed in the paper-thin universe that revolves around the edgiest/gaspiest character since Shadow the Hedgehog, then this game is the game for you.
But if you are looking for engaging combat, a deep story, and enjoyable characters paired with decent voice acting, turn around now.
The game is advertized as a 2d hack-n-slash platformer. When I think of hack-n-slash, I would expect a full tree of different combat moves, strategies, and styles. However, 15 minutes into the game, you have the same abilities as you do end-game. The skill roof is high, but unnecessary because the game is a cakewalk, no matter how you cut it. Of course, you could play on the hardest difficulty, if you are looking to be killed in two hits in the tutorial. There is hardly any real platforming, the game is based mainly on its combat, which is odd, seeing as it is as expansive as a popcorn kernal.
You don't have to worry about remembering each character you come across, because each character is about as deep as a bottlecap. But the main characters each have qualities that distinguish them from the other non-essential characters, such as unsaturated color schemes, flamboyant accessories, different method of locomotion, or existing in an entirely different state of being. And there is an unusual trend in that the more a character appears in the story, the more obnoxious the voice acting is. The voices are all overenthusiastic and exaggerated. The main character sounds like he is holding toothpicks between his teeth the entire game, and it gets painful to listen to real quickly. It's almost as if one character was voiced as a blueprint, and all the other voice actors followed blindly.
As for the overall design, that's really up to you. I'm indifferent towards the anthromorphic community, typically, I try not to associate with it. But regardless, I feel that this game could have easily have been created in a different universe, with more human characters, and still have had the same impact it meant to have, or greater. This whole game was the manifestation of one person wanting to show the world how he create a great world with great characters and put that world and those characters together to create a great story. In his head, this was perfect, but a game needs gameplay. The gameplay was created not to accompany the story, but to merely make the story into a game.

I think you are better off just buying the soundtrack (which is just absolutely amazing) and leaving this game alone.The whole randomized levels thing isn't very well implemented. You start with the same items on every level you often end up severely lacking in some resource, be it a weapon, healing items, armour, shovel etc. It also leads to a lot of shenanigans such as: Starting off right next to the miniboss (all of which have a near global aggro range btw) and a bunch of tought to kill cronies, teleporting into 5+ mobs most likely leading to death because the monsters stepped onto the floor switch but haven't moved off the destination spot, and the ole classic "Shopkeeper's on fire". The whole beat gameplay thing is fun for a while, and it is, but late game enough you are better off ignoring it since you get plenty of gold without needlessly putting yourself at risk. I think it's kind hilarious that a lot of the monsters will move/attack to the beat as well, sometimes putting you in a bad spot as long as you are playing the game the way it's meant to be played. That makes it seem near discouraged. This may sounds a bit mean, but the cutscenes are quite poorly made, I would even go as far as compare them to Zelda CDI games. Of course they don't stoop to that level but the resemblance is very strong. I don't expect something insane from a 15 dollar indie game, but there are other ways of adding story content without excess animation, take the old school dialogue box scenes they used a lot in RPGs in them good ole days. Voice acting is pretty odd, I'm currently playing as the protagonist (the game does feature a variety of playable characters), female character Cadence and her voice seems to change during battle, certain spells and hits from certain attacks will cause her to sounds like a deep voiced bloke. KoH is an excellent medieval RTS, very underrated and unknown by many players. It was originally released in Belgium 2004 by Sunflowers and then by Paradox for North America in 2005. Developed by Black Sea Studios, (now Crytek Black Sea) they did a fantastic job on this game. However, there are some things I don't like about it, and it's merely personal preference.
Despite KoH being a great RTS, it does tend to get a little boring and repetitive after awhile. The developers could have done some extra things to spice it up more, such as more historical units, random events like disease, fires, barbarian/mongol invasion, the plague, a royal family tree, etc. I find it a little odd that knights live forever unless killed in battle or by a spy, and your Kings only die of old age or in battle or by a spy. Didn't the developers know people died of disease and other things in those days, just like we do in today's world? I'm not trying to flame, not at all, the game is great, but a little more realism would have made KoH the best RTS ever.
All in all, and despite my personal thoughts, KOH is a great game that everyone should try.

This review is a shortened version of my review published here:
"LiEat" is a series of three short, simplistic story-driven RPGs with a strong focus on the relationships between the characters and the tension between the two races of the world: humans and dragons. At the same time, while this theme overarches across all three games, "LiEat" doesn't let its main story overtake the story of any individual game.
Before I really begin, I want to clarify that this game will not be for everyone. As a writer myself, I found the story to be lacking and, as a gamer, I found the balance of the game to be even worse. That is not to say this is a bad game, because it isn't... but it does mean you will be less likely to enjoy the game if you focus too much on either aspect of the game. Both parts are equally important and should not be ignored. That said, for the purpose of this review, I will be analyzing the aspects separately.
First, let's discuss the music, which was one of my favorite parts of the game. In all three games, you have interesting, well-composed tracks that fit beautifully not just with the game and the scenes they appear in, but, as actual songs, they also fit well with each other conveying a smooth story-progression through their melodies. While there were a couple songs that felt somewhat generic, the game's composer did an (overall) excellent job at matching the moods and tones that needed to be conveyed.
While there are plenty of parts in the graphic design of the game that feel like a generic RPG Maker game, there are just as many unique design choices. While the interfaces may be plain, they are still functional; and, while the overworld feels initially uninspired, it is very clear there was effort put into making the game feel both familiar and new at the same time. While the overworld is far from original, the real prize is found in the cut-scenes. Just as the monotony of the overworld and the repetitive combat (more on that in just a moment) got to be tiresome, the beautifully stylized cutscenes (and even the stylistic still-frames) appeared, and, with them, a breath of renewed enjoyment in the visual experience of the game would arrive. Finally, we have the character sprites. While most of the enemies look like generic black slimes, each of the actual characters was visually beautiful and had their own unique charm.
I feel "LiEat"'s combat deserves its own discussion... for how overwhelmingly bland and generic it is. In "LiEat", you really only have 2 main enemy types: Lies and Bosses. While each Boss looks unique and different, and while there are different appearaces for the Lies, combat in this game is really just "Stab... Stab... Stab..." with no need to act differently. During my first playthrough of "LiEat I", the game accidentally made my party completely incapable of taking ANY damage from the game's BOSS due to its poor balancing of stats, enemies, and EXP gains. The only thing noteworthy about the combat is the artwork of the bosses and the lack of too many combat animations gives the game a sort of neo-classical sort of charm to it as though it is trying to be reminiscent of older games... otherwise, it's a no-thought-involved cookie cutter system that makes you actually have to try in order to die.
Fortunately, in the overall gameplay, you can avoid most of the sLIEmeS if you want, and I encourage it if you want the game to have an ounce of difficulty, but otherwise, gameplay is almost as simple and generic as combat was... But it worked well with the story and actually felt fitting for the overall feel of the game. Most of the puzzles were exceedingly obvious, but never felt like chores to solve because, unlike many games, the puzzles reward you as you do them with interesting dialogue, access to new areas, and overall story-progression in the moment and not just at the end. While combat was underbalanced, general gameplay was quite well-balanced and well-done. The way gameplay integrated the story into each action of the quests... it was a breath of fresh air. During typical quest completions, I usually don't actually have fun, but that was not so for "LiEat". The fact the story is given to you as opposed to needing to be hunted down was another nice touch. While the game does reward you handsomely for investigating and looking for secrets, it also doesn’t make you need to do any needless hunting in order to find where you need to go next; the game maintains a nice, consistent flow that is only added to by searching and not detracted from, which is something most games try and fail to do.
Finally, we have the (spoiler-free) story. The story is essentially a modern take on classic noir fiction. While the setting may not be black and white, many of the other core elements are there. Overall, the story is fairly predictable if you know the standard tropes and patterns associated with classic noir fiction and if you picked up on the foreshadowing used throughout the games from the very first scene. That said, if you're unfamiliar with the genre, this game can serve as an excellent gateway enabling you to see the charms while still being family-friendly. However, the story did have some issues. To begin with, the story felt shallow from its over-devotion to a central story line over three terribly short games. Generally, maintaining a persistent narrative would be a virtue, not a vice, but it actually worked against “LiEat”. While the writer tried to sprinkle foreshadowing into each game to show what was yet to come, there was still little build-up. The writing was amazing for a children’s game or if it had been a longer series, but for general audiences as it is right now, it would fall flat. The other major problem was the lack of dimension to the characters: only the anti-hero and the "bad cop" (of sorts) had more than one dimension to their personalities. Overall, I still liked the story, but it irritated me how quickly the Chekhov’s Guns went off and how the characters needed more than one game to develop even slightly.
Despite how harshly I criticized “LiEat”, I actually enjoyed the series significantly. I didn’t have to go out of my way to find the story. The game still rewarded me for being curious. The music was great and the cut-scenes were eye-grabbingly beautiful. There really isn’t a reason to outright dislike “LiEat” if you look at it as a whole. While combat was rubbish and the writing weak, it was still enjoyable for as brief as it was. Everything contributed to the series equally. Even if the combat was absolute garbage and even if the writing wasn’t where I would have liked it to be, the way the individual parts of “LiEat” interacted with one another created a beautiful tapestry of a series. My only regret is that “LiEat” was as short as it is and lacks any real replay value, as even a self-imposed “hard-mode” does little to increase the difficulty of the games.
"LiEat" is a beautiful series and may have just become one of my favorites. While it seems odd that I can have so many complaints but still love these games (possibly more than I do some of my childhood classics), "LiEat" had an interesting story, despite not being as fleshed out as it should have been. The music and cut-scenes were amazing. The gameplay, bar the combat, blended well with the narrative and pacing. If you think of a game as being about mostly this or mostly that, don’t spend a cent on this game… but if you can accept the bad qualities of a game because those qualities themselves are actually made better by the other qualities of the game, "LiEat" should be in your Library and thrown to the top of your Queue.
~Sora

LiEat is a three-in-one trilogy mystery RPG series about a young dragon girl capable of materializing and eating lies.
Pros:
+3 games in 1, totaling to five hours of playtime
+Each game is varied from one another, identical in gameplay (aside from some parts in the third game) but vastly different in storyline
+Each storyline is surprisingly deep, offering a unique take on the reasons why people lie, and how even lies with good intentions never prove to be worth it in the end
+Charming characters with witty dialogue
+8-bit visuals are detailed enough to not grow stale over time
+A unique art style for the character portraits and CGs
+Mini animated cut scenes scattered throughout
+Plenty of CGs
+Excellent soundtrack
+Able to listen to soundtrack, view CGs, and watch the animated cut scenes at your leisure upon beating each game
+Optional collectibles hidden within many of the game's maps
Cons:
-RPG gameplay is far too easy; one can EXP farm a few random enemies and grow over-leveled in a matter of two minutes, making even the final bosses a breeze
-Lots of backtracking. It doesn't take very long, but the sheer amount of it required across all three games adds up
LiEat is a quirky series with a charming cast and compelling mysteries. It's themes about lies are memorable, and the price during steam winter and summer sale is a steal for how much content you get. Furthermore, you can beat the first game in under two hours, so if you buy it and don't like it, you can always refund. But it's more than worth giving it a try!

2.  The modules system is one of the most unique features about Star Crusade, and is much better than the hero powers of Hearthstone.  They really feel like they're meant to be a part of your strategy, rather than a backup option if you have no cards to play.
3.  Gameplay is quick and streamlined.
4.  Lots of deck variety.  Most of the races have multiple competitive strategies to pursue.
5.  This is big - the devs are very active.  This game gets balance patches and new features constantly, and they are quick to fix problematic cards and modules.
6.  The collection grind isn't nearly as bad as most games.  I dropped $20 (mostly to support the game) and I have PLENTY of deckbuilding options.  I've opened probably a dozen paragons and crafted a few more.  And I was doing fine even when I was Free to Play.
Cons:
1.  The modules system is a double edged sword.  It often feels like your module choices are more important than your card choices.  It does give you a nice guideline for deckbuilding, but not all modules are created equal.  Some are much more powerful than others.  And because you start every game with them, any imbalance is that much more obvious.
2.  The single play campaign could use a little work.  Some levels are brutally unforgiving, and only two races are playable so far in the campaign.

Hey all,
I recently tried to play FATE after upgrading to Windows 10, but was experiencing the "Application error" issue. The solution that worked for me was to start the game in window-mode and make sure that the window-width and -height (including the border) were small enough to fit inside the screen’s set resolution.
To start the game in window-mode go to "C:\ProgramData\WildTangent\FateSteam\Persistent" on your computer, open the "config.dat" file with Notepad, and change “FULLSCREEN:1” to:
FULLSCREEN:0
Also, ensure that “WINDOWWIDTH” and “WINDOWHEIGHT” in the config file are set to something that will allow the application window, including the border, to fit within your screen resolution. For example my brother’s screen resolution is 1366x768, so we put our values at:
WINDOWWIDTH:1366
WINDOWHEIGHT:725
For some reason, if the window is set to a size where even the border is to the outside of the screen, it creates a graphical issue where the gameplay is located in a small box to the left corner within the application window.
I hope this helps someone else. Cheers!

I honestly don't care if this is an 'Overwatch Clone' or if Overwatch is the opposite. This game is FUN. Period.
....Still here? Alright, alright. More details comin' up.
So it's a Hero-based PvP shooter. So what? TF2's a class-based PvP shooter, and the same argument happened there. Yet TF2 and Overwatch are NOT the exact same.
Yet this game is...almost the exact same. What's different?
Well, for starters, there's upgrades that you can purchase at the beginning of each match. They retain with you for the entire round/match. I say that because it varies on which gamemode.
The heroes, even though they look a little too much like their Blizzard counterparts, aren't completely copied. In fact, they have their own feels to it, and they play a lot more differently.
For instance, let's talk about Torbjorn and Barik. Both build sentries. Torb's sentry can withstand a lot of bullets, and he has to hit it with a hammer to heal and upgrade it. Barik creates mini-sentries that repair themselves whenever he's close enough, and they don't upgrade (yet they are fragile AF, and two fully charged sniper shots could destroy 'em). Torb throws armor. Barik places a bulet-sponging shield. Etc, etc., I can do this for hours.
Oh, and how's this for 'originality' (I say it like this because I honestly have NO idea if any other game use it. You know what to do if this sounds familiar). There's cards that buff your abilities, and you can make loadouts with 'em. And then there are the Legendary cards that extremely buff one of your 4 stand-points (weapons and armor, and your 3 abilities).
Plus, you can ride on a horse...only when you respawn, though.
Lastly, you don't have all the heroes. BUT you can unlock 'em in two ways (one way might be gone as soon as the game's out of beta, though). One way is to grind a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton and get a lot of gold (Oh, yeah, currencies. Crystals and Gold are used to unlock Heroes and cosmeticals. Crystals cost RL-moneys, while gold is obtained by playing in matches). The other si that you purchase the Founder's pack: all heroes, a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of Esssence (Whoops. Essence is used to craft cards.) and some beta-exclusive items.
...I'm not going to do a TL;DR this time. Mainly because I want you to read the whole thing.
Lastly, be glad this isn't something like the pretty obvious Overwatch rip-off Force Gaming looked at.
I'm not giving a number this time, it's just fun. OK? Go get it if yer broke, or you're interesting.

If my score and stance on not recommending this sound harsh, that is likely because I had hopes for this title and it simply didn't meet them. The art turned out to be the only enjoyable thing about this visual novel, which is why I even bothered to get all the endings.
+ Pretty art and character designs
+ Developer provides restoration patch
+ Skip button works perfectly so replay is easy
+ Going back on text is easy in case you missed something
- Faceless protagonist
- Horrible choice system
- Very short and shallow story
- Animation effects are not used to their full effect
☆☆☆☆☆☆☆☆★★
2/10 - Awful
I chose not to recommend this game for three main reasons that I will discuss in detail below, but here they are completely spoiler free: story, characters, and decision mechanic. These are the core of any visual novel and none of them hit the mark on this one. Before going over those, there are couple more things to mention about Divine Slice of Life.
The game has a restoration patch that will include nudity in your game. I'd personally argue that they aren't really needed as the H-scenes are definitely lacking, and out of the five girls your protagonist will only be shown having sex with two (third one is simply described but not shown). If you are one who needs very good H-scenes then you might be disappointed by this title as those scenes are definitely unsatisfactory.
This visual novel is partially animated, but only when it comes to mouth movement when the characters talk. Adding this is definitely peculiar since the animation doesn't  match what the characters are saying, and the effect is never used anywhere else in the game (to emphasize movement, for example). Divine Slice of Life also comes with complete voice acting for everyone except the protagonist, but I will refrain from saying anything about its quality as it's in English and I simply ended up muting it.
The story is a mix of slice of life and supernatural, following the faceless protagonist Aaki as he laments his inability to make a move on the girl he is interested in when suddenly he encounters two girls fighting in the park and his life takes a sudden turn. The girls turn out to be descendants of Aphrodite and Athena, respectively, and they've come to make Aaki choose one of them as his wife, because he is a reincarnation of Zeus that via marrying one of them he would be able to enter Pantheon. The catch is that if Aaki falls for a mortal girl instead, he'll lose his godly heritage and neither goddess wished this to happen. Pretty basic idea, but definitely not well executed and it becomes clear that the creative team did not put research into the mythology they wanted to incorporate.
In total there are seven characters in this visual novel, five girls and two guys. The other guy, Ronan, only exist to offer weird competition for Aaki in the form of “you fight this guy or lose the girl” and that's it. It basically only serves to make you realize the girl you are going for isn't really all that great, and even getting her good ending isn't sweet after you remember what she's like. The biggest problem with the girls is that Aaki doesn't connect with them and all the romances feel completely unnatural.
– the two goddesses, I decided to lump them together because they start from the same line with their relationship to Aaki and have the same motivation for going after him. The problem is that their personalities are almost exactly the same to a point where you only want to choose one of them based on their looks and nothing else. Even when you can choose one of them their reactions are identical, there is literally no variation in their dialogue.
– Aaki's crush from the start, it's made clear he is interested in both her looks and wits. There was potential for a nice love story there, but unfortunately she herself turns out to be not-so-great person. The good thing is that depending on your choices, Aaki can also realize this way before she tries to do anything about it.
– The childhood friend, so there is obviously an established connection with her and Aaki. She is quirky and maybe even stalker-ish depending on how strongly you view her actions. But Aaki's feelings about her are only revealed to the player after you've already made your choice regarding her, which is a terribly writing choice as it isn't even meant to be Aaki realizing what he has passed up on.
– Classmate and the girl Aaki has least interactions with. He explicitly stated not having even thought about her before actually ending up with her, and there is no connection between them. The story tries to patch that up but it comes off as very weak.
This brings me to what might be my biggest gripe: the choice system. Out of those five, three girls are ones that you will only get to be with based on a single decision. That would not be bad if the choice was what you think it is, but these choices have nothing to indicate to you that you are actually choosing a girl by doing that. I'm trying not to spoil the choices themselves, but there's a point in the game where you make a choice that will automatically determine if you will end up with Ryn or Yui, provided you don't try to go for the other three girls after that or get yourself into a Not-so-good ending instead. When it comes to Akame, the choice has nothing that would lead you into thinking that you are choosing a different romance path but once you've taken that turn, you will have no other outcome left for you.

Divine Slice Of Life is a visual novel developed by AJTGames and published by Dharker Studio. Take on the role of Aaki, a seemingly normal if somewhat self conscious young man, whose life is suddenly turned upside down after a casual stroll through the local park late one night. After disrupting a battle between two mysterious demi-goddesses, Aaki learns that he is the reincarnation of the god Zeus and they insist that he must marry one of them and take his rightful place in the Pantheon as ruler of the heavens. If that wasn't enough it seems that several women he knows have also decided he must go out with them and all the while he has his college exams to deal with too. It's a tough time for Aaki in this little Divine Slice Of Life.
This is a fun and light-hearted visual novel with an interesting story based on Greek mythology which is a topic that I love. The story has some talented voice acting with lots of tongue in cheek humor as well as an adbundance of choices to make as the storyline branches. There's also a number of romance options available to Aaki as he attempts to choose his future wife be they goddess or mortal.
Graphically this novel looks really great. The artwork is spectacular and vivid. One favorite thing to note is that in many of the scenes the characters are somewhat animated in that they have various facial expressions when speaking, they blush or frown and their eyes blink as they stand silently listening to others during conversation. This is a very refreshing take on the typical static nature of the characters in many visual novels that I've previously read and it's a quality of presentation that I could easily get used to seeing more of. This title also has many other features such as multiple alternate endings, a original soundtrack, an unlockable in-game gallery and Steam trading cards but sadly only one Steam achievement to earn.
Divine Slice Of Life was a fair read but definitely not one of Dharker Studios better visual novels in my opinion. To me there was alot more emphasis on dating than on the story which is what I would have preferred more of. I would merely recommend trying Divine Slice Of Life to fans of the visual novel genre and more so to dating sim players but a pass to casual gamers.

Little Inferno looks like a simple, casual game, but it's actually a little deeper than that. Yes, you get to throw stuff into a fireplace. A lot of things, in fact. But way, way into the center of it all there's also a storyline to be found. I won't spoil it so I'll just talk about the gameplay a little bit more. While burning things you'll earn coins and stamps. You see, all items have to be ordered and the stamps will give you the ability to instantly deliver an item to your doorstep. Coins can, of course, be used to buy items or increase the number of objects you can stock.
A few hours into the game these items will dramatically increase in price.
Now, the real goal is to find and create combos. Combining certain items will unlock an achievement and earn you lots of money. And what for ? To buy new items, you got it ! These combos are a must if you want to complete the game, by the way.
Most gamers should be able to finish it in 3,5 hours or so. So it's not all that long, and the time limit for deliveries artificially lengthens the game as well, which is a real shame.
The graphics and animations are cute and beautiful. And the fire looks quite amazing, with all the ashes and whatnot. Impressive stuff if you ask me.
The music is minimal, but memorable. Especially the Weather Balloon song got my attention.
All in all it's a fun game but I wish it was even deeper than this. It's still a bit too shallow for my taste.

If this weren't Stardock, I might give a thumbs down. I've run into a few game-stopping crashes, but the devs are reliable when it comes to customer support, so I'm not too worried about that.
Now this game isn't Space Empires IV in terms of complexity, but it's not GalCiv1 either. It strikes a good balance between attention to detail and simplicity. It's got a nifty ship designer that lets you spend hours customizing the entire look of your fleet, but that's completely optional; you can just use the stock designs (of which there are plenty), or tweak the components on them without actually customizing them cosmetically, if you so desire.
One thing I like that's unique to GalCiv is the starbases, which give a variety of bonuses to ships and/or colonies in their area of effect. The effects are pretty small, though, so I'm not sure how worthwhile they are to build compared to the cost of defending them. I also like the MOO2-esque "specialization" techs added in this iteration - do you want to unlock cheaper armor, lighter armor, or tougher armor? You can only have one, unless you trade with other empires! (Can you steal techs from other empires? If not, that totally needs to go into an expansion.)
Overall, GalCiv3 is a fun 4X game that needs a bit of work, but given Stardock's record, I'm sure that work will get done!

I knew I was going to love this game right out the gate. Made by the same company that made World of Good, The Tomorrow Corporation, I knew I could expect a few things from this game:
-An eerie but endearing artstyle.
-A more than mildly distressing distressing story.
And of course, absolute insanity.
I can safely say that it disappointed in none of these respects. In this game, the main character is a child, burning toys and other objects in a fireplace to stay warm through a mysterious and never-ending winter. Burning items gives you currency and unlocks more things to burn, allowing you to gradually unlock more things to play with as well as more of the story.
Items burn in unique and often realistic ways, and the game give the player enough item variety and space to work with to keep this fresh for several hours, just long enough to see the story through to it's conclusion.
My only gripe with the game lies in the item cooldowns and delivery times, which seem to be nothing more than a tool to extend the gametime due to an overall lack of content. There is a system in place to combat this, in the form of stamps awarded for solving rather simple puzzles involving burning specific combinations of items, but I didn't really feel that it added much to the game.
The character dialogue and the design of the multitude of burnable items in the game are absolutely charming all the way through. I certainly enjoyed Little Inferno while it lasted, but it's hard to say whether or not it was quite worth the $15 pricetag.
I'll just say that if a game where you haphazardly order items out of a catalogue only to shovel them into a firepit and see how well they immolate together sound like fun, you may want to give Little Inferno a look. (Though you may want to wait for it to go on sale.)

Well, how do we start this? It’s pretty much a compilation pack of three short, story-driven RPGs, telling the story of a conman traveling with his trusty loli dragon that eats lies, Efina.
I won’t say that this game is really good, but it certainly wasn’t even close to mediocre as well.
There... isn’t really much to write about regarding gameplay. Combat’s there, but it’s pretty basic—attack option, skills (which most of the time is just multi-hitting attacks, but there’s also HP-to-MP conversion, so I’ll give you that), items, and flee; things you’d expect from these kinds of games.
There are also, in fact, things you can find and equipments scattered throughout the game(s) in a non-linear fashion, so you can, for example, cheese your way through fights with that “endgame” weapon you (somehow) found in the first game
There’s also emphasis on puzzles in the third game, but it’s not really that difficult either.
Which brings us to our next topic...
What LiEat lacks in gameplay, it makes up in the narratives, and it does them well—really well.
Every character (well, at least those who have portraits) are well-rounded and really memorable (arguably even the four maids in the third game, who just serves as a puzzle setpiece!). vgperson are partially to blame for this.
World-building is also there, solid enough for you to understand what’s going on, but also loose enough at some parts to be open to interpretations.
The last but not least...
The artwork is somewhat of a middle ground here. It isn’t
distinctive, impressive or anything like that, but there’s a certain charm to it that makes them really interesting.
The same also applies to the music. It’s not good, it’s not bad, but it definitely served its purpose well.
Also, there's animated scenes/CGs! Granted, the animation's just the "one person goes pose one to pose two, end" kind, but still.
I’d like to re-emphasize that, again, LiEat as a whole is a story-driven RPG, albeit a short one. If you want a strategy-heavy RPG, this isn’t the one for you; but if an interesting setting, characters, etc. is what you’re looking for, this is one of the better choices.

Alright, im gonna keep this as short and as informational as possible with not much experience with the game, so bear with me.
First of all, what the hell is this game about?
Well, basically, it's about this developer that needs to upload a game before his publishing licesce expires. However, as luck  would have it, it fails epically. And his licesce expires tomorrow. But, lucky for him, there are five other developers in his apartment building, and they all have developed one game. His mission now is to source hack all of thier games and put something on the app store.
Alright, so what's the gameplay like?
Well, the camera follows your character as if its on a wall. Its sorta hard to describe, but you'll know what i mean if you download it. Your character (his name is warren, so we'll use that from now on) travels on this grid, sorta like an old Pokemon game. You use either WASD or the arrow keys to control Warren, E to inspect, and R to interact.
Now for the main part of the game: the minigames.
When Warren hacks a game, all you have to do is play a short minigame. I'm not gonna spoil anything, but the minigames are actually very short. The longest minigame is about 15-20 minutes, assuming it's your first time. That's really it. It is a very simplistic game; some would even call it humble.
This leads me to the next category: Graphics, Sound, Interface, and Stability (GSI&S)
The graphics are , as i said before, simplistic. not much else to say. The sound also is simplistic, but it has a cartoonish sort of ring to it. The interface is... AGAIN, simplistic. It's simply drawn out, and the hud only appears  when you can interact with an item (e.g, hacking a game, etc.). The game is extremely stable; i havent run into any problems yet, not even lag. Overall, it has a very simple feel to it. Games today (Especially freemium clash of clans ripoffs) try to overexaggerate, both in ads and in the game. I mean, seriously, when some chick with triple G's in metal lengere (nailed that spelling) pops on your screen and starts yakking about how you must RISE TO POWAR AND CONCAR YAR FOES FOR THA GLARY OF YAR KINDAM and all that shtuff, its... overwhelming. This game, however, dosen't shove triple G's in your face (execpt for one part but thats not the point). It offers what it has, nothing more and nothing less. But, im ranting too much. Lemme talk about the cons.
What are the cons?
Well, there arent many cons i can think of that shtick out. I mean, some of the dialouge needs some proofreading, but, aside from that and a couple other things, it dosent really have any cons. A simple game dosent have room for cons. Big ones, that is.
So, ive listened to you up to here. What do you think?
Well, if you have 35 minutes to spare, get it. It's a neat little game that has some humor sprinkled in there with simplicity for all. So, I say get it.
Before you leave, i just wanna thank you for putting up with my B.S. for however many lines this is. I really hope this review helped you choose to download this game. Now, i hate begging like a betch, buut imma beg like a betch. If you though this was funny and/or helpful, please gimme a thumbs up and/or a smiley face. Thank you, and stay away from chicks with triple G's with metal lengere.

This is the story of
, a person with extraordinary capabilities. When I first met Dust, I did not think much of him.
He felt generic, not showing his face, having amnesia and struggling to find out where he came from. I did not connect much with the furry man, as such a story is hardly original.
Fortunately, his gameplay did connect with me from the start. He hacked and slashed like a true soldier, finding keys, treasures, abilities, upgrades and many more fine, fun things in true MetroidVania fashion. One could even find a small funny easter egg related to the horrible CastleVania II when you look hard enough(You'll chuckle when you find it). With such gameplay and 2D graphics, one might ask if such a game has still the right to exist amongst contemporary gamers. The answer is a loud and clear YES.
As I travelled through the world of Falana, I was amazed how much I did start to connect with Dust now. The man was truly regretful of his past and sought to redeem himself through every possible noble deed he could manage. My little companion Fidget started to grow on me too. Being a flying whatever-the-♥♥♥♥-its-name-is with a high-pitched voice and a knack for being scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and knowing everything better, the little critter soon turned into a lifelong friend of mine.
And of course there was Ahra, the mystical and mysterious (Wow, never thought to use 2 words in the same sentence starting with 'my') sword. What was his purpose? What was our purpose with him? What did he know about us and what did he keep silent from us? The plot started to deepen, becoming ever more emotional from chapter to chapter.
The journey felt like a personal growth, a new sense of understanding the world.
Hacking and slashing through hordes of enemies is fun, but not necessarily very hard. Granted, I finished the game on normal, but even on normal I did not die many times. Fortunately, there are two extra difficulty levels (tough + hardcore), which can be set from the very first playthrough.
As mentioned, Dust can be upgraded and level up, giving you the option to invest more in Dust's defense, attack or Fidget (the flying critter has interesting powers). Items can be crafted from materials that you gather from fallen enemies, such as pendants, rings, armor and augments. The only downside to the crafting is that you do not actually see Dust wearing the item. Also old school I guess.
If grinding to get all the materials you need isn't your thing, there is a nice mechanic with a travelling salesman that follows you throughout your travels. Sell him one piece of a particular material he doesn't have and he'll "catalogue" it. After that, he will update his stock over time and provide you with the materials you once sold him.
After clearing the final area and defeating the final boss, I realized something. I actually cried at the ending of this visually stunning video game. Being created by just a SINGLE person (aside from the story and music), this game is something very, very special. For little money you get at least 10 hours of gameplay, make that 20 hours if you're a completionist like me.

Final Fantasy VII is one of my favorite games of all time.  I had the original PC version back in the day and it ran flawlessly if I remember correctly.  I played it with my Gravis gamepad.  Again, with no problems.  This version is a disappointment all around.  The first thing you will be required to do is to create an account with Sqaure.  Makes no sense at all, but hey.  Still, it is an annoyance.  Once I finally got the game fired up, I immediately started having problems with my gamepad.  The cursor was flying all over the place.  I had to download a profile for Pinnacle to fix that and the fact that a few of the buttons would not respond at all.  Again, an annoyance.  Despite this effort my character still wants to walk to the left much of the time.  This I cannot seem to fix.  Sure, I can just plow forward and try to ignore it, but it still detracts from the game.  Lots of people have complained about the music or the fact that the graphics look terrible on current HD monitors.  That really does not bother me at all.  The same great gameplay is there if you can get to it.  The horrible controls completely wreck it.
A person much wiser than me, who also owns this "updated" version, told me that it was a better idea to just use a psx emulator to run this game if you really want to enjoy it again.  He was right.  Square totally dropped the ball on this one.  They have pretty much dumped all over the game that literally put them on the map.  I am definitely NOT saying that Final Fantasy VII is not a great game.  It is.  This is just not the version you want to play if you want to enjoy it.

Some games require a long anecdote to explain exactly how good they are. I played this a long time ago on the playstation. I had a friend who used to be an all-state running back, played college ball and flunked out because he wasn't exactly committed to academics. He and I used to hang out, smoke a certain substance and play games. He was mostly into shooters, John Madden and racing games.
One day we bought a racing game that came out on playstation, played it and beat the whole game in a day. We took the game back to the store, which had a policy allowing you to return a game if you "didn't like it" within a week of purchase. Naturally we became very harsh game critics who thought every game sucked.
Anyways, getting to the point, we took the crappy racing game back and my friend (who had bought it) asked me what I thought he should get. I, having never played an ff game, had read a review of Final Fantasy VII and thought it sounded interesting.  I suggested the game to my friend. He bought it and we both became completely hooked on the game, playing the game stoned frequently until 4 am. My point is that the game is so excellent that it made an rpg fan out of my friend, an fps and John Madden lover, and me, a guy who didn't pay much attention to gaming as I generally preferred playing basketball, reading books and going out to concerts. This game (and diablo and warcraft I & II) turned me into the hardcore gamer I am now simply by being a fascinating experience.

If you don't know FF7, you're weird. I'm not going to comment much on the actual game itself, because there is no point. It has been beaten into the ground for years - this is one of the best JRPGs ever, and it has aged incredibly well. There is still a ton of fun to be extracted from this. It might be a bit tough for a new person who has been raised on the 360/PS3 generation to get in to this, but I guarantee that if you can look past the goofy models and surreal translation, you'll find an excellent game. The game is long, the gameplay is great, the story is pretty cool, the music is top notch, etc, etc. It's worth it, trust me.
The port itself is my focus here: It's not so bad, but it's not what it should be.
To start, you're going to have to sign up for Squaresoft's useless service. It really isn't much trouble, but adding on a useless layer of DRM doesn't really benefit anyone. After getting past that, every time you turn the game on you'll be greeted with a useless launcher. You can change a few options, including using some ridiculous cheat that maxes your characters out, but that's about it.
Secondly, they didn't map this game to the controller very well, despite the fact that it was made for a controller, and you're stuck with using the analogue stick, even though it is designed for the D-pad, and there is no way to change this. You cannot run from battles with the controller, and instead you have to use Page Down/Page Up to do it. I'll be referring to the PS1 controller for reference on the next bit - Triangle is switched to Square, Circle is switched with X, Select is moved to... Pushing the analogue stick down... it doesn't make sense. Having to use A trigger button during some minigames is kind of annoying, but it's not too bad.
Third, the graphics are slightly improved, and things are smoothed out, but the character models have not aged at all. Battles look nicer now.
I think the definitive version of FF7 is the original PSX release, but, this works just as well for playing the game. Beyond some minigames being mapped terribly and being forced to use the keyboard to run from battles, this is a pretty good port.

A classic brought to you through Steam, experience the all-time popular hit Final Fantasy 7.. The Shinra Corporation is sapping precious life from the planet to fuel it's machinations, and it's up to Cloud and his friends to put an end to it before the world is beyond saving. But a larger threat looms over the planet still...
If you have played the original on the Playstation, you'll find not much has changed, and that's definitely a plus. Originally, the soundtrack had been muddled, and given a substitute in the form of sub-par midis, but that's been long resolved, leaving us with a exact replica of the original experience.
The story is original and engrossing, and while at times, the dialogue can be a bit unintentionally humorous, it only adds to it's charm. There is now an option to play with the graphics looking slightly more crisp than the original PS game, which may or may not be something you look forward to. In any case, if you are looking for a classic JRPG experience, and to witness one of the most influential and well-known entry of the 90s and series, do yourself a favor: get your hands on this.

I used a PS4 controller, and there was built in support for it, even though the on screen graphics show a Xbox One controller.
Trying to avoid spoiling the story, it does have enemies and friends. Plus a narrative that speaks in the same emotional tone as Journey. The soundtrack responds to what emotions are supposed to be conveyed and I really enjoyed the refinement that has happened between the release of Journey and this game. It really feels worry free and complete, worthy of a high price tag. My first play though was 118 minutes, but I would suggest taking your time in each area to look around and enjoy the completeness of the world and the continuation of the art style consistently.
TLDR: Really pretty. Runs great. PS4/XBO controller support. Wear headphones.

Character creator is a good addition to SGB. Definitely worth having, although one of the cheapest DLCs for SGB it is a DLC you can use on any project. Free DLC  if  you owned SGB before 2017 steam summer sale.
Edit characters while you are in the game editor. Neat.
You can customise characters easily and very quickly indeed, or use the random button for instant new characters. Note that so far all the characters use one mesh for the head, but more advanced users than I already import character meshes (and 3D models) made with software like Blender.
Use this on the normal SGB character meshes and right away they will be a bit less "stock asset" looking, another important little step in stamping your games identity as a bit apart from the one the other guy is making with out of the box characters simply by swapping faces, body, legs, hair, clothes and colours.
If you want to go a small step further there is a built-in editor with which you can "paint" onto your characters.They reckon there are over 3,500,000 combinations using the slot-together character parts, and that's before you start changing colours or painting your own.
Dead easy to use, bug free, built into the game editor and it works well.

As someone who loved World of Goo about as much as someone can possibly love a game, buying this was a no-brainer. But should you do the same? I'm not sure.
This is definitely one of those "love it or hate it" games (if it can even be called a game). I personally loved it, but I wonder how many others will. On one hand, the gameplay consists of burning things... lots and lots of things. This is an act of primal enjoyment for most human beings. But on the other hand, that's really all there is to it (for the most part). I mean that literally - the entire 4+ hour game consists of burning things in a fireplace. I know that sounds boring, but it's actually kind of not. It's fun to throw different items in to see what they do, and finding combinations of items that, when burned together, reward you with tons of cash and more items. How much mileage others will get out of that experience I can't even being to predict.
Aside from burning things, the only other notable aspect of the game is its story (which for 90% of the time takes place more in the background). The end of the game changes this significantly, but I shan't say more about that ;). The story is a sort of societal commentary built of mounds of metaphors (some subtle, some not so much), with a major revelation at the end... basically, it's the kind of thing that goes over well with the "artsy" crowd. I dug it, but again, I'm just not sure how that translates to a mainstream audience. It does, however, lend itself perfectly to the overall atmosphere of the experience (along with the unique art style and music).
If you're open to unique indie experiences and don't mind the $15 price tag, go for it. Just be warned that there's not all that much to it. World of Goo, this most definitely is not - but it's definitely something very unique (in its own very, very weird and addicting way), and all-in-all, a worthy successor.

Pretty sure the jeep doesn't have the heft to anchor a winch for this (haul a B-130 out of the drink? yes. This? ... oh boy.).

This game stood out on the market place because of its Age of Empires II graphics coupled with a seemingly total war "esk" strategy dynamic. Upon reading reviews it had a zealous fanbase. (always a good sign) When this game booted up I was suprised to see that this was published by Paradox Games. That was when I knew, that I would be in for a treat.
This game's most valuable asset is the real time mechanic. Most often I avoid real time stategy like the plague because I like to take my time playing turn based stategy games. However, Knights of Honor has a real balanced approach to real time and made a real fresh experience in my primarily turn based game library. With a trade system like Settlers of Catan KoH frees you to focus on the land grab and military aspects of the game. In addition, this game is not so much do or die. Most games I play: Crusader Kings II, Dark Souls II, LoL, require a well planned and finesed approach to everything you do. They will stress you out after a while. The game handles a lot like Sid Meiers Civiliation, its got a relaxed approach that gets only as serious as you want it to be.
The last gem within this game is the randomization of the map resources. I cannot tell you how many games are limited by a single game breaking exploit based on an area, character, or strategy. The randomization frees you from the burden of starter placement. It gives you a reason to expand, instead of being passive. It gives the game all the replay value and ultimately drives the game.
I would describe this game as Sega's Total War + Settlers of Catan dressed up as Age of Empires II masquerading as Crusader Kings. Very unique.
If this game had only received a better name and more marketing it would have been a gaming Giant.

TL;DR Verdict: A solid recommendation! Pick it up!
While about a 10-20 hour game (Main vs Completionist), Dust offers plenty to do for the duration and offers a fun and acrobatic combat system in a visually impressive Metroid-vania esque frame. It's short in that good way where it doesn't overstay it's welcome, and the journey itself is a great one with a high amount of polish not seen by many indie developers. An Elysian Tail also exceeds at offering just enough for both sides of the coin to make it a solid recommendation for most any action/adventure (with light-rpg element) players.
Price: $15 is a completely fair for this game given the amount of content and how well polished it is. On a sale it's a steal.
Pros:
The biggest strengths of this game are it's very fluid animation and bright visuals (especially so given the modern brown and grey tones most games are plagued with) and a combat system that is easy to get a grip on.
It rewards those who backtrack to find older inaccessible areas with gradual upgrades to make fighting the hordes of enemies significantly easier, but doesn't require it. This gives completionists something to do, while people who prefer to charge ahead to the end can do so without too much punishment.
The upgrade/crafting system is also very rewarding, and helps to give meaning to running back through areas hunting for components. Those that hate "farming" can utilize the merchant to give you the components you need over time.
Multiple difficulties are available, so if you find the game is not challenging you enough, you can always switch over to a different difficulty. (Note this is not a menu option, it seems to require starting over.)
Cons:
If you are expecting a grand and epic tale like you've never heard before, you may want to look elsewhere. While the story is far from awful, it is rather by-the-numbers and few will be surprised by it's twists. Think of it as a solid summer animated film in terms of story quality.
Your mileage may vary on some of the main characters. I will say that from a story and flow persepctive, each character fits in nicely and none of them ever seem redundant, however if you do not particularly care for one of them, the number of voiced cutscenes may be irksome.
