I enjoyed my playthrough of Abzu though it didn't reach the emotional heights of its predecessor Journey. Many of the moments didn't feel earned. In journey, you understand your objective from the outset - GET TO THE TOP OF THE MOUNTAIN. Your start in a desolate environment and as you progress through the story you can see the fruits of your efforts visually through ever changing and ever more beautiful scenery, The feeling of kinship that develops with a stranger/s over the course of the game, whom you feel very attached to by the end and finally the lengthening and shrinking of the scarf.
Abzu instead starts you in an environment which is much the same through the course of the game. Its objective isn't immeadiately clear. In fact by the end of the game, I wasn't really sure what I had accomplished. Having played journey I am able to assemble together some story, but for those who haven't played journey, I wonder if they would be able to piece together much of it.  It is obvious that the story, is not the primary focus of the game and that it is intended to be a much more meditative experience than journey. Oddly I found jorney to achieve this affect much more for me. Abzu almost feels like its trying too hard to be profound.
Abzu does not utilise multiplayer, and has replaced the other player with little robots that you can find along your path. I'm not sure if players are supposed to develop a bond with these, but I did not. They are easily lost and replaceable and merely serve to open a few doors.
Technically this game is amazing! The schools of fish are drop dead gorgeous and you can easily get lost following all the various fish around.  I can see why the developers added a mediation mode the main menu.... aka. Fish tank mode.
I am tempted to record a few hours of this and have it running on my second screen while I work.
Overall this game is a nice experience, and some of the visuals are absolutely stunning. Pick this up if you are looking for a game to escape the stress or real life or if you want to show your friends the best PC fish tank simualtor available.

There are bugs, the optimization isn't perfect. The gameplay gets repetitive soon. Still I'm recommending this game for anybody who enjoys a good story. I haven't finished the game yet, but it already got me hooked. It's something different from GTA for sure, and frankly speaking, as somebody who loves GTA 5 and 4, i would NEVER compare Mafia and GTA. They are just two too different series that put emphasis on different things. In GTA the fun factor is alway pumped up. Mafia relies on gripping stories and interesting interactions between player character and others. Even Mafia 3 has that, though some people accuse it of having very bad story. It's not bad, it's just different from the Italian Mafia stories from both previous games. It's so different people don't like it. I get it. Not everybody likes GTA 4 either, it's too dark and grim compared to other GTA titles.
The gameplay is also different from GTA. There you have 20 guns under your belt, with thousands of ammo for each. Go and kill! Wreak havoc. In Mafia you can carry only two guns, and the ammo is limited to 2-4 extra clips. That, plus the fact that you will die after two shotgun blasts or a good burst from a machinegun means you have to rely on stealth, takedowns, the silent approach. The FATE series is definitely starting to show its age now.  But if you’re a fan of classic dungeon crawlers or are interested in exploring the history of Diablo-clones, it’s well-worth checking out.
Among other things, it used to be a popular Diablo-clone in its day, attracted a dedicated modding community around it for a number of years.  Plus it might especially interest fans of the Torchlight series, because the different developers behind Diablo II and FATE are also the same people who eventually got together to co-found Runic Games and made Torchlight.
Not only was Torchlight directly influenced by Diablo II in that sense.  But it likewise inherited a lot of features from FATE.  Sure, you could point out that even long before FATE and Torchlight, dungeon crawlers such as Nethack had pets, too.  But FATE was really the first one to introduce pets into the gameplay in a Diablo-type game, and to give them features such as their own inventory interface, so they could carry some of your loot, and at the click of a button be sent to town to cash-it-in for you.  Plus it introduced some other new things to that gameplay too, such as being able to fish for loot at fishing holes scattered throughout the game.  That’s not to mention it also came up with how the user-interfaces look and work for all of those things.  Other than maybe give them a lick of paint and a tweak or two, Torchlight barely changed many of those things at all when it inherited them from FATE.
For better or worse, FATE also influenced Torchlight’s toon-like style.  That conspicuously didn’t come from Diablo II.  And it’s a design-choice which might put off some players at first.  But it can also make FATE a perfect game with which to introduce younger players to Diablo-clones if you have kids.  That certainly proved to be the case in my household when my kid was growing up.
Despite how child-friendly and lighthearted FATE might look on its surface, once you get into it, it’s also still quite an expertly made and solid Action-RPG deep-down.  In that respect it’s still a blast to play today, because that well-tuned gameplay it had beneath its surface as a Diablo-clone is still there in an ageless sort of way.
You also needn't worry about having to get the whole FATE series.  The sequels mostly just add some additional content and include previous content in them.  Otherwise they essentially play and feel the same.  I happen to prefer the first FATE game a bit for my own nostalgic reasons.  But you’re good to jump into the series wherever you want.
Anyway, the bottom-line is the FATE series might not be for everybody.  But I’d still heartily recommend it to any fans of classic dungeon crawlers and Diablo-clones, young or old.
(Note:  This review also replaces a previous review I did for the FATE series.  It was a mixed review just to alert buyers to an issue it used to have being unable to run under Windows 10 for some users, despite trying many popular workarounds to fix that.  But as near as I can tell, it no longer has that issue.  So that means I can finally give FATE its real due with my new review here.  Not only that, but on Steam it also has more resolution-options now than it used to.  So it’s not only fixed, but it’s also improved.  That’s another real plus.)

A cute and adequate diablo clone but without the capacity for multiplayer -- which frankly is a standard of games like this ever since... well, Diablo. I got sucked in initially by it's subtle charm and my affinity for the genre, but frankly stayed with it to beat the game on a grudge. The loot system is flawed in that the majority of gear is unusable without certain stat requirements -- for example, to wear plate mail you'd literally have to win the game more than once, perhaps several times. That frankly is ludicrous, considering my character was literally defined as a hero of great reknown who was DRIPPING in strength-giving gear and focused on developing strength... what, is plate mail made of depleted uranium in this world? This is just one example... the vast majority of equipment you find or see in stores is reserved for people who (somehow) have the time and facination to remain on the hamster wheel. I hate-played this game just to see what was waiting for me when I finally beat the creature designated to be the target of my adventure... and it was the "opportunity" to start all over from the beginning. Bottom line - if you want to play a game like this play Diablo, or Titan Quest, or Path of Exile (which happens to be FREE!) -- those are ALL better games and finer examples of the genre. Barf. Oh, one last thing -- the difficulty scale on this game is literally offensive... it just multiplies (or divides, it would seem) monster hitpoints, and in the case of "Hero" difficulty (which I chose expecting a challenge, not a boring punishment) just makes monsters rapidly scale out of reach of being able to keep up with them. It won't make the monsters more challenging, but it WILL turn the entire game into button mashing the potion key while holding the attack button down. Also, most anti-climactic final battle ever -- it basically filled the screen with summons to the point the player cannot remain engaged to one target for more than an instant, making it literally impossible to swing more than three times at the same creature before dying. Luckily there is a (stupid) mechanic in the game that allows you to respawn exactly where you died at the loss of some xp and (mostly pointless) fame, so to beat the boss, (or anything for that matter) you merely need to swing twice before you die where you stand and keep coming back UNTIL you kill enough of the annoying summoners to face off with the boss, and if needed die numerous times to get him as well. Awful. Awful. Awful. If you played the game as a youngster and feel the need to retread this path somehow, be my guest. Those without the benefit of nostalgia have been warned.

Isometric action-RPG dungeon crawler. A bridge between Diablo and Torchlight. Everything we have in the Torchlight we have because of this smooth project... And Fate itself is based mostly on the Diablo Hellfire best patterns.
If you're familiar with the Torchlight (and I guess you are), then you'll know everything the Fate got from the first sight.
Cartoon-styled graphics. Mild music, yet reminiscent to Matt Uelmen tracks. Very basic RPG elements but rich grinding system, making you constantly looking for more power-ups and new guns, which will be bigger and brighter... And many-many randomly generated levels (over 2 millions, and that's not a joke). Basically, you can keep playing in the Fate year by year and still be far from its depth (that's what Diablo 3 is only dreaming to be).
Comparing FATE to all other "Diablo killers" and especially Diablo 3 itself may not be the best idea, though. While generally all those games, would that be the Diablo itself, Titan quest, Sacred (etc.) - have some story on the plate, you can't say same thing about FATE. It is so random in every point, that even the main quest is not stable, and will be procedurally generated and different for any player. You'll not get any background there but only the very basic: you have a town with some folks, half of them will be traders or item randomizers, while other half will be sending you on some irrelevant quests. And all the quests in the game will be like "reach the level X and kill the monster Z" or "Bring me an item Y from level X".
Now, the main question: should you buy it? Yes.
Point one: it is good for any dungeon crawler fan. Hardly FATE can take your heart now, with all new titles like Van Helsing or Bastion (or dozens of others), but still it provides a very solid gameplay. A lot of challenge awaits!
Point two: even if you are not so deep in dungeon crawlers, but making numbers on Steam (would that be score of games in possession or achievement statistics, or both) - it is a good buy (especially with discount, of course). To make a gold on achievements, you'll probably need less than 5-6 hours.
Finally, this game has very high valued cards, so you have a good chance to buy the game and even make some money back on top of it!
Overall, it's not a hit or something you can't live without, but it's a very good pick. My mark 7.5/10

I I'm a big fan of these types of games and I get that there is a nostalgic air around these modern versions of the old games. Still, there are some improvements in general gaming that shouldn't be ignored just as it was how they did it back in the 90s.
This game has nice graphics and charming art. I enjoy the "press your luck" monster gathering mechanism and in general, it is exactly what I am looking for in a game.
Yet, walking from one part of the world to the other, exploring, levelling up over a decent amount of play time all getting lost as the save point was when you left town it soul-crushing.
I lost hours of game time and saying "well that was how it was in the old days" doesn't not cut it. It sucked back then as well. Easily one of the most complained about things in the entire genre.
With modern computing and the speed of a save there is NO REASON not to have autosaves of some sort as you move through the world. Simply having the player loose hours and hours, then forcing them to repeat all that gameplay is one of the things that we DO NOT want back from the old days.
Level by level dungeon saves in this game are fine, IMO. They are about clearing and exploring a level and there is a saves in the dungeons I tried at appropriate points. I'm talking about the free-range exploration zones on the map. Where there are no saves and you can spend as much time as you like looking about and levelling up.. all to be lost if you die.
This was so demoralising I may never load this game up again.
There are many things we want in a retro-inspired game, but we do not want all the stuff we used to hate, only the good stuff. Retro-inspired games should be about taking the best of the old games and leaving all the rest.. this game, unfortunately, took one of the worst aspects of the entire genre and chose to keep it... and it ruins this game completely.
Whats better than shooting guns? Shooting guns..as a duck, and killing other ducks. MURDEROUS DUCKS ARE FUN!

Not a terrible game but definitely not a top performer in the genre.  Nice unit choices and a variety of building options.  However the buildings are somewhat weak with their effect and really don't do much for the playability of the game other than give unit recruitment and some resources used for the kingdom advantages part of the game.  The "Royal Court" only consists of 9 slots regardless of how many provinces you own and that gets to be a real problem with expanding your kingdom.  Somehow you have to fit marshals, priests, governors, merchants, spies etc, into these 9 slots to manage your expanding kingdom.  That is pretty much impossible.  I usually went with 1 merchant, 7 marshals and left a spot open for whatever else I needed at any given point which makes the whole kingdom court a useless part of the game.  Even with this strategy it was advance a few provinces and then wait and quell the constant uprisings in the newly conquered provinces.  This takes what seems like forever as you have to wait for the "Nostalgia" effect to drop before the rebels stop spawning in the recently acquired areas.
Diplomacy is unpredictable as nations that you have had good relations with will eventually turn bad for no apparent reason.  Marrying into the noble family of another nation is no guarantee that the nation will have good feelings for you and seems to do nothing but cause problems in the future.  Marrying off a princess is, most of the time, the worst thing you can do.  It doesn't help your standing with the nation your princess is married to and if they claim rights to your lands it goes bad for you either way you decide to handle it.  If you agree, you lose land. If you disagree you lose more than half your kingdom power which effects several aspects of the game to include income, happiness of the populace, and overall standing with other nations. princesses in my kingdoms were all spinsters, never married and an overall waste of the king and queens lustful energy.
There are a lot of things I like about this game. Unfortunately there are a lot of other things I find very undesirable.  Now for the reason I gave this game a "NO" in the recommendation.  With all the little things that are either small irritants or just plainly useless in game play the thing that makes no sense is thus.  I played several campaigns and they all ended the same way.  For no apparent reason or some reason that completely escapes me all of my marshals will just quilt and turn against me.  With population at a content level and everything going well they just decide to turn rebel and start destroying anything and everything around them.  When new marshals are recruited to replace and fight the old ones they too turn rebel and continue the onslaught against their former king.  The developers may as well have just added a message that says: "You have played this particular game enough and even though you have done well and managed your kingdom like a pro, YOU LOSE! please play again soon."  I guess that is one way of getting out of writing a good successful end game screenplay.
If you do decide to purchase this game I'm sure you will get several hours of enjoyment playing it, just don't expect it to be the greatest game of all time because that one hasn't been written yet.  I do wish this game was better than it is.  It had the potential in development but I think they either ran low on funding or just got sloppy towards the end and rushed it out.  Nevertheless I hope you find this helpful and as I said earlier if you do play this I truly hope you find it enjoyable for the parts that do make it fun and take the rest in stride.  Its not a perfect world after all.  Cheers :)

Knights of Honor is a medieval strategy game which mixes the style of the Total War and Europe Universalis series with real-time elements. It is almost ten years old now, but is still a competent game in its genre.
Pros:
Nice mix of kingdom management and military strategy. Provinces can be taken over, developed and defended when needed. Military units can be moved with marshals through the map in real-time. Leveling and perks are deep enough. Fights can be simulated or played on one of the many pre-built battlefields. Sieges and engagements need strategic decisions. Diplomacy is important, every move influences the way how others will act. The whole map of Europe can be seized and dominated. Many nations can be controlled in three different period. The world feels living due to the many events occurring constantly. Pre-rendered graphics look decent even in 2014 and the menus are also usable.
Cons:
Only two game modes available, campaign and battle. Multiplayer campaign would add to value. Some features are too simplistic and leave some more to be desired, like the importance and use of trade and exotic goods. The limitation of knights/nobles available for actions are frustrating, especially when a bigger kingdom is governed. The way military units transported and used in slots and their numbers feel less appropriate at cases. Also, units moving on the battlefield can collide with each other causing well set formations to break. AI sometimes prefer annoying and dumb decisions both in diplomacy, map movement and battles and can be exploited at times. Graphics engine lacks options demanded nowadays, like higher resolutions and widescreen.
Overall, I highly recommend this game to anyone who wants to play a complex military strategy game with many ways and choices available. The game features long campaigns with dozens of played hours and also has a high replay value.

When you get to the ball you may have to circle back to it once or twice to even pick it up, but by then the AI will have picked it up in one swoop.
I have played 4 hours in and haven’t even unlocked any European teams, so I do not know how hard it is to unlock them.  However, if you want to play your home country and it happens to be Japan, Australia, Mexico, Canada, the US to name a few, then good luck.  You will have to win a specific tournament on Professional (hard).  For the US, you have to beat 5 tournaments to even unlock the specific tournament.  So if you can get good enough, by the time you do, you may be tired of the game.
My keeper has gotten caught multiple times behind his own net during corner kicks, where I have to go in and out of menus to try to get him unstuck (then I often give up a goal because of it).  My keeper has run off the screen with the ball until the half ended.  My keeper has kicked balls backwards on goal kicks and passes, once scoring an own goal (since the last update), and that is not counting the time he leaps out of bounds with the ball…or leaps with the ball into his own net.  On low difficulties this is forgivable, but on higher difficulties it is infuriating.
This game has potential, and I would consider changing my review if they fixed two big issues: allow players to unlock everything from easy modes and remove the new passing update.  However, I can’t recommend it in its current as I feel it has strayed too far from being an arcade-style soccer game.

Final Fantasy VII is a great game! However, if you plan on trying to save this game via cloud saving as advertised, then this probably isnt the game you want to buy. The cloud server for ffvii is crappy. It worked only once for me and then all of sudden it stopped. I looked at forums online, and it seems that is big issue. Don't get me wrong, the game itself is great. The amount of customization you can put on your character is great, and there are hours of sidequests along with a great main story.
Here are my favorite points about this game:
Story: Honestly, it's really great story, and no I'm not a FF7 fanboy (though I am a Final Fantasy fanboy in general lol). Great characters really made a difference in the game. Of course the most famous is probably the antagonist of the game, though I won't spoil it (I'm pretty sure every gamer knows that character haha).
Materia system: Materia=magic. Magic includes damage spells, healing spells, buffs, summons, special attacks and stat boosts. This is where customization comes in. Your weapons and armor have materia slots in them, which you equip the materia onto. Unlike most Final Fantasy games and RPGs, you have a finite amount of materia you can carry. This means there are a massive amount of possibilities on what you can build for your characters. Also summons are really cool in this game, though you have to go through the animation everytime which can be annoying. Oh and you can actually level up your materia to do greater damage and new spells! EX: Fire materia=Fire 1 (automatic) Fire 2 (1st star) Fire 3 (2nd Star). If you get a third star, then that means you mastered it, and an new fire materia is created for mastering it. Though the new one starts at 0 again.
Note: You will need endless hours of grinding to master the materia.
Limit Breaks: For those who have never played Final Fantasy, think of this as your Ultimate attack. Final Fantasy VII utilizes this system well and can be useful when your fighting bosses. There are usually 4 levels for each companion and usually contain 2 per level, and one on the 4th level. You have to acquire the 4th limit breaks through sidequests though. The more damage you recieve the higher the limit gauge, and there are some status effects that can affect your limit gauge fill speed. Once at maximum you can use the limit break command.
Sidequests: There are a bunch of sidequests you can do. They even have a location, Gold Saucer, where all you do is play games which help you get awesome items. You can do pretty much anything like buying your own house, getting amazing materia, limit breaks, and items, fighting epic boss battles, and even raising your own chocobo (you might need a guide for that last one). You literally can spend hours on it.
Party: You have 3 party slots total. Also there are hidden characters within the game so keep that in mind when playing. One thing to remember is that you cannot switch out Cloud (main character).
Items: There are a bunch of items in the game, including ultimate weapons. Weapons and armor have tradeoffs usually for materia slots; some weapons and armors may be stronger, but may not have that many slots. You also get accessories in the game which can help you by boosting your stats to granting immunity to things (the legendary RIBBON!!!).
I'm sure I maybe missing things, but that's the jist of it. Im only giving a thumbs up for the game because it is a good game, despite the crappy server for this game. Also, character booster is unnecessary. You can easily complete the game without, but it will probably take more time haha.
P.S. Locate your save files immediately and place copies elsewhere in your system. If you save on the cloud, it will remove the files from you local system and put it on the cloud. And if you can't access the cloud...well there goes your save files :'(

I enjoyed my playthrough of Abzu though it didn't reach the emotional heights of its predecessor Journey. Many of the moments didn't feel earned. In journey, you understand your objective from the outset - GET TO THE TOP OF THE MOUNTAIN. Your start in a desolate environment and as you progress through the story you can see the fruits of your efforts visually through ever changing and ever more beautiful scenery, The feeling of kinship that develops with a stranger/s over the course of the game, whom you feel very attached to by the end and finally the lengthening and shrinking of the scarf.
Abzu instead starts you in an environment which is much the same through the course of the game. Its objective isn't immeadiately clear. In fact by the end of the game, I wasn't really sure what I had accomplished. Having played journey I am able to assemble together some story, but for those who haven't played journey, I wonder if they would be able to piece together much of it.  It is obvious that the story, is not the primary focus of the game and that it is intended to be a much more meditative experience than journey. Oddly I found jorney to achieve this affect much more for me. Abzu almost feels like its trying too hard to be profound.
Abzu does not utilise multiplayer, and has replaced the other player with little robots that you can find along your path. I'm not sure if players are supposed to develop a bond with these, but I did not. They are easily lost and replaceable and merely serve to open a few doors.
Technically this game is amazing! The schools of fish are drop dead gorgeous and you can easily get lost following all the various fish around.  I can see why the developers added a mediation mode the main menu.... aka. Fish tank mode.
I am tempted to record a few hours of this and have it running on my second screen while I work.
Overall this game is a nice experience, and some of the visuals are absolutely stunning. Pick this up if you are looking for a game to escape the stress or real life or if you want to show your friends the best PC fish tank simualtor available.

What can I say? I loved this game. The indie charm of it was magical.
No...  *endearing.*  That's the right word
Sure, there are plenty of issues to nitpick over, but nothing game-breaking. The animation is mostly stiff, the writing was a little odd, the jokes don't often land, the camera is inconsistent, most of the condition icons are impossible to interpret, and there's a little bit of grindy filler, but overall it's a lighthearted love letter to the RPGs of the mid-to-late 90's.
The combat is simple, yet enjoyable, with a lot of well-designed boss battles. Some clever choices like the pairing mechanic, a wide array of mix-and-match damage types, and a spin on the always-popular limit break, added just enough strategy to keep combat from ever getting stale.
What you'll find here is something less than Final Fantasy or Chrono Trigger, but far superior to all but the most acclaimed of RPG Maker games. If that sounds like fun to you, nab this game. And with the promise of an ungraded version on the horizon coming free to those who purchased this version, it's easily worth dropping $10-$15, if not a little more.

*If you don't want to read all this, you can go to the bottom of the review to see the conclusion.
I'm not gonna tell you that this game is similiar to "Final Fantasy Series" because I don't want you to think that It's somehow comparable to that. It felt more like "Golden Sun" to me however this game is also not comparable to "Golden Sun" but as an indie game, it does it's job.
I'm not going to give you any spoilers but the story overall is not new, It has been used in many games with different styles. The biggest issue with this game is that: I didn't cry, I didn't feel anger, I didn't feel any excitement, I didn't feel any emotions at all. I just smashed my buttons and fought all the bosses to get through to the end and yes, I read every single dialogue in this game, most of them were stupid to be honest tho.
Graphics wise, It's almost the same as Torchlight's which is a game I love. If you like cartoony characters I don't think that you'll hate this game's graphics either.
So It's a little turn-based RPG which most people will enjoy playing, but if you have high criteria, you won't like the game and probably return it after an hour.
PROS
*It has a variety of play styles like the old RPGs. By this, I mean: Going full DPS and beating the boss in no time, going for a tank/healer combo and playing it safe, choosing magic/ranged combat rather than melee combat etc.
*It has a talent system which allows you to improve your characters' stats and perks, even to play as a mage with a healer character by changing it's active abilities.
*It has a little crafting system if you like crafting and going for better stuff rather than keeping what the game gives you through the game.
CONS
*The story is not that great, It's more like nostalgic.
*It leaks sub story.
*For me it's nice, but the game is not easy and it takes time to figure out stuff.
*The game does not allow you to interact much with the world, It's so limited.
*Crafting system could be better.
The Conclusion
You can get this game and give it a try if it's on a discount, otherwise, It does not worth the price. If you like hard games and those with many boss fights, leveling up your characters and bringing out their capabilities, It's a good oppurtunity to give it a try but If you're a casual gamer and generally play games for  their stories or to relax after a long day, this is not your game.

A great game, but two aspects kill the experience for me.
The first is the randomly-generated cities.  If you don't have certain resources in any of your cities, too bad, you're stuck; the RNG is too real.
The second is that you cannot zoom out in battles.  When I can't see my whole army from a reasonable distance, some mechanic is wrong (or missing) from the game.
Other than that, Knights of Honor is a well-crafted, funnily-narrated, deeply-intricate strategy game.  I'm impressed with the scope that KoH manages.  I recommend it ONLY if you're willing to put up with those two major issues.  I hope you can look past them and love the game for the rest of what it is; I cannot.

Earthlock : Festival of Magic is a turn-based combat RPG similar to the old Final Fantasy series. You play as Amon, a thief/explorer who has found an artifact that is wanted by the cult of Nadir. Your hammerhead shark uncle, Benji, gets captured and it is up to you to save him. Along the way, you will pick up your motley crew of Ive, Taika, Frogboy, Gnart, Olio, etc. The start tutorial at the Suvian Academy is extremely lacklustre.
Gameplay-wise, you control a team of 4 heroes taking turns to act. The game is designed for a controller where you use the arrows to choose from 4 main categories of actions; combat, items, running/escaping and ultimate. Each hero has 2 stances to choose from, a combat stance and a support stance. Combat stances are basically for damaging/casting spells while support stances do support roles like tanking, stealing, trap laying and buffing. All special actions require Amri points and range from 1-3 costs.
There's base building on Plumpert Island where you get to garden, barnacle and craft. The crafting is slightly cumbersome but easily done. Gardening only encompasses watering plants to a certain level and harvesting them until they mutate/upgrade. Every item or vegetable collected has a minor, normal and magna level which requires you to get a normal, + and ++ recipe respectively. It's basically Levels 1,2,3.

Conclusion, the overall feeling is that it's okay but not great. It's very close to mediocre. The game is missing many components to make it feel impressive. However, it is decent enough to play. At the time of this review, only 3.4% of all Steam purchases bothered to complete this game. It is like almost like Earthlock is trying to be like Final Fantasy 7 but seems to be lacking in certain key areas. Perhaps, the Unity Graphics Engine is not robust enough?
21 Dec 2017: I had to change my review from positive to negative. After playing for a longer period and seeing how shoddy the later part of the game is and how nothing has changed over a period of 1 year, I am greatly disappointed by Snowcastle Games. Bugs have not been fixed and the overall gameplay is just not passable. It would be unfair to other developers who put in the effort to make a proper game. To give it a + would be trying to reward developers for churning out unfinished games for money-making purposes.
Note: Snowcastle Games is an independent game developer based in Oslo, Norway. Founded in 2009. After five years in development, including a successful Kickstarter campaign, they are now back with their highly anticipated RPG; Earthlock: Festival of Magic, the first in the Earthlock Trilogy. CEO is Bendik Stang, COO is Erik Hoftun, Lead Designer is Thomas French.
1. Base Building/Gathering
Build a garden, barnacle beach, blacksmith, emporium, airship, rest stop, crafting, etc.
2. First Strike Clicking
Keeps you attentive with only a small amount of effort.
3. Seeing Your Enemies on the Map
I love this compared to the old Pokemon-grass random encounters.
4. Unique Stances and Abilities
I kind of like it except for Ive and Amon who both have Steal.
5. The Burning Desert Level
Kind of immersive when you have to run from shade to shade. It's like one is in a real desert.
6. The Moving Frog Statue
I like how it moves and bows whenever you warp.
7. Frafnir's Lair
The moving stairs are a nice touch.
8. Different Hero Interactions
Ammon has an Amri Attractor to turn on devices. Gnart and Taika are short.
1. Dead World
There is seriously little or no interaction with the world. Every object is a decoration. You hardly interact with the world at all.
2. Skill Build
Horrible. Once you connect up the first 3 skills, what else is there to do? There is no real customization since once you form the main skill links, you are just filling up empty spaces.
3. The Strategic Map
Too little and too small. Once you get to the desert, it's like 50% game explored. Almost like an entire beginner's island. I was expecting more.
4. Repetition for Ive and Amon
Steal x 2? Kind of breaks the unique character aspect.
5. Fire, Water, Electric Attacks
So boring. Fire does additional damage called Burning. Water does additional damage called Drowning. Electric does additional damage called Electrocute. The problem is that all the effects are the same. It's just a matter of finding out what weakness the creature has.
6. Bosses Have Pure Immunity
The bosses have Confuse, Silence, Slow, Taunt Immune. So, your status effect skills don't matter.
7. Crafting Ammo/Lances Only for 2 Heroes
Only Ive and Amon use it.
8. Changing Stances
Absolute waste of time just to reach another set of skills. This is horrendous and doesn't add anything good to the game.
9. Limit of 4 abilities per Slot
Each ammo and item type is limited to 4 slots. So, having ammo + and ammo ++ requires 2 different slots. You have to manually remove them the weak ammo and replace them.
10. Dead Zones
The game is very linear and goes in one direction only. Once you complete a zone, that's it. Move onto to the next one.
11. Bugs/Glitches
Taika's Elemental Absorb creates a bubble that absorbs any Fire/Water Attack once. However, once you absorb one attack, the bubble animation doesn't disappear. Tooth Cactus does not shine for harvest. PS4 controller can't be detected.
12. Bad Zooming
If you run too close to a wall in the foreground, the game automatically zooms in onto your character causing you to lose sight of the map. For some reason, they have no idea how to use translucent foregrounds. Also, combat with certain monsters results in the monsters appearing outside of the screen so you can't see them.
13. Repetitive Creatures
If you look at the bestiary, you will see that the monsters are different coloured versions of themselves. E.g. Barghest is red and Simoorg is blue. Red, yellow, blue lanterns.
14. Mini-map sucks
It's a compass not a map.
15. No Different Weapons/Item Customisation
Picture show Olio with Paddle and Sickle, game does not have item customisation.
16. Unfinished Game
If you look at the trading cards, Brynn would be a hero. Olia would have different armour and items. The gardens would be more interesting. There would be airships and a blacksmith. There would be more shops.Barnacles poo.
1. Gardening
Cumbersome but easy enough to do. It's a good idea but I think it can be improved to make it more fun to do. Currently, it feels like a minor chore. It does not look like anything advertised. The plants are all "dead" and are basically the same thing. This is what I mean by okay but not great. It is a good concept but delivery is extremely mediocre. Also, you are collecting vegetables to make weapons. No wonder their damage sucks. You are basically firing potatoes.
2. Barnacling
Minor chore but the barnacles are cute.
3. Hogbunny Design
Perhaps, the hogbunny is not as cute as it seems? Over 20% of the purchases stopped playing after seeing the hogbunny. They didn't even want to reach Plumpet Island. It's neither cute nor cool.
1. World Interaction
Secret zones, climbing on, destructible objects for obviously breakable things, sitting down on a chair, hidden wall bookcases, jump puzzles, cracked wall breaking, swimming, picking up throwable objects, mini-games, talking to NPCs for rumours, NPCs that react to your action, increase/decrease population size due to your actions.
2. Ive's Special
Sniper shots. On the map, if there certain objects that need to be shot down from a distance, changing to Ive will allow you to aim and shoot it. E.g. Levers, power circuits, buttons. Olio can use her strength to move rocks, boulders and heavy objects.
3. Level 5 Garden
Don't make me plant 2 Level 3 plants. Make them Level 5 with 30 at once. 1 plant, 5 growth stages, 3 different parts to harvest.
4. Remove your +,++,+++ System
It's a horrible crafting system and makes your game look mediocre.

[UPDATE 24/08/2016 - after Online Multiplayer patch]
As I promised, I want to update my review by including a feedback about Online Multiplayer.
My overall opinion is Online Multiplayer is badly implemented, plain and simple.
Nice to choose the different modes, too bad you click on 2v2 and you get put in a 1v1 match.
This would be solved easily by introducing a lobby before the match start, so players can join and wait for the game to be filled with enough players to have a 2v2(3v3,4v4 etc.) or quit before the match starts, no?
You can't choose the teams, you can't switch sides if you end up 3v1, you can't do nothing.
Very meh.
Another issue is ping.
This game heavily depends on a good ping to be decent, otherwise it's a torture.
Sadly you can't see your or other players' ping, you only find out while playing and that's not really fun.
I think the Online Multiplayer can be improved A LOT with some little changes here and there, sadly this game has a little online community (I've seen 50 to 70 players online).
The game sometimes randomly freeze, btw.
And players don't hook correctly the ball even if you run over it, that's very annoying.
I recommend this game only if you buy it with some friends to play together, otherwise it may not be the best purchase of your life.

It is always exceptional when a game manages to be minimal while retaining the essence of what games are. Removing all the cruft modern titles are burdened with often leads to an experience that is refreshingly pure. Typically, this approach also leads to innovative, experimental mechanics that are fun to explore. Abzû looks like one of these titles, and I was very disappointed when I realised it wasn't.
There is a fine line between distilling elements to their core components, and removing them altogether. Unfortunately, Abzû crosses that line, and then some. The near-absence of mechanics turns the play-through into a radically passive experience, and without any form of compelling challenge or interaction, its status as a game becomes glaringly debatable.
Not that, as an art piece, it has no value. The soundtrack is particularly well executed, and the visuals, while nothing special, still hold up in their naive simplicity.
Still, while Abzû hits a few right notes, the extreme brevity of the experience (you will find that two hours are more than enough to consume it), compounded to the lack of interaction, make it a very hard title to recommend.

If you don't want to worry about team formation, tatics and you want to play quick and short soccer games, this game was made for you.
Kopanito is a soccer game on Early Access that already has a lot of content:
-16 tournaments and cups to play, but you can also create your own tournament.
-100+ teams from all over the world.
-4 AI difficulty levels
-Super-moves
-Achievements
-Leaderboards
-Controller support
It's an extremely simple soccer game. You pick your team (5 players + 1 goal keeper) and you can play a friendly match or try to win a tournament or cup.
There are no fouls, no referees, no team formation, no tatics, no stamina.
The game has a smooth gameplay, you can tackle as much as you want, but that doesn't mean you're going to easily steal the ball.
When you press and hold the kick button the game slows down and you can change the ball direction, making the goal keeper's life difficult.
The super-moves are a nice addition to the game: you can freeze your opponent, you can use a magnet to pull the ball, you can teleport to another region of the field, you can perform a super shot or use a windmaker to blow the ball away from your goal.
You can play locally with your friends: up to 5 local players, using gamepads and a keyboard.
In the beginning you can play just one tournament. You need to win it on the Beginner level to unlock another tournament and so on.
Even though the game has 100+ teams you can pick just a few in the beginning and you need to unlock the other teams.
9/10

A solid game, well made, enjoyable, but with a few frustrating problems.
After playing through all the quests (siding with Roach) and finishing the game in 38 hours, here are my impressions.
Positive:
+ Graphically impressive, running on everything maxed out, this game is a visually phenominal. Both open and closed areas are very detailed, textures are crisp, animations smooth and lighting for different time of day is just perfect
+ Story - although it is a positive here, it is not a perfect one. Seems like a story was just made for the sake of making a story. The whole premise of Gerald following Letho was to find the real killer of Foltest (and maybe clear his name?) Well after he finds  Letho - he can either let him go or kill him, which doesn't make sense, right ? Shouldn't you put him to the trial - not kill him or let him go ? And even after he kills him he just walks away. Good job, now everyone will think you are Foltest killer right ? Then why did you bother in the first place....
+ World - although it is not an open world, it still feels alive when you play it. Now that we have many great titles trying to put more emphasis on the world itself (such as GTA 5, Skyrim) Witcher series still does it well, if not the best.
Negative
- Bugs, Crashes - Don't know what's up with that, but for some odd reason as soon as you pass some magical number of saves the game starts to hang/crash pretty much all the time. The only solution to this problem is to manually go to the game folder and delete saves yourself, wait for them to load from the Steam cloud and play few days more.
- Combat - I am not sure if combat is better than in Witcher 1, I have a feeling that it might be even worse. The great idea of selecting a foe and attacking him is great on the paper but it just doesn't work, you are always surrounded by multiple foes, and you cannot properly hit them because Gerald is always trying to do a long hits that take time, while you are getting hammered by  everyone who surrounded you. Switching and targetting another opponent is also a problem, you have to stop what you are doing and select one in order to hit him effectively, takes time and makes combot not as enjoyable. He is also gets himself stuck in all kind of items on the map, the areas that you fight are very small, you cannot dodge properly without running into barrels, lamps, chairs, whatever. And what is the idea of always getting hit first whenever you go to combat after conversation ends, isn't there a way to put a small delay, so you would have some time to react ? Sometimes when you go into combat you have your sword drawn, sometimes not, requiring you to draw on first while dodging fireballs in the process, why it is so inconsistent ?
- Witcher ? - The last one is probably the thing that bothered me the most, what did I like the most about Witcher 1 was the whole  fact of discovering the world and doing the thing that Wichers do - slaying monsters, and not go and play political games that Gerald was doing this time around, where is a fun in that ?

After playing the disasterous remastered version of Beach Bounce I have become very skeptical of Dharker Studios. As for Divine Slice of Life, it was not the best Visual Novel I have ever played. Far from it, it still has it's problems but that doesn't change the fact that it was a major improvement from Beach Bounce.
First off, having our main character as the reincarnation of Zeus was too funny, and having these two girls, Yui and Ryn fight over you because of your "destiny" to ascend to godhood and choose one of them adds a very interesting story instead of just having them fight over you because they want you.
As for Aaki himself, not a very interesting protagonist. He's very weak in terms of other VN protagonists, even though he's a reincarnation of Zeus.
Yui and Ryn are just too funny that you can't help but fall for them, as they continously refer to you as their "king" made me laugh a bunch.
Then you have Sakura, the hottest girl in school who's dating the most popular guy in school and how you and he but heads over her. Then there is the typical childhood friend Taka who has loved you since you were kids. Not original I was rolling my eyes the whole time.
One thing Dharker does get right is the music and artwork. Music sets the mood in certain situations and the artwork is absolutely beautiful.
And in this VN we actually have voice acting. Very cool as most VN's don't have voice acting. Unfortunately, the voice acting in this game is not good. Even if you turn the volume down, it's still hard to hear. But if anything, I'm glad they decided to include it rather than not have it at all.
5/10: Average. It's not really the best but it's not bad either. I just wish the protagonist was more relatable and that some of the other girls besides Ryn and Yui were original. All of that and if the game was longer, I would've gotten a 6 or maybe a 7.

It's a step in the right direction from Beach Bounce and I recommend buying this after a price drop. This game has also given me hope that Dharker has learned from Beach Bounce and will try their best to make better VN's.

First off, the positives: The artwork is nice and detailed, and the voice acting is pretty good. It looks really nice and professional.
Then, the major issue: The writing. Looking at it on the store page I was expecting something cute and silly with a plot a bit like Shuffle!. The premise is like something straight out of an anime, so I was expecting an anime-esque romp. I was rather disappointed. It reads like a first draft. I don't want to be mean, as there is clearly a fair amount of work put into this game, but the writing really lets things down. The characters are barely formed at best, and actively unlikable at worst, and the plot logic is disorienting in its randomness (the bit with the parents walking in on the demi-god girls naked...it's not even funny, it's just weird). I feel that if the game had just gone all out in terms of sillyness and been a bit more self-aware, (maybe a bit more like Huniepop), it would be better for it. As it is, things are just kinda awkward. It's a shame because the starting premise is pretty decent and some of the plot elements (the one girl turning out to be a demon, or the protagonist getting one of the love interests pregnant and stuck on earth) are kinda cool - overall it just feels rushed though. And I'm not even going to start on the weird emotional manipulation and nasty relationship bull...I make allowances considering it's supposed to be a rom-com sort of thing and all but it really made me cringe.
I got this on sale, but even then I don't feel it was wholly worth the price considering the state of the plot. There are far better romance visual novels out there in my opinion. Cute art though, and if you can put up with the cringey plot, fair play to you.

GC3 is less than it what could be or what I had hopd it would be, that it is not to say it is without merit.
Some of this may just be that it feels incomplete. It has a very small campaign, but a lot of room for customisation, modding, and user created content.
Some of it is due to over-engineering, so that things that should be at the fore-front of the interface are hidden away in obscure corners or just not presented to the user, as if the developers or the playing community just take these things for granted. Information on how the economy, combat, tourism, influence, etc works, is just not obvious or even explained in the game or the manual, and you could find yourself doing hours of research to find out simple stuff that should have been at the forefront of the interface. The game also has a very weak diplomacy interface, and a currently weak AI.
There are also some long standing conventions from strategy and turn based games that are (currently) not implemented in GC3. For e.g. you can't execute all ship movement without ending your turn, and if a ship has movement points left over you don't have an opportunity to use them before the turn is executed.
By design, you have no control of tactical combat. Not even a card system like in Endless Space. It is just a calculation with only a vaguely related animation (combat viewer) to go along with it which often has no bearing to the actual combat results, and the actual combat system is not explained anywhere in the game or the manual (you have to go to the wiki page for that).
Much is made of the ship designer, but actually 90% of it is purely cosmetic, in that you can pretty much draw anything you can imagine, but in terms of actual ship performance and stats, you just add a combination of basic modules (engines, weapons, sensors etc) to determine a ships combat attributes, but many other attributes you might expect to have control over are NOT in the game (weapon size, line of sight, power levels, repair rates, critical hits, subsystem taregting, etc.).
It's also so 1980's to be limited to a 2d galaxy map (the models may be 3d, but the stars are laid out on a flat surface), and the game could really do with a well-developed controllable 3d tactical combat engine, rather than just a plain hands-off combat calculator.
In the end I was somewhat disappointed that the game wasn't all I had hoped it to be, and therefore felt that I had not quite got my moneys worth, but it is engaging. I might have been happier had I bought it on a sale. If you are hoping that this is the ultimate space 4x game, then I didn't find it so. I do want it to be thouigh.
I would have scored it a 7/10 at release, with the potential for getting to 8/10 (maybe even a 9) after a few patches, some AI improvements, and a lot more user created content.
If customisation, mods, and user created content is what you are after, then you might be happy with it eventually. If you are expecting a well-polished game with all the bells and whistles and a decent campaign and strong AI for single-player games, you will be disappointed right now.
It is certainly not (yet) the 9+/10 that most magazines gave it.

The addition of a 64 bit system within the game is a welcome change--something that never happened with Gal Civ II unfortunately. However, Gal Civ III just don't bring enough good to the table, and often times brings nothing but wretchedness in it's place. CTD's, stupid AI, slow as hell multiplayer, and wildly disproportionate civ bonuses (I'm looking at you Altarians) ruin good game play. Seriously: only two people are ever playing mutliplayer, and it's for a good reason,  Often times you'll be waiting three minutes for another player to finish their turn, which leads to a lot of boredom. AI Civs cheat endlessly, building huge slews of warships and developments despite not having the economy or happiness to do so--their colonies can be deep in the red and they'll be fielding fleets that can kick your♥♥♥♥♥no problem. Their research is also not tied to their economy or improvements, leading to them getting a huge edge early game, and staying there until you're dead. The issue's so bad, it often leads to one AI being a master of everything. How Stardock thought this was and is good game design is beyond me, and the fact the game's been an unbalanced and broken mess for 8 months speaks volumes about the company's desire to actually fix the game.
The UI is good for the most part, but the idea to map the rotation button (in ship designer) to the mouse wheel of all things is idiotic, and there is no way to remap the key.  The tutorial is garbage and doesn't adequately explain things, leading to you jumping into the main game in order to figure things out. In all, the technical failures of the game bog down the experience. This game is definitely not worth 60 dollars. Avoid entirely. Do not reward Stardock for such laziness.

I wanted to like this game. I remember playing GalCiv 1 and 2 and enjoying them. However, something is just not right in this one.
Something feels off. Like each piece of the game, such as research, combat, and the various empire managements just don't work together. It was almost like different teams worked on each and they tried to fuse them all together in the end. However it didn't quite work.
For example, you can build combat ships with different types of weapons and defenses with each type of weapons SUPPOSED to have different ranges and damages. Also, each type of defense is supposed to be better suited at countering certain types of attack. However, once you actually use these ships in combat, there seems to be something that doesn't quite work correct. It seems there are several factors at work here. The combat viewer has a habit of not actually showing what is actually occurring, making the player think that the ships are behaving differently that they should, and perhaps then changing the ships and their roles to make them better at combat, when it might or might not. It all seems sloppy and needs to be tightened up.
The AI acts strange. Sending colony ships to take planets right next to my capital for example. Other than the fact that this should be an act of war, it's just a dumb move on the AI part, because a few turns afterwards the planet will flip to my side automatically because its in the middle of my influence zone.
However, they can still send starbases in and build them right in the middle of "my" space. Steal my resources. This seems ok for some reason. (and the stations don't flip like the planets do)
Edit: I think stations not fliping is a bug, there are parts of the game that say that they are flipable, I have never seen one do such however.
Edit: I have put some more hours in and have sadly only come across more issues that I feel I need to bring up.
-Planet invasion was a big issue in the last games. I seem to recall taking well defended planets with troops was a diffcult proccess in the other games. It's way to easy in this one and the population seems to be alright with you taking over pretty quickly
-The game shows you "unlocking goverment types" in the research tree. It implies that you can have different goverment types in the game. However, there is no where in the game you can change your goverement. It seems the feature was never added??
-The AI is way to passive most of the time, even when the more aggressive types declare war they hardly ever actually attack.
Overall the game needs some work still. Perhaps with some love they can still fix it.

I... Love this game. Not in the way you love a game for opening your eyes to a brilliant new way to experience gaming, or in the way you get sucked in to addictive mechanics and extremely well crafted gameplay, but I love it because it is exactly what it sets out to be: An homage to the late 90s early 2000s JRPGs.
The storyline is not new, but it is nostalgiac. The art style is not particularly unique, but still it is beautiful in it's reminiscence of games past (you might be sensing a theme here). The gameplay is not prticularly difficult and there are not too many fights you will be sweating, but that's okay because I think this game should be approached as a joy ride and not a grit and grind challenge.
This game is relaxing and the sound track reflects in that with piano dminant tracks that remind you of a Studio Ghibli film opening.
When you do dig deeper, the character customization system is something more unitque and actually quite engaging. The bond system in which pairing your party members off results in different minor (and some major) boosts adds an extra layer to party design that I'm surprised doesn't exist in more games. Really, the bond and customization systems are not done full justice because of the games lower complexity, but it is still fun to play around with and there are a few battles that will necessitate their strategy.
There is a small crafting system with a couple of small and nice touches that make it feel slightly less grindy. I invested about 25 real hours playing the game and a chunk of that was due to my desire to do more than the minimum (as is the way fo most JRPG players right??).
tl;dr
If you have nostalgia for the JRPGs of old and you are looking for a game you can turn your brain down on and relax to, this is a good one.

It is always exceptional when a game manages to be minimal while retaining the essence of what games are. Removing all the cruft modern titles are burdened with often leads to an experience that is refreshingly pure. Typically, this approach also leads to innovative, experimental mechanics that are fun to explore. Abzû looks like one of these titles, and I was very disappointed when I realised it wasn't.
There is a fine line between distilling elements to their core components, and removing them altogether. Unfortunately, Abzû crosses that line, and then some. The near-absence of mechanics turns the play-through into a radically passive experience, and without any form of compelling challenge or interaction, its status as a game becomes glaringly debatable.
Not that, as an art piece, it has no value. The soundtrack is particularly well executed, and the visuals, while nothing special, still hold up in their naive simplicity.
Still, while Abzû hits a few right notes, the extreme brevity of the experience (you will find that two hours are more than enough to consume it), compounded to the lack of interaction, make it a very hard title to recommend.

Played it's demo before in my childhood but didn't manage to finish it. Don't be fool by my game time i played it like for more than 12 hours and finished it. Fate is a simple and old game, it's a really fun dungeon crawler game.
The NPCs gives 1-3 level high quest depending on what dungeon level you are on, which is really convenient if you are heading to the main quest dungeon. The bad part about it is that once you've reach a dungeon level you can't get the quest in the dungeon you are in or any dungeon below your current dungeon you've explored, some quest have normal rewards but others have item rewards, but in this case you can manage the quest that you wanted to do even though it is limited.
The monsters in every level is different and they have different types of attacks, if you're making a summoner build you are going to die... a lot... so its best to cover up your character weaknesses.
One of the best part in this game is that you are able to turn your pet into a monster( not like slime, goblin or anything that has 2 hands and 2 legs) by feeding him fish, the fish you fed to your pet have a duration of how long your pet can be turned into a monster, you can turn your pet into a monster permanently if you want. And yes you can go fishing in the game in town or in the dungeon if you're lucky you can get rare items just by fishing.
Finally the skills in the game, there is no skill perk trees just old fashion Str, Dex, Vit and Int. But instead of a skill tree you can spend points on Weapon skills, Critical strike, Spell cast time, Attack spell level, Defence spell level and Charm spell level. You can use magic too, you can choose to buy them from a NPCs or explore the dungeon for it.

An amazing RPG and good sequel to its predecessor. The Witcher 2 abandons the Aurora engine (used originally in Neverwinter Nights) for its own game engine. With this comes a shift from traditional RPG to an action RPG more in the vein of Demon's Souls or Dark Souls.
True to the series, the game pits you into a fascinating scenario filled with interesting characters, a strong plot throughout, and deeply profound decisions that you're prompted to make around every bend—decisions that are not easy, because you cannot foresee the immediate consequences, and the game avoids comical good-versus-evil situations for a morally gray setting.
These decisions lead you down two fundamentally different, branching paths throughout the story, and combined with the character build options, offer great replay value. The different skill trees feel very different in how they inform or complement your playstyle, and are well balanced in the sense that you can focus on any skill path to complete the game. If you import a save game from the previous game, you will even see some consequences of certain decisions you made back then which helps add further dimension to the setting.
The game also has a nice range of difficulty settings and solid controls. Easy will serve people well who are only interested in the story, while Normal is fairly challenging. Hard, Dark and Insane modes add a lot to the game, making you rely on every single tool and technique you can get your hands on, and encourage you to fully utilize the game's extensive alchemy and crafting system beyond simply mastering combat and magic signs, delivering a satisfying experience to those who enjoy games with a difficulty like Dark Souls.
This is a great action RPG with a couple of fresh approaches to classic ideas, and an excellent story. Do yourself a favor and don't miss it.

Earthlock is a throwback to the better parts of old school JRPGs.
It really feels like someone really wanted to make a great JRPG... and a year into development remembered they needed a plot. In some ways this is a great thing. It's more about the mechanics, the need for grinding has been removed (until the part where you get a couple of characters who are 5 levels lower than the rest of your party), and some of the mechanics allow you to scale the difficulty a bit to what you want to play. All without a bad story constantly getting in your way- scenes with dialogue in this game are usually 30-60 seconds long max... which is fine, as this game is about the gameplay and not the talking.
You'll get about 30-40 hours of gameplay out of it, and for the most part that won't require any back tracking. There's side quests, optional bosses, in-game hobbies for rewards.... All in all, a satisfying experience.
Of the games cons, the 'on the ground' vs. 'in the air' enemy positioning doesn't really add anything tactical, just makes fight take extra turns. The method of grouping enemies together could be more reliable (especially if you're trying to get that trophy for the tournaments), the dog has a move where she learns abilities from only specific enemies that's never fully explained and only works randomly, and not having a faster way to level up your teammates who are taken away from you and come back WAY behind, even when you're not grinding could all be improved in an expansion/sequel.
As a, it is what it is decision, the regular battles against enemies, even in large groups are usually really easy. And then the bosses, will murder the sweet hell out of you if you don't figure out their strategies pretty quick. There's no real training for hard battles, you just have push-overs to bosses that will make you use more items than you've ever used in a JRPG to keep your people alive. And the final boss' difficulty is questionable, because even with max level characters, you're still most likely going to die on your first run for not already knowing and understanding all of his moves, and having the correct members in your party who are practically required to beat him. That being said, I beat him on the second try, was just annoying to spend 20-25 minutes of a fight to end up dying solely because I didn't have the right members in my party.
All and all, a great little thing to spend some time and money on. Not super memorable, but fun and solid.

I bought the game during a sale since I have very fond memories of games that look like this one.
First of all, I don't really regret to have bought and played this, yet at the same time, I can't really recommend it as well.
All in all the game shows a lot of promise, but it during developement some short-sighted decisions were made, at least in my opinion. But let's mention the good stuff first:
- Earthlock runs smoothly. I haven't experienced any crushes or major bugs during my time with it.
- The idea of building pairs in the party (which consists of 4 characters, chosen from a total of 6) is quite nice, especially because you can unlock certain perks and thus customize your party. A grid-based talent system adds to this as well.
- There's a hub you can teleport to from any save point. There you can craft, regenerate and quick travel.
However, those are the only features which stand out positively.
As for the story, it's a mediocre one that hints on a vast world with rich history, yet most of it is told in bland cookie-cutter dialogue. The best example I can give for this is that in the last quarter of the story your main character suddenly is a descendant of an old race who have been around since forever doing cool♥♥♥♥♥♥ you know the drill.
It's seems there might be more to it, but that's really it. Someone mentions this fact, everybody is astonished, scene ends, nobody ever cares again.
The characters themselves are walking stereotypes, albeit they do have a certain charm to them.
Now for the bad stuff:
- The combat is repetitive, bland and tedious at times. You are introduced to some strategy druing the first quarter of the game, but you barely need any, besides the few instances when the game demands it for certain bosses.
- You are level capped. This is one of the short-sighted decisions I mentioned earlier. I hit max level about two thirds into the game and from then on fighting seemed even more like a drag than before.
- There are random difficulty spikes here and there which can render a party you deemed overpowered for the last two hours dead in a few turns.
- There is no gear at all. You have to improve your characters through the usage of talent nodes which you can not craft. Unlike ability nodes which you can craft, but they are quite expensive and you may only obtain currency thorugh fighting and stealing since you are unable to sell any loot.
- Lastly, you can not buy ammunition for your characters, you have to craft it. This involves growing plants which take forever to grow. After this, they need to be harvested and tended to which really disrupts the pacing of the game at certain points. I, for example, went out of ammo shortly before facing the final boss which really killed the little mood that had built.
In conclusion, I really want to like this game and I do see the potential it holds, but after having played it, I was just glad it was over. If you really like rpgs that feel like they are 10 to 15 years old, this is your thing, but if not, you might not like this game at all. However, I still would play a sequel or even back it up.

An overall decent turn-based RPG, but while it draws inspiration from the classics of the late 90's, it does not live up to their legacy. Unsurprising, considering those were produced by industry giants.
Earthlock offers a pretty simple turn-based combat system, but what makes it stand out is how you can lure enemies on the overworld into groups and fight up to 8 enemies at once for massive XP bonuses.
However, this can be something of a daunting task since there's almost no reliable area damage in the game.
There's no MP. Rather, abilities(even basic attacks), use a resource called Amri that regenerates slowly during battle.
This forces you to wait or use items to use your more useful abilities, but your maximum Amri increases as the game progresses.
The interface is relatively simple. Each action is tied to its own button, rather than being accessed through a menu. One can change which type of actions(combat, item, misc) is available by pressing a direction, and pressing that direction again changes to a second set, allowing 8 abilities of each type to be accessed per character.
Unfortunately, many of these slots are taken up by upgrades of old abilities. Two characters, for example, use weapons with ammunition, and each ammunition type has two upgrades. You'll have to go into the menu out of battle to re-arrange the order of these to get the right ones to show up.
Each character also has two stances, granting them another set of combat abilities. Changing stances wastes a turn, and is in general a feature that provides nothing but frustration.
The item list is incredibly small. There are several tiers of health potions, one revival potion and a few status cures.
Many items must be crafted (I've only found 2 shops in the game), which while kind of neat is also time-consuming since you have to wait for ingredients to grow. Yes, most of your ingredients are plants.
Also, you can't craft anything without a recipe, some of which you can buy but many which you must scour the world for.
There's no equipment. None. You cannot equip weapons, armors or accessories. If enemies in an area tend to inflict a certain kind of status ailment(like Stun), there's nothing you can do about it except try to kill them first and hope your healer doesn't get said ailment. Fortunately, escaping from monsters is easy and battles aren't *too* hard.
What you *can* do is switch out your level-up bonuses. Each time you level up, you gain a Talent Point that lets you equip a talent. Most of these must be found or won from boss battles, but a few can be crafted.
You can always switch the ones you have equipped from the menu. There's no downside to doing this, so if you've built your characters wrong for a boss, you can try something different.
Of course, this means that you CAN build your characters wrong, which adds a bit of frustration to the game since you don't know if you're doing it right.
Characters are also paired in battle, depending on the party order. Each pair gains unique bonuses, and share a meter that lets them use super abilities when filled. Leveling up all of the bonds is a good idea, since each pairing provides each member with Talent Points at certain bond levels.
I should note that there's a bit of a difficulty spike towards the later parts of the game. Your level is capped at 20, so you can't grind your way past the challenge, and the final area has a bunch of annoying battles you can't flee from.
I cannot call Earthlock a bad game, but it could certainly be better. Battles *can* get tedious and the story feels like it has some holes in it, but if you just want a smaller kind-of-retro RPG that won't take you 70 hours to complete, this is a pretty solid choice.

The lack of play time wasn't due to it being glitchy or anything, rather I had a few other games on my plate and didn't think there was much depth to Crypt of the NecroDancer. TIME SKIP. The game leaves early access and I suddenly decide that it's worth picking up and playing for a bit after getting a little burned out on The Witcher 3. Returning to it, I hadn't recognized how much depth there truly is in Crypt of the NecroDancer. You have to really plan each of your runs carefully: are you going to try to collect as many diamonds as possible? Are you trying to get to the exit as quickly as you can? It reminded me so much of how my girlfriend and I played through Rogue Legacy, where we had to determine if we intended on collecting as much gold as possible or if we should try to get to the boss rooms as quickly as possible.
No doubt the games soundtrack is really catchy and fun to listen to as well, as it should be. What I appreciate is that you're not really hindered significantly if you fail to keep in time with the music, outside of losing a coin multiplier.
I can't recommend Crypt of the NecroDancer enough. I have only a few hours logged in currently, partially due to the fact that the game is perfect for just picking up and playing for a few minutes at a time.

An amazing RPG and good sequel to its predecessor. The Witcher 2 abandons the Aurora engine (used originally in Neverwinter Nights) for its own game engine. With this comes a shift from traditional RPG to an action RPG more in the vein of Demon's Souls or Dark Souls.
True to the series, the game pits you into a fascinating scenario filled with interesting characters, a strong plot throughout, and deeply profound decisions that you're prompted to make around every bend—decisions that are not easy, because you cannot foresee the immediate consequences, and the game avoids comical good-versus-evil situations for a morally gray setting.
These decisions lead you down two fundamentally different, branching paths throughout the story, and combined with the character build options, offer great replay value. The different skill trees feel very different in how they inform or complement your playstyle, and are well balanced in the sense that you can focus on any skill path to complete the game. If you import a save game from the previous game, you will even see some consequences of certain decisions you made back then which helps add further dimension to the setting.
The game also has a nice range of difficulty settings and solid controls. Easy will serve people well who are only interested in the story, while Normal is fairly challenging. Hard, Dark and Insane modes add a lot to the game, making you rely on every single tool and technique you can get your hands on, and encourage you to fully utilize the game's extensive alchemy and crafting system beyond simply mastering combat and magic signs, delivering a satisfying experience to those who enjoy games with a difficulty like Dark Souls.
This is a great action RPG with a couple of fresh approaches to classic ideas, and an excellent story. Do yourself a favor and don't miss it.

A sweet little series of stories about Efina, a baby dragon girl who can eat lies... and the con artist she travels with.
The three chapters of the story expand on some details of her caretaker's history, culminating in the third story.
Combat is fairly minimal, and if you uncover the legendary weapons in each chapter you can completely remove all pretense of strategy.
(Exception: the first one has a section where you have to dodge swarms of enemies or face 8+ in combat at once. You can get wrecked pretty fast even with legendary weapons.)
Meeting each of the characters, and seeing their interactions was worth the price.
You'll get maybe 4 hours of overall story and play to reach 100%. Its a pity there's no further story, or games involving Efi, as she would be interesting to watch in the world you've barely set a foot in by the time the last chapter closes.

With FATE now arriving to Steam, I figured I should share how great of a game it is! This is the precursor to Torchlight and Torchlight II. It's a very simple loot-fest with a never-ending and randomly-generated dungeon. It's an awesome game, it's easy to pick up and put down, doesn't require a lot of commitment or effort and it's very enjoyable. It now even has 1920x1080 resolution, which I'm pretty sure was a thing of the future when it was originally released. Some people are complaining about bugs with the Steam version, I've never had a problem with that one or the WildTangent download. This game is a classic, and it deserves no less than what I'm giving it. Amazingly fun and simple game, and very nostalgic to me and I'm sure a lot of other people that grew up with this game. It has tons of weapons, multiple skills to learn, and a great system to build your character towards a desired style. If you want to be a wizard, upgrade magic and the multiple magic skill perks. If you want to be a warrior, you can upgrade the type of weapon you want to use as well as your strength and dexterity. Tons of different ways to play it that will keep it interesting despite the very simplistic gameplay.
It has insane replay value as everything is randomized and there are hundreds of different ways to play through it. The main goal of the game is to traverse the dungeon doing tons of quests until you reach a certain level deep down which contains the main boss (it will take a long time to reach this level). Then you kill it and you're then allowed to retire (or continue down the dungeon for eternity if you so wish), which locks your current character, but passes down (and empowers) an heirloom of your choice. For example, if you get the best bow currently in the game, defeat the main boss with it and pass it down as you retire, you will be able to start a new character with this, now even MORE powerful bow. And so on...
Nothing not to love about this game, despite it's simplicity and lack of variety when looking at it materialistically, the game is just so damn fun to play I still play it to this day, along with it's other three successors: The Undiscovered Realm, The Traitor Soul, and The Cursed King, which by the way are all just as good! Get it now!
