As with most strategy games, Knights of Honor is a little difficult to learn, if one is not accustomed to the genre. The developers thought it was a good idea to prevent players from skipping through three different introductions from gaming companies and an intro that is almost three minutes long. This is absolutely unacceptable. To stop this, you are forced to hold down the left Ctrl key while clicking repeatedly the left mouse button (this took some Google searching to discover). What kind of idiotic idea is that? The tutorial is adequate, and the text is accompanied by an ideal voice actor. Voice acting as a whole is excellent. The in-game help system is also very good. There are some issues with crashing from time to time. The user reviewers here were spot on about this game. It is extremely addictive to grow, expand, rule Europe and its surrounding areas. Knights of Honor sucks you in and doesn't want to let you go. The hunger for more power, territory expansion, and blood grows each and every minute. The fun, tension, and excitement increases in strength after every battle, and every province won. You will not notice at all how the hours pass while playing this game. Easily, six our eight hours will expire before you notice. Restroom breaks will also become nonexistent. You will not want to stop! Nothing else will matter! Your eyes will be glued to the monitor! When you are not playing, you will be thinking about strategies to improve your kingdom and to win the game. The game is so good, I even lose sleep thinking about it. I want it all! The entire continent! There is near infinite re-playability, as each of the many kingdoms to choose from will play differently than the next. In addition, each game will also differ from each other, as near limitless alternative history scenarios will evolve and transpire. I would have liked for the game to have the in-game date for perspective. I would have also liked for the player to have access to more than just three religions from the period, with a choice to convert to atheism or at the very least paganism. It would have also been nice if the game included information on what language each kingdom spoke as well. What is also nice is that you can choose to not micromanage the battles. You are allowed to utilize the knights' AI to battle for you. This is one of the most engrossing and absorbing games I have ever played. I admit, that towards the very end, I had grown a bit tired of fighting all the time, but winning the game brought on a natural smile to my face.
Knights of Honor is amazing.

If you like sometimes-frustratingly-brutal challenges, this will probably be a welcome addiction.  Only after you've mastered it, pick up Wrath of the Lamb (WOL).  WOL launches automatically if installed (there does exist a launcher to prevent this, so if you make the mistake, it's not irreversible), and the content assumes you've already mastered the original.
The WOL powerups feel a little less balanced and a bit more broken than the original content (a few invincible conditions),but it does add a welcome level of additional challenge, so I recommend it.  I will say WOL does do a better job of making your resources more valuable all the way through (the original tends to devalue certain resources after certain choke points).
Average play-time for a round is about an hour, which gives it a nice arcade feel.  You're bound to have a few play-throughs that just begin with terrible luck, but you'll probably die quickly and get to start afresh in those cases.
No pun intended, but this game is deeper than you think.  The game grows with your mastery of it in a pretty satisfying way.

Short Background.
I have purchased a physical copy of the deluxe edition of this game, always found New Orleans and 60s quite fascinating. Music, culture, daily life and century defining events happening all around you. This game delivers incredibly on carrying you back to those times, putting you in an old muscle car with radio talking about space race and presidents before blasting some raw Creedence Clearwater Revival. It is amazing to be in it.
Gaming Virtue
The game follows the story of a young Vietnam veteran, struggling to adapt back into his old life before it is taken from him. You see the criminal world knows no limits, blood defines new rules and your only friend is yourself. You lose your loved ones, you lose your home and place in the city but you are on your way to take them all back or die trying. You aim to take back the city district by distric, make your way to the man who took everything from you. You have contacts on the way, small choices to make and patterns to follow. Sometimes it gets repetitive on how you deal with each district but the story behind them differs, the motive and the people, their location make the difference on your efforts on that district. There are lots of things to do apart from the city scale war, you have to gain the trust of your associates, explore the darker side of the city, take part in the equal rights movement and profit. You need the DLCs for a complete experience, explore all the game offers.
Technical Aspects
I have a gaming labtop with a GTX1070 and i770HQ, 16GB Ram and game running on the SSD. It is not perfectly optimized, there is an unfinished feeling of the what the artwork might have been but it is still beautiful. It is a demanding game, I used ReShade on it and it is very pleasent with the colours being adjusted in the way I feel it is true. It is not very light on your CPU and needs you to do some tweaks but I played it on high settings with nearly stable 60fps on 1080p.
Verdict
I recommend this game. Music, world, feeling of the city, story, things to do all around with the DLCs. It is a unique experience that presents you a very interesting city in a very, very interesting time. Immerse yourself in it and enjoy the enviroment, enjoy the music and French Ward. Collect every collectibles like I did, you will not regret it.
Suggestion: Would be amazing if they added a real in-game camera, a polaroid or a 35mm that you can shoot sceneries as much as you want and collect them.

DO NOT BELIEVE THE POSITIVE REVIEWS. Here's the truth:
This game is obscenely Pay-to-Win. If you don't like being blackmailed into purchasing digital goods that you never actually possess (and which you can't turn into cash), there's one thing you should do: RUN.
This game has some interesting mechanics, but they mean nothing if someone with premium cards dismantles everything you do without any tactical planning or strategic finesse.
This game fails to create true, fun duels. It creates a comparison NOT based on skill, but rather who's stupid enough to pay for intangible goods so they can defeat one of the approximately 20-40 players in this game (the few who can actually tolerate this unethical business practice). Which brings me to the next point.
You run into the same people again and again. That's because the devs focus too much on short term gain, instead of delivering a cool experience to people who would like to remain f2p.
Again: You can't blackmail people into purchasing some digital, mundane crap.
The way this FREE game punishes you for not wanting to buy some intangible crap is appalling. I can understand why so few people play this game. It's a wasteland.
I've had some good matches against people with similar amounts of cards or I should rather say "similar level of rarity".
In other words: If you accidently run into someone who's free-to-play, you might have a good duel. You know... the way it's supposed to be. But the rest of the time, you'll be used as cannon-fodder to give their "paying customers" a quick, meaningless win, at the expense of everyone's fun.
I can understand that the Devs want money. But damn, do they have to be so greedy and desperate about it?
They have proven that matches without pay-to-win mechanics are perfectly possible (whenever you happen to stumble across an opponent who's f2p). Which means they actively decided against creating fair and balanced matches, just so they can make a quick buck.
I feel sorry for everyone who actually falls for this kind of unethical "let's restrict access to CRUCIAL game-elements" manipulation tactic. It's transparent to everyone with 2 braincells to rub together.

Esto es Jogo Bonito: Kopanito
Juegos como FIFA y PES se van a los puños en sus intentos de ser el mejor simulador de fútbol, fallando de vez en cuando en sus intentos pues no logran ser lo esperado y se vuelven todo menos divertidos. Pero Kopanito All-Stars Soccer no es un simulador, es un arcade total, solo te preocupas por pasar la bola, disparar y barrerte, no hay truquitos ni jugadas de pared, esto es una legitima mejenga de barrio, sin arbitro y en eso es que brilla Kopanito.
Las físicas, los gráficos de lujo y jugaditas a los Neymar se dejan de lado en Kopanito, siendo reemplazadas por risas, barridas al hueso, tiros especiales, con un estilo gráfico muy ameno –Algo parecido a SouthPark, y llamativo que incluso niños pequeños encuentran super divertido. En Kopanito todo es diversión y aunque no logremos ganar, nos vamos con una sonrisa en el rostro pues el juego es pura loquera y no hay absolutamente nada malo en él.
El juego es fácil de aprender a controlar, como ya mencionamos antes, es super arcade, y más si usas un mando de Xbox, pasas el balón con A, disparas con X, centras con B al atacar, al defender lo único que tienes que hacer es usar B para barrerte y eso es todo. También tiene alguno que otro truco muy divertido como tiros especiales, tele-transportaciones (si, eso que hace Goku), hasta un abanico gigante nos ayudara a evitar que nos anoten.
Es muy entretenido hacer barridas como desquiciado por todo el campo de juego, tanto que había momentos en los partidos que solo me concentraba en intentar barrer a los contrarios en lugar de tratar de anotar, y fue divertidísimo, pues para lograr hacer contacto con los jugadores del otro equipo también hay que tener pulso, pero valió la pena ja, ja.
El juego es en 2D, acompañando su estilo arcade “semi-retro” de una manera excelente, su atractivo estético es su segunda mejor virtud, los detalles en los jugadores los hacen muy graciosos, nos harán reír a montones y más si jugamos acompañados en linea o de manera local, con jugadas increíbles y tarjetas rojas que nunca veremos llegar.
Aún en Early Access, Kopanito All-Stars Soccer viene con un sin fin de selecciones nacionales, muchas deberán ser desbloqueadas al jugar distintas copas o campeonatos de selecciones,  con posibilidad de hasta 5 controles a la vez de manera local (4 mandos y 1 teclado), con dificultades que incluso los niños pueden probar sin problemas hasta el más difícil que nos hará intentar romper el control.
Kopanito es divertido, rápido y  sencillo, los juegos de fútbol ya no te hacen reír, Kopanito All-Stars Soccer lo hará de sobra.
Más de 100 equipos nacionales, 16 torneos, 7 estadios y hasta 600+ jugadores únicos no son suficientes, pues también tenemos la posibilidad de crear nuestros propios equipos, estadios y balones. Los desarrolladores han incluido 4 distintas ligas por medio de Steam Leaderboards, empezaremos en la Liga Bronce donde conforme ganemos partidos de torneo (solos o co-op) obtendremos puntos de fama, lo cuales necesitamos para avanzar a las ligas mas altas.
Kopanito es divertido, rápido y  sencillo, si los juegos de fútbol ya no te hacen reír, Kopanito All-Stars Soccer lo hará de sobra. No me reía tanto al jugar un juego de fútbol desde… Bueno, es la primera vez que me río demasiado jugando un titulo de fútbol, no sabia que podía haber “friendly fire” en un juego de soccer, ja ja. Incluso si no te gustase el deporte practicado en Kopanito, te puede gustar demasiado jugarlo con amigos.

I did not want to give a negative review for this game as it is in early access, and the developer does seem to listen to the gamers and work hard, but after only few hours playing, I feel it was more negative then positive at this stage, even though there is a bit of potential in the game as well as an arcade football game.
However, the way the game is right now, all be it in early access, it is very tedious and frustrating and gets boring quite quickly.
The difficulty jump between each setting is quite high I found, and even on amateur was a challenge because the computer AI tends to be able time things very well indeed when for the player it is much more of a challenge, this is ok, but does get frustrating.
There also is not a lot to the gameplay, it gets very samey with so little options and things going on, you tend to get very bored quite quickly. pass, shoot, pass, shoot, pass, shoot with the odd sliding tackle now and again when you can time it right, and trust me, it's more difficult then you think.
As I say, I reluctantly make this a negative review, I wish there was an option for 'neutral' or 'mixed' as I did not hate it, but it did get tedious.
But I will still be following the progress of the game, and see where it goes as there is potential, but it does need a lot more things added to it because even as an arcade game there isn't much to it, obviously we don't expect Fifa options, but basic things like heading aren't even in the game, which while isn't a gamechanger, put ten or so little things like that to the game and it becomes better, The developer does seem to take notice of the feedback and I applaud him, but right now I won't be playing it again for a bit, but will still follow its progress.
Also PLEASE DO NOT listen to people saying it is a sensible soccer or kick off successor, it really isn't at all.

TIME SKIP. The game leaves early access and I suddenly decide that it's worth picking up and playing for a bit after getting a little burned out on The Witcher 3. Returning to it, I hadn't recognized how much depth there truly is in Crypt of the NecroDancer. You have to really plan each of your runs carefully: are you going to try to collect as many diamonds as possible? Are you trying to get to the exit as quickly as you can? It reminded me so much of how my girlfriend and I played through Rogue Legacy, where we had to determine if we intended on collecting as much gold as possible or if we should try to get to the boss rooms as quickly as possible.
No doubt the games soundtrack is really catchy and fun to listen to as well, as it should be. What I appreciate is that you're not really hindered significantly if you fail to keep in time with the music, outside of losing a coin multiplier.
I can't recommend Crypt of the NecroDancer enough. I have only a few hours logged in currently, partially due to the fact that the game is perfect for just picking up and playing for a few minutes at a time.

Short version: If you like JRPGs - particularly those from the sixth-gen before shooters with stats took over the RPG market - then I highly recommend Earthlock despite its flaws. If you don't like RPGs, then this one won't change your mind.
Most of the Earthlock reviews are very, very mixed, and this one will be no different. The easiest way to deal with this is to lay out everything it does well and everything it does badly.
What Earthlock does well: The game features a excellent combat system that's more tactical and satisfying than in most RPGs but without getting too quirky for its own good. It features a character level system that allows the player to easily build each character in several different ways. The overworld features yet another neat series of mechanics that allow the player to avoid random battles or manipulate them to increase experience. Basically, the developers tweaked the basic RPG gameplay enough to avoid the more common old-school design errors. And while the graphics aren't stellar, the design is exceptional - a visually unique world with a level of detail rivaling that of some S-E titles.
What Earthlock does badly: The game is pretty grind-heavy (especially with the poorly implemented farming system that means a patient player never runs out of healing items or ammo), but the big problem is the story. It's hard to explain the many problems with the plot without spoilers, but here's the gist: There's not much of a story for the first half of the game, just a series of extraordinary coincidences and unmotivated decisions to get the party together. Once the story does start up, it moved with headache-inducing speed, introducing new characters and plot points without really establishing them at all. I gather that this first game was meant to establish the world (and it is an interesting world with an interesting history), but the game doesn't even do a great job of that since most of the worldbuilding is in optional flavor text.
I still recommend Earthlock because when it comes to RPGs, I'm willing to forgive a weak story if the game has interesting mechanics - and Earthlock definitely delivers that. It's just frustrating because the developers avoided the world of old-school RPG gameplay snags while burdening the plot with excessive devotion to old-school RPG cliches. I hope they release another title, because I suspect that they will get better at this with time, and they're already more than halfway there - they just need to unlearn what they think they know about writing for video games.

I would suggest staying away from this one.
It adds nothing new to the 4x genre.  The development focus was on anything-but-4x.  Stardock focused on graphics.
The result is a buggy engine that is a total resource hog.  (But there's 3 layers of star fields to provide this amazing parallax scrolling effect!!! Lol.  Just what every grand strategy game has always been missing.)  This 4x game will require far more RAM and VRAM than any highly immersive FPS/RPG that you play.  Why?  God only knows.  The graphics aren't even that good.
with the graphics turnt up[sic] is less demanding than this game with them on low, and for the life of me, I cannot fathom why other than terrible, lazy engineering by Stardock.
But good luck turning down the GFX settings, even if you need to.  The game will not save the changes you make, even though you have to restart the game for them to take effect.  You will need to manually edit the pref.ini file, and do so again every time they patch the game.  That's quality assurance, right there.  Most of the time Steam shows me as playing this game has been working with Stardock support trying to debug it.  They have offerred nothing.  Not even an apology.
You don't get anything that GalCiv2 didn't have.  Personally, I think the UI is a regression.  Where all their development efforts apparently went was the ship designer.  You can spend an hour making one of your ships look like an Imperial Star Destroyer.  Exactly how long is that going to entertain you?  Especially when you consider that the camera work in battles is shoddy, at best.  If you want "gratuitous space battles," there are many SciFi games do better with flashier, more immersive combat.
All-in-all?  1 of 5 stars.  Stardock has ruined their brand in my eyes.  Everyone bombs a project once in awhile, but their utter lack of true customer service damning.  EA and Valve have been more willing to take responsbility for their mistakes, and that is truly saying something for anyone who has dealt with either of those companies.

Not a very good game. Not as good as any of the Civ's. Not even as good as Master of Orion 2. I have the impression that the software team was really tallented (the game runs well, no bugs, beautiful graphics etc), but the gameplay is just plain bad. Here is my list:
1. The tactical combat screen is pretty, but you have zero control....I have no words....Unbeleavable. I can't imagine why they would do this.
2. The AI is brutally bad. I played about 20 turns on beginner to get the hang of it. Then played a game on normal and won easily. Then played a game on expert and won easily. The AI makes a ton of obsolete ships and is rarely aggressive in any way. Also way too easy to see how an enemy is designing his ships (heavy on lasers, missles, or guns), and design against him. AI is oblivious to rock/paper/sissors system.
3. The diplomatic engine is bad. By 10% of the way through the game every civ hates me. But they still trade with me, often at pretty even terms. Even after I've pummeled them badly and offer peace they refuse. Your only options are: declare war and trade. You can't do anything else with the other civ's.
4. You can build pretty fancy starbases, but they are fairly weak, and get weaker as the game goes on. The AI NEVER attacks them. If the AI, or you, attack a planet with a starbase, the starbase is not part of it. This for me was another unbelievable WTF. The starbase doesn't defend the adjacent planet?
5. Obviously quite a bit of effort into the custom ship building, but you'd have to be nutty to be bothered doing it. So tedious. When you deck a ship out with 10 guns, they seem to all be able to fire at once, even if they're on the back of the ship.
6. Planet building is not great. Seems like every planet is always full and you can't do anything else. Gotta wait till you can open up a new hex.
7. The entire money system is trivial. You don't have to build any markets etc and it's easy to have enough money. I 90% ignored the monetary part of the game and it didn't matter
8. ok, the tech tree is pretty nice and well implemented
9. There are a bunch of galactic resources that the AI seems huge on collecting, but they have a trivial outcome on the game. They can be completely ignored
10. There is this insane mad scramble at the start of the game to colinize every available planet. No regard to how to defend these far off empires.
11. it is crazy easy to capture an enemy planet. You create a ship, put 3 million (or is it billion?) civilians in it, and it will defeat almost any enemy planet, even if there are 15 million people on it. The defensive improvements you can make give a trivial improvement to defence and you don't actually create solders or tanks. Lame.
12. I liked the way you could have multiple planets support a ship building dock
13. No spying. All you have to do is talk to other civs and you can see what techs they have and how they are decking out their ships.
Wow, that's more lame stuff than I would have guessed. Well, it's maybe not all that bad. I enjoyed it, but it wasn't a good game. I really think this was a result of the bad management dictating bad decisions. Oh well.

I'm giving this game a thumbs up with an asterisk.  This game's current state as of June 26th 2015 is uncomplete, but playable.
Normally I would not give a game a thumb's up for that, but this is the first 4x game that I'm aware of that truely utilizes multi-core processors and is built around a 64bit technology.  In the 4x world, this means far larger map sizes than you are used to dealing with, and finally make space feel like a vast expanse.
I can't state enough how big of a deal this is for this particular genre.  As a modder myself, memory restrictions have played a big part in not being able to go as far as my imagination would have liked to go.
Having played the previous two GalCiv games, I have complete confidence that the unfinished features will find themselves back in the game at some point.  If you're new to the series, or 4x genre in general, you may want to stay away from now, but if not, feel free to reward a developer for pushing the technological boundaries further.

I started playing this game about a month ago. I have attempted to play enough to finish the daily quest each day
as well as earn at least one booster pack per day when possible.
My opinion of this game is as follows.
The game is a scifi clone of Hearthstone...
That being said i feel it stands on its own two feet and surpasses Hearthstone.
The game is fairly user friendly but i do suggest new players go through the new deck guides found on the steam forum and within the game to get explanations about mechanics.
As a new player there will be some frustration as with any ccg you will start out at a disadvantage. But if you build one of the cheap decks found on the forum it will allow you to play and earn card packs to slowly get better.
The mechanics can be confusing at times because its not always made clear as to how they work or interact with each other.
The online matching system can be difficult since in the absense of someone your level or below you may get paired with someone much more skilled than you.
They balanced that by making ranked matches of person beyond 5 levels of your rank cost you  no rank points/rank exp.
The game does have many features which make it more appealing due to in game mechanics give weaker players a boost at the start of a match.
The developer is russian and i highly recommend participating in there twitch streams as they allow you to ask questions in both english and russian of the developers and they give out free packs etc.
I will say that some of the cards or paragons cannot be made via fusion and the only way to get them is blind luck through booster packs. Unlike Hearthstone you will not get duplicates of the same cards within the same pack.
I have found the booster packs very fair in distributing new cards vs repeat copies. the game also allows you to directly purchase specific cards with in game credits not real money but i have a hard time saving for them and would rather buy boosters with my in game money.
I high recommend giving the game a try. I play it on both PC, Ipad & Iphone.
the game plays the same on all devices with the random issues of ipad app closing once every blue moon or prolonged gaming on the ipad causing a memory leak effect to slow the game down forcing you to reboot the tablet. Granted that was after a 5 hour stretch of constant matches.

I first heard about ABZÛ not too long ago and was intrigued after finding out that the art director and composer from Journey, along with others who worked on the project had started their own studio and made ABZÛ their first project. The first question I had was, “What exactly is an ABZÛ?” Queue wiki, where an answer awaited:
Well, color me interested! How would this apply to ABZÛ the game?  As I was to find out through my journey into the deep waters of an unknown ocean, Giant Squid Studios ably crafted a fitting tribute to the legends while creating some lore of their own in the process. However, as is said, the journey is often as important if not more so than the destination itself, and with ABZÛ, this cold not possibly ring more true.
The story in ABZÛ is as much a journey of self discovery as it is an exploration of an ancient and lost world. Through various hieroglyphs, architecture, and ancient creatures found through the length and breadth of your journey, you find the remnants of a once great civilization. However, ABZÛ doesn’t hold your hand with its storytelling. Rather, the player (you) are left to seek out meaning as it best suits your sensibilities and love for a personal narrative experience. To me, this journey was about finding peace through observation, and the world specifically seemed like the lost land of Atlantis. You, a nameless diver/robot are quietly tasked with rebuilding this lost land that was clearly ruined and subjugated by an apocalyptic event. The beauty of a story like the one presented in  ABZÛ (and in its sort of predecessors, Journey, Flow, Flower) is that while some aspects of the story are clear, the rest is subjective and you can truly find your own story here. There is a strong resolution to the story, but revealing anything about that here would be revealing far too much. It is worthy of experiencing with no prior knowledge of what is to come.
8.5 out of 10
The gameplay was very good overall. ABZÛ is definitely a game that requires a gamepad to get the maximum effect, and the Steam product page recommends it directly. So, while you can use a keyboard and mouse, it is not recommended.
You will be underwater for the majority of this journey and will need to learn to swim. I didnt find this to be completely intuitive, as swimming is a twin stick affair. Initially, some of the controls will be inverted, but fortunately, the customization option is simple and an easy way to accommodate your preferences. That said, swimming will still be a trial and error deal for most. Once you get the hang of it, it becomes a seamless and awesome experience, but until that happens, ABZÛ can be frustrating. In addition to the twin stick camera and direction controls, you can also get a swimming speed boost, can roll to increase this boost, and as you get more familiar with the controls and your timing, you can string these together for limitless boosting of speed.
A popular and pleasing aspect of ABZÛ is your ability to breach, and as you get better at the controls, you can perform cool flips and such while breaching. Additionally, you can grab on to larger sea creatures, essentially riding them, and can also use them to perform awesome water acrobatics. This is an aspect of the game that has players coming back for more long after finishing the game.
You will find meditation statues to rest upon throughout your journey, and you can use this time to attach your mind to the various fish and other underwater critters in your area, travelling from on to another at will, and gaining a birds (fish) eye view of things. This is great example of how serenity is used as a gameplay aspect to grant you moments for introspection and at times, wide eyed wonder. The simple pleasure to be had with this gameplay aspect will also have you revisiting ABZÛ long after you complete the story.
For the most part, the other aspects of gameplay involve solving puzzles and interacting with objects to unlock or open up the next part of your adventure. There are some traps in certain sections of the game that you will need to try and avoid, and that is pretty much it as far as what you will be doing gameplay wise in ABZÛ.
I encountered zero bug, crashes, stuttering, or anything else that would break immersion. This was a seamless experience.
9 out of 10
The graphics in ABZÛ were sometimes very much reminiscent of Journey (which is no surprise as the Art Director for that game is the founder of Giant Squid Studios), but at other times, the graphics far exceed those of Journey, and reach awesome new heights. ABZÛ is imaginative and creative in appearance, and you can never really tire of taking in the impressive set pieces and scenery that make this game the amazing experience that it is. Brilliant, lush colors, excellent use of lighting to emphasize emotion….this is brilliance incarnate.
9.5 out of 10
The audio for ABZÛ were all about emphasizing mood. This means that  throughout your time with ABZÛ, you will presented with music that drives home a sense of peace and/or wonder, adventure and mystery, and at times, tension and almost fear. Austin Wintory, another of the folks that came over after working on Journey, truly does amazing work in capturing the moment perfectly through innovative and imaginative compositions. There is an unspoken tale to be told, and Wintory’s music is as much a part of it as anything else in ABZÛ. I daresay that without his brilliance, ABZÛ would be but a shadow of itself.
10 out of 10
ABZÛ is a game that will take you on an exhilarating adventure of body and soul. I rate this as a must own, must play game, and one of the premier offerings of 2016.

What a pleasant surprise! I bought this game on a whim, looking for JRPG-ish fare. While not a AAA title, this game is well worth the asking price.
Pros:
- Polished. No crashes or clunky controls.
- Decent, colorful varied graphics.
- Decent sound.
- Solid development system that includes skill trees, recipes, crafting and even bonding bonuses between characters.
- Constant challenge in both combat and puzzles.
- Unique party members. No two members alike.
- Cliched, yet adequate story.
Cons:
- Minor technical bug; if my controller gets disconnected, I can't get controller support without restarting the game.
- Few side quests. The ones that were there are unique and fun, but there aren't many of them.
- No gear. All development is done through stats. * I didn't miss this at all. Between the stats and the talents, customizable was satisfactory to me.
- Dialogue could be polished.
If you've played Oceanhorn, this game is to Final Fantasy 7 - 9 what Oceanhorn is to Zelda; a solid and enjoyable effort.
Plenty of room for a sequel! This game was a Kickstarter game and I'd gladly back a sequel.

I would like encourage dev with a thumb up because the game has some interesting positive but I can't because overall it's a very average RPG. In comparison Rip Mass Effect Andromeda looks like the 12th world marvel it isn't.
The controls port for PC are tedious because the mouse is almost not used. The combats are are weak, typical quick combats alas lacking a lot of interesting aspects. And the combat issue becomes major because there's a ton of boredom grinding and boring pointless repetitive combats. And even worse there's an intense respawning system making the repetitiveness infuriating. Finally the game is too much targeted to kids for my taste, it could be ok but I'm not in the mood for that. Even when considering it's more targeted to kids, it's still very average writing, too much average, or too often.
Still I admit the game has its charm and that's probably what's explaining its surprising success. Some example of positive in my point of view:
- The character/party building has interesting aspects.
- Despite it's too much kid oriented the game build a cute mood anyway, from graphics and world and a bit from lore writing.
- The first main character appealed me and increased my curiosity, but not at all the second main character and I lost patience before to find back first character.
- Despite map world is objectively with too simple graphics and too much lacking in details, the closer view than usual avoid to fall into boredom of never ending walk of those RPG open world with close range perspective, and it's an interesting approach even if obviously it could be improved.
- Despite plenty elements bring back the game to JRPG standard cloning and clichés, overall the game succeed build something partially original and that's pleasant.
I don't consider my review fair at all it's just reaction after some hours of play.

I've never reviewed a game before but this one compelled me too. I bought it for the beautiful graphics, but this was massively overshadowed by the dull, uninspiring and empty combat and dialogue. Do not recommend.

Bosses simply get one devastating attack, that you have to prepare against and the rest of the tactic becomes "who deals more damage faster". Also nearing the end the story and dialogue take a drastic turn towards the negative as if someone tried to rush the end (i. e. Aderyn).
I stopped playing shortly after arriving in the ice plains. Despite the fact that I was high-leveled fights just became harder and harder to a point, where even that was no fun anymore.
For anyone who loves old RPGs, grinding and doesn't care too much about a good written story, buy it please! They certainly deserve support for trying it, but I guess I'm just to spoiled by the games of my youth.

"Well if that's just the jokes they're showing in the trailer, the game must be awesome" i thought, unfortunatley not.

Crypt of the Nercodancer is a Dungeon Crawler game mixed in with a Rythem Movement system, as in you have to move to the beat of the song.
the game itself is pretty simple and Really easy to understand, The artstyle is really nice and pretty clean looking aswell and the soundtrack is easily one of the best, all 3 of them, original, EDM and Metal. Edit: 2 more were added a while ago! A chiptune soundtrack by the same person who made the shovel knight soundtrack & a Synthwave Soundtrack by Girlfriend records, Never fail to amaze with the different styles of remixes!
There are 10 Characters total, Each every different things, like bolt who moves at double the speed, or Aria who can't get hit or miss a beat (as in dies in 1 hit or missing a single beat.)
There are a bunch of different enemies, which also move to the beat with different patterns which are easy to understand, Each as moving every 2 beats or lunging forward after being hit once or even teleporting the player.
Even if you're someone who isn't great with hearing/listening, there's a guideline sort of thing at the buttom of the screen, which you could use to learn the beat.
Its a great game and i'm amazed the Devs Created this unique game. Easily Recommedable to friends, Especially with the OSTs.

Ok so this game here is a prime example of why Steam should allow users to have an 'its ok' button with which to review things, because thats exactly what this game is: its ok, its right smack dab in the middle of whether i could reccomend it or not. However, thats not to say that its a bad game, quite the opposite; it runs smoothly, the controls are intuitive, and the art style and graphics are fine at the very least.
But it is limited. If you get this game then dont really expect anything more than a time waster, a good time waster mind you, but thats about it. The simplicity of the game is also it downfall, making it very hard to play for advanced tactics, as you can LITERALLY run circles around the opponent and win.
It may also dissapoint anyone whos a fan of the more serious football games e.g. FIFA, because some basic game mechanics that you would expect to see are nowhere to be found. For example I will constantly pass to my team mate and start running with him, only to find that HE LEFT THE STUPID BALL BEHIND!!! And that was from a pass directly to him! So, yeh, players wont always latch onto the ball if you pass to them, also your friendly AI can be so stupid and not auto-run onto the ball if its landed right near them.
Dont be put off though, it still has some great mechanics which it utilises perfectly: for one, the slow-mo precision shots are great and pulling off a shot curved right around the keeper feels fantastic! Furthermore the power up system is a nice touch and all the power ups tend to balance out nicely, with some being more O.P than others but never to an unfair extent - yes im looking at you Blue Shell    >:(
I picked this game up on sale so really I'm quite pleased, but looking at its current full release price it would be hard to make a case for buying it, especially as its currently single player and local co-op only, though the developers are quite active and have said that theyre working on an online multiplayer feature, which honestly it really needs as the AI can be laughable at times, and ridiculously skilled at others, basically seems a little unbalanced.
If you do pick this up then I would strongly recommend playing with a controller, makes the game way more friendly for new players, however be aware that if you pause a match using the controller, you will have to press A/X (xbox/ps) to resume the match which, because of the button mapping, will make your player pass the ball unintentionally, or just change players all together - Very Annoying so try and remember to use the mouse to close the pause menu.
In summary, yes definitely pick this game up on sale, but give it a little thought before purchasing at full price. However you can completely ignore me on that one if the devs have added in more features, because online multiplayer would definitely make the price tag more appealing.

Knights of Honor, while certainly not unique from the dozens of other Paradox published or produced map based games, Appeals to me as the most accessible for new time players, while still easily one of the more fun ones for more advanced gamers. Its core gameplay was easy for me to understand with 25 minutes, and I had mastered many of the simple tasks by the end of an hour, allowing me to start bigger and better parts of the game.  The game is laid out similar to Total war, where you control a country during a time of war and unrest (In this case, during the medieval ages). The game is largely map based, and while it has RTS type battles, I recommend leaving it to the AI auto battle system, as that is a lot less frustrating and tedious.  The games highlights for me are based around its well balanced uses of espionage, religion, economy, military and diplomacy. Any of these may be used to achieve total victory, or a unique combination of them. This allows the player to choose their play style, unlike Total war, where you are trapped in a looping cycle of battle.  Like all games, KoH has its share of problems, and a few of them are major. On some machines, the highest available resolution is 800 X 600, which looks very odd on modern monitors. Un-skippable start up logos that last around 1 minute each time is annoying and makes launching the game a pain. Actual in game issues are few in the area of glitches, but some sections of the game are cruelly tedious, like rebellion and currency inflation. While it may be open for debate if these ruin the game, it definitely adds another dimension to the gameplay.  While KoH may not be on the same level of polish as other map – based strategy games, it should not be forgotten, especially for the bargain price of $9.99.

A good light grand strategy game to get your feet wet in such games. In comparison to Crusader Kings 1/2 and Medieval 2: Total War, it is very arcadey.
You can take the known world by pure conquest or by subterfuge using spies, or even by demanding another kingdom recognize your right to certain lands due to to a royal marriage.
That said, there is no family tree history. There is just your current ruler (King, Emperor, Sultan, Caliph, Khan, whatever), his wife (either an "ordinary noblewoman" or a woman they married from another kingdom), and their sons and daughters. Only your sons may inherit, you can choose which one becomes king but this can cause some issues. Your daughters can only be married off for royal marriages/alliances.
The campaign map is akin to a total war game's campaign map, except in real-time. You can pause or speed up time, however. The battlemap plays out with you actually ordering individual units, and even your marshal (you can not send an army out without a marshal) + his bodyguard, to fight (whether in a field battle or siege). It has the look of a cleaner age of empires 2: the conquerors, in terms of graphics. You may opt to instead let battles auto-resolve (certain marshal traits only apply in auto-resolve). Naval battles are always auto-resolved, and can never be fought manually.
The A.I. was purportedly developed simply to entertain the player (it was discussed on the old black sea studios forums), rather than actually challenge them, even on Hard difficulty, but this is more or less the case with pretty much any video game in existence that has functional artificial intelligence, anyway. The game has surprised me a few times, like when I had no heirs to inherit the throne, and it turned out the nobleman whom took the throne for himself (a lord I hired to act as a merchant to earn more gold) was actually a spy for another kingdom... And so he dutifully handed the crown over to said kingdom, and suddenly game over.
It still has great entertainment value, however. And there is even a modding community for it, and once you've mastered the game on the "Hard" difficulty setting, there is a "Hard" modification that makes the A.I. into a totally unrepentant warmonger once you've reached a certain amount of provinces, though they can declare war before that point.

I'd been wanting to play this game for many years after first hearing about it back when it was new -- a Diablo clone during the action-rpg drought of much of the 2000s, with all these nice features like a permanent pet that can hold and sell your junk for you while you adventure?  Sounded awesome.
Of course, much time passed and I ended up playing Torchlight and its sequel before this game.  And on that note, I can go ahead and give you the meat of the review:
And yes, I know it's by the same guys and came before Torchlight -- but there's really no reason to play this instead; there's absolutely nothing that this game does better, or even as well, and they're quite succinctly the exact same game only with Torchlight being newer and more improved.  It's not like how they're both direct clones of Diablo 1 but that game has a unique atmosphere and gamefeel that makes it still very much worth playing separately; no, these games are *the exact same thing*, except Torchlight is better.
Torchlight has classes; Fate does not.  Fate makes you play a generic character whose un-alterable starting stats are those of a warrior class, even though, for example, playing as a mage is very powerful.  Likewise, Torchlight has an actual skill tree system a la Diablo 2 whereas Fate has a flat page of skills of which no playstyle will ever need to put points into more than 3 or 4 max.
Torchlight has a variety of visually luscious dungeon areas, a unique backdrop to each set of floors, whereas Fate hits you with a generic and unappealing handful of locales randomly chosen floor-by-floor.  Torchlight also offers enemies cohesive to the area at which you fight them to some degree whereas Fate throws a random mishmash of almost every enemy in the game in your direction each floor, with lower floors having you see a bit more larger stuff along with 'elite' and 'legendary' versions of the smaller stuff to make their HP pools monsterous; there is no rhyme or reason.
Torchlight has a massive amount of powerful equipment to find and collect, offering you many build options and ways to increase your power, while Fate quickly makes you realize a simple and painful truth; farm the shops until you have the maximum gem slots possible in every piece of equipment, then farm the mage shop until you have the required amount of superior gems, asap.  There's your endgame equipment; if you're lucky enough to find higher-tier stuff later with the required sockets then good for you, but don't hold your breath.  And this goes for all playstyles.
Torchlight has a defined endgame, final floor and final boss, and then a separate 'infinite' dungeon to test your skills if you want to keep playing.  Fate gives you a randomized boss monster on a random floor and then gives you the option to go deeper in the same dungeon for no real reason.  I will say that the 'descendant' system is interesting, but is it really worth it?  Oh sure, you can become insanely powerful and tear up the dungeons for hundreds of levels if you really want, but you've seen all the game has to offer by floor 20 or so max, and by the time you get to your final boss situated 2 or 3 times deeper than that you'll be well and truly done with the game.  Even the powerful endgame unique equipment that serves as the carrot-on-a-stick for many action-RPG players is a joke, here -- as far as I can tell, you can get *all* uniques even extremely early in the game via fishing holes, and though some seems tantalizing at first you quickly realize their benefits are still not comparable to a socketed, plain version of the same item; and while a socketed unique may be the ideal, good luck with that.  You'll never find them socketed already, and if you dare spend millions of gold at the enchanter in the tiny off-chance you'll get one added (when ideally you'd want 2 or more), you're liable to revert the item to a powerless piece of scrap.
So all in all?  Yeah, no.  Skip it.  Play Diablo, Diablo 2, Diablo 3 (yes, Diablo 3), Titan Quest, Grim Dawn, Path of Exile, the Van Helsing games, and any other action-RPG before you think about this one.  And especially Torchlight.  Because it's literally the exact same game but better in every conceivable way.
That being said, I am still going to check out the other Fate games and see if they're... fated... for better reviews.  Heh.  Haha... *cough*

FATE is really good, particularly for a decade-old game. The graphics are simple, but cute and colorful. The music's cheerful. And the gameplay is a simple concept that really keeps you engaged. In my case, this definitely isn't nostalgia speaking, and I'm not looking at it through the rose-colored lenses of my childhood. I never played it, or any others in the series, until recently. And it's kind of impressive just how well this game has held up over time.
The game's premise, borrowed liberally from the original Diablo, is a basic dungeon-crawler RPG. Each level of the dungeon is randomly generated and filled with items and monsters. Villagers in town will give you quests tied to specific levels, and you journey in and out of the dungeon as you complete your tasks. You can only take three quests at a time, and it's up to you whether you take the maximum on every level and explore every corridor, or rush through on your way to the final boss.
As you complete quests and hack and slash your way through the dungeon's monsters, you gain experience, and leveling up allows you to increase your skills and stats in specific areas.  Looting dungeons gives you gold and items, and there are also several vendors in town who can sell you items, or perform various services. You can also earn money (and find rare items) by catching fish in the fishing holes found throughout the game.
Got too much stuff to carry around in the dungeon? No problem. You'll have a pet, an un-killable companion that can also ferry your junk to town in exchange for gold. Your pet can also help fight enemies, but it will flee if its health gets too low and be no use in the fight. If the basic cat or dog isn't powerful enough, you can feed your pet fish in order to transform them into different monsters found in the game. If this sounds an awful lot like Torchlight, it's pretty evident that FATE was a huge influence on that game.
There is a main story quest that is basically just a harder boss on some random level close to lvl 50. Since the levels are generated randomly, you could just keep playing by continuing down for thousands of levels. Even without the practically unending dungeon, randomly generated levels and a pretty big combination of skills and gear gives FATE almost infinite replayability. This is actually featured in the game well, since finishing the main quest allows you to create a "descendant" character. This new character can keep one "heirloom" item but begin his or her own adventure. It's especially cool that you can also import characters from FATE into the sequels as well, heirlooms and all.
As an RPG, FATE is not terribly deep. But it is a lot of fun, and it's a great – if somewhat casual – way to blow off steam while crawling through maze-like dungeons and blasting or slashing your way through colorful mobs of creatures.

A good successor to the first game.
That said, It did have problems.
The gameplay, more specifically the combat, in my opinion didn't get better, in fact it just turned more frustrating.
For starters, the targetting system is an utter failure.  Now you say, "Can you elaborate?".  My response to that is not really, so if you are expecting Batman Arkham Asylum smoothness in regards to targetting, prepare to be disappointed.  Second, the practicality of Geralt's sword combat.  When in comparison to the first game it had three fighting stances:  The strong stance, reserved for heavy/bulky enemies; the fast stance, for the quick and agile enemies; and the group stance, for those times when you were outnumbered and surrounded.  In the Witcher 2, those stances were thrown away and combat became streamlined by replacing it with light attacks by clicking the left mouse and heavy attacks by pressing the right mouse.  That doesn't sound bad, right?  In some cases, yes, it worked out fine.  But there were some instances where this new combat mechanic just sucked completely.
The big problem is that the new mechanic didn't leave it as straightforward as the first game.  Geralt in this game does his super stylish spins in the worst of occasions.  Where in the Witcher 1, he did his spin attacks more in his group stance to keep from being overwhelmed, and in this game he does his spins for the sake of spinning, whether you are surrounded or not.  Sometimes when you want him to do a wide slash spin when surrounded, he doesn't, or when you want to do powerful but quick attacks on one or 2 opponents, he does his spins and all that time he used up spinning he gets hit like the idiot he was.
TL;DR  You have less control of the swordplay in the Witcher 2 in comparison to the Witcher 1.
Next up is the potions/enhancements.  Oh god...  This was probably the most frustrating bit.  In the Witcher 1, you could go into your inventory and drink a potion.  Before or during combat, and the effects lasted much longer.  Simple as that.
In the Witcher 2, you have to predict when combat will show up, sit down, drink, have him♥♥♥♥♥♥around for another 10 seconds, stand up, then you are good to go.  And no, you can't drink potions during combat.  So, if you show up at a boss fight with no potions in your system, you are screwed.  You either have to go back a save or two, drink the potions on the prior knowledge of meeting the boss/hard part and beat it/them, or you have to bite the bullet and beat it/them without potions.  Hilariously enough, you can enhance your armor and weapons during combat.  Why not stay consistant?  I don't know.  Even worse, the potion effects only last 10 minutes (a tiny bit more if you have devote your levels to the alchemy skills).
TL;DR  Your potion usage is restricted (in comparison to the prequel again).
What else...  The game is shorter in content overall and in my opinion feels just a little bit more linear and less open.
Oh, and the game's soundtrack doesn't feel as memorable as the first.
So far, everything from the above is dedicated to those who played the first game.
If you haven't, then it won't really change anything.
OTHER THAN THAT....

I'm sorry I have to write this. First of all, I love Galactic Civ 2. I think it was and arguably still is one of if not the best 4X TBS games, and I have 1000+ hours in it. I did buy the $99.99 elite edition so I get all of the DLC and expansions free, so I still have hope.
Unfortunately, GC3 just isn't as fun. I have many problems with the game; here are a few that really annoy me.
1. Economy/Hapiness- This is the one thing I really hate about GC3. In GC2 managing the economy, taxes and production capacity was one of my favorite parts of the game. It's all gone. Tax rate can not be adjusted, instead you only get the wheel to adjust where spending goes. Hapiness also sucks now. For example, I was playing on largest size map. I was suffering from large empire penalty, an awful addition, and was building two stadiums per planet to maintain hapiness. Finally, I just stopped caring. My global hapiness dropped to 7%, with most planets at 0%. Guess what happened? Absolutely nothing. Planets are supposedly more suceptible to invasion and grow slower, but not a single one leaves. In GC2, you would literally die if you did this. One time in GC2 I changed tax rate from 39% to 100% for one turn to bail our my economy, and my citizens literally killed me, taking 119 of my 120 planets, leaving my relpacement I played as with a clsss 4 and half a fleet.
2. Pacing- Somehow this is pure awful also. I am 250 turns into a game, and havent met a single other civ. I dont think exploration was changed; what changed is how long turns take. All units must have orders, and this doubles turn length. In GC2, I could get through 50 turns in 5 minutes if I wasn't at war. In GC3, I would be lucky to get 50 turns out in an hour. The era lock on technologies is also bad, making all civs make mearly identical research choices.
3. AI/War- GC2 has an amazing AI. Better than the AI from any other strategy game I have seen since or before. GC3 throws this legacy away and instead goes in the direction of CIv V's AI (Not that Civ IV had great AI, and Civ V is good enough that I have 2000+ hours on it) aand is awful. Especially in warfare, AIs are completely incompetent. GC2 Ais were on par with me most games, but GC3 AIs suck at politics completely.
4. Ideology- While I very much like the concept, many policies need to be curbed or removed. There is a neutral on tthe FIRST level that makes it so you cant declare war on whoever gets it for 50 turns(about an hour of gameplay) which I hate, especially because minor races will always take it and other majors as well righht as you are about to invade them. Many others are overpowered; for example a malevolent one gives 5 transports, which have 6b population each. At the point of the game you can get it, this literally doubles your population if you land them.
There are other things that annoy me as well, but theses are the most game breaking. If the devs want to fix this game, they should:
-Re-Implement GC2 economy features
-Remove large empire penalty for all civs- May be why many races stay small and never meet you
-Let players end turn if units need orders
-Fix AI- Need to be way more agressive and expansionist
-Rebalance economy
All in all, I do think that this will eventually be a really fun game. As for now, GC2 is better. If you are considering buying this, instead go for GC2. It is really modern despite it's age, even supporting 1920x1080 resolution, though the UI is dated.

This is similar to a rogue-like game (procedurally generated, permadeath, hard to beat). I'd recommend FTL before this, but it's still a great game, a sort of bridge between casual gaming and hardcore gaming in that you can play it for 20-30 minutes at a time without having to sink all the way down into an immersive experience.
Despite the adorable aesthetics, the subject material is incredibly dark. The story unfolds more through the glimpses between levels rather than a direct narrative, but (mild spoilers ahead) it deals with child abuse, depression, suicide, the perils of religious fanaticism, and ultimately the freedoms and dangers of imagination. But I don't believe it quite hit the mark...
Heavy subject material doesn't necessarily
a heavy handed narrative. Psychonauts is a great example of representing deeper issues through colorful facades. However, in the Binding of Isaac, the full tilt whimsy out-shouts and undermines the messages or emotions we might take away from the game. It feels a bit akin to watching an Adam Sandler movie about the Holocaust. It's hard for me to be affected by an emerging theme, when the theme is drowning in poop jokes.
But as far as simple, fun, repeatable gameplay, it's the worth the low price of admission.

Music

Combat
Combat is turn based with each character using a set action points, that are regenerated each turn with differing upper and starting limits, that are used to for different actions.
Story
The story line is fairly generic to RPG's, but is enjoyable none the less.
Exploration/side quests
There is a limited amount of exploration/side quests in the game as it is a short game, but I don't think that is a bad thing. The limiting of exploration/quests keeps you moving through the game at a good pace, without having to really grind to acheive good progress.
Character types
The character types again are steriotypical:
Mage/healer
Tank/Warrior
Thief/Ranged
Trapper/Ranged
Blue mage/Support

I really wish the ratings system was not binary, because while I do recommend this game, I have my problems with it.
First of all, its a JRPG through and through. I will say that it does a lot of things RIGHT. The combat and experience felt good and unique. I never found the normal battles to be a slog, and while the bosses weren't incredibly difficult, they all had their own mechanics that would usually take me a bit to understand. The gameplay itself is very good, and I think that's the only reason I recommned this game, because literally everything else is very hard to recommend.
A huge part of being a JRPG is having a believable world with fleshed out characters and understandable motives for why certain things are being done. In this game I found next to none. While the game went through the motions of "character development", nearly everything is done for the sole purpose of "that's where the game wants us to go next". I found nearly every bit of dialog to be incredibly shallow, and the story really takes a nose dive near the end where it seems like development was rushed.
In short, the game itself is just a classic JRPG with a unique and fun twist to combat and character progression and customization, but falls extremely short of being a satisfying game due to extreme flaws in the story telling and world building. If I could rate it numerically, I would say it is a 6/10. The game is not bad, and it kept me entertained, but by the end I was playing just to finish it to say I got value out of the game, not because I particularly cared what happened to any of the characters.

Do you like copious amounts of dungeon crawling that never ends? Then Fate might be for you. I've clocked in over 50 hours on this game this past year and I really had no idea what the end game goal was. I got it into my head at some point that it would all be over at Level 100. There'd be this grand baddie that I'd face off with my minions in an epic battle and I'd prove victorious. When that never happened and I was at Level 103 I became suspicious. Turns out I just had to go to floor 51. I over shot my goal by 52 floors.
That proves 2 things. One, I clearly wasn't informed of where I had to go and two, the game doesn't do a good job of informing you of your goal except at the very beginning. I would have never guessed that the old wizard at the entrance was who you needed to talk to to get your end goal. Unlike all the other town folk who have a big exclamation mark above their heads when they have quests for you the guy with the end quest was just chilling at the entrance so I never spoke to him every time I went to town. That's just poor informing on the game's part. Not to say that I didn't thoroughly enjoy this game and if I wasn't trying to complete the achievements, one of which I didn't get until I was somewhere around Level 100 I probably wouldn't have played for so long.
This game is a grind but there's lots of loot and villagers supply you with endless quests for you to keep going and going and going. Weapons and armor are plentiful but I found item enhancements to help more than picking the weapon with the highest attack power. My favorite armor was one with a defense rating of 42 but it had a bunch of buffs that increased my damage by 40% and my dexterity by 70%. It also helped that it absorbed 9% of damage dealt. You'll also find out pretty quick that your starting animal is useless. Find fish to transform it as much as you can until you get one that you can live with. I particularly liked the Ebony Stalker. Summon spells are also your friend. I can't count how many times I was killed in seconds by mobs of enemies. So get yourself a Venomous Wyvern summon and always have 6 around you. They don't do much damage but they sure do come in handy when you want enemies to target something that isn't you.
This is Duracell bunny of dungeon crawlers. That being said if you like Fate you'd love Torchlight. It's just like Fate only better and it has an actual story as a plausible reason for your dungeon crawling that comes to a clearly defined end.

Well, I did it. After about 13 hours of total game time I've perfected hotline miami (four of those attempting to get the "Plain luck" trophy) so I feel like I can give a decent review now. Short story: hotline miami is a fun game that'll make you tear hair out from time to time. Long story: hotline miami is a fun, fast paced over the top slasher game with many different weapons; melee and ranged, masks (each mask give you a certain perk or weapon you start with) and niches. You can play quietly with melee/executions only, or you can go guns blazing with shotguns, rifles, uzis, etc. The story itself is very confusing, you take control of a
man named jacket who is recieveing strange phonecalls that tell him to go to certain locations and kill everyone he comes in contact with.  You don't get a definitive answer as to where these calls come from unless you find all the hidden puzzle pieces, assmble them in the right order, and enter them as a password on one of the final levels. Otherwise, it's a big "Oh you don't know, lol" mystery. It isn't until hotline miami 2 that you get your background and real answers. As for how the game performs the combat is MOSTLY smooth and fluid, however there are times that bullets will go through people, enemies will shoot through walls, or melee hits don't register, but you're dying so much anyways it's not a big deal.
Overall I feel hotline miami is a great, fun, gory game with a few problems that can be overlooked.
If you can, buy this and hotline 2, then play them back to back.
Edit: after researching the lore a lot, jacket isn't schizophrenic but rather suffers from memory loss and the "schizophrenic moments" are actually coma induced dream sequences. Woops.

**NOTES:
- I played around 50 hours of Mafia III on the PS4, so don't be fooled by the few hours I've spent on the PC port. Check my username on PSN: Goldenhawk5219 and see my Trophies from Mafia III I have earned.
- I will be updating this review as I play the game and finish everything. I will also talk about the DLC's as I finish them.
- I have had the game crash to the desktop without errors while doing races and while I am aware that everybody's PC's have different hardware and software setups, somebody has shown me a solution to this problem. If the game crashes to the desktop, it may be your graphic's settings. First, turn your V-Sync on and turn your framerate down to 30 FPS. If that doesn't work, turn your graphics settings down until the game stops crashing. I seriously doubt the developers will be releasing anymore patches or updates since they are probably done with this game and don't give a damn about quality unfortunately, so I wouldn't go waiting for that.
-------------------------------REVIEW---------------------------------------------------
- GRAPHICS/DESIGN: The world they have made is really great and feels like the developers put a lot of time into the map with well put together buildings; parking lots in the right spot; well correlated and consistant street signs, and road paintings; pedestrians talk to eachother and make comments and react to what you are doing; different districts having different levels of economy with diverse vehicles, police behaviors, and so on to give it a sense of being in a different part of town; so on and so forth which is VERY MUCH appreciated. The world feels very alive. In fact, the world's design is one of the most detailed and well put together I have ever seen in an open world game and tramples over GTA V's! The game's textures certainly look much better than Mafia II, but it feels outdated already and the graphics certainly don't feel like a 2016 game and feel more like it's a few years behind. Alot of the textures are low-res. Also, the sky is the most ugly looking blotch I have ever seen in a modern video game and looks like something you'd see if you were on mushrooms. Sky in Super Mario 64 looks way better. Also the world always looks like there is a extremely annoying brown haze to it whether it be the weather affects or the lighting itself. This may be due to the developers trying to give it this "oldies" look to it but it is more annoying than anything and looks so ugly.
- GAMEPLAY: The PC version is not very well optimized and you will need a beast to run it at full constant 60 fps at high settings. With other games I can play like Forza Horizon 3, Forza 7, and Rise of The Tomb Raider on high to very high at a constant 60 fps, but with this game, it jumps from 35 to 58 fps at high settings. Driving in the game to me is really fun, especially the weight the vehicles feel in the game. A lot of vehicles feel pretty realistic when it comes to drifting and weight distribution which is really neat in making them feel unique to their time era. The map in the game is pretty cool and this time around there are swamp areas, suburban, and city areas to explore in which you can now drive boats. There are also aligators in the game in which you can kill to defend yourself. There are collectible magazines, propoganda posters, albums, and paintings you can collect and rather than trying to figure out where they are by yourself or by Googling them in Mafia II, there are blips in the map this time to tell you where they are. The combat is terrible, very repetitive, and gets hilarious to see that the only two or three kill moves you have are ones that are one-hit kills. The police AI is terrible this time around from previous entries and is not fun at all. Alot of the little details like turning light in your apartment or house on/off, opening and closing the hood of your car, turning the faucets on/off, strategic combat, refilling the gas tank in your car at a gas station, washing your car, sophiusticated car damage, so on and so forth are not present in this game either like they were in Mafia II. Much less attention to detail. There are still many bugs and glitches that can even prevent progression in the game.
- STORY: It's just bleh... Thats it. It's ok. There are a few pretty unique things to see like being on a sinking boat, infiltrating and drugging people's drinks at a golf country club, and interrupting a big KKK meeting at night with molotov cocktails, but that's about it. They did very good in how the story is presenting with very well scripted cutscenes and surprisingly great voice acting! IT's just sad to see that potential wasted on what could have been a really good story. Not only is the story unimpressive, but the missions are EXTREMELY repetitive. For the most part it's: "Go kill these people and destroy things in stores in this district. In result, have the underboss come out so you can either kill him or have him work for you to get more money." Rinse and then repeat many times until you have all the districts. Many of these underbosses look the same and is so obvious they used the same character models for different underbosses. Now the ending....well you'll just have to find out. Let's just say it's not really satifying.
- DLC'S:
a) Faster, Baby!: There is a whole new area added to the map at the South-Western side called "Sinclair Parish". It is about 3/4 the size of the swamp area, Bayou Fantom. It's a huge countryside with farming fields, a cute town area with a sherif's department and A LOT of jumps. This time they added select destructible stores which you can drive your car through. There are also conveniently placed truck trailers with tree logs on the side of roads that you can shoot and the load falls over after you pass by them to temporarily stop cops in their tracks. The first few missions are really fun because you cut through wheat fields, make jumps, and run away from the cops like you are in a 60's or 70's action movie. However, later on it gets boring as you do favors for people and the ending is really anti-climactic for me as it ended earlier than I thought with an unsatisfying conclusion. The story itself isn't all that interesting and the characters are forgettable. The missions from this DLC can be beaten within just a couple of hours. Within the first couple missions, you get a new sports El Camino-like vehicle that is almost as indestructable as the armored van. You also get to grow your own weed as you plant, grow, and sell your crops to certain districts and each district has their own stats with different numbers of profit margins. As you grow weed in your greenhouse, your weed crops level up and you can upgrade things like the lamps, fertilizer, water, etc. to grow them faster and get different seeds and create new strands to get more profit.
b) Stones Unturned: This one has you tavel in a laughably small boat with your partner, John Donovan to a beautiful uncharted island in Vietnam via cutscene after the first few missions. The island is ABSOLUTELY gorgeous and the scenery looks almost identical to the scenery in Dead Island remaster. The rain forest is Uncharted-level Grade A design with cool looking abandoned buildings and old wrecked planes and an abandoned WWII underground Russian bunker. Unfortunately, the Island level is built for linear play and cannot be returned once the story mission is finished.
- OVERALL/CONCLUSION: Is it worth the $40 price? No. As of now, this game is on sale for $20 and that's when I got it. Is that price justified for this? Maybe. It feels unfinished after a year and still needs work done on it. If the developers would have given it at least another year, it would have been much better. I still like the game in many ways, but I feel it's an unrecommended purchase.

No game could possibly live up to the hype that has been created around Final Fantasy VII for the last decade and a half. It would have to be the second coming of Christ to meet half of the inflated expectations built up around it. So let me be clear: this game is not perfect. In fact, in a lesser JRPG, this many flaws would absolutely ruin the game. The dialogue is wooden when not completely stupid, typos and mistranslations abound (at one point, an ally tells you to do the EXACT OPPOSITE of what you're supposed to), and the battle system is derivative at best (yes, even for the time it came out). The villain is not nearly as awesome as many would like to think, lacking any reasonable motivation, and the game pulls Aerith out of your party after an entire disc's worth of levelling her up.
All this makes it sound like I'm coming down on Final Fantasy VII, but I actually really love this game. For all its myriad problems, it still manages to have the most important thing in any game: it is a freaking blast to play. While the battles are nothing new, they are fast and furious, with all kinds of explosive spells and special techniques to play with. Each character also has a Street Fighter-style meter that fills up when hit or attacked, which lets you pull of some truly ridiculous super-moves when it's full. The story is simple and to-the-point, and cribs quite a bit of plot and concept from the 1988 film "Akira", but provides more than its share of fun set-pieces, including a giant casino and amusement park, and a truly apocalyptic final boss fight. It delivers its environmentalist message with all the subtlety of an anvil storm ("The planet's dyin', Cloud!"), but you can't help but cheer the colorful cast on in their struggles against the Shinra Electric Power Company. Even if it's not told in the most professional way, the spirit of the story shines through clearly.
Which may be why this game succeeds in the end, the
of the thing. The gameplay, despite the jump to 3D graphics, has changed hardly at all from the previous SNES and NES adventures, and the fusion of old-school gameplay and modern(ish) graphical style makes this one a compelling play. Nobuo Uematsu's concert-hall ready compositions give the game a great cinematic feel, and the epic scope of the game's story is complemented perfectly by the sound and visuals. in spite of its (many) flaws, you can tell the development team at Square put their heart and soul into this one, and it pays off.
