I know i've only played for 22 hrs, but i've played enough to notice some very fundamental things about this game.
First time playing a Galactic Civ game and was dissapointed. I usualy love strategy games of all types, and especially anything space based or science fiction, but this game was a dissapointment. I'm not saying it's a terrible game, but it's definitely not better than a 6/10- and definitely not worth 60$, but with the price drop now to 38$- possibly, but I wouldn't expect much. Here are my main reasons why not and why to get the game:
Why not:
1. AI is suuuuuuuuper easy. I played through the campaign on normal(keep in mind this is my first time playing a Galactic Civ game), and winning basically came down to 2 things. Build factories and shipyards, build fleets, and build money factories, then repeat 1000 times. This makes the game highly repetitive, unless you go out of your way to make it harder on youself- which is ridiculous. This also kind of nullifies 90% of the rest of the content in the game that is entirely unnecessary to learn to win. Research for example; all I did was research weapon technology, hull stuff, and logistics(fancy word for how many units you can stack in a tile), and I was able to win almost all engagements.
There are dozens of ship classes which STAY WITH THE SHIP FOREVER which tells the ship in battle what to target and where to go. Assault ships for example, will rush right in and target another class.(I managed to win the Campaign without learning what any of the classes do). You can either build preset ships with classes, or build your own ships and assign it a class. All of this is completely unnessary to learn in order to win. This is just one of many examples of features in game which make things unnessarily complicated.
2. Game is highly repetitive. I kind of mentioned this above, but there's a lot more features in game which are a grind.
I'll highlight my petpeeves; Galactic events/Planet Events/Player Event choices/Building stuff on planets/ Micromanaging planetary production, wealth, and research(I didn't even bother doing it, and only build production and money factories every single time). Also, the choices you make in game are a joke. You either have Benevolent, Pragmatic, or Malevolent, which means 90% of the time you're either: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and love everything(even non-sentient robots), use things strictly to your advantage, or are a psycopath. There is no reasonable, rational person choice, and there are hardly ever win-win decisions. The EXACT same dillemas will often appear in the same game over and over again as well.
3. The campaign is 3 missions long. I kid you not, and the story is just as short the missions. It's as follows: SPOILERS(not that it's interesting or surprising anyways) Earth needs to be saved. Rebuild Civilization, Build Fleets, Take back Earth. I was expecting conflicts with other races, other than the one you're fighting, but there wasn't. You have the option to declare war or ignore other races, and I ignored them, and it didn't matter at all.
4. The story was bad. Yes. It had NO MAIN CHARACTERS too. It was as follows(spoilers); Earth taken by Drengin, you fight Drengin and take area around Earth back with ships. The whole game I was annihilating the Drengin and tried to negotiate ANYTHING, and they wouldn't even SPEAK TO ME.
5. Micromanaging is a headache. It would take a while to go into detail with this point, suffice it to say there are a lot of terribly inificient features and designs which make doing simple things a hassle. From managing production of planets to using the galaxy map, this is not user friendly and takes a while to learn, and once you do it's still very annoying and inificient.
6. After playing for 22 hrs I still havent figured out fully how to watch the ship battles the way I want to. Every time I try to go into the free mode and move my mouse a TINY TINY bit, my view is instantly jerked a mile away from the battle, and I'm luck if I can get back with the non-sensical sidways inverted 10000 sensitivity controls.
Why to buy:
1. THOSE CINAMATIC GRAPHICS LOOK GREAT!!!!!!
2. The pictures in the galactic events/planet events/ diplomacy look fantastic. Only wish the rest of the game was up to that level of work.

Overall, disappointed.

7 hours in and I feel okay doing first impressions:
This game is solid. Insane amounts of ship customization, lots of interesting stuff to do, decent UI, and generally a pretty good game.
There are a few minor gripes:
It's entirely possible that I'm just missing it, but there doesn't seem to be a place to set ship tactics (evade, assault, hold at distance, etc), nor does there seem to be a place to set a patrol route for ships or anything like that. It's not end of the world, but being able to set ship tactics seems like a good idea. Again, maybe I'm missing the place for it, but then again that'd be a problem with the UI.
There doesn't seem to be a password protection thing for setting up multiplayer games. Again, minor annoyance since you can kick anyone you don't want in your game during the lobby, but still.
The ship designer isn't super intuitive when you're making an entirely new design. It seems alright for altering existing designs, but making a new one is a bit odd.
All in all it looks like this will have a lot of staying power. Not bad at all.

Lieat is a very good story. Isn't much of a game. I recomend it.
Short story long, Lieat is a peice by peice story that entales the "Current off the past" Story of a Con man who cares for a young girl. THe what and the why is for you to find out, as this game lives and, dare I say, dies by it's story. This is not a game, it is a story with game elements. A cut ahead of visual novels but a cut behind an RPG horror game. I think it wears its place well.
The game has a nice style. Everything is original to the game, and it's all well done for it's miniscual scale. It has it's own artwork for each character, and even some small animated scenes. The music sets the stage alright enough, and is something I like to listen to casually.
I'd like to empisise miniscual though. This game is a very small game, easily completed in 2 hours for a first run for a normal player. The game is made even smaller by being cut up into 3 peices, each a labled "game" You'll pick from once you start up the game. Each one is self contained, but they all add up into a complete plot of the main characters. I like how it was handled, too. It gives it a sense of progression within each of the chapters without having to ellate farther down the road.
Ultimately, this game a bit sized story broken up into bite sized senarios. It's handled well through and through, but do not expect a ton from it.

If you like Medieval Total War, you'll probably like this. The battles aren't as memorable, and it really places a focus on kingdom building and diplomacy. As such, it can be a fun little jaunt into the byzantine politics of dark age Europe. A good buy at $9.99, and an excellent time-sink. Not as engrossing as Europa Universalis, thank God - approachable, with a fully voiced tutorial. Simple but deep mechanics. Extremely dated graphics. Good stuff, though.

It's not a bad game.  And more's the pity, actually.  If it was, it'd be more laughable at least.  The most that can be said for it is that it's weird and unnecessary.  And that sounds silly to say over a video game, which are primarily time wasters to begin with, and dating sims which tend to skew towards really freaking bizarre.  But in this case, it's the best words for it.  I love VNs and dating sims and even harem games, but nothing about this stands out at all. There was a lot of wasted potential regarding the routes and "divinity" (spoilers: You're Zeus) that just never got used (you give me a reincarnation of Athena and Aphrodite, and they do nothing with that characterization, wtf).  It's a little too cliche well beyond familiarity, and honestly, save your money and get a different one instead.  Even most of the free games of this genre are a lot better.
That said, it's still not bad, but that's what makes it so unnecessary.  It's kind of difficult to glean much other than cards out of the game tbqh.  And at the end I was simply left with a sense of "well that was weird," and nothing more.  And given that I love absolute crackfic series, it wasn't even good weird or bad weird or funny weird.  Just weird and vaguely pointless.  I do want to see more and better from the artists, but hopefully paired with better writers.

is a game I didn't really expect to like much when first playing considering I didn't know what I was expecting when I went into it. As soon as you enter the game you are drawn by the aspects of the game, the color, sounds, and most of all the game play mechanics. Much of the game was a blast for me spending a good week to try and complete the game due to it usually drawing me in with all of its elements. The voice acting is good enough and frequent enough to let you not get tired of their voices and much variations of accents and characters help with that. The character you play provides a mystery as you try and uncover your past and reasons of why you have all these things happening to you but it has a linear story which I did not like due to the fact there should have been choices to things later on in the story I would like to have made. Gameplay wise it controls very smooth for what it is, as you level up the enemies develop new tactics and fighting styles as they add more to combat you getting stronger and learning new moves as well throughout the story. Sad to say that even though you are a melee character with different moves and some ranged moves with the help of your sidekick, ultimately I usually had an indefinite combo of defeating every enemy and boss except for a few rare exceptions. Story wise I think they should have expanded on the concept and extended it more since it only takes place in 5 different kind of biomes such as forest, caves, mountains, volcano, and a cemetery area. Most of the areas consist of forest with the other biomes only have 1 area for them. Enemywise there are many different kinds but sometimes there are reskins in later areas but at least they don't reskin much and also they develop new moves and get stronger as you continue through the story. The side missions are the only way of adding more to the game but they are mostly just to help level up and gain materials. The economy in the game seemed a bit too forgiving as most of the time I would end up with items and gold I needed after defeating so many enemies finishing an area in the game. Variations of attacks pretty much you only develop new range attacks and get better dodging techniques but you should have to develop new tactics each time you get later on in the game.
In the end this game controls well, the game looks good, and the story is a little lacking. It ended so soon and I would rather have more added to it.

(My reviews assume you have read about the content of the game in terms of gameplay. I am simply reviewing each individual aspect based on my opinion. This allows for my reviews to be spoiler-free. You may find I rate by different categories in each of my reviews. This is because every type of game is different, and will not have the same content. I think it is pointless to leave a category blank or write 'unrelated', or something similar.)

Pixelated RPG, Indie
**** - As mentioned above – pixelated, but in anime style. The cutscenes have higher quality graphics, as well. I feel that in this case the pixel graphics are not a hindrance to the game, or a product of lack of developing money, but a way to add a different feel to the game. If the game had Final Fantasy graphics (an example) or something similar, it would not feel nearly as cute and the player would not feel as at home in Effie’s world.
**** - The music really suits the game, it’s (mostly) fun and upbeat with a different style depending on the chapter or the happenings in the game at that moment. When simply strolling around a new area while ‘Papa’ is off working, the music has a pleasant tune. But when someone has been hurt or disgraced, the music conveys the character’s anger, sadness or malice.
*** - Once you start the story, it really makes you question the nature of Effie’s world and how she even came to be. When I was playing it, I thought about it even when I was far from my computer. So I will give it three stars for catching my mind’s attention to the point where I always wanted to play it more.
***** - As mentioned above, the story is breathtaking in complexity and the characters are closely related to their world, which is why I combined those two categories for this review (and also so I don’t have to say ‘as mentioned above’ every five seconds). The characters are complex with intertwining relationships and there are some you might be able to relate to or empathize with in some way. The dragons in this world are often mistreated, with Efina being lucky to have a (somewhat) caring companion, so you can also hear a bit about other dragons’ experiences, although most like to keep it to themselves.
*** - It’s pretty easy really. The battles are even easier if you find the incredibly overpowered Legendary Gear. Even if you don’t, you shouldn’t have a problem. (P.S – There is already a guide on Steam that shows you how to find all of the gear, so use that as you will!)

** - It’s kinda just one of those games you play again once you have forgotten about it, really. XD
*** Standard RPG controls, basically. Nothing special and nothing too difficult.
*** - 6/10 (although I consider it a 10/10!)

BLUF:  Don't download this game if you value using your computer and/or keeping your HDD from eating itself.
I'm a network security specialist and an network intrusion incident responder supervisor... my job - all day, every day, is investigating malware and determining root cause.  I'd like to think, given my experience and rapid promotions, that I'm at least halfway decent at the job.
While the game is fun, there is something broken badly in the game code that has it continue to run and read/write constantly to your HDD, making most any system highly unstable.  After fighting valiantly to have my computer remain functioning long enough to diagnose the problem, and removing every other reasonable possibility, the only remaining culprit was this game.
It was the last change I made before the problems arose, and removing the game (after much wrestling with a very grumpy, unstable computer) immediately alleviated the problem.
After an analysis of my Anti-Virus logs, and running a few of my work tools on the system, it was obvious that this software was the culprit.
As with any piece of "freeware"... BUYER BEWARE!
And so the alleged developer comments (since deleted, so no one else is exposed to their malfeasance)... and wants me to go to a .ru website.  I think not.  That more than answers how and why this game is querying my HDD...
Let me clarify, since apparently some folks don't "get it".  The developer asked that I go to a page and give them my system settings... but the page they "linked" in their comments was to a JPG, not an HTML or other webpage.
When you go to a link with a picture file (as a JPG is), your system will automatically scan and execute the code that makes up that picture file.  Malicious code is easily and EXTREMELY commonly embedded in such files.  Why, if this developer wanted my honest input, would they send me to a webpage that was NOT intended for user interaction, and when the page they linked to was scanned with a malware scanning engine, came back as containing malicious content?
Anyone letting Russian freeware onto their system is just begging for trouble.

TL;Dr-Version: Get this game if you are into dark-fantasy RPGs and played the first installement. And if you want to kick♥♥♥♥♥
First of all, while it is questionable if the graphics of a game play an important role for the recommendation or not,
it is truly clear, that this game has excellent, i repeat excellent graphics. Modern PCs are still not able to run this game in 4K fluently maxed out. Besides this, the graphics are still completely amazing at Full HD, too.
Back to to topic:
The story of this game is really well "written", having many memorable moments ( eyes and spoon, for those who have played it) and the decisions one makes do really impact the outcome of the story, letting this have 8 different endings. As if this wasnt enough, the game has two storylines, which can only be seen by doing a second run (i am glad about that) or even more, if all achievements want to be collected.
The characters: One word: Unique. (Besides that they are based on books, of course).
The main character, Geralt of Rivia, is a fantastic protagonist, and playing as him is extremly joyfull, especially when the progress he made throughout the whole game regarding skills and weapons and so on... can be seen. You then feel like a boss, putting it simply.
But Geralt isnt the only one, is he? No, while you may cant play different characters, there are compagnions you wish for in reallife: Triss, Zoltan, Dandelion: All these folks are following Geralt since the first Witcher, and they grow to the heart of the player (so: YOUR heart).
And as we are mentoining the first title of the series, it has to be mentioned that the game (and the developers, ofc) made an extremly good job adding new features and freshening up the graphics (i said this already, btw, the part about the party). The combat system is thought-through, make it not too easy nor to hard, just... right (although if i am missing the different, manually selectable combat styles from the first installment).

In the 08 May 2015 article "The 25 Best Puzzle Games Ever Made,"
"Sokobond" made number 21 on that list.  I disagree.  If you really, really like Sokobon-type puzzles and would like to see a chemistry twist to those, then the 144 levels in this game (124 regular and 20 bonus) should keep you going for a while.  But, I had issues with it ranging from my own mistaken desires on up (or down, as the case may be).  From least important to more important:
- This one's my own fault.  When I bought this, I figured it would be more of a way to see how molecules got built within a game framework.  Instead, it's a Sokobon-type game using clumps of atoms as the "blocks" that you move around until you get the final molecule.  "Sokobon" as most of the name ought to have clued me in.  So, just disregard this one.
- The interface is keyboard only.  It would be a lot easier on the wrists if we could use the mouse to move things around.
- The progression through the game is indicated by the filling in of a periodic table.  For whatever reason, the periodic table used appears to be wrong.  Even taking into consideration the developer's desire for contiguous pieces in that table, their version still appears to contain four extra elements.  Sort of odd in a game based around chemistry.
- There's no "proper" progression through the puzzles.  I'd have thought the puzzles would start with the simplest molecules (restricted to the organic set of Hydrogen, Carbon, Nitrogen, and Oxygen (they throw in Helium, but it appears to be a type of mobile blocker to the puzzle since it doesn't bond with anything) and work up from there.  Instead, there's only a fairly general increase in molecular complexity.  Similarly, it's fairly open which order you proceed through that periodic table of puzzles.  So, at any given moment you might be working with different atoms, different complexity, and different game mechanisms to build things.
- I'd expected more of an educational bent to the game:  show us the molecule, explain what it does and what bonds the atoms use, and, perhaps, talk about the geometry and how it's built in reality.  Instead, we're presented with a puzzle space containing some atoms, we move them around in such a way that they'll fit through the blocks, and when you get everything stuck together, you're presented with a blurb about the molecule.  The atoms stick together based on their valence electrons and there's some work with single, double, and triple bonds.  But, none of that is ever explained.
- The above is also a problem because unless you know enough chemistry to know what the end product will be (there are 40 molecules used in the game) when shown a list of atoms, you really don't know what you're trying to build.
So, as I said above, even ignoring my mistaken pre-purchase impression of what the game was, I'm not recommending it.

Sokobond is an old-school puzzle game. It is simple, it is hard and it is good fun if you're into challenges.
The game is controlled via keyboard only, even in the main menu, which may seem odd at first. It's probably part of a certain old-school aesthetic and will become second nature to you after a few minutes. The ruleset is surprisingly simple: There are circles with open docking ports in a confined space. You are one of them. Move and push circles around until all docking ports are filled, creating larger structures of circles.
The natural beauty is that this simple, incredibly logical ruleset is based on how chemistry works in real life. In chemical terms: You are an atom and move other atoms around until all atoms have their outer electron shells filled via molecular bonding. Chemistry knowledge is not required to beat the game, but it certainly helps, giving you an intuitive idea of what your target molecule will be. After creating it the game will reward you with interesting chemical factoids and more levels.
I really enjoyed the streamlined minimalist design and the non-existent load times. The game is technically rock solid and never caused any problems. It's fascinating to see how long a very basic mechanic can be kept interesting with good level design. I wasn't a fan of this kind of puzzle and honestly pretty bad at it, but I gradually got better and started enjoying the game more. There are 124 basic levels followed by 20 very very hard bonus levels. Of the 15 hours I played, I spent about half on these last levels, sometimes coming back to the same level across several days to try out new ideas. Thankfully the game is very forgiving, having no time limits and allowing infinite undos and resets, so you can experiment to your heart's content.
Among my gripes is that the progression is pretty bumpy. The difficulty of any basic level seemed utterly random. The game gradually introduces more mechanics (double bonds, noble gasses as spacers, bond breaking, etc.) and I would have liked a little more control over that. Some mechanics I really enjoyed and would have liked more of, but there may only be a hand-full of levels. Sadly there's also no endless mode or level generator, which would have been a great addition, especially to get some more relaxing, easy levels.
Beating the last levels felt really really good, but there was some frustration and annoyance here and there through-out the game due to the high difficulty and due to being forced to play levels/mechanics I didn't enjoy. I'm not sure I would pay full price for this game, but I can definitely recommend picking it up during a sale, if you're into mind-bending movement-based old-school puzzles.

Depite some tepid reviews, this is a terrific game. The open world is gigantic and convincing, encompassing multiple different sorts of locales: urban, rural poor, the French Quarter, privileged rich... The narrative is good. The cut scenes and documentary framing work. The animated acting is nuanced. And the game play is ... good. (More on that in a minute.)
Most of all, it's awesome to have a game set in reality, aware of the issues of the day, and aware of the gulf between the black and white worlds in America in the 1960s - a gap that obviously we still haven't entirely healed. The game isn't *about* that, and it isn't preachy. It's simply set in a time when grotesque discrimination was taken by the privileged as normal and proper.
I liked the game play, but I'm not very demanding. Most of the missions involve wading into an area with five or six enemies, shooting them, retreating a bit, and then setting up to shoot the next one. You'll learn some techniques based on the limitations of the AI that make it easier, but the difficulty rachets up over time, with more enemies, and sentries that can bring in another wave if you don't get to them in time. The side missions are more of those along with driving challenges. The larger and more complicated shooting missions often took me several tries, but I'm not particularly good.

Mafia III, man.. Such controversy about this game. Main hero, setting, not playing as actual Mafia as-we-know-it etc etc...
The game gets flak for repetitivness and seemingly nothing to do in the game-world New Bordeaux.. well, yeah. It's true. If you go into this game expecting similar fun-factor to GTA V or God forbid The Witcher 3, you're in for a one wake-up call. There's not much to do besides main missions, races, car tuning and collectibles-hunting. Well that, and the DLC (which I heartily recommend, but let's not go there just yet). But, as I was going through the story, I began to think "It was never intended to have those activities".
Instead, we got top-notch revenge story (well, yeah, it's cliché, but hey - it's a game about Mafia. What do you expect? Goodfellas?!), spot-on VA and probably the best looking faces and characters in the game industry, tons of guns, colorful and diverse city of New Bordeaux (with Bayou) and...yeah, THE best in-game soundtrack in the entire Mafia franchise. The minute All Along The Watchtower starts blasting in the main menu, you know this game has style - you can't deny that.
Driving is kinda good, cars feel heavy and like to slide alot (which is good), but the damage model could have been better.
Shooting is among the most satisfying features in it - once you fing your signature gun - you never go back. They are loud, powerful, they look good and oh-my-God do the wreck the foold who happen to be on the receiving end of your gunbarrell. Poetry, I tell you.
Stealth is pretty much broken - you can ghost entire areas if you AT LEAST try. There is an option to choose between lethal and non-lethal takedowns, which is a welcome addition to those pacifists among us.. (pff,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
Cover system is fine, helpful and works when it needs to
Story itself is great, I think the best in the series. Mostly because of the acting and quality of the cutscenes. That, and likeable villain(s). Every time I was watching a cutscene I couldn't help myself but think that I'm watching an old Scorcese gangster film. High quality stuff right there. It starts and ends just perfectly.
Graphics...well, they are OK, I guess. Definitely not on the top of the game of this gen. In fact, some textures are quite blurry and low-res. Especially cars, damnit. You had 1 job!
The soundtrack - probably the thing that stands out the MOST. Hangar 13 sure did their homework and included the most iconic and well-know hits from artists like CCR, J. Cash, Rolling stones and so on.. (yes, there is Elvis, you can exhale now). There are 3 radio stations and I had a hard time deciding which one I'll leave on - there was a hit on every single on of them.
There are 3 expansions - with my favourite being "Stones Unturned" - a buddy-action fun packed with some backstory to one of your main characters and several new locations. But, frankly, all 3 expansions are solid and defo worth your money and time. 2 of them also add some sweet activities to do around the map, which is always welcome - more content - more worth for you money.
I gotta give it to this game and dev team. They done goofed at launch with some unfinished features and hilarious and game-breaking bugs (lol), but they pulled their heads outta their asses and tried and fixed at least some of the addressed problems. Feedback is always good, guys.
I enjoyed every single hour I put into Mafia III and am currenty planning a second playthrough. If you are a fan - go for it right now, if not or weary - wait for some sale (it tends to be on sale pretty regularly, so be patient).

This review has been completely rewritten for version 1.4. Prior to 1.4 I gave this game a thumbs down because I did not find the game fun and couldn't in good conscience recommend it to anyone. Patch 1.4 brings in a simplification of the economic system and improvements to the AI. Combined with the previous patches since release, it turns out the game is fun to play. Well, fun enough, anyway. I still maintain a long list of things I'd like to see improved, some of them already acknowledged by the devs to be on the roadmap. For those of you who have been delaying getting this game, I will say that it is no longer a complete waste of money. I apologize in advance if you now go out and buy it, but you come to the opposite conclusion. YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED!!!  As before, I will try to update my review as Stardock continues to develop the game.
The game is fundamentally a good one. It is a big step up from GalCiv2 in many ways, while keeping to the formula that makes GC2 a fun game. Absolutely humungous hex maps, better graphics and battles, more complex battle mechanics, a focus on planetary specialization, more complex diplomacy and trade. All these things plus more make the game concept very exciting. That's not even mentioning the plans they have for DLC and expansions, which will make the gameplay even more rich. I've been playing and providing feedback since Beta 1, have watched all the dev streams live or same day. I've seen the game improve significantly, and I fully expect it to continue to improve and eventually be a great game, whereas now I categorize the game as just "kinda good".
To those who have played the game, patch 1.4 removed the planetary production wheel, opting now for the global wheel plus economic focuses. As a person who used the planetary wheel extensively, I was skeptical because it meant less planet specialization. But in practice I find it to be a good thing as tweaking the wheel for optimal output was repetitive, annoying, and deteriorated immersion. The new system reduces specialization, but there is still a lot left so the change doesn't completely dumb down the game. I would have preferred other solutions, but we don't always get everything we want. In my initial post I had six main annoyances. They have addressed three of them with this one change.
A fourth annoyance was trivial-to-beat non-cheating AI with average play. That is no longer the case. I'm getting beat right now in a large galaxy with a good start on normal difficulty because I failed to maintain awareness of my enemy's military buildup. The latest patch is said to have improved AI management of planet buildings. But I've seen some very bone-headed setups, so there is a lot to be desired. And that's the general story for this game. Some good things, but much to be desired.
What is left on my initial annoyance list is constructor and starbase management and a cluttered main map with no declutter capability. The former is supposedly set to be addressed in patch 1.5 (I'm not holding my breath) and the latter is probably never going to be addressed.
Stardock has had a history of saying they want to do X, but not coming through in a timely manner, or in some cases ever, going back to at least beta 1. As I play through 1.4 I'm finding more things that bug me, some are gameplay and some are UI. Ideally all those annoyances would get addressed, but Stardock is now in DLC/Expansion mode, so they have bigger fish to fry. The more I play the game, the more I get desensitized to the things that bug me. That may be a desireable result for Stardock, but I suspect it will turn off newer players.
In summary, Stardock has made sufficient progress on my "annoyances" list to allow me to declare that this game doesn't straight-up suck, so I dutifully yet begrudingly changed it to a thumbs up. It is closer to where it should have been at release, though I think there is still a long way to go. I promised I would keep this review updated as they develop the game, and now I have fulfilled that promise. I look forward to future improvements, and will be keeping a keen eye on progress so I can scratch more items off of my "annoyances" list.
Some annoyances. I'm sure there are more, this is just what I wrote down when I encountered them in my most recent game:
- Pirates are pointless hazards. They will continue to be so until ships gain XP for beating them.
- Planet governors still suck at least half the time
- There should be a global option for auto-upgrading because sometimes I don't remember to turn that option off for every planet I colonize.
- You get no context when you encounter pirates while surveying.
- You get no indication in the trade window which techs are exclusive specializations. If you get such a tech in a trade you cannot choose a different specialization to research later.
- The large empire penalty is lame, and very damaging on large maps. Is that really a good mechanic?
- The shipyard building list gets very cluttered, and decluttering it is very click intensive.

LiEat is a simple RPG-maker game divined into three short stories that follow the lives of a young man and his dragon-girl companion. Each of these episodes centers around a single area where you mainly talk to people, solve puzzels and encounter fights. While these are all essential (and only possible) features of every RPG-Maker game (and usually how well you incorporate each of these determines the game's success), I personally enjoyed a lot how the fighting encounters were incorporated as more of story element rather than forcing them to play a bigger part in game's overrall flow. Granted, this means that the fighting part overrall feels very one-dimensional and easy, which can make the bossfights feel like a letdown.
The stories are mainly detective-like, where you spend most of the time uncovering what has happened. There's a lot of characters, and luckily those that you meet in all three episodes are the most with most substance. Since the game overrall is pretty short (It took me 4 hours to get every single ending & achievement), it does have quite a lot going on and its emphasis on exploring the background of the other MC can feel a bit tedious. On the bright side, most of the dialogue between charachers flows well and the game is sure to leave you warm-hearted after experiencing all of it.
I'd say that the biggest problem I had with the game was the fact that getting a neutral/good ending of the final episode is heavily obscured compared to earlier ones. Nevertheless, its a very warm and fuzzy game with a solid artstyle and writing, and totally worth the few dollars.

Divine Slice of Life is a visual novel with more fantasy than the usual visual novel you would play. It is a little hard to explain without spoiling the story, but i'll just mention that you meet 2 goddesses during the story, so it is a bit surreal.

LiEat shows that even with a basic engine like RPGMaker, you can still make some truly interesting and emotional stories.
The story follows a human and a dragon-girl with the ability to eat lies. LiEat has three different arcs, with each one containing a different adventure of the duo. While it may sound too long, LiEat's arcs are bait sized, and can take between half an hour to two hours, and they keep themselves interesting with well made, entertaining characters.
While the stories and gags are great, the battle mechanic is almost non-existant. While both characters do level up and every arc does end with a boss fight, the battle system itself is basic, and can easily be broken by getting the "legendary weapons" hidden at the start of every arc.
although, LiEat can sometimes use the battle system to its merits, having you fight "lies" to progress through investigations and even involves the character's levels into considerations when picking an ending.
despite all of its flaws, LiEat is short, sweet, and interesting, and is recommended for everyone who can see past its visuals.

SAMOLIOTIK is short, story oriented shoot-em up game. The game features multiple different levels that feature different enemies. Each level comes with an added difficulty. The game has a constant rate of fire, no ammunition values and time based power ups that either give your gun a shotgun like effect, shooting a rapid stream of 3 bullets, slow down effect or a speeding up effect.
The games difficulty lies in the fact that movement is relatively sensitive, and touching an enemy will cause death. There are no lives in the game so it is an instant restart upon death. The bullets shoot out of the front of the plane in the center, so you cannot just sit on one side and shoot, because you risk getting your plane clipped.
The bosses in the game are relatively easy. Shooting the boss 10 times will cause it to recede and fall back. It is not as gratifying as seeing a big explosion, but it works the best with the 8 bit graphics due to the constant gameplay.
The graphics are styled in an 8-bit fashion. It is all very blocky, and simplistic. The colors palate is limited with most levels using three colors in general.
The biggest, game breaking, bug I found was the fact that you can move you plane on the pause screen, allowing you to evade enemies that would otherwise trap you.
In all, I would give this game a 6/10, it is a fun and simple little game to play in your free time, or to collect achievements.

Earthlock: Festival of Magic is a good indie turn-based rpg that takes around 20 hours to finish entirely. While the combat system itself is a classical turn-based mechanic, the way you level and customize the characters is quite unique and refreshing. You can also decide whether you want to fight enemies in small or big groups, as you can aggro your opponents on the map. You gain bonus XP when you fight bigger groups, so this is also a nice and unique gameplay mechanic.
While some enemies do offer a bit of challenge as you need to figure out which abilities and talents can counter them, the game is not particularly difficult (unless you want to fight some optional bosses early on, which you can do). This is a rather chill rpg where none of the achievements are missable and the chests are (relatively) easy to find. This is not the "grindy kind where you click on all the npcs in every town because you may miss one of eight pieces that unlock a special summoning" type of rpg.
The game is visually pleasant, with a cartoonish feel. The music is also nice and quite atmospheric. Overall, the game is artistically well done. The story might have been presented in a more scenarised way, as the game lacks some really memorable moments. In particular, the way some characters/bosses are introduced could have been more scenarised. Some people have commented that the game feels boring and this may be due to the way the story is told (because I actually think the story itself is nice).
In conclusion, I recommend the game for its original gameplay mechanics, while pointing out that this is a more casual rpg that is enjoyable as long as you are looking for a nice and chill experience.

Great collectible card game. Nice combos and lots of different strategies you can use. They took great ideas from several different CCG’s and blended them in nicely. It has several unique features. The developers seem to be very good about play balance – waiting for the community to respond to new strategies before changing cards. A growing community of players that are fun to play with.
Pro’s: New CCG with lots of new strategies to unlock. If you want to join a CCG and be able to compete even if you are new, you can, because you don’t have to learn an extensive existing play book of strategies. Enough variety that you can easily find a play style for you. You can play for free with great starter decks - one for every race/faction - which unlock very easily. You can develop the cards you want just from the in game money. In my mind, a very good free CCG. Great in game help for features – basically, you can lot at any card, lot at its ability and watch a short video on how the ability works. A really nice feature is that for each race you can pick 1 – 3 modules that are your abilities rather than being stuck with only one race ability.
Con’s: Raid mode is still very confusing (think of sealed deck play). The layout for the deck you are building is a little confusing to look at to figure out the cards you have already picked – not horrible but not the easiest. If you simply want to build a deck from a guide you will not find different decks to pick from – although that is slowing starting. There are no cards you play during your opponent’s turn so you have to use other features (like cyphers – cards that respond to certain opponent actions) to anticipate and counter some strategies. No special boss decks to defeat as you develop through the first few levels (in case you really enjoy that idea).
Overall: Since its free and VERY playable free, a must have for anyone who likes or loves CCG’s

I always enjoy seeing a well made traditional turn-based JRPG style game that has come out of somewhere other than Japan. There are often subtle differences that make it feel a bit more diverse while still being the kind of game I grew up loving. This game didn't disappoint. The characters in particular were nicely designed, the art style was unusual, I liked the battle system and the game engine in general, the world well thought out. The music was good quality, the game had a good balance between taking itself seriously and having fun, there were none of my personal pet hates (unreasonably hidden true ending, forced replays, no Game Over tune...) and overall it was well worth buying.
There were a few flaws. The biggest ones to me were how literally dark the graphics tended to get, I had turn the game's brightness way up to see what i was doing; and also the endgame was very irritating, with the savepoint too far away from the final boss (savepoints in general annoy me, there was no reason not to save anywhere) and several non-evadable pointless battles before the boss. In general, the system of having the monsters on the map was a good idea but the execution was annoying, it was too easy to accidentally aggro things you can't fight and can't shake off. The music, while good quality, was a little unenthusiastic and didn't fit the mood. The game felt short in a way that came across as unfinished rather than compact. Sequel please? The English was weird in some places, not sure if typos or bad translation. The comic was near unreadable as well, not sure if it was my display or the resolution settings or what. Also, I got stuck on the map once or twice and in general the camera angle sucked.
Overall? Yeah, buy it.

Music, Artwork, Gameplay, Story

Technicalities:

UI is okay, took some getting used to

Now, i first saw this game on Orlygift, which gives out codes in raffles for steam games, and it actually looked really fun, despite the simple premise and design. So I decided to pony up and buy the game for myself, after not winning it. First of all, even though it looks like an HD asteroids  remake meets a pong ROM hack, the vibrant backgrounds and EDM soundtrack support it, allowing you to stay enveloped in the game.
Unfortunately if you want to play every mode, you need at least one controller and a sperate human being (unless you're really good at multitasking). And even though the two multiplayer required modes are more for fun and playing around, that is what they are designed to do. The single player modes (which can be played with up to 8 players like the rest) are more focused on survival, which is well fitting. These three modes are Acrobat, compression, and Core Defence, with each mode getting a couple more mechanics than the last, and are varient enough to not get stale.
Acrobat is a mode where you simply have to not get hit. This is for players who are more run than gun, as it doesn't include the gun feature like the other modes, though this is not a bad thing, as it allows the player(s) to focus on dodging the bullets, or enemies as they're called in the game. This mode also spawns "Seekers" occasionally, who will follow you until you die. They are stopped by the center aroun the core, but it's a circle, so they just slide around it, adding a better challenge to the simple mode.
Compression mode is like acrobat mode, you still have to dodge enemies, but three things are different. 1. You can get powerups. 2. You have a gun mechanic. 3. The walls are closing in on you. There are no seekers, but the walls are a bigger problem. Now touching them won't kill you, but getting squished isn't impossible. The walls move in slowly, but they get closser every time you shoot the core's circle, or the walls, which ou will do a lot, so only grab the multishot power up if it's absolutely neccessary.
Now Core Defence is different. Veeeery different. In core defence, you are ctually siding with the core that has tried to kill you over and over again, and what do you get to protect it? Defences which I call "cores", because it's easier. These cores vary from powerup genorating factories, to the classic shields and turrets. You will have a _lot_ of cores if you can place them close enough to the center core, and there will be many lines close up, and that's good. Now you cannot control when or how you get the power ups, you can just hope you get a good one, but over all it is one of the best modes in the game, and it gets even better from the fact it's the most... "in depth" single player available mode.
Overall this game is just fun, fun, fun, and fun, although I reccomend it to people who have a lot of gamer friends, so you can enjoy it how it's supposed to be played, with friends. Get this game.

After a few hours into the game, I can't say that this is a bad game. I can say its boring though.
The game had me at several points, wanting to see the potential of the game. But for every positive I can list, I can also list a negative that almost makes you forget about the positives.
The graphics are charming and good, the characters and word being bright and contrasting well with the environments. But after several optimization patches the game still runs poorly. Frame stuttering is normal, and the game hangs from time to time after certain actions.
The boss design is great, with many having a certain weakness that destroyes them. But man the difficulty is all over the place. Beat a boss that took you to the edge of you limits, then the next one is a walk in the park.
The battle system is unique and refreshing. More along the lines of final fantasy 10 turn based style with chrono cross combat points(I forget what they were called). While the system is great, the battles are SLOW. The game rewards you heavily by pulling in and fighting multiple mobs at once, but you lack any consistent AOE for several hours into the game. This is by far my biggest gripe with the game. While its not to terribly difficult, its extremely tedious. You do build a meter to unleash strong attacks, but its not frequent enough to help speed up the pace. And I hope you like to grind, because the pace made the game feel like a grind.
The talent system is great. Its a solid effort at something unique, and its very customizable. You could just add a ton of might on a single character and have a powerhouse. However, you will always be low on whatever it is you need. Always. You have 2 or 3 talent points but no might or magic? To bad. And yes, you can switch around talents for others when you get the one you want, but it will be a long while till you feel comfortable with what you got.
The dungeons are simple and straightforward enough. But several times the camera was just obscuring what I needed to see. The camera wasn't always a trouble, but when it was the problem was maddening (burning desert im look at you).
I could go on and on, the problems ultimately outweigh the positives. And that sucks. I wanted to like this game. The style and presentation was present, and I could see the potential it has. But I kept waiting for the game to reach its potential, and it never did.

During my entire playthrough of EARTHLOCK, I was never really sure whether I enjoyed it or not - the game tiptoes between enjoyable and boring, never really falling into either category.
For everything it achieves, there is a "but":
The locations are lovely, but nothing memorable.
The character design is interesting, but the characters themselves are not.
The battle system fun and challenging, but grows old quickly.
The JRPG grind is mostly absent, but now you have to wait around to literally farm your upgrades.
The music well produced, but not all that fantastic. (The battle theme being the most disappointing.)
Perhaps the worst offender is the story, or what constitutes one. It's borderline generic involving loosely tied together plot points. You go from location to location with only the thinnest of motive before discovering the main antagonist and from then on pursuing him.
As many have mentioned, the ideas are there, its just the content that is missing. EARTHLOCK never truly feels finished.
I'm recommending this game because I genuinely see potential in Snowcastle's series. With EARTHLOCK: Festival of Magic it has started shakily, but with a little finesse they could have a magnificent series.

There are five game modes in total out of which three can be played single player. All five of them can support up to 8 players so have your controllers and friends ready! The game modes vary nicely and I found each one to be very enjoyable.
Collider is very much a time-burner. Once you start playing you don't realise just how long has passed until you stop. I found myself constantly thinking 'Okay, just one more round' then playing for another ten minutes.
The co-op part of the game is where it really gets fun though. It's really awesome to work with and compete against your friends. I found single player to be rather relaxing whereas co-op was the complete opposite; we all found our competitive sides coming out. We ended up playing for around 45 minutes when we only planned to play one round of each mode.
I think local co-op is often under appreciated these days and I'm glad there are still games like this that understand some people just want to play with one copy of a game on one device. There is a lot of re-playability due to this and it doesn't run the risk of having no-one online like so many multiplayer games end up with.
The gameplay itself is great, the game runs fine with no issues and the controls work perfectly when using a controller like recommended. You can still use a keyboard but I found it a lot harder and not as enjoyable. The graphics are very nice yet simple, though I feel this works in favour, everything is beautiful yet there isn't too much going on.
There are a few tiny, tiny gripes so far I have with the game but nothing that stops me from playing. My first is the distinct lack of a pause feature. Now I know games like this don't require one but when I'm playing and I've gotten pretty far in a mode and have no choice but to die to take an urgent phone call it sucks. Secondly some options would be nice so you are able to adjust sensitivity and volume.
. Lastly there could be some form of tutorial or explanation to each game mode (I didn't realise I could shoot until reading an achievement and even then it took me pressing every button to find it out). The last two the developers have said they are working on though which is great and shows that the developers do listen which is rare.

Excellent puzzle game based on pushing and linking atoms to form molocules. You don't need to know anything special about chemistry, it's just the framework for a set of devious puzzles. The core of the game is pushing around blocks, sokoban style, except they form bonds, linking to each other. As you progress some puzzles feature multiple bonds, splitting and reconnecting atoms, and rotating molocules till you have just the right shape to reach that one last atom you need. Every level ends with a bit of chemistry trivia about the molocule you just created.
Most puzzles aren't trial and error or brute force, but tempt you into making assumptions that keep you from spotting an elegant solution, which makes solving them very very satisfying.
As you can see from the screenshots, graphics are purely functional, but in a puzzle game that's not a bad thing.

If you've never played a GalCiv game before, you'll probably have read that this is a 4X game in the style of Civ in space. While that comparison is somewhat accurate, even Civ players might not end up liking this. But for those micromanagement junkies - the ones who only use the biggest maps, who meticulously plan city placement, who feel that even the longest game setting is too fast - this game is heaven.
To be clear - this game is at its best if you love the detail of building structures individually on each of your planets (and you can have hundreds), and rejigging every single one when you make a significant new research discovery. Of my 232 hours played, 200 have been on one game, and I'm only just starting to take down my first enemy opponent. The systems themselves aren't complex - it's time-consuming because the choices you make are wide, not deep. The mechanics at a core level are very similar to any other 4X game.
Also, make no mistake - it's buggy, and even when it does work, it's incredibly challenging on hardware. The UI is functional, but not even close to optimal.
Taking all of this into consideration, I have every reason to believe that 95% of gamers will hate this game. But in spite of that, I have to recommend it strongly. Because if you are that target gamer - obsessive, patient and wanting to command a sprawling empire - you'll cope with all of the challenges and frustrations because there's literally no game on the market this deep. You have to buy it. Nothing else matches it.

Kopanito All-Stars Soccer:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
“What a superb pass from the midfielder to the winger - he beat the defender fair and square, he is going to score without a doubt! What a move, Ladies and Gentlemen. Exceptional talent displayed from this player but . . . Hold on, WHAT A CRASHIIIING TACKLE from the second defender, so hard that his boots are the only remains on the pitch! Did you see where he landed, guys?” I love commentating Kopanito All-Stars Soccer matches; we see great moves, great tackles and no dives! Plenty of boots here and there but definitely no dives.
Kopanito All-Stars Soccer is a fast paced arcade-ish sports game. As per the intro, this sports game is absolutely frantic, to say the least! Well, there are no referees on the pitch and we do not care about this silly offside rule. All we have is two teams of six players each who go in to battle fiercely to win the match.  You will be able to use super moves when you fill the energy bar (I call it that), every successful pass, tackle, shot and goal will help you to increase your charge bar. Then you might get the super shot and score; you might get the magnet to pull the ball back to you (this is what Germany used in the Semi-final against Brazil in the latest World cup, for sure); you might teleport a player up field, or even get a massive ventilator behind the net so the ball can’t cross the line! JUST FUN!
16 tournaments and leagues to play either solo or with friends on local multiplayer which supports up to five players (four on gamepads and one at the keyboard) and four levels of difficulty. I would recommend that you start playing on the beginner level for a while and familiarise yourself with the gameplay. As soon as you move up to the amateur, the difficulty increases dramatically.
During each match, you will be given a challenge - if you manage to succeed you will receive points and in-game achievements. 114 national teams to choose from but a large number of them need to be unlocked.
I really like the cartoonish graphics; the game is very well balanced and the controls very responsive.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Really fun gameplay
-	Great cartoon graphics
-	100’s of national teams to play
-	Great number of tournaments and leagues to play (including custom ones)
-	Local multiplayer
-	Trading cards
-	Stacks of achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	The levels of difficulty increase rather steeply
It is fast, fun, competitive and even frustrating at times. Kopanito All-Stars Soccer is a must-have!
9/10

Ever wanted to play Dance Dance Revolution but with a bit of action and narrative added to the mix? Well Crypt of the Necrodancer is a good waltz in the right direction! Crypt of the Necrodancer is a rhythm, rogue-like dungeon crawler that has you moving and attacking to the beat of the tune.
The gameplay as stated above generally has you doing everything to the beat of the tune by using only the arrow keys, whether your in the main lobby or fighting your way through the next level. You can even set the game up to be played with a dance pad! In the main lobby you're able to buy permanent upgrades to weapons, armor, spells and trinkets found in the levels,  practice against certain enemies, read background about the game and choose which zones you'll be "dancing" through along with a few other options. In the zones themselves the overall objective is to find the stairwell to the next level, however that doesn't necessarily mean you should be racing for the stairwell with all due haste. Diamonds, your currency for permanent upgrades, can only be found while exploring these levels, and once you are done with a zone you will only have those diamonds in your next trip to the lobby. Once you decide to go back into a zone you will lose all the diamonds you collected on the previous trip! So finding enough diamonds to buy those ever increasingly costing upgrades can be well worth the exploration. Remember how I said those permanent upgrades to items only affect what you find in the levels and are not given to the characters themselves? Those items can either be found throughout said levels or in the shop in each level. Enemies drop gold in order for you to purchase these items from the store, and if you keep up with the beat, a coin multiplier is added when you kill enemies so you get more gold for your kills. With that being said the levels are on a time limit, can you guess what that time limit is? The music! If the music you are playing to finishes before you get to the stairs you are immediately dropped to the next level. On top of this each level has a boss, and not only will you lose your multiplier combo if the song ends but rather than being dropped into a relatively safe room at the beginning of the next level you will have to face that levels boss immediately if the previous levels boss wasn't defeated.
The games uses pixel art and uses it's musical theme in some of the enemy designs. For example the Minotaur enemy's  horns are actually a harp and the reaper has a microphone attached to his scythe. This leads to a very visually pleasing themed art style that looks and plays it's part.
The music is electronic and catchy, even making you want to stay on a level just to keep listening. In lower levels of each zone the beat is actually slower so that players adjust to the beat as it get faster with each level.
Crypt of the Necrodancer is a fun and enchanting game and is well worth your time and if you have a love for rhythm and rogue-like games alike, this original gem will not disappoint you.

Here's a recipe for waffles.
1 cup all-purpose flour, spooned and leveled
2 tablespoons sugar
1 teaspoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1 cup milk
2 large eggs
4 tablespoons (1/2 stick) unsalted butter, melted
Maple syrup and butter, as desired, for serving
Preheat waffle iron according to manufacturer's instructions. In a large bowl, whisk flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt; set aside.
2. In a small bowl, whisk milk and eggs; pour over flour mixture, and whisk gently to combine (don't overmix). Gently whisk in butter.
3. Following manufacturer's instructions, cook waffles until deep brown and crisp. (For a standard waffle iron, pour a generous 1/2 cup of batter into center, spreading to within 1/2 inch of edges, and close; waffle will cook in 2 to 3 minutes.) Serve warm, with maple syrup and butter, as desired.

Mafia III is the story of Lincoln Clay's fight to avenge himself and his foster family against the powerful mafioso who controls 2K Czech's fictitious take on New Orleans, Sal Marcano. The game makes no bones about the fact that its protagonist is a dangerous sociopath whose ultimate objective will entail carving a bloody path of murder, extortion, theft, arson, kidnapping, and other felonies too numerous to count. He's certainly no hero, but as with all of these kinds of games, he's generally portrayed as being at least marginally better than the people he's trying to take down.

After a prelude, the game is divided into a series of racket and district takeovers with the goal of replacing Marcano's lieutenants around the city with Clay's own associates. This typically involves going after a racket's enforcers and fiscal and physical resources until you've drawn out the boss, at which point you can intimidate or kill him after you assault his stronghold. Lincoln starts out with one associate who controls her own small army of hired guns and eventually recruits three others. As Lincoln slowly takes over New Bordeaux, he doles out these districts to his associates as a way of currying favor and gaining bonuses such as upgrades to vehicles, guns, or Lincoln himself (such as extra health bars).

In addition to the main story missions, there are loyalty missions to boost your popularity with your associates and a number of collectibles. Like its predecessor, the game has its set of collectibles that remind you that game audiences are mostly male (Playboy centerfolds), but it also has several other sets of items, including album covers (which are pretty cool), Alberto Vargas paintings, communist propaganda posters, Repent magazine covers, and Hot Rod magazine covers. The other item that Lincoln collects is fuses, and the fuses are used to rig up junction boxes around the city so that Lincoln's CIA friend Donovan can tap into local communications and gain intelligence on various targets. The practical effect of wiretapping is that it shows collectibles on the minimap and also allows you to "see" enemies through walls, which makes stealthy approaches to combat a bit more feasible.

One thing the game lacks is anything resembling fast travel. If you want to go anywhere in New Bordeaux, you will be walking or driving. The game's fantastic '60s soundtrack takes the edge off that point but only for so many hours. And the soundtrack is great--2K managed to procure compositions from virtually every major artist from the late '60s except for The Beatles in an array of music that ranges from zydeco to blues to R&B to rock. The game also has a few radio shows and pseudo-vintage ads that play on the in-vehicle radio stations but after over 100 hours you really start wishing that 2K had put some kind of fast-travel system that would allow you to travel across the city in less than 10 real-world minutes.

Each of the single-player DLCs in the season pass adds a few new mechanics to the base game. Faster, Baby is the most interesting of the three, although the only significant additions to the game are the customizable cars and racing. The story in this first DLC revolves around the efforts of The Voice and his daughter, Roxy Laveau, to combat Sheriff Slim Beaumont's efforts to suppress voting rights of people in the fictitious Sinclair Parish. Of the three DLCs, Faster, Baby feels of a piece with the main story of the game far more than the others--having a black protagonist in the late '60s in the Deep South, there was no way to avoid the issue of culturally-embedded and institutional racism and 2K Czech handles it well both in the main story and here. Roxy also feels like a blaxploitation-era Pam Grier, which makes her character that much more endearing.

Stones Unturned follows John Donovan's quest to track down his old war nemesis who has resurfaced in New Bordeaux with a small army of mercenaries at his command and a sinister agenda on his mind. This DLC adds sniper support that is so finicky it's virtually useless and a few bounty-hunter missions.

Sign of the Times wears its Manson influences on its sleeve, but it is primarily a story about the relationship between Lincoln and Anna, a young woman who figures into the plans of a murderous cult that has emerged in New Bordeaux known as the Ensanglante. This DLC introduces some investigation mechanics that are only used in certain segments of this story and the use of throwing knives. There is also a series of missions that allow Lincoln, along with his adoptive aunt Lily, to rebuild Sammy's Bar, which is destroyed in the game's prologue.

The game's main story is well-written and populated with interesting characters. While the driving mechanics are just okay and the driving itself gets excessive after a while, the shooting mechanics are well-done. I spent over 150 hours on the game, but I did many of the available side-missions and sought out every collectible and activated wiretaps in every area, so a playthrough that adheres more strictly to the story missions is probably much shorter. The game is not without its bugs. One of the official patches forced players to disable the Steam overlay or deal with weird controller stick issues that made the shooting parts of the game considerably more difficult. Also, some of the mission markers will occasionally disappear from the map, making it effectively impossible to continue them.

While it feels like Lincoln Clay's story is done, I could definitely go for a fourth installment in this series. It sounds a little Vice City, but a story set in a different part of the country in the '80s has potential to be (totally) awesome.

This game, Wow. At first, I didn't have high hopes for it. I bought it one day, Then left it sitting in my library for about a week. I decided to finally play it when I had nothing to do for around 30 minutes while I waited for my game to update. I ended up playing the whole story 4 hours straight, and I did not regret it.
The story was lovely. I loved the dialogue, and the personality of the characters. Especially Elfi. Her dialogue was adorable, how she was really clueless about many things. The art was really good as well. It isn't as sparkly, and shiny as the art of really good artists, but it gives off a really nice charm.
I wasn't expecting cutscenes from this game. Though really short, I feel that it gave a really big impact to the story. Text, and pictures can't always tell a story better than it being animated.
Though saying that, The cutscenes are just around four seconds, but it was still a nice addition overall.
The first two games are pretty much the same thing, but the third game really starts getting into the characters. That's all I can say about the three without spoiling it to much. Though I'm not saying the first two are repetetive. They both have a unique story. The second one teared me up. Don't even ask me about the third.
For the mechanics, The battle system is pretty simple, and most monster fights are pretty easy. The bosses have really high health, but they don't hit as hard if you do the right thing. Though the main part of this game is solving problems, I wouldn't necessarily say it's a puzzle game. I don't know the word, or how to explain it, but it's like piecing the parts together to get the answer. I guess it's like that.
OVERALL:
The game has a lovely story, and the puzzle part of the game isn't to hard, but it can be a challenge here, and there. Overall a wonderful experience, at least for me. I recommend it for anyone who's in for a good story.

Ok, at first this game is awfully similar to HS. The mechanic, the cards, the ability keyword etc.
But there are some distinct differences that makes it much deeper than HS:
- Each commander (hero) can use up to 3 different modules (abilities)
- There is a sub resource called energy (besides the main supply - mana), which is gained by hitting face or destroying units which can be used to play various cards and modules.
- Commander starting HP is affected by the number of cards in the deck. Each deck can have 25-40 cards
Just those subtle differences give the game a much better strategic play and deeper deck combination.
There are still some issues with balance and raid (draft mode), but this is one of the better CCGs on the market. Give it a try and you'll like it.
The dev are actively working on balancing cards, and NOT adding RNG like HS

Earthlock is an indie developed (somewhat rough around the edges, no AAA content), adventure (you follow a linear series of events) RPG (there are no decisions in the story, no Role to play) inspired by the classic 3D RPGs (early Final Fantasys with must reduced content) of the late 90's (more early 90s), with a fresh take on turn based combat (nope, old hat. Unapologetically difficult, but simple to play. If you have a place in your heart for old-school addictive arcade games that punish your incompetence, this will be right up your alley. While it’s core is simple, it has plenty of twists on the dodge-em gameplay.
Collider has 5 game modes, all of which support up to 8 players and 2 that require a second human to play. I found all of them to be fun and frenetic in their own way, ranging from the one-handed play of Acrobat, to the complex base building of Defend the Core (my personal favorite). Adding players simply ups the chaos, as every player shares the same circular arena.
Controls are simple, just move and shoot. You can use a mouse and wasd, but I preferred a PS4 controller where you just use the two joysticks. The action is tight, and the controls are extremely responsive; you can start and turn on a dime. When you die, it’s not the game, it’s your own damn fault.
While not spectacular visually, it’s a whole lot of fun and only gets more insane as you add players. I eagerly await the online multiplayer.

I have yet to be dissappointed by Alan Hazelden's elegant puzzle games. Typical of his style, Sokobond employs simple, self-explanatory mechanics in a series of small, self-contained puzzles which nevertheless manage to be frustratingly challenging.
The difficulty builds up naturally -- each new mechanic is introduced on its own, first with simple levels to give you an idea of the basic tricks, and then with harder levels. Then, the different mechanics are brought together in later puzzles. Stopping to think logically through the situation is a must; if you don't, you get stuck trying things that don't work over and over, and many levels seem impossible.
The chemistry theme is well done, supported by random chemistry facts after each level. The graphics are smooth and aesthetically pleasing. The overall atmosphere is relaxing and minimalist.
One drawback is that there are some levels where repeated guesswork leads to the solution. When I beat these levels, I had no idea what I did or what the key to solving them was. I realize that guessing is not the smartest way to play a difficult puzzle game, but I am sure many players will guess anyway. Another minor drawback is that bonding order is unclear -- if you push a molecule next to two things it could bond with, which bonds first? This ends up being relevant in several puzzles, but there is no explanation so you just have to try and see what happens.
It took 15 hours to finish the game including all the bonus levels. I did look up one solution, in the end (the last one I was stuck on).

Unlike its predecessor, TW2 has a much more political plot in addition to the regular Witcher-business of killing monsters, playing mini-games and sleeping with as many women as you can. While some criticized this Game-of-Thrones-ish aspect of TW2's plot, I came to absolutely love it. The game starts in Temeria and develops slowly but constantly from there until the point, where you start to feel as if you were at the center of the intrigues and power fights between the Northern kings, the sorcerers, powerful individuals and last but not least the Nilfgaardian Empire.
It is precisely this new aspect of the game which made it one of the most enhancing and breathtaking experiences of this year for me. In some ways, The Witcher 2 resembles a movie, where you can influence the way the plot continues, rather than a game. I don't think this is a bad thing, however. Hell, compared to TW1, where all you were doing was running from one end of the map to the other, it's a definite and huge improvement.

After about 2 weeks now of near non-stop playing, I feel as if I am now entitled enough to give a proper reveiw.
Pros-
--This game is going in the right direction, I love turn based games and the setting, scope, and style of GC3 is totally amazing. To be immersed in such an amazing universe, having to aquire unique resources, spreading to differnt habitable planets, createing peace or war with other civilizations. This game has everything I wanted and I love it.
Cons-
-- Here is why overall I give this game a no. 1st off, I am not one to complain about cost, I have a 3k expensive alienware so I can get the best experiance possible. And I actually like when games cost around $60 because I feel like there has been a lot of work done on it to make it worthy of my time. So I bought this game about 2 weeks after it launched offically (i knew there would be bugs so naturally i wanted until some fixes were available).
So to begin, Learning how to play has been the most troublesome and encumbersome feat I have had to distainfully deal with in the longest time. I understand these are very large games therefore as a gamer it is my duty to study up and learn the mechanics before i can expect to have fun and win chanllengeing games. So i began the tutorial with a notepad and was ready to learn how to become a galaxy master. Unfortunealy the tutorial  is so short and the explinations are so non-existant that i litteraly had to check and search online to make sure that i wasn't missing something. Then i searched for a guide, a rule book, an explination at the very least of how some things worked. How pathetically unforunate i am to have to endure such a total slap in the face.
After about a week of learning most of the game mechanics myself trhough trial and error, or looking online and watching hour long videos of other peoples games, I became sorely disappointed. Some aspects of the game are so in detailed and wonderful, like the ship designer and being able to name any ship and any planet or starbase. But those are minor points, how could the game designers put so much effort into that, but make the major componets like the technology tree and civilization diplomatic engagements the most basic and mundane thing ever. I wanted to throw up when i discovered how basic and non-creative the tech tree and the ideology tree were. Then i realized that because of this, my next games would all be the same. I wanted to win this game in every way possible, war, peace, trade, yada yada. how dissapointing that this is all.
I was exspecting a game with an awesome campain (campain is a scam, joke, lie), a HUGE tech tree with mulltiple pathways. I mean how can someone create a game that can have 100+ planets, which means i could be in the same game for over 2 weeks, yet have the mechanics be so basic and boreing.
Therefore i recommend that if ur looking for a turn based strategy star game, that you wait for a different game to come out. I have tried a few in the past and was simmilaily disapointed. One will emerge sometime soon, that will actually have mechanics that are as deep as the universe they govern. Not another game that had such great potential but got rushed by the company owners and was released without the complexity we all desired.
