Greetings Everyone!  As always I try to review every game I own and occasionally like to buy a game here and there on my wish list, even more when they are on sale.  Today, we have a new RPG using classic mechanics with a healthy splash of new and exciting.  The graphics are also low in that indie way but charming.  Anyone looking for a new RPG knows what to expect but some younger players may have never seen a turn based RPG that focuses on story not leveling mechanics and although there is challenge the mechanics themselves are not meant to be the focus.
Timeless Setting:  Let me start by focusing on the most important part of any RPG, the story.  Before I can start with the story itself I must mention the settling.  I absolutely love the setting, I won’t get into the big ‘thing’ that sets this world apart but I absolutely loved it…what annoys me is that the game focuses so little on it.  There is an amazing part of the world you are in that the game only bothers mentioning part way through and with no fan fair; they don’t’ try to ‘show you’ and just tell you but don’t make anywhere near as big of a deal as they should.  It turns out that this is even partly central to the story but only because some happened already.  I feel like I would have rather see the original event and not this second coming.  There is an amazing story that I hope they will focus on in a sequel but as it is the story is left with a ‘bleh’ feeling where the setting is amazing.
Press Space to Attack:  The combat revolves around classic turn based selection where you line up on one side and the enemies line up on the other.  I know many might think this outdated but I found it refreshing to see an old school system but that is also revamped with modern components and strategy.  Not only is the combat solid it is difficult to a decent degree, requiring attention and strategy but not so difficult that you have to spend hours of grinding.  The leveling system has a unique ‘talent’ system that is innovative but forgoes weapons and armor or stat improvements from leveling.  It is a nice system though I would have liked to have seen more depth in the end (and a level cap higher than 20) including weapons, armor, etc.  The Amri system is a nice addition that creates resource management in addition to turn based.
Time to Completion:  From my research the game takes about 20 hours to play though I spent several hours more.  But, none can argue that it isn’t a bit short, the game picks up about halfway through but feels more like a speed bump due to some of the story issues.  I can’t help but feel there is a much larger story here and this is only the first chapter, I want to know more about the cities mentioned, the final continent, etc.
Some Minor Bumps:  I normally stick to three points but I felt it was needed.  There are some non story related issues that I have.  The ammo system in the game and the items themselves are managed poorly, I should be able to remove items from my shortcuts that are no longer needed but all I can do is exchange them.  In addition the way the items are numbered is odd.  The much larger issue is that there are a small number of venders but you can’t sell anything and many of the rarer items require you to kill very specific enemies you don’t really remember where they are causing some minor annoyances when you are just trying to prepare for the final push.  The game also has area based level caps for experience which is both a blessing and a curse.  Finally, we have some odd pulls where the enemies seem to bug out and you end up having to kill them in another battle hurting both your experience and time; to make matters worse some enemies are single enemy packs that are just basic enemies wasting more time for no reason.
Let me end by saying that if you like classic RPGs with a solid combat system you should grab this.  Yes it has problems (mainly some of the story bits) but overall an enjoyable game that really could use a bit more depth in the story and some additional content.  Oh, Olia’s victory animation needs some work; she looks like she is jerking her spear around instead of flourishing it.  Other than that, this game is a solid piece of callback to the old ways of RPGs with some solid attempts to improve on it.

This is the product of what would happen if the fast-paced and thunderbolt world of Super Mario Strikers met the charming and intense world of Sensible Soccer. Sprinkle some unforgettable scenes from Shaolin Soccer and you have Kopanito All-Stars Soccer.
+ I have never had so much fun slide tackling in to opponents. Traditional grassroot rules do not apply, so get out there and break those legs!
+ Gameplay is solid and fully responsive between keyboard and gamepad. There is a learning curve involved, but once you discover the importance of team work, dribbling and tackling, everything feels a lot friendlier.
+ Visually a very charming game. The cartoony art direction is certainly a good call and works well. Player animations are solid. Goal celebrations are... ahem... animated.
+ Not a lot to offer in terms of sound effects and soundtrack, but the current offering delivers to a satisfactory standard.
+ A large assortment of competitions to unlock and play through including custom tournaments, practice and friendly matches.
+ Powers can be huge game changers and injects new life to the sport. There are four powers in total with individual strengths and weaknesses.
+ Support for up to four additional local players. Grab your friend(s) and charge through various tournaments as a team.
+ Full keyboard + mouse and gamepad support. Keys can be configured to your heart’s content.
+ The greater the goal difference, the more resilient and alert the AI becomes to your tackles and dribbles. Something I have not seen before, but it's a mechanic which works extremely well in an attempt to avoid further catastrophes.
+ Leaderboard and fame points work really well side by side. Adds a whole different layer of depth for players to continue playing and reach the Platinum League.
+ 225 achievements and in-game trophies. That’s 225 individual pieces of effort and excruciating dedication to unlock.
+ Match challenges offer objectives for players in search of small modifiers (ie. avoid using powers, score three goals in 30 seconds, and so on). You gain fame points in return for your efforts.
+ Friendly user interface with all the standard options you would expect from a PC title.
+ Online multiplayer is planned for release with the final version of the game.
- A friendly warning: The AI will torture you during your first few sessions/hours until you figure out how everything works. You may even grow suspicious of cheating AI. I most certainly did. The important thing is to try and play as much as you can to get to grips with the gameplay.
- Slight overkill with AI catch up speed compared to player catch up. I don't feel like the sprint button does anything when chasing the AI.
- The need for more power ups or other methods of scoring (ie. volley or header) is great.
- There is an audio balancing issue. Almost all audio during play comes through the right speaker/headphone. I have tried using two perfectly functional headsets and a speaker to cancel any malfunctions on my end.
- Only international teams are playable. It would be great to be able to play in a league filled with fictional teams/players, just to shrug off the feeling of international play. Pro Evolution Soccer has done this for many years with great success (ie. North London: Arsenal; Hampshire Red: Southampton; Merseyside Blue: Everton).
- It would be an even greater feature to allow players the freedom to create their own teams, team names, players and kits from pre-made designs, then to incorporate this team to a randomly generated and fictional league.

This is a review from somebody who owns GalCiv I + II but never got into them. Why I don't know. Installed GallCiv2: UE severeal times, played for a little while and got bored to hell. So I was quite sceotic with all the GalCiv 3 beta pizzazz.
BUT
It is sooooo good. I don't know what they did, but it suddenly clicked with me. Everybody says galCiv 3 is to similar to GalCiv 2, this I don't know, but they did something with GalCiv 3 which utterlay fascinates me.
The thing I am looking for in a Space game is SPACE. The vastness, the endless possibilities. Never was I more frustrated when I realized that "Endless Space" was very restricted in terms of Space. Enter GalCiv 3 you can create maps which are so big, that the UI (and mybe your computer) can't handle all the planets and star on the map. You can play with 100s of Factions if you want to, the ship creator doesn't let you outfit your own schips, no, you can create them from predefined 3D parts and then put your weopans, sensor, whatnot on it. I instantly created ships from Battlestar Galactica, modded my "race" so that I have Commander Adama as my leader with all the logos. How awesome is this?
Gameplay wise it creats all sorts of interesting decisions. How do I outfit this planet? Oh I got attacked, in which why should I construct ships, that my retaliation is successful? Do I need special rescources? Where do I find them? Is this region stable? Should I station a fleet there? Which planets do I take first from the enemy? Where is the best place for my new shipyard. It goes on and on.
PLUS Stardock has itself committed to support this game for years to come and I have no doubt that they will do it.
It is my most played game since Steam records your playtime.
Nuff said.

Beatgames (or rhythm games) tend to be very hard at first, but when you practice, you can literally see your improvement. Although this game is not a pure beatgame, it has the full characteristics of one. The concept of two different game genres put into one is incredible, but it is just
when the execution of it is perfect.
The soundtrack of this game is simply amazing. I've never really had a taste for electronic music or jazz, but the stuff they put into this game definitely made me change my mind. The way they've designed everything, I think, was so you, the player, could jam to any music that would hit you. Every moving object in the game has an animation that moves to the rhythm of the BPM (beats per minute; determines how fast a song is) of the song, the shopkeepers' singing is just perfect, and the rest of the sound effects (voices, attacks, monsters) flow so astoundingly. Sometimes I play this game just because I want to listen to the soundtrack. Custom music is a plus, and I have not found any errors working with it so far. It has it's own BPM detection that works fine.
Randomly generated-ness (well that's rogue-like, isn't it?) makes this game never get old. The story mode is of moderate length, and surprisingly, or at least, for me, I have gotten tied to the characters and I have grown to have sympathy for them! If you don't have a thing for rogue-like games, this will surely change your mind (That's what had happened to me).
The pixel art is adorable, and the character concept art for those monsters are.. dark and horrifying. Think you have a slow/old computer and can't run this game? This game ran at 60 fps on mine, so you're fine. (In case you didn't get it, my computer is
bad.)
When you first start playing, the thing that you need to remember is to
give up. If you die five times in a row, you should either take a break for a while and come back to the game later or keep playing. You
see that improvement and it will just feel amazing. You actually feel accomplished about something, which is what very few games are able to do.
As for going into more depth about the gameplay, no need for that. It is all for you to discover yourself. But here's something to remember: although the content of this game doesn't seem that abundant, trust me. It was way more stuff than you think. They also have a level editor after you complete the game (or should I say, a fraction of the game [Note what I said to remember]), so you can upload your creations to the Steam Workshop that is connected to the game or just play them alone. Nothing wrong with that.
To sum it up, this game deserves every one of those awards that you see to the right. If not, more than that. This review cannot express how much I enjoy this game. It is one of the most unique and unforgettable gaming experiences ever. Get this game if you're looking for something new to enjoy.
Also, sorry if I have any grammar/typing errors. I did not read this over.

EDIT (300+ Hours of Play):
WOW!
You know a game has you in its grips when you start scheduling your life around your game time!
I have now been completely sucked into GC3.  I knew this game was pretty solid when I first started playing it, but now that I've had some serious time to play it and actually figure out what I'm doing (mostly), I just have to say that this is what a 4x game should be.  A game that makes me say "Just one more turn!"   Just one more custom race tweak.  Just one more try at a new build strategy. (etc.)
I have not been this addicted to a game since probably World of Warcraft (even though they are in two completely different genres), and I really have to give credit to Stardock for doing a great job at making a game that is infuriatingly addictive,has literally has kept me up until dawn the next day, bloodshot eyes and a sore mouse-hand.
I think that Stardock has found a happy balance between being so simple of a game as to be boring vs. being so deep that you need a 100 page manual just to understand the game.  It's really easy to get into GC3, but once you play through a few games (400+ turns) on insane szed maps, you really get a feel for how this all works, and the game design is brilliant.  The sheer number of potential win strategies on display is staggering.  There is no "best" tech tree utilization.  Every decision has pros and cons and there is both short term and long term strategies that need to be mapped out.  Between the map design, your race (custom or not) along with planet management and tech research, there are potentially billions of ways to attack this game.
Personally, I play my games with "Conquest" or "Alliance" as the win strategies just so some race doesn't outbuild me and ascend to a different dimension while I'm stilll building capital ships to wipe them out.
The planetary map mini-game is really the stroke of genius to me.  SO much of your empire's success hinges on good planet management, and good planet management means paying attention to every detail, coming up with a solid build stretegy, having the right tech trees unlocked and then being able to switch gears on the fly.  What you build, where you build it and when you build it can mean the difference between rolling over your enemies like a steam roller, or getting your butt kicked before round 200.  The interplay between your research within the tech trees, your planet management and shipyard management are really where this game happens.  (I haven't even begun to use the custom ship editor!!!).  The planet mangement aspect of the game is very simple to get into, but this part of the game gets more and more complex as time goes on.
I haven't even begun to be an expert in this game even with 300+ hours under my belt.  I see MUCH replay ahead!
One last note:  The game has only crashed once on me in 300+ hours.  THANK YOU STARDOCK!
------
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
Anyway, I just wanted to provide an update to my previous review of GC3, and raise my score for this game from an 8.8 out of 10 to a solid 9.5 out of 10.  (The .5 left over is really just bug fixes, but I have found the game incredibly stable at this point).
GC3 is a game modder's DREAM!
I just started poking around the various game directories last night, and you really can customize the crap out this game.  Not only can you load in your own icons and photographs and backgrounds and videos for the races, but you can also use the ship designer todesign your own star fleets AND you can replace most of the game UI graphics AND they have included the ability to create "total conversion" mods for the game, right out of the box.
So, even beyond an already flexible game (no modding required), the replayability of GC3 is great!  Add to that the ability to tweak this game into the next century and that adds another whole dimension to it.
Next, I confirmed with some fans that Stardock has committed to 2 expansion packs and several bug fix patches along the way.  This is a big deal to me because if you have seen the end result of GC2, you will realize that this released game is just the START of a development cycle that continues well after the game is released.  Bugs will be fixed, new features will be added etc.
So, I'm not just happy about this game as is (and I am already addicted to it!) I am very much looking to the future as well.
IF you are a fan of 4x games, I think this is defintely a must have!  I've been looking for a while for a decent way to burn time, and GC3 definitely fits the bill for me.
Hopefully my other review will go up at some point... I don't want to have to write all that again!  =(

Soo i haven't played the game as much as the most people here but i can say that - I think this is the best sandbox game ever created, and i will explain why.
First off you can do whatever you want ( like with most sandboxes ) but Gmod if you have the skills, the technique and the brain you can create your own world, because it enables you to do it, you can insert plugins, make them and use them and your server.
Second the game system requirements are really good, thanks to the amazing performance creating system of Source Engine which applies for like almost every single one of their games, you can run this game with its good graphics without lags even with low budget pc.
Third it has a lot of gamemodes so if you get tired from sandbox with friends or alone you can go explore them, but here is the catch: Because most of the servers use a specific graphics pack ( addon pack ) you will need it if you don't want to see errors and pink ( missing ) texture, you will need this specific addon pack which is a little larger then the normal ones but its worth it i gurantee you it will fix every single missing texture that you have if not too specific - just go google gmod cs source cheater
textures and open the site then go to Garry Content and download Cs Source addon and map pack and you are good to go. A little more i can add to this review is that the player base is really good I'm not really sure of the region system ( if there is one ) but I'm from EU and i can tell you that there are more than 200,000 people playing almost every 24 hours a day. Playing with friends is even more fun as you do silly things together in the sandbox mode or join a specific one. The steam workshop page for Gmod is the biggest one in Steam as there are more than 1mil addons you can download for free and use them in the game. The only negative side i can say is that the more complicated stuff you do the bigger performance damage you will suffer, for example if you join server that has a lot of plugins and addons you will have lower performance then playing in a casual server with a little bit of addons but still enjoyable, even in singleplayer mode the more things you do ( spam, use, change ) the lower performance but i think that is something normal for a sandbox game. The other negative thing is that you have to wait long often when you join servers even if you have the maps and also the more addons you have the longer you will wait at the beginning of the game when you launch it because they will need to fetch. Thats pretty much what i can say i really enjoy the game with and without my friends I can say 9/10 but still the best sandbox and one of the best Source Engine projects ever created. Its worth the money also really often on sales.

Over the last two week I have been taking a grand trip down memory lane to my all time favourite game, Final Fantasy VII, the 1997 Playstation 1 blockbuster that won a place in my heart all those years ago. But I’m 26 years old now, so I was more than tempted to see if this game has aged as well as I hope it has, or if my own memories of this game have clouded (see what I did there?) over a lot of the games issues.
When it launched back in 1997, Final Fantasy took the world by storm, selling 2.3 million copies just in the first 3 days and that was only for Japan and by 2010 the game had sold well over 10 million copies worldwide, so it has has obviously earned is self more than a few fans since its initial release.
Since then it has been re-released on the PlayStation Network as a digital download, where again it saw a rise in sales and popularity, but the crowd that was really left out were the PC gamers, given a somewhat shocking port of the original PlayStation 1 title, with poor controller support, lower resolution videos and a midi soundtrack that had lost all the charm from the original release, but now with this new release I aim to find out if all this and more has finally been addressed, giving us PC gamers the Final Fantasy VII port we want and deserve.
While I’m sure there are many fans that are crying for a full blown remake of this game, please don’t hold your breath for it, it may or may never happen, no one really knows, but for now, this will have to do.

This is kind of like Winged Cloud's Sakura series, really, except that it's a poorly put together erotic visual novel rather than a poorly put together fanservice visual novel. On the plus side, it has English voice acting, which is a nice touch even if it's oddly quiet in a lot of scenes, such that I could barely hear it even after turning the music volume down to like 20% and leaving the voice volume at 100%. On the minus side... well, everything else.
The biggest technical complaint I had with Divine Slice of Life was how obtuse a lot of the choices are in terms of what they affect - basically every choice affects which ending you get, but it's rarely clear why or how it should when you're making it... or ever, sometimes. Beyond that, it's just clumsily written romantic/sexual hijinks over a few days, with the two main girls often sharing the same lines in different branches despite being incredibly different in personality when they get their own lines and plenty of writing that just made me think the writer was a space squid attempting to understand how human relationships work.
It's also fairly short - despite what the designer has said about five hours, I finished up with the game in 99 minutes, a good bit of which I spent trying to figure out what choices were making me automatically pick Ryn at the end, since the ones that affect that mostly seem to have little to no bearing on anything.
So yeah. Not recommended to anyone, might well be worse than Winged Cloud's similar Sakura Angels.

Earthlock harkens back to the early days of 3D JRPGs with gameplay inspired by games like Final Fantasy 7-9.
One of the initial draws for me was the art and music. Very clean and polished. The music is high quality and fit in well with the art direction. While it can look bland in some areas, overall there is a considerable amount of detail. Though not particularly unique, the character designs were also good.
The gameplay itself was mostly as expected. There is the world map you wander around in, towns and dungeons you can visit, and then battles you can fight in an oldschoolish JRPG battle system.
Although the towns looked great, there wasn't much interaction to be had outside of story. This is true in general. There are very few optional things to do and it takes the liveliness away from the world.
The dungeons had weak designs. They weren't particularly challenging. While there are elements that resemble puzzles, they were not puzzling at all. You simply go through each section guided by whatever path is made available to you.
The battle system was ok, but too many things that just weren't useful. I found that I only used a few skills because of how useless most of them are. Changing stance to use a different set of skills was a cool idea, but took way too long to recover from to be practical in most situations.
It was an excellent effort, but in the end, it was a mediocre experience and did not satisfy.
Update 7/11:
I played through the game with the new stance cost reduction and the battle system is a little more interesting now. I am using skills and party builds that weren't feasible with the old stance costs.
Playing the game again also made me rethink my recommendation. I wanted something a little more hardcore and in that respect, I still would not recommend this game. However, it is a decent game, not too casual, that should appeal to genre fans that don't mind a little less depth.

So, I am not sure why my last review isn't on Steam now... did I say something wrong?
EDIT (300+ Hours of Play):
WOW!
You know a game has you in its grips when you start scheduling your life around your game time!
I have now been completely sucked into GC3.  I knew this game was pretty solid when I first started playing it, but now that I've had some serious time to play it and actually figure out what I'm doing (mostly), I just have to say that this is what a 4x game should be.  A game that makes me say "Just one more turn!"   Just one more custom race tweak.  Just one more try at a new build strategy. (etc.)
I have not been this addicted to a game since probably World of Warcraft (even though they are in two completely different genres), and I really have to give credit to Stardock for doing a great job at making a game that is infuriatingly addictive,has literally has kept me up until dawn the next day, bloodshot eyes and a sore mouse-hand.
I think that Stardock has found a happy balance between being so simple of a game as to be boring vs. being so deep that you need a 100 page manual just to understand the game.  It's really easy to get into GC3, but once you play through a few games (400+ turns) on insane szed maps, you really get a feel for how this all works, and the game design is brilliant.  The sheer number of potential win strategies on display is staggering.  There is no "best" tech tree utilization.  Every decision has pros and cons and there is both short term and long term strategies that need to be mapped out.  Between the map design, your race (custom or not) along with planet management and tech research, there are potentially billions of ways to attack this game.
Personally, I play my games with "Conquest" or "Alliance" as the win strategies just so some race doesn't outbuild me and ascend to a different dimension while I'm stilll building capital ships to wipe them out.
The planetary map mini-game is really the stroke of genius to me.  SO much of your empire's success hinges on good planet management, and good planet management means paying attention to every detail, coming up with a solid build stretegy, having the right tech trees unlocked and then being able to switch gears on the fly.  What you build, where you build it and when you build it can mean the difference between rolling over your enemies like a steam roller, or getting your butt kicked before round 200.  The interplay between your research within the tech trees, your planet management and shipyard management are really where this game happens.  (I haven't even begun to use the custom ship editor!!!).  The planet mangement aspect of the game is very simple to get into, but this part of the game gets more and more complex as time goes on.
I haven't even begun to be an expert in this game even with 300+ hours under my belt.  I see MUCH replay ahead!
One last note:  The game has only crashed once on me in 300+ hours.  THANK YOU STARDOCK!

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
Anyway, I just wanted to provide an update to my previous review of GC3, and raise my score for this game from an 8.8 out of 10 to a solid 9.5 out of 10.  (The .5 left over is really just bug fixes, but I have found the game incredibly stable at this point).
GC3 is a game modder's DREAM!
I just started poking around the various game directories last night, and you really can customize the crap out this game.  Not only can you load in your own icons and photographs and backgrounds and videos for the races, but you can also use the ship designer todesign your own star fleets AND you can replace most of the game UI graphics AND they have included the ability to create "total conversion" mods for the game, right out of the box.
So, even beyond an already flexible game (no modding required), the replayability of GC3 is great!  Add to that the ability to tweak this game into the next century and that adds another whole dimension to it.
Next, I confirmed with some fans that Stardock has committed to 2 expansion packs and several bug fix patches along the way.  This is a big deal to me because if you have seen the end result of GC2, you will realize that this released game is just the START of a development cycle that continues well after the game is released.  Bugs will be fixed, new features will be added etc.
So, I'm not just happy about this game as is (and I am already addicted to it!) I am very much looking to the future as well.
IF you are a fan of 4x games, I think this is defintely a must have!  I've been looking for a while for a decent way to burn time, and GC3 definitely fits the bill for me.

First of all I want to say congratulations TREK Industries, for making a revolutionary product that will change the way we look at games forever. I have logged over 500 hours in this game on a seperate account and bought it again for this one and all of my friends just to prove my loyalty to the product. Now for the actual review.
Orion: Prelude is an amazing game that can be easily compared to AAA titles such as Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare, the Halo franchise, the Counter Strike titles, and is better than mostly all FPS indie titles out there.
Graphics: Oh my god the graphics. This is a timeless piece of art that will be revered for as long as video gaming is alive. The graphics are simply timeless and they make the enviroment look absolutely beautiful. Low graphics in this game are basically equivilent to Ultra graphics in Far Cry 4. Water reflections are amazingly vivid, the dinosaurs are textured amazingly. Really nothing else can be said but this is an absolute must have game for anybody who enjoys beautiful scenery and amazing gameplay.
AI: If you can call it AI... it feels like you're actually playing with real people when offline. The grunts that help you move and act like they were real war veterans and move into and out of cover as well as taking positions to give them the upper hand. Advanced manuevers are no problem for this AI. Aside from the humans, the dinosaurs are superb as well. Amazing tracking, great movement recognition. Be careful, these things can spot you from  a mile away.
Gameplay: This gameplay is honestly some of the best I have ever experienced. The best way to describe it is a mix of Call of Duty, Halo, and the balance of Counter Strike. While in the game I have had extremely intense situations where the entire team relyed of me to win. Its stuff like that that makes the game fun. In one instance I was being charged by several velociraptors and a T-rex. I turned on my absolutely flawless cloaking device and fled the scene back to the hut where i bought my sniper rifle and killed each and every dinosaur to win the game. Lets say i was sweating after that intense experience and was extremely proud of my self and my abilities to master this amazing game.
Overall I think this is a must have for any video game player looking for an amazing, intense FPS situation with not only good graphics and fun gameplay, but with balance and a cheap price as well. Honestly, this game should be at LEAST 10$ for a copy. I have bought it for all of my friends and we currently all enjoy the game together and play it whenever we have a chance. Keep up the amazing work TREK and make sure you buy this game before the price goes up! It's definitely worth the money!

A top down, insane mixture of stick shooter, stealth, and melee combat. You play a man who I can only conclude is whacked out of his gourd, completing missions that mostly boil down to "Go to the next level and kill all the dudes" but it is WAY more complicated that that sounds.
You have to sneak around the building, avoid being seen, try to get the drop on your enemies. You can just run in guns blazzing but unless you have reflexes like the friggen flash, you are going to find yourself neatly perforated by all manner of objects righ tquick.
Despite the retro aesthetic and top down look, the combat feels very visceral and quite satisfying, especailly once you beat the tar out of the levels boss after your 25th try .
The game is hard, and it is not apologetic about that, but the fast respawn back into the action helps alleviate that somewhat. It's not as unforgiving or unfair as something like I Wanna Be The Guy! but I did have a few moments where the cycle of death and restart was feeling very familiar.
If you are looking for a difficult, but mostly fair, fast paced combat game, you won't do much better than this.

Crypt of the NecroDancer. So what is it? It is a dungeon crawler where turns are taking place in a certain (dictated by song) rhytm.
Basically you go on andventure of 4 zones, each having 4 levels. Design of each zone is unique and entertaining, each with different enemies traps and hazards. At end of each level you will meet a Miniboss (7 different types, which most have upraged version of itself), and at the end of each level you will meet a boss (4 types).

When you finish a "run" (beat 4 zones in a row) you will meet final boss. But if you are able to defeat him it's not over. After it you will have 2 more characters that push story to play with. "What story?" Every time you beat any zone with a character you will get a cutscene (don't worry you can skip it).
"But why did you say 2 more characters
?" Because you will have 6 differeant characters that do not push story and are there to make this game even longer!
Gameplay feels slick and nice with amazing songs (3 differeant song packs {normal, kind-of-disco and metal one} + a beat analizer so you can adapt your own songs to the game).  Game is quite well balanced and only issue that i have is bosses at end of zones are too easy (excluding "main" ones). Local Co-Op is sweet, game has controller support and achievment system.
What could i say more?

"Mafia III could have been so much more"
Mafia III is a contination of the timeline from the previous Mafia II game, but this time it takes place in fictional New Orleans (New Bordeaux) during the early 1960's "Jim Crow" era of segregation in the United States.
At times the racism and long held beliefs feels geniune, but MOST other times it feels forced and the game only seems to show one side of the story to make the player seem justified in his actions.
I understand that this problem was paramount in this time period, but this is a game about being in the Mafia and fighting the Mafia, not MLK vs. the KKK.
I'm not even kidding, every white person in the game is either a rich snob who sticks their nose up at your black character, or they are a renegade redneck Klan member who wants to murder you  right there in broad daylight.
The black people are all potrayed as either poor and unable to function or hardened criminals who have to be criminals just because "racism".
This unfairly paints ALL people who lived during segration as racists and all people of color as victims or thugs.
There seems to be only one character in the game who has any sense of right and wrong, but at the same time, he gets on the radio and calls for the killing of other people, right after telling your character to seek God.
Why they chose to focus on this to the extent they did feels like a cheap way to get the player to side with the main character, who is pretty horrible person in his own right for some of the crimes he commits throughout the game.
But the game makes it feel like "hey it's okay you just killed 20 people, because racism".
The character you are playing is not a good person, he is a CRIMINAL who uses people for profit and kills people for a false sense of justice, so why go all heavy handed with the high-horse political crap is baffling to me.
This political divide didn't even need to be in the game to begin with and it seems as if it was put in the game as an excuse to hate the people you are killing rather than focusing on character development of the enemy.
All the bad guys feel like cookie cutter, worst of society types.
Only the very last enemies feel a touch unique, but even then, any veteran of gaming plot lines will see the ending coming hours before the game is even close to finished.
I did enjoy the part where the CIA is involved and the under running subplot, that part felt somewhat realistic and geniune, I wish they had focused on reality more like that and the game would have felt like a geniune succesor to Mafia II rather than a side story.
Some of the side characters you deal with are so arrogant, annoying, and just down right nasty people to deal with, there were times when I wanted to side with the antagonists rather than the "heroes" of the game.
The mission structure and the constant driving over 85% of the map to get 1 out of 200 of something makes the game feel like a chore rather than fun or engaging.
It feels like the devs were so proud of this big map they made, so they wanted to force the player to cover every single inch of it, as many times as possible.
When you get sick of driving from point A to point B in game, you know something wasn't done correctly.
I spent at least 60% of the game just getting to a place to collect or do something that wasn't part of the main mission.
The other problem, is once you unlock certain vehicles, there is no point in using any others for the rest of the game.
This happens pretty early in the game and makes the entire concept of using different vehicles pointless.
There are also many, many techincal problems with the game.
From a graphical stand point, this game CAN look good, but not without tinkering with .ini files and tricking the game into disabling some of it's "features".
Without editing game files, the game's best modes look like someone smeared grease all over your screen.
From skys that look like hell has arrived to sudden changes in weather every 5 seconds, there is def. a problem with the graphics engine.
Gunplay/ Combat feels like an MMO.
The entire cover, shooting and aiming aspect honestly feels like the type of "action" you would encounter playing
an RPG MMO with super accurate AI and 50 bullets to drop a single guy.
I played this game from start to finish, I have over 100 hours in it, so yes, I did get my money's worth, But:
Would I play this again, knowing what I know after playing it?
No. That's the problem.
When I finished I didn't feel resolution or happyiness at finishing an amazing story.
I only felt relief and boredom as anyone over the age of 20 would have seen the "ending" coming after the first hour into the game and everything else just felt like filler to pad the game clock.
If the devs want me to purchase Mafia 4, they need to go back to their roots and analyze what made Mafia 1 and 2 so succesfull.
Stop with the political and progressive echo chambers and make a game where you are in the Mafia, not some 'good' side guy who runs around avenging 1 wrong by killing every single person in town who may or may not be bad, just because they happen to live in a time period where some people had the wrong ideas about color and race.
I was crying playing this masterpiece. If you are into music, art or just beautiful nature this game is for you.

Abzu very different kind of game but I thoroughly enjoyed it. The visuals, soundtrack, and overall artistic style really sucked me in all the way to the end. Although there is a focus on taking your time and enjoying the game's atmosphere, there are a few mysteries in the storyline which the game will keep to itself right to the end, but constantly pique your curiosity with clues and twists.

gamepad controls are great, wouldn't change a thing about them. If you plan to use a keyboard, don't. Playing through this game for the first time is a once in a lifetime experience you won't want to sour with the wrong controls. Not that the keyboard controls are poorly designed, it's just that with your character swimming through 3D space and a need to rotate the camera at will, keyboard and mouse really aren't the right input device for the job.
If you're after a challenge or long campaign, this isn't the game for you. The gameplay consisted of finding buttons and unlocking species to advance to the next area, and I completed it in about 2 hours. This didn't bother me at all though since there was plenty of fun to be had gliding through the incredibly diverse scenery while hunting for secrets, and actually being surprised (there are plenty of surprises) and entertained by how the game changed themes as I progressed.
You might want to think of those 20USD like a conert or movie ticket as you're more or less buying an experience.

If you go into the three LiEat tales expecting a typical or expansive RPG experience; don't.
It's much more narrative focused with the gameplay amounting to little more than a barebones "examine around until you find the powerful gear and extra restoration items, then grind just a tad" affair with the occasional puzzle to drive home the mystery theme. Sadly, most of the interesting puzzles and gameplay consequences are exclusive to LiEat III and kept sparse between the other two.
LiEat's appeal primarily lies with its snappy personality filled dialogue exchanges between characters, utilizing bittersweet tones to good effect and visual presentation, featuring some nice dark and not so dark fairy tale motifs and the occasional non-sprite animated segment (something rare to find in Wolf RPG editor titles). It's a cute/neat looking game to be sure and a nice little collection of reads if you have the patience to figure out what to do next, but alas it finishes off like a read that was just getting to a good part before snapping shut with no continuation in sight.
I found myself quite enjoying the setting and general idea of LiEat but was also finding that, as deduction + lie eating as a gameplay mechanic was never capitalized on nor amounted to anything outside of flavor text, perhaps the whole thing would've worked better as a novel like the prequel was rather than using a not so great RPG as a medium to relay the story. But for that bite-sized price that nets you three games, which occasionally becomes nibble-sized sales depending, I'd say it's still worthy of checking out if one finds the basic premise appealing.

The music is very good and memorable, and the environments are sufficiently detailed, especially the town of Grove, which is a bright and lively antithesis to the dark dungeon.  It has a unique replayability in the form of retirement.  Upon slaying the monster assigned to you at the beginning of the game, you are given the option to retire and pass on an heirloom to your heir.  This heir starts over from the beginning with the heirloom, of which the magical attributes have been doubled.  If you get the game, don't expect some deep RPG with lore to blow you away, but expect a fun little Diablo-esque hack-and-slash dungeon crawler.

Before you disregard this review due to the little time played on this account, I actually went and purchased the MG version and played through all of it.
Honestly, waiting for this game for months really hyped it up for me, but in the end I was severely let down. The fac that it was made by a Western team doesn't elevate its status in the least bit, other than the fact that the art work was stellar.
The voice acting and lip-syncing were off to the point that a character would continuously make lip movements although only interjections or very short sentneces were made. The voice acting had awkward volumes at some points in the game and it wasn't even of decent quality to boot.
The story was largely unaffected by most of the choices except for a few, putting very little weight and actual thinking into each choice being made. Two of the bad endings were basically copied and pasted with different voices, which is honestly a lack of effort on AJTilley's side. The story was also rushed to the point that I had to replay it just to properly understand what happened after making a couple of choices.
I'm no visual novel connoisseur, but I've played through enough of them to know this barely hits the level of mediocrety. Also if you're curious as to whether or not you should get the MG version or the Steam version, there is honestly next to no difference except for the rather soft and unfortunately forced H-scenes that pop up every here and there. You're better off spending your money on a decent on either a better visual novel on steam(I reccomend Cho Dengeki Stryker) or any other game for that matter that isn't this.
P.S. Mangagamer usually does shell out pretty good content(take eden* for example) so you can check out their other works and not be disappointed by this, lack  of better words, awful visual novel.

10/10 Best time sink simulator for the price.
Let me preface this by saying that I have put almost three full days of playtime into this game at time of writing, so I obviously like it.
Fate is a Dungeon Crawler that came out in 2005, while the music is somewhat similar to that of Diablo, it does fit the setting and does aid with immersion quite well. The graphic are great for 2005 and can hold their own in a modern gaming market given recent events. (I am looking at you, AC Unity.)
A very basic gist of the story is this: big bad monster in big bad dungeon. Adventurous hero of unknown origin and unremarkable (non-existant?) achievement must go and slay this baddie as s/he is clearly our last and greatest hope. So off you go with little more than a pointy stick and your trusty pet compainion to try and stomp a monster's teeth in.
Every floor of the dungeon is random, in the sense that is a series of rooms with sporadic and often unyeildy connecting paths. As a whole, the entire dungeon has a nice and bumpy difficulty curve that, if you are strategic and don't mind some grinding, you can completely kick the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of.
I think one of the drawbacks of this game is one key game mechanic in particular. I won't be disclosing which mechanic this is, as once you figure out why it is useful, you are going to abuse this machanic like you just found out the button combination to get free soda in the soda machine at the office. Once that happens, the game loses quite a bit of difficulty. One of many things that really makes up for this is another mechanic, Enchanting, which is really more of a gamble than the actual "gambling" mechanic.
Another thing I really like about this game are the items obtainable and the playstyles available, FATE wholeheartedly supports the idea of having your cake and eating it too, though various stat selections on leveling up, you can do just about anything, or do everything if you really want to. This is great for me, because I am the type of person that if I get a massive '♥♥♥♥ you' sword, I want a second '♥♥♥♥ you' sword or a superpowered sheild of 'I don't give a ♥♥♥♥'. And the game lets you do that! And I love that about it.
All in all, it is a great game if you are looking for something to introduce you to Dungeon Crawling, or if you are looking for something to eat up free time cheaply.

To summarize, I wanted to like this game so much, but there are too many flaws to overlook. The concept is original, and the visuals are pretty, but the game lacks in length, writing quality, voice acting quality, and good, unique characters.
Naming the positives of this game is easy, as they are exactly what the game flaunts most in promotions.
- The artwork and visuals flow well, and look good. Some might disagree, but I like the charm, and it definitely adds to the game's quality.
- The story concept is a relatively good one. Two goddesses suddenly attach themselves to a random guy, and he has to deal with everyday life while they call him Zeus, the king of gods, fawn on him, compete for his affections, and generally make his life a hectic mess. If the game was executed better, this would have been a fabulous opportunity for comedy gold, awkwardness aplenty, and a diverse cast.
- The game has a good number of endings, with outcome diversity that makes them at least worthwhile to see how they differ.
- The music is decent and fits the mood, though it isn't the highest quality I've heard from a visual novel.
Despite the positives, there are many issues with the game that leave a bad taste in my mouth.
- Length. The game claims to have 5-6 hours of play time if you play through all the endings. It took me closer to 4 hours, though that might be due to my reading pace. Still, however, I don't think that it's quite how much as I expected.
- Voice acting. I'm not the best judge for voices, but those that the game used didn't sound very professional in quality. The voices weren't normalized to a set volume, clearly used recording equipment of varying quality and sound, and generally seem more thrown together as a promotional feature than crafted to enhance the story.
In my opinion, this game's writing quality is what holds it back the most. It's rushed, repetitive, and worst of all, fails to make its characters unique besides their appearance.
- The game is rushed. There isn't a lot of conflict, except choosing between which girl you want to get intimate with, with a few other choices that determine good/bad endings. The game skips over time periods frequently, to the point where I lost track of what day it was many times. Plenty of things go unexplained about the goddesses' cultural differences, reduced to just a few lines of explanation. There's also a lack of casual talk and events that aren't crutial to the plot. The game just passes by, preferring to move on with the story content and choices instead of taking the time to give the reader some flavor to savor, and develop the characters.
- The game repeats itself often. For example, in the first two endings in the game, (which happen within the first 20-30 minutes of play) the script is literally a copy+paste, with two characters swapped out, and a few names changed in the text. I would have much preferred some variety in both the characters and the script for those individual endings. I would think that The goddess of wisdom and justice would react different to the goddess of love if either is
That isn't all of it, though. Even the good endings for each of the goddesses are eerily similar, with lines that don't differ much at all. The bad endings share a lot of the same text as well. This makes replaying the game for new routes tedious in a lot of ways.
- The characters aren't unique. While the game does have an interesting premise, it doesn't do much with its characters at all. The two goddesses seem like copies of each other in terms of personality, history and background, power level, and so many other things, that choosing between them seemed meaningless. Given how much copy+paste text they seem to share, I think I could almost replace them in my mind with one single goddess character, and the story wouldn't be much different. The other two heroines are better, but both are classmates with the protagonist, and still seem very similar. They also fall into the "childhood friend" and "popular girl" tropes pretty solidly, not trying to be much different from what consumers have seen time and again.
For consumers,
This game might look attractive, but it has a lot of flaws. If you really like the concept, or you're not picky about quality, you can pick it up for a decently good time, but don't expect it to leave you with a fulfilling, meaningful experience like other visual novels might.
For the game devs,
Your game is not bad, and it gave me a good run for the time I spent with it, but you haven't put in quite the amount of effort it needs to seem professional, and worth my time and money. To improve your game, I'd highly suggest working on the script, rewriting repetitive scenes, and making the characters more unique and genuine. The script is the core of the reader's experience, and while great visuals and art improve the game, and voice acting is a lovely feature when done right, it won't compensate for lazy, repetitive writing. When you're working on your next game or improving this one, make sure to evaluate your priorities, and make sure your game is appealing in every aspect.
Note: I played the Mangagamer Adult Version, so some differences may be apparent between that and the steam version.

Loved it when I was a kid, love it now!

OVERVIEW
This game is a lot like a sci-fi themed Hearthstone. If you've played Hearthstone, then it will feel familiar to you.
MECHANICS
Like in Hearthstone you get one supply (mana) per turn to a maximum of 10. There is an initiative token similar to The Coin.
Where this game is different is that you pick a race, and then up to 3 modules that can be considered your class abilities. There is a fairly broad pool of modules, but they must be collected or unlocked. Some are much more powerful and useful than others, but there's still room for tactical flexibility.
Your HP is determined by the amount of cards in your deck. You must have a minimum of 25, to a maximum of 40. In other words, you sacrifice consistency for more HP. Rush decks or very focused decks tend to be closer to 25, while control decks usually have more.
For people who are used to having a maximum of 4 per card from Magic, or 3 per card in Duelyst, this game allows only 2 copies of a card per deck — except Paragons (Legendaries), of which you can only have a single copy.
You can craft cards in this game and break down duplicates or ones that you are not using.
PRICE
The game is fairly priced compared to similar DCG's. You can earn a pack a day if you do your daily quests and play a couple of rounds. You can earn more if you Raid (Arena) and are good at it.
The thing I like about the game is that you can build a fairly competitive deck for cheap. The HajirGog and Heirarchy both have budget decks (around 250 scrap) that can get you fairly far up the ladder before you may need to invest.
Of course, some of the better decks are more expensive. But these budget decks are pretty effective.
INTERFACE
The interface is not as polished as Hearthstone. I personally think it's ugly, but it's functional — it clearly displays all the information you need to know.
It's missing some filters in the deckbuilder that would be handy, such as sorting by creature type. You can type in things like rarities, but it's not as useful as just being able to toggle a button.
CARD ART
You can't really judge card games by their graphics, as they're usually pretty light. The card art is decent. Nothing spectacular, but good. Most of the aliens and such look good. It's really only the humans where the art looks a bit strange or amateurish.
SOUND
The music is your typical spacey / industrial theme. I muted it after a while.
Sound effects are chunky and satisfying, particularly for some of the Terran tactics that rain fire.
OVERALL
I recommend this game to people who may have liked Hearthstone, but didn't particularly care for the Warcraft theme. I prefer the science-fiction theme. Like Hearthstone, there is a lot of RNG, but there's enough room for tactical flexibility with modules and what not that it feels slightly more strategic.
You can play a couple of matches in a small amount of time. I would say it's not as deep as HEX or Duelyst, but it's satisfying for what it is.
All in all, I recommend this game — especially given its budget-friendly decks.
Do not forget to check the Steam Discussion boards for the promo thread and try out all the codes. Many are time sensitive, but there are a few that are still active to boost your colleection.
UPDATE: I can no longer recommend this game due to the imbalance of certain cards that has gone unaddressed. Play it, by all means — but I would not spend money on it.

First of all I want to say congratulations TREK Industries, for making a revolutionary product that will change the way we look at games forever. I have logged over 500 hours in this game on a seperate account and bought it again for this one and all of my friends just to prove my loyalty to the product. Now for the actual review.
Orion: Prelude is an amazing game that can be easily compared to AAA titles such as Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare, the Halo franchise, the Counter Strike titles, and is better than mostly all FPS indie titles out there.
Graphics: Oh my god the graphics. This is a timeless piece of art that will be revered for as long as video gaming is alive. The graphics are simply timeless and they make the enviroment look absolutely beautiful. Low graphics in this game are basically equivilent to Ultra graphics in Far Cry 4. Water reflections are amazingly vivid, the dinosaurs are textured amazingly. Really nothing else can be said but this is an absolute must have game for anybody who enjoys beautiful scenery and amazing gameplay.
AI: If you can call it AI... it feels like you're actually playing with real people when offline. The grunts that help you move and act like they were real war veterans and move into and out of cover as well as taking positions to give them the upper hand. Advanced manuevers are no problem for this AI. Aside from the humans, the dinosaurs are superb as well. Amazing tracking, great movement recognition. Be careful, these things can spot you from  a mile away.
Gameplay: This gameplay is honestly some of the best I have ever experienced. The best way to describe it is a mix of Call of Duty, Halo, and the balance of Counter Strike. While in the game I have had extremely intense situations where the entire team relyed of me to win. Its stuff like that that makes the game fun. In one instance I was being charged by several velociraptors and a T-rex. I turned on my absolutely flawless cloaking device and fled the scene back to the hut where i bought my sniper rifle and killed each and every dinosaur to win the game. Lets say i was sweating after that intense experience and was extremely proud of my self and my abilities to master this amazing game.
Overall I think this is a must have for any video game player looking for an amazing, intense FPS situation with not only good graphics and fun gameplay, but with balance and a cheap price as well. Honestly, this game should be at LEAST 10$ for a copy. I have bought it for all of my friends and we currently all enjoy the game together and play it whenever we have a chance. Keep up the amazing work TREK and make sure you buy this game before the price goes up! It's definitely worth the money!

When I hear Zach Barth say that a puzzle game made him want to stab himself, I expect that game to be made from the stuff of Satan's nightmares. As it turns out, Sokobond is made from more palatable material, and Zach's quote is made from hyperbole. This is not a criticism, mind you - when you have 124 puzzles in your game, you don't want inordinately difficult roadblocks impeding access to the rest of them. Progression is handled by way of a grid in which each puzzle is represented by a square and successfully completing it unlocks adjacent squares. The challenge curves out nicely, and if there was one puzzle I had grown tired of there were usually at least a half dozen others I could divert myself to.
The trailer shows you pretty much everything you need to know about the game mechanics. In every puzzle you take control of a single molecule which has a certain number of bonds it can make - anywhere from 1 to 4 - and will automatically bond with any molecule it comes into contact with, provided that that molecule also has spare bonds available. If it doesn't, then you are able to push that molecule elsewhere in the level. At fixed points in the environment are spaces which will separate bonded molecules, increase the strength of molecules' bonds (i.e. if 2 molecules are bonded, and each have another bond spare, running them through such a space will remove the spares by giving them a double bond), and reorientate the molecules' positions. That's it. It's essentially a block-pushing game with a novel twist.
The goal is to connect all of the provided molecules in such a way that there are no remaining bonds. In some levels the challenge lies in working out in what order and in what arrangement a small number of molecules need to be collected and placed to use all their bonds, while in others the challenge lies in piloting a huge snaking line of molecules around a very limited space, making sure that certain parts of its body never touch others in order to avoid undesired bonds. Some levels even see you take control of helium, which has 0 bonds available, meaning that you can only create the end product indirectly, via environmental manipulation. Though, as other reviewers have pointed out, the chemicals you will be making are frequently the same, the way in which you make them is always fresh and different - no small feat, given the amount of content on offer.
I enjoyed my time with Sokobond and would recommend it to anyone looking for an intermediate level of challenge. It's certainly not even in the same universe of hellish difficulty as Zachtronics games. It's not the most amazing or memorable puzzle game I've ever played, but it is thoughtful and well designed.
Overall score: 3.5/5
As a footnote, I'd like to say that I did not enjoy the bonus levels unlocked upon completion of the other 124, however as they are presented in the context of a bonus this did not affect my opinion of the game one way or the other. I will talk about them anyway, because they serve to illustrate the difference in 'feel' regarding the sort of puzzles I enjoy, which is useful info if you share similar preferences. The bonus levels adhere to the 'needle in a haystack' school of puzzle design, in which there is only one route to the solution and a single misstep will render the puzzle unsolvable, however this will not be apparent until several steps further down the line, leaving you to wonder which of the many previous moves you have made was the wrong one. With a few exceptions, the main game's puzzles allow you enough leeway to experiment and come upon an 'a-ha!' moment organically, and if it has become unsolvable this will be immediately apparent. The latter feels as if I'm slowly being guided to a solution via process of elimination, while the former gives no feedback whatsoever, making it more frustrating than fun. The great majority of the puzzles in Sokobond are fun.

First off and probably most importantly: The game is about as stable as a house of cards built over a geyser. It took me about two hours of researching to find solutions and playing around with the game's files to finally get it going for that first time. Then, the game continued to crash during play time. So, yet another hour or so of my time to find methods of keeping it running properly. The mothertrucker still crashes to this day at times.
That right there costs the game some big points in my esteem. When I pay 50 bucks for your game, it better damn well work the first time I click on it (unless my computer is the problem-- which it was not in this case.)
Technical issues aside (as glaring as they are), this is a really lackluster, mediocre game. Nothing special to see here folks.
Diplomacy is pretty standard with nothing deep going on there. It's the standard trade agreement that we have already seen in hundreds of such games before (give me this tech for that tech, declare war, etc). The diplomacy system in older games (Alpha Centauri among others) is probably much more complex. If anything, diplomacy is pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with the AI factions acting all bi-polar on you. They shower you with praise and credits at one moment, then they declare war two turns later. I enjoyed the quasi-United Nations thing they had going there though (planetary alliance or something). That was a neat highlight.
There is no ground combat / planetary invasions - defense game system. It's a very random thing. In most of my playing, taking over a planet is pretty automatic. Very rarely did I need to send in a second wave of invading forces. You don't need to prepare too much in advance. Planets that are outfitted to the wazoo with defensive things still get taken down fairly easy. Honestly, why has no game of this sort not put some thought into the ground game? Look at Emperor of the Fading Suns. There's a great old game that did that in a very fun and engrossing fashion. Seriously, no one has even touched the ground game in years.
The space combat is ridiculous. You have zero options or control. Starships fly and charge at each other like cavalry. Once close to the enermy, they then begin to rotate around each other in a dancing fashion and deal their damage. Seeing capital starships fly in circles around one another like fighters in some kind of demented NASCAR dogfight took a lot of punch away from the highlight of the game (starship battles). I found myself skipping the combat scenes pretty early on because A) You can't do anything anyways and the ships are governed by the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cavalry charge tactic. 2) It makes me laugh because it's so off putting... the way the ships dance around each other in a circle.
Seriously, give the player some tactical control. Make the game interesting by still having a chance to win even if you're the underdog with the smarter opponent having an edge of some kind.
The universe is pretty dead. Ships take forever to get to all the corners of the open space. No jump drives or something that could speed up fleet movement over the map. This isn't even slow burn tension, it's like driving a golf cart for 8 hours.
The only thing that I really enjoyed about the game was the custom faction option. I had fun populating my map with Warhammer 40K and Mass Effect inspired races / factions. I played with my own custom made Kilrathi Empire faction. I had more fun creating factions than actually playing the game though.
So, no, on the whole, this game isn't worth 50$.

I got a lot of enjoyment out of Dust but at the same time I don't agree that it is as great as some reviews make it out to be. First, the gameplay: Combat is solid but what you see at the beginning of the game doesn't evolve or add new moves aside from 2 spells for your sidekick, Fidget. You'll perform the same few combos over and over. They are flashy and feel weighty but there is a limit to how many times you can see them before they become stale; a limit I reached considerably before the end of the adventure. I will commend the game for the innovative ability to supercharge Fidget's spells by combining them with your Dust Storm technique. I just wish more was added on as the game progressed.
The voice acting is another area of contention. From a technical standpoint I think it is very well done. In particular, your sidekick Fidget has a unique, emotive and amusing voice-over that, while cartoonishly exaggerated, demonstrates a lot of talent from the actress. It is that artistic choice to go with a fairly light and at times silly tone that I question. It fits great with the visual design but not so much with the rather dark tale that is told. It is also bound to turn some people off.
The first half of the game has a pretty standard plot involving an amnesiac protagonist. It isn't until near the end of the game when you discover his origin and backstory that things became interesting to me. Without spoiling anything I will say that the concept is really cool and an adequate payoff after a predictable beginning. Fortunately, some lively and likable characters are able to keep things enjoyable even when the plot is dragging. My only noteworthy complaint with the cast is that no background or motive is given for the main antagonist, making him a very shallow character.
Visually Dust is an appealing game with great use of color but it doesn't stand up very well to close scrutinization. There's just not a lot of detail in it. A good artist can make a simple design look elegant and appealing but there are frequent examples here where simple just looks amateurish. A lot of the character designs fall into that category as do environmental  objects like trees. Still, there is enough that is good about it that it has most reviewers saying it has excellent graphics. The whole package is complimented by a compelling soundtrack.

The game is really Gal Civ 2 with a few changes that could be done as a DLC. The same graphics, icons, portraits, civilizations, technologies, buildings' names. There are a few new technologies, buildings, ship modules and a new ship creator, but overall it is still the same game - all basic functionality did not change: you can survey anomalies, build starbases, build buildings on planets in exactly the same way. If you want a few extras for Gal Civ 2 you may like this game, but if you got bored with Gal Civ 2 and expect something new - you will be disappointed.
-
- game crashes when trying to load certain saves. This prevents you from interrupting the game because you never know whether you will be able to load that saved game or not, which in turn makes a game unplayable
- you can sometimes build unique buildings twice
- sometimes the technology tree shows that the technology was not yet discovered even though it was, you have to close and open technology tree again
- the technology tree doesn't show descriptions of other specializations than the one you researched (specialization is a technology such that you have to choose one of 3 available, however you can buy the other two from other races)
- bugs/mismatches between technologies' descriptions and actual effects
- AI is pretty dump, they will declare the war against you because they don't like you, but will ask for peace next turn because you are too strong
- path finding is dump, it will often choose a path through enemy teritory even though equally long path through your teritory exists
- impossible to rename the planet immediatelly after colonising it, you have to go to the map and back to the planet
- if there are multiple messages after others turn (war declared, new race found, auto-surveying ship found an anomaly) only one of them is shown
- when you change production distribution (research/manufacturing/economy) the buildings queue is not refreshed, you have to either change something in the queue or switch to map/another planet and then come back
- multiple typos in technology tree
- various graphical bugs (shots not displayed correctly, some weird textures behind some of the texts etc.)
- ideology traits saying that they give you some bonus which in fact is not applied at all
- on larger maps the performance is really terrible, when you scroll the map you have to wait for a few seconds for it to load, opening any other view such as planet management or diplomacy also takes 5-10 seconds, a "quick battle" actually takes about 10 seconds of ships waiting on the map before one of them shoots and the other is destroyed; if you try to zoom in (to see actual models of entities instead of their icons) you will probably decide to zoom out again after 20 seconds of game being stuck
- you cannot see the path or the range of the ship, click will initiate movement which cannot be interrupted
- if a ship is moving towards destination and you press "next turn" button, the ship will move but all remaining movement points are lost, you are not promted to do something with the idle ship
- the same happens if the ship is set to "automatic survey", once it reaches a destination anomaly site, all remaining movement points are lost
- it is very difficult to control enemy ships movements - all are done at once and there is no log or "enemy turn replay"
- all remaining manufacturing/research points are lost at the end of turn so if you have 2k manufacturing points per turn and want to produce a frigate which costs 200 points, you can only produce one per turn anyway
- you can assign multiple planets to provide their manufacturing points to single shipyard, however you cannot assign single planet to multiple shipyards
- buying ships/buildings ceases the normal production, i.e. if building A has 1 turn remaining and you buy building B, next turn building A will still have 1 turn remaining
- although in ship designer there are tabs for "core" and "user" ships, there are no such tabs when upgrading existing ship, which means that you have to scroll through 20 "core" designs to find the one you made
- micromanagement - each planet's potential can be split between wealth, manufacturing and research (defaults to 33% each). Let's say that you want a research focused planet so you set research to 100%. Once you discover a new type of laboratory, the upgrades will be put onto the building queue automatically, however they will not build because you have 0% manufacturing. On the other hand, if you have 20% manufacturing only for this purpose, once all laboratories are upgraded and building queue is empty, you just lose 20% of planet's potential
- there are list to view all your planets/ships/starbases but the order in them is completely random with no sorting options
- music is different in every view (map/ship/planet/governing planet/menu) which gets pretty annoying e.g. when you need to go over 20 ships to upgrade them and you hear 3 first seconds of two different tracks over and over again...
however it
address any issues listed above... Stardock is promising regular extra content with the first expansion at the end of summer, however the game is so full of bugs that it is really unplayable. Don't waste your time and money on it.

Beatgames (or rhythm games) tend to be very hard at first, but when you practice, you can literally see your improvement. Although this game is not a pure beatgame, it has the full characteristics of one. The concept of two different game genres put into one is incredible, but it is just
when the execution of it is perfect.
The soundtrack of this game is simply amazing. I've never really had a taste for electronic music or jazz, but the stuff they put into this game definitely made me change my mind. The way they've designed everything, I think, was so you, the player, could jam to any music that would hit you. Every moving object in the game has an animation that moves to the rhythm of the BPM (beats per minute; determines how fast a song is) of the song, the shopkeepers' singing is just perfect, and the rest of the sound effects (voices, attacks, monsters) flow so astoundingly. Sometimes I play this game just because I want to listen to the soundtrack. Custom music is a plus, and I have not found any errors working with it so far. It has it's own BPM detection that works fine.
Randomly generated-ness (well that's rogue-like, isn't it?) makes this game never get old. The story mode is of moderate length, and surprisingly, or at least, for me, I have gotten tied to the characters and I have grown to have sympathy for them! If you don't have a thing for rogue-like games, this will surely change your mind (That's what had happened to me).
The pixel art is adorable, and the character concept art for those monsters are.. dark and horrifying. Think you have a slow/old computer and can't run this game? This game ran at 60 fps on mine, so you're fine. (In case you didn't get it, my computer is
bad.)
When you first start playing, the thing that you need to remember is to
give up. If you die five times in a row, you should either take a break for a while and come back to the game later or keep playing. You
see that improvement and it will just feel amazing. You actually feel accomplished about something, which is what very few games are able to do.
As for going into more depth about the gameplay, no need for that. It is all for you to discover yourself. But here's something to remember: although the content of this game doesn't seem that abundant, trust me. It was way more stuff than you think. They also have a level editor after you complete the game (or should I say, a fraction of the game [Note what I said to remember]), so you can upload your creations to the Steam Workshop that is connected to the game or just play them alone. Nothing wrong with that.
To sum it up, this game deserves every one of those awards that you see to the right. If not, more than that. This review cannot express how much I enjoy this game. It is one of the most unique and unforgettable gaming experiences ever. Get this game if you're looking for something new to enjoy.
Also, sorry if I have any grammar/typing errors. I did not read this over.

So, I just finished ABZU and I think about posting my thoughts about it while they're still clear in my mind.
First of all, if you like very visual games, by all means, get this game. There are many different colorful environments to explore.
This game has no dialogue. Absolutely no text in spoken nor written form. The story is told solely by visuals - just like a colorful picture book. So it leaves a lot for the player to think about. The way I see it, the story is told very much by metaphors. The world is in no way realistic - it's more like a beautiful dream. You can think what your dreams might mean - this game is very similar.
What annoyed me a little was the pacing. The climax arrived a bit too quickly. However, the fade out after that was on point which smoothened the rather spiky climax part making the game more enjoyable towards the end.
If you feel like seeing a visually beautiful story, by all means buy this game.
