SAMOLITOLOK... SIMILOTIKOK... SALITOLILOL... SUKALO... whatever the hell this thing is called, is a plane fly-y, shoot-y, weave-y, meme-y game that's out for you to play on your computer machine contraption right now. Use the mouse to control a silhouetted plane as it flies upwards, while trying your best to either shoot or avoid various other silhouetted shapes moving downwards. Hit a certain amount to reach a boss, shoot it, move on to a different "stage"/background colour with different shapes coming at you, and don't crash into anything or you'll reset to the start. Do this over a small handful of stages, unlock all the achievements, have the game automatically shut down on you, move on with your life.
It's a short game, clocking in at anything from 10 minutes to possibly half an hour, depending on your skill level or patience, the only other complications being some pick-ups that will have brief, temporary effects of either giving you a multi-shot, speeding you up, or sending out a row of projectiles to clear the screen. There have been a couple of updates to add two new stages and bosses to the game, bringing the total to 5 at the moment, but there may be more in future. It has a certain appeal to its super basic visual style, and the music is actually pretty good. But for better or worse, that's all there is to the game. I think the more interesting discussion here may be about products and their value or worth.
I may have only gotten 20 minute's worth of play out of this with its current content (the rest of my play time being for card drops) but for only 99 cents, I'm not actually going to complain about that. Some people feel hard done by the game because of this and feel it should be free, but I don't think that's entirely fair. Trying to view this from a creative perspective, had I spent any decent amount of time and effort putting something together with sincere intentions of entertaining people, then I wouldn't feel the price was too unreasonable. Sure, what it's worth to you, only you can say - maybe you'll love the game, maybe you won't - but I think it's fair. I mean, if you can afford a device to play this on, the electricity to power it, the bill for your internet access to download it, and however many other things that might come into play, are you really going to complain about something as trivial as 99 cents and say you were ripped off because you only got half an hour's worth of content that someone else put some work into? I'm sure we've all wasted more money on worse things than this and barely thought twice about it. Like I said, value is pretty subjective and the worth of anything will vary from person to person, but I still think this is justified in this case.
So, while I'm not exactly in love with the game or anything, I was still entertained and enjoyed my time with it and hope there will be more updates to come. Get it on sale, at full price, or not at all, it's your choice, and either way you're not wrong in which you prefer, but if you do get it at least don't make the same mistake I did and do yourself a favour - don't play this in the dark sitting really close to the screen. I don't think my eyes will ever be the same again.

I didn't expect this game to be good. I bought it for like $.99 or $1.99 on a sale expecting a generic game I could play for laughs. Instead, I got a game with a compelling story that, while I only spent 3 hours playing, I enjoyed every minute of. The normal price is $2.99, and I'd say that the price is worth it for what you're getting. Unless you're a soulless husk, I gurantee you'll enjoy the game. The storytelling is top tier, with a narrative that does wonders getting you to care about the characters in a relatively short time, which is something many AAA titles have trouble doing in 60 hours. The pixel art looks decent in game, but really comes to life in the short cutscenes and other artwork (such as portraits). These really help the characters pop and really brings them to life. The soundtrack is just phenomenal, with the boss music doing a great job to set the mood. The only 2 things I didn't like about the game was the lack of an options menu (so no volume adjustment or fullscreening) and 2 of the 3 endings for Chapter 3. Other than that, it's really a phenomenal game with great music, a great narrative, and great artwork. Spend $3.00 and you won't be disappointed.

I can't deny that the game is fun to play when you get the right champion, but it's horribly one sided due to its pay to win nature. All but 7 champions are locked and have be purchased with in game currency, or you can fork over your money and get them right then and there. That isn't fair to anyone who can't just buy every champion to play them in game.
For instance, say you're trying to play Kinessa and suddenly the other team has a Maive. If you haven't bothered going and testing every champion in the training, which I'm sure most people don't, then you won't know what she does. You try play Kinessa and the enemy Maive bodies you. What can you do about it? Nothing. The game restricts you to one champion per game without switching.
In a game where there are champions who obviously counter other champions or are simply unbalanced in the terms of them not being fun to fight against, why are you not allowed to switch champions to better you're team and the sernario the enemy puts you into? If the enemy team simply has champions that are either stronger or counter you and your team, then you're♥♥♥♥♥♥out of luck.
I hate comparing these games, but both TF2 AND Overwath allow for you to at least switch you're class or hero respectively. Why should we be forced to be only one champion? If the team doesn't work or if you aren't doing well as a certain champion then it seems like a no brainer that you should be allowed to switch.
Another glaring issue is the card system. I have nothing against it, in fact I really enjoy being able to adjust the playstyle of champions, but it falls under the pay to win aspect as well. If you have a loadout or a certain card that another player with the same champion, you could easily give yourself an advantage over them. How exactly is that fair? Especially considering the fact the the only two ways of getting cards are through the loot chests that you occasionally get or buy, or just outright buy the card.
Look, I don't hate the game. I really do enjoy playing it, but I can't look past the fact that game is trying to force in game purchases down our throughts for things as basic as playing any champion you want to play as.

Not worth it at $30 for what it offers. It looks beautiful, I'll give it that, but the gameplay is more tedious than fun. I know it has JRPG-like combat, but even with that, battles feel so incredibly slow. Attack animations take a long time and some attacks look clunky. The big issue I have is attacking flying vs. ground enemies.
Some enemies can decide to fly up in the air, and these can only be hit by ranged attacks (usually in ranged stance). To get to ranged stance, you have to take a full turn to switch stances (letting the enemies have a round of attacks on you) before you can start shooting. The problem here is that your party is usually more efficient in melee stance.
The dungeon puzzles/gimmicks are annoying and obvious, not innovative. The bosses feel too strong. I died to the first boss and felt that I needed to grind before fighting it again. For every boss, the whole fight is usually just 2 of your party members attacking while the other two are trying to keep your party alive with items and heals (which barely heal for anything).
Currently, this game feels like an early access game with the lack of optimization, clunky animations, and random bugs.
Edit: Beat the final boss.
- The flying/ground thing eventually ceased to be a big issue.
- Ghosts eventually got so annoying to fight that I just turned off the item that allows you to see them. Their attack animations take way too long.
- Farming (literally) to make potions and ammo was probably my favorite mechanic in this game.
- The last fight basically forces you to use a certain party composition to even stand a chance.
- Overall, still can't recommend it for full price unless you really enjoy classic JRPGs.

I found myself deeply enamored with the world of the Witcher. My first exposure being the book, “The Last Wish” by Andrzej Sapkowski. I started in on Witcher 1 after reading and found the mechanics slightly overbearing. Even with some background I found myself being overwhelmed by the vastness and seeming complexity of the mechanics brought fourth by what, to me, was a very cool prospect. Alchemy.
The idea behind it was not as its traditionally seen, even in fantasy. It wasn't some equal exchange of two completely unrelated things. Or when it was considered theoretical science, turning common metal into gold. It was poison, concocted from traditional alchemical ingredients. This poison would kill anyone not used to it. It took years and years of borderline torture to build this resistance. All in exchange for what was essentially, a high. Which in game mechanics turns into stat buffs and regen of various meters. AND on top of all this people were kidnapped before the age of five, trained in swordsmanship and forced to build a tolerance to the poisonous alchemical drinks. All to become “thugs for hire” and slay monsters. That, is the coolest♥♥♥♥♥♥ever.
Sadly I never completed the Witcher 1. Due to the overbearing nature. Suffice it to say. The Witcher 2 is a vast improvement. Mechanically, Narratively, and boy is she pretty.
My first play through I found some of that residual vastness to get to me. But I decided to forge ahead. I found myself understanding the times at which potions were needed and when they were not, even if most of time was due to trial and error. I am sort of an obsessive quick-saver. I found the dichotomy between Steel and Silver swords very real. Making the action feel much more tactical than your standard, run into that room and whack at stuff with a sharp stick.
You make decisions in this game like every other RPG. Only these choices are not so clear cut. There isn't really ever a clearly good or clearly bad option. Moral ambiguity at its best. Rather both sides seem to have very real unforeseen consequences. In fact in the mission “At a Crossroads”, Literally 20+ hours of content lay behind a single choice. My second play through I had a lot more fun because I could focus less on worrying about how to spec or do I have enough ingredients for the potion I need. I was able to focus on the story and actually see some of the political tension much more clearly and take a stance that was well informed.
I love this world. Its probably the most fleshed out fantasy world I've gotten involved with. That's likely due to the fact that this game is based on a book series and not vice versa. Much in the way the Metro 2033 series is.
No prerequisite reading required to enjoy but it will definitely enhance the experience.

I backed this game on kickstarter on a whim. I liked the cutesy artstyle and felt like playing a classic RPG again, so I just pressed the button and prepared for a let-down. Fortunately, I was proven wrong. The developers gave frequent updates, reacted to bug reports and criticisms (although one bug in particular, that you can fall through the ground on plumpet island on occasion, hasn't been fixed in the finished game) and delivered a finished game more or less on schedule.
That alone almost deserves a recommendation. But how is the game?
Let's be honest, it is not brillant. But I still enjoyed it.
The
is pretty lacking. There is no voice acting, so the story is conveyed through speech bubbles, and since no one wants to read endless dialogue, there is not much to it. There are some books you can read for some additional lore but there is no rich story to be found.
There are still some
, the aformentioned falling through the ground on plumpet island, and the game gets slower the longer you play. It also crashed a couple of times. But I didn't encounter any game breaking bugs or save corruptions so it is definitely playable.
I really enjoyed the
, you can see it in the trailer and the pics, so see for yourself if it appeals to you. The background
was varied and relaxing, no complaints there.
I liked the actual
quite a lot. The fighting system is pretty straightforward. I strongly recommend playing with a controller, though (I used an xbox controller). ETA: The game is definitely playable with keyboard and mouse, I just found it more enjoyable with a controller.
The
allows you to give your characters different perks (mostly partial immunity against different attack types, strengthening different attack types, but also some special ones) and character upgrades (defence, offence, evasion, quickness, accuracy) and you can also add new abilities that you can find along the way.
There is also a bond system: Depending on which two characters you pair with each other they gain different perks which can be quite powerful. You have 6 characters to choose from (you fight with 4).
Taken all together, you have quite a large variety of fighting styles, whether you want to be more defensive or offensive, rely more on physical attacks or magic, melee or ranged or area of effect attacks, it is all up to you. All 'talents' (perks, abilities, upgrades) can be exchanged at any time so you can experiment quite easily and even adjust them to a particular boss fight if you want.
I recommend the game for people who like classic RPGs, enjoy the artstyle and are looking for a not-too-complex game that still provides lots of variety in fighting styles. I would wait for a sale, though, 28 Euros are a bit steep, in my opinion.

**Disclaimer: I love the game and recommend it highly but I have one specific area of extreme disappointment which is completely based on my opinion of a single gameplay element.**
So, 200+ hours in and I have lots of great things to say about this game. I have fond memories of previous installations of this series and I was immediately rewarded with enjoyment and relatively bug-free gameplay from day one of install. I have been a pre-release backer of this game for a good while, and I almost uniformly hate pre-release games and early release iterations of the "finished" product. This game, however, is an exception.
I spent my first half-hour post-release immediately building a custom civilization, modding in leader foreground and profile pictures and generally tinkering with the galaxy and opponent settings. I love the customizability of the game, the depth of scope is up to you, the density of worlds, number of foes, opponent preferences and play styles, the ability to define your race, its ships, styles and techs, and so much more. The game is deep and yet streamlined to really make for easy navigation and hands-off (if you prefer) gameplay through governing, templates and auto-building (using star-base requested constructors etc.)
I am in the middle of a game currently and will expand on this review shortly, after the Drengin succumb to my planetary bombardment of their home world, but alas I was driven to write regarding a particular feature of the game that can be exceedingly off-putting to some players. This feature is as-intended but could (and should be) modified slightly for players who dislike it for reasons noted below.
As in Gal Civ II, there is a built in surrender feature that the AI will use to effectively give-up and hand over the remnants of its civilization to either the player or a friendly AI (based on diplomacy and relations). This feature can be exciting when it works in your favor, or even when it doesn't. This feature can also add to late-game fun or end a long-slog of conquests planet-by-planet that can end a "won" game. Now, the problem I have with the feature is its inability to be turned off, as it can drastically alter a game you might have been enjoying, for example, a huge build-up, an initial invasion and then sudden, irrational and instant capitulation of every planet in your enemy's empire after the loss of a single border world, or even just a few ships.
This is entirely my opinion but I see it too often. I see empires, thirty worlds strong, casually give their home world and all their people to another race, and just "quit," based on a relative difference in power to their foe, without even fighting, trying, altering strategy (or ship weapons/defenses), going after strategic resources or using diplomatic means to isolate the foe or recruit allies. This feature is too vaguely defined, and often far too quickly enacted. Would humanity just capitulate outright to an alien species or would we fight, even to a bitter last stand? Now, there are times where it makes sense, but races surrender sometimes to enemies, often ones they are already at war with, to spite the stronger aggressor. This can quickly unbalance games, throw off strategy and realism and steal your fun if you haven't even begun to fight and they are immediately giving up.
This is a personal nit-pick for me, and I don't want it to discourage people from buying the game, as it's the only thing at all I have had any issues with, the game is polished and otherwise excellent. I only want people to be aware that you can very quickly see your long-time allies causally surrender without losing a planet to their most random neighbor, or a race across the entire galaxy at the opening of a conflict. You might also unfortunately inherit a cash-drained empire, whose ships and worlds sink you into instant debt. You cannot refuse the surrender, you cannot oppose it.
My one hope is that this feature will be able to be toggled on and off at some point, as I would love to fight my foes to the end, or see the weaker of two forces try other tactics to tip the scales. Change their force consistency to target enemy weaknesses (ex.: exploiting the enemy’s lack of shields, or countering their missiles with point-defenses), maybe target star-base mined resources, recruit allies diplomatically, ask for embargos, petition the United Planets for a peace-keeping force/funds or sanctions or simply fight on until they cannot resist any longer. Too often I get the Thalan empire randomly surrendering their whole populace and territory, despite my having nearly no contact with them, simply because they lost a single world to rampaging Yor forces. I've had Altarians surrender with twenty planets and a huge military (larger than my own in fact), simply because they fought a few turns with the Krynn who were only slightly more powerful.
My only gripe, my only wish would be to see the surrender mechanic changed to be toggle-able.
Beyond that, throw your money at this game, it's worth it. I have another three or four hundred hours to go before I even consider another game, and with the frequent patches, updates and interesting tweaks, I may find myself dragged in even longer. Please support the game, do purchase it, and do have long late nights of losing sleep to the one-more-turn nature of this amazing game. And thank you, if you've read this far. I'll expand on specifics and features in a tl;dr format soon.

It's incredibly difficult to review this game without already saying what so many people before me have. This is primarily a rhythm game, with some light rogue-like elements: randomly generated dungeons, perma-death, loads of items/spells and difficulty. I would emphasise that rogue-like elements are, as I said, light, compared to other games. And, frankly, that's fine by me.
The two most important parts to any rhythm game are, unsurprisingly, gameplay and music. Firstly, the music. They can rise and fall based solely upon how good the music is, and thankfully, NecroDancer hits a home run. The songs have clearly been designed entirely with the game in mind, as the beat is always very easy to find, though difficult to keep in the heat of combat. I listen to them outside of the game all the time, they're just so great.
The gameplay is bizarre, unique and a lot of fun. Every time the beat plays, as indicated by a scrolling bar along the bottom of the screen, one may perform an action. In this way, it is turn based, but also real time. It's such a strange mix, and I'm shocked it works as well as it does. Failing to keep the beat, or missing it, results in the player missing a turn, something your enemies won't. The gameplay, at it's core, is really that simple.
A plethora of items affect one's damage, armour, health, visibility etc., as well as weapons affecting how one's attack functions. Enemies all have different patterns that must be recognised, learned, memorised, and reacted to, all while keeping the beat. It gets very hectic when there are 10 enemies on screen, all with different patterns. Death is expected and common, but every death I have experienced could have been avoided through my own actions.
The graphics are great, and fit the style of the game. They aren't quite as sensational as the rest of the game elements, but they are certainly good. The monsters are varied and look quite nice, fitting the particular level well.
This is possibly and quite probably the best game to come out of early access. Before I played NecroDancer, I considered the rhythm genre to be dead, after the massive saturation caused by Guitar Hero/Rock Band and it's numerous clones. I cannot think of a single other game that has solely and completely revitalised my interest in an entire genre before.
Simply put, this game is a fantastic achievement, and about as close to perfection as can be. Unless you don't like rhythm games, I cannot understand how anyone could dislike this game.

Rhythm based roguelike thing. Roguelikes have become quite commonplace. Some sharing more with the original rogue than others.
This game is a very basic roguelike. It's main mode is divided into 4 areas with 3 randomly generated levels each, then followed by a boss.
The enemy pattern is quite simplistic, you can predict where most enemies are going to go.
Equipment wise there's far less than you'd expect in a roguelike. So why is this still a recommendation when it's so simplistic?
Rhythm. Where most other roguelikes revel in powering up enemies, having you take a risk drinking a potion which might turn out to be acid, have your equipment be cursed or break out of pure chance, this game sets the difficulty with the music. Each beat is a turn. Miss a beat and you won't move, but the monsters may. This makes all the huge difference. Suddenly the simplistic enemy patterns get tricky when you're faced with multiple enemies closing in .
That's pretty much it. Music gets faster. Enemies with new trickier tricks show up, and of course mistakes which can ruin your run for you.
Once you've beaten the necrodancer there are 9 other characters to try out, each with their own twist on the gameplay style which can make things easier or harder, like the monk who will die if he touches gold, or the bard who turns it into a turnbased game without the music egging you on.
It's simplistic, and yet I cannot stop playing it.

ABZU is a very similar game to the previous success from Matt Nava (JOURNEY for PS). ABZU's story is a typical call against technology, the return to nature's prime. While I think it fails in delivering a powerful message, its mysterious setting and mesmerizing visuals create and interesting (if short) experience.
On the good side, ABZU's visual aspect is extremelly polished: the breathtaking color palettes and underwater scenery as well as the arab-inspired architecture feel just right. The music, as wih JOURNEY, is terrific: the score never manages to get in the way of the gameplay but is always on the background following closely the intended mood for the player. The schooling simulations felt particularly impressive, with very realistic behavior albeit with a noticeable drop in framerate. (Also, as someone working on the origins of multicellularity seing ANOMALOCARIS in the game gave me a nice chuckle).
On the other hand, the game contains no challenge or choice for the player: it's completely linear and has a single puzzle in the whole game repeated beyond good taste. Also, the controls feel very clunky, especially on the ground where turning and walking are done at an abismal and non responsive speed. In striking difference fom JOURNEY, some of the scenes in the game feel spoon fed to the player and almost out of place (like that of the whales).
Bottomline: don't buy it if you expect something better than JOURNEY or if you don't think JOURNEY was worth it.

tl;dr It's literally Journey under the sea. Score - 6.9/10
This game is just asking to be compared with Journey. LIke Playdead's game Limbo and Inside -both feature a similar situation, similar gameplay, and some tweaks here and there-  now there the protagonist had a red shirt! This has been called just a retread of the past game and that's not bad, Limbo is still a great game. The same thing can be said about ABZÛ.
You start somewhere and are told vaguely where to go, just like Journey. The character lacks characterisitcs so you can identify with it, like Journey. There are optional things to collect, like Journey, though this time there are THREE instead of ONE :O The story (what there is of it) is told through (similar) murals, like Journey. It also follows the same overarching story of 'machine vs nature' and how the destruction of the former lets the latter thrive; the story also moves in the same patter: don't know what's going on, discover it, try to change it, get hurt trying, make it and happy ending.
The story itself is the biggest offender. In Journey even the name told you what it was going to be, so when you booted the game you knew you'd have to move and get somewhere. The story arcs in that game are directly connected to "The Hero's Journey", the Monomyth, and the game benefits greatly from this since it gives a powerful payoff in the end. The player character has gone through a life changing Journey and has been affected to it's very core, and the player itself has done the same as well. The moments of strength and weakness are also masterfully shown through gameplay. This story format doesn't benefit ABZÛ as much since you didn't feel the need of going somewhere, and it feels somewhat shoehorned.
Now, back to ABZÛ.
Truth be told this game shines when it's /not/ being like Journey. Exploration was not strong in Journey since you could get to see most of the amazing visual just by going through the game. In ABZÚ however you can go up, down, left or right, watch the sky from above (very reminiscent to the Wind Waker's skybox), or just explore the masterfully modelled underwater ambients. You can also observe the multitude of fish in the game interact and move about the water. One great aspect of this is the meditating statues (which strangely look like dog-sharks) in which the camera focuses on the different animals of the area. This lets you appreciate each fish model better and makes for a wonderfully relaxing time specially with the music.
Another strong point is the interaction with the many species you can find. If they are small then they'll swim away or with you (if you boost), and if they are big enough you can hitch a ride and swim with them. You generally move faster this way, which is nice, but you can also turn and breach if you feel like it.
Have in mind this isn't an action packed game but more of an experience you can swim through. If you feel there isn't much gameplay it's because it wasn't meant to have much as it would distract you.
What would I've changed? The story since it doesn't benefit from the monomyth formula– what's more, you didn't even need one! Just a big, wide blue to explore with many secret places and you're set. Each area should've been bigger too. I understand that could be taxing to both the team and the hardware but the sea in this games just begs to be explored. Not open world, no, just bigger areas.
My score: 6.9/10
This game is at it's best when it's not trying to be Journey. This game can't be bad though since Journey is awesome but it could've been its own thing. This game is for you if you want a peaceful time with relaxing music and vistas.

Fate is pretty decent.  It's an RPG that could be considered the father of Torchlight.  Made a few years earlier, it incorporates a number of things that Torchlight did, particularly the use of the pet as both a beast of burdon and as an ally which is transformable by fish.  It has randomly generated dungeons, which is always nice, and has been produced well.
That said, I am finding it a bit boring.  As a fighter specialising in swords, I've found most of the drops to be magic-geared, or aimed at axe-wielders.  I'd say about 95% of the drops are of no interest to me at all, and this tends to make hacking your way through the levels a bit monotonous.
I'm also finding it annoying that it is all too easy to die in the game, especially if you're focusing on what's happening on-screen.  The warning that health is low seems to come too late, so you end up having to divide your attention between the fighting and supervising the health bar.  The pet also seems to spend about 50% of its time fleeing.
My last moan is that the resolution doesn't seem adjustable, and I'm finding that I'd like to be able to zoom out a little more and with more detail - many of the characters seem rather large and chunky, as though this game was aimed at kids.
All said though, the game is cheap enough, and I bought my copy during a sale.  If you like RPGs, give it a go.

In Earthlock you’ll play as Amon and his group of have-a-go heroes as they adventure through Umbra. The story is light-hearted but fits well with the JRPG genre and though it isn’t overly ‘deep’, it does the job of keeping you interested in the characters and wanting to find out more as the game goes on. There are some nice bits of lore throughout the game and some character development that, hopefully, will lead into a sequel.
The gameplay is intuitive and relatively simple to learn - a huge plus for me is the fact that the game is fairly straightforward. There are dungeons along the way you can explore and you can veer off a little and do you own thing but your direction is clear and the story path is easy to follow.
Earthlock uses the usual JRPG turn-based combat style of choosing whether you want to attack/use items/rest and though it seems easy at first, once you start meeting new party members and unlocking new talents and abilities you’ll find yourself having to think about your technique a little more. Your party members can be ‘paired’ and will gain a battle bond whilst they fight together, giving them added passive advantages and a super ability when fully levelled. The combination of skills, abilities and stances gives you a huge arsenal to play how you prefer and allows you to take different approaches to taking on enemies.
There is also a fleshed-out levelling system that allows you to pick and choose what you level in what order you want but also allows you to switch out talents/abilities/some stats if you’re not happy with them, if they don’t suit your playstyle or they aren’t working in a specific battle. You ‘craft’ talents which can then be used on any of your characters and also swapped out if you need to. Abilities are found throughout the world and sometimes gained when you level, these are mostly character based and can’t be changed. You can also earn ‘stat slots’ which increase a certain stat (e.g. magic, armour, agility) – this is the only way to buff your stats beside levelling.
The graphics aren’t amazing but they don’t feel underwhelming either, they fit with the game style. The little pieces of art on the loading screen are fantastic, I wish there was a little more of it in-game (though there is a comic you can buy that I’m hoping has a similar art style).

++ Easy to learn gameplay. Everything is explained as and when you encounter new things.
++ Delightful story with likeable characters.
++ Intuitive but not overly complex puzzles. None of them are too difficult but not even one feels cheap or easy either.
++ One of those games you can find yourself getting lost in for hours – 22 hours playtime in a week.
++ Brilliant soundtrack that fits with the game world. I probably spent longer than I should have just planting and harvesting seeds because the music was so relaxing.
++ Really nice lore if you take the time to read it which is hopefully continued in the comic.

--Cannot skip enemy attack animations. This can become time consuming if you’re like me and prefer to fight a large group for more XP.
-- You can only control your camera at certain points in the game, which has led me running into enemy ambushes unintentionally and not being able to see around me properly at times.
-- No dungeon mini-maps. My memory is pretty bad so remembering which routes I’ve taken in corridors that all looked the same was kind of hard.
-- Can be a little difficult at times with no warning meaning you need to grind up a level or so to pass some of the bosses.
-- Little to no replayability. Once the game is over there isn’t really much to do.

Overall, Earthlock is absolutely worth trying, especially if you’re a fan of JRPG’s that are a little more light-hearted. The gameplay is fun, the story keeps you interested and the overall experience is great. I completed the game in a week and had a lot of fun getting all the achievements so I’d happily recommend Earthlock: A Festival of Magic. The ending was fantastic and closed the game perfectly, and has kept me wanting a sequel so I hope these guys have something else coming.

I found myself deeply enamored with the world of the Witcher. My first exposure being the book, “The Last Wish” by Andrzej Sapkowski. I started in on Witcher 1 after reading and found the mechanics slightly overbearing. Even with some background I found myself being overwhelmed by the vastness and seeming complexity of the mechanics brought fourth by what, to me, was a very cool prospect. Alchemy.
The idea behind it was not as its traditionally seen, even in fantasy. It wasn't some equal exchange of two completely unrelated things. Or when it was considered theoretical science, turning common metal into gold. It was poison, concocted from traditional alchemical ingredients. This poison would kill anyone not used to it. It took years and years of borderline torture to build this resistance. All in exchange for what was essentially, a high. Which in game mechanics turns into stat buffs and regen of various meters. AND on top of all this people were kidnapped before the age of five, trained in swordsmanship and forced to build a tolerance to the poisonous alchemical drinks. All to become “thugs for hire” and slay monsters. That, is the coolest♥♥♥♥♥♥ever.
Sadly I never completed the Witcher 1. Due to the overbearing nature. Suffice it to say. The Witcher 2 is a vast improvement. Mechanically, Narratively, and boy is she pretty.
My first play through I found some of that residual vastness to get to me. But I decided to forge ahead. I found myself understanding the times at which potions were needed and when they were not, even if most of time was due to trial and error. I am sort of an obsessive quick-saver. I found the dichotomy between Steel and Silver swords very real. Making the action feel much more tactical than your standard, run into that room and whack at stuff with a sharp stick.
You make decisions in this game like every other RPG. Only these choices are not so clear cut. There isn't really ever a clearly good or clearly bad option. Moral ambiguity at its best. Rather both sides seem to have very real unforeseen consequences. In fact in the mission “At a Crossroads”, Literally 20+ hours of content lay behind a single choice. My second play through I had a lot more fun because I could focus less on worrying about how to spec or do I have enough ingredients for the potion I need. I was able to focus on the story and actually see some of the political tension much more clearly and take a stance that was well informed.
I love this world. Its probably the most fleshed out fantasy world I've gotten involved with. That's likely due to the fact that this game is based on a book series and not vice versa. Much in the way the Metro 2033 series is.
No prerequisite reading required to enjoy but it will definitely enhance the experience.

is a more old-school style turn-based RPG that has some good things going for it as far as originality that make it really stand out.  From the start, the game seems a bit familiar.  I can't really come up with anything to compare it directly with, but it seems to have the makings of a solid game right off.
I'm about three quarters finished now, so I feel pretty comfortable writing a review at this point.  Most of what I'd mention up here in the introduction I've already pointed out below.  While there are some flaws and things I don't particularly care for, the good things override a lot of the negatives in my opinion.
The graphic style is very appealing.  Reminds me of old RPG games I liked from the late 90's or so, when the more 3D style games started to get popular.  There are many varied areas so far, which is great!
There are some jokes here and there.  Humor is a plus,  generally, so this is welcomed.
Some fun side quests and other extras to work on during your journey.  I won't get into any details, but I do enjoy having some extra stuff to do, rather than follow one single linear plot.  Not a ton, but I do like the extras that are added in.
Music is nice for the genre of game.  Definitely fits the style, and there is nothing annoying about any as far as I am concerned at least.
Easy teleport system to move around from fairly early in the game.  This is helpful moving from point to point easily, and there are a good many spots to jump from.
There is a nice multi-level crafting system in the game.  While a lot of what you can create might not be necessary in many cases, some aspects can be pretty handy.
The concept of using talent points on a talent grid and changing your stats and adding to other abilities through the talent points system is a nice idea.  The various cards are also interchangeable between characters for the regular stat ones, and then there are more specialized ones that apply to certain characters in ability and perk nodes.  The system is not too complicated, and simply gaining levels gives you access to more spots you can fill.  As long as it is touching one that is previously activated, you can keep activating more that are further down.
There are several informative menus you can check during the game, like a bestiary, tutorial recaps, or journal so you can recall where you were if you stopped, or just got confused or didn't know what to do next, etc.
The bond system is a great addition too that adds to battle customization.  As you pair with another member of the party and fight, you gain up to five levels in the system.  They generally will give passives for whenever the two are paired, so you can mix and match depending on situations.
There are various different things you can do in dungeons and places you explore.  I like that it's not just moving from place to place and killing stuff.  It makes it interesting to see new things as you are going through various areas of the game.
I like the fact that you can change to a secondary stance depending on the situation.  Sometimes one might be more useful or helpful than another depending on what you are battling.
The difficulty of this game is kind of tedious and there is one.  No changing it in any way.  I found myself having to use a lot of heals on some bosses if I skipped battles, and it kind of makes the game less fun than it could be, since I cannot pick up on particular strategies for certain fights that might make it easier.  I simply seemed to be under-leveled and would need to grind a bit first, or else no strategies would work due to lack of health.  Just a fair warning from my own opinion about this particular facet of play in the game.
A slight freeze for a second or two after each super move for me.  It's just a small delay, but it is noticeable.
Some sounds are very loud compared to others at times.  This might be a bad thing if you are already playing the game pretty loud and you get hit with one of these.
No voices at all.  I think it would be a lot better if this were incorporated into the game somehow.
I wish the towns were a little busier and had more activity and size.  They are pretty straight-forward and there isn't much to them besides a path or two.  More would have been nice.
Camera at times can be a little tricky, especially near borders of areas.
There is no skip screen if you find yourself having trouble over and over at a particular spot.  This could really help out, since there are some difficult bosses with small bits of dialogue.
Not much substance to the characters or story so far.  I would have liked to see more interaction between different characters.
On one particular boss, $AbilityName came up for one of the moves, and I am not sure if this was intentional or not.  Seems like a bug.  It was a seemingly robotic/golem-like boss, but it was a bit strange to see this.

Earthlock: Festival of Magic is a classically inspired, turn-based, 3D Adventure RPG. Rather than setting out on the typical cliché RPG quest to the save the world, the ragtag band of misfit characters all have their own reasons to be exploring the world. They simply join each other out of convenience rather than some misguided heroic notion. With the ability to change your stance and thus change your abilities, the combat system in Earthlock: Festival of Magic adds an extra layer of strategy to what otherwise would be common RPG style fights.
Earthlock: Festival of Magic is much like any other RPG of this style that you have played. Your team of up to four characters all head out to the world map to find their way to their current destination. While they all have their own motives and reasons, they will slowly grow bonds between them and be stronger for it. The Bond system is one of the features that sets Earthlock: Festival of Magic apart from other typical Role Playing Games. You can have up to four characters in play at any given time, but there is an extra layer of strategy that will come in to play here as well. Characters are grouped into pairs on the battlefield, and the characters that are paired together will form a bond between them. The longer they are paired, the stronger it will grow and new abilities will be added and talent (skill) allocation points will be earned. This encourages you to not only ensure you keep rotating your partners to make certain they gain all the talent points they can, but also to partner those together that give the best perks for whichever area or battles you are in.
Another unique element is the farming system. Rather than just buying your ammunition or items, you have the ability to grow the plants required to produce them yourself. The simple farming system has you finding seeds, planting them in your garden and watering them. One they are ready to harvest, which takes only moments, you can harvest them. The plant itself is not damaged, and will grow again if you water it. Harvesting from a plant a sufficient number of times will cause it to level up or possibly mutate. Leveling up produces more crops per harvest, and a mutation gives a seed for a new variety of that plant. You can then take all your crops you have and craft them into the various ammunition or items you will need during your adventure.
As mentioned earlier the game has talent points rather than typical RPG automatic skill increases purely at level up. These talent points allow you to shape your character’s stats and abilities. To upgrade your character, you have a proper tile to place and a talent point to place it. There are some generic tiles that will work for anyone and then there are those that are tailored for specific characters. The generic ones come in two flavours, the one that just boosts your stats, and the other than changes an aspect of the game or adds new abilities. Typically, after a boss battle you will gain one of the latter tiles as well the ability to craft additional units of that tile. The others are commonly found after some battles or in chests.
The game is broken into two types of screens: the world map and the zone map. Both are basically the same idea, however, the world map lets you walk between zones, fighting battles on your way, and the zone usually has unique puzzle elements to it as well as the battles. Battles in this game are to some degree optional. If you don’t feel like fighting, you can avoid the enemies as you are able to see them wandering around. Each unit you see walking around the screen is typically a single monster for you to fight. A more unique feature however is the fact that you can deliberately attempt to fight multiple enemies at a time. You simply run past an enemy and have it pursue you until you have wrangled up as many as you are willing to fight. This will make the battle far more challenging than had you soloed them all, but it also gives you bonus experience due to being outnumbered. The battles are a speed-based turn system. You can see the order in which the battle will unfold, and unless an ability is used that slows or speeds up a unit, the order shown will be how the battle will play out. This adds a layer of strategy to the game as you are able to make a plan about who you should be focusing on for your current turn rather than just always targeting the weakest one.
There are puzzles in each of the zone maps that you must solve to progress. These puzzles can be as simple as finding the key to unlock a door, or using coloured lights to unlock a device. One zone even had a unique twist where you had to try to make it to the next sliver of shade in order to avoid passing out from the extreme heat of the area. These puzzles add a level of challenge and interest to the game and makes for a more fun experience overall.
The game works well with both the keyboard and mouse or with a gamepad. I played it mostly with the gamepad and found it to be highly responsive and worked well with that setup. The interface takes a little getting used to but once you have it figured out, it actually works very well.
The only really bad things I have to say about this game is that it requires you to grind a lot of enemies fairly often and that you can't usually rotate the camera. If you have been attacking single enemies everywhere you went, you will be in severe trouble when the boss shows up. Even if you have been heavily overwhelming yourself by wrangling every enemy you can into battle, you will still have trouble when the boss shows up. This leads you to need to waste time fighting the same groups of enemies repeatedly until you gain enough levels to be able to struggle your way past the boss. Some might argue that bosses should be extremely challenging, and while I might agree, having to redo the battle repeatedly and getting lucky is far less fun than having a fair shot at killing the boss due to being a sufficiently high level to face it in the first place.
This is a very charmingly cartoonish looking game. The visuals really do fit well with this style of game and is sure to have nostalgic appeal to those of us who played games at the turn of the millennia. Each area you visit also has its own design and look to it which greatly enhances the experience. No two areas really look that much alike and it shows that a lot of care and attention to detail went into the planning of the graphic designs of the game. The enemies on the other hand are not that varied in design. While there are plenty of enemies in this game for you to fight, there are quite a few that are just recolours of ones you previously fought. This leads you to fighting pretty much the same enemies everywhere you go with a few new ones tossed into the mix. It’s mildly disappointing, but is something that is common to these types of games so it shouldn’t really be considered that much of a detractor.
The music is wonderful and really helps with the charm and appeal of the game with each area pretty much having its own theme music. For the most part, the sound effects are your standard RPG ones that are common to the genre. There is a distinct lack of voice acting in the game which I am not sure if it was done to add to the late 1990s feel of the game where speaking wasn’t that common, or if it was simply because they didn’t have the ability to record all the dialogue with the budget they had for the game. I know I always prefer it when the characters talk aloud in games, however at the same time I wouldn’t avoid a game for lacking that feature. Plus this way it avoids the risk of having a really annoying sounding character spoiling your experience!
Overall Earthlock: Festival of Magic is a welcome addition to the RPG Adventure games available on Steam and has enough unique elements to it that I found it to be quite enjoyable.

Fun game with a huge amount of potential, but it still needs a lot of work. I've encountered a few nasty game-breaking bugs (with the worst one being unable to load your saved games, though the opt-in beta patch fixes this)and a bunch of balancing issues. Gameplay wise, there are a few things that bother me:
-Diplomacy is somewhat lackluster, you can't really do anything aside from making trading deals (which also include alliances and the likes) with other factions. I really hope this will become better in the near future, as it - as advertised - should also be a diplomacy-heavy game.
-No espionage.
-Issues with the AI. The Drengin Empire seems to disregard upgrading its logistic capabilities, and thus can only field small fleets, even though their ships are pretty powerful. (but due to the lack of logistics are pretty easy to take down) I also noticed that other factions, until they are threatened by war or wishing to start one themselves, have little to no military ships. (and thus, make them easy targets for a military-heavy faction to conquer)
- The game's a little too easy unless the difficulty is cranked up immensely. (which will give the AI handicap bonuses)
- Planetary invasion feels weird and shallow.
However, these are pretty much my only qualms. Apart from this, the game is absolutely fantastic and a real treat, and is in my opinion, the best 4x game on the market, (only contender would be Endless Space in my opinion) especially when you consider that the game shows a lot of potential to improve and expand in the near future!
Final verdict: Avid fans of the genre will definetly enjoy it, those who are more skeptical, wait a few months until they flesh out the bugs and improve it a bit.

The game could have been fun even though it is a carbon copy of Hearthstone, but as of 9/15/16 the game is already broken because of a recent update that gave beta players a severely unfair advantage over new players (who have only had a week to play the game since the official release).
Card games like this heavily rely on a players ability to analyze the board and make calculated decisions and actions in a particular order to gain positive results. By cutting the time on the turn clock by a third (80 seconds down from 120), there is not nearly enough time to make careful decisions. Every turn becomes a race against the clock rather than playing against your opponent. This becomes especially true in the final seconds of the turn, when it's a coin flip (and usually a losing one) whether or not your cards will deploy before the clock runs out.
There's a lot this game has going for it. The community is not terrible (rare for me to say so as community is usually what turns me off of multiplayer games). The game takes an already popular formula and copies it into a new, exciting setting. The background visual effects are awesome and fun.
But when it comes down to core mechanics, it's hard to get into a game where you can barely begin to learn and have to join a field of players with more skill, more time, and better equipment.

Thank god this game is free; it's just a compilation of 8 newgrounds minigames slapped together into a wholly uninteresting and uninspired plot. What you see in the trailer on the store page is *exactly* what you're getting, and very little else. The dialogue is bland and riddled with punctuation and spelling errors, and doesn't motivate me not to spam the continue button instead of reading it, in the hopes I might stumble into something interesting for a change. The only semblance of difficulty this game portrays is in a minigame which the game literally gives you an option to skip by hitting the F key. As such, I have deemed this game a children's game, which is a genre I wish I could reinforce if not for the game's choice use of curse words and references to simulated eroticism throughout.
For example, 'Cabe what the f***' is a focal humour point midway through the game, and overdoes it in what little time it grants the joke. It also likes to make fun of other infamous indie game developers; while I'm not discrediting the slander is usually expected and in most cases deserved, they could have been a lot more graceful about it. I suppose I could be far more convinced the slight mockery attempt made towards bronies was actual mockery, if the developer hadn't put so much more effort into the pony segments of the game.
I want to emphasize that my major complaint is that this simply wasted my time. This is the sort of game you expect to find on Newgrounds, not on Steam. If I wanted to spend time playing minigames, I'd be there, not browsing my steam library. If this game had charged more than dollar to buy on here, it would have been a major problem to many potential customers.
If a game's free-to-play on Steam, it's usually for a good reason, be it microtransactions or a general failure to profit with an initial release price. I suppose if the Dev's willing to put down the $100, anything can get up here, huh?
See 'Citizen Burger Disorder' for a far more simple, engaging, enjoyable and free game.

I wanted to like this game and certainly it's better than Beyond Earth (admittedly a much different game) but I'm surprised I'm giving it a thumbs down.
Two big issues for me:
(1) Way, way, way too many technologies. You wouldn't think too many is bad but it is. They all are so similar.  Honestly, the tech tree could be cut down by 2/3s. Most of the techs are forgetable as you just click next your next research goal without really thinking of what you just discovered. Many of them are just filler until you get the one that actually has a benefit. The devs should have taken the lead from Civ V. The tech tree was excellent. Every tech you discover gave you something.
Another problem with having so many techs is the benefits you get when they do pop up are so minor as to be unimportant - 1+ food, 1+ research, meh. This is similar to the problem that plagued beyond earth.
If I had one wish, it would be for a pared down tech tree with significant beneits gained with each discovery - in the vane of Civ V.
(2) Diplomacy is so boring. It's hard to believe but Civ V's diplomacy is better. For one, making any agreement is a chore. IF you offer something for trade you can't just click a button to say what would you give me for this like in Civ V, you have to go by trail and error to finally find something they'll trade you. I just gave up.
Also, most of the interactions from the AI are either them begging for money or telling you they're unhappy or happy about open borders.
There is the odd taunt but you can never give it back to them as in Civ V.
I was expecting much, much more with diplomacy given Gal Civ's history and it being from Stardock. I am very disappointed.
There are fun parts of the game, certainly tweaking the position of your buildings to get the optimum bonuses is fun. The exploring and settling part is good too as are the ideologies.
Unfortunatley, overall the game doesn't do it for me. I was surprised they didn't take more ideas from how Civ V did things to really make Gal Civ III shine. I keep coming back to CIv V because there are so many great things Firaxis did to make that game accessable, fun, and easy to play. Stardock certainly could have brought over some of the ideas. I mean there isn't even an option to have the game automatically end your turn. You always have to click the button.
I really, really, wanted to love this game but I can't recommend it.
Short review:
(1) Tech tree is too expansive and the individual techs are forgetable.
(2) Diplomacy is worse than CIv V.
(3) Exploring is fun as is settling your planet as is optimizing your building position.
I don't recommend it, unfortunately. The game has been uninstalled.
Sorry Stardock - I'm still a fan and I hope you can fix it.

I'll admit it: I came for the piggy.  His name's Gnart, by the way, and apparently he's a hogBUNNY.  I don't really see the bunny part, but I guess they were using that to justify the white fur.
I'm glad I stuck around, though.  This game is worth it.  It's a real nostalgia trip to early 3D roleplaying games, but done effectively with nostalgia goggles.  It looks the way I REMEMBER games from that era; other developers looking to capture that feeling would do well to take a page from this game, using sleek modern lines with classical intent.  SnowCastle figured out which buttons to push and they delivered, over and over throughout this game.
The Good:
The music's fairly good for an indie game; it starts to drone on after a while but it has a lietmotif that is memorable and the transitions are well done.  The scenery is breathtaking and believable from a geological perspective (desert surrounded by mountains, forest in the lowlands, swamp at a river delta).  As an audiovisual experience it hits its mark.
The world-building... wow.  While it's a little back-loaded, the creators went out of their way to make the setting robust.  In particular, the game sets about establishing its own idioms and jargon.  A little vocab for your convenience: Lys is the sun, a Cycle is one orbit around Lys, and a Moonrun is equivalent to one day (not a month, as I originally thought).  The concept of Earthlock’s planet Umbra is a heart of fantasy gold: the planet has stopped rotating and one half of it is in perpetual day, while the other is in perpetual night.  They track the passage of time by the movement of the moon (which is implied to circle the planet once a day by our standards).  The game puts a lot of lore in the fire and not all of it comes to fruition… that’s good if it’s the start of a series and I’m hoping that’s the case.
Each character has their own flavor… you’re not likely to care for all of them but you will probably like at least one of them.  The game has context-sensitive cutscenes which trigger based on who is leading the party.  As such, you can switch in somebody you like to be your map icon and they’ll get more screentime.  I didn’t care much for the protagonist (Amon) so I had Gnart running around the entire game (Yes, I like piggies).  I thought this was a very novel approach to player preferences and I’d like to see it used in more JRPGs.
Combat is excellent: each character has two “stances” which boast a separate set of abilities, doubling the utility of each team member and allowing them to fill two roles.  The aesthetic is sleek and easy to follow; icons on health bars let you know how long an effect will remain and give you the gist of its purpose.  You also have the freedom to customize your character’s stat priorities, so you can create interesting synergy with unusual strategies.  I loaded Gnart with speed-boosting talents and put him into Focus stance: he became a lightning bolt of buffs and whenever somebody else got a turn they hit like a mountain.  There are ways to make any team of four viable which is nice to see; often games with more than three characters will just write some off as throwaways.
I have two issues with the combat system I’ll discuss later, but for the most part it was perfect.
Random encounters aren’t random (a great move in modern RPGs): you can see opponents on the map and each represents one enemy.  One of the most entertaining components of the game is kiting them around so that more than one enters battle at the same time (which gives a bonus multiplier to experience).
Stuff that could use Work:
Stances are the big allure of the combat system, which makes it a pity that switching them in combat is so punishing.  Not only do you lose a turn switching stances, but your haste takes a hit and it takes longer to get your next turn.  This is incredibly frustrating and prevents you from switching stances more than a few times the entire game.  To the developers: I’d make normal stance switching accelerated (like the Quick Switch talent) and upgrade Quick Switch to make stance swapping instantaneous.
Stances are also particularly punishing for Olia and Gnart: Olia loses her counterattack immediately on switching stance (rather than holding out until her next turn, like it should) and all of Gnart’s buffs fall off the party immediately when he switches stance (something no other buffing character has to deal with). What can I say about this sick, twisted little game that hasn't been said already? The Binding of Isaac is nothing short of EPIC!
Let's break it down, shall we?
* Graphics/Art Style - While not the prettiest of ducklings, BoI is gorgeous in it's own "wrong" way. The thing that makes it somewhat stand out from other games of the sort is the fact that 90% of the items you pick up change your character, turning it, almost every time, into an abomination - from the embodiment of the devil itself, to a dead cat or a flying ghost sperm.
* Music - One of the greatest elements of a good game, the sounds and music really set the mood for a situation. And The BoI really nailed it here. The music fits it perfectly and makes you "feel" the game.
* Gameplay - **CAUTION - ANGER AHEAD** While seemingly simple, the gameplay can be a pain in the behind sometimes. Nothing really difficult about it, is there? 4 movement buttons, 4 shooting buttons, 1 for using bombs, 1 for a special item. That's easy! Right? Right? WRONG! YOU try dodging all the homing tears coming at you from all directions while a couple of vagivags on legs puke menstrual blood at you while five failed abortions with bombs for brains go all kamikaze on your bottom! It's hard as fock (*cough* that'swhatshesaid *cough*)! But when you DO manage to finish the game without taking ANY damage, you will feel like a GOD!
* Story - The story, like many other parts of this game, seems fairly simple and easy to understand. But it is made up of layers upon layers of hidden messages and meanings. Most of the items you will find in the BoI have a "hidden" symbolism behind them. Take the "COAT HANGER," for instance. It's an item that increases your damage and changes your character, making him look like he has a twisted... well... coat hanger coming out of his skull. Hidden symbolism? Abortion. Aye, I told you this is a sick little game.
* Replayability - The Binding of Isaac has 100 collectible items. The expansion has 198. To that, add 35 Trinkets, 28 Tarot Cards, Pills and what-not. And each and every one of those items may react differently if combined with another one. That means that NO two gameplay sessions will be the same. You can play it again and again and again and again and... must I go on? And it will ALWAYS feel fresh.
All in all, should you get this game? You betch'yer♥♥♥♥♥you should! Why would you NOT get it?! And it's cheap as hell!
To conclude, Edmund McMillenn, I tip my hat to you. You have created one of the best games I have ever played and I am trully thankful for that.

If you liked OMD and OMD2, this is now - FINALLY, after years of wanking around with MOBA gameplay and stuff - the same game with a layer of F2P fluff on top. I was a huge fan of the first two and was really disappointed with the "lane running" game. But now it's orc slaying madness with tons of maps, more traps, traits, guardians, and a couple dozen heroes to choose from.
OMDU is a little more of a slog to upgrade your traps than it used to be; trap upgrades and development are more involved than they used to be. But also, the F2P aspect can be annoying, if you're impatient to unlock stuff. It's brutally expensive to buy things in the game; if you don't buy things you will have to be patient hoping for loot drops to upgrade and earn traps. But that's OK to me because the base traps and hero abilities are so much fun.
With the exception of Bionka (who is slow and boring), I've found all the heroes to be really fun to play. The newer heroes (Brass and Deadeye) are my favorite; they aren't covered in the Heroes pack but are worth shelling out the extra ten bucks to acquire if you are having fun with the game.
Get on hangouts or facebook chat with a couple buddies and have tons of fun slaying orcs.
My favorite moment thus far was on a flight of stairs with push traps overlooking a lava pool, I used Bionka's bounce ability to chuck a horde of orcs into the air. My buddy, using the Sorceress, triggered the push traps, flinging at least ten airborne orcs into a cauldron of death. Second favorite moment was watching an orc get bashed off a three story drop and land on a flip trap, which hurled him into the abyss.
There has only been one correct way to play the OMD franchise, from day one: KILL ORCS AS CREATIVELY AS POSSIBLE. Who cares about stars, rift points, ladders, rankings, upgrades, skins, any of it. If you are worried about these things you are missing the point. They add a fun superficial layer or two, but it's the core mechanic that makes it all shine. The whole thing is about building insane killboxes, using physics traps and fire and lightning and bombs and ballistas and ice and arrows and magic and huge axes and claws and stuff to dispatch hundreds of thousands of stupid monsters. I watched across the map as my friends placed flip traps that launched orcs up to a high wall, and placed blade traps on the wall so that the orcs could be chucked into a whirl of chopping blades.
Lots of bad business decisions have led to an exceptionally fun, free game that somehow has a small and dwindling player base. If you're thinking about giving it a shot, get a couple friends and come play.

Also the fact that you can't use all characters makes it so you'll get beaten from heroes that you don't know how they work (looking at you samurai and your sword aura, that insane pushback on your cursed sword is just sad to fight against D: )
This game could benefit a lot from a better matchamking system, as in allowing us not to queue to only to either ffa or team games, but to all games, cause I never got to play team since it requires 6 persons. Allow us to browse rooms while in matchamking please.
For people having a hard time, the game is called HUNGER dungeon, it's important to check your hunger, as it can give you insane mana and health regen. But the problem with this is that when you're dead, you don't restore mana. You might end up with no mana in most fights if you're already low on the hunger meter.
I wish we had something like a +100 mana when respawning.
Also there's the issue of not being to type in game, emotes are nice and all but... Not having a way to communicate is hurting more than anything in my opinion.
Another thing that might help is being able to see what other people are using but in game, it's hard to know how they got the edge over you in a fight when items can be really crucial sometimes.
What could make the fun factor multiply would also to be able to make some more customizations, rounds last longer, more rounds for ffa... It needs some variety!
The game has some nice depth, to me more than one round is the way to play it since gold doesn't matter in single rounds games.
Get some friends, play it a bit. Enjoy it with strangers.
TL;DR with some quality of life optimizations the game would be way more popular imo, as in chats (so we know there's actually people wanting to play), an easier matchmaking (since the already low playerbase), and a possibility to check what heroes do or test scrolls with no gold limit (would help new players a lot).

Not worth the $75.
$20-30 would be more reasonable, although it feels as though the developers were forced to release the game before it was complete.
Being a hardcore fan of the series, especially the second game, I was really expecting something special for the third (and possibly final?) game in the series.
Something about this game reeks of clashes between designers/developers. I feel almost as though there was a group of talented designers and developers with experience working on this game, trying to add quality where they could, but ultimately held back by the poor choices of other designers and developers.
Mafia III runs on an updated version of the engine that powered Mafia II. This feels evident in a subtle way; the dynamics and movement reflect that of the second game in the series.
You play the role of Lincoln Clay, an absolute monster of an ex-soldier who is out for blood at the neck of the most powerful crime boss in the city of New Orleans. Along the way, you build up your own team of lieutenants, complete missions and take over the city region-by-region.
THE GAMEPLAY is good in general, but it is executed and applied poorly. Prior games applied the beautifully crafted experience where you would meet up with fellow gang members and discuss details, work out what your goal was, and then work your way through a set of unique obstacles to each mission such as sneaking into warehouses or following cars to remote locations, sometimes with sabotage from the other team.
In Mafia III, each mission consists of a 'cutscene' in which Lincoln stands in front of some generic random person in the exact same way, and both talk about what you're going to do. Almost every single mission (around 98%) are identical in gameplay, and simply take place at different locations. They usually consist of "Drive to this gang area, interrogate and/or kill the boss, and trash the place while you're at it. This is the games weakest point, and it becomes repetitive within half an hour of beginning missions as you predict what comes next. The cutscenes are re-used over and over for every single mission, with Lincoln simply standing over an enemy and holding a knife to his throat, then either knocking him out or killing him.
THE ENVIRONMENT of New Orleans is masterfully crafted. I was personally excited to experience the "French Ward", based on the French Quarter of New Orleans in reality. Each area is detailed with gorgeous buildings, vivid lights and a whole group of beautifully subtle features that make the world feel 'real'. Walking past houses, you might walk right up to a random front door and hear muffled music inside.
There is one flaw however, there is absolutely nothing to do in New Orleans! You cannot eat at bars, find new clothes, steal from weapons shops, do any kind of interesting activity (bowling, use strip clubs etc).
THE CARS seem to handle pretty much how you'd imagine cars from the 1960s would. Big, boxy designs of the late 60s barrel around corners with horrendous understeering which in itself, actually becomes a fun mechanic; you must navigate your environment carefully.
However, you cannot own your own vehicles in this game like the previous ones. There is no car that is special to you, you must simply steal one, or request a lieutenants man to bring you one of a tiny handful of custom selected cars .
THE WEAPONS have absolutely no guts. Instead of massive revolvers that punch holes in enemies and machine guns that rip things to shreds, each weapon feels like a cap gun shooting bb pellets. The sound design is clear but poorly suited to each weapon, and the gunplay segments are repetitive. Enemies shoot back blindly with no co-ordination or tactics. One thing that did irk me is the inclusion of weapons from the 1980s when the game is allegedly set in 1968.
Something Mafia II did well was allow you a sense of progression in the world. Vito had to work his way up (often for the rug to be yanked back out from under him) and it was apparent through different houses, cars, amounts of money etc. In Mafia III, you actually own no more or less at the end of the game than you do at the start with the exception of territory. There is no acquired sets of clothes, no arsenal of weapons, no garage of cars.
For MAFIA II fans; The game does give a definite, but extremely quick closure to Mafia II, but I would recommend simply searching youtube for 'Mafia III Joe Barbaro' to find out what happened. Vito has changed a fair bit since his time in Empire bay. His way of speaking and his accent are different, now resembling the fast-talking chicago-type gangster rather than the logical Vito once represented in the previous game. He's become extremely aggressive, fast-talking, and seemingly bitter with everything.
+ Very authentic New Orleans Environment
+ Atmosphere is incredible, can be very beautiful sometimes.
+ Incredible Soundtrack
+ Interesting lieutenant mechanics, being able to call in favours from others and try to keep everyone happy with owning a piece of the city each is a challenge.
+ Driving can actually be quite fun, steering and maneuvering is quite satisfying.
- Story is stretched out and predictable
- Extremely repetitive gameplay
- Poor weaponplay
- Buggy, low framerate from time to time, repeated crashes.
- Inaccurate for the period (ie weapons from the 1980s in a game set in 1968, cars from the 70s in 1968 etc)

I really did not expect this much appreciation for this game. I saw this game a while back and being a lover for pixel graphics, I placed it in my wishlist for a while. Bought it on sale, and pursued to try it out. And I loved it.
The game actually splits into three hour-long games, depending on how you play, and each has it's own interesting and individual story. You follow the characters Theo, a con man, and Efina, a lie-eating dragon, as they travel to town after town, figuring out information they can later sell to earn most of their money. However, they come across some dangerous situations, from vampires to a phantom thief.
The "RPGness" of this game is rather simple. There's no real strategy to winning, other than using powerful weapons you find while exploring the area around you, which is the best way to complete battles. Hence, the game focuses more on character development, dialogue, and exploration to drive the game forward. The different endings add a good small variety to the game, and the game progresses as there is an actual universe in the game that conflicts impact the ending.
All in all, I really enjoyed all three games. Althought the slight limitations of doing your own thing are low, the story is genuinely good and original. Even though the puzzles sort of play themself, I was immersed in the story greatly, and actually felt emotinal with all the endings.

Sokobond is a nice little puzzle game with some questionable views of chemistry.
The game involves you controlling one atom in a grid structure, and you move the atom around the grid forming bonds with other atoms [or not, in the case of noble gases]. Each atom is a simplified representation of its real-world counterpart, focusing mostly on the number of bonds it can form.
The puzzles in this game range from simple to quite tricky, and it took me quite a few hours to complete the entire thing without cheating. [Don't cheat, it's very satisfying when you solve a puzzle]. The mechanics require you to do a lot of lateral and reverse thinking, which is quite good.
Simple graphics and sound design, which works well for a puzzle game. The controls use either a keyboard or a controller, both of which are again, very simple [LUDR + undo/reset].
Definitely a good simple [but not easy] puzzle game.

I definately recommend this game to everyone who loves a good, immersive single player experience. This is one of the best single player games I have ever played!
The story is interactive and incredibly good. Most of the characters are very well made too. The game is just very engaging. You can really forget all about the world around you and play in this different world for hours straight. It almost never got boring for me. You do have to like cut-scenes though, because this game has a lot of that!
I also really loved the fact that your decisions matter. You can occasionally choose the path you want to take and based on your choice the game will play out. This really makes it fun and because of this you could even consider playing it more than once.
The graphics are not mind boggling, but they are fine.
The biggest problem I had with this game was the combat system. It is just super complicated. You can fight, dodge, run around in circles, use magic or use potions. If you are extremely good at multitasking and adapting mid-fight, it will still be very challenging. I found it a little too complicated and somtimes even a bit awkward: You can craft potions using materials you find around you, wich I like, but you have to meditate in order to drink them. And the problem is: They rarely announce that there is a boss waiting for you around the corner, so you don't even have time to drink your potions.
But that was the only thing that I didn't like about this game and the single player takes actually quite long to finish! I spent around 40 hours before I finished the game.
