Now I rarely write reviews, but since I feel like this game is often judged unfairly, I will make an exception.
First off, I'm a fan of the Final Fantasy series (up until 10) and purchased the game after seeing it on a random Twitch stream because of it turn-based combat system. So, as many people I started playing with good memories of the FF games.
I have played many similar games, but so far, this is actually the first one that managed to capture the mood and greatness of a past era. I wasn't blown away at first, but given time, I grew attached to the game's atmosphere, its characters, music and its combat system. It actually managed to do something that Final Fantasy VII never could: having likeable characters, of which you can't decide which ones you take into your party, since you don't want to leave any out.
I feel like many play about 4-5 hours and give their review, which results in the reviews not doing the game the justice it deserves. But I'm now almost 40 hours into the game and I'm really enjoying it. It has clean, well-polished graphics, a bug-free system and a very interesting background story. I spend about twenty minutes reading through all the shelves in the Owltide Library, which give an insight into how the civilizations and races found in the game came to be. I especially liked the detailed little side-stories, where someone accidentally finds something important, but ends up short of funds, looks for a sponsor, but after some struggle ultimately makes an impact onto the world (Not going into detail to avoid spoilers). All those credible stories and character's interactions imbue the game's world with life and allow you to immerse into it and enjoy the time you spend there.
I can really recommend to support this game's developers by purchasing it and sincerely hope that they will continue creating such games, ignoring all those nasty ratings of people too narrow-minded to appreciate something great even if it stands right before them.

Echo and the Bunny Men noticed back in 1988 that “People are Strange”, this is very true when it comes to our attempt to justify something we like.
We often feel compelled to compare something new that we enjoy, to something old which popular opinion of yester-year agreed was good, as if pointing out a connection between the two things somehow validates our enjoyment.
Music is a perfect example of this.
I’m sure we’ve all heard pretentious people talking about new music and how it resonates with “classics” from the past.
New punk bands on the scene will have “a raw sound reminiscent of the Sex Pistols”, any mixed Scandinavian group will almost certainly be labelled as “the new Abba” and I’ve lost count of how many boy bands I’ve heard referred to as “Beetles Inspired”.
The gaming scene isn’t immune from this either.
Point and click adventures are always “in the same vein as Monkey Island”
If you’re talking about a city builder it’s almost obligatory to mention “SimCity”
and even some relatively new games have established themselves as a point of reference.
Have your read a review for the excellent episodic adventure “Life is Strange”?
Did it say something along the lines of
“A similar feel to the tell tales games of recent years” or “Fans of the Walking Dead and The Wolf Amongst Us should feel at home here?"
I bet it did. (If I get chance to review it, that’s the sort of thing I would say!)
It’s understandable why we do it.
It’s easier to use a point of reference than to describe something from scratch, its short hand for those “in the know”.
The problem is that if you’re referencing something that is so very old, like for example, an obscure 80’s band that had a song featured in popular vampire movie of the period, the chances are that unless your audience was around in the 80's and remember "The Lost Boys"  movie, then they aren't going to get the reference.
Another side effect of this historical referencing is that it tends to add value to the “classic” being referred to; it elevates it to a level that the music, game (or whatever) never actually reached.
The whole thing feeds on itself and we continue to recycle the classics name for more than it was ever worth.
Consider the 4X space genre.
If you mention this particular genre to a PC gamer of a certain age, they won’t be able to resist name dropping “Masters of Orion”.
It’s definitely a classic 4X title and one which deserved all the praise it received “back in the day” but as the years have passed it seems to have been placed on some sort of pedestal.
If you want to bask in its genre defining glory you can only do so wearing rose tinted glasses.
To say anything even remotely negative about it is considered gaming blasphemy.
The fact is that it’s now a quarter of a century old, sure, it deserves credit for what it did for the genre back in the early 90’s but there have been many better 4X titles following in its wake.
If you fired up MOO now and actually tried to play it without wearing your “red shades” then you’re going to be disappointed. It’s long in the tooth, the visuals are archaic and the game mechanics are dated. It’s time to do what princesses Elsa did and "Let it go".
So what of the better 4x titles following in its wake?
Well, the original Sword of Stars was an amazing game, (the launch of the second one was a disaster but even that came good in the end and at least it tried something a little different).
Distant Worlds Universe is an outstandingly deep space-opera romp, but one which doesn’t get the publicity it deserves (which is probably because it’s expensive and has a “face fit for radio”).
Another great 4x Space title, and one which might actually get a mention by our “mature” PC gamer when he finally stops delivering his Master of Orion Monologue, is Galactic Civilizations.
Ahh... Galactic Civilizations.... now that game takes me back....
Whilst Justin Timberlake was asking everyone to cry him a river and Jennifer Lopez really wanted  people to know she was "from the block" Galactic Civilizations was released.
It was a hugely enjoyable and pretty much universally well received 4x title
(unsurprisingly a lot of people compared it Masters of Orion at the time...).
It included all the usual tropes of the genre, explore the map, find suitable planets for colonisation, build fleets of ships to defend your territory etc.
It was good.
By the time 2006 rolled around, Jenny "from the block" had decided she was an actress and Justin Timberlake was singing about someone with a "sexyback"
but " Sexy" wasn't the only thing back in 2006, so was Galactic Civilizations.
At the start of that year GalCiv II was released to eager 4x fans
(who probably compared the sequel to Masters of Orion).
Again it was well received and had everything we wanted in a sequel, including a shiny new ship design feature!
Like the original it too "was good".
So the original GalCiv was out in 2003 with a sequel in 2006 and being good at finding patterns where none actually exist I was all set for another instalment of GalCiv in 2009.
I'd waited patiently for three years, it was time, even the Black Eyed Peas "Had A Feeling".
The year slowly unfolded  without news, Lady Gaga pulled a "Poker Face",
Jennifer Lopez decided she was a singer again and Justin Timberlake was trying his hand at acting but sadly there were no GalCiv3 announcements.
Another four years passed by, Jennifer Lopez had discovered a TV show about Idol Americans and had decided that she was a judge and Justin Timberlake, after crying a river because he couldn't see his own sexy-back, was now happily singing about "Mirrors".
But the big news in 2013 was the announcement from Stardock that, after seven years of waiting they were finally working on a sequel to GalCiv2!
Fast forward to 2015 and following 2 years in development Galactic Civilizations 3 is finally here, but is it any good?
Well, to quote a Justin Timberlake inspired and incredibly annoying ad campaign,
"I'm Lovin' It!"
(I could also really go for a burger right now, I guess advertising really does work.)
So we know that Galactic Civilizations 3 is a 4x space title, the third instalment in a franchise and like its predecessors, "It is good" but why is it good?
Well, for starters, the alien races you know and love from the previous titles are back, only this time they all look a whole lot better, not in a beauty contest kind of way (The thought of A Drengin in a bikini talking about world peace is as horrifying as it is improbable.), but the HD makeover does an excellent job of making the ugly look uglier...
In fact everything in GalCiv3 looks lovely, from the aliens and the ships, through to the stars and planets themselves, which you can see  up close and in plenty of detail thanks to the impressive level of camera zoom on offer.
There is a new alien race joining the ranks for this outing too, The Iridium, an ultra capitalist corporation which prioritises economic wellbeing over other concerns.
You also have the ability to create your own custom races, along with custom biographies, AI play styles and pictures too!
Want to create a race called "The Lost Boys" with Echo as the leader and the Bunnymen as his overlords?
There's nothing stopping you my troubled friend!

I will write in 2 sections about my experience in points, first section overall, second comparison to Galciv2.
OVerall :
1 + Decent/good AI. I wasnt able to beat the game at highest setting, despite a few tries. Sure its mostly due to its bonuses I suppose but im still happy i wasnt. On  tough and challenging diff it still  bite back and overall did reasonable stuff. I wish there  was another setting between  tough and sucicdal.Also it would be nice if the AI was playing abit smarter , not mostly being hard due to bonuses.
2 +The game is slow, as with all GalCiv, so you have to give it some time, learn its mechanics to have most fun.
3 +The art and music is very nice.
4+ Overall everything one could expect from a good  4x game: Many races, custom races, long tech tree, many events,ship design, shaping your own ideology, good writing and humour...As with all Galciv games, there is no tactical battle tough. (for some its  a plus for soem a minus)
5 + Stable. I had one crash in the 65 hours.
6 - Imho the early game  pace is off. The expansion race is just silly. There is no mechanic to slow you down. its colonize colonize and colonize some more with maybe a few mining starbases. In galciv2 the economy stoppped you from overextending, it doesnt seem to happen in Galciv 3.
I would give the game a 8/10 i think atm. There is still some balancing and AI refining to be done imho.
GalCiv 3 new features, compared to Galciv2:
1- There are now strategic recources that you can use to build very powerful weapons and improvements early on. So you got this tottaly new layer, if you want to race to grab them on , and rely on them. On other hands they are scattered
and its hard to defend the bases that are mining them. It changed my Galciv2 playstyle in a  big way.
2-The affinty/morality is  abit different. You got a tiered tree with upgrades that you unlock. Its imho a nice change, i have i  think more fun with this then in Galciv2 approach.
3-There are now adjecancy bonuses on planets, so you got to think a bit more about designing it.
Overall i hadnt the impression to be playing a reskinned GalCiv 2, imho its a proper sequel.
4- Very nice addtion of planet independent shipyards , to which you can assign up to 5 planets. Reduces micromanagement a lot.

What can I say about this sick, twisted little game that hasn't been said already? The Binding of Isaac is nothing short of EPIC!
Let's break it down, shall we?
* Graphics/Art Style - While not the prettiest of ducklings, BoI is gorgeous in it's own "wrong" way. The thing that makes it somewhat stand out from other games of the sort is the fact that 90% of the items you pick up change your character, turning it, almost every time, into an abomination - from the embodiment of the devil itself, to a dead cat or a flying ghost sperm.
* Music - One of the greatest elements of a good game, the sounds and music really set the mood for a situation. And The BoI really nailed it here. The music fits it perfectly and makes you "feel" the game.
* Gameplay - **CAUTION - ANGER AHEAD** While seemingly simple, the gameplay can be a pain in the behind sometimes. Nothing really difficult about it, is there? 4 movement buttons, 4 shooting buttons, 1 for using bombs, 1 for a special item. That's easy! Right? Right? WRONG! YOU try dodging all the homing tears coming at you from all directions while a couple of vagivags on legs puke menstrual blood at you while five failed abortions with bombs for brains go all kamikaze on your bottom! It's hard as fock (*cough* that'swhatshesaid *cough*)! But when you DO manage to finish the game without taking ANY damage, you will feel like a GOD!
* Story - The story, like many other parts of this game, seems fairly simple and easy to understand. But it is made up of layers upon layers of hidden messages and meanings. Most of the items you will find in the BoI have a "hidden" symbolism behind them. Take the "COAT HANGER," for instance. It's an item that increases your damage and changes your character, making him look like he has a twisted... well... coat hanger coming out of his skull. Hidden symbolism? Abortion. Aye, I told you this is a sick little game.
* Replayability - The Binding of Isaac has 100 collectible items. The expansion has 198. To that, add 35 Trinkets, 28 Tarot Cards, Pills and what-not. And each and every one of those items may react differently if combined with another one. That means that NO two gameplay sessions will be the same. You can play it again and again and again and again and... must I go on? And it will ALWAYS feel fresh.
All in all, should you get this game? You betch'yer♥♥♥♥♥you should! Why would you NOT get it?! And it's cheap as hell!
To conclude, Edmund McMillenn, I tip my hat to you. You have created one of the best games I have ever played and I am trully thankful for that.

I get that it's F2P, but you need to give people something at the start.
Now the game is so much better! It focuses alot now on PvE with one mode to a bit of PvP. There's 'survival' where you need to survive a pre-set number of waves with up to 3 friends. There's endless mode where you can fight endless waves with 3 friends. Then there's the PvP mode that you can play with more then 3 friends if I recall correctly. You can ofcourse group up with random people and make your game public when you need just 1 person or when you're playing solo. At the early stages I found that it was do-able with just 2 people but I can figure that in the later parts of the game you'll need a full group of 3. Luckily I found the public chat to be very nice and funny! People are having a blast and asking for invites left and right so making a group of 3 shouldn't be that hard. There's still a bit of a grind ofcourse, but it's way more do-able then before! Upgrading your traps cost alot of points however, especially for new players. If you don't upgrade any traps buying a new champ (the cheapest ones) should be do-able within 3-4 hours, depending on your skill level with the game (if you played any of these games before). I'd say that how it is right now, it deserves more players. Even though it feels somewhat weird you can't earn skins FOR AS FAR AS I KNOW. Games like League etc have ways to earn skins, even if it's a horrible grind. But I can see how they don't have the playerbase right now to hand it out. Be sure to grab some friends or tell about the game if you like it! If you're planning to play the game more, it only will get better the bigger fanbase it has.
tips: Navigating the enemies is key. Use barricades to guide them trough your maze of traps. Don't forget that if you have enemies coming from multiple lanes, you can use the barricades to redirect the enemies from those other lanes to one place. It needs a bit of planning before hand but that's the key to reaching 4-5 stars every game at the start.

It's pretty fun so far, and tough as well. The music is also pretty great, which of course is a must for any rhythm-style game. Keeping with the beat and reading the enemies' patterns go really well together as well. Nice to see a roguelike that does things to step outside the box.

I play only the PvE modes in this game at this time. There are two things I need to say about this game.
This game is fun.
You should *not* expect exactly the same experience you got with OMD1 & 2.
Here's the thing, the game is definitely the same basis. Traps, shooting, and orc death! Elementals and runners! Chasing down the ones that got through your kill hall/box, and avoiding getting assasinated by mobs who know nothing but of their need to murder you! All fantastic things, you can agree, if you even liked the first two games.
But. It is not those two games. Because it is F2P. If you are someone who just played the first two games to casually slaughter orcs, you probably won't like this game as much, even though it hits all the right points.
The reason is this: the "grind" is simply about challenging yourself to specific tasks. In order to progress with trap upgrades in the previous titles, you needed only to manage to "pass" a certain level with a minimal number of orcs reaching your rift. The way you get upgraded traps here is one of three ways: you must either 5-star things, play a certain map/difficulty on different characters, or do Rift Keys which are interesting in that they add specific weird debuffs/buffs to the levels and you progress through the key until you either fail 3 times or you get a sweet truckload of loot at the end. I believe there's some flavor of rewards to the endless mode, however I'm not familiar with them. It should be noted that these will earn you chests of the respective level that drop an RNG set of traps of that tier.
Now, I know what you're saying. RNG OMG PLS. Well, sort of. If you are paying attention to my original point, you'll notice I mentioned that you progress by specifically challenging yourself. I've found almost no difficulty in getting enough traps to do the damage I needed to do to progress to the next map if I put my nose to those tasks. Do a level and couldn't 5-star it? No big deal, hop in with another character I like to play, get not only the chest for first-time on that map/difficulty with that character, but try again for the 5-star.
In that vein, do you get to choose your traps you want and grind them up? Not exactly. You can choose to save up your upgrade points for when it drops the specific trap you actually want to upgrade, but you're only making it harder on yourself that way. You'll get the trap you want eventually and just as much upgrade points if you're playing naturally in the pattern I mentioned before.
So in conclusion, if you do not enjoy challenging yourself in this manner, and just want to kill orcs like the past two games, this is unlikely to be your cuppa. If, however, you enjoy very structured, disciplined methods of play, this could be just fine for you. It is for me. Good luck!

I just uninstalled this game after investing a bit over 34 hours and $30.  It happend like this: I was playing a Master-level Endless map called "Frostbite" and had attempted it about 7 times when on the 8th attempt, at wave 3, I found myself being attacked by 2 assassins at the same time.  The rift was overrun in seconds.  It was my 8th attempt, and at over 30 hours of experience playing the game, I couldn't survive more than 3 waves.  I force-quit the game and immediately uninstalled it.
Playing Orcs Must Die Unchained *can* be fun.  But much of the time it is not.  And therein lies the carrot the game dangles in front of you - the prospect that you will succeed this time even if you just failed 7 or more times.  Apparently, hope does spring eternal, because even though I lost a match roughly 66% of the time, according to my personal statistics, I went into every match assuming I would win this time.  Losing in a game, whether because you failed to time a jump just right or because your rift was overrun by orcs yet again,  is never fun.  To fail 2/3 of the time really sucks.
What contributes to failure in OMDU?  Here are the things I've noticed in 34 hours of play:
1. Balance.  The game is carefully balanced so that without a proper strategy you will fail.  Part of it is learning the map, part is memorizing the waves.  But it seems as if each inividual level is balanced by hand, so the experience is not consistent.  Some levels are super super hard, while others are just merely hard (there is nothing "easy" in OMDU).  The difficulty is in the level design itself and in the design of each wave that comes.  Maybe a level has very few places to build roof-mounted traps, or has floor areas that don't allow traps to be placed (grid irons over lava for example).  Or maybe an early wave is a bit too difficult and needs to be fine-tuned by the devs.  Each level is so varied in design, features, and waves that the difficulty is all over the map.  Some levels you'll love, some you'll grit your teeth and barely pass and never play again cause they suck.
2. Sappers.  Sappers suck.  But they are not the only things that can destroy barricades.  There are multitudes of enemies that can do so in various ways.  In fact, the developers, in their quest to add challenge to the Orcs Must Die formula, have made barricades so incredibly delicate (there are so many more things that can destroy them than in past games) that its best to play without them whenever possible, which makes the game that much more difficult and frustrating.
3. Assassins.  Asassins either hunt you down or sabotage your traps - some of them do both.  They are often more powerful than boss orcs and can wreck a perfectly good run in seconds.  The game does give you tools to deal with them, but I find that they often sail right through my traps anyways.  Assassins make the game UNFUN.  Why play something that isn't fun?  Exactly.  That's why I uninstalled it.
4. Level design.  In past games, there were at least some maps where you could mount a defense of the rift in one spot - find a choke point and build on that spot through wave after wave - this is very fun and very rewarding.  In OMDU, there is, as far as I have seen so far well into the Master levels, not a single level that features anything like that.  Every map has orcs coming at you on multiple fronts, and even if you manage to barricade some of those routes off, something inevitably will destroy one or more of those without you realizing it until it's too late.  Another aspect of their level design, consistent throughout the game, is purposeful placement of trap cancelling features: floor features that forbid trap placement in key areas to prevent you from routing the orcs down one path, a lack of a roof low enough to place ceiling traps in critical spots except a select few unhelpful spots the devs built in.  The devs *want* you to feel frantic, overrun, at the end of your rope.  They don't want people complacently barricading the heck out of their beautiful levels and just sitting contendedly in a kill zone blasting away wave after wave.  They want players dashing madly from end to end taking out one crowd of orcs at one end, racing to the other side of the map to deal with a stuipd "unstable rift" that threatens to undo everything, to racing madly elsewhere to bolster a small killzone, to resurrecting a champion that has fallen (again).  Meanwhile they are beset by hordes of orcs, bosses, assassins, exploding things, unstable rifts, and stupid barricades that can't survive more than a couple whacks by an orc axe much less a kobold with a pack of TNT on his back...
What has improved with the new OMDU:
1. Game engine.  The previous two games, I understand, where built on custom game engines.  These were pretty good because the levels were finely tuned to stay within the confines of the engine's limitations.  But once folks began modding the game, that all went out the window.  I have a fairly high-end PC and with OMD2 + mods I've seen the framerate dip into the single digits very quickly and consistently.  It also likes to suddenly crash to the desktop fairly consistently.  Mods are a lot of fun, but slow frame rates and crashes are not.  OMDU uses the Unreal Engine, which rocks.  It looks good, is stable, and has excellent frame rates.
2. Level design.  The levels *look* incredible.  Kudos to whoever built them because visually they are a feast for the eyes.  Textures are beautiful, design is interesting, exploring locales from a ship on the docks to a castle floating in the sky and lots and lots of "castles."
3. Features.  There are a billion "things" in OMDU.  Much of it you can get for free, but just as much requires you spend some money.  But whether you like traps or champions or accessories, or costumes, or consumables - OMDU has you covered.  Notice I haven't said anything about the marketplace.  OMDU has done a good job of integrating microtransactions into the gameplay in such a way that you can play and have a good time for free for a long time before the itch to speed things up with money hits you.
This review is quite long.  Let me sum up for you:  Fantastic game hampered by a few key design decisions that for me totally ruin the experience.  For you all/some of those things (balance, level design that forbids effective routing, delicate barricades, and assassins) might be a non-issue.  I believe you will come to hate at least one of them, if not all.  But the only way to be sure is to try.  If you've enjoyed the previous games, give it a shot and see for yourself. I hope you have a great experience and better success than I've had.

Heroes rather than Traps

The fact of the matter is that there are a lot of game modes, the problem is that most of them aren't terribly good. Survival and Conquest are Co-Op, PvE, round based modes. For a general reference point, think Killing Floor - or less accurately

You may be asking yourself, "Why is all of this in the 'Cons:' sections? None of this sounds too bad." In PvP and PvEvP you spawn with the basic kit assigned to your class, this includes unlocked skills/augments. Again, "Well, that means that everyone is on even footing. What's wrong with that?" Simply put, equal doesn't always mean fair. Example, a player spends hours ranking their favorite class in Survival and Conquest and then all their work is stripped away from them. Fair? Perhaps. The maps are extremely varied. There are Forests, Deserts, Tundras, Box Canyons, Building Interiors, and even Cartoon Maps. So yes, I would recommend this game, and I have to a few friends. Just don't expect a flawless experience.

Sokoban (not to be confused with Sokobond, the game I'm reviewing) is a puzzle originating from Japan (hence the japanese-sounding name). It's a fairly simple puzzle that tends to have overwhelmingly convoluted solutions. You control a person in a warehouse, and your job is to put all the boxes away into designated places. They are heavy, so you can only move them by pushing them around. You can't move through boxes, and you can't push a box if there's a wall or another box behind it. Simple rules, incredibly complex solutions.
Sokobond takes this premise and adds chemistry to the mix. You control an atom, and your goal is to get all the valence electrons in all the atoms to bond. For example, you might control a Hydrogen, and another Hydrogen and an Oxygen are somewhere. Your goal would therefore be to bond both Hydrogens to the Oxygen to make water. Or mayble you'll control a carbon amidst another carbon and six hydrogens to make ethane.
Just like Sokoban, in Sokobond, you have a maximum of four options available to you at any time: move up, move down, move left, or move right. Just like Sokoban, if you try to move into an atom, you'll push it. Unlike Sokoban, if two atoms with free valence electrons become adjacent, they will bond, and bonded atoms will move as a group.
Later, you'll be introduced to three more puzzle elements: debonders which remove a bond you made, rebonders which add another bond to a pair of atoms (allowing for molecules like ethene or acetic acid), and rotators, which let you rotate bonds.
Just like Sokoban, Sokobond has a simple premise, but loads of depth, and all those extra-convoluted solutions.

GalCiv III is another solid entry in the series from Stardock. It is your typical 4x space game, with somewhat dry lore, with the addition of a racial morality system, complete with perks. The early gameplay is actually quite peaceful and focuses on expansion and diplomacy. It is not until the mid-game is reached that the technology for invading planets with billions of soldiers is unlocked. As with the previous entries, there are a multitude of win conditons: diplomatic, cultural, ascension to a higher plane of being, research, military, etc. The combat is automated and is based on a sort of rock-paper-scissors model, which allows the AI to be a competent oppent. Overall, solid AI provides a decent challenge. If you like creating and building neat spaceships, fear not, for this game features an extensive ship creator, allowing huge freedom in designing the look and loadout of your craft.

This is a beautiful game, no question about it - the music is perfect, the aliens look good, the ships and map are pretty much perfect, but... It has a few flaws that are quite frustrating among the stuff that actually are good.
To begin with, aliens declare war at the drop of a hat for no good reason, and as soon as war is declared, it's a pain to get peace. That means that between warring aliens and pirate bases trade become useless unless you provide escorts (slow, expensive escorts that would be better used at the frontlines) to maybe reach a currently reasonably friendly alien planet.
Secondly, the ground combat is resolved with a mouse click. That's it. No invasion cut scenes, no ground combat tactics, no fighting done. And it is done within 1 week. Yes. With one transporter, you will take over a planet in one week. That's so bad words can't describe it.
The game is a bit silent. The music is perfect, and it's never tiring to hear, but there is the usual (scientifically wrong) booms in space, and there's no voice acting, not even from the science advisor in your team. That's a pretty bad flaw too.
It does get a bit repetitive over time, especially on large maps when you are in a perpetual war from pretty much the start: build a star base to increase the operative range of your fleets, invade a planet, collect your fleets again, rinse and repeat.

A great 4X game all in all - Although you may want to hold off a bit if you're coming from it's predecessor, Galactic Civilizations 2. It is still a bit barebones in some areas like Diplomacy/Espionage but they seem committed to adding all of those features down the road as free content patches while expanding on existing mechanics through DLC and Expansions.
Is it fun?
Yes, definitely.
Is it pretty?
As pretty as you can expect a 4X to be - And then some.
Replayability?
Oh yes - You can create your own races with unique traits and give them personalities so the AI will play them as you intended. The game also features a very robust Ship Designer tool, which lets you design your own ships from scratch. The sheer size of the larger maptypes means you can create games that will potentially last you for weeks - Not unlike that of Distant Worlds with up to (and potentially beyond) a hundred or more unique races provided your hardware is up to the task.
Campaign - In a 4X?
I'm not entirely sold on this concept - While it works in some games better than others, it is definitely more of a lore introduction / tutorial campaign than a full on campaign as you would expect from a series like Heroes: Might and Magic, or Age of Empires. It's short but serves as a great springboard into the meat and potatoes of the game - Sandbox games.
On a final note - The developers are very active with the community, taking lots of feedback and suggestions from forum posts and livestream comments. These are definitely people who care about the genre and the game - It's not just about the bottom line.

EARTHLOCK: Festival of Magic is an adventure RPG game with fantasy themes, and enjoyable single-player gameplay.
Earthlock's story is something that I am still learning, but its story takes place in the world of Umbra, where a cataclysmic event occurs that stops the planet from spinning. This leaves part of the world scorched by constant sunlight, part of it perpetually cold due to lack of sunlight, and a patch of livable land in between. The incident ends up burying much of the past advanced civilization, but humanity survives and society begins anew in the habitable part of the planet. The story follows the adventurer known as Amon, a boy from a desert city called Zenit. Although he usually scavenges ruins, he eventually gets entangled in a conflict with a ruling Empire, when his uncle is kidnapped, and an artifact he owns is trying to be taken from him.
The game's combat is reminiscent of some older RPG games, and has a turn-based system where each character can choose their attack, magic attack, or buff. There is also an MP system in the game, called Amri, and you must use it in order to use characters' special attacks and magic attacks. There is also a "battle bonds" system that gives passive buffs to characters that fight together over time, and they seem to increase the more battles you do.
In its combat, there is an EXP system, and when characters level up, you can apply talents to their talent boards that increase stats, give them a new ability, or give them special defenses and buffs.
Earthlock's open-world gameplay is quite fun. In the cities, there are NPCs and buildings that you can visit, as well as some shops in certain areas, but in the overworld areas, there are enemies of numerous kinds, each having their strength and weaknesses. Many of the game's enemies have an elemental weakness and strength, or a weakness to a certain type of attack, be it piercing, slashing, crushing, etc. There are many different types of locations to be found in the game too, from swamps to deserts to temples, and more! The locations and the soundtrack of Earthlock are my favorite aspects of the game, and the environments are beautiful and unique.
The game also has a crafting system that allows you to create ammo, potions, spells, talents, resistances, and some other things as well. As you explore the world of Umbra, you'll find various seeds for plants that you can plant when you reach an island in the game, and when grown and harvested from, they provide you with key ingredients that you'll need to make important items. Though the plant-growing and harvesting process can be time-consuming, as long as you have a plant, it will be able to provide infinite resources, and as it levels up to level 3, it will give you more items per harvest than a level 1 plant.
So far, Earthlock has been quite enjoyable, although the difficulty curve has been a bit difficult to adjust to, and I'll probably have to do some more grinding. Some of the puzzles can be tricky, as well, but overall, I quite like this game, and I think it should have some more recognition.
Previously, I was encountering a glitch where the game would crash often for me. I contacted Snowcastle about the issue, and they released a patch that made it so that the game would work better for Windows 8 users, and I appreciate their efforts a lot, as I haven't had a single crash since then.
I do have a few complaints that I have so far in playing Earthlock. There is a difficulty spike after a certain area in the game that other people have noticed as well. You will also likely have to do some grinding of some enemies in order to reach levels that make certain difficult future boss fights doable in a way that gives you a chance. Each boss has a different strategy, and it can be hard to guess what it is sometimes, but after time, you'll be able to find their weaknesses, and with enough patience and levels, you'll be able to finish the fight. Fortunately, the game seems to consistently have save-game statues before every fight, so that you can warp back to the island and rest up, as well as make items you might need, like more potions or ammo.
I've also noticed a few issues with the dialogue, and sometimes I feel like the dialogue could be fleshed-out better, but the characters do seem to have their unique personalities.
Overall, Earthlock seems to be a very nice game so far, though. The unique and beautiful environments, gameplay, its absolutely lovely soundtrack, character designs, and graphics so far have been very enjoyable and quite nice to experience, and I think that this game is quite fun to play, and it has quite a bit of potential. I hope that the developers can recognize and deal with the difficulty spikes, and make the game a more smooth experience, but I still like the game quite a bit so far, and I do not regret buying it.
I would recommend Earthlock to anyone who enjoys RPGs with turn-based combat, and anyone who enjoys open-world adventures. ^.^

I have never had mixed feelings about a game like I do about this one, I mean it's a bad game but there are some things done right and we must aknowledge this. Other developers can draw inspiration from them. A good example would be the police response time and witness mechanics.
Mafia III is a lot like Game of Thrones and by that I mean that it has several brilliant moments that make you wanna see what happens in the end, but between them it's rarely anything worthwhile.
Graphics : Tehnically, this game looks good  but the color pallete used in portraying the environment is very washed out so that the real beauty that this game would be capable of is never in the spotlight. The game looks better at night cause of that.
Bugs: Many game breaking bugs as well as minor bugs and glitches plague this game from start to finish.
Sound: The sound FX are borderline decent. Like in Mafia 2, the highlight is the awesome radio soundtrack but this time around there are cool news and ads that help immerse you in the era. That being said, they manage to entertain you for 15-20 hours but considering this game is very long, they become boring. This problem is highlighted even more by the fact that 75% of the gameplay time you are driving trough the huge world back and forth between interest points.
Gameplay-wise this game is only repetitive because of its length. I guess if it were the same length as Mafia 2, it would've felt better. Problem is, they wanted to give large mission content but instead of putting the least important missions of the storyline as optional, you have to keep doing them between the missions that matter  to the point they become tedious.
Story: When there is story, the story is very good. It's exactly what you would expect and what you'd hoped for. The problem is where it ain't any. The characters are great, have diverse motiviation and you have reasons to choose anyone of your underbosses over the other. This is due to good motion capture and better voice acting, the characters being the main reason why you wanna reach the conclusion.This game has 3 endings which you are allowed to come back and visit but only 2 of them are good.
The World: The city is the biggest one I have ever seen in a video game and I just finished GTA V so that's saying something. Problem is... the map is empty. Sure, it looks exactly how you would expect 1960' New Orleans to look and it's huge but you ain't got nothing to do. There are 6 types of collectables but you get absolutely 0 if you get them all. So there's not even that. There are a few racing events but they aren't that cool either. They are just ok and the cars drive realistic I guess. The huge world is a burden when all it manages to do is putting lots of kms between you and your marker, especially underlined by the fact that the cars are EXTREMELY SLOW. Also the AI is dumb, like pedestrians jumping under your car than away from it when you speed by kind of dumb.
I finished it just so I can be qualified to write this review and I liked the story but really that's all there is. The game is a development disaster. It behaves like an Early Access.

FATE is A RPG dungeon crawler brought to you by the people at Wild Tanget. This game is A classic. Only thing that would make me love this game anymore is if it had multiplayer. The game centers around YOU be you Dicky Gobblkoque or John Doe. And unlike some games, this game only has ONE dungeon. With an infineite amount of levels of which new monsters come and they also increase in levels. These monsters change in variety from a basic slime to yetis. This game, although stable can have bugs every once in a while. One of which i had where my normal cursor stayed on the screen when i started the game. Not allowing me to click any options and FATE took over my computer. Forcing me to cold reboot. But once you are in the actual game, I doubt you will find any glitches. Like i said eariler the monsters level up the deeper into the dungeon you go. So playing on the harder difficulty like I do you can sometimes rush into A level you just can't handle. The spells in this game are extremely varied, sometime even pretty unique. From making monster your friends to attack other enemies, to poisonous clouds that drain the life from your (Not undead) Enemies. There is also a stamina system in the game. Because even heros get tired. This really is only to slow you down. Making it so you can't run forever so thats pretty bad. And one of the best parts... FISHING. Yes, the developers decided fishing would make a great part of their game. Fish can be used to turn your pet into magical ceatures. And fishing can also get some of the rarer items in the game. The quest system is your standard. "Go kill this for me/get this for me and ill give you gold EXP and sometimes an item" its not much to talk about but its worth a mention. And mage is the only extremly remarkable class, albiet the hardest one to really lift off on.
So all in all, fate is a pretty good game. If you like dungeon crawlers then you will love this game without a doubt, if your not a fan of dungeon crawlers i still recommend it. You might just find an exception to your distaste.

First of all, ABZU is not a game. In order for a game to be a game, it needs both winning and losing conditions. If you cannot win and if you cannot lose, it is not a game, and, in ABZU's case, you cannot lose. There is absolutely no real danger and, therefor, there is nothing at stake. In my opinion, ABZU would have been much more immersive if you have to be cautious around certain creatures, which may or may not attack you if you get too close.
If anything, ABZU a simulator, but a simulator of WHAT is the question. It's not a scuba diving simulator, because the protagonist does not suffer limitations real scuba divers do. The protagonist never runs out of oxygen and, therefor, never needs to resurface, and he or she can resist the pressure of the deep sea, even going as deep as the abyss without the need of a submarine. I feel I needed to address this, because I've seen ABZU been called a scuba diving simulator around the net.
The graphics make ABZU look like a painting, which may or may not be intentional. If the developers intended for the game to simulate a painting, bravo to them, for they succeeded brilliantly. However, for me, the flat colors made the game feel artificial, hindering immersion. ABZU does, however, have beautiful lighting effects, and is beautifully animated, from the protagonist, to the animals, and even the plants, even if you occasionally run into one that spasms for seemingly no reason.
To sum up how I feel about ABZU, the simulator is beautiful to look at, but is not really worth experiencing. The simulator is short (will take you around 2 to 3 hours to complete), offers very little to do in a gameplay standpoint, and the story is something seen many times before (even if there's no dialogue). Until the developers add to ABZU, or reduce the price, this simulator is not worth your time.
By the way, for merfolk fans like me to know, there are no mermaids in ABZU whatsoever, at least in the time I wrote this review. If you're looking for a mermaid simulator, get The Sims 3: Island Paradise.

I played The Witcher series since the first. I knew the game from a PC magazine, it was a walkthrough and it seems the game is kinda interesting, so i bought myself a copy of the first The Witcher, and i got myself engrossed in it.
Honestly i played this game before for many times and had a lot of alternate routes before i got it on Steam (okay, i used to pirated the game, sorry).
And now the review.
The Witcher 2 starts out with a war between two kingdoms which one of them has Geralt the silver wolf with them, and so is Triss. The beginning of the game starts off with a great prologue, you will see a lot of nudity in this game and of course sex scene. The battle system is tight and fast paced, it's really great so you will use all of the game had to offer such as many kinds of potions and four upgradable spells of the Witcher. Though the battle is kinda different to the first one, doesn't mean it's going down, if i may say it's even going on another level.

This is a really great puzzle game. I've never played sokoban (which this is based off of if it's not obvious to you), but it's a great spin on the concept, as instead of just being able to push things, you can pull atoms around when you bond with them (but bonding in the wrong pattern can make the puzzle unsolvable if you can't bypass an obstacle as that shape). You can infinitely undo any number of actions, so if you get into an unsolvable scenario you don't have to start over, just undo the last X steps until you can try something else.
The mechanics that let you rotate a bond, make more bonds and split bonds are well executed, and they often get in your way just as much as they help you complete the puzzle, which makes you have to figure out just the right set of moves to execute.
I resorted to a guide for a couple puzzles, as I had an idea of what I needed to make happen but I didn't know how to get there. Despite this, I thought each puzzle was well designed and none of them felt impossible; I just needed a hint to nudge me in the right direction.
I hope the developers add steam workshop support with a puzzle editor; I'd love to play more levels. Definitely get this if you at all like puzzle games!

Okay to start off: I played Gal Civ II - so I'm mostly going to  write the review as a migrating Gal Civ II player.
What Gal Civ II had going for it was a great AI, but that seems to be gone in this game. The AI is definetly competitive in the sense that it's able to colonize the galaxy and expand pretty well, but it's not very dangerous necessarily - at least not in  the early to mid game. The AI - even the aggressive races will sometimes not attack - maybe because of their life support tech being poor? Or them forgoing  research of the exploration tech. Their reasons aren't clear to me. Sometimes it seems that the AI's are pretty slow at developing a military too and they get pretty cocky once they do develop a small military.
An unwelcome addition is the addition of pirates. To be perfectly honest - in a game where the militaristic side is slow to develop - I don't think they're very necessary and they serve little purpose that I can see other than like in Civ being a nuisance and destroying your unescorted colony ships.
The tech trees have also been more streamlined to follow the universally same structure between all the races. This makes the tech trees certainly less interesting and nothing like they were in the previous game but on  the other hand you don't need to make drastic changes to how you play races anymore and it's easier to get into the game from the beginning. They also set up a tech requirement that you need to research X amount of techs in your tech tree before you're allowed to advance to the next era. This is certainly nice as troop transports aren't availible until the second era: "The Age of War". This also means that civs can no longer shoot for distant techs spec strategies, like choosing a massive galaxy and just researching tech ascension. However there are only 3 Eras in the game so it's not a lot of gating going on here.
Edit: Another thing I failed to mention is that I don't like the user interface at all, but I don't think it's so bad that it makes the game unplayable.
However all these changes are sort of making Cal Civ III lose it's identity. How is this title supposed to compete as a space 4X game when it has very little that makes it unique? This makes the  game also very hard to recommend or not to recommend. But ultimately I feel that the game is enjoyable enough to say: Yeah! It's good enough.

A great mixing of genres that leans more heavily on the roguelike side, Crypt of the NecroDancer is a great example of Early Access done right.  The game is pseudo turn-based as each "turn" is one beat of the soundtrack during which you can either move, attack, cast a spell, or use an item.  Keeping the rhythm allows you to build a multiplier, while acting out of rhythm resets it back to 1.  Although this mechanic is strange at first, you'll soon find keeping time is no problem due to the amazing soundtrack by Danny B.  The progression system is standard roguelike as you can find diamonds during your run which you can spend to upgrade your character.
Best Feature:  The soundtrack and animation are excellent.  The way everything hops to the beat is fantastic.
Worst Feature:  The music can get repetitive when starting out, however this is fixable by changing the track or using your own mp3s.
Final Thoughts:  Explore the dungeon to the beat and while the shopkeeper sings.

Earthlock: Festival of Magic is the game I would reccomend to people who get turned off by staple features of 90s console RPGs.
Earthlock manages to lovingly emulate the enjoyment of playstation and SNES RPG Titles, but in a truly surprising way actually progresses and reinvigorates the style. While the titles this game is based on are great, they require those who weren't fans or unable to get past certain pet peeves to put up with it for the entire game.
Things like repetitive battle music, slow battles, oversimplified commands (generic Attack command), and the dreaded grinding of fighting the same short encounter list makes classics and modern retro RPGs harder to enjoy for many people. Earthlock addresses all of this while forging it's own identity.
The Soundtrack is incredible and diverse, but what makes it more than just nice to listen is that battle themes are rearranged versions of the area themes they belong. It truly makes the game more enjoyable when your favorite battle themes can be traced to fighting in the sewer or on the glacier. But most importantly you never go into the hundreds upon hundreds of battles hearing the same opening over and over, also the switch is seamless as a nice touch.
Slow battles is a little harder to explain, but just expect no ATB bars and being able to input commands much faster than most turn based games. In the few instances where the battles drag on a bit, the game shells you a bit of bonus EXP for sticking to the end.
Very early the game teaches you a simple trick, slashing attacks kill plant enemies better. From this point on, you realize that the generic attack technically dosen't exist in this game, the game puts it in your best interest to explore and adapt since the stances can radically change your battle strategies and with more useful attack abilites (Gouge, traps) and becuase such logic as only ranged attacks can hit flying enemies, stops the players from mashing an attack command for 40 hours.
Last but not least, Grinding. There are too many good games classic and modern that need warning labels about how much they block your progression or enjoyment because of this curse. It seems way too hyperbolic to state that Earthlock simply has no grinding, it techinically does, but with good mechanical and subtle design it never needs to plauge the average player. Encounters are visible and can be avoided or engaged quite easily, but another feature is to lure encounters into 1 large outnumbering battle. When you risk these battles, your exp is dramaticly increased based on the size of the encounters, in fact fighting single enemies produces pitiful gains. In this fashion, the game encourages you to seek battles that might be more than you can chew. You never find yourself fighting the same list of encounters with a static exp increase. A more subtle feature is how the hub garden let's you literally farm for ammo and craft potions, but it's used when players are spending downtime between the more active chunks of the game. Other small things help like getting extra exp for not having anyone die, or making the level cap 20, or how upgrading the bonds gives you points to level up with. The amount of options and characters and pairs, while not staggeringly large, give players lots of room to deal and adapt to bosses and tough areas all the better.
In terms of cons this game does have a handful or so. The engine and the collsion can be a little spotty when walking around, the control scheme takes a bit to get used to for using abilities and items, PAT takes a small while before he truly holds up as good as the other characters. A less nitpicking issue is that gold (or as this game labels it Daler) has very very little use in this game thanks to how the garden and crafting system works, or how items worth having are found in chests and at the end of boss battles. The game has some good consumable (non health restoring) items to use, but you never get them outside of the arena, and you cant take them elsewhere, so things that could be bought with currency just dont get to be used for some reason. In the end your Daler becomes obselete really fast, I felt that removing the Daler or making more shops would have integrated Daler perfectly.
There's more subjective things to talk about like how the story and characters are begging to have more time in the spotlight at times, or how the game simply dosen't offer optional areas and even a fraction of side content that more popular games offer, But I state that for a kickstarted retro style RPG this is one the most polished and refined original titles to come out of 2016 and for a first time title from a new indie studio in Norway, That is incredible.

Pros
> The battle experience system is good - taking on more mobs gets you bonuses. It's almost always worth rounding up lots of enemies, than fighting them individually.
> The gardening/growing ammo is a neat idea.
> The artwork and animation is pretty good
> Good boss battles, challenging and require some though
Cons
> The normal battles are fairly boring. Same tactics used each time. No in game help that lets you see what enemies are weak to what.
> The gardening is a good idea. But like the plot, it feels half finished.
> The frog island feels unfinished - like, they had plans for weapon upgrades and clothing and stuff, but then didn't implement it. There is clearly space for a blacksmith, and some other stuff at the base Island, but it's never used. Eg, the library also seemed like it was going to be used for something. Instead, you just go in and then use a room upstairs to rest. A lot of the game spaces in towns are like this - no purpose to them, but it seems like they were planned to have a purpose at some stage.
> Extremely frustrating to have to leave an area to replenish HP. Why not just have the frog statues let you replenish your health? Instead, you have to teleport to base, run around, find the rest area, warp back, and all the monsters have respawned. Instead, just make 99 of the cheap health potions and use them to heal up.
In summary, the game is enjoyable, but feels unfinished, like only half of the ideas they had made it into the game. Search google images for "Earthlock Map" and you'll find two different maps. One is a small map of a peninsula and the other is a huge multi island map. The small map is the entirety of the game. The other map is just lore as far as I can tell. There are three "over world" areas and all of them are tiny.
Once again. Feels Unfinished.
Hard to recommend. I'm giving it a thumbs up, because it's not a bad game. It's just not what it could have been.

I have never had mixed feelings about a game like I do about this one, I mean it's a bad game but there are some things done right and we must aknowledge this. Other developers can draw inspiration from them. A good example would be the police response time and witness mechanics.
Mafia III is a lot like Game of Thrones and by that I mean that it has several brilliant moments that make you wanna see what happens in the end, but between them it's rarely anything worthwhile.
Graphics : Tehnically, this game looks good  but the color pallete used in portraying the environment is very washed out so that the real beauty that this game would be capable of is never in the spotlight. The game looks better at night cause of that.
Bugs: Many game breaking bugs as well as minor bugs and glitches plague this game from start to finish.
Sound: The sound FX are borderline decent. Like in Mafia 2, the highlight is the awesome radio soundtrack but this time around there are cool news and ads that help immerse you in the era. That being said, they manage to entertain you for 15-20 hours but considering this game is very long, they become boring. This problem is highlighted even more by the fact that 75% of the gameplay time you are driving trough the huge world back and forth between interest points.
Gameplay-wise this game is only repetitive because of its length. I guess if it were the same length as Mafia 2, it would've felt better. Problem is, they wanted to give large mission content but instead of putting the least important missions of the storyline as optional, you have to keep doing them between the missions that matter  to the point they become tedious.
Story: When there is story, the story is very good. It's exactly what you would expect and what you'd hoped for. The problem is where it ain't any. The characters are great, have diverse motiviation and you have reasons to choose anyone of your underbosses over the other. This is due to good motion capture and better voice acting, the characters being the main reason why you wanna reach the conclusion.This game has 3 endings which you are allowed to come back and visit but only 2 of them are good.
The World: The city is the biggest one I have ever seen in a video game and I just finished GTA V so that's saying something. Problem is... the map is empty. Sure, it looks exactly how you would expect 1960' New Orleans to look and it's huge but you ain't got nothing to do. There are 6 types of collectables but you get absolutely 0 if you get them all. So there's not even that. There are a few racing events but they aren't that cool either. They are just ok and the cars drive realistic I guess. The huge world is a burden when all it manages to do is putting lots of kms between you and your marker, especially underlined by the fact that the cars are EXTREMELY SLOW. Also the AI is dumb, like pedestrians jumping under your car than away from it when you speed by kind of dumb.
I finished it just so I can be qualified to write this review and I liked the story but really that's all there is. The game is a development disaster. It behaves like an Early Access.

Used to play this all the time. Lost the CD, found it again on Steam, and had a blast.
What you've got here is a decent Diablo clone with a ridiculous amount of depth. There's lots of customization in the way of attributes, skills, equipment, a pet, and magic, and the game constantly rewards your efforts by allowing you to improve more and more in each of these departments. It can get quite difficult and hectic at times (seriously, why must I fight more than 10 enemies at once), so if you don't like the idea of teleporting back to the town every five minutes, micromanaging your armor based on stat bonuses, or bringing up your inventory a million times in one battle, this probably isn't for you. If you can deal with all that, then get it, install it, and ready yourself for one awesome, yet often overlooked, game.
-----
Now then, be warned, this game has its share of problems. I ran into a few in-game bugs, but none of them really broke the game or made it easier or harder. More important than that, there is a serious issue of some Steam users not being able to run the game, and while WildTangent (the devs) have made an effort to address this problem, there is still a relevant portion of people who have bought the game and just had it sitting in their library since. It isn't always necessarily the same thing giving everyone this problem as well, so what works as a solution for one person may not work for you. I got it working after a few months, but if you want to play it and have any doubts about whether you can run it, you probably want to read the forums and see what people, for their specific cases, have done in the way of trying to fix the problem.

I received FATE through a bundle that contained other games I was interested in getting, so I did not actively seek it out. However, I'm a huge fan of some RPGs, so I figured I would try out FATE. After all, I was obsessed with WildTangent back in the day. (Still hoping for a Steam version of Blackhawk Striker 2!)
Sadly, FATE turned into a game that I do not wish to play. However, I would still recommend it, which is why I'm giving it a positive review.
The best way for me to describe FATE is that it's a never-ending dungeon. Whereas other RPGs will have you encounter multiple dungeons alongside the main story or as side quests, FATE is simply one gigantic dungeon. There is little story here; it's all about becoming the most famous adventurer to conquer what lies beyond the Gate next to the town of Grove. There are quests that the villagers of Grove will give you, but they're simply "Get back in that dungeon, to a specific level, and beat up this specific monster there. Get the item he drops and come back." This furthers your progress with experience, gold, and fame. Way more focus on gameplay (see below) than story.
The aesthetics are not Battlefield 4, but they completely match with the time period the game was developed in as well as in the style of RPG the game was going for. It's very much old-timey. However, don't let the graphics mislead you into thinking that this is one of the really difficult RPGs of old; it's actually quite easy to pick up and play when you get through the opening loading screens. I would have liked a tutorial or quick "here's what you're doing and how you do it" conversation with a tutorial NPC or something, but it's fine as it is. Level 1 of the dungeon is straightforward and pretty much sets the bar for what players should expect.
Of note, however, is that there's a difficulty setting. I set it to Page, the easiest. So it might just be me. The hardest difficulty, Legend, might be what the veterans from old RPGs would like to start out at to really get a challenge. :P
Gameplay is interesting, to say the least. Battles and encounters are real-time, so you have to stay on your toes and watch where you're going. Thankfully, it's easy to discern an enemy approaching you, so you have time to react. But enemies do have various speeds, both for "walking" and for attacking. I highly appreciate that an enemy's important statistics are mentioned just by hovering over it; it's very easy to tell what it's weak or strong to.
The music and other sound effects are top-notch, and I'm definitely going to research into the FATE soundtrack after posting this review. Very enjoyable, even to just sit in town or the main menu and listen for a while.
tl;dr FATE is simply one giant dungeon, but it does it pretty well. This is not my kind of game, and I didn't enjoy it as much as other people would, but I would definitely recommend it because, for the kind of RPG it is, I think it's worth a look for all RPG fans.

Watching the short trailer video for LiEat, I already knew I wanted to play it as I adore RPG's. LiEat is a trilogy of short games lasting around one - two hour each and you follow around a young guy and his pet dragon called Efina solving mysteries. It's one of the only games I own on steam, that I would recommand to every friends I have. The game is worth the money and doesn't feel like a $3 game at all. If you're just considering buying the game because it's cheap, do it. It's well worth it.
It took me a total of nine hours to complete all three LiEat games and also complete all the achievements for each game. Sometimes I did have to start a new game to do an achievement but as a completionist and i forgot to save it two times, I didn’t mind, it was worth it.
So let’s talk about the  style, it was lovely and cute imo, kind of has an anime/VN vibe to it and the little characters in the game are adorable as well!!. Simple but with the perfect amount of detail when it’s needed. Also, when you progress through the game, you will come across crucial moments where there would be a short animation clip, just to make the game more visually appealing which I really appreciated. If you can’t get enough of the clips and you would want to view it again, once you complete the game your character will be transported to the ending room where you can look back at images and clips you came across in the game and also read more information on the characters in the game.
The games themselves aren’t hard to beat, really, but the last installment will require the player to look up a walkthrough if they want the good ending, due to the very random, very specific requires that must be achieved in order to unlock the good ending.
The mysteries in the games were very good and a lot of fun to explore and figure out, and the characters were all very diverse. I was incredibly pleased when the police dragons continued to show up throughout the series as well. Awesome game. Ten out of ten. (What can I say? I’m a sucker for a good story.) I would probably have to rate this teen and up though for the blood and the second chapter’s setting, which while not too graphic, is something kids probably shouldn’t be learning about quite yet.

Spintires is a simulation games similar to Euro Truck Simulator, Farming Simulator, and other simulator games of that type. The main objective of the game is to deliver loads of logs from one part of the map to the other. To deliver these logs you have several different cold war era Russian military vehicles which can be modified with a plethora of different attackments form log loads to fuel tanks. Each vehicle has its pros and cons for different situations.
The maps consist of basic themes which provide diffenet challenges from steep hills to a flood plain. One constant of these maps you will come to find is the pools of stagnant water you can easily drown your vehicle in and the waist deep mud you will constantly be getting stuck in. After playing the game and I mean actually playing the game you will see these obsticles as minor speed bumps and carry on as if they were not even an issue.
Playing with other veteran players all the maps can be completed in around thirty minutes. That being said for beginners even playing with other beginners expect to be playing for hours and do not expect to finish the first map you play. This game is hard in the beginning but is simple to learn if you actually just sit and play the game.

I played The Witcher series since the first. I knew the game from a PC magazine, it was a walkthrough and it seems the game is kinda interesting, so i bought myself a copy of the first The Witcher, and i got myself engrossed in it.
Honestly i played this game before for many times and had a lot of alternate routes before i got it on Steam (okay, i used to pirated the game, sorry).
And now the review.
The Witcher 2 starts out with a war between two kingdoms which one of them has Geralt the silver wolf with them, and so is Triss. The beginning of the game starts off with a great prologue, you will see a lot of nudity in this game and of course sex scene. The battle system is tight and fast paced, it's really great so you will use all of the game had to offer such as many kinds of potions and four upgradable spells of the Witcher. Though the battle is kinda different to the first one, doesn't mean it's going down, if i may say it's even going on another level.
You will need to prepare yourself for every possibilities lies ahead, even before some cutscenes, since there are possibilities that after cutscenes you may find yourself surrounded by enemies and without any buff from potions, since you can't drink any when you are in the middle of the fight. There are also kinds of enemies, starting from human, harpies, gargoyle, troll, etc. Each of them (monsters) has lore of their own, this may be a friendly reminder or a spoiler but you may find the knowledge about monsters before you fight them so you won't get a hard time, to find the knowledge about monsters, you could learn by experiences (means you have to fight them enough until you know what's what) or you can just buy a book from a merchant in town. The choice is all yours.
Talk about choice, as you can see on the tag of this game, your choices DOES REALLY MATTER to define the game stories. You will find yourself a totally different route for the story everytime you choose a choice differently, and this is what's makes this game so great. You will get served a new kind of adventure for every choice you made.

Sokobond is a neat puzzle game.  You start with a board with a finite amount of space, and a single piece (an ion) that you can move.  Move it next to another ion and the two will bond.  Bind all the free ions together to make some compound and you're done.  The thing is you can neither rotate your molecule, nor unbind ions, and the board is designed such that you have to be careful how you bind the first ions or you won't be able to get your molecule to bind with the last ions (the molecule'll be too fat to maneuver).  Sounds simple, and the early puzzles are, but they get harder.
Successfully create a molecule, and you get a little blurb about what that compound is, and how it's used.  Chemistry ftw!
Your progress through the puzzles is tracked on a grid with one puzzle per grid block.  Solve a puzzle and the adjoining puzzles become available.  You start in a red area with red puzzles.  Finishing the puzzles leading to an arrow opens up a new, differently colored grid section.  Sometimes the different colors offer new mechanics, sometimes they just offer harder puzzles.
The graphics are as good as they need to be.  The sound is adequate.  The background music is the ambient, puzzle-game sort (think World of Goo).  It's unobtrusive enough not to bother you while you're trying to figure your moves, but keeps you from listening to nothing.
You don't need any chemistry knowledge for this, but you'll certainly pick some up.  The amount of free electrons an ion has is indicated by floating circles slowly orbiting it.  This is the sort of thing that gets ingrained in a mind over time after moving nitride and oxide ions around for fun.
This game is cool for its elegant simplicity, and because chemistry, yay!

I would recommend this game to fans of the Galactic Civilizations franchise and 4x strategy games with some minor caveats.
First, this is a solid game, with similar gameplay to other GC titles. Most things work well, with a few bugs, but as the closed/purchase beta was fairly long, they fixed most major issues.
Still some problems in there, but these will probably be worked out in a not very long while.
My reservations about this title are a few:
1. Stardock seems to be going down the same DLC path as other game companies, and I do not see this as a good thing. Up to now, they have done a fairly good job of not nickel and diming people to death. They have been putting out some reasonably weak expansions for their other titles, so I am not terribly hopeful on this front.
2. The gameplay is extremely similar to GC2 w/expansions. There is not a whole lot new in there, that I have seen at least. It is very much evolutionary in design, and in places, not very much of that even. GC3 is certainly not revolutionary in design. New graphics, cleaner look and play, much better under the hood, but not a fundamentally different game than GC2.
3. For a game so similar to GC2, the full price of ~ $50 is a bit high. I myself bought in during beta, and paid far less. Had I paid full price for this title, I might have been less satisfied with it.
So, it is a good game for fans of 4x strategy, and the GC franchise, but even with a few things that need work, the game is worth buying, especially if you can get it on sale.

GalCiv 3 has a lot of potential. It could be the best space strategy game out there. However, two major shortcomings prevent it from fulfilling its promise. First, the interface is entirely inadequate to manage large scale empires - one of its supposedly major advantages over its predecessor. Once you control more than a a few dozen worlds, star bases and ships, this game becomes micro management hell. For example, there is no way to upgrade a whole fleet, you'll have to do it piece by piece. GalCiv's other major weakness are bugs. It's not unplayable but there are just too many to really enjoy it. Why is the guard function not working? Why does it crash or hang every so often? Why does the AI behave so erratically, declaring war and begging for peace the very next turn?
I've decided to stop playing for now and give it another try in a couple of updates. Stardock did improve GalCiv 2 a lot during its life time. I'm confident they'll make an enjoyable game out of GalCiv 3, too. At the moment, it just isn't.
