I’ve played GalCiv 3 since late beta, running an i7 with 12 GB of RAM.  I haven’t tried the in-game campaign and have played only single-player using medium and large galaxies vs. all 8 in-game AI factions + assorted minor factions.   You can go much bigger than that if your machine will support it, but I've found large galaxies make for very satisfying games.  I highly recommend smaller galaxies for your first games, so that you can get going more easily.  As others have pointed out, the bigger you play, the more RAM you will need.
:  Fun game, your decisions matter.  AI factions are entertaining, imperfect, and improving.  Ship designer keeps game interesting.  Stardock user community is active and helpful.  There is a learning curve and some rough edges, but lots of entertainment value for my money (more than most games).
:
- Most of the decisions you have to make matter.  Each tech you research, each colony improvement you build makes a noticeable improvement -- your ships become more powerful, colonies are more productive, your influence and bargaining power increase.  You aren’t overwhelmed by near-meaningless busy-work or grinding to grow your empire.
- Every faction feels different, much more so than, say, in the Civ series. Tech trees change depending on which faction you play, and the strengths and weaknesses of each faction feel important.  Plus, you can make all the custom factions you want, or download others' factions from Stardock's website (Steam workshop support should be coming soon, too).
- AI factions have personality and give you feedback.  An AI faction might warn you off if you're amassing ships near their border, or let you know they value the trade route you have with them.  I quickly get to like/despise/fear each faction in the game, and this also changes from one game to the next depending on your choices and how the game progresses.  One game, I was planning to go to war with one faction, but then they surprised me with a small gift, expressing admiration for my society.  So I gave them some help, we became friends and are now fighting an enemy faction together.  This has made for a much more interesting story than the old smash-em-all slog that many 4x games become.
- Ship combat is more interesting than GalCiv 2 -- not just rock-paper-scissors, but ships are assigned roles like assault, guardian, escort, support, and these roles affect combat.  Your ship designs and fleet composition make a big difference.  Much like Civ, I would say the battles are fought strategically, not tactically (you're the admiral directing the war(s); you're not the captain making in-battle decisions).
- The ship designer lets you make any ship you want; customize load-outs and/or appearance as you like. You can even download and use others' ship designs – some users have already posted some interesting designs.  I get weary of 4x games where every faction has the same old units -- not here.   While I haven't seen it myself yet, word from other users is that the AI will learn to use the units you design too.  Never the same game twice!
- Adjacency bonuses – e.g., two factories next to each other make each other better – make planning improvements on your colonies more interesting than just loading up a build-queue.  It adds some strategic planning to your colony management without overwhelming you in too many details.
- If you love to micro-manage, you can tinker with just about everything, and most of the numbers you see have pop-up tooltips showing you where they come from.  If you prefer, you can play a rewarding game without worrying about min-/maxing every little decision.
- The UI and graphics have improved dramatically over GalCiv 2.  It's easy to move through the turns and most decisions can be enacted quickly and intuitively.
- Nebulae, black holes, wormholes and asteroid fields add more “terrain” features to the map than GalCiv 2 had, and these can be relevant for positioning, hiding, or escape.  As well, there are more galactic resources which can be mined for improved technologies.
- The Stardock user-community is generally helpful and respectful; if you have questions, ask, and someone will answer pretty quickly.
:
- If you're not really familiar with the GalCiv games of the past, or even if you are, there's a learning curve.  There is a manual on Stardock’s site, and you may need to scout the web or forums for help.  I’ve gotten answers to my questions from the Stardock user community usually very quickly.  When playing your first game or two, expect to make an occasional unfortunate decision only to learn later that it wasn’t what you might have expected.
- Game is a little rough around the edges (some spelling errors, the odd tech doesn’t work the way it’s advertised, AI occasionally does something dumb), but no disastrous issues and improvements are happening all the time:  2 patches since release and version 1.1 is coming in June.  I've had one CTD, but with auto-save I lost only a couple of turns, so no big deal.
- Espionage is non-existent, and Diplomacy is fairly basic – you can trade and ask another faction to go to war with/for you (for a price).  Like with any other 4x game, I expect more to come in future patches/expansions.
- Not all information is accessible when you want it – e.g., you can’t review the state of your empire before responding to an AI’s trade request.  While once in a while this can be awkward, it’s far from game-breaking.

: Brace Yourself Games
: Brace Yourself Games, Klei Entertainment
==========
Crypt of the Necrodancer is a rhythm rogue-like dungeon crawler. You navigate your character through randomly generated dungeons divided into zones, while avoiding traps, defeating enemies, and collecting treasure, weapons, and armor. The game encourages you to move to the beat of the tracks played in each zone, offering you a coin multiplayer as long as you stick to moving with the beat. The longer you stay in rhythm with the beat, the higher your multiplayer goes. The multiplier affects how many coins you earn from defeating enemies, as well as providing boosts to some of the items you find. So it's really in your best interests to try and keep a good rhythm going as you explore!
==========
As said above, you move your character in-time with the beat of the song being played on each floor. The starter character, Cadence, has the perk of having an assistive tool at the bottom of the screen, which helps you to time your button presses with the beat. The game is divided into 4 zones, each consisting of a few floors and a boss floor. Each floor has a different tune playing, which in turn has a different beat that allows you to move at a certain pace. Some floors have a slower beat, some have a faster beat. Also important to note are how monsters move with the beat. Certain monster types have specific patterns, and learning these patterns will help you greatly in navigating the dungeon safely. Some move every beat, some move every other beat. If you happen to move onto a square at the same time as a monster, you take damage, which further emphasizes how important it is to learn monster movements.
You are also able to utilize several tools, including a shovel, bombs, and various charms that have different effects. Also scattered about are shrines, which offer several different effects depending on it's type. Some are positive effects, while others are negative. Smart use of every tool at your disposal is crucial to survival. One tool I really like to utilize are bombs, as they have several exploratory and combat uses. The shovel is used to dig through walls, which can lead to lots of hidden rooms with secret items! Some walls cannot be dug if your shovel isn't good enough, and there are several tiers of shovels, as well as weapons and armor. Gold, Blood, Titanium, and Obsidian are a few examples, each providing different modifiers for the items.
The game also features a level editor, with which you can create and upload your own dungeons to the Steam Workshop for others to play and enjoy. The only downside is that you need to clear Zone 4 with a character to unlock it initially. It's also a bit odd in that it's very difficult to use until you learn how to navigate the menus and how to place items. Despite this, it's a powerful tool that works. One thing I'd like for them to add in the level editor is the ability to have specific enemies drop specific items when defeated...such as keys!
==========
Boasting a pixel art style, everything is surprisingly detailed. The sprites are amazingly rich and colorful, and often times you are able to tell where monsters will move and what they are about to do, as well as spot secrets hidden in the walls...like the glinting tip of a diamond in a stone pillar! Such small details are what make this game great. Armor also shows up on your character, so it's easy to tell what they are wearing. Some weapons have battle animations, such as the whips, but most you don't actually see the weapon. Instead, you see a sort of "slash" animation depending on the weapon type. Needless to say, these are minor graphical grievances that are more than made up for by the rest of the game's details. Traps are easy to spot, and items laying around are easily identified as well.
==========
The music of this game is where the game shines. Catchy tunes accompany every zone and floor, offering a variety of beats and toe-tapping goodness. Danny Baranowsky is the one responsible for most of the songs in the game, and he has done a fantastic job in really giving this game life. Sound effects are basic and they work, signalling damage, movement, and enemy presence. There really isn't much to say here, other than the soundtarck is amazing. You can check it out or buy it
. It's 100% worth a listen, and even a buy if you like it! There is even an extended soundtrack available for you to further customize each zone. The game also allows you to use your own MP3's in-game for endless fun.
==========
This isn't really a very-demanding game, so most people should have no issues running it. If you have any doubts, make sure to check the minimum and recommended specs for the game on the Store Page. During my playtime I did not run into any bugs or glitches. I expected to run into at least 1 bug during my several playthroughs, but surprisingly not a single one appeared. Bravo! There are options for several resolutions, as well as Windowed and Fullscreen modes.
==========
Crypt of the Necrodancer is a worthy additional to the library of anyone who is a fan of rogue-likes, music-based games, dungeons crawlers, or people who just love fun unique games. There hasn't been a game like this before, so it's worth diving into if you are looking for a new experience.
==========

==========

Earthlock is a nice little gem of a game. I'm quite happy I purchased it and it was well worth the money. I'm hoping for a follow-up game from the devs with better writing. However, when you have 7 other languages to translate it into I understand.
Pros:
-Graphics - are nice and colorful but can also change as you progress in the game to be dark and dense nicely matching the place you are currently going. The diversity is great and the maps are littered with beautiful vistas. Seeing the battles and the artwork were the main draws to the game for me.
-Battles and Fights - are really quite fun and every character has two stances. Some characters might focus on buffing and damage which others focus on healing and damage and others have a melle and ranged stance. It's quite nice and you'll find yourself switching in and out of stances at times to get the best results. You don't have magic either you have a number of amri (abilitiy points) that you can use and some moves require more than others. It's fairly wel balanced and tweaking the talents and bonds system allows for more customization.
-Leveling up system/talents/bonds - Leveling up does make a difference but something else that is quite cool is the bond system. Every character can bond with another. The point of doing this, outside of adding 3 unique points to your talent board is that it will grant the characters more unique abilities that when they are paired can make them stronger. This comes in handy when fighting certain bosses. On most fights you don't need to tap into these abilities but it's worth it when you fight difficult bosses. If you outlevel the bosses they can be easy but if not considering how to fight can be quite fun and worth your time. If you take the wrong character combos and don't consider what you need to win you will die in battle.
-Music - The compositions and score are quite nice. I had a great time listening to the music and never wanted to turn it off. Of course battle music may wear on you after awhile but I still enjoyed it. The sound effects aren't brillant but they're decent and they worked and were never immersion breaking.
-Languages - Lots of support for other languages in an RPG is hard to find. If you want to pratice another language or learn one it's not a bad idea to open the options menu and have it switch over. You don't need to restart the game and it works like a charm. I tested it with Chinese, since I'm learning Chinese and it was fast and easy. It's something most people won't care about but it's quite nice!
-Fun Factor - I always felt like I wanted to play the game. It rarely ever felt too grindy or like a chore. I wanted to progress and explore and kill all of the bosses. Dungeons weren't too long and the game was just a blast to play through.
Cons:
-Storyline - It's not brillant. It's not awful but... being a veteran to many rpgs I was rather dissapointed with quite a bit of the dialogue. One of the characters who arguably does draw/stretch out the lore is often told to zip it. While this makes sense it would have been nice to find ways for the characters to ask questions as opposed to just ask him to shut up most of the time. They character dialogue when they spoke to each other wasn't interesting either. They didn't really say anything witty or clever most of the time. There were a few jokes but they didn't do it for me. If you want a wonderful story you will be a bit crestfallen.
Minor Annoyances:
-There are 2 characters who did not have an animation when they finished two sections of the game that are required. It just seemed off though since I started grining this to level up my bonds/abilities.
-Garden Growing - Early in the game you are taken to a garden section where you grow plants to get the best items for two characters as well as healing items. This section can be quite fun but it is also grindy and you HAVE to do this for the best attack items for 2 of the characters in the game. I said this earlier and didn't mind it much but it might bother other players.
-Teleportation is nice but there to teleport anywhere you first have to teleport to a main hub. It's not a huge deal breaker but it will take you about 15 extra seconds to do this and you may do it a fair amount of times.
-No weapons/armor to upgrade. I personally don't mind but if you love equipping new gear you will be a bit upset.
TL:DR
+ Graphics
+ Battles
+ Leveling up/Bond and Talent System
+ Nice Music
-Storyline and writing isn't great because of 8+ languages supported.

Dust is a 2D platformer/fighter, like something from the nineties, but a bit more up-to-date and surprisingly polished.
Movement and platforming mechanics are solid and reliable - it's never unfair and, providing you've at least a little skill, at no point is it likely to become tiresome.  Combat is straight-forward and fairly fluid.  While it requires no great skill (you can button-mash through most of the game), it is quite fun stringing together the various simple combos.
The audio-visuals are extremely polished, the game looks and sounds good throughout.  Characterisation and storyline are the game's weakest points - it feels somewhat like a cross between an old Disney movie and a generic Japanese anime episode - and these days, seeing as Disney/Pixar turns out the likes of The Incredibles, Monsters, Inc and so forth, producing a sub-par old-Disney-style story with added anime stereotypes really isn't impressive.
Voice-acting is as good as it can be, given the paucity of the scripts the actors have been given.  Kimlinh Tran as Fidget has the most to work with and sounds like she's having the most fun.
On balance, this is a good game.  I've finished it on Normal Difficulty and I didn't feel like the game outstayed it's welcome.  I'll be playing through again on a higher difficulty later.  Recommended.

Honestly overall I thoroughly enjoyed this game. Enought to play it one more time to enjoy the DLC and gain a more satisfactory ending.
The things I liked
1) Visuals
(Ill talk about the bad visuals further down in my review). I enjoyed the 1960s southern american city setting. I loved how the cars looked and how the game generally looked when it was in action.
2) Story
The story was refreshing somewhat, it wasnt some mobster trying to climb up the mob ladder and become capo of some family. Here you are trying to tear a rival family down and build the foundation of your family on the ashes of the previous one.
3) Music
The music choice in that game was superb. Loved almost every single song.
4) Gameplay
Pretty straight forward and enjoyably smooth to play. Controls werent clunky or weird. Overall it was a blast to play through.
The only real issues are the bugs and other developer choices.
1) Customisation
When I started playing there were no options to customise cars, or your outfit; which was disappointing considering in MAFIA II you were able to purchase clothing and vehicle modifications. In Mafia II you were more free to customise your character. In mafia III on the other hand you have no power over the character other than how your allies preceive you. Some very limiting customisation options were added as DLC later on but by that time the damage for me was already done.
2) Visuals
The game looks good but sometimes the lighting goes all out of whack. Everything looks nice but all of a sudden you are the silver surfer and everything is excessively reflective and silvery. The good visuals arent constant and the bad ones are extremely noticable. Its not something you can try and ignore.
3) AI
The AI is not that good. Actually its quite bad. Pedestrians keep getting scared and jumping into oncoming traffic even if you are not driving in their direction or at any speed. Lincoln Clay is talking to someone and there is no lip movement. There are times where I have cleared a whole warehouse of baddies by just 1 whistle. I just hid behind a door and kept adding bodies to that same spot over and over again until only the districts boss remained.
4) Bugs
One noticable bug for me is that when I start the game sometimes it stutters. Im driving fast down some highway and my game is running at a smooth 60+FPS. Then any movement from the mouse is stuttered. I try looking to my left and the game is turning at -60FPS and it seems like it is struggling.
Also if you are in full screen mode and you tab out and back in again, dont have any hope that your game will be running smoothly. The sounds for me dont work and the cutscenes have no video, just the audio. When my sounds bug up like that only voices, impacts (bullets) and footsteps can be heard. Nothing else...
5) Gameplay
I enjoyed the game. I loved the during/post Vietnam era the game was based in. I loved the music choice, the cars and guns. THe one thing I genuinly got bored of was the tedious task of gaining a territory. You speak to some underboss or whatever, they tell you who runs things. You interrogate some guy, you kill some other guy and you bust some of his rackets and then you go talk to your underboss and go face the enemy in the same racket you massacred half his crew in 5 minutes ago. Then you just repeat that whole process a total of two times per district. The first time it was cool BUT by the time you had taken over half the city, had made a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of money and could invest in upgrading weapons, health etc. You are unstoppable whether you blast your way through or go in Sneaky Beaky like. Honestly this gameplay choice makes this game very easy to speed run.
I know I might of mentioned more bad than good in this review but honestly, I replayed this game regardless of some bugs and nuisances. If you enjoyed mafia II you will most likely enjoy this one as well. Maybe not as much as mafia II but you will enjoy III non the less.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is an action-RPG that really gets it right.
RPG mechanics are strong and very well balanced. You gain abilities as you progress through the game. Combat difficulty stays leveled right along with you. Simple crafting and shops make item upgrades a cinch. If hack-and-slash games are your thing, you're in for a treat. This is a side-scrolling hack-and-slash with lots of delicious combo action.
The art style of the game is incredible as well. Everything oozes with lovely hand-drawn charm, and the animations are smooth. Music is decent, but not stellar, and matches the mood when it needs to.
Characters are lovable, even the enemies. Every character is fully voiced and animated, but text is provided if you'd rather skip past long dialogue sequences. Cutscenes have a certain charm to them as well.
Story was a good length, too. Not too long and drawn-out, not too short. Playing through and collecting everything felt like the right amount of time, and I was never bored.
Quick disclaimer: Every character is some sort of animal-human hybrid (read: furry). Might bother some people.
TL;DR: Buy it if you like hack-n-slash RPG's with a great storyline.

TL;DR: LiEat is a fun and charming game that is more than worth 3 dollars despite not being gameplay heavy and harboring 3 episodic chapters.
I purchased this game looking to kill time for under six dollars and was returned with much more than I was expecting.  I believe that LiEat is a very easily enjoyable game for those who don't mind playing something light on gameplay.
The game is split into three chapters that each follow a pattern of the main characters, Efi and Leo arriving at a town, the player meets and interact with the other characters, a mysterious event occurs, the police captains, Brett and Neil, show up and investigate the mystery alongside Efi and Leo and they catch the culprit who is one of the previously introduced characters.  A heartwarming ending follows if the player chooses to achieve the good ending of each chapter. Each chapter takes 1-2 hours to get through.
The gameplay tends to be on the lighter side as it is almost impossible to die unless you are trying to achieve that.  Until the last chapter, you are already given all the healing materials needed and it is possible to find extra. You will be fighting small monsters called little lies throughout the duration of the game and leveling up, gainging strength and skills to fight with until you reach the end of the chapter which results in a boss fight.  From these fights you usually take very little damage until the boss fight and it is very easy to heal.  In fact, it is possible to pick up special, stronger, weapons if you look for them within the game which makes fights pretty easy.  The characters walk at a nice pace and the controls are easy to figure out but i would have prefered if there was a screen that listed the controls, especially since the title of the game window was left untranslated from Japanese and as a result many don't know that F4 will convert the screen to take up the desktop.
Despite the lightness of the gameplay (if light gameplay does not suit your tastes), and the episodic nature of the chapters this game boasts an incredible amount of charm and likeability that is unshakeable to me.  Leo and Efina are fun and interesting characters which create nice foils to one another.  Leo's cunning and mysterious past as well as Efina's innocence and many other childlike qualities  are fun to watch on screen and make interacting with other characters twice as enjoyable.  Though, the characters introduced each chapter tend to be likeable by just themselves. The animated cutscenes and music look and sound especially nice adding just another reason to like this game.
LiEat is definety worth your 3 dollars and is a charming and enjoyable to pick up at anytime.

Interesting puzzle game.
Unlike Sokoban, which is a block-pushing game... here, you push atoms which can form bonds when two atoms are adjacent to each other, with an objective to form a single coherent molecule involving all the atoms (or, in some levels, multiple molecules).  Various puzzles have noble gasses (which don't bond with anything else), locations on the grid which break bonds, locations which strengthen bonds (double-bonding and triple-bonding, for instance), and locations which bend your molecules.
Later levels can be very, very non-obvious.

This game was developed back in 2013 by Herrero Games, a videogame company based in Cantabria, Spain. They have made other games, but it would seem that this is their first and flag game. This review is for the Steam version, it is available on Wii-U and has recently become available for mobile devices (Play Store and iTunes entries verified).
In this game, JOB -actually, it is pronounced “hob” in Spanish- is a leprechaun, which is set to find, rescue, free -whatever- his “Friend” (note the “”) Erin. I think that this could be a relatable character and that although you will perhaps not spend much time playing with him, you would perhaps be able to set him apart from other non-relatable platformer characters.
The game itself was pretty fine for this kind of platformer. One big mistake is that it takes a little while to figure out somethings, which are perhaps not as self-evident for as one could hope for. Once you discover that there is movement and two main keys (jump and attack) it is pretty simple, but the interaction with the surroundings give it something additional. Basically, to pass a level one must collect all leaves in it. After 10 or so stages there was a boss encounter which I was really hoping for at that point. I did not make it very far into the second “world” in around 45m, but the game was delivering and I was not having a particular great “platformy” day. The music loop of the first level is fine, but a bit tiring, but after the first boss the music changes. Overall, I think this game is finished in around 2 hours.
Levels are well made, entertaining and after a little while you pick up on the way the game is supposed to be functioning.
There is no controller support. As I just mentioned in a review before, I find it really difficult to understand why platformer styled indie games are not supporting the use of a controller. This could have worked great on my NES styled controller, and it would have added so much to the game. Come on platformer game developers, add controller support to your games!
No, it is not the best indie retro-styled platformer. Still, if you are in for an hour or two of platformer action with an 8bit inspired leprechaun, it is the way to go. For the price of 0.99 (at the time of review) I think it is a fair deal.

The similarities between this game and another, very popular digital CCG, are undeniable. HOWEVER, there's no shortage of unique mechanics and it absolutely stands as its own game. People need to realize that when a game in an otherwise unpopular video game genre becomes a massive success, it DEFINES that genre. Other developers would be unwise and stubborn not to form a template based on said game. That being said, it brings it's own flavor to the mix and I enjoy it much more than other digital CCG's that I've played in the past.
The business model is a little more fair than the common system, but comprarable. I suggest playing a few game against the computer (practice mode) and some casual games against other players and then see how it feels. If you like it, the best route is to invest in the 19.99 captains pack. You support the devs and give yourself a much needed boost in your card collection. It gives you some crafting material to play with, too. You don't HAVE to do this, as the ranked matches are balanced very well for a new game.
TLDR; check it out. Don't get too turned off by it's similarities to other games. Appreciate it for what it is and you may find your new CCG. It won't be for everyone but it's FTP so if you're looking for a new card game fix, this is your best bet.

: Brace Yourself Games
: Brace Yourself Games, Klei Entertainment
==========
Crypt of the Necrodancer is a rhythm rogue-like dungeon crawler. You navigate your character through randomly generated dungeons divided into zones, while avoiding traps, defeating enemies, and collecting treasure, weapons, and armor. The game encourages you to move to the beat of the tracks played in each zone, offering you a coin multiplayer as long as you stick to moving with the beat. The longer you stay in rhythm with the beat, the higher your multiplayer goes. The multiplier affects how many coins you earn from defeating enemies, as well as providing boosts to some of the items you find. So it's really in your best interests to try and keep a good rhythm going as you explore!
==========
As said above, you move your character in-time with the beat of the song being played on each floor. The starter character, Cadence, has the perk of having an assistive tool at the bottom of the screen, which helps you to time your button presses with the beat. The game is divided into 4 zones, each consisting of a few floors and a boss floor. Each floor has a different tune playing, which in turn has a different beat that allows you to move at a certain pace. Some floors have a slower beat, some have a faster beat. Also important to note are how monsters move with the beat. Certain monster types have specific patterns, and learning these patterns will help you greatly in navigating the dungeon safely. Some move every beat, some move every other beat. If you happen to move onto a square at the same time as a monster, you take damage, which further emphasizes how important it is to learn monster movements.
You are also able to utilize several tools, including a shovel, bombs, and various charms that have different effects. Also scattered about are shrines, which offer several different effects depending on it's type. Some are positive effects, while others are negative. Smart use of every tool at your disposal is crucial to survival. One tool I really like to utilize are bombs, as they have several exploratory and combat uses. The shovel is used to dig through walls, which can lead to lots of hidden rooms with secret items! Some walls cannot be dug if your shovel isn't good enough, and there are several tiers of shovels, as well as weapons and armor. Gold, Blood, Titanium, and Obsidian are a few examples, each providing different modifiers for the items.
The game also features a level editor, with which you can create and upload your own dungeons to the Steam Workshop for others to play and enjoy. The only downside is that you need to clear Zone 4 with a character to unlock it initially. It's also a bit odd in that it's very difficult to use until you learn how to navigate the menus and how to place items. Despite this, it's a powerful tool that works. One thing I'd like for them to add in the level editor is the ability to have specific enemies drop specific items when defeated...such as keys!
==========
Boasting a pixel art style, everything is surprisingly detailed. The sprites are amazingly rich and colorful, and often times you are able to tell where monsters will move and what they are about to do, as well as spot secrets hidden in the walls...like the glinting tip of a diamond in a stone pillar! Such small details are what make this game great. Armor also shows up on your character, so it's easy to tell what they are wearing. Some weapons have battle animations, such as the whips, but most you don't actually see the weapon. Instead, you see a sort of "slash" animation depending on the weapon type. Needless to say, these are minor graphical grievances that are more than made up for by the rest of the game's details. Traps are easy to spot, and items laying around are easily identified as well.
==========
The music of this game is where the game shines. Catchy tunes accompany every zone and floor, offering a variety of beats and toe-tapping goodness. Danny Baranowsky is the one responsible for most of the songs in the game, and he has done a fantastic job in really giving this game life. Sound effects are basic and they work, signalling damage, movement, and enemy presence. There really isn't much to say here, other than the soundtarck is amazing. You can check it out or buy it
. It's 100% worth a listen, and even a buy if you like it! There is even an extended soundtrack available for you to further customize each zone. The game also allows you to use your own MP3's in-game for endless fun.
==========
This isn't really a very-demanding game, so most people should have no issues running it. If you have any doubts, make sure to check the minimum and recommended specs for the game on the Store Page. During my playtime I did not run into any bugs or glitches. I expected to run into at least 1 bug during my several playthroughs, but surprisingly not a single one appeared. Bravo! There are options for several resolutions, as well as Windowed and Fullscreen modes.
==========
Crypt of the Necrodancer is a worthy additional to the library of anyone who is a fan of rogue-likes, music-based games, dungeons crawlers, or people who just love fun unique games. There hasn't been a game like this before, so it's worth diving into if you are looking for a new experience.

I'm a huge Civ fan, but have also enjoyed Stardock's galactic take on the whole genre.  I've always liked Galactic Civ, but for some reason, they just really nail it with III.  I've found if very enjoyable with a lot of replayability and feel like I'm engaged enough to finish an immense game.
I like the fact, also, that the Civs themselves are a little more believable.  In the past in most Civ games, if you get too big, your enemies are afraid to attack you and you ultimately steamroll them.  In GalCiv III, you get too big and they realize they have no choice but to attack you, just to survive.  I find that refreshing and getting tagged by several weaker enemies at the same time has introduced some interesting strategy changes to my game.
I do wish, however, that they would add a little more meat the the battle engines.  I'm good with the cut scene battles, which are kind of fun to watch, especially if you have a large fleet.  But I'd like to see something in the line of experience or veteran rewards for a vessel that has seen a lot of action. That seems to really be the only thing I find missing in the game.
Overall, solid game. Very enjoyable.

Earthlock is a western take on the classic jRPG formula and should be instantly familiar to anyone who enjoys that kind of game. Besides its own charming cast of characters and beautiful world, it has a number of mechanics that set it appart from the rest:
Character progression:
Characters level up, but unlock skills and talents on a talent board - different talents are collected or crafted, then sloted on the board as the player earns more slots. To use a slot, a character has to have an available point to spend, a talent to place in it, and must have a talent in one of the adjacent slots. There are different types of slots - some reserved for the character's abilities, some for stat boosts, others for passive abilities such as damage reduction, extra damage or the ability to ressurect once per fight.
Stances:
In combat each character has two stances tehy can switch between. Thus Amon, the main hero, can either be a dagger wielding rogue, able to cloack himself, mug and steal from opponents and slice and dice them, or he can grab his trusty gun and shoot opponents with ammo harvested from his garden (yes, you grow your own ammunition in a garden).
Bond:
In your party of up to 4 characters, you can pair up sets of characters and their bond will increase, giving them unique boosts whenever these specific two are paired up. It adds another layer to party selection, as you will not only look at what four characters to take along, but also how better to split them into two pairs to gain the bonuses you need in a given situation.
On top of that, each pair shares the typical "limit break" style bar used to power specials. So once you can trigger a special, you still have to choose which of the two characters' ability will be more useful.
Overall, it is a fun, beautiful little game. It is not the longest, it is not the most challenging, but if you give it a chance, it can offer you fun with some nifty character systems, enjoyable gameplay and some tough boss fights.

This game is clearly made with effort. The art assets, especially the environments, are wonderful, the characters each have some interesting mechanic to play around with, and the monster designs are cool. It harkens back to slightly older JRPGs with its use of classic tropes and terribly named inconsequential objects. The mechanics for the battle system are interesting, and at times quite fun.
However, this game has so many problems, I cannot in good faith reccomend it.
The writing is entirely devoid of voice. Each character sounds like the same person's speech, with a few quirks hastily pasted onto them. What could be relevant and relatable character designs are ruined by one-dimensional exposition lines and a lack of reactive dialogue. The tutorial messages placed into character dialogue are arguably worse, taking what could be an opportunity for cheeky 4th wall breaking, and removing all flavor.
The navigation is inconsistent at best. In most places, the character models are prone to get stuck on corners of walls and whatnot. This is far from a major gripe, but it's important, as walking is a good portion of what you do in this game, and it determines the position you're in at the start of a fight.
[Edit: One of the major gripes I had with the walking, at the time of 5/17, has been fixed. The character models have not fallen through the floor and cost me progress yet.]
The progression could be interesting, but it takes a good deal of grinding the thief's Steal ability on different enemies to craft objects needed to use the talent points you have gained, and oft creates spaces within the game where the player is underpowered and overleveled when facing enemies, and leads to a less-than-smooth leveling experience.
I found the puzzles quite boring. Not very good by any stretch. Many of them will require that your have a single character selected, something the game only ever mentions once, almost at the very start of the game. Some will require you run into stray geometry until your character finds a hidden passage, and all of them require repeated use of a quite awful context-sensitive interact button.
All of that combined with the fact that the game has a number of edge-case bugs which can cause save corruption and crashes. [Edit: Some of which have been fixed]
This is not a very good game.
I hope that the Developers can learn from the mistakes they made with this game and move on to something greater, because everything in this game reeks of untapped, unpolished potential.

Kind of like hearthstone but hate RNGesus shenanigans and like some more depth? Oh, and don't mind a lack of polish (yet) and a spacey theme? Try Star Crusade! You'll probably enjoy it.
Read a few other reviews and thought: is this hearthstone in space? Well, yes, -but- with a few very important differences that make it a -lot- more enjoyable for me. Here's what different apart from the obvious theme:
- Your "heroes" can equip 3 different modules that in essence are hero powers. These powers use either your basic resource (supply) or energy, which is gained by attacking your opponent and killing his units. These things add a layer of depth on the "hearthstone" strategy you're used to.
- RNGesus plays nicenice! I really hate, Hate, HATE playing a flawless game of hearthstone and get absolutely destroyed because of 1 redonkulous yogg-saron, a knife juggler + unleash madness, a doomsayer pilot or whatever else Blizz seems to find great game design. I like to win or lose a game in a ccg (mostly) because of my plays (and deck of course). If you like that too, Star Crusade is way better in that respect. There are a few cards that do (semi-)random damage or summon a random unit but nothing that breaks the game.
- the draft mode is slightly more interesting and decently more rewarding. You you start off with 3 fleets (ie. max losses) on a map with planets you need to "liberate" which are connected via warp lanes or somesuch. Some planets offer bigger rewards and are harder to liberate, with planets taking 3 wins to liberate being the hardest, -but- those also offer you an extra fleet. All in all it doesn't make a -lot- of different which route you choose, but it's kind of fun nonetheless.
Breaking even in draft mode (arena) is fairly hard. Let alone make a profit. It seems in Star Crusade it's a bit more forgiving (after tweaks in the last few months by the devs). Get just 2 wins and you're break-even-ish. You'll still get wrecked if you have no idea what you're doing, but seems way more viable for the decent/good player out there.
- The devs! They listen to feedback, aren't afraid to balance, tweak and improve and seems to be rather thankful for our comments and criticisms.
- The UI needs work and the overall game could use polish. For instance: when a player uses a "hero power" that deaks 2 damage a target at the end of his
turn, there really is no indicator on that unit that shows you attention needs to be paid. If you did not see your opponent target that unit or if you didn't look at the battle log you have no way of knowing that unit is in trouble. There's lots more small stuff like that.
- Less cards. There's less than half the amount of cards hearthstone currently has. HS is also 2.5 years older. Shouldn't stop you from trying out this game though. The more people enjoy this, the faster it'll grow. Probably :)
- Less players. Like: a few hundred online at a time. Only one way to fix this: install the game :D
Right now finding a game doesn't take long at all. You -do- get the same opponent a decent amount of the time though.
Like a CCG somewhat more complex and less rng-focused than hearthstone? Don't mind or even like a spacey/sci-fi theme? Don't mind a somewhat worse UI and polish? Give Star Crusade a try!

There's no point in playing this over Orcs Must Die! 2. Setting aside all the bugs and random errors, even when OMDU works it fails to live up to to its namesake. It's the game you love stripped down and then partially sold back to you through infinite microtransactions. But no matter how much you spend, it will never be as good as the game it's following up.
One of the biggest missteps here is that they've removed the weapon system entirely, so you're now stuck using the same boring attacks for the entirety of the game because you can never move to a different weapon. Like Maximilian but don't like the crossbow? Tough. Unlike in OMD2, where you could use any weapon in the game with either character, each character has a baked-on weapon that never changes. In the place of the weapon system from the previous game, they have added multiple heroes into the game that are locked behind paywalls. Max and Gabriella, the main characters of the franchise, have also been stripped of their movement abilities (double jump and hover). Presumably this is meant to push us towards the new heroes, unlocking them by purchasing in-game currency.
Trap customization has also moved backwards in big ways. In OMD2, you upgraded traps using skulls to add new features or change how they worked in tangible ways. Now you're just grinding for hours to get enough RNG loot boxes to level up a trap and get...a +8% damage modifier. There is no real sense of accomplishment or progress. Everything is tediously incremental.
Visually, the game looks great. The character and world design are stellar. The graphics are nice, and one of the only improvements over the previous game. The gameplay is still smooth, and the actual act of killing orcs is enjoyable enough. But the features that previously made this core gameplay meaningful and rewarding are gone. They've been replaced by a P2W microtransaction scheme that dogs every single aspect of the experience and pulls the whole thing down.
I wish I could recommend this. Maybe someday we'll get a real sequel, but until then I can only recommend playing more Orcs Must Die! 2.

Duck Game is a side-on pixel art local and online multiplayer shooter where you can win by preaching to opponents. Duck Game has a vast arsenal of lethal and non-lethal weapons ranging from fire extinguishers to bazookas to suicide pistols, not to mention any guns you mod in. Duck Game has a variety of pre-built maps that are well designed and enjoyable to play and learn, there is also the ability to turn on random maps that are procedurally generated, but these can end up with unfair spawns and can get rather boring. There is also a singleplayer mode that is based around challenges using a certain mechanic from the game, these can be fun and frustrating but also sometimes a bit lacklustre and not a reason to buy the game. By completing these challenges you get points than can be used to unlock modifiers and hats from the shop. After a while the maps, hats and weapons in the game can get boring and lack the variety they originally had, this is where the workshop comes in. The workshop for this game is consistently active with new hats, weapons and maps being added daily so you can keep your game fresh every time you play. You can also add to the workshop by using the built-in map editor, it can be a bit fiddly but is overall OK.
Duck Game is a fun and fast paced action game that is great for a group of friends to play either on the couch or over the internet. It is very well made but can get boring after a while though it can be refreshed easily with the wide range of high quality and easy to access content on the workshop. It is only majorly let down by the singleplayer aspect of it and that isn't even too bad. Overall I would highly recommend Duck Game to you if you are looking for a game to play with 3 or 4 friends, but if your looking for a great singleplayer experience you won't find it here.

I enjoyed the witcher 2 quite thoroughly. It has an excellent, mature storyline that takes some thought to understand properly, expecially the relationship between the northern kingdoms and it's rulers. The side quests are fairly interesting too, if a bit poorly directed at times and througout the game is an excellent morally grey set of decisions to make. The game looks georgeous on maximum settings and is very well optimised for pc, even though some of the controls are clearly designed with gamepad in mind. The one major gripe i have with the game is the combat system. The potions and oils and other equipment management are well conceived and the basic concepts of the combat also have great potential, however it required more polish. The full combar rebalance mod made by an employee of CD Project RED helped iron out a few issues, however it still suffered from awful hit detection that caused attacts that should have at missed by more than a metre to cause deaths that feel cheap and frankly make the game a frustration. This is not difficult combat like dark souls that punishes the player for their mistakes, its one that punishes the player for not recognising that if you don't roll at least several metres away from an attack, it will somehow hit you magically and kill you. It simply feels like the game is cheating at these points and it is hard to continue playing. When you do get hit, you barely notice, there's no sound of impact, no screen indication, Geralt doesn't even flinch. The health bar just drops with every strike and you end up seeing the same boring death animation over and over again. Its almost like the developers weren't counting on players being hit at all and just said, "Eh, just lower the health variable if anyhthing touches (or in some cases doesn't) the player". This is not responsive and it slowly becomes infuriating. Don't misunderstand, the combat has it's moments and can sometimes feel really good, but the simple fact is that the majority of deaths feel cheap, as you feel that it is the games fault, not yours. You simply need to dance around this airy combat to make the most of it. Even so, the game is great. It has so much depth in characters and in customisation that it feels like a living, breathing world. It also has lots of replay value, with 16 different endings based on choices througout the game and branching paths that change the whole quest structure from the first chapter. But is it the rpg of the decade as some people profess, or is it even my game of the year (2011)? The simple answer is no.

If you've played Journey on ps3 and loved it; you definitely will love ABZU.  The similarities between Journey and ABZU are noticeable.  The same vibrant colors and even the same composer, Austin Wintory. The relationship between you and the environment around you is satisfying to watch.  Firstly, the game takes place underwater whilst Journey took place on a desert.  However, I need to commend that the level of detail and environment interaction is much greater in ABZU than it was in Journey.  Don't get me wrong, I loved Journey.  I enjoyed roaming through that vast empty desert.  But the amount of work the creators of ABZU put in was overwhelming.  The variety of fish, sharks, eels, coral, and much more; it was all pleasing to the eye.  Not only that, but each animal having their own interation with the player is amazing too.
If I could give one piece of advice is that you should take your time playing this game.  Enjoy exploring, take a few minutes to look at everything.  Meditate. Yes, meditate. The game gives you that option when you find of the statues spread across the levels.  But so far,  I've been reading reviews on how they managed to complete the game in a short amount of time and how it's not worth your money.  And I think they got it all wrong.  This game isn't about getting from point A to point B, you need to take your time and be in the moment.  You don't pay 15 bucks to an art mueseum just to see how fast you can get to the exit.  No, you look at the art in between and enjoy it.

OK, this is actually the first time I would write a review on Steam, so it may not be perfect, but I tried at least.
Garry's Mod, the game that has shaped my childhood.
No, really. GMOD is what I can call possibly one of the best Sandbox games I've ever played. I remember discovering GMOD thanks to popular animators, and one of those 2009 animations. The visuals on this game is what made me scrounge a few pennies for this game, available right here, right now. The game is simply what I like to call a sandbox version of Half-Life 2 (UPDATE: I bought HL2 for a good deal and I feel satisfied that there's so many maps to begin with) with a few mods. The first time you boot up the game, you will be greeted with a picture slideshow showing all of the amazing renders made by community users, which actually gives you lots of ideas of what you can do in this. You can build an automated rocket chair, you can build a floating car from the future, you can build a beautiful landscape, based on your style. The sky's the only limit here. (also your computer if it can handle all of the graphically intense processes)
The first time I started playing GMOD, you're greeted with two maps, the classical gm_construct, or the Flattywood branded district of gm_flatgrass. Being the good old me I was, I decided to go for gm_construct because I thought it looked nice. I was blown away instantly by all of the graphics, because I thought the map looked beautiful. After walking around, I began to wonder: "How can I add items, and how can I play around with them?" Little old me decided to mash the keyboard until I found random menus started popping up, I finally found the Spawn Menu, a man's dream of sandboxing. I interacted with a lot of stuff, you can open things, you can close things, you can break 'em, you can build 'em. You can even grab yourself a bottle of root beer and break it, and start to party. It was the best.
During my great adventure in Garry's Mod I found out that this game had little "addons" you could subscribe to and that would implement tons of good stuff, like more weapons, more props, more maps, or even an automated GUI so you could do anything. I felt excited that I could add myself tons and tons of Ferraris and so many rich cars. (thanks SCars, you're the best!) There was just one problem, I couldn't subscribe to all of the addons easily, for some "weird" reasons. I resorted to using other methods of downloading Workshop items. I stuffed everything I wanted in the game, and boy did I get surprised eventually. Heck, when I was bored, I'd usually boot up GMOD and spawn in some NPCs, only to kill them to relieve my inner stress. It was basically fun at that point.
Multiplayer is something I wouldn't like, as you can see. There are so many servers out there that shaped the game so much. You could download various game modes, and play with friends and family. However, it seemed that in a lot of servers I play in, most of them lag, most of them are crappy, or just plain empty. I began to wonder why, until I realized that I was playing the game in an old PC, and mostly due to having slow internet speeds, topping off at a whopping 512kbps. I wouldn't recommend this game if you are a "budget" PC user that is hoping to play with friends, but finds out you actually can't, because it "times you out" randomly while you're connecting, or it is downloading a ton of crap that you don't like. However, this does not mean I would discard the multiplayer feature at all, there are some good servers out there, and maybe you can just find the one you like the most at just the blink of an eye, just look hard enough, I know you will find it.
The community is...OK... in some cases. You see, there are some fandoms out there that just go against the game, or others, just make tons of bad game content. Either I see some random posts saying "how can i use the physgun?" or "how do i spawn new npcs?", it just freaks me out. However, the community is very nice and helpful, and can guide you through some tips and tricks to help you get started playing the game. However, I would stand against the forums, since sometimes, they can become overflooded, or just plain full of posts that doesn't interest you. Like I said, that doesn't mean I would discard the forums. Forums are just a type of social media, but instead of regular conversations, you get helpful answers, and good people just waiting for you to hop on in their server and play together. Just don't make sure to go far, if you know what I mean.
And my final thoughts, this game is worth your 10 bucks, and it is multiplatformed, which means you can play in Windows, macOS, and a few popular Linux distros out there. I would give this game a 8.5/10 as a result. This game is so good in any way possible, build anything, destroy anything, have a party, you name it. All I can say is, thank you Garry Newman for making this beautiful sandbox, and I will look forward to S&box.

If I could describe Earthlock in a single sentence it would be something along the lines of this: A simple, unpretentious rpg heavily inspired by NES/SNES jrpgs. The game has numerous flaws, but if you temper your expectations you'll be taken on a rather enjoyable journey.
I'll begin with the game's strengths. The music is absolutely brilliant. Almost every track fit right in and strengthened the atmosphere of the entire game. The dynamic music, how the overworld track would go right into the combat version of a song then seamlessly right back out once combat ended, was a great touch.
The story is simple. This is actually a boon to the game as it keeps the focus where it needs to be. The characters all have their reason for going on the journey, and it's never hard to follow.
The world is pleasant to look at. Visual design for most places ranges from 7/10 to 10/10. I do not know if it was intended, but the stark contrast in appearance between the ancient technology and the modern, rediscovered/reinvented technology was pleasing. The world felt as fresh and unique as it needed to be. In addition there are lots of little bits of lore scattered around for those who wish to look. Even the character Gnart, a scribe of sorts, keeps a little journal of the adventure one can read at any time. You can tell they cared enough to flesh out their world beyond what the story required.
There are many great systems similar to those used in other rpgs. There are no random encounters, all enemies being visible on all maps. One can choose to engage a large group or lure them off one at a time. There are benefits to both approaches. Obviously fighting fewer enemies at a time will make life easier, but fighting more builds a large experience multiplier skyrocketing levels much faster. It's a great risk vs reward system. Although the difficulty spikes make it near manditory to fight large groups when you can or else you may have to go back to grind levels later.
You have a party of 4 out of possible 6 characters. Each character can be 'paired' to any other and they work together. They gain passive bonuses based on their bond level, which can change up how they play. Furthermore every character has two seperate stance which give them multiple different abilities. You can have the character Amon play as a rogue/thief, or as a ranged heavy hitter.
Instead of physical equipment, each character has a large talent board. On the talent board you can put stat cards, ability cards, and perk cards. This further changes the way characters can play, though each one is locked into a general role. The mages are never going to be as effective fighters as the characters made for it, but they can be made somewhat passable if one chooses.
The use of teleport and saving statues is nice. They're well placed so one is never far from being able to save or teleport back to a town, so the lack of being able to save anywhere was not noticed at all.
The gardening is a cute addition. I mean that both literal and sarcastically. It's not required except to craft healing potions, or if you plan on turning either of the two character with ranged weaponry into ranged specialists. It is the only reliable way to gain potions or ammunition, and can be quite time consuming. Perhaps being able to purchase second best ammunition and potions from shops would alleviate the frustration I had with the game design behind it. Using it to craft the best items would give incentive, while giving the second best items to shops would have made it 100% skippable by those not wanting to touch it.
The enemy visual design is a little hit and miss. In general I like it, even though there's not a wide variety of enemies so some models are simple retextures. I adored the old enemies from the ancient ruins.
Now the bad. Like I said the flaws are numerous but most are relatively minor, considering the small team and inexperience behind the people involved. Some minor spoilers about characters lie below, but nothing pertinent to the story.
The scope felt a little bit too big for the story. There wasn't a whole lot of character interaction, and I could feel any footing of investment I had in a few of the characters slip as time went on. Gnart and Amon end up being the most interesting of all the characters. That's not to say the others couldn't potentially be, but there is so little ever mentioned of them that it's easy to forget that they are more than cardboard cutouts holding weapons. Olia, a mysterious spear wielding warrior/scholar, obviously has an interesting backstory that is constantly hinted at, but never properly told. Taika is an odd and special breed of magic dog, but we're never told what makes them special. PAT is an ancient robot from the pre-magic-apocalypse, but he tells almost nothing of interest before that pre-magic-apocalypse. I think Ive is my least favorite character, but that may be because of her introduction to the game and lack of consequences for a particular action she commits rather than her demeanor. The game shares a lot of backstory on Amon and Gnart, on the other hand. While it serves to flesh them out a lot and is wonderful in and of itself. It also highlights just how little the game tells us of the others. In short, I think the characters have character, but the lack of interaction makes one easily forget.
The dialogue is also rather simple and a little strange at times. Some of it could be due to translation, but it never bothered me personally.
In addition I wish there was just more interaction between all the characters. They all had their various reasons for being dragged into this adventure, but the party banter felt very lacking. Maybe an easy solution to this could have been various interactions on the Isle of Plumpet (your home base more or less) depending on how far into the story you are. Interactions with things leading the chosen leader of your party to comment with their thoughts or feelings.
The fights, or rather the game difficulty, seemed very spotty. You're driven in a linear fashion through the world, or else this wouldn't be much of an issue. However more than a few times you'll enter an area or find a new boss, and there is no way forward except to go back and grind out a level or two. Maybe it was because sometimes I preferred to not fight large groups of enemies so I became underleveled, but even so it was an annoyance. In addition, the AI seems really bad. For example, it will bring a character to the brink of death and then focus on another before actually finishing said character.
Animations are a little clunky and character models felt stiff. In contract to the music work, the sound design for everything else was mediocre.
This is very spoilerific for the ending, so reader be warned. I'm wondering how the party managed to escape the memory of Maato after destroing the Valvur'ed Ichabo. To my knowledge there was no proper way to leave once you entered. Them just magically pooping out after winning the fight seemed very hamfisted. I can forgive everything else in the game, but that was one thing I felt really needed an explanation. Perhaps this is due to the general feeling of the scope of the game being slightly larger than what the devs could feasably pull off, which I feel is the reason for a lot of other story/character interaction related things. But still, this if anything needed some sort of explanation.
In short, the story is nothing spectacular but passable and unpretentious. The game systems are hit and miss, but with a lot of novel things thrown in. The world and music are delightful. I paid around 27 euros for this game. I'd say it's at best a  15 euro title, for those that like this sort of game. Although I feel no regrets paying the amount I did and am glad the money went to this studio. There was real talent and real love fueling this game. Despite the pockmarks and cracks, I found it to be a great experience.

Remember that awesome moment in Journey, where you're floating around in the liquid-sand and the carpet-whale comes out, and you ride it and you just don't want to leave that room? Well that's kind of what ABZU is... a whole lot of THAT.
LIke Journey, this game is atmospherically beautiful. A lot of the things you loved about Journey are back: large explorable spaces, ruins of a cyclopean culture, a narrative on the hubris of technology delivered via diagetic props, fragments of a lost religion, a gorgeous soundtrack by Austin Wintory.
Perhaps it's the similarities to Journey that make the differences disapointing. It might be an unfair comparision but I missed meeting random strangers, ABZU being a much more solitary experience.  The mechanism of replayability as part of the overall narrative of reincarnation in Journey was a unique meta element that required a very short game to work. ABZU is just a short linear story. And perhaps it's a nit-pick but whereas collecting runes in Journey gave you immediate visual and gameplay rewards (those wonderful scarves and extended flight) shells seem merely to give you trophy bragging rights outside of the game,
Minor dispointments aside, tt's an accomplishment for sure. It is clearly the spiritual descendant of it's imediate predecessors (Flower and Journey) but also invokes the wonder and awe of ICO and Shadow of the Colossus. This is art.

I enjoyed the witcher 2 quite thoroughly. It has an excellent, mature storyline that takes some thought to understand properly, expecially the relationship between the northern kingdoms and it's rulers. The side quests are fairly interesting too, if a bit poorly directed at times and througout the game is an excellent morally grey set of decisions to make. The game looks georgeous on maximum settings and is very well optimised for pc, even though some of the controls are clearly designed with gamepad in mind. The one major gripe i have with the game is the combat system. The potions and oils and other equipment management are well conceived and the basic concepts of the combat also have great potential, however it required more polish. The full combar rebalance mod made by an employee of CD Project RED helped iron out a few issues, however it still suffered from awful hit detection that caused attacts that should have at missed by more than a metre to cause deaths that feel cheap and frankly make the game a frustration. This is not difficult combat like dark souls that punishes the player for their mistakes, its one that punishes the player for not recognising that if you don't roll at least several metres away from an attack, it will somehow hit you magically and kill you. It simply feels like the game is cheating at these points and it is hard to continue playing. When you do get hit, you barely notice, there's no sound of impact, no screen indication, Geralt doesn't even flinch. The health bar just drops with every strike and you end up seeing the same boring death animation over and over again. Its almost like the developers weren't counting on players being hit at all and just said, "Eh, just lower the health variable if anyhthing touches (or in some cases doesn't) the player". This is not responsive and it slowly becomes infuriating. Don't misunderstand, the combat has it's moments and can sometimes feel really good, but the simple fact is that the majority of deaths feel cheap, as you feel that it is the games fault, not yours. You simply need to dance around this airy combat to make the most of it. Even so, the game is great. It has so much depth in characters and in customisation that it feels like a living, breathing world. It also has lots of replay value, with 16 different endings based on choices througout the game and branching paths that change the whole quest structure from the first chapter. But is it the rpg of the decade as some people profess, or is it even my game of the year (2011)? The simple answer is no.

Get five attribute points to distribute per level up - check.  Get a skill point to apply to warrior skill, mage skill or ranged weapon skill - check.   Have a pet - check.  Can transform pet - check.  Use fish to transform pet - check.

The popularly accepted theory that Jazz stemmed from a simple combination of African rhythms and European harmony is in need of a little revision. Both African and European rhythms were employed. African music supplied the strong underlying beat (absent in most European music), the use of polyrhythms, and the idea of playing the melody separate from or above the beat. European music provided formal dance rhythms. Combined, these rhythms give Jazz its' characteristic swing. Likewise, the harmonies and musical ideas of both continents are present, the blue notes derived from the pentatonic scale, "call and response" and unconventional instrumental timbres of African music together with "conventional" harmonies and, most important, the formal structure of European music. The multiplicity of ethnic, cultural and musical conditions needed to spawn Jazz was thus unique to the United States, and specifically to New Orleans. The necessary philosophical impetus for Jazz, i.e. , democracy and freedom of individual expression supported by group interaction, are also American institutions.

You only know how many atoms can be joined to each atom (by the number of little circles swirling about it). As the game progresses you get additional options like the ability to cut links using cutting intersections, but sometimes this hinders more than helps.  Overall an impressive and very well thought out game.  Highly recommended.

I wrote this a couple of years ago. While it was true at the time, there is no reason to buy this game. Instead check out its sequel: The Binding Of Isaac: Rebirth. In comparison, this game is horse♥♥♥♥♥♥
By far the best value for money on Steam, The Binding of Isaac guides you through layers of depth and despair. The main story is that the child, Isaac, must flee through the randomly generated levels of his own basement to escape his homicidal mother. The rooms are filled with terrifying monsters and Isaac must fend them off by shedding his own tears. At the end of each floor, there is a boss room and there are many different kinds of optional rooms that will provide Isaac with powerful bonuses or fearful punishments.
The game is fiendishly difficult, with a health meter shown as a few precious hearts. Once you die, you have died for good and you’ll have to start afresh. The game has about 200 items that change the stats of the player as well as provide extra methods of survival and by the later floors Isaac should have a few helpful assets to help him achieve victory. It's sad the way that almost every decent digital CCG has gone down the crapper due to incompetent mismanagement, isn't it? Might & Magic: Duel of Champions was shut down because it was owned by Ubisoft (who literally cannot do ANYTHING right), Spellweaver just completely stopped development while waiting to complete a pointless tablet port, Duelyst sold out to Bandai-Namco who began milking it for all it was worth, Shadowverse succumbed to ever-more-insane Legendary card power creep with every expansion, the devs of Chronicles: Runescape Legends revealed that they actually didn't give a damn about their own game, Blizzard don't have a damn clue how to balance Hearthstone (as always), and now Star Crusade wound up its swing to hit a home run with the release of its first expansion and ended up knocking itself out with its own bat instead.
My previous (positive) review called this game "sci-fi Hearthstone but better", and that pretty much still stands. It's still a pretty blatant sci-fi rip-off of Hearthstone, only throwing aside the twin-millstones of dumbed-down, oversimplified gameplay and a reliance on insane, unrestrained RNG that make Hearthstone such a chore. Star Crusade gives you a lot more choice than Hearthstone does, with the module system allowing you to customise your hero powers, the Energy system giving some cards (such as the basic Sniper) more ways of using them, and the changes to deck construction (your deck can be from 25-40 cards rather than being fixed at 30, with you having the same starting life) gives you much more flexibility. There was almost NONE of the unrestrained RNG that turn HS games into cases of "your opponent gets insanely lucky and you instantly lose". So yeah, it was better than Hearthstone alright, despite its core elements being almost a direct copy.
The problem, however, came with the release of the first expansion, Shadow of the Council. Now one area where Hearthstone DESTROYED Star Crusade was in keeping the game shaken up and fresh with new cards. While the SC devs had added semi-regular infusions of new cards to the game (including a mini-expansion where they added an entire new faction, the Vraxxian pirates), they'd never released a complete expansion, something HS did about every 4-6 months or so. So they eventually announced Shadow of the Council and released it earlier this month (September 2017). Aaaaaaand... well, it was a catastrophe. The set itself was utterly perplexing- aside from a single new keyword (Link, which requires you to play  Council units that have it next to other units of certain tribes for bonus effects) there were no new themes to any of the new cards. In the core set each faction had their own themes, as is standard for this kind of CCG- Annuaki were Psychic Charge and neutralising enemy units, Hierarchy were Cyborgs and healing synergy, Hajir-Gog were weapons and self-damage etc etc, but none of the cards in SotC played to ANY kind of theme at all aside from the aforementioned Link mechanic. While SC had been more complicated than HS for a long time now, a lot of the new cards just ramped up the complexity to insane levels, to the point that it's hard to work out what exactly they even DO (a matter not helped by badly-translated card text, missing keywords, and other misprints). There were WAY too many hard-countering "magic bullet" cards designed to do a single specific thing, perhaps most gratuitously Kong's Blockade, a unit designed to counter Mobility (can attack the turn they're played) units, when the last balance patch before the expansion's release had just nerfed almost ALL Mobility units into the ground anyway (making several of them outright unplayable). Worst of all, there seemed to be an increasing number of "infinite RNG" cards added to the set, cards with a completely unpredictable range of possible results, sending the game blundering headfirst into the same problem it had previously neatly sidestepped. There were several good new cards, of course, but the set as a whole felt underwhelming and confusing.
The real nail in the coffin, however, was the change to the economy. Star Crusade had always had a VERY generous free-to-play system, especially compared to Hearthstone, with countless systems in place to give you free stuff- not only did you get 2 dailies worth a guaranteed 60 credits per day every day, there were also daily login bonuses, the Exploration system which gives you a random goodie (ranging from a puny 5 credits to a stack of 3 booster packs) every few hours, and Loot Crates that you could both get to drop and also open for free (you could pay to buy them and to open them immediately, but with you having about a 50% chance of getting one from every win and them opening on their within 4-24 hours depending on rank, why would you ever buy them?). This reached the point that the devs were apparently struggling to make enough money- so when the expansion came out, they applied the thumbscrews. Rather than doing something
like cutting back on the amount of free stuff they were giving away or providing more cosmetic things that can only be bought with Fracta (real-money currency), they instead doubled the credit price of core boosters, TRIPLED the credit price of expansion boosters, and if that wasn't enough,
And just to add insult to injury, they also massively increased the crafting price of most of the cards from the expansion to make it that much harder to acquire them without getting boosters. They could not say any more clearly "either buy Fracta or you don't get proper access to the expansion, your choice". It's
anti-F2P customer behavior, and made all the worse by the fact that they didn't NEED to do it. There were so many things they could have done instead to try and increase profits, but they went for the most openly malicious and shamelessly extortionate option. I was so incredibly angry when I discovered the restriction on buying expansion boosters that I nearly blew my top- and I wasn't even affected by it, as I'd preordered the prerelease 50-booster stack and had a nearly-complete collection of the expansion anyway. It's the principle of the thing- I won't tolerate this kind of anticonsumer rubbish from ANYONE. I felt dirty for having supported them. If I'd known they were making this change (because while they'd announced the booster and crafting price increase, they HADN'T told anyone about the artificial restriction on buying boosters with credits), then instead of preordering the expansion I would have
But hey, if the expansion is weak but you're not allowed to buy it properly without spending real money, I guess it all evens out, doesn't it? Bah.
Star Crusade is sick and dying and writhing in agony, but instead of giving it a dose of morphine, the developers shot it up with heroin instead. Barely anyone is playing the game any more and both the casual and ranked queues are populated almost exclusively by incredibly-stupid bots playing pathetically weak decks. Only about 1/10 of all the games I play are actually against a human. The expansion they'd been banking on managed to be simultaneously long-overdue and obviously rushed. And in the face of these problems, the developers decided the best solution was to put what free-to-play players they still had on the torture rack to try and juice money out of them? Absolutely mind-blowingly dumb. I don't believe Star Crusade is going to live even half a year longer, and frankly I struggle to sympathise.
ADDENDUM: As predicted, game's dead. Nobody is playing it and developers have gone silent. What a waste.
