It's not a deep review.
I am fairly disappointed by this game because even the tutorial area and your first "fights" are bland and uninteresting.
All doors locked, NPCs that don't say anything meaningfull, not a single drawer to open or anything somewhat hidden, basic combat as a flavourless turn-based thing that doesn't even try to hook you in, not a single line voice acted, not even the intro video...
Granted, it could be an amazing game after that, but you are switching out to a different character with no explanation, and not showing me anything remotely interesting (hell, not even a level up from the two tutorial fights).
I know that it says "inspired by the classic 3D RPGs of the late 90's" on the description, but it completely fails to show any of the "fresh take on turn based combat" when it presents it to you for the first time.
The soundtrack is not bad, at least.
If it had been a 5-10€ game, I could understand getting a rough game, but first impression is really important in games, you want to hook the player with "look at what we promise you during the game", presenting the world (we got a bit of lore at least), the main character(s) (not even sure who is the "main" at this point), and giving a glimpse of the cool things that the player can get later on (be it flashy skills, complex combos, or at least OP stats).
Not all games need all of those of course, but if you remove the games that purposedly set you up as "you are not a legendary hero, just a common person that will have to work hard to even just keep up", those that miss those are usually not purposedly choosing it for an actual effect (dramatic or otherwise) and more of an indication that game designers are still working on their basics (or lack of interest/funds for the project).
It does need to be noted that I am biased against the turn based battles (FF style), because it was playing with the hardware limitations at the time.
Nowadays, if I see a game use it, I go in thinking "it's lazy".
Granted, there are a lot of good games that use this, but if they don't seriously rework the combat, then those games shine for other reasons (graphics style, animations, characters, world, story, take your pick).
TL;DR: The start of this game is really sub par and doesn't give me any hope for an actual good game worth nearly 30€.

EARTHLOCK: Festival of Magic (EL:FoM) is a decent and a competent RPG, inspired by various JRPG released last decade. However unlike those JRPGs, EL:FoM lacks originality and depth. Underneath the passable graphics are layers of wasted potential and missed opportunity.
One thing I really dislike about EL:FoM is the absence of an equipment system. Players cannot equip nor buy any weapons/armours. This makes money widely unimportant to gather as the only thing you will be able to buy are mostly crafting materials. No, you do not get to craft any weapons/armours.
Battles are a breath of fresh air after a lot of Final Fantasy clones made using RPGMaker sold on Steam, though it might take some time getting used to it using the keyboards. It does have it's own weakness, however. For example, players are forced to remember the enemy weakness since you cannot view the details of an enemy in battle. To make matters worse is there's no indicator for exploiting enemy weakness, like in Persona 3/4 and Pokemon. This causes me personally question whether my attacks are effective or not.
Another disappointment are the story. The story is hardly interesting, with some overly complicated lore made probably by Kickstarter backers. The awkward dialogs does not make it any better, I'm afraid. Basically, your character found an ancient artifact and goes on an adventure (with a complete stranger) to find out what exactly does the artifact contain. After a few hours, I got bored with it and simply stopped caring about the whole plot.
The biggest turnoff for me about this game are the characters. I swear, sometimes I could not even remember the MC's name due to how incredibly uninteresting he is. The other characters are no better, especially the dark skinned and bright hair coloured woman. Some might call her character tough with a no nonsense attitute, I'd say she lacks empathy and can get obnoxious at times.
Final Verdict: Good enough RPG but clearly not enough meat on it's bones. Better buy it on sale.

Strikes a perfect balance between providing the backtracking and exploration the Metroidvania genre is known for and maintaing a constant sense of knowing what you need to do. Recommended to anyone with even a passing interest in the genre.

-Fantastic visual design

-Clear, yet interesting level and quest design

-Impressive enemy variety prevents using the same combat tactics for too long
-Voice acting for the main cast is very well done
Cons:
-Several minor characters are poorly acted. They're not awful, but there's a noticeable drop in quality between them and Dust/Fidget in conversation.
-Although the way you approach combat has to change throughout the game, mashing left click is generally all you need from the combo system, at least on Normal.
Other:
-It took me about 9 hours to finish Normal with around 70% completing. Going for 100% would probably take another 4 hours, and I'd expect higher difficulties to add to that significantly.
-Some of Fidget's abilities can utterly destroy the balance of the game if you go all out for them. This may not be true on higher difficulties, and it's your choice to use them in combat regardless.
-I was disappointed that only one quest had a branching ending and that, (MINOR SPOILERS) (EXTRA WARNING SPACE) although the villain's dialogue is written in a tone that implied he wasn't totally evil, his actions are never justified as anything other than genocide. (END SPOILERS) I don't consider either of these a con since it's expected from this genre, but it is missed potential.

"It's Halo with dinosaurs and it costs a dollar" 7/10
It's pretty obvious that this game is trying to be exactly like Halo...with uhhh, dinosaurs. They really make it no secret either; the graphics, art style, and gameplay are almost identical in every way possible. The layouts of the maps are also very similar, you drive around in vehicles that bare a striking resemblance to Halo vehicles, and oh yeah, you're in space too. Which I suppose isn't a bad thing,  Halo is now dead for the PC anyway, and if you're going to steal from a game, Halo is a pretty good one to steal from. Don't believe me? Well pay the dollar to see for yourself!
Which brings me to my next point, this game only costs a dollar, the price of a cheeseburger. It also works perfectly with a 360 controller, feels like a AAA title from a few years ago, has dinosaurs galore in it, and like I said only costs 99 cents. What more do you want from a game that costs less than a taco? Sure it's got some problems, but they seem pretty minor when you take the price into consideration. Even if you get just a few hours of gameplay out of it, you're still getting a great deal.

All-in-all, if you're looking for something familiar, without having to shell out a lot of money, and are really into first person shooters, then you can't go wrong with this title.

My brain is now puzzled.  Even though you don't need any understanding of chemistry what so ever, if you enjoy puzzle games this game is most certainly for you.
At first glance, we may be reminded of the classic Atomix from the Amiga and C64 era. Apart from building molecules, this is an entirely different game that feels very unique and genuine. The staggering 144 levels will keep you busy for quite some time as it took me about 12 hours to beat. The puzzles themselves are easy enough for the average person to beat while not feeling silly doing so and difficult enough to challenge every mind. The basic premise is controlling one atom to move, bond, break, turn other atoms to complete a molecule - all within a set of boundary. The only letdown is atom variety as you'll only be seeing C, O, H, N and He which can and will get boring once you're close to completing the game.
It is worthy of mentioning that the game runs on Adobe Air and there have been reports coming from Linux users that it does not run on some occasions as Adobe has ceased linux support.
Although the game would greatly benefit from Steam Workshop integration, the developer has stated he does not wish to implement such features in the foreseeable future - a shame as user created levels would keep the game and its community alive for longer.
For the fan of the puzzle genre, Sokobond will quench a thirst for simple 2D puzzlers. The average gamer should give it a try as its addictive nature may surprise you playing it more and more. If you have a personal vendetta against these types of games - stay clear of this one.

The Good:
This is a solid 4x space game.  If you have played MOO or Galatic Civ II, you know what you are getting into.  While it has some minor bugs (which I am sure will be fixed soon), it is a very solid game.  The graphics are good, and the time between turns, even in a large galaxy is quite fast.  It has pretty much everything you expect from a modern space 4x game in a streamlined UI.
The Bad:
There is little in game documentation, and the manual is pretty weak.  There are a lot of mechanics which are not explained.  For example, planet population.  Sure more is good, but exactly how does it affect production?  I spent a lot of time in forums to figure the various game mechanics instead of having some in-game explanation.
There are three ideologies, which you can think of as skill trees.  The problem is that most of the stuff in the trees is very "meh".  This was an exiting feature of the game, but in reality it is almost totally forgettable.
The diplomatic AI is pretty poor.  While each faction is supposed to have a personality, they really don't.  They will all end up hating you.  They will hate you if you are too weak. They will hate you if you are too strong.  They will hate you if you are losing.  They will hate you if you are winning.  People you have never met, who are far-far away will declare war on you, even though you will never see their war ships because you are so far beyond their range.
The ugly:
The strategic AI is abysmal.  Unfortunately GC III is not alone in this.  It seems to be the the status-quo for the genre.  I can't think of a TBS in recent memory that had a decent, let alone good strategic AI.  In this case it does an abysmal job of managing its planets, economy, tech, fleets, you name it.  The only thing is the difficulty does beyond "normal" is  add multipliers for the AI's various resources.  They are just as dumb as before, they just get a free ride in production.  I personally do not find this very satisfying.  This is not an unsolvable problem.  For example, in GC III there is buildings of the same type get an adjacency bonus.  The AI never takes advantage of this and just throws stuff randomly on each world.  5 factories next to each other are far better than 5 factories scattered.
There is nothing new under the sun:
GCIII really doesn't bring anything "new" to the table.  Its just another 4x game.  There are no new mechanics that are game changers.  Nothing that makes you go, "Oh WOW! That's Cool!".  Perhaps the Ideologies were an attempt that that, but due to the poor execution, they are quite forgettable.
TLDR; Version:
If you want a solid space 4x game that is like other 4x games, then buy it.  If you want something genuinely new, then skip this title.  It is simply more of the same.

I want to like this game, but there's just so little game aspect that it feels unfinished. I'm reluctantly recommending it, but only really for the summer sale price of €6.50.
Pros:
- Looks great, especially the water dynamics
- Unique genre
- Vehicles respond realistically to the environment
- Some workshop content
Cons:
- Lack of game content and explanation
- Frustrating controls and camera movement
The main problem is that it's unclear what you're supposed to do. I tried picking up lumber and delivering it to an objective, but that doesn't appear to do anything. Through a YouTube video I discovered that loading up lumber automatically from a log kiosk works, but doing it by hand is of course the real challenge (which I haven't gotten working). Per chance I found that driving garage parts to a new garage unlocked it and that concealed parts of the map could be revealed by driving to a cloak point. It appears that these three elements are the entirety of the game. There are six maps and a dozen trucks, I believe, along with some workshop content.
There is no kind of campaign or progression; your objective is just to deliver logs in half a dozen different maps.
It also wasn't clear to me if there were penalties for reparing vehicles or using fuel, especially when recovering them to a garage. It seems these statistics are simply presented to you when you complete the objective and don't mean anything otherwise.
Driving around is fun, but constantly getting stuck can be a bit frustrating, especially when in general the vehicles don't go very quickly, even on pavement. With the commenter below's recommendation I played with the gear box a bit, and it certainly helps against getting stuck. Also the winch is useful in a pinch.
I'll say in all the controls are very cumbersome with a keyboard and mouse. I'm also often struggling with getting the camera pointed where I want to look.
I think the game has a lot of potential in a unique genre, but is still somewhat of a letdown.

Galactic Civilizations III is a game I've been looking forward to getting my hands on once i began to read and see about it. I got it for cheap £15 to be exact and I would pay that all over again, I felt there was a little bit of a steep learning curve to begin with but there's nothing sitting and staring at the tech tree for a while can't solve.
The sheer scale of the game is something i adore, even choosing a 'Huge' size map will guarantee you hours of fun in a single match! There are so many features in this game I love compared to other games of it's genre, like when you build a new ship and right click for it to move to a fleet of ships say 20 tiles away to meet up with them the ship will follow the fleet and not just go to the tile they were on, making it easy to manage fleets more effectively. The ship designer is a real neat feature, allowing you to customize your ships into whatever your heart desires, making your match yours in a completely unique way. As well as being able to make your own ships the ability to make your own Civilization exists in the game too, choosing unique personality features, creating the lore, having a unique tech tree all add to make this feature one that hardcore 4X fans will love!
In a nutshell i love this game, it goes without saying there are some AI balance tweeks needed and multiplayer from what i gathered is a little flawed too, but honest to god i can see myself sinking hours and hours into this title, hope you guys have fun with it too!

We just know that Job the Leprechaun need to save his/her friend Eri and will know later which one kidnapped him/her by playing the different levels.
The game features 2 worlds for 35 levels this includes normal levels, bosses levels and a bonus level.
The aim of the game is to clear each normal level by collecting all the clovers and reaching the door which appears after having all clovers. Of course the is some platforming, fighting and some puzzle to make your journey challenging. There is also a time limit to finish each normal and boss level. Hopefully Job is resourceful : he can use his hat to knock out foes and can also reflects with it fire balls. Job is not alone, several big ears Leprechauns, plants and cows will help him through his journey. Finally you begin the game with 3 lives and can acquire several more in some challenging area or in some trees.
You can always quit the game and resume where you left it but beware to not press enter before choosing Continue instead of the default choice of New game. The game isn't too long, less than an hour is enough to beat the game.
(#):
One achievement is earned after finishing the game (easy difficulty) and another one is earned after finishing the game without using a continue (medium difficulty). At the beginning I didn't really got it, but after finishing the game I can confirm that a continue is granted when you have lost all your lives. So it's really easy to finish the game.
(*):
Even it's still difficult for you to finish the game without using any continue you can save some lives by escaping the game before your life is taken and resume the game. But this is mostly doable when you fell off the screen or running out of time and hard to make in the other cases.

Slipstream 5000 is a futuristic flight and combat racing game by Gremlin Interactive.
This game is a child of the 90s, from times when future was not all apocalypse and racing games dared to have other vehicles than automobiles.
The sounds of the planes, the craft and course design, radio chatter between competitors and the pre-race TV hosts introducing the upcoming track are few of the highlights which really make this futuristic world believable.
The game is challenging and the controls are really tight PROVIDED you're using a joystick or even analog gamepad. This game NEEDS analog controls. Period.
One negative is the low in-game resolution which makes it hard to judge turns at distance and you to rely on track memorization. While the graphics are mostly OK and at times quite good for a 3D DOS game, there is no option to increase resolution past 320x200. Play it in 14" CRT telly and it'll be much better.
It would be nice for DosBox to exit itself though. Not a dealbreaker but some people might find this confusing when quitting the game.

IF you like Hearthstone, then you will like this game as well because it plays very similarly. The key differences are in the deck building. Your commander at deck creation can have up to 3 hero powers (out of a pool of about 10 per commander) if he chooses and anywhere from 25 to 40 cards out of a pool of about 400 cards currently. The more things you put in your deck, the less focused it becomes, the tradeoff, but also you get more hit points. Another difference is that this game is much more strategically deep than Hearthstone as it has more mechanics to factor in to your strategy, such as an additional resources other than supply (mana) known as energy. As you could imagine this boosts the fun factor way up. In addition 2v2 will be implemented at some point. Can you imagine how that will play out? So this may be spacestone, but the devs are thinking outside of the box. At this early state of the game some of the creatures/robots/aberations/vehicles/etc. (minions) are missing sounds. Same is true of some of the tactics (spells) and modules (hero powers). But with every patch more and more comes alive. Also the game is still being balanced here and there and the foil cards are not out yet (golden animated versions of each card). Some functions such as hero skins, adventures packs, and other aspects are grayed out indicating they will be here at some point. The raid (arena) part of the game needs more players to make getting a match more faster. The game is free to play  but a FTP player can compete with players that purchase boosters, albeit their win rate will not be as high as it could be. You regularly get boosters if you perform your quests (missions) at the rate of about 1 per day in about 1/2 hour of playing daily if you wish. Well, all in all at this early state I would highly recommend if you like Hearthstone but tire of the fantasy swords and spells theme. And even if your not tired of Hearthstone (like myself) I would definately try this game out as I'm enjoying both concurrently and both are free. A no brainer.

JRPG's are a rather broad genre, and can focus on quite a few different things. This one is mechanics focused: lots of effort was put into making the battles easy to control and the game itself flows smoothly. The game is "streamlined", in that you don't spend time messing with equipment optimization, but there's still some choices to make with your character progression thanks to the ability to put different kinds of cards on your talent board. Level up, get a point, pick a card and slap it on the board, and you're on your way. Easy and efficient.
The battles themselves are the usual turn-based type, and that's a good thing. The main innovation is that you get a multiplying XP bonus based on how many enemies you fight, so you're strongly incentivized to set up huge battles against swarms of enemies. Don't bite off more than you can chew...
Mechanics-focused indie RPG's usually don't look like much, and this is the best thing about Earthlock. The game is beautiful, both in terms of the vibrant 3D environments and the high quality JRPG-style music that goes with it.
Then there's the parts that didn't get as much attention. Namely, the story and characterization. There seems to be some sort of plot here, but the best thing I can say about it is that it mostly stays out of the way of the actual game. This is not a cinematic or plot driven game of any sort, so if that's what you want from your JRPG's you won't find it here. Likewise, the translation, while competent, is really awkward in some places, and i find the characters to be utterly forgettable.
On the balance, I quite like this game. It's exactly what we were promised from Kickstarter: a game that captures the feel of the 3D RPG's of the PS1/PS2 era. And those games weren't exactly famous for their plots or translations either, exceptions excepted. It feels like this game is being overlooked by ... pretty much everyone, and that's a shame.
[Disclosure, I recieved this game due to a Kickstarter pledge, which I do not consider to be getting the game for free.]

I really love this game, and its universe, but I have a hard time recommending it.
EARTHLOCK has some great ideas, but the game is too small, too short, to allow these ideas to breathe. Making them feel halfdone. I'll definitely look forward to any game these guys create in the future.
Let me first talk about the combat system; There are 6 characters, each with two different combat-modes that you can switch between. There is also a battle-bond system, you team your party members up 2-and-2 and they'll form a bond. From 1 star to 5 this battle bond unlocks unique passives that strengthen different playstyles. (You can change bonds whenever you want without loosing any progress)
There is a third mechanic to the combat system and that is the talent board. Each character has a talent board with set amount of plugs. There are Abilities, Perks and Traits. Perks gives different passives and buffs, Traits give you statpoints and Ability gives you skills you use in your combat-mode. Unlike other talent-tree systems in other games, EARTHLOCK allows you to change what is in the plugs whenever you want. So as you play the game, you'll find new abilities that you can change out the ones you already have. Meaning if you prefer one battle-mode over the other you can build your talent-board around this.
The negative to this is that there isn't enough options, making the system feel halfdone, or too big for the game. Throughout the game, you feel you have options, you're finding skills and changing them out. But in the end, there's barely any choices. Not to mention the characters whose second combat-mode is simply buffs,
The universe is beautiful, with no UI when walking around you get to truely appreciate the backgrounds and the details the developers have put into it. And god! Some scenes are amazing. But again, it feels rushed. At the beginning, I'd explore like I'd explore a proper rpg: I'd talk to bookshelves and crates lookings for loot and idiotic lines from books. But nothing. I could not interact with anything outside of the quest items, and that felt.. odd to me. It wasn't natural. Especially considering later in the game there WERE bookshelves I could talk to, in the giant library, out of the dusin bookshelves I could talk to TWO. TWO!! Who the heck programmes only two bookshelves to be interactables and not the rest?
The game is advertised as an old-school JRPG, and that casuals should look elsewhere. I disagree. Oh how I disagree. This game isn't hard, this game is laughable easy. Sure, sure, if I ran into a boss without healing up or preparing I'll swear and wish there was a flee button so I could prepare myself. Did I die? Sure, yes, of course. But because of my mistakes. Because I tried to avoid mobs and ended up in a combat versus 12 mobs when I had half HP and no ultimate ready. But the combat is easy, tedious at times (considering before Taika my skills would each hit 10%) But slow combat doesn't equal hard combat.
Once I unlocked Taika as a party member, the rest of the game became a breeze, only difficulty came from me going for 100% achievements which forced me to run around the game with random characters with random bonds together. I don't know if Taika is simply broken, or if this is some bug. Taika has many AOE skills, if you meet 8+ mobs, Taika will hit them for the normal 10%. But unlike the other few (and rare) aoe skills the other character has, it seems Taikas damage stacks.
Thats a bad way of describing it. Normally, an AOE will do X amount of dmg to X character. Taika's skill does XXXX dmg spread out. Meaning if I meet 8 mobs, she'll hit all of them for 10%. But as the mobs die, at the end her skill could one hit a monster. So yes, boss fights became very, very, easy.  (While the other characters aoe would do the same dmg no matter how many or few monsters we encountered)
Part of the difficulty of this game is lack of information: There is no information on skills, buffs, debuffs, dmg, or levels. You don't know what level monsters are, and you don't know what that debuff does. Your own skills got descriptions but they are limited. Which meant every time I encountered a new debuff, or buff, it was a trial-and-error playstyle. They had some interesting buffs and debuffs. Like one that reflexs all magical damage onto who casts it. I killed myself once or twice trying to figure out what that new icon under their hp bar meant. But once you figured it out it was "oh I cannot kill him now, I'll just click rest for three more rounds untill it disappear and then kill him".

I've never played Final Fantasy 7 before it hit Steam, so I bought it and played to completion. So I can say honestly, with neither bias nor nostalgia getting in the way of honest critique, that this game is fantastic.
The Good:
Combat is simple, but has a lot of depth. You can put the best gear on your party and slog through enemies with high damage, but the Materia in this game can not only make things more interesting, but easier. Link up a health drain Materia with a high-damage summon to instantly recover while devestating your opponent. Or the game breaking 4x-Cut linked with a poison materia, leaving any survivors of your micro-onslaught poisoned and near defeat.
The story is also good. Admittedly weird in places, but come on. It's a fantasy game. Leave your logic at the door.
The Bad:
The first is the somewhat slow start of the game. It takes a long time to leave the first city, Midgar. To be fair, it's a big city with lots to do, but it's not surprising that a lot of people stop playing before the game starts proper six hours in.
Another downside is the game's backgrounds. They look fantastic, and kind of give me a warm, fuzzy feeling of nostalgia (since Resident Evil did the same thing). That being said, they haven't aged super well, and it can get a bit difficult figuring out where you're supposed to go.
Lastly, although this is something that comes with the genre, there's a lot of grinding involved. Grinding battles for experience and money, and to level up your game-breaking Materia. Sinking money and time into raising Chocobos that are needed to get to the secret areas of this game. Saving Battle Points at the Gold Saucer's Battle Square to get the best Limit Break skills (which, may I add, go away if you leave). It'll take time to beat this game.
To sum this up, this game is far from perfect. But that doesn't mean it's not one of the best JRPG's in the whole genre. I cannot reccomend this game enough to beginner and veteran alike of turn-based RPG games.

Sokobond is a puzzle game with a learning twist. You see not only are you trying to reunite, or combine the different objects in the level, but these objects are actual periodic elements, and you are putting them together to create different chemical compounds. All I have to say is who knew science could be so fun? You will be faced with level after level of differing elements and obstacles to overcome. If you successfully put all the elements together not only do you unlock additional levels, but you get to learn about the compound you just created.
Graphically you are not going to see anything 3D, but in this puzzle game, the beauty of the simplicity of the graphics shows that this is definitely more about the elements. All the colors are varying subtle colors such as red, green, yellow, blue, etc. The levels are laid out in a grid base format where you will be trying to combine the elements by moving up, down, left, and right. The little added pieces to the game also come off as subtle, but are very recognizable after you use that functionality the first time. The pieces I'm talking about are the - and + which will take away bonds, or add bonds.
The music and sounds follow the same path as the art style. It is a soft sound that gets other sounds added in when you make a bond, or lose a bond.
The controls, as described before, are simply moving up, down, left, and right.
So here's a game that has no story, but has many rewards to be had. The rewards you gain are that you complete a level, open up other levels, and if you so choose you can learn something about the compound you just made. As the levels increase, the difficulty increases. There are many many levels to sink your teeth in, and for those parents out there you can not only educate your kids with this game, but you can secretly help out if you have a controller plugged in. The best part about this puzzle game is that the developers did not want to stop the chance for someone to learn about all the different compounds, so there is an option in the menu that allows you to unlock all the levels.
I personally found this game a breath of fresh air, I did not have to worry about monster attacking, or having to watch certain statistics to make sure I could survive a level. I was able to play at my own pace, and hell I actually relearn some stuff that I had long forgotten about. So with that I have to give this game a 9.5 out of 10.

I was pretty disappointed to see that Star Crusade is a carbon copy of Hearthstone's gameplay right down to the hero powers. Not only that, but the devs couldn't even bother to attempt to create their own card mechanics as many of them are simply renamed ones from Hearthstone (Activate = Battlecry, Shield = Divine Shield, Revenge = Deathrattle, Fury = Enrage, etc).
Granted, the Energy and Firepower mechanics take a slight detour from the game being a complete mimic of Hearthstone, but it would still be a stretch to say the game offers anything new. This is reminiscent of the MMO era when devs decided to just clone WoW and change a few things so the game was only a 95% clone of WoW. Remaking Hearthstone and draping a sci-fi theme over it is lazy development and wasted effort in my opinion; why make a game if you don't even have your own ideas.
There is a difference between drawing inspiration from a game versus copying it. Star Crusade feels, looks, and plays exactly like Hearthstone; which begs the question: why play a poor man's version of Hearthstone when you can just play Hearthstone? It's quite mind boggling why the devs decided to go this route - compete directly with Hearthstone, the biggest online CCG, but do nothing better and offer nothing new. Look to Runescape Chronicles or Spellweaver for unique CCG alternatives.

Sidescrolling RPG with very clean, beautiful graphics. Really good soundtrack, although it doesn't really stand out while playing. The character designs and their personalities are really well done, as is the dialogue. Lots of funny moments involving the main character (Dust) and his side-kick (Fidget.)
The story is good but isn't very deep. Most of the gameplay revolves around sidequests or things not super directly related to the story's main premise. It's not until the last chapter that you even really learn the spoilers.
The combat is very smooth and fluid, although it really starts to get repetitive a little over half-way in. The only real reason I didn't notice it so much is that you can build hits together for combos, and so I tended to always try to beat my previous record during fights. There's only a tiny bit of variation to the combat later on in the game, but it feels like it's introduced a bit too late and isn't all that different and exciting. I would have really liked a more complex system with more variations, but the combat is still really good just due to how smooth it is. The only negative I really have about the combat is that the game will often orient your characters automatically towards  an enemy or nearby object... so you'll be fighting something or trying to move into a specific position, and your character will somewhat auto-lock onto the thing it thinks you're trying to attack. It's fairly frustrating when it causes you to get hit during combat and break your combo.
The last chapter drags on for an extremely long time as far as gameplay goes... it's a lot of fighting over and over. The last boss battle is too ridiculous and drags on far beyond even the most patient person's attention span. It reminds me of Cave Story, where the game's flow is very well done, and ramps up as you progress.. but then the final battle is just way over the top to the point of being much harder than any other part of the game, and really frustrating.
There are lots of things hidden away for you to find, namely keys that are used to unlock chests with goodies inside, and a bunch of "friends" which are just cameos of characters from other games. They're all fairly well hidden and it's fun to figure out how too get to keys that are just out of reach.
Overall, this is a really well done game with a sizeable amount of gameplay. If you're trying to 100% it, you will spend many more hours trying to perfect  the challenge areas and get all the collectables.

There are some video games in life that cannot be compared to anything else, and most likely, will never be comparable and will remain in their own category.
I very vaguely remember hearing about ABZU when it first was announced, and so when the day of its release arrived and all of my social media accounts were bombarded by screenshots, videos and articles about the game, that is when I realized what would make me buy this game in a matter of seconds: Matt Nava the art director behind what is hands down one of the absolute best and most beautiful game & experience I ever had in gaming, Journey, was the founded of Giant Squid, the studio behind ABZU, which is their very first game. If this wasn’t already amazing, I quickly learned that Austin Wintory, the composer behind Journey’s soundtrack (again, one of the best soundtrack of anything you will ever get to listen to), was also in on the project.
I was sold. That was it. I went on steam, purchased the game, and nearly cried at the excitement and feeling of privilege that I was suddenly filled with.
I played ABZU that very same night. I waited until everyone in my apartment complex went to bed, for the streets to go quiet, and for a nice breeze to settle and travel throughout my apartment, I wanted the right setting for what I knew without any doubt was going to be an absolutely amazing experience. After Journey, and now after ABZU, Giant Squid, and especially Matt Nava & Austin Wintory have my unwavering support in whatever project that have planned for the future. They are geniuses.
So, ABZU.
In ABZU, just like Journey, you follow some sort of neither human not clearly animal creature who is set in a beautiful and intriguing environment that you have to explore. In Journey, the goal was to get to the tower, as you learn about your people, their culture, and what possibly could have gone down in a distant or not so distant past. In ABZU the game is similarly linear but the way the game is constructed and looks invites you to explore every piece of it, its depth, its population, and to interact with the very various aquatic life that surrounds you, sometimes passively, sometimes not so much. As you are given the option to free some various types of fish, you learn a little more about the people that used to coexist with them, your people, their past, their culture, and some other things that may or may not be all that ambiguous to you.
In moments when I thought that I understood ABZU, its setting, the story it was trying to tell, things turned up on me and a lot of the aspects of the game that were simple and beautiful, remained beautiful but touched on a lot of darkness I had not expected.
As you swim, sometimes something that was a bit challenging to do in terms of being able to control your character and move exactly like you mean to, you are surrounded by what is one of the most beautifully designed video game world I have ever had the chance to experience. The color palette, the way that fish, whales and seaweed moves, and the way that the world interacts with you, truly going the opposite direction from some sort of silent observer.
Just like in Journey, Austin Wintory offers us such an incredibly amazing, powerful and unique soundtrack, songs that brought me to tears so many times, as I smiled for very various and complex reasons: that is what video game music should be like. That is what music should be like. Austin Wintory’s compositions are the hands holding the art design of ABZU, working so perfectly well together in order to transport us into a world, an atmosphere, a place that although I expected the quality of due to the amazingness that is Journey, reached a new set of highs. Went where Journey had not, excelled all of my expectations.
10/10 – In one night, ABZU became, without any possible, even the smallest of doubt, one of the very best game I have ever had the chance to play in my life. And for this, I am so proud and grateful for the existence of video games as a medium for magical storytelling.

So after 2 and a half years of development, we'd finally get this game: Dust: An Elysian tail.
And please tell me if you get the gabe newell reference, but this game was worth the wait in every way.
Throughout the game, i'd search for plotholes and flawed gameplay mechanics, and needsly to say, i couldn't find any.
Dust's controls are the opposite of stiff. The game is really responsive to controls, and it leads to some fun platforming and fast-paced gameplay. And while this game does have a rush bros disease of slow walking and fast rolling, I had an easy time ignoring it to the game's combat.
Not only are you given a however small variety of attacks to dish out pain with, there's loads of combos that you can test yourself to execute and memorize with your keyboard, and you get rewarded for each combo. Not only do you get extra experience, you also get achivements, and your enemies of course die faster. While that does sum it up, this game also has its way of disapointment.
At the beginning of the game, you're given the blade of Ahrah, Fidget, And dus'ts glorious control to utilize and THATS. IT.
Later in the game, you're informed ahrah is only ONE of the blades of elysium; Why couldnt we find and use the others? I wouldve liked more variety than just being stuck with 2 weapons to use. Fidget got more than one mode of attacking, why cant we?
Gameplay aside, the graphics, which are hand drawn by the way look GLORIOUS. They dont cause any eyestrain and there isnt a spam of color palette like rush bros had. The game is really pretty to look at and i hope you buy it for that reason.
Now, lets go to the plot. In the beginning you see an unknown warrior charging through a variety of people for an unknown reason, and later find out he's killed by a child. In the next scene, you see our main character, dust, kneeling in the middle of an unknown forest.
Anyway, we're introduced to our 3 protagonists, dust, fidget, and the blade of ahrah, which as i said earlier is the main weapon you'll be using throughout the game. We then see that dust has forgotten his past and that he summoned ahrah for yet another unknown reason. Dust doesnt even know why he did it, but he chooses to ignore it and go on a quest to find out more of his past, kill a bunch of racist knights, and simply bring justice where justice is needed with the help of fidget and the blade of ahrah.
This is why i like indie games like this, they keep the plot simple and fast to keep the player wanting to play their game. You might call it lazy, but it works.
So after all that said, I do like this game for a variety of reasons, (One i'd rather not say) And also, I think that this game has perfect potential and setup for a sequel. If there were a game called Dust 2 (No pun intended), I really hope they'd keep what made this game good and add onto it.

This game is pretty awesome overall. I want to start off by saying this game is inspired by the great JRPGs of yesterday, with a unique artstyle and an amazingly genuine and beautiful soundtrack. The mechanics of the game are similair to any JRPG and has many of the tropes expected.
The battle system takes a unique position on the stance/position mechanics which is refreshing and makes combat interesting and adds a layer of strategic resource management. Overall battles start out generally pretty easy and ramp up in difficulty in the fist few hours. Enemies are encountered similarily to Chrono Trigger or more specifically The Last Remnant, which is a positive becuase it does away with a bad JRPG trope, random encounters. (Yay)
The world is beatifully designed and again the artstyle and colour pallet used fits the experience very well. The game is more vibrant than many RPGs in general and reminds me of Super Giant Games art director Zoe's colour choices for Bastion or Starbreeze's Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons with a bit more variety. It definitely has an indie game vibe about it's aethetics and thats not a bad thing by any means (Unless your a graphics nazi). Overall puzzles are quite easy but fun so solve and treasures are not difficult to find. I was hoping for a more playstation era vibe when it comes to secrets and hidden treasure or quests. Things that take a little more consideration and thought to discover.
I love the soundtrack. It is very remenisent of Nobou Uematsu, Yoko Shimomura, mixed with a light version of Darren Korb, also from Super Giant Games (Bastion, Transistor, soon to be Pyre). Each song syncs up with the desired atmoshperic feeling the developers want to convey. I cannot say enough good things about this OST. Eiko Nichols is outstanding in my books.
There is a fun crafting/gardening system. Ive never played many traditional JRPGs with a gardening system, let alone one that was simple to understand yet fun to indulge in. Skill/talent/bond systems are quite unqique and allow a degree of customization in where and how you level your stats and abilities. The talent system for example allows you to determine which type of attributes you want to gain depending on your play style, and in turn, your placement of these attributes on a grid system, also determines which abilities you obtain and when. Its not perfect but it is different and does allow some customization.
The story so far isn't about crystals, or people being crystals, or searching for crystals so its decent in my books. The writing reminds me of a PS1 era JRP so thats great.
Overall the game is very enjoyable. Ultimately its a great first installment in the series that appears to be a light version of a Final Fantasy JRPG type game. I have a lot of faith in this game and this company. Moving forward I know they will improve upon the things mentioned above and continue to produce outstanding experiences.

When I first purchased this game, I had quite a bad first experience. Since then, the studio have been in contact with me over the problems highlighted in my origional review, and gave me a key to review changes they recently made (as I had actually refunded the game, the first time I had ever dome this for a steam game.)
The changes made in the recent update really overhauled the opening, and I know that my first experinace of the game would have been much much better if had found the game now. The tutorial was completely overhauled, and this section now guides you through their battle system bit by bit, rather than paralysing you with a wall of text information. The delivery of dialogue by characters has also been improved, now with small flourishes of acting from some characters when speaking, which really is a huge step up.
I do wish the characters acted more, but this just didn't seem to be their aim with this game-- and that's ok. Since bringing it up, they have even worked to improve this, and I find that pretty admirable. From reviews I've read, I know this game is a pretty seizable experinace, so I cannot expect the same characterisation to be added into the entire length of the game; but it's now there at the start and it would have won me over if It was part of my first experinace.
So yeah, if I bought this game now, I wouldn't refund it. I feel I can recommend it if you're looking for a longform RPG experinace with all the trappings of it's genre predecessors.
Thank you to all the guys and gals at Snowcastle for taking the time to respond to player feedback in a bigger way than I have ever seen from any other studio, And thank you for not taking negative feedback as badly as many many indie studios seem to be doing these days. I wish you all the best in the future and look forward to seeing more of your games!

Okay, this game intrigued me since I first heard about it. As a huge fan of old school JRPGs such as Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest this was right up my alley. So naturally I backed the Kickstarter, and was thrilled when it exceeded funding.
I've been eagerly awaiting this game on the same caliber as Dragon Quest VII and Final Fantasy XV. So was it worth it? Oh yes. The game was developed by a small team, so it has that "indie game" vibe to it, but it takes the classic JRPG formula and throws some awesome unique flavor to it. I'm not one to read super long reviews though, or write them for that matter, so here's a list of pros and cons for the game
Pros:
- The art
Oh my god is this a beautiful game. The colors, and areas are beautiful, with unique character designs, amazing locales, and an old school overworld. The best part of the already amazing art though, is it's unique style. Unlike many Japanese style RPG styles developed by a small team, it doesn't look like it's stealing it's style from FF, DQ, Tales of, etc.
- The battle system
A turn based RPG really has to have a unique battle system to shine, and Earthlock really does. The characters can build bonds between each other through combat, and learn passive abilities. Also in battle every character has two stances, which really makes combat strategic and fun. Also, a lot of turn based RPGs in general suffer from long battle animations which make battle a slog. Not Earthlock. The battles are crisp and smooth, delivering fluid beautiful combat, that flows perfectly, and doesn't slow down the game a bit.
- The story
Admittedly I'm not super far in yet, but it's been very good so far. No JRPG tropes of amnesiacs, destroyed hometowns, awkward romance between childhood friends etc. I'm not quite at the point where the story has "took off" per se, but I have no reason to believe it won't be great.
- The characters
Once again, I don't believe I'm far enough to see the characters truly develop but every character has had a unique personality without relying on a tired trope. Plus there's a character named Frogboy. How can you not love that?
- The music
The music is absolutely gorgeous and captures the feel of the game perfectly. Like the art style, it's a completely unique style that doesn't feel like an intimation of another game.
- The hub island
I'm not a fan of "crafting" games, but the hub island you find a few hours in adds a lot of fun and depth to the game. You can grow plants to craft items from, and as someone who put 100 hours into Stardew Valley, this is an absolute joy to have a Harvest Moon lite thrown into an already very beefy RPG.
Cons:
- Controller buttons don't appear on screen
I'm playing with an XBOX 360 controller, as it's my weapon of choice in my PCMR arsenal. Although the game recognizes it just fine, it shows keyboard buttons instead of the controller buttons in the menu, battles, tutorials, etc. Once again, it doesn't ruin the game by any stretch, as I've gotten used to it, but it's a bit of an annoyance. Hopefully the devs fix this and I can remove this as well.
There you have it, overall there's a few small things that annoy me, that hopefully the devs patch out soon. However the pros overwhelmingly outweigh the cons. This game gives me that feeling of excitement, wonder, and awe as I had the first time I played FFIX, and I hope for the devs this can reach "Overwhelmingly Positive" so that they can maybe make a sequel one day.

The approach I take when I review any 4x game is to evaluate whether I feel drawn back in to finish "one more turn". Unfortunately, with this game that is not the case. In pre-release videos developers lauded tools that would help players more effectively manage their empires, however this game is filled to the brim with micromanagement once you build the massive empires that the game advertises that you can build. That is, if you can build a large empire. Currently the "large empire happiness penalty" is extremely crippling and really hurts the ability to build the large empires that most people love building in a space game. I don't mind building a small, extremely efficient empire, but if I want to do that, I'll simply play Civ V, because right now that game does that better. People want to play a space 4x because you don't want to have the same constraints as a game like Age of Empires, Civ, or Rise of Nations. Instead, you want to build an empire that has hundreds of planets and hundreds of ships. At this point, it's best to keep playing GalCiv II until they get the game balancing figured out. While it is playable if you have a good machine, it isn't very entertaining at the moment and instead of me telling me self "just one more turn" I think "ugh, another turn". (5/10)

I can say that I'm probably not even halfway through this game, and I've found it rather addicting.
I could say that my first exposure to Sokoban, the inspiration for this, would be through the arcade game Pengo and a non-visual example in Zork III. (Yes, I'm showing my age. Get off my lawn.) Sokobond takes it a step further by having you maneuver different atoms to form bonds and ultimately get a molecule form them all, with the exception of the helium atoms. The challenge lies in the space to move for each board, and in later levels, the placement of certain features, like bond splitters, bond enhancers, and rotators. Be prepared for a mental workout, though, as levels will range from 'piece of cake' all the way to 'dear God, are you freaking KIDDING ME??'
The game itself is minimalist, as advertised. Controls are simple, graphics are not fancy, and sound consists occasional beeps with a slight droning chord in the background. The focus on this puzzle game are the puzzles themselves, with a little bit trivia to go along at the end of each puzzle with that feeling of a job well done. Total game time-- as well as the amount of Angrish used while playing-- will vary with the gamer.
All in all, this is a solid puzzle title and well worth having in one's collection.

I bought LiEat because I am nothing if not a sucker for interesting aesthetics. And JRPGs. The premise is a young dragon girl who can eat lies; that combined with the art style was enough to convince me it was worth the very small price tag.
This game is broken down into three 'parts'. Essentially, each is a self-contained adventure in a confined space that takes about an hour to play through. I'll be honest...I got stuck quite quickly. They take an odd format and presentation that completely stumped me; it dumps your character in an almost empty town and says to go do stuff. What follows is a very linear series of events that are so loosely connected that I highly recommend following a walkthrough.
This sounds like it should be a negative point, but the fun of the game isn't in working out the next step. Instead this should be seen more as a visual novel with token battles and movement that go a long way to investing you in the story. And it is the writing that gets this game a definite recommendation.
You experience the events - that take the form of a series of 'mysteries' to be solved - both from the eyes of the naive and childlike Efi (the lie-eating dragon girl) and her 'father' Leo (an early twenties conman). This split perspective works very well and lets you see the various characters with whom you interact in differing ways that would have been unavailable if your protagonists didn't act independently.
Efi is endlessly cute and acts very much like an actual child would; playing, exploring and making friends with all the shady people Leo regards with cynicism and weariness. She is initially the focus of the game's attention, but this regrettably shifts to what I hesitate to call the 'over-arching plot' in the last part.
Okay. Cards on the table. This game is very short. Four hours to 100% it on my first run. And that includes leaving it running a couple of times while I got distracted and wandered off. I would have absolutely loved if there had been another three or more of the little 'episodes' even if that doubled the price of the game. As it is, the game peaks with the second part and the third part kinda lost me.
The first part focuses largely on the combat which varies from impossible (if you didn't stumble randomly across better weapons) to trivial (if you happened to find the best ones). The second is a mostly conversation-based little story with less combat where Efi is at her best and the third takes a very 'puzzley' attitude that almost forgets combat exists until the end where you need to grind for a couple of minutes.
As I said, I think this game is best played with a guide open (made easier by the fact the resolution CANNOT be changed from a 480p window), allowing you to find the good weapons and get through the weird sequence of interactions you need. Without the 'gameplay' to slow you down, you can explore everything and talk to everyone. It's the talking to everyone that makes this a fun adventure.
Considering I bought this very cheap based mostly on its aesthetics, I am pleasantly surprised by how much I like it. It is crammed full of a cuteness and charm that appeal greatly to me and smother any ill feelings about the relative lack of gameplay or the short runtime. While the third part is by far the weakest, it does end in such a way that a sequel or expansion is not impossible. If one is ever released, I'm sure I will play it and enjoy it simply if it is more of this.
Oh. And the idea of having all art stills and cutscenes viewable at the end of the 'part' is brilliant. They're pretty if few in number and they're worth that second look at the end.

So after 2 and a half years of development, we'd finally get this game: Dust: An Elysian tail.
And please tell me if you get the gabe newell reference, but this game was worth the wait in every way.
Throughout the game, i'd search for plotholes and flawed gameplay mechanics, and needsly to say, i couldn't find any.
Dust's controls are the opposite of stiff. The game is really responsive to controls, and it leads to some fun platforming and fast-paced gameplay. And while this game does have a rush bros disease of slow walking and fast rolling, I had an easy time ignoring it to the game's combat.
Not only are you given a however small variety of attacks to dish out pain with, there's loads of combos that you can test yourself to execute and memorize with your keyboard, and you get rewarded for each combo. Not only do you get extra experience, you also get achivements, and your enemies of course die faster. While that does sum it up, this game also has its way of disapointment.
At the beginning of the game, you're given the blade of Ahrah, Fidget, And dus'ts glorious control to utilize and THATS. IT.
Later in the game, you're informed ahrah is only ONE of the blades of elysium; Why couldnt we find and use the others? I wouldve liked more variety than just being stuck with 2 weapons to use. Fidget got more than one mode of attacking, why cant we?
Gameplay aside, the graphics, which are hand drawn by the way look GLORIOUS. They dont cause any eyestrain and there isnt a spam of color palette like rush bros had. The game is really pretty to look at and i hope you buy it for that reason.
Now, lets go to the plot. In the beginning you see an unknown warrior charging through a variety of people for an unknown reason, and later find out he's killed by a child. In the next scene, you see our main character, dust, kneeling in the middle of an unknown forest.
Anyway, we're introduced to our 3 protagonists, dust, fidget, and the blade of ahrah, which as i said earlier is the main weapon you'll be using throughout the game. We then see that dust has forgotten his past and that he summoned ahrah for yet another unknown reason. Dust doesnt even know why he did it, but he chooses to ignore it and go on a quest to find out more of his past, kill a bunch of racist knights, and simply bring justice where justice is needed with the help of fidget and the blade of ahrah.
This is why i like indie games like this, they keep the plot simple and fast to keep the player wanting to play their game. You might call it lazy, but it works.
So after all that said, I do like this game for a variety of reasons, (One i'd rather not say) And also, I think that this game has perfect potential and setup for a sequel. If there were a game called Dust 2 (No pun intended), I really hope they'd keep what made this game good and add onto it.

This is an utterly fantastic metroidvania and i enjoyed it from start to finish. This game doesn't necessarily do anything new or groundbreaking but instead offers a highly polished experience. You play Dust who wakes up with no memory of who he is to find a talking sword and it's guardian Fidget who decides to join Dust on his quest to discover who he is and to stop General Gaius who's army is devestating the land.
The Good:
- The graphics look beautiful and remind me of the cartoons i grew up watching in the 90's particularly the Disney cartoons like Ducktales and Chip And Dale:Rescue Rangers. It really gives the game some character and personality.
- The story isn't too bad either which surprised me as i had been misled by the cartoon looking graphics into thinking the story would be childish but it can be quiet dark at times and did keep my interest.Also the characters are likeable including Dust himself as well as Fidget with some humourous dialogue between the two.
- There's plenty to do in this game with lots of side quests and loads of collectables (including collecting various characters who players of popular indie titles might recognize) so there's enough there for a 15or sohours of gameplay.
- The levelling and crafting systems are simple and effective. It doesn't feel tacked on and you will notice the difference after levelling and upgrading equipment when fighting enemies.
- The game also introduces a good idea in that instead of having to grind for different materials to craft items you merely need one of each type,which you can sell to the merchant, who will then sell that material from that point onwards. So no grinding for ages to craft the armour you need.
The Bad:
-While there are several different types of attack,combat sometimes just boils down to button bashing against hordes of enemies.
- I played using a 360 controller and while it generally worked fine with the game, at times it was a bit sluggish and unresponsive. Though not enough to impact on my enjoyment of the game.
To summarize this game is a must buy and is truly deserving of all the praise and accolades it has gotten. 9/10 from me.

After playing the DLCs I finally decided to write a review for the game. It has been criticized a lot, and I can't say that game doesn't deserve it. For myself, I'm a fan of the Mafia series since the first game, and I can say a lot of bad things about Mafia III. But I don't want to. Mafia II was worse than the Mafia, and Mafia III is worse than the Mafia 2, we all know this. But all of them have something, that force you playing in it. Previous parts hace a good stories. And the third continues this tradition.  Conquering the districts is annoying, and at fourth-fifth district it become so disgusting, that sometimes you have a desire to delete the game and never play it again. But if you can overcome this, you will see that behind the monotonous routine hidden a good story.  The story about personal war of a man, where is no place for right or wrong, good or bad. In fact, you can't say that Lincoln is a good guy and Marcano is bad guy. All of characters have a point, reasons to acting their way. This is rare in today's triple-A games, and this gives a Mafia III a big plus. The game mechanics are relatively good, except some stranges with the cars behavior (notably the turning). And the main thing why you should play this is the atmosphere of the 60s. On the radio playing Rolling stones, Jefferson Airplane, The Animals, Johnny Cash, you name it. News telling about the GIs fighting in Vietnam, people ringing ones of the first, classic, muscle cars. You even can have a Vietnam flashback if you want to :). One exception is the Avengers' cover on Paint it black, it was terrifying.
The DLCs of the game (story ones, not the ones that give you weapons) shows how the game could be if there wasn't conquering part. Fun, dynamic, and with the good story.
I won't urge you buy the game on full price, the routine parts doesn't worth it. But if it on sale, I strongly recommend to spend your money on this game. It will give you some hours of great atmosphere and story.

Call it sour grapes if you want, because that is what most negative reviews usually are, however I will say I have a few, even in just my short time of playing.

To my point there are six factions in the game and you start only being able to play one of them, even though you have starter decks for each faction.  The only way to unlock a new faction for playability it seems is to defeat an opposing deck, which is all well and good until you run into the BS psychic decks.

-Also the arbitrary rule that you can only have X number of units on the field, I believe seven or eight.
*To the devs who I highly doubt will ever read this:  you need to balance out the psychics, you need to make it so that units with no attack (read 0 attack value) can still attack inorder to be able to sacrafice themselves so you can clear you own board, or remove the arbitary unit on the ground limit.  Additionally you should also add in a better tutorial that explains more of how to unlock your other factions or just have them unlocked from the start.
Last thoughts Spellweaver is probably the best pure old school style CCG out there right now, it both plays and feels like a table top card game and it is easy to be a free player and still get all the cards.  Hex would probably be the best New school style CCG.  How I define the difference between the two games is new school uses random token generation and random number values in card effects, and old school does not do any of that, it follows the rules of what you could do if you were playing with someone in person.

The Binding Of Isaac is definitely a love-hate relationship. This game is truly addictive if you really get into it. Although at a glance it appears to be repetitive and at times it can be, it has hours upon hours of fun on it. It is incredibly hard and seems to be made only for the true hardcore gamers (like me!), which I truly find amazing. You will find yourself playing this game for maybe 10 mins (or more maybe) and end up dying having to start ALL over after having some of the best powerups and getting so close to the mom battle. I love it's incredible hard gameplay. I was skeptical about the game at first and at a glance found nothing for me here, and thought not much of it due to the fact that I bought it on sale. I quit for a while, then got back into it and found myself getting sucked into it. Unlocking characters, trying to get achievements, unlocking items, and finding secrets was a lot of fun. This game is insanely good for $5 and if you're lucky like me, then you will find the game on sale at the right time. Mafia III is a really one of those games that has its moments and really has bad moments. It’s a definite “meh” overall which is why currently it has “mixed” ratings overall. The game has a great story with a totally unexpected twist that changes the entire story, however the story doesn’t do so much from just killing all the racket bosses one by one and destroying their crime operations. It’s really just: new area = target 1 of 2 crime sub bosses and destroy a high estimate of their income to draw them out to of course kill them. After that you kill the main crime boss of the area and do that for about 7 areas. The graphics are yet again one of those moments where they seem good sometimes but other seem god awful, however the gameplay and combat, driving, etc. are are top notch and I found myself loving to come back to just drive or shoot people. However there are several, several bugs that seem very easy to fix and instead the dev’s throw out ♥♥♥♥♥♥ hour long DLC’s for $15.
+New Bordeaux is a beautiful rich city that is very vibrant and alive and definitely feels different in every area
+I love the animation style of how Lincoln runs, shoots, and just overall moves in the game
+Driving is super realistic, you’ll actually die several times from high speed impacts or being shot to death whilst driving compared to a game like GTA where that’s impossible
+Felt that several of the blood splatters and deaths looked really realistic
+The “Brutal Takedowns” are so badass
+Several very awesome characters with lots of character development they are all very interesting and crazy individuals
+Besides the fact that the game is just running around going through the chain of crime bosses to the godfather, the game does have it’s moments of epic and fun missions
+Many different characters outfits
+Many cars to choose from and customization as well!
+I love the fact that you can just call someone to bring your car, or to bring a mobile armory, guys to help you, call the cops off, etc.
+Great tracks from the 60’s
+Being someone who was born in the 90’s this is a great history lesson of how life was like in the 60’s
+Some of the DLC’s are really fun and take you new and exotic areas with new and crazy characters plus new weapons and equipment items
+Love how you can see your mph
-Glitch where cutscene will play but you can’t see anything but a black screen and still hear it playing

-The mirrors in the game are so awfully put together they are like laggy on crack♥♥♥♥♥♥mirrors

The bad:

Game is either bugged, people cheat, or tooltip is entirely wrong/bugged. In some of those cases all you see is a lightining icon between the cards in combat logg so you have no clue what actually happened and why your card didn't do the damage it was supposed to despite no cypher being used by opponent, why their card did more damage than the initial tooltip said, or why that card that was intended to split it's damage did all of it to a single unit literally cheating you out of victory.
Balance seems to be bonkers, cheese strats are king, like having your opponent  hierarchy player create som 8/8 shielded monster on 2 supply, consortium flooding the entire deck and your hand with sabotage cards on 2 supply etc.
I believe this is due to the vast ammount of no cost cards, which makes these cheese strats so powerful, literally making many games pointless to play past the first or second round or even past card drawing phase.
Raid seems to be a waste of time unless you are a pro.
Game is predictable, I can literally guess which BS card my opponents will topple me with most of the times by now, I'm generally rather surprised when they do NOT play that particular BS card as they seem to always have an answer to everything you do. Especially in the ranked environment.
Game takes alot of patience, especially due to the cheating/tooltip error or whatever it is and neverending cheese strats, mine has run out.

While I only played this steam version of the game 38min, I did 4 complete playthrough in the last years with another version of the game, so I think have more than  enough experience with the game to write a short review.
It's a gorgeous rpg in a dark, gritty and mature fantasy  world. It has an very intelligent, complex and amazing written story. It has memorable and well written characters with their own motivations, actions, which doesn't just exist to help/oppose your hero. The world feels alive and is a fresh breath to all the "perfect" high fantasy world rgs. It is a world full of violence, greed,  sex, schemes, swearings and political intrigues with choices that really matter and have a huge impact on your further story Also there are no good/bad choices, only grey ones, which is a huge olus for me personaly.
Combat is average.It's a big clunky and sometims it's difficult to target enemies. They tried to make it like Dark Souls but unfortunaly failed with it. I wouldn't call it bad, but it definitly stands out in a negative way when the story, charcters and world atmosphere are so brilliant. There are also some problems with the balance. While the game is rather difficult at the beginning your character becomes to strong at about the middle of the game.
Voice acting and music is good, Graphic wise it's still one of the most beautiful rpgs, although it was released more than 3 1/2 years ago.
Summarized: If you want to play a beautiful looking (action)rpg  in a dark, gritty and atmospheric fantasy world with a brilliant story, memorable characters and huge choices and consequences you should give this game a try.

There are some video games in life that cannot be compared to anything else, and most likely, will never be comparable and will remain in their own category.
I very vaguely remember hearing about ABZU when it first was announced, and so when the day of its release arrived and all of my social media accounts were bombarded by screenshots, videos and articles about the game, that is when I realized what would make me buy this game in a matter of seconds: Matt Nava the art director behind what is hands down one of the absolute best and most beautiful game & experience I ever had in gaming, Journey, was the founded of Giant Squid, the studio behind ABZU, which is their very first game. If this wasn’t already amazing, I quickly learned that Austin Wintory, the composer behind Journey’s soundtrack (again, one of the best soundtrack of anything you will ever get to listen to), was also in on the project.
I was sold. That was it. I went on steam, purchased the game, and nearly cried at the excitement and feeling of privilege that I was suddenly filled with.
I played ABZU that very same night. I waited until everyone in my apartment complex went to bed, for the streets to go quiet, and for a nice breeze to settle and travel throughout my apartment, I wanted the right setting for what I knew without any doubt was going to be an absolutely amazing experience. After Journey, and now after ABZU, Giant Squid, and especially Matt Nava & Austin Wintory have my unwavering support in whatever project that have planned for the future. They are geniuses.
So, ABZU.
In ABZU, just like Journey, you follow some sort of neither human not clearly animal creature who is set in a beautiful and intriguing environment that you have to explore. In Journey, the goal was to get to the tower, as you learn about your people, their culture, and what possibly could have gone down in a distant or not so distant past. In ABZU the game is similarly linear but the way the game is constructed and looks invites you to explore every piece of it, its depth, its population, and to interact with the very various aquatic life that surrounds you, sometimes passively, sometimes not so much. As you are given the option to free some various types of fish, you learn a little more about the people that used to coexist with them, your people, their past, their culture, and some other things that may or may not be all that ambiguous to you.
In moments when I thought that I understood ABZU, its setting, the story it was trying to tell, things turned up on me and a lot of the aspects of the game that were simple and beautiful, remained beautiful but touched on a lot of darkness I had not expected.
As you swim, sometimes something that was a bit challenging to do in terms of being able to control your character and move exactly like you mean to, you are surrounded by what is one of the most beautifully designed video game world I have ever had the chance to experience. The color palette, the way that fish, whales and seaweed moves, and the way that the world interacts with you, truly going the opposite direction from some sort of silent observer.
Just like in Journey, Austin Wintory offers us such an incredibly amazing, powerful and unique soundtrack, songs that brought me to tears so many times, as I smiled for very various and complex reasons: that is what video game music should be like. That is what music should be like. Austin Wintory’s compositions are the hands holding the art design of ABZU, working so perfectly well together in order to transport us into a world, an atmosphere, a place that although I expected the quality of due to the amazingness that is Journey, reached a new set of highs. Went where Journey had not, excelled all of my expectations.
10/10 – In one night, ABZU became, without any possible, even the smallest of doubt, one of the very best game I have ever had the chance to play in my life. And for this, I am so proud and grateful for the existence of video games as a medium for magical storytelling.

Hi there,
I write long detailed reviews for video games. My name is FATAL and I'm reviewing the game Mafia III.
I will review the gameplay, storyline, glitches, pro's and con's.
Introduction: Mafia III is about a soldier "Lincoln Clay" who hunts down everyone and everything connected to the man who betrayed him during a mission they went on together, Mr Marcano. Seems simple but Lincoln Clay has to put his time and effort into taking this man down.
Gameplay: The gameplay is great you have different options of dressing your character up, upgrading items such as cars.
two things I did notice that I did not like is the fact you can't fast travel, you also can't manually save I mean, what game doesn't have these two options?! You can drive a car in either simulation or normal and they also added a mirror to the top of your screen when driving to see behind you. Which I never look at it, for me it's a cool but unccessary feature.
Storyline: The storyline is fantastic I love the feeling I get when I've put all my hard work into doing missions to get a cutscene so crisp and clear. The style of it all fits in perfectly with everything. Who doesn't want payback on a man who betrayed you? Who doesn't want to kill every person who ever got in your way from killing this person who betrayed your trust? I love the storyline. But also it's an obvious storyline to go for.
Graphics: The graphics in cutscenes are just beautiful. Stunning. BUT in actual gameplay it takes some time to load the textures thus making everyone and everything look glossy and all one colour, which is fine as it doesn't stay that way. So I've no complaints.
Side missions: The side missions are mixed up but they are the same as every other game. For example: "Steal a semi-truck" You steal vehicles, hunt down bad guys what's new here? Them side missions are every side mission ever made in a game. Which does make it boring and feel more like a task. I also found a lot of glitches such as side missions not appearing on the map. Or the objective just wasn't at the mission mark which means you have to progress through the story BUT they don't tell you that. Which wasted your time driving there.
Conclusion: I love mafia III's storyline but the side missions I'm not a fan of when they glitch out all the time and become repetitive after a while. I also don't like the glitch where you try to talk to someone to unlock a side mission and they don't talk... so you try to talk to them again and the option is not there. Which is annoying. But if you are into open world games with plenty of missions and a long story you're going to have a field day buying this game. I do recommend it simply because it is a very underrated game although I can see why people would be put off when there's tons of annoying, unwanted glitches.
Pro's: Long and amazing storyline
Lots of missions
Amazing graphics
Cool upgrading system
Con's: Glitches left, right and centre!
Side missions are repetitive.
Can't fast travel.
Can't manually save.
