I have played the game for 75 hours on Xbox One. Don't let the time played fool you. Here is a nice video preview which I made which'll help you decide if you want it or not.

Music is beautiful – Through the most RPG games I play the music is always top notch and beautiful. Earthlock is no exception to this and provides a beautiful soundtrack to go a long with the game. Although the soundtrack is nowhere near the level of Final Fantasy or any other big RPG games, it was still enough for me to highly praise and enjoy it.
A great RPG experience – Earthlock is everything you seek from a more ‘classic’ RPG experience. This game is turn based and relies mostly on strategy. You are level capped at 20 and towards the near end of the game the enemies get tenaciously strong. If you don’t pay attention then it’s easy to get a party wiped and hit a game over screen. There aren’t any voice overs in the game and it relies more on just being able to read the text on the screen as it pops up. I preferred this over the voice acting as it gave me more engagement.
Not the farming you’d expect – In RPG’s, especially MMO’s farming revolves around killing the same monster repetitively in the hopes of getting rare loot. Earthlock however takes the meaning literally as you have farm land in which you can plant seeds and then harvest them for materials when they are ready. I spent quite a lot of time doing farming because I enjoyed the relaxed style of it.
Character change – This is a really minor positive but one I enjoyed. I really liked how you could swap between characters when in the actual game. In some instances this required swapping to a smaller character to get to a place inaccessible by other characters.
Unique Talent and levelling system – For each character you are presented with a board full of squares where each time you  level up you get a talent point and can put a talent card in an empty square. You can also get talent points by levelling up bonds with each characters and certain squares required skills which you can find the cards in loot and chests.
Selecting an enemy to hit – Depending on your camera angle, choosing an enemy to hit can be frustrating and annoying at times because it’s super sensitive and only rotates to certain characters. This sometimes left me hitting myself and healing enemies.
A lot of the NPCs are just filler – Most the NPCs in the town just wander around aimlessly providing no text option or talk. Even in certain cities they were walking around and into each other stuck in an endless cycle of doom. The walking detection on them was very poor.
Camera Angles – The camera angles on the game are not so great. It uses the fixed camera pivoting in one position. On some scenes this caused a huge amount of frustration and some scenes where running into a blind corner led into me running straight into enemy mobs.
No option to sell – Being a hoarder sometimes I would get duplicates of items I wouldn’t want duplicates of, for instance seeds and recipes. I wish there was an option to sell so I could sort my inventory out perfectly the way I want things.
No minimaps – The only map on the Earthlock is the overworld map. I would’ve loved if they had an area map too with the location name. For instance, I had no idea where “Konkylian Plains” were and when referencing a boss is located there makes it hard to find.
You. Are. Dead – Later on in the game there is Ice Regions of Nunaar Station. This part of the game is absolutely dreadful and almost ruined my entire experience of the game due to frustration and unfairness. The enemies are mobbed together in clumps meaning there is no way to sneak around very well or escape them and you will most likely fight between six to eight enemies per fight. These monsters are overpowered with deadly aoes and a very high attack speed that even when it was their turn I knew my maxed characters were going to die. The sound of ice constantly crunching and crackling was a very big nuisance and one which I did not like, I had to mute the games audio.
Overall, I really enjoyed my time playing Earthlock and it provided me my fix of turn based RPG games which I really missed due to them being viewed as “outdated” or “old”. Earthlock was not brilliant and certainly flawed at times but I still enjoyed the experience it provided and really enjoyed my time playing it. DISCLAIMER: I have almost no time online, and the few times I did so, I had an awful connection.  I will not comment on net code, because I almost never have access to reliable, playable internet.  I will say that I did not have an issue finding a lobby during the day, but that may have changed since writing this.  This review is 100% centred around local play.
This game hits everything in the right spot.  The physics and overall speed make for a very enjoyable game.  The lack of control of your aiming is actually a feature, and adds to the fast paced competitive nature of the game.  Some guns(such as the magnum revolver) will raise your aim due to rapid fire recoil.  The AK47, as well as shot guns, have various spreading techniques that can be used to hit an enemy despite not being at the exact same level of height as them.  There aren't too many OP weapons; the weapon spawn/pickup system makes it so you can get yourself out of sticky situations if you are skilled enough.  Though I will say right now, the net gun is frustrating.  Fast firing and projectile speed, helpful physical properties, above average range(it will beat out medium range weapons), is unaffected by prop cover, and leaves you completely vulnerable to just about anything if hit.  The most comparable weapon to it is the mind control gun, which is much shorter range and leaves the user vulnerable while using it on someone else.
This fits the bill(ha...) for a competitive, pick-up-and-play style of multi player game.  The controls are simple and responsive.  The workshop has a lot of hats for you to add to the already absurd in game collection, as well as a few extra weapons and a plethora of maps.  Quality of said workshop items are all over the place, but there is enough good stuff to make it worth looking into.  The potential for "HYPE" moments is very high in this game; even without adding modifiers, you will have a lot of jaw dropping moments of awesomeness, that you may or may not see in another round ever again.  Even with the RNG elements and basic game play, this game is very skill based.  It will be clear as day who the best duck is in your group.
The retro style soundtrack isn't something to write home about, but it fits in nicely and gets you in the mood for action.  The pixel graphics move smoothly, and are overall pretty appealing.  As far as the in game sounds... satisfying, every sound is top notch and fuels the aforementioned hype.
The single player isn't much to talk about either, but its a decent addition for the game for when you don't have anyone to play with.
The price may seem a bit steep for what your getting, but the value comes from the game play, not the content.  Sale or no sale, this will always be a great addition to your multi player get together game collection.

I've found this game on
and instabought it, worth it.
The mechanics are based on 倉庫番 (sōkoban) which is a type of transport puzzle.
In this game, the player will push atoms (displayed as Lewis' Ionic dot structure) to form molecules (Lewis Theory of Bonding).
After completing the task, it will display a small info card about that completed molecule.
It is pretty educational but if the molecule repeats, it won't give you any new factoid :(
The sound of this game is just special and unique. The feedback sounds are diffused amazingly in the ambient background, building up a very calm scenario. For a non time-based puzzle, I didn't expected such good sound works. But like the molecules information, the sounds are very limited too.
The game progression is very simple, it follows the complexity of the molecules. The maps can be solved using single-agent search algorithm. But sokoban are known as NP-hard problems (Non-deterministic Polynomial-time hard). The puzzles can exponentially grow the branching factor of the moves which can be very challenging.
Sokoban can be a very entertaining way to keep your brain active but cannot be considered a game for the casual.

Sokobond features a minimalistic and yet slick artstyle, underlined by great, atmospheric music (by Rob Roth, who you might know from Starseed Pilgrim and Electronic Super Joy). The gameplay is a block-pushing puzzler at it's very core, however with increased bonding, your molecule grows larger and thus movements gets restricted. This unique twist adds fresh flavour to the genre and without much knowledge in chemistry, you'll soon find a lot of intriguing fun facts thrown towards you for completing level after level. The game does grow very challenging later on, but only after you grew accustomed to the basic mechanics. Progression is well done. I do have some minor gripes with the rather classical Helium levels and some levels that require larger molecules, nontheless, overall Sokobond is a
game and should be picked up by fans of the genre. The average gamer should wait for a sale though, as Sokobond is not ground breaking, however competent in what it wants to achieve.

LiEat is a super simple JRPG that features the extramily adorable Efi- Efina if you want her full name- and... Well he's got a lot of names. I loved them both as well as the supporting cast, each with a visually distinct design and their own little quirks. The story of the first two sections is very simple and are likely more focused on getting the player accustomed to the controls and aquainted with the characters. It builds up the mystery that is much more elaborated on in the 3rd part- not that it doesnt introduce its own cast of course. Think of them as one game rather than three, least thats how I do it. They are enjoyable on their own of course, but they are fairly simple imo.
I absolutely adore this game, miwashibas works are some of my favorite of these little rpgs [and I guess perhaps visual novels as of 1bitheart, would you call it that?] and their art is honestly just beautiful. That alone makes me love the game just a bit more- I'm a sucker for art as an artist myself.
The combat is simple [Albiet perhaps a little too much so, but I'm not particualrly skilled at games a lot so it's a easy game for me to pick up and play] and the controls are easy to get accosomed to. I only had one problem when I was starting the 3rd one, my controller wouldn't get picked up by the game. But, I played something else for a bit and when I went back it was fine. Who knows what happened.
While the writing and story are very much simple but very nice to read I did feel it was a tad short. Even spread over 3 games. The buildup is very nice but the finale of the 3rd game felt just a tad fast. This isn't a problem exclusive to this game- I had a similar problem with 1bitheart [I haven't experienced AliceMare recently, I might pick that up soon] but I don't retract much with it.
Overall, I'd defeinitely recommend this game. With a very nice soundtrack and a incredibly heartwarming story I'm glad its reached a bigger audience [aka on steam and not just online haha]

The Binding Of Isaac is definitely a love-hate relationship. This game is truly addictive if you really get into it. Although at a glance it appears to be repetitive and at times it can be, it has hours upon hours of fun on it. It is incredibly hard and seems to be made only for the true hardcore gamers (like me!), which I truly find amazing. You will find yourself playing this game for maybe 10 mins (or more maybe) and end up dying having to start ALL over after having some of the best powerups and getting so close to the mom battle. I love it's incredible hard gameplay. I was skeptical about the game at first and at a glance found nothing for me here, and thought not much of it due to the fact that I bought it on sale. I quit for a while, then got back into it and found myself getting sucked into it. Unlocking characters, trying to get achievements, unlocking items, and finding secrets was a lot of fun. This game is insanely good for $5 and if you're lucky like me, then you will find the game on sale at the right time. The thing that sucks about the game is the fact that it is written in Flash which really limits what the game can do and you can definitely notice the limitation. It also lags my computer and can get annoying occasionally but definitely a small price to pay for this truly addicting fun game. If you don't want to deal with the limitations, lag and all that with The Binding Of Isaac then I would recommend waiting for The Binding Of Isaac: Rebirth which in case you don't know, is a full remake of the game that isn't in Flash. It consists of the original game, Wrath of the Lamb, and even more in 16 bit with tons of fun packed in! Sadly there isn't a specific release date announced yet, but is said to release in the first quarter of 2014. So you should expect to see Rebirth by march at the latest hopefully. But I would have to give this game an 8/10. It would get either a 9/10 or 10/10 if it weren't for Flash but like I said, Rebirth is coming out and that will probably be 10/10

This game combines rhythm and roguelike like fried chicken and waffles. If you haven't experienced them together, you think it's a bizarre combo that won't mesh well. Then you try it and you wonder why you haven't had the two together before. Where has this magical combo been your entire life?
Gimmick aside, the game is still beautifully designed. The enemies all have tells and literally have choreographed attacks. Everything gives signs before the action takes place, much like many roguelikes. It's just that this game took that dance and set it to a kickin' soundtrack. You can even practice against enemies without needing to throw yourself into the deep end to figure out their tells.
Even the characters are more upbeat and lively than your average roguelike. The little things, like how they greet NPCs (shyly VS boldly VS force of habit) and their surprised reactions to teleportation make them seem less like digital avatars and more like humans. A little detail that adds a lot of magic to the game.
[edit] THE STORY. Add the story to another fantastic bit of this game. Only frustrating bit is how hard it is to complete story mode, but hey, it's a roguelike. That's to be expected from the genre.
TL;DR - A wonderfully charming game that blends two very different genres in a lovingly-designed piece. I strongly recommend you pick up the game and the soundtrack!

The answer is yes. I know what you're thinking, and this game pretty much plays just like Hearthstone.
PROS
If you've played Hearthstone, you'll pretty much know how to play this game right away. Firepower and Spell Damage, Assault and Windfury, or Cyphers and Secrets, etc. etc. In my opinion, it's not a bad thing to be similar. You know what they say, "if it ain't broke, don't fix it." The core Hearthstone mechanics are here. Draw some cards, gain a point of mana, play some cards, rinse and repeat... Though there's only a handful of mechanics that are different, there's enough to force different strategies. Take for example, the Module mechanic, it's pretty much a Hero Power, but you're allowed to customize these in a way that dictates your deck.
And on a side note, the cards are pretty nice to look at.
CONS
Game plays very slowly and it's quite easy to screw up your turns. Hate to sound like a broken record, but with Hearthstone, you can pretty much play all your cards, end  your turn, and watch it play out. Try this with Star Crusde and I guarantee you it'll ignore 50% of your moves and still let you end your turn. So what happens is, you have to play one card at a time and wait for it to play out before playing your next card.
This game's version of Arcane Dust is Scrap. However, disenchanting/scrapping cards barely returns any Scrap and most of the cards are friggin' expensive. Almost not worth it to even try and scrap anything.
And lastly, this game's  version of Arenas, called Raids. You have to pay with your Gold/Credits or use real money just to get in. It's a giant barrier to entry when you get bored of the standard play mode.
EXTRA
Yeah, this game is Early Access, so it's a given that there's not that many people. However, more often than not, I find myself paired up with the same person over and over again. Almost becomes habit to just take turns and concede.
There is a few non important bugs but this game is one of those games that is just extreeemly fun to play

A great combination of a roguelike and a rhythm game. It borrows elements from games like Speluny and Binding of Isaac - permanent item/character unlocks, a daily challenge, and of course random level generation and permadeath. The rhythm aspect makes it unique - unlike most rhythm games, you don't have to hit a particular button at a particular time, but there is a lot of strategy in getting the timing right to kill enemies and avoid damage - strategy which is enriched by the variety of enemy move/attack patterns and a number of items that affect your own movement and attack. It's all about planning ahead, and thinking fast so you don't lose the beat.

Currently this is my favorite CCG.  I say this as someone who has played Hearthstone, MTG (online and IRL), Might and Magic, and Runescape Legends - just to name a few CCG.  Yet I like this one the best, why?  First of all I simply prefer the aesthetic of this game.  It is the only futuristic card game that I have played in a seemingly endless tide of medieval-fantasy.  That and it is the only CCG I've found where it is truly possible to excel and progress meaningfully, in terms of rank and card collection, without throwing tons of money.  Many CCGs are free-to-play but, oftentimes, pay-to-win-more.  Note that this is how things stand as of the moment I am writing this review; and, as it stands, I have been able to keep a solid winrate and acquire many high-end cards without needing to pay anything.  As someone with not a lot of cash, this is fantastic.
Many will compare this game to Hearthstone, and while that is true (they are very similar on multiple points), the new mechanics of having multiple, exchangeable hero powers and also have Energy as a second resource to Supply makes this game feel completely new and fresh.  As someone who played Hearthstone from the beta, I now find Star Crusade to be a much more compelling experience simply because the devs are not afraid to print cards that are extremely powerful or can create mega combos.  Right of the gate some of the best cards in the game are given to you as basics - it's just up for you to figure them out.
Personally, I have had tons of fun with this game and I cannot understand why it is so poorly received.  Most likely, people have not given it the time of day to understand that Star Crusade does enough different to excite someone who has played other CCGs while maintaining a similar formula that will leave you feeling comfortable.  It is vastly underrated - I love this game, as it stands so far.

But it is definitely worth a play, especially if you can pick it up for cheap, which it regularly seems to be.
One thing I will say, when playing full screen this game forced my 144hz monitor into displaying 60hz. I tried the most commonly referenced fix listed on forums (i.e. setting hz rate in nvidia control panel) which didn't fix the problem for me. Playing in windowed was fine and allowed my monitor to run at 144hz but as soon as i entered full screen it capped back to 60hz. This game does not have a borderless windowed mode option. What did work, was using a very small, tidy, unobtrusive bit of software called windowed borderless gaming which forces the windowed mode into borderless windowed, this worked a charm and I played what looked like full screen but was actually windowed so 144hz. That said, even with a 1080 I was only getting roughly around 60fps at 1440p (most settings on max) - but it does look good!!

Orcs Must Die! Unchained is an absolutely wonderful game. Over 120 hours so far and counting.

Earning the regular currency called "Skulls" is quite easy to get. You can earn them from playing matches, completing missions, buying them from the shop, or claiming the daily rewards that are offered.
Earning the special currency called "Gold" is harder to get as you can only get it from daily rewards or by buying it from the shop.
This game does not make you feel pressured to buy anything in the shop. The game is not pay 2 play and you can earn everything with time and skill.
The traps that are unlockable by opening chests or buying them for a one time deal in the daily trap shop are not unlockable using gold, or skulls. You need to level up in order to have the traps appear in the chests and trap shop. Sure, you can buy lots of skulls and upgrade your traps as much as you can with them, but that requires that you actually have the required amount of that trap to upgrade it, which as I previously stated, you cannot buy unless it is in the daily trap shop.
I could go over more but I won't because I am too lazy.
Overall, 10/10, not a pay 2 play.

What comprises a good game is something very different in each of our minds. To each is own. But certainly one of the most important aspects of a successful product, is one that moves you. Makes you think. Or stops you from thinking and allows you to just be in the moment. That is Abzu.
Giant Squid, makers of the uber popular mini-game on PS3, Journey, are back for more with this beautifully rendered emotional underwater adventure. Abzu is just that, an adventure. There aren't any creatures or baddies to fight. There aren't any major obstacles standing in your way of completing the charming--albeit short--story line. Just like its predecessor before, Journey, the story is one that slowly rolls itself onto you by the unique, cleverly scripted story that happens around you as you explore your surroundings.
The art design is beautiful and simple, the sound and music are all wonderful and appropriate. And the gameplay is smooth and elegant. I had some framerate issues with my settings on ultra, but I only have a mid-range gaming machine, so that is understandable. If, however, you needed to, the game scales well to your hardware without losing a ton of fidelity. The beauty isn't in the fidelity anyway, the real beauty is in the charming art direction and execution.
Giant Squid loves to pull on your heart strings and make you consider existence. Make you think about the fabric of life and the universe around us. Journey had you take a trip to the afterlife, and I feel...I feel like Abzu took me on the journey of creation and evolution. Starting in the sea as we once did, Abzu's linear story paints a portrait of creation to its player. New species are unlocked and seamlessly become a member of the ecosystem as you play. A great many larger underwater creatures are spawned...er...created as well, like the Blue Whale who makes an appearance in the later scenes of the game. One of the joys and cool mechanics of this game is the ability to grapple on to the larger aquatic creatures and have them pull you along. While latched on, you are able to control the creature, or just hold on and see where she takes you.
Overall Abzu succeeds at what it wants to deliver. An experience that moves you, and allows you to let go and sink into the story. Although too short, I definitely think this is worth the purchase.

DISCLAIMER: I have almost no time online, and the few times I did so, I had an awful connection.  I will not comment on net code, because I almost never have access to reliable, playable internet.  I will say that I did not have an issue finding a lobby during the day, but that may have changed since writing this.  This review is 100% centred around local play.
This game hits everything in the right spot.  The physics and overall speed make for a very enjoyable game.  The lack of control of your aiming is actually a feature, and adds to the fast paced competitive nature of the game.  Some guns(such as the magnum revolver) will raise your aim due to rapid fire recoil.  The AK47, as well as shot guns, have various spreading techniques that can be used to hit an enemy despite not being at the exact same level of height as them.  There aren't too many OP weapons; the weapon spawn/pickup system makes it so you can get yourself out of sticky situations if you are skilled enough.  Though I will say right now, the net gun is frustrating.  Fast firing and projectile speed, helpful physical properties, above average range(it will beat out medium range weapons), is unaffected by prop cover, and leaves you completely vulnerable to just about anything if hit.  The most comparable weapon to it is the mind control gun, which is much shorter range and leaves the user vulnerable while using it on someone else.
This fits the bill(ha...) for a competitive, pick-up-and-play style of multi player game.  The controls are simple and responsive.  The workshop has a lot of hats for you to add to the already absurd in game collection, as well as a few extra weapons and a plethora of maps.  Quality of said workshop items are all over the place, but there is enough good stuff to make it worth looking into.  The potential for "HYPE" moments is very high in this game; even without adding modifiers, you will have a lot of jaw dropping moments of awesomeness, that you may or may not see in another round ever again.  Even with the RNG elements and basic game play, this game is very skill based.  It will be clear as day who the best duck is in your group.
The retro style soundtrack isn't something to write home about, but it fits in nicely and gets you in the mood for action.  The pixel graphics move smoothly, and are overall pretty appealing.  As far as the in game sounds... satisfying, every sound is top notch and fuels the aforementioned hype.
The single player isn't much to talk about either, but its a decent addition for the game for when you don't have anyone to play with.
The price may seem a bit steep for what your getting, but the value comes from the game play, not the content.  Sale or no sale, this will always be a great addition to your multi player get together game collection.

Combat is fun, although since you can't choose which heroes are free on each week, you might have to stick with boring heroes or ones that don't fit your playstyle (unless you're willing to pay).
There should be a sort of tutorial mode against dummies where you could try out heroes you don't have and then make a decision on whether you want to buy them. Right now, the only way to tell if they're any good is if a bot randomly picks it or if you play against a player who bought that hero.
Dragon Mode (the PVE mode) is has a lot of potential but is pretty glitchy: AI spells (such as Totems) don't consider the dragon nor the floating balls as enemies, so they do nothing, and equipment items that benefit from hitting targets don't consider the dragon nor crystals/barriers as targets, so they do nothing. That's a huge chunk of the store that becomes useless in PVE.
Rewards for killing the dragon are ridiculously low (3 doubloons per kill, while a new hero costs over 1000 doubloons), which makes it a pretty unrewarding way to play.
Net code is also a little weird, as I can't even figure out if hits are decided from the attacker's perspective or the defender's. Even in games with ping below 50ms, hit detection is pretty wonky.
In the end, it's a free game which can provide you with a few hours of fun, but there's a lot of room for improvement. Even playing with friends doesn't make it significantly more fun, especially since the PVE reward is so underwhelming.

If anything, this game is cute, fun, and totally worth the price. LiEat is about a partnership of a lie-eating dragon and a master liar. Together they solve mysteries and find out the truth. The concept itself is interesting and fun enough already.
The story and the gameplay are very simple, which is both a positive asset and a shortcoming. On one hand, you get to understand what's going on right off the bat and it doesn't get any more complicated as you go. This allows you to enjoy the characters' personalities and dialogues rather than having your mind preoccupied with every detail you come across. On the other hand, it takes away the mysteriousness of the detective-esque scenarios. There is no wrong answers or missed clues. All you need to do is talk to everyone and kill monsters to finish the stories. The plot comes off as shallow and it makes it too easy but it's fun to go through nonetheless, and at the end of the day, that's what matters most.
A biggest part of the experience is the very stylish design. From the interface, to the sprites, to the CGs. Not to mention the beautifully animated cutscenes. The music throughout is also very ambient and appropriate to the situation. The second biggest part is the characters. The energetic and optimistic Efina is easily the most fun character to interact with or play as. She is ever so energetic and optimistic. Her childish personality is very entertaining, and it complements the serious, albeit playful, attitude of her partner, the master liar.
What I personally liked most about this game is the chemistry of the two main protagonists which I think is very cleverly constructed. The game has three parts. Each deals with different stories to tell and mysteries to solve. It would be nice to see more sequels for this series.
Would I recommend this game? To a particular group of people, definitely. This isn't a game for all tastes, but for its target audience, I'm sure it will be highly appreciated, especially Efina.

I've played a lot of basic rpg games that have mediocre music and graphics and unispired stories, and let me tell you, this is not one of them!
First off, the graphics in this game are beautifully stylized. The characters look colorful and unique without overshadowing the very pretty, if somewhat small, world maps. The game generally sticks to a 16 bit style, although its cheating and going a bit over that limit- to good effect. Interspersed in there are hand drawn frames, stills and animated scenes normally about 3-5 seconds long, that have a simple but colorful style to them that mesh with the normal graphics very well.
I was not expecting anything more than a 10 second loop track or four with this game and boy was I wrong! This game has at least 8 tracks that are over 1-2 minutes long for each chapter, and I rather liked quite a few of them. They are left open in the games files so you can drag them right onto a music player. They are very soothing to listen to, many of them are quiet music box ones but there are some others that are more robust.
The gameplay itself is rather basic rpg format. turn based with limited ability menus. There are item upgrades if you want to search the wold maps but I found that it really wasnt neccessary until the final chapter when you have to battle a fairly tough boss without your AP recovery guy around. The game itself is extremely short, clocking in at around 4 hours for me to unlock all endings, but I still haven't unlocked over half the acheivements.
The story is engaging if you like fantasy. Its nothing too mind blowing but still enough to make you cry a little. Reminds me of a Miyazaki film a bit. The characters are easy to grow attached to.
Over all I really enjoyed Lieat a lot more than I thought I would, and highly recommend it for anyone looking for an easier game to chill and get lost in for an evening.

Decent graphics for a game its age, and quite a lot of bang for your buck given its relatively low price tag. That said, the story is essentially non-existent and the gameplay is pretty shallow - you basically just run through randomly-generated dungeons killing hordes of monsters while completing meaningless quests. Gameplay follows a pretty simple formula:
- Go to town. Buy gear. Get quests.
- Go to dungeon. Kill monsters. Find loot. Complete quests.
- Go back to town. Sell loot. Get quest rewards.
And then you more or less just repeat until you get bored. It's pretty standard dungeon-crawler faire.
Now, if you really like generic dungeon crawlers and are a big fan of the action/RPG genre, you'll probably have fun with this game, though you might be better off going with something like Titan Quest if you want a bit more depth.
In sum, FATE is a good game to pick up if you're just looking for a simple dungeon-crawler to play. It won't be the greatest game you play all year, but it won't be the worst either. All things considered, it's worth the $7.99 price tag.

Let me start by saying I cried twice while playing this game.
The second time it took me a while to stop.
Never before have i played a game with a story so strong and heart-tugging that i had to constantly stop just to take a deep breath.
Dust: An Elysian Tail is a side-scrolling adventure like no other. The character development. voice work, and plot are so prefected i can't even begin to describe it.
The gameplay is smooth and flawless. While yes, you can only have one sword (It's essential to the plotline), its one hell of a sword. The enemies, minibosses and bosses are colorful and unique, and through my 10 hours of playing my first game i never stopped experimenting with combo's. (That 1000 point combo.... damn!)
Your little companion, Fidget, has to be the most adorable character i've ever seen in a game of this type. I fell i love with her sarcasm and tough-girl act immediately. Her range moves also helped me through many a tough spot. But really the main reason i like having her around is becuase i can always count on her to make me smile in the darker parts of the game.
This game may be rated E, but thats a stretch. Some moments in this game really play your heart strings. Like i said before, i cried twice, and i dont cry often. The story makes this game, it really does.
The item and shop system is a masterpiece. I found myself returning to familiar places to collect up on new supplies to sell, trade and send to the blacksmith for better stuff. There are hundreds of items from sword augments to armor to food (Don't eat the Mysterious Wall Chicken. It's mysterious.) to jewelry.
The soundtrack hit spot on in this game. I did, more than once, find myself standing still on a level just to hear the beautiful, spooky, or just plain awesome music.
The average playthrough of this game is about 10 hours. That;s how long it took me. If you rush you could probably do it in 8. if you take the time to do all the side quests and collect all the best items you could be at this game for 50 hours or more.
It's worth it though.
NOTE: Once you complete the game, you cannot return to the world. make sure you do everything you want to BEFORE you take on the ending.
This game is (If played in normal or higher) not a cake walk. It's a hard game that challenges you to experiment and get creative. There are moments where you will be gritting your teeth. The final boss battle was so intense i was off my chair.
(If you play on casual, the game is MUCH more relaxed, since the death sysem reverts to a "Lose EXP, but keep playing" system.)
As far as visuals go: My god. The game is beautifully crafted. Never before have i seen a side-scroller quite like this. It's just breathtaking, it really is.
All in all, this game is a masterpiece that deserves far more attention than it gets. Buy it now, i promise you you will not be sorry.

It doesn't feel like you're losing games on a 50/50 coin toss, but rather on the strength of your deck and your piloting of it.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a side scrolling combat game, it has the look and some - thank god - downgraded combat from Street Fighter 3/4.
The story is heartwarming and very interesting. It never felt boring or long drawn out.
You are starting as an unkown soldier who gets called "Dust".
He is constantly trying to find an answer who he really is and soon he will realize that he will face a bigger threat than he actually thought of.
As you progress you will remember more and more of the past and learn who you really are.
Your cute, little flying companion called Fidget is  travelling beside you on the adventure, she is the gatekeeper of the sword.
The sword that got awakend through your "hands" is called Ahrah and can talk to you. I would describe Ahrah has your mentor.
The NPC' s in this game are all very unique. Each with its own dialogues and background story.
By far the most interesting NPC is your companion Fidget imo. Her dialogues are funny and pretty well structured.
The mainstory and the characters bound to the main story are well thought and I had a ton of fun doing and listening to the main story quests.
While this game has a lot of funny dialogues and easter eggs it also has some really sad parts which made me sometimes cry.
(Not sure if good or bad, lol)
The dialogues are all unique and most of them are pretty funny. Some of them are sad.
The element of sarcasm was used alot and.
I really liked the voice acting in this game. It really felt "alive".
Most of them are decent sized, but 10-20% are pretty large.
Its a cartoonish look with some really detailed combat animations. It really fits this genre and theme.
Some of the environment changes as you use specific skills.
Every area has its own climate.
There are grassy, rainy, windy, snowy and dark areas.
Not really much more to say.
(I played this game from the beginning with a controller, never tested it with keyboard + mouse)
The combat is pretty smooth and easy to learn. You are starting with only some bunch of sword attacks but as you progress you will get more and more useful combos and your companion also will gain new skills which you can combine  with yours while fighting.
Pretty interesting is also the aspect that you can parry enemy attacks and counter them afterwards.
As you progress - learn new skills - and master them, the game becomes more and more fun to play.
At the beginning of your adventure the enemies are pretty weak and not a big threat. But as you progress through the game and discover new areas, the enemies will get stronger and stronger.
Some of the enemies you will encounter are dodging and require some decent tactics.
After every level up you gain 1 skill point. There is not an in depth skill tree.
You can choose between 4 attributes. (HP, Damage, Defense and Skillpower)
I dont really think an in depth skill tree would make sense at this game. It would only complicate and slow down the action oriented gameplay imo.
All in all you gain level quite quick. Pretty fast leveling until ~40ish.
After some 2-3 hours into the game you will get to a blacksmith.
In exchange for the blueprints and the materials you will get some really good equipment.
There is a weapon slots, armor slots, 2 rings and 1 amulet slot.
The equipment is not visible as you change it.
You dont have to farm for materials.
If you collect a specific material one, and sell this to a vendor, the vendor starts selling this specific material in the future.
All in all the equipment and crafting is pretty simple.
While the game was developed by 1 person, the sound actually came from a specific sound studio.
Every map has its own sound and music.
In most of the games I played, the sound got pretty boring after a while and I switched to some own background music.
In my 15-20 hours of gameplay the sound and the music never got on my nerves.
There are like ~20 sidequests beside the main story which you can optionally complete. They will grant you Exp/ Gold and sometimes items.
At most of them you have to collect items, kill monsters or find some lost NPC's.
Good thing is: You will complete most of them by actually following the main quest.
Every map contains some puzzles or hidden treasures. Some of them are easter eggs from other games.
After you enter a new map which contains a treasure, your companion Fidget will tell you that.
Your minimap will also tell you if you collected all treasures of a map.
A circle on the map means that you have treasures left to collect, a dot means that you collected all treasures of that map part.
Most of them are easy to find and simple to unlock.
There are 6 instances called "Cirelian Trials", you will stumble across them while progressing through the game.
The are a great help at keeping the gameplay fresh.
They are basically a mix of jumping puzzles and speedrunning through a specific area.
You have to make it through the whole trial in time, without getting hit by the traps and beside that you have to destory some sort of "candle bearer" to get points.
After you completed a trial you will most of the time get really good equipment parts.

It is a real shame, b/c the game has a lot of good ideas, and it's only a few decisions that really screw it up; but I have to give it a thumbs down.
The problem really comes once you get your 2nd party member, & realize that the action choice is for the ENTIRE party. As is item & magic.
That's right... each turn of combat is picking ONE thing the ENTIRE party does, you literally can make ONE decision per turn.
Also, the fight action for both you and the enemy is un-directed, attacks from ea. character/enemy tries to hit every opponent in the combat.
Both of these choices combine to throw almost all tactical depth out the window.
This is the first RPG game I have ever played where getting a 2nd character became a liability... b/c instead of that character giving you an additional tactical choice each turn,
they essentially just become an extra fight attack. An extra attack with its own, lower health bar that you have to waste time with defend/item action to keep alive,
sacrificing the attack that could have come for your other, full health hero.
The simple additions of letting you choose an action for each character, and requiring players to choose which enemy/group of enemies to attack,
would have made the experience so much better. As it is the grind is REALLY noticeable, and tactical choice is restricted to knowing to cast the element the enemy is weak to a lot.
I have an inkling that they were trying to mainly imitate the original Dragon Quest... without taking into account that in the original DQ you didn't have a party, and you fought only a single enemy at a time.
Later DQ games, with more player characters, you got to do multiple actions per turn, and you had to decide what enemy you hit with an attack command.
In addition to royally screwing up the battle mechanics, they game cheaps out on having towns you can actually explore. most cases you walk over a town and just get a menu to rest/shop/etc.
I'm just really, really disapointed. The game runs well, they got the aesthetic spot on, the world & story are interesting...
& if they had just put the time in to flesh out mechanics instead of taking shortcuts, ESPECIALLY with the combat, this would be a positive review.
And the changes to the battle mechanics are not, to put it bluntly, rocket science. We're talking basic features present in some of the oldest genre games.

Another Star isn't going to wow you with incredible cutscenes, complex battle mechanics or a very intricate story. But what it will do however is surprise you with a very heavy dose of nostalgia, especially if you grew up with a Sega console.
The game is basically a tribute to the RPGs of old where the mechanics couldn't be complicated and the presentation was very basic due to hardware limitation. If you ever played the early Phantasy Star or even Dragon Quest, you'll feel right at home.
The game has a few options to configure the overall look, defaulting to using a shader to emulate the feel of a CRT screen. While it can be disabled rather easily, I would suggest leaving it active while adjusting the curvature to your liking. The shader will also add scanlines to make the pixels stand out somewhat more as well.
The music track uses a soundchip similar to old Sega consoles and the score is rather pleasant to listen to. Props to the composer as the music, even by the game's end, wasn't hard on the ear. Sounds used for combat were simple but also intended as such.
The overall story is told through very short cutscenes with textboxes without actual animations. In fact, the game have characters show up instantly in their places then disappear when no longer needed. The world design uses a similar simplistic look which requires a good dose of imagination to enjoy.
Towns are visited on the world map and while there are no transition to 'town maps', the options offered usually offer a bit of lore about what is currently going on in the world. In fact, I was surprised by how quickly the dialog changed with every step of your quest and how each consultation often described an event in the form of paragraphs you'd usually find in "Make your own adventure" books. It gave the game a lot of personality and was unexpectedly engaging.
The overall experience of the game can be configured to be either inline with old games' difficulty by adjusting the difficulty of battles (enemy damage vs player damage) and growth rates (rapid gain of XP and ressources or slower up to including a 'need 4x more XP than normal).
The battle system is turn-based, using simple commands that determines the party's actions. An unique trait is that there is no actual targetting since any action affects either the player's or enemy's party. For example, if a regular attack is used then each character in the party will attack every other character of the other party. If a spell is used, then all enemies are affected or all allies are.
Speaking of which, the magic system in the game doesn't use MP but are all cast from HP. This would be problematic if the game didn't also let you recover roughly 40% of your HP when the combat ends and about 15% while defending. Each character receives a unique set of spells and using one takes the whole turn, meaning your allies do not attack. Luckily, the same is true for enemies using any form of ability : if an enemy uses an action other than attacking or defending, then only that character acts.
It is an interesting way to speed up combat and once the variety of spell elements and their effects are mastered, some rather unique strategies can be made for boss battles.
Encounters are random though you have the option to ignore a warning "!" to skip a battle if you only wish to zip through  an area (much like the system used in Wild Arms 2)... however, any "!!" must be triggered else the party gets ambushed on the first turn. Considering how short battles are however, grinding for XP and ressources isn't too taxing.
Another Star is a fun experience. I went in not expecting much but Vision Riders Entertainment surprised me very much by their product. When you hear about steam and its massive library of games, people sometimes talk about hidden gems. I'm talking about the real hidden gems here, not the ones that are well known by now, but those games with not many reviews and which are fairly unknown. I can now say i've stumbled into one of those with 'Another Star'. This retro 8-bit console RPG insipired game is just awesome and a must have if you are into the whole retro-vibe/feel in modern games.
It plays its retro card very well, for example the CRT emulation is the best i have ever seen, even in official emulators. It was just so convincing that while playing on my big TV in the living room, i sometimes forgot i was playing on a modern LED TV. The music and sound effects are all delivered through Yamaha sound chip emulation which is again spot on. An amazing effort in making the game look and feel so retro authentic.
And with the feel we hit another topic that is executed to perfection. It has all the mechanics and limitations of those early JRPG console games. There is no build-in world map, there is no mission log, so keep paper and pencil ready to take lots of notes. The combat is turn based, operated through menus, that will be familiar to a lot of retro gamers. However, a lot of the frustating bit, that plague the original classics, have been left out or have been improved.
Combat is very balanced, not to easy and not to difficult, you will die a lot of times (there is a battle-retry option after you die), but it is fair almost all of the time. In case it does get too difficult, it is possible to decrease the difficulty.
Being an RPG, the story is important, and it is a great tale, with the usual unexpected twists and turns, funny moments, deaths of popular characters and a slew of memorable characters you start to take in as the story progresses. Excellent writing and never a dull moment as there are so many side quests and hidden secrets in the game that in my +30 hours playthrough i feel i have only discovered half of it.

So, if you screw up and want to reload a game you cannot use 'quit' and reload, because it will overwrite your only previous good save.
In short, I can't recommend this game enough, if it would have been released in 1984 instead of 2014, it would have been one for the books, one we would still be talking about today as we do of the original Final Fantasy series. It really is that good.
The game works perfectly on SteamOS/Linux, i don't suspect it to be that resource heavy, so it should play well on less powerful machines. Excellently playable with the Steam controller and streams like a charm to the Steam Link for you to fully enjoy on your big TV.

I'm don't normally write reviews or recommendations, but I truly enjoyed Another Star.  It was a throwback to classic style RPG games, but can be played at a much faster pace.  I enjoyed the retro sprite graphics and the music was overall fitting and catchy (like an earworm, but enjoyable).  Random Battles are not an issue since you have the option to skip them.  Leveling does not have that significant grind-y feel and fights can be fairly quick since all characters in your team attack together (no micromanaging turns) and if you take the time to explore learn magics and exploit enemy weaknesses most enemies fall within 1-2 turns (except bosses of course).  It is easy to near the end max out your characters and feel very overpowered, but it was an earned feeling.  The game itself can be difficult or hard depending on how much time you'd like to put into exploring the very vast overworld.  There are secrets in almost every map, so it encourages you to check out every nook and cranny (and revisit some areas later on).  My main complaint was the limited inventory space.  I would frequently have to throw away items, to make room for new ones, which can be an issue when you don't know what they do.  Near the end, I felt scrolls were the most useless once you learned all the basic element spells for each character.  Anyway, if you'd like an enjoyable short 10 hr rpg experience that satisfies the old-school turn based itch.  This one does it.

I STILL play OMD2.  This game is in no way OMD3.  This is a shameless cash grab.  Traps are an afterthough; they will do some dmg to orcs and slow them down a bit, but not much else.  They hide behind their greedy pay-to-win attitude by saying "Its free!  What do you expect?" even when it is obvious that this game was designed from its core for micro-transactions.  I would have paid money for OMD3.
It seems they tried very hard to make this game the next League of Legends.  Its is all combat related and highly focused on team play.  Its an eyes on the mana and cool down bar to spam specials kind of game.
Most combat is like this - Run to trouble spot. Primary attack spam, special. Primary attack spam, special. Primary attack spam, special.  Repeat.
You will not be able to set up trap-oriented strategies to win maps.  You will not plan and plot the perfect trap set up to clean up the orcs so that they die enmasse.
In the previous games did you ever have trouble with a map to sit back and think how you could use different traps, move your choke point, or select different weapons to win?  That isn't going to happen here.  There is absoultely no trap strategy whatsoever.  Traps are an afterthought in this game.  You can't put a barricade in certain spots because it blocks the orcs... That should tell you right there that the developers couldn't care less about traps and they don't want you ruining 'their' FPS combat game with your trap setup.  They want you engaged in combat.  They want you running back and forth between points you can't control.  You won't setup traps and sit back to clean up stragglers.  Gone are the days of trap focused play.  You won't play a map without using mana or weapons.You could win these maps without traps, you will never win without weapons.
Now there are a ton more things that will walk through your tissue paper barricade after a couple swings, or just go over it.  Barricades don't channel the orcs like they used to.  The orcs mostly follow the path they were assigned and attack a barricade if they come to it.
The characters feel slugish, too.  I don't mean this in a latency way, its that OMD2 the characters were snappy and responsive.  In Unchained they feel like they are slow.  They move back and forth like in League of Legends.
Headshots are gone.  Sprinting is gone.
Weapons feel like they do next to nothing, and can't be changed from character to character.  Choose a character and that is the weapon you're stuck with, forever.
Maximillian doesn't double jump.  Gabriella doesn't hover.
Since this game is so engineered towards team play, you won't be able to finish most of the maps by yourself.  When playing with other players your dmg is nerfed to ridiculously low levels.
What little strategy with traps that there is will be useless when playing with other people who will not understand or who have different ideas.  There is generally ONE way to setup traps for a map, PERIOD.  This is mostly just how you set up barricades, all other traps are a little extra dmg as gravy and it doesn't matter what they are or where they're set.
They went off the deep end with complexity as far as leveling up everything and random boxes needed to get anywhere.
PAY TO WIN.  There are children on here whose mommy and daddy gave them unlimited access to a credit card so that they could buy their way to the top.  Good luck competing.
Prepare to grind.  Much of this game is built on chance - to upgrade traps you get boxes that have random contents that you must use towards upgrading.
Prepare to wait in queue for games so that you can get some turd who wants to AFK or take pleasure in sabotaging your game.

I should probably write mroe reviews for the Steam games I play, but I haven't.  This game defintiely deserves one, however.
I went into this game expecting a retro experience with maybe just a bare minimum of a game, like most retro games out there.  I liked the premise, but the battle system seemed simplistic, and I was skeptical when I read that the game was ~20 hours.
Thus, I was pleasantly surprised when the mediocre impression I had before firing up the game proved completely wrong.  This game is definitely old-school in that it will be hard, even on the regular setting, but it rewards you for exploring everywhere all the time.  Even up to the final endgame portion of Another Star there was more stuff to find and more of the games world and lore to learn about.
And to that point, the plot is actually pretty darn good as far as retro games go.  It's very Star Ocean/Phantasy Star-esque, which is what drew me to the game in the first place.  Yet, unlike a lot of games that go down this route, Another Star doesn't fall into the trap of doing too much with it's plot and fully explores the gameworld without feeling like there's too much extraneous padding.  I can say without a doubt it's a very satisfying and good plot, even if some of the running gags got a little old by the end.
My only complaint is that the difficulty balance seems planned around the "High" growth rate.  For most of the game, the battle system is surprisingly deep, with a wide variety of enemy strategies employed throughout the game, and much more thought involved than you might initially think!  However, I played ~2/3 of the game with the "Standard" growth rate, and a number of brutal encounters, but around that point it's almost unwinnable without large level gains for their HP increases.  Enemy magic is also brutal--elemental resistance equipment is worth its weight in gold.  So much so I would advise everyone playing this to keep those Waterproof Ponchos on hand the second you can get them early, because they were useful essentially until the last stages of the game.
TL;DR: Buy this game if you like older, turn-based RPGs!  It will be worth your cash and time, for sure!

When I got Orcs II, I fell in love with the game.  I loved playing the Sorceress, warping minds and turning minions against each other like a true manipulator.  The traps were hilarious, the enemies satisfying to kill or convert - especially the big ones - and being able to fight alongside the turrets and traps was an experience I've only found in two other series - Dungeon Defenders and Sanctum
Unchained manages to capture that feel, at least initially.  The hectic back and forth as sheer numbers overwhelm your traps, forcing you out of favorable positions to scramble to survive, the satisfaction of triggering every trap at once and decimating an entire cluster of enemies, the fun of playing coop with a friend and splitting up who does what and having to trust and cooperate with each other...  etc.  That's all here.  And for people like myself who have played 100+ hours of OMD2 and are looking for some variety, this game will give exactly that and can be a lot of fun.
It even adds a fresh dose of fun with new mechanics that blend with the old.  There are lots of new heroes with different mechanics, giving players much more variety to work with and find one that suits them.  The players gain up to 10 levels per match, and at certain tiers they can enhance their abilities (think Heroes of the Storm, if you're familiar with that).  You get to customize your hero to a degree beyond choosing which core mechanics you want, and the combinations can be very potent toward solidifying how you play a character vs how someone else does.  The difficulty is increased by having boss monsters, powerful versions of normal foes that you have to spend a lot of effort to defeat - and don't let them hit you because they HURT.  New mercenary foes have unique mechanics that you have to address while dealing with the horde, making the managing of your time and resources trickier in a good way.
There are three major problems though, and they're tied together under the same core issue.
1. You don't get to decide which traps, equipment, passive upgrades, etc. that you unlock or upgrade.  Traps gain experience through level-up lootboxes that give it randomly to whichever trap that level chest is compatible with.  It might be the ones you like, it might not.  Either way, the game controls how you improve everything except your own reaction time and ability practice.
2. Skulls have become a much broader currency in this game.  You get 3000 just for completing your very first mission with 4 stars.  You don't get a small amount per map victory, you get flat amounts.  It doesn't have the same feeling of accomplishment that OMD2 gave when you got JUST enough skulls to upgrade that favorite trap to be even better than it was before.  And unlocking new heroes takes a STUPID amount of skulls.  If you have OMD2 you get the Warmage, Sorceress and a Gnoll Melee expert for free, but any new guys are going to take some grinding to get.
3. Some of the newly-introduced Boss Monsters have a serious drawback that makes you quickly come to dread their appearance - not because they're difficult, but because they do something that breaks any attempt at strategy and enemy path control: they destroy barriers.  They're not little squishy sappers, where if you're fast enough you can take them out and return focus to the main horde.  No, they're durable, strong and extremely dangerous, AND they destroy the only thing that keeps you from getting overwhelmed by multiple enemy paths.
The core issue: Microtransactions.  Unlike Overwatch (where the lootboxes are appearance and cosmetic items only and if you're crazy/wealthy enough to spend money you can only pay to swag), this game encourages you through rapidly-scaling difficulties to bypass the grind and spend real money to get things that make the fight easier.  It's pay-to-win microtransactions that are almost shoved down your throat.  Spend $X to improve your barricade now so the boss can't destroy it so easily.  Spend $Y to unlock this hero.  Spend $Z to control which traps you get to upgrade.  The game cripples you at the starting gate, then sells the cure after you've taken three strides forward.
I hate the fact that microtransactions are becoming a thing.  I hate that loot boxes are the primary means of spending money on stuff now, randomizing what you get so your real money might not even get you what you want.  It's ridiculous.  That said, if you have the sheer stubbornness to keep your wallet out of this game, the base gameplay itself is still everything OMD2 offered with a few fresh twists and turns.  You can play earlier levels and still enjoy yourself, and you'll eventually earn the heroes and trap upgrades that fit your style.  It may be shorter, it may take much longer, but you can get there and still leave rivers of orc blood&giblets in your wake.  And as long as that core is still in the OMD games, that's good enough for this enchanter.
TL;DR: If you enjoyed OMD2 this game offers a fresh take that can be a lot of fun, but be warned the game will try to shove pay-to-win microtransactions at you by ramping up the difficulty extremely fast.  Your traps and upgrades will come randomly, heroes are a pain to earn, but you still get that satisfying feel of slaughtering wave after wave of orcs with good trap and ability usage.  A free-to-play game that's worth at least trying to see if you can enjoy it despite the crap-filled baggage that comes with it.

At first impression this game is quite underwhelming and seems to be nothing more than a re-skin of Gal Civ II but as is often the case, first impressions can be very wrong. After you get your rear end handed to you in the first few games and once you start to "get" what is going on this game really comes together and shows its abundant depth and fun. It may lack  that level of super polish and marketing bells and whistles that some other recent 4x games have, what it doesn't lack however is pure unadulterated PC space strategy goodness. This game has so many systems all working together at once it can become exceedingly complex but never seems to bog down and become a chore. Decidedly old school in its interface and gameplay (a good thing) but with a nice snappy modern engine backing it all up, the game can handle a huge universe with tons going on without seemingly batting an eye. Gal Civ III is the first 4x to truly bring out that "just one more turn" feeling for me since CIV IV. With a bit more fine tuning and some Steam workshop addition of races, mods etc (Star Fleet Command universe I am waiting for you) this game will undoubtedly stand as a space strategy classic.
Pros:
+ Massive levels of customization, from races and ships to game settings you can play this game how you want.
+ Huge maps that could setup some truly lengthy and involved games, or small skirmishes if you so prefer
+ Has Multiplayer (but is bare bones and has issues)
+"Feels" comfortable for anyone who's played Gal Civ II or M.O.O. before, yet adds new systems and depth.
+ Turns are very fast. even in late game with tons of units and things going on. Huge plus
+ Steam workshop support coming soon in patch 1.1 (not currently implemented in 1.01)
+ AI does a respectable job of making you feel like you are playing real humans (or aliens)
+ Good writing, even amusing at times
Cons:
- Default races are a bit bland.
- Battle viewer is somewhat simplified
- No planetary invasion animation or battle viewer
- $50 price tag
- Multiplayer is crash prone at this time.

I've played a lot of basic rpg games that have mediocre music and graphics and unispired stories, and let me tell you, this is not one of them!
First off, the graphics in this game are beautifully stylized. The characters look colorful and unique without overshadowing the very pretty, if somewhat small, world maps. The game generally sticks to a 16 bit style, although its cheating and going a bit over that limit- to good effect. Interspersed in there are hand drawn frames, stills and animated scenes normally about 3-5 seconds long, that have a simple but colorful style to them that mesh with the normal graphics very well.
I was not expecting anything more than a 10 second loop track or four with this game and boy was I wrong! This game has at least 8 tracks that are over 1-2 minutes long for each chapter, and I rather liked quite a few of them. They are left open in the games files so you can drag them right onto a music player. (Game received for free not for promotional purposes, but as a gift from a kind redditor.)
tl;dr
I don't often care about games enough to write a review, but Abzu has easily rocketed to the top of my 'favorite games of all time' list. Abzu is what I would consider to be a masterpiece.
Pros:
+ Stunning art style and consistant art direction
+ Beautiful soundtrack
Subjective:
= Loose storytelling. You're very much shown rather than told, and for those who would rather not interpret their own meaning, this may not be the right game for you.
= Relatively short main storyline. I finished in about 3 - 3.5 hours, though I haven't gone back and collected everything yet. That said, that time was all killer and no filler, so personally, I'd say that it's well worth it.
Cons:
- Simple puzzles. Honestly, I didn't mind this, since I felt this was very much an atmospheric game, but if you're the type to get bored or lose interest because the puzzles aren't complicated, this may not be the game for you.
- Set control scheme. You can invert certain options, but it may take you some time to get used to the swimming controls in this game. (I'm a bit under 4 hours in, have beaten the story, and still don't feel used to them. That may be because I'm notoriously bad at video games though, so your mileage may vary.)
----
Let me start off by saying that I have roughly the emotional range of a toaster. It's very hard to get me to /feel/ anything based on the narrative in a game, but Abzu absolutely managed it. There were points in the game, without getting into too many spoilers, where I felt genuine joy, mourned certain events, felt insignificant due to the vastness of aspects of the environment, or felt genuinely angry over something that happened. I felt sympathy for a character I had previously only felt anger for, and I felt joy when I wouldn't have expected to. This game absolutely runs the spectrum, and in my experience, does so effectively. When Abzu described itself as an emotional experience, I was skeptical, but having played it, it's absolutely accurate in that description.
The soundtrack for Abzu is beautiful. There's haunting melodies, songs of joy, and everything under the sun. I frequently find that I wish to play games with the music off, but Abzu joins the likes of Transistor in having a soundtrack perfectly executed, and masterfully made. Not once did I even THINK about turning off the music, and for me, that's saying something.
Similarly, the aesthetic of Abzu is beautifully crafted. It was very, very clear that each environment had a LOT of love put into it by the developers. Every little detail comes together to create a beathtaking world filled with colors, emotion, and beauty.
I honestly can't even begin to say how much I love this game. I've tried in this review, but I don't feel that I've truly done it justice. I strongly recommend trying it for yourself.

Where do I even begin with this game. First off ive been playing this game for about 7 years now and every playthrough ive had of it was exellent. There is alot of variety when it comes to builds. There is the obvious Light/Dark or Grey option for the game but there is also Force user builds, Ranged builds, Pure combat focused guardian, etc. I find the combat to be enjoyable (In my opinion) since its tactical and you can really plan attacks and things of that sort. Take DA:0 for example. Its pretty much the same system. You can start with 3 beginning classes: Guardian (Combat focused), Sentinel (Better skill progression), and Consular (Force powers). You then later in the game get different set of prestige classes depending on your allignment. Now, lets get to the writing of the game. This game has one of the best stories I have ever seen. You'll see once you play it for yourself. The reason I prefer this game slightly over the first is just because I prefer the darker, philosophical, grey aspects of the atmosphere and story a bit better (Kotor 1 is also one of my favorite games). Anyways, this game presents the idea that Dark is not necessarily evil and Light isnt nessesary good and you really get to see the Flaws of both sides. For example, you play as the Jedi Exile, who was exiled from the Jedi order for rusing to war to protect innocents. The Jedi were lazy and waited to "evaluate the threat". The dialouge and voice acting in this game is absolutely fantastic (Especially Kreia). For this game, you dont even need to be a fan of Star Wars. A non Star Wars fan would look at this game and just play an RPG. However a Star Wars fan would look at this and play an amazing Star Wars RPG. The reason for this is because the game is set in an era wayyy before the Movies. One flaw however, would be the cut content presented this game. Obsidian (The developers) were rushed to release this game by lucasarts, resulting in them needing to cut out content for the game. Luckily, a group of community modders managed to get into the games files and restore alot of the content that was cut. You can find the mod on the steam workshop. Anyways, hurry up and buy the game! You wont be dissapointed.

Another Star is a remarkably well made nod to RPG games of yore with some unique elements sprinkled in to make the gameplay still feel fresh. The game offers varying difficulty and character growth levels, with even the harder difficulties relatively well balanced. Personally, I think the enemies that can heal/absorb hitpoints are a bit overpowered, especially on higher difficulties, but that's the only thing that bothered me. Playing on Hard difficulty and Old School (25%) growth rate, I still felt very little need to grind to advance in the game, so I never felt like I was stuck on an insurmountable obstacle.
Despite the imposed limitations, the graphics are quite pretty, especially the enhanced battle sprites. The game also allows you to disable the CRT scanline effect or adjust its curvature, as well as letting you toggle screen flashing/shaking and vsync.
The music is spectacular, each track giving the proper tone in the scenes they play and never gets repetitive. Fortunately, the dev has put up a free download for the soundtrack on his website with some unused tracks, too.
The story is interesting, though admittedly has some cliché moments, but it fits well with the type of game it is paying homage to. The game does have a number of typos and small errors, but they're getting fewer with each update.
Overall, I greatly recommend this game. Even if you're not familiar with the old RPG style, you might still be able to get a kick out of this game. I am anxiously awaiting the recently teased Another Star 2.

I play lots of JRPGs: retro, modern, indie, AAA- I dabble in them all.  Another Star is among the most compelling and original of them I've played in years.  Before you dismiss the game based on its apparently gimmicky retro feel, consider that this game is NOT made using RPGMaker and IS made by people who actually played those old games when they were new, and who loved them, and whose lives were affected by that experience.  This game is a love letter to a lost friend, a time and place we can never return to but will never forget.
All that being said, Another Star feels fresh and original despite its archaic appearance.  I have found the writing especially compelling.  The world building is spectacular and immersive, reflected in the dialogues among characters, the excellent character portraits, and the game systems themselves.  This is a primitive world experiencing its own Iron Age.  Small settlements dot the lush landscape, populated by numerous ancestral clans, each with their own goals and histories.  There are allies, uneasy peaces, rivalries, and wars.  The central protagonist is son to the patriarch of one such clan.  As you can imagine from this setup, a GoT-like cascade of betrayals, deaths, and heroic acts crashes through the narrative.
The adventure begins when a falling star crashes into the wilderness and the clans send their heroes to retrieve it first, hoping it will give them godlike powers to defeat their rivals and secure their longevity.  It becomes quickly apparent that the falling star was in fact a vessel from a technologically advanced society.  I was immediately reminded of Vernor Vinge's sci-fi masterpiece
, which, among many other things, chronicles the effects of such an event upon a primitive world.  Another Star won't be winning any Hugo Awards, but it does confront the issue with depth and nuance, and it doesn't flinch away from the catastrophic damage and transformative unravelling that inevitably occurs when the primitive crashes against the advanced.  It's happened on our own world, again and again.  But even while grappling with these themes, the writing remains personal and intimate, such that I always feel invested in the fate of the individual characters.

Ok let's talk a little about the gameplay itself.  There is a standard overworld spritemap dotted with settlements and other points of interest- some of which are hidden, so explore.  Entering a settlement brings up a menu that allows you to visit the clan's chief, talk to villagers, sleep at the tavern, or shop.  Visiting the chief requires a donation relative to the clan's power, but bestows a buff on the party for some time.  The responses of the villagers are very interesting and change as events progress and relationships among the tribes evolve.  If you find yourself stuck this can be a good thing to do because you may hear an important clue.  Also, any "loot" acquired from battle is automatically exchanged for cash whenever you enter a settlement.
Battles. The battle system is excellent.  First off, random encounters are usually optional. An exclamation point flashes above your head and you can press a button to engage.  However, I would recommend fighting every single battle you can, because dungeons and bosses are often quite challenging and you are going to want every point of xp you can get.  There is a standard "fight-skill-item-defend" type menu but its execution is quite different.  You only get to select one command and then your entire party fulfills it.  For example, if you attack, everyone in your party attacks. Furthermore, they each attack all of the enemies at once.  Healing items are dear so most healing comes from a small boost you get from defending- a technique your enemies will also use.  Magic is powerful but items are uncommon and actually casting spells costs hit points.  Battles take thought and require careful risk and reward assesment and boss fights can be long and arduous but also tense and ultimately fulfilling upon victory.  The system is so compelling and so tactically satisfying that I'm hoping others will take note and adapt some of the principles into the tired menu clicking paradigm most JRPGs still employ.
I'm going to stop here because I don't want to over-discuss this game.  Part of the joy of a game like Another Star is the wonder of self-discovery.

At first I looked at it and went meh, I'm so burned out on retro-console-style games. Everyone with some half baked story thinks they can make the next Final Fantasy using RPGMaker. But then I looked closer.
IT WASNT MADE IN RPGMAKER. Cool! Just like One Way Heroics, a console-looking but really unique game (also not made in RPGMaker) that I love.
So I picked it up. Ive played literally thousands of RPGs. I remember the 8bit and 16bit eras. I remember when RPGMaker  first came out,. For the most part, its games were donation-only, and teams worked to make great (but limited by RPGMaker itself) games. I'm so burned out on console style turn based RPGs, that to be interested in one got to have a compelling well written story, decent balance, and something that sets it apart from the herd.
Another Star has all that. If youre a fan of console RPGS, this one is way better than paying who-knows-what for another RPGMaker yawnfest. Even if youre burned out, its worth picking up. It is set so you dont have to grind if you dont want to. Always a plus, as grinding just to progress is one of those things that should be left in the past. You can also get rid of that annoying "CRT scanlines and convex screen" effect in the options. Its cute, but thats another thing that should be left in the past.
Overall, its well done. Keeps the good parts of retro console RPGs and dumps the annoying parts.
EDIT: I  would like to point out that the overworld music is seriously the most awesome retro-rpg music ever!
