Enjoyed this game thoroughly. I entered the franchise with this title, so the deep story was a little hard to follow at first, but once I caught up I was immersed in a rich world of swords and magic. The characters are all very well put together. They all have their own little backstories explored, all interacting in different ways with the main character. In this game you have to make a lot of hard choices, and they all hinge on your feelings for these characters. These feelings are introduced to you through storytelling of a depth and degree that is rarely seen in games today.
The gameplay itself is fun! With 3 main trees to branch out into, RPG style, replayability is high. Hacking and slashing your way through swathes of monsters is a hoot, maybe throwing in a cheeky fireball in there for good measure.
In some situations though, combat can feel a little... clunky. 1v1 boss fights, where forced victory mechanics are unclear but concequences for copping a hit to the face are high leave you reloading multiple times trying to figure it all out. Some of the mandatory powers you have to use in most fights (quen) are a little slow to actually enable during the fight, leaving you static and vulnerable.
One other thing I would improve upon is the general gearing throughout the game. You get some serious swank towards the end of the game. I would've love to have played through more than 10% of the story with it!
All in all, fantastic game in a fantasy setting. Happy to be accustomed to the franchise now. Bring on 3!!!

Final Fantasy VII
"... She smiled until the end." - Cloud Strife
Oh, dear. Where do I even start with this epic masterpiece? I guess I'll start by saying that yes, I am a huge FF fan. However, 7 is tied with two other Final Fantasy games for my top 3, which are 6 and 10. So I had to get that out of the way before everyone starts ragging on me assuming I'm biased because my picture is Cloud. The truth is, I'm probably one of the most reliable people you could choose to read a review from, because I have been playing this game since it was released on PSX in 1997 and I will still be playing this game 50 years from now.
I have beaten this game so many times that I've lost count, and I have done everything there is to do in this game. Why should you trust my review? Because I have a ridiculous amount of experience with this game. So let's get started...
STORY - Epic. That's the best word I can use to describe this game's story. What starts out seeming like a story based around destroying an evil corporate giant unfolds into a much larger catastrophe where the entire planet is in danger. You play as Cloud, an "Ex-SOLDIER 1st Class" who has deserted SHINRA Inc. and has joined the anti-SHINRA group known as AVALANCHE as a mercenary. AVALANCHE's goal is to stop SHINRA from sucking all of the life out of the planet, and for the first bit of the game it seems as though this is what you'll be doing, but no. Within the first couple hours of the game's first disc you will attack the SHINRA-HQ head on and learn that there's much more to this than you think. A presumed dead 1st Class SOLDIER named Sephiroth who went insane is showing signs of resurfacing, and for some reason it's driving Cloud mad. I don't want to spoil anything more, but this story will pull at your heart and make you feel every emotion you could possibly feel. Love, hate, regret, confusion, sadness, anger, frustration, happiness... And a crazy amount of twists and turns will leave you feeling a part of this story and playing it through to the end - and loving every second of it.
CHARACTERS - This has always been a strong thing coming from Square games, characters are always relateable and human. It's so easy to get attached to these characters and feel like you've known them forever. As the game progresses you learn more and more about these characters, revealing things about their childhood and their motives. It's easy to feel sad whenever something bad happens to one of these characters, they are so well created.
SETTING - The massive world of Gaia. You are only restricted for the first hour or two of the game and once you get out of Midgar this world opens up and it's lovely. As events unfold the world map will completely change, and the entire layout of it is very detailed. There isn't much I can really say about this so you'll have to experience it for yourself.
GRAPHICS - Definitely not one of this games strongpoints. I'm willing to admit that. I mean, sure, 15 years ago this game was beautifully crafted and stunned people, but now? You can't get someone who's never played this game before to try it out without giving them the longest talk ever about how worth it it is. This remaster doesn't help it THAT much. Yes, it looks a little better now than before, but it still is hard on the eyes of newer gamers who don't understand how unimportant graphics really are. However there are so many graphic mods for this game it becomes a nonissue once you get the right ones plugged in.
AUDIO - HOLY♥♥♥♥♥BUCKET. Square's soundtracks have ALWAYS been masterful and this game is no exception. Sometimes when I'm on my computer doing nothing I just listen to the soundtrack on YouTube because it's so beautiful. Nobuo has done a wonderful job as always and the music in this game is beathtaking. Every piece of music has been selected and placed perfectly into the game and it's all the better for it. HOWEVER THE AUDIO QUALITY IS STILL GARBAGE AND THEY COULD HAVE DONE A MUCH BETTER JOB 'REMASTERING' IT.
GAMEPLAY - The most important part of a game, in my opinion, is the gameplay. Afterall what's the point in playing a GAME if the GAMEplay is lazy and boring? Great news... This is the main strongsuit of Final Fantasy 7. Walking or running around the game world is responsive and simple, dialogue is nice to read, and combat is incredibly fluid and fun. Final Fantasy's trademark ATB battle system comes into play here and it works insanely well as always. The game's menu is very well done and the materia system is so great and easily figured out. There are so many sidequests and minigames to play that it's very hard to get bored in this game and will take you many MANY hours of playing time before you've done everything this game has to offer.
Obviously I have an insane amount of positive things to say about this game but I don't want you guys to take up all your time in the day reading a review so I'm trying to make it as short and helpful as possible. But let's get down to my negative points, which there are few.
NEGATIVES - I said it above... The audio quality isn't good. It would have been so easy to remaster the game's soundtrack but SquareEnix has once again dropped the ball in order to cut more corners. It's still a beautiful soundtrack and amazing, but they could have done more considering this Steam version was released in 2013. The graphics, while breathtaking at its time, have not aged well even with this 'remaster'. With mods this is repairable but that isn't an excuse to half♥♥♥♥♥the remaster. The story, while incredibly well thoughtout and engaging, can be very confusing/hard to follow and it's easy to get lost and have no idea what to do next. There are also some bugs and glitches in the game, some unnoticable and others (like the fact that MAGIC DEFENCE DOESN'T EVEN WORK) are gamebreaking. The save system can also be a hassle in this remaster and that's inexcusable.
OVERALL I don't think I've ever recommended a game to more people than I have with Final Fantasy 7. Buy it. Buy it now. WHAT ARE YOU WAITING FOR? Buy this god damn game, you will not regret it. And if you do? Well, I'm sorry, but you're in the minority and maybe one of those people who won't even give it a chance because it's "overrated".
Is it overrated? Yes, but it deserves to be.

Wow, what a whirlwind. When I first tried this title out, on the heels of Orcs Must Die 2, I was very disappointed. At that point, Robot seemed to be primarily focused on creating a MOBA game, and the survival mode just didn't feel very good. Though I can't say for sure, it seemed that many others felt the same way, and the survival mode was retooled over the next few months. When I returned, I found much more to like.
First of all, I absolutely love the characters. Many of the characters feel viable, and all are oozing with personality and require specific playstyles. Although towards the end, attempting to achieve 5 stars on the few maps we had left, we gravitated towards Oziel and Midnight, I found uses for many of the characters. For close-combat, Blackpaw ruled the roost for me. Cygnus is fantastic in maps that don't require much mobility (especially if he can set up close to the rift). Max is awesome at dealing with unstable rifts and getting a quick cash infusion to get barricades arranged. Oziel is just amazing all around, and is very self-sustaining (he can regenerate his own mana). Temper and Gabriella were my other favorites - Temper has some of the best quips in the game, and his bull charge move can be outstanding on certain maps, while putting Gabby in the middle of a well-developed killbox feels just SO effective. The other characters I purchased (I bought all characters with skulls and gold from log-ins) were Bionka, Hogarth, Midnight, and Zoey. I received Tundra and Smolder from some special website reward key I found online. All of these characters, though they had great personality, were just underwhelming for me. Midnight is actually very good, but I just couldn't get in the hang of using her well. Smolder, at the time of this review, seems like the worst survival character.
The characters were a wonderful addition to the Orcs Must Die experience. It really feels quite expanded in comparison to just Max and Gabby (in Orcs Must Die 2).  Orcs Must Die is at its best, in my opinion, when you're asked to contemplate (especially with a partner) what enemies you're seeing, the traps you have available, the initial routes and routes you can create, and the strengths of the characters you can choose. Many times while playing, we'd run into a specific enemy configuration or lane that would give us trouble, return to the drawing board to try different traps or configurations, and come back victorious. This is immensely satisfying. Unfortunately, for much of my time with the game, this wasn't made easy. You were unable to restart a map, and therefore had to quit the game and often wait for a "failure" screen.
I'm sure that at this point, the score you saw at the top of this review doesn't seem to make sense. However, there are quite a few design decisions, many dealing with the F2P model, that make it difficult for Orcs Must Die to be "at its best."
First of all, you have traps. Traps are given to you in the form of "cards" that are found in chests after completing daily quests and maps. You must find at least one of the card to have access to a trap, and then to maximize the power of the trap, you need to find more and more copies of the associated card to "level" the trap. The maximum level is 7, and it takes more and more copies of a card (as well as skulls) to level it each time. As you level a trap, it becomes more powerful and allows for more and more "parts" to augment the trap and make it more effective. The "parts" are also found randomly. After playing for more than 100 hours, there were still two traps that I had yet to find (of the 53 in game). I still lacked 5 of the 37 parts in the game.
Secondly, you have traits. You can take 4 traits into battle with you, which can do anything from increasing your defense, increasing the coins you earn (that you must spend to drop traps), or increasing the damage you do to a specific type of enemy. Traits are also found randomly in chests. After playing for more than 100 hours, there were still 6 traits I'd yet to find (of the 48 in game).
Third, there are guardians. Each map has "guardian spots," and each guardian spot has a specific symbol associated with it. If you put the associated guardian into the "correct" spot (the spot associated with its symbol), it will often have much more health and do much more damage. For some guardians, 35% more of each in the correct spot. After playing for more than 100 hours, I still lacked 7 guardians (of the 18 in game). I did not find a guardian that was associated with two of the symbols, the horseshoe and the jail.
Lastly, and definitely worst, you have account level. All maps have a recommended account level. As you play, your account levels up. When this occurs, you do more damage with all of your character's attacks.
Taken altogether, these elements do their level best to sabotage player strategy. Think about it: if I play a map and fail, how do I find the issue?
1. Could I have better traps? Could those traps be leveled up more? Are there parts that I do not have that might greatly enhance one of my traps (perhaps something like floor spikes or arrow walls, which are omnipresent)? These are all subject to random chest drops.
2. Could I have better traits? There are a few traits that seemed strictly better than almost all others. One I received very early (a trait that reduced the cost of traps that deal physical damage), and one I did not get until I only had one map left to complete the game (a trait that increased a character's damage by 10% as long as that character had higher than 50% health). With a ranged character, this is basically a strict 10% damage buff! The traits I have depend on what I find in randomized chests.
3. Do I have a guardian that matches the symbols in the guardian spots on the map in question? 35% guardian damage is not to be taken lightly - but it won't have it if I haven't found the associated guardian in a chest.
4. Is my account level not high enough? If you can't figure out a viable strategy, you may just choose to "overlevel" the map in question. Since your account level is tied to the amount of damage you deal, you can keep leveling until you can clear the waves fast enough to meet the par time. There were a couple of maps with extremely difficult par times (Shark Island, Temple Graveyard) that my co-op partner and I just skipped and came back to when we had a higher account level.
I loved playing the new characters, and had fun with the degree of strategy that existed. However, the game had the potential to be something much more special.
Also, please allow your players to simply buy the skin they'd like to see on their favorite character. Most character skins, like everything else, are found in random chests. You can actually find character skins and dyes for characters you don't even own. I spent about 25-30 dollars overall on the title to support the developers and acquire some cool skins. I got a few that I liked, but my lack of Oziel's Knight Walker skin when I finished my time with the game is a sore spot for me.

I can't recommend it. TLDR at the bottom.
To start, it's fun and the free to play model seems fine, with you unlocking new traps pretty regularly and ooh! Upgrade!
But here's the rub. It quickly starts to grind. The level pool is really, really shallow and when you go up a difficulty, not all the maps are carried through and because the match making makes it so you won't get placed into certain maps due to your account level (eg. Crogon Keep on Rift Lord is recommended for 60-66, so you won't get placed there before lvl 60), it means that with 3 players, you wind up playing the lower level maps of that difficulty level over and over.
Also, I don't know what multiplayer actually adds to Orcs Must Die!
You have a great strategy? Good luck implementing it with someone placing a weak trap in a key spot.
And the worst decision they made was that melee charactars block the shots of ranged allies. All the shots. So if you're a ranged and your team mates both go melee, you're going to do next to no damage, no matter how you position yourself.
On the note of damage, it's a jarring disconnect between solo and multiplayer. In multiplayer, your damage is reduced to about 1/4. 3 people + a little extra since you have more stuns and such, which is fine in theory. But it makes you feel weak. Even a medium orc takes a lot of shots to kill with ranged charactars and that's not fun. Feeling weak and powerless is never fun.
All of this would mean I'd prefer to play solo, except for the existence of trap cap and the design of the maps. Now, in Orcs Must Die 2, the maps were designed so you could either divert all enemies to go down one path or there was a position where you could keep an eye on multiple paths and provide assistence where needed. Now, in Unchained, they fully wall off a lot of the maps, meaning the party has to split up to cover them all, which is fine except when you're playing alone. So you think that since you get more money in solo, you can just use traps right? Nah, you can only place a limited number of traps, which is only enough to think the herd, rather than stop it. I would dismiss this as a case of "get gud" but my traps are tier 5 or 6 (out of a max of 7) and I've done a lot of research to make sure my trap placement is optimal.
And then we get onto sabotage mode, which is ok in theory. It places two teams on an identical level and you can play cards to send against your opponent, which are either extra minions, debuffs for the enemy heroes or buffs for minions in the wave. And it's not actually bad fun.
But it's pay to win.
Now, I mentioned trap tiers a moment ago but let me explain in more detail. In this game, you open chests and they contain traps. They might contain 15 barricades for example. When you get enough barricades you can upgrade your barricades by paying skulls, which you earn in game for doing levels and quests. In the case of the barricade, this will increase barricades hp, but for damage traps, it will increase damage and for physics traps, their fire rate. This means that a player with a T7 bladewall, is doing nearly double the damage a T1 bladewall, for the same cost. This gives players with higher level traps an objective advantage over players with lower tier traps and also, minions have the same health as in the higher difficulties, meaning if you get a player with T1 traps, you end up suffering.
But more than that, you can buy consumable chests, giving you the ability to pull consumable cards for Sabotage! Which is insane! One of the most common ways of winning is get a boss called Swifty Hooves. He's a fast guy who ignores barricades, with not much hp so play him in combination with stun cards to knock out enemy heroes and stop them pursuing and you win. But you get Swifty unless you pull him out of a chest, meaning a player who pays money for consumable chests can get better cards in Sabotage!
The concept for sabotage is alright. The implementation is awful.
Also, perhaps I'm one of only a few people who care about this, but the charactar is gone. The tutorial makes you think it might be like a standard Orcs Must Die game. Witty reparte between charactars, orcs exploding into gibs, well designed levels. But after that, it dissapears. It's gone. The level designs are poor, the charactars spout the same lines verbatim, there's no progression or end goal. Also, it gives no explanation as to why I'm fighting alongside an orc or why I'm fighting against order soldiers, since the order was supposed to stop orcs reaching the rift.
So the TLDR of OMDU is that it's a game which should never have been made multiplayer. The multiplayer aspects cost too much of what made OMD great. They saw that sweet, sweet F2P cash and wanted a piece of it, but in the process, they reduced their game to a husk, sacrificing too much of what was brilliant about it to make way for the multiplayer mechanics, which do more harm than good. And the sad thing is that multiplayer could have been a fun option in OMD3, but we're unlikely to see that now. OMD may die here and that is sad.

This game takes the traditional top-down roguelike and puts a simple however game-changing spin on it: Moving only at the beat of the music.
. This adds a bit of a turn-based stratergy to it, with the enemies having very predictable patterns (except the bats. I hate
of them), it gives you the ability to plan your attack so long as you can plan it in under a second. Remember: you move at the beat of the music. If you are thinking that this is simple enough, WRONG! This game is fffffffffffffffffHARD! Throughout the game - especially in the later dungeons - you are fighting off hordes of monsters so you have to take a lot into consideration: the range of one monster, the movement patterns of another, the traps laid around the room and the attack patterns of your weapons, which flows perfectly into the next subject.
The weapons in this game are greatly varied, however I dare say biased because I see some a LOT more often than others. With each weapon having its own attack pattern, everybody has the ability to choose their own favourite weapon. Do you like having extra space on the

.

I was fortunate enough to receive this as my first-ever review copy (yay!). Very, very excited to try this game because I adore the rogue-like genre and enjoy beatmatching when I mix my electronic dance music (EDM) at home. Crypt hit on many of the themes and concepts that I’ve always loved, and I thoroughly enjoyed my gameplay experience. This is easily one of the best staples available in the rogue-like genre.
If you like rogue-likes, rhythm mechanics, dungeon crawling, electronic music (Danny Baranowsky’s score), and constantly unlocking new things, then you will really love this game.
The aesthetics are great – the amount of detail in the different levels and characters is well-done. The retro, pixel graphics combine with the electronic musical score to provide a very fun, fast-paced experience reminiscent of old-school arcade games (including the high difficulty that usually accompanied them). Danny Baranowsky’s music is critical to the gameplay – since you have to time your movements with the beat – and fits well with the heavy rogue-like elements found in the game. If you are partial to electronic music, then you will enjoy the great soundtrack. If you don’t, however, like EDM and/or Danny’s style, then you can always use your own music (MP3 format). There is a unique track for each level, and you have the option of loading your own playlist for each level. Note, I have a very wide taste in music, so I tried an assortment of genres – EDM tracks work very well with the rhythm mechanics (because of the consistent beats per minute), but Ariana Grande (I love her) songs DO NOT work very well. That being said, Danny’s composition is fantastic, and I don’t mind replaying levels over and over again, listening to the same tracks every time. Another advantage of using EDM tracks in a custom playlist is the length – the levels end in line with the track playing, so EDM’s lengthier (on average) playtime gives you more opportunity to explore the floor. The story involves you falling into a dungeon, your heart being magically tied to an ominous beat that you must dance to.
The controls are fairly easy to learn – a tutorial is offered that teaches you the basics of gameplay. I personally prefer using a controller over the keyboard, and I suggest you use that instead. The learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your experience with rogue-likes and/or rhythm games. Before you start playing, you will have to do a latency test for visual (the heartbeats and beat prompts) and auditory (the actual beat) cues; you can redo the test whenever you want. There is an “easy” mode that you can play, however, I sincerely think you will find a fair challenge playing the regular difficulty. Also, if you want a break from the beatmatching, you can play as a character (Bard) who does not have to move in time with the beat.
Difficulty is something this game does very well, especially for a rogue-like. Characters you unlock will usually have harder playing conditions (ex: cannot kill enemies, die when you pick up gold), ramping up the challenge factor. To combat this, you can unlock a character/room that allows you to practice against the different enemies you may encounter – this allows you to recognize their movement/attack patterns and how to best deal with them. A character/room also exists that allows you to train against mini- and regular bosses. I highly recommend you at least check these out once you have them available, especially if you are having difficulty progressing through the levels. There is even a room that provides levels where you can learn advanced tactics, like how to kill the shopkeeper in different ways. I appreciate this approach to difficulty because it provides you with the tools to improve your playstyle, should you so choose.
Gameplay involves you moving around a grid-based dungeon floor, most times in synchrony with the beat (unless you are playing as the Bard). Monsters on the floor also move in time with the beat, and they attack based on a chess/checkers-style pattern – if you move onto a tile that a monster was about to move to, you will take damage. Also, if you move into the attack range (varies based on the monster) of a monster, you will take damage if it is ready to attack – they usually have an animation cue (ex: skeletons raise their arms) to let you know an attack is incoming. To take advantage of monster movements (all units have to move each beat, or “turn.”), you can do things like backtrack or hit a wall (which will keep you on the same tile). As you progress through the level, monsters will drop gold. To increase the amount of gold dropped, you will have to build up your gold multiplier by hitting all track beats (when you move/attack) within a small window. Every time you miss a beat or take damage, your multiplier will decrease by an increment. Picking up armor will decrease how much damage you take, but will not affect your multiplier. Gold is used to purchase items from the large variety of stores available. Multipliers are especially effective when paired with multiplier-based equipment (ex: damage dealt is based on your current multiplier).
Overall, the game is an immense amount of fun and always a fair, interesting challenge.
If you are any bit interested in the rogue-like series or rhythm gameplay, then I implore you to give this game a try. It definitely is one of the best rogue-like titles available today.
ABSOLUTELY RECOMMEND!

If you're looking for a game to waste thousands of hours on, then this is the game for you. Garry's Mod is a game where you can add addons made by the community. These addons can be maps, gamemodes, playermodels, ragdolls, npcs, snpcs, saves, dupes and even clips made by other people. Here's some reasons why you should buy Gmod (If you don't own it already).
(Warning! The following review might sound very cheesy!)
_Positives_
1. Very fun maps: Just want some maps to play on? You won't be disappointed, Gmod's got many different maps ranging from the standard sandbox map to the action-packed adventure map to the chilling horror map. (Well, MOST horror maps, others are just loaded with cheap screamers).
2. A variety of gamemodes: Don't feel like playing the Sandbox gamemode anymore? Don't worry, there's gamemodes like Prop Hunt, Murder, Zombie Survival, Trouble in Terrorist Town, ect. that'll keep you occupied.
3. Plenty of addons: Want a skin for your Physgun or an additional playermodel? You're in luck, there are thousands of addons to choose from and the workshop might even have exactly what you want! (Though I wouldn't guarantee it).
4. Additional fun with friends: If you have some friends who own Gmod (assuming that you also own Gmod), don't hesitate to invite them to join your game, with friends around, Gmod can get very chaotic.
5. Tons of replay value: No matter how long you play Gmod you'll never be able to get bored of it! With all the maps, gamemodes and other addons this game has, the possibilities of a new experience never ends!
Of course this wouldn't be your average generic game review if I didn't add some bad things about Gmod, so here are a few that I came across while playing.
_Negatives_
1. Some maps need the Half Life 2 Episodes or Counter Strike: This is mainly just a personal gripe from me because I don't own either the Half Life 2 Episodes or Counter Strike (Jeez, I'm missing out).
2. Your friends need to have the same addons as you do: I've had this problem occur a couple times because a map was missing, and not having the addons that your friend has can make loading times significantly longer.
3. In multiplayer you can't spawn anything in (i.e props, ragdolls, npcs): This is just another personal problem that's occured when I tried to spawn anything while I was playing in a multiplayer server I created. If anyone knows a solution to this problem it would be very appreciated.
4. Having way too many addons can cause your game to lag: I can see why this is a thing but can't a guy play Garry's Mod and mess around with all his addons?
All in all, Garry's Mod is a very fun game to play, even with the bad things that hinder this game from being perfect (then again, NO game is perfect), the positives that I listed above greatly outweigh the negatives. Thanks to it's replay value, Garry's Mod is one of those games that you can keep coming back to and still have lots of fun each playthrough. I highly recommend that you buy this game. If you haven't bought it already, you don't know what you're missing out on.

The Last Express is, surprisingly, a unique point-and-click (P&C) adventure game in first-person perspective taking place on the Orient Express train, journeying from Paris to Constantinople in 1914; only a few days before the First World War starts. While it is an adventure in its own right, it combines genres such as murder mystery, suspense, romance and an Indiana Jones and Sherlock Holmes like adventure all together in one solid package.
The story starts off with Robert Cath, a young multilingual American doctor, getting a telegram from an old friend, Tyler Whitney, about a recent discovery he made while Cath was retreated in Paris after a firefight involving Irish nationalist and British policemen. The proposition is to meet on board of the Orient Express going to Jerusalem, but just when Cath manages to get on board illegally (since he was followed by policemen), he soon discovers his friend was murdered in his own comportment. From this point on, the game begins as a simple murder mystery case, but the plot thickens as the story progresses. With Tyler gone, Cath takes Tyler’s identity throughout the journey as means of disguising himself, making his task of finding the murderer a lot easier and safer without anyone else knowing he actually died. This is where the game shines because it always provides something fresh and keeps the player invested in the plot. There is always an unexpected twist just around the corner, and you will eventually discover that everyone on board is not who they seem to be at first glance; a solid inceptive to find out what is actually going on. In fact, almost all characters are related to the main plot to an extent, like a big masquerade. Ultimately, from start to finish, this is one heck of a journey. Something big and eloborate is behind the plot and Tyler's death is only the catalyst. A memorable adventure throughout the 10-hour plot, at a normal pace.
What is unique about The Last Express is the real-time simulation mechanism. Nearly all the events happen in real-time, giving the player a certain amount of time to complete tasks non-linearly on board of the train. These can range from talking to characters, eavesdropping conversations (which can provide invaluable information on characters’ backstories) and searching compartments for clues. Time does indeed pass in the Orient Express, with every single clock tick. Moreover, all the NPCs are excellently programmed as well, since they go about their own things in real-time, so there is always the possibility of missing out on their acts in any playthrough.
It is correct to say that everything can be approached non-linearly within a time gap in the game. However, there is at least a certain point in the game which may require the player to do the specific tasks in an exact order since otherwise you end up to a dead-end due to a bug, I believe. In my case, avoiding any spoilers, I was supposed to put a certain briefcase (what is in the briefcase is for you to find out) which I retrieved in my own comportment but due to the chronological order I approached things, the briefcase would always disappear from my inventory when I was entering the comportment. Nonetheless, the simulation is nothing I have ever seen in an adventure game before and it is entirely functional and, yes, revolutionaly.
And this leads to another interesting thing which is the number of possible “deaths” the game can offer. Since tasks are meant to be done in a certain time gap, failing to accomplish them can result in different outcomes ranging from simply being killed to getting arrested (in different circumstances). Most of these trigger when you are too late since time never stops. For instance, at the start of the game, you have to find Tyler before anyone else on the train, otherwise they will find the corpse and stop the train to check every passenger on board, ultimately discovering that you do not have a ticket, leading to your actual identity. Thus, in a way, it is rather interesting to see the different ways you can “die” and increases the tension without actually being a frustrating experience. There is almost never that feeling that you are running out of time, forcing you to rush. How come?
Well, even if you die or made a mistake, The Last Express features a functional and unique Rewind button which always you to go back to whatever point in time you want. This way, you can approach things differently without getting the game-over screen. It works like a save file, albeit much more immersive. In reality, it works like in Prince of Persian (2003), but instead of seconds it can range from minutes to hours. And this is not a surprise since the same person who designed Prince of Persia also designed The Last Express, so the similarities can be spotted in this rewind feature.
The bottom line is that the player can take different paths in the game, leading to different final endings. Thus, chances are no two people will play the same game, increasing the replay value. For example, without any major spoilers again, there is a point in the game where you can either run away with the briefcase or hand it back.
The puzzles are definitely not hard to solve and the hint system in the Gold Edition is useful if the player ever gets stuck. In general, the puzzles are adequate but hardly a strong point of the game. Not because there are poorly implemented or illogical, but because they are less memorable. Actually, there are not that many puzzles in the game in the traditional sense of combining inventory items and placing them on things to see what happens. If applicable, the puzzles are mostly of “be there, at the right time” for the event to trigger.
While The Last Express shines brightly as an adventure game with a great plot and believable characters, it is visually outdated by today’s standards and did not age well. While the character drawings are acceptable, it might put off a number of people used to more realistic 3D graphics by how pixelated they look. Since the game back then (in 1997) used up 3-CDs, it can be clearly noticed that the developers had to compromise in the animation department to save up space. For example, travelling in the game is more or less static, along with the cutscenes. But bearing in mind the circumstances, being a 17-old game at the time of writing this, I strongly believe it does not break the overall immersion and spark if you accept the fact that the game is old. In fact, it might have been a great looking game back in 1997 on the 640x480 resolution monitors given that the developers tried creating characters which look more human than some cartoony sprites like in other old P&C adventure games. I respect that. Also, there are some fighting scenes with required QTEs which can be frustrating at times though. Lastly, one last grip might be the advertised length of the game. On Steam, it says the plot lasts more than 20-hours, however myself and other people completed it around 10-hours. While it is still a relatively lengthy game, especially for when it was originally released, I personally felt a bit disappointed by that because I always had the impression that there would be more stories to tell by the time you arrive in Constantinople.
Conclusively, as an adventure game, despite being visually outdated due to its old technology, The Last Express is an amazing game and a true masterpiece. It has everything: a great branched plot with many twists, well-written and voiced cast of characters, realistic circumstances with a choice-and-consequence mentality, and most importantly a unique and revolutionary real-time simulation mechanism to advance the plot. Easily one of the best adventure games ever made. If only the visuals were to be remastered accordingly, I would easily see this game wiping the floor with most other similar games out there, new or old. And to hear that the game flopped commercially at launch, it breaks my heart!

If you like point-and-click noir-style adventure games, then this one might be worth checking out. It was made in 1997, but as i was playing I found I didn't notice that fact as much as I thought I would. I think it's the combination of the unique art style and the solid voice acting that drew me into the story and distracted from any graphical shortcomings. The gameplay stands up on its own as well, and though the clicking system can be a bit clunky at times, overall it's a fine interface once you get used to it.
Another strong point of this game is the cast of characters. Over the course of the journey, you come to know each of your fellow travellers and have to piece together the mystery that, as you proceed, you realize everyone else has a hand in as well. Despite the fact that the characters all come from different backgrounds, for the most part the tired stereotypes are avoided inasmuch as they can be in this style of noir investigation. If the game doesn't create all new archetypes, then it fulfills the existing ones very well.
Overall I'd say this is worth the asking price, as it will probably occupy a good 3-4 nights of gameplay for the casual gamer, all while offering a new perspective and a rather unique gameplay experience, the likes of which are rarely seen in titles today.

**minor spoilers for the beginning of the game ** This game has a lot of positive reviews, and I must admit there are some interesting and unique aspects to it, but I cannot recommend it unless you get it extremely on sale and are very curious. This is supposed to be a point and click adventure game where you are tasked to solve a mystery, but what I found while playing it was that you wandered around trying to find things to click on while hoping that said things didn’t suddenly and inexplicably end the game for you. This happens a lot. “Oh, that’s the E-break to stop the train? Guess I should have left that alone, but it was so shiny and clickable!”
The animation style is unique and it might appeal to some people. It looks old-fashioned, and since the game is set on the Orient Express, that’s probably on purpose. The gameplay consists of wandering around the same five or six locations while trying to “catch” people in conversation to further the plot, or sometimes people simply show up and talk to you. Often times I felt like I performed an action and had no idea why until the game explained it to me. For example, very early on in the game you come across a dead body. You have no idea who it is but the only thing you seem to be able to do with it is throw it out the window. If you do nothing, the game ends on your failure to act so I threw the body out the window and wondered what the heck was going on. Later on, the game finally told me who that was and why I threw him.  I don’t feel like I’m actively solving a mystery when the game has to explain to me why and what I did after I already did it.
As I said, some people might enjoy this game. It’s a bit of a curiosity and it’s not a bad game per-say, but I could not enjoy it because I didn’t feel like I was solving a murder mystery (especially when I threw the body out the window).

The Witcher 2 improves upon the first game in the series in several aspects. The graphics are much better and can be quite gorgeous at times. The combat system was changed from the first game to be more controller-friendly. This is good and bad in a way. The combat system in the first game tended to be a rock/paper/scissors affair depending on the enemy you face (which was usually cast Aard-stab-stab-change stance-stab-stab-stab), while in the second game I tended to face encounters the same way (cast Aard-stab-stab-roll-stab-stab-roll-cast Aard-stab).
The story though and voice acting is the biggest sell for this game. Not going to spoil anything but the storyline is quite rich and full of excellent world-building.
Choices that were made in the first game very minimally affected Witcher 2. Mostly as just a one-off comment that would change depending on one or two plot points. A lot of decisions were made though in this game that I believe will affect Witcher 3 so for those new to the series that want to play 3 I would suggest jumping on here, although Witcher 1 is also a good pick-up for an RPG itch.
It'll take some getting used to if you moved here from Witcher 1 with new controls, UI, alchemy system, but its definitely worth it. Pick it up if you don't already have it.

A true love letter to all the great adventure movies from back in the day. This game is by far one of the best point and click games money can buy, despite the aged graphics and animations. If you are a lover of adventure games, this is a must own title from one of videogames legandary  creators. I got this on sale and maybe that is why I am over the moon about it, yet if you are a point and click gamer, this is still a no brainer.
The story is well written and keeps a nice pace from start to finish. The voice acting really does shine and has to be the best part about the game. It is as if you are watching a film sometimes and every now and the game just looks amazing for when it was made. The world around you functions without you having to set all the events into motion. The way things play out is very entertaining and you are rewarded for searching the entire train.
There are a few bugs here and there for windows that you might notice. These are not at all gamebreakers, just a bit annoying. Your character from time to time will get stuck in an action, for example you might move too many paces ahead of yourself and have to turn around. Also, the icons to move and interact with things get mixed up from time to time. These bugs can be fixed with a quick reload and don't happen often enough to destroy the fun.
If you are a lover of the classics and have some money to throw at this gem, then do just that. It won't let you down unless you allow the age of the animation and graphics bother you the entire time. Everything you need to get invested into a story is right here. Enjoy your adventure.

Good game. I finish it in a little less than 30 hours. At first I was not sure about getting it, cause, as you can see, it was badly rated. Then i realized that most negative comments came from people that barely played it. So, it was pretty cheap and with cards, so not much to lose in any case.
For the way people talks about this you would think is a bug fest that crashes all the time, but that's simply not true. I had zero crashes. Bugs, not exactly, just a few mechanics that could be better. At times a character can get stuck for a bit behind another or might need a few extra clics to shot or hit a zombie. Nothing is game breaking and you get pretty much accustomed to it rather quickly. Also, there's no real issue with the interface. And, most important, you can give instructions while the game is paused. So, actually, is very easy to control the action.
The game is not a combat game, is a tactics game in the likes of Commandos. Nevertheless, you can shot plenty if that's what you like. At the end, the objective is to complete the maps in the most efficient way. As in Commandos, is a little bit of a puzzle where you need to think for a moment about the best approach to any situation. There are traps to lure the zombies in, for instance. There are blood packs that you can use on one of your characters or throw them to the zombies.  That would work in different ways. There are a few surprises regarding the zombies too, at times there are much more of them than you would think.
There are six characters with different skills. There are several weapons, even granades, so is not like it's lacking variety. The graphics are good and the game is good looking overal, with nice effects and decent voices. The story is just your typical zombie story but, really, what's so original about zombies since the "Night of the living dead"? It's always about some dudes trying to survive.

It is a wonderful game, a great shame that it wasn't a success when it was new. I absolutely recommend it to anyone who enjoys classic adventure and mystery games, especially the fans of historical settings. And I have to say, re-released on the centennary of World War I, this game is current as ever.
There are a few minor caveats though, that I need to mention...
First, the control scheme is extremely unusual, and not very intuitive, especially if you are used to point-and-click games. It definitely takes getting used to, but once you get the hang of it, you won't even notice this.
Second, the Windows version at least seems to be somewhat buggy - I have ran into a few crashes, peculiar slowdowns and speedups, and action icons getting mixed up randomly (like "turn around" being shown instead of "go forward", or having an item icon stuck as your "interact" icon, even after you've disposed of the item...)
Third, there are a few genuine design glitches, especially surrounding the artifact missing from Tyler Whitney's compartment. It is nothing major, but it's definitely something that the creators, or the remastering team could really have tackled better.

I hear people say all the time that paladins is a ripoff of overwatch. But honestly, that's ridiculous. The difference between paladins and overwatch is the same difference between League and Dota. Overwatch is League, while Paladins is Dota.
Paladins is much slower paced, The MOBA elements are much more pronounced, and it plays much more like TF2 than overwatch does. While overwatch is a very simple, minimalistic game, paladins has much more depth.
There are more champions in paladins, each of which can be played in several different ways depending on which loadout you select.
The gameplay and gunplay feel a lot better to me as well. My big problem with overwatch is that it feels like there's way too much movement, the camera is constantly moving and bouncing around. It's trying to be immersive, but it's just obnoxious to me, especially coming from TF2 where there is no camera movement like that. It's just jarring as hell. Paladins has some camera movement, but it's much more subdued.
I would personally say that paladins is already better than overwatch.

Orion: Prelude is a FPS where you (primarily) defend your base against waves of dinosaur enemies. It's not well-explained where you are or why dinosaurs are attacking your base (especially the herbivorous ones, like Stegosaurus and Triceratops), but that perhaps misses the point: shooting dinosaurs. This aspect feels pretty solid; big dinosaurs are hard to deal with and can easily kill you, little ones surround you and can take you down in a short period of time. I'll tackle major aspects of the game below instead of a list of pros and cons. If you're looking for deep gameplay, look elsewhere. If you're looking for a little bit of fun, especially with friends, this is well worth your one dollar (but perhaps not much more). OVERALL: 5/10
Gameplay 6/10
I've only ever played the standard co-op wave survival game type (with bots and/or friends), but there are other game modes. Each of three classes has a specific ability and set of weapons, which are adequately differentiated. Difficulty scales nicely over the ten waves, and rewards for defeating dinosaurs allows you to purchase weapons, turrets, and/or item upgrades. This all feels pretty good, but the weapons could be slotted into 4/5 categories which feel almost exactly the same. Vehicles (which seem mostly ripped from Halo's assets) are an interesting addition and are fun to use, but somewhat difficult to steer. Dinosaurs' models match their power level neatly, and you'd better be packing top-tier weapons when more than two at a time are nearby. Killing an enemy while downed allows a self-revive in addition to teammates' ability to revive you.
One of my biggest issues with this game is the AI. The dinosaurs will not know what to do if you are outside of their attack range and will waggle back and forth below seemingly forever. Cloaking immediately breaks aggro of ANY dinosaur and seems to prevent re-acquiring you as a target for a few seconds. Teammate AI is even worse. They rarely revive you, fail to efficiently capture points, routinely fail to headshot dinosaurs sitting in front of their face, and have garish joke outfits like sandwich hats and wizard cloaks. Playing with bots is really only worth it for two reasons: they aggro dinosaurs and can (for some reason) accurately take down dinosaurs flying at/near the game ceiling.
Graphics: 5/10
Looks solid most of the time, but things get wonky when dinosaurs die, and when playing in 3rd person. Switching weapons results in a very low-quality model for the first second or so. Dino models are solid, character models less so, (bot costumes -> horrific). Environment looks good all around, weather effects look great, but hinder visibility in ways that are counterproductive to a FPS.
Music/Sound: 4/10
I have only ever heard two songs in this game, both of which are rousing and I quite like. If you didn't like them, they'd get old fast.
Sound is less good overall. Sound balance is wonky: one pistol is about twice as loud as every other weapon; T-Rex roars seem to badly clip the audio (and my eardrums); slow-mo start sound blares unreasonably. Could be better balanced and menu audio options don't seem to affect all sounds. Everything else is solid, but leaves something to be desired.
Performance: 4/10
The game seems to be very poorly optimized and freezes for a few seconds when awarding class level ups, and uses far more system resources than I would expect from a game like this.

I gave Star Crusade a try whilst casually getting up to speed with the current situation on card game front. Do I recommend it? Yes and no: the game is in early access, so whatever I say now might become irrelevant in a week or so. If you're looking for a finished product or want to invest money into a hobby, you probably won't be interested in an unfinished title in the first place. However, if you're more adventurous, this might be worth a look.
Early access or not, the direction here is obvious from the outset. This is a Hearthstone clone. It might sound a bit rough, but that's essentially what it is - not a "Hearthstone-style" or a "Hearthstone-inspired" game - a straight and honest clone. And that, I think, is not necessarily a bad thing.
I've played absurd amounts of Hearthstone in the past, probably more than I should have. And I have no regrets about it, it's a great game and it's popular for a reason. But eventually I stopped, and so did many people, because it has some glaring, hard-to-ignore issues: unhealthy meta, boring ranking system and stubborn, corporate customer support just to name a few. What started as a great CCG with seemingly limitless potential gradually devolved into a braindead netdecking grind. And most of those problems, I think, stem from the fact that Hearthstone has gone effectively uncontested for too long.
So this is where Star Crusade comes in. It copies Hearthstone at the very basics, card-for-card, system-for-system. Even the card stats are mostly the same. And I can see the potential benefit from this strategy. Star Crusade promises Hearthstone veterans a fresh start and could be less intimidating for new players. Plus, the devs seem to be adding new concepts to the game and attempting to fix some of Hearthstone's most obvious mistakes.
The way I see it, this experiment could go both ways. If they manage to take the initial concept of Hearthstone in a whole new direction (Space is a good place to start, no doubt), this could be a big win - especially with a few improvements on the business model. However, if they stick to the source material too much, I don't see why anyone should choose a carbon copy over the original, unless they really prefer space ships over orcs. If the game doesn't evolve into something completely different, it will simply repeat Hearthstone's mistakes, and we'll have two netdeck-dominated grindfests instead of one.
Also, Hearthstone didn't earn all that credit on gameplay alone. It has some hugely impressive art direction going for it, and, in all honesty, I think in many cases it wins people over more than the game itself. Plus, it has all the richness and familiarity of Warcraft lore. If Star Crusade is to succed at all, the art team will have to topple that. At the moment most of the cards in Star Crusade are well-voiced but visually uninteresting, everything is mostly grey and navy blue, and the factions look very similar to each other. I'm afraid they will have to do better than this. But hey, it's too early to pass judgement on the looks. All I'm saying is, this is an area that needs a lot of improving.
As for now, I'll give this game a thumbs up just because I think it's about time someone attempts to give Hearthstone a run for its money. Let's see what happens next.

FATE is the spiritual predecessor of Torchlight, and it shows.  Mechanics like "pets carrying loot to town" were developed right here.  The graphical style is similar, the play style is familiar, and the entire game revolves around procedurally generated quests and dungeons.  If these are the elements of an Action RPG that you enjoy, then do pick up this game and play a little slice of history.  If, however,  you want a thoroughly modern and highly polished experience, then stick with Torchlight 2 or Path of Exile instead.
That all said, it has been my experience that most fans of ARPGs have a little bit of retro-gamer in them.  If this describes you, then stop reading this right now and start playing FATE.  It will give that pin-prick of retro style in a package that is just as fun as other ARPGs.
The only detractors for me are the lack of any sort of skill tree system, or anything else that truly differentiates one play style from another.  While it is true that FATE's character progression is intendedly more organic than a class-based game like Diablo 2 (and succeeds, as far as it goes), it comes off as retrograde as compared to character progression in a more modern game like Torchlight 2 or even Diablo 3.
Bottom line: If you enjoy Action RPGs, then pick this up on sale.  You won't be disappointed.

I keep travelling back to the old school and the next stop is "The Last Express", an adventure game by Jordan Mechner, who is most famous for creating the original Prince of Persia. In "The Last Express" you play a man who answers the call after recieving a telegram from a friend who is bound for Istanbul on the famed Orient Express train. That's as far as I'm going plotwise because it would be doing a disservice to future players because it's one of the best things about this game. It's like a historical spy adventure murder mystery with some romance thrown in. The story, voice acting and music are all top notch. The graphics are "rotoscoped" and are early examples of all that sensor wearing/green screen technology so common in movie making today and they work very well. Another thing of note is that the game runs (mostly) in real time. The passengers will go about their business so if you miss something, you'll really miss it. However you do get a lifeline with a "rewind time" mechanic which allows you to run back the clock. It's pretty helpful when you make a bad decision. Unfortunately you will do quite a bit of wandering waiting for the next action to occur and the train isn't terribly big but you will know the layout very well by the end.  Some of the QTEs are somewhat wonky but you get used to them fairly quickly.  If you're an ADD type player looking for quick satisfaction, then you may want to look elsewhere. But if you savor slow burn, plot driven games where you take your time then this is for you.  The story gets a 10/10 from me. Overall an 8/10 though.

This game is like if Endless Ocean tried to be Journey. I can't say it succeeds, but it's still a good game.
The world of Abzu is gorgeous and it was fun finding and interacting with a lot of my favorite marine wildlife species. There were several species that I did not expect and was delighted to see. (No cuttlefish, though. What the heck?) There were a lot of surprises that brought a smile to my face, and I felt like the game was encouraging me to experiment and explore. There were moments where I felt genuine glee, and others where I felt genuine terror. (Like, slightly nauseous terror. Maybe I just have a fear of the ocean.)
But those moments made the disappointing moments even worse for me, when the game's similarities to Journey became a little too overt, or when it took the reins away just to show off how pretty it is. The swimming controls feel good and natural, even with mouse and keyboard, but there are a few places where the camera goes wonky, and trying to swim vertically can be weird and troublesome. The limitations on where you're allowed to swim could also be strange or unclear at times. The story is interesting enough, but it certainly doesn't seem to be the "universal myth that resonates across cultures" that they've been touting it as.
Another issue I have with the game is the illusion of danger. In Journey there were monsters that would permanently tear off half of your scarf, meaning losing half of your flying capability. That feels like a big deal, and it has long-lasting effects on your playthrough. In Abzu there are things that stun you for a few seconds. That's not a big deal, it's a minor annoyance. But it's treated with the same gravity as in Journey. And I think that's Abzu's core problem, at least for me: It tries too hard to be like Journey rather than its own thing, and it fails to measure up.
This review sounds very negative, but that's just because I'm disappointed that the game isn't as amazing as it could have been. It is a great experience nonetheless, with fantastic visuals, immersive diving, and a wide and (mostly) realistic variety of sealife. I can wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone who doesn't mind the short length and simple gamplay.

As a fan of adventure point-and-click games, I decided to take a risk and buy The Last Express to see if it actually lived up to all of its hype.
The short answer? Yes. Yes, it absolutely did. Buy this game. NOW.
Weirdly enough, I almost stopped playing this game after the initial five minutes. My one  caveat to anyone playing this game is to expect a very narrow game screen. After playing (and being spoiled by) modern games that fill up my entire computer screen, I was surprised and temporarily frustrated by narrow gaming window (can't remember the name for it, but basically black bars on either side of the screeen with the game "window" in the middle). While this screen does open up for cutscenes and certain areas, if you give the format a chance, you'll be used to it in no time. After about 15-20min, I got my bearings and roughly knew the layout of the train, as well as important functions like looking around.
Unlike the vast majority of games out there, The Last Express is in real time, so conversations don't wait, people move around, and important events may unfold regardless of your presence, which often lead to a very abrupt end. Not to worry though; the game has a handy "Rewind" button which allows you to go back before your mistake, so the ends aren't that problematic and occasionaly are even funny. As such, you are immersed into a living, breathing world set just before World War I, where every moment contains actions and dialogue that can be caught or missed. If you turned left during one playthrough, turn right during the next, and so on; you never know what you will find or overhear! As far replay-value goes, The Last Express is a gem: the script for the game was apparently over 800 pages long.
You play fugitive Robert Cath who has managed to get on to the Orient Express at the behest of his friend Tyler Whitney. On board, you go find to find Whitney, and are quickly swept up into an engrossing tangle of murder, political intrigue, covert operations, and even a bit of romance. I'll be honest, I didn't expect to become so invested in the story, and there's no two ways about it, chances are you will (unneccesarily) rush through your first run because of the inital pressure of real time (turns out, you can actually do and explore a lot more than you think), but by the end, you will be right there with the characters as plots intertwine, secrets are revealed, and the world stands on the brink of World War I. By the time the credits roll, you'll want to start it all over again.

I have been a fan of Galactic Civilizations since its first game and a Fan of Stardock for a very very long time. Although some of their titles have been plagued with bugs this game is pretty stable.
The game is Civilization in space, and instead of plopping cities wherever you wish your limited to habitable planets that can sustain your race. The good news is you can create your own race with its own perks and limitations. The race to colonize the galaxy is a fierce one as you will be competing with many different major alien empires as well with local independent planets that will hinder or aid you in your own conquest.
Customizing your race is fun, there is a lot you can edit including your portrait, name, abilities, ship colors, ship styles, and even your opening text as you boot up your game. The race you choose can evolve the way you want by the way of morality by special events that occur in the galaxy or planets. Your morality works like a religion as the other alien empires will judge you based on your rule style.
The bad news is the game can be a little complex as the technology tree is very large and diverse. Although it has improved since its earlier titles it still very large and will take a while to get through. The galactic map can become very difficult depending on how the map is drawn you could be in the center of the galaxy surrounded by habitable planets or stuck in an asteroid field with dead planets.
The game is very random which is a good thing, even playing the same nation it will play out differently, no strategy will work every time. It is worth the money, I just wish they would open the game up for modding as this game has enormous potential for expanded content.

The Witcher 2 improves upon the first game in the series in several aspects. The graphics are much better and can be quite gorgeous at times. The combat system was changed from the first game to be more controller-friendly. This is good and bad in a way. The combat system in the first game tended to be a rock/paper/scissors affair depending on the enemy you face (which was usually cast Aard-stab-stab-change stance-stab-stab-stab), while in the second game I tended to face encounters the same way (cast Aard-stab-stab-roll-stab-stab-roll-cast Aard-stab).
The story though and voice acting is the biggest sell for this game. Not going to spoil anything but the storyline is quite rich and full of excellent world-building.
Choices that were made in the first game very minimally affected Witcher 2. Mostly as just a one-off comment that would change depending on one or two plot points. A lot of decisions were made though in this game that I believe will affect Witcher 3 so for those new to the series that want to play 3 I would suggest jumping on here, although Witcher 1 is also a good pick-up for an RPG itch.
It'll take some getting used to if you moved here from Witcher 1 with new controls, UI, alchemy system, but its definitely worth it. Pick it up if you don't already have it.

The Last Express is a classic adventure game with a riveting story and brilliant atmosphere, it is perhaps my favourite story told in a mystery adventure rivalled only by some of the LucasArts classics.
I've played through this game multiple times over the last decade and I always enjoy the experience, it's like watching an excellent mystery movie, with interesting narrative and likeable characters and conversations which stick with you even after the game concludes.
However.
DotEmu has sacrificed what made this game a 'must have' in any collection, marred the game play with tool tips and icons which ruin the atmosphere of the game.
Sure, it plays in a higher resolution, and has compatibility with newer operating systems, but in the process DotEmu seem to have removed sound effect files such as the bustling wind from the carriage windows when they're opened.
I know it seems silly to nitpick on such minor details, but these minor nuances are what made me fall in love with this game.
Back on the subject of tool tips, the achievement icons that pop up in the middle of the screen when cinematic are playing.
And these can't be turned off. Not at all.
There is no option to turn off achievement or character bio/unlock popups, and they linger on-screen for up to 10 seconds.
The inclusion of (but to merit the ability to disable) tutorials is an insult to this game. Sorry you had to take the time to write them into the game, sadly they don't scream "GOLD EDITION" when the original title was a test of wits and observation skills, rather than telling you that the person you needed to talk to was currently having breakfast and you should annoy them.
I wouldn't recommend this VERSION of The Last Express solely that there are better, unadulterated versions available from other distributors, and simply put the term GOLD EDITION only exists because of a unlockables screen, which ultimately ruins the experience.
If the above could be toggled on/off or even removed, or even a purist setting, which disables on-screen prompts and hints, I would instantly regard this as the best version of the game available.

Released in 1997 during the final stages of the golden age of point-and-click adventures, the game was eventually a commercial failure and out of print nearly a year later. It was extremely expensive to make at the time, and a lot of effort was made to make it as historically authentic and convincing as possible. They even found an old abandoned Orient Express stowed away for 50+ years on a rail yard somewhere in Athens giving them first hand sources to make the legendary train come to life.
The game itself in a nutshell is a murder mystery. You have received a telegram from your friend Tyler Whitney to meet him on the train to take a journey from Paris to Jerusalem, as he has found something that might interest him there. Unfortunately the protagonist misses the train thanks to unforeseen circumstances with the law, and the only thing Tyler is greeted with is patrolling police on the lookout. Still that doesn’t stop the protagonist from boarding the train thanks to a friend and her motorcycle. On board you are free to explore the train, but your first task is to reunite with your friend whom should be waiting in his compartment. As you open the door you are met his mutilated and clawed up body. Determined to find out what happened you hide his body, take his identity ready to seek out and find the killer of your friend.
What makes this game so unique and not like anything you have ever previously played is how the whole game is played in real time. The clock is always ticking on the Orient Express and you have both passengers and crew going about their own things no matter if you’re there to catch them in the act or not. By making it this way you never feel like the game is tailor made for you. Just sitting in the smoking car eavesdropping as the passengers babble on might give you important information or clues to your case or impertinent discussions about anything 1914 related topics or just ordinary daily life stuff - which is still very interesting mind you thanks to some of the most realistic and deepest characters I’ve ever seen in a video game.  Never have I played a game with this level of historical authenticity, you are immediately immersed in this game and convinced that you are a passenger on the Orient Express on the eve of World War 1.
Being in real time you will obviously miss tons clues, discussions, dialogue and events the first times playing it. Every time I come back to this game I always find new and undiscovered information. You are of course still able to rewind or fast forward the game at your leisure if you feel like experimenting with different routes. The game features a bunch of endings and only the most determined will make it all the way to Constantinople and find out the truth about the fate of his friend.
I highly recommend this game for any fans of point-and-click adventures who wants to try something different. It contains a compelling story, excellent characters and great voice acting who all speaks in their natural language; may it be Russian, English, German, Serbian, Arabian or French. The graphics are cartoony, but very stylish – I think it fits great for this game. All the characters are based off real actors who were mo-capped into the game so it still contains a very realistic look despite having cartoony colours.

So did you ever wonder how it would be like to be a game developer? An indie one whose livelihood depended on it? I doubt it would be all fun and games (pun intended) but you surely wouldn't resort to the same schemes as Warren, the protagonist of Dev Guy. You wouldn't, right?
Dev Guy plays like an adventure game with just controlling the bearded fella who can merely interact with stuff and use the single item he might be carrying at the time. The deadline for app store uploads is next day but he manages to lose all his files (okay, he's apparently not heard of cloud storage before) and goes on a hacker-equivalent of burglaring frenzy.
Hacking plays out as mini-games when Warren tries the various games whose assets he's stealing. Probably the only challenging one is the platforming mini-game with lethal spikes; the rest are mostly very easy, rather shallow mini-games from various genres like visual novels and puzzles. They are fun enough to play or try once so they get the job done.
Dev Guy is perhaps a parody of indie development scene. Indie games may be short, artsy games; (relatively) hard, punishing platformers; one-trick ponies that charm for a couple of sessions that you then leave to rot to your ever-growing gaming library. Why, some even look like they have their assets stolen from other games. Dev Guy looks like all the described games above at the same time.
Being a free single-player game, should you play Dev Guy? Well, it's got a load of funny enough gaming and pop-culture references for less than 1 hour of play time. It's not bad - though it's not that good either, but I think it could be worth a buck if there was a price on it. In retrospect it looks like a mediocre compilation of a small developer team's handiwork that does not really break the point to be considered a commercial product but just *might* work as a showcase for something bigger to come.
I'm still just saying *might* because its visuals are unpolished (perhaps by design, I cannot say) and there's not much replay value unless you really like the jiggly mode that looks like something they threw on top of it because it looks funny. For a completionist, Dev Guy is easy one to 100%.
If after this review you find yourself thinking you might want to play it, I propose you install it. Then, one day if you find yourself having nothing better to do, play it through: you'll get that nice 1 hour of entertainment you were craving for. It might also get you thinking of programming, development or ethics of those things (if you are into such things) but that I cannot guarantee.

It's pretty obvious that this game is too much of a Hearthstone ripoff. Too many of the same rules apply. You basically race to be the first player to knock the enemy's HP down to zero. However, I am willing to give them the benefit of the doubt as I can see some differences in their gameplay. If I were to score them from 1-100, they would get 50-60 marks, barely passing because they copied too much from Hearthstone. Packs of 50 cost $62.29 and each pack has 6 cards (300 random cards). The price is kind of unaffordable for an online game that doesn't need to worry about shipping costs.
PROS
1. Cool Sounding Names
Hajirog, Annuranki
2. Modules
The commander abilities can be swapped out with modules allowing you to change their abilities.
3. Non-Hearthstone Abilities
The abilities are not unique but at least I don't see them in Hearthstone which is where the developers primarily copy from.
Soak: Your units take 2 less damage
Hero Ability Mutate: Units take 1 damage and gain 2 attack
4. Interesting Storyline
The story is pretty good and is reminescent of a game called Twilight Imperium.
5. Energy
Interesting idea. It prevents games from dragging on for too long.
6. Turn order token
Well done. It's much better than Hearthstone's End Turn flip.
CONS
1. Pay To Win
Totally forgot that a CCG is always P2W.
2. Ripoffs from Hearthstone
a. Number of cards in Deck = 25-40
b. First Player draws 3, Second Player draws 4 and gets an Initiative card (Same as Crystal in Hearthstone)
c. Hajirog Thrash = Mage Firebolt (Deal 1 Damage for 2 Mana)
d. Terran Rally = Paladin Reinforce (Summon a 1/1)
e. Hierachy Nanite Conversion = Priest Heal (Recover 2 HP)
f. Stacking limit of 2 of a card per deck
g. Credit: You pay for the card next turn.(Similar to Overload)
3. No Trading of Cards
Your cards are virtual so they have no secondary market value. This ensures that Rare, Uncommon, Common and Legendary are meaningless.
However, they have no secondary market to trade cards. This ensures that players are unable to find the cards that they severely lack for cheap. Fusion mode might sound great but you need to sacrifice many cards to make 1 card you need.
If you are worried about multiple accounts focusing all the cards to 1 account, you can track the cards with a trade log to find account spammers.
NEUTRAL
1. 2-Player Limit
Sadly, all CCGs seem to be unable to play more than 2.

I'd been itching to play this throughout the Early Access, but just because of that, I waited till the release so I would be even more impressed. And heck, I was impressed. The more I play Crypt of the Necrodancer, the more things I find to appreciate. Ultimately simple using only four keys to play the game, but with a good amount of items, monsters, songs, bosses and characters to suit your disco of a dungeon crawl to make it both challenging and leave plenty to try as I continue exploring the crypt. Danny B's soundtrack is wonderful, it's fitting and mighty fine to slay monsters to, with the alternative soundtracks and the custom track option, even more opportunities open up. Monsters are both terrifying and downright adorable with their individual dances, and the bosses are simple in theory but perform so well. The inclusion of a daily challenge is entertaining and feeds the desire for so many players to just keep going, and something I was very glad to see included. I've noticed a few comments about the levels being timed, since when the beat drops, your heart stops. Personally I feel fine with this, not only do I feel the songs give you about the right time to explore everything, but it helps keep a pressure on your back that I would far rather have than not in keeping the drive of the crawl. It's not the Binding of Isaac, sure, but I don't want it to be. Absolutely I recommend this game as long as players jive and zombies thrive.
