Released in 1997 during the final stages of the golden age of point-and-click adventures, the game was eventually a commercial failure and out of print nearly a year later. It was extremely expensive to make at the time, and a lot of effort was made to make it as historically authentic and convincing as possible. They even found an old abandoned Orient Express stowed away for 50+ years on a rail yard somewhere in Athens giving them first hand sources to make the legendary train come to life.
The game itself in a nutshell is a murder mystery. You have received a telegram from your friend Tyler Whitney to meet him on the train to take a journey from Paris to Jerusalem, as he has found something that might interest him there. Unfortunately the protagonist misses the train thanks to unforeseen circumstances with the law, and the only thing Tyler is greeted with is patrolling police on the lookout. Still that doesn’t stop the protagonist from boarding the train thanks to a friend and her motorcycle. On board you are free to explore the train, but your first task is to reunite with your friend whom should be waiting in his compartment. As you open the door you are met his mutilated and clawed up body. Determined to find out what happened you hide his body, take his identity ready to seek out and find the killer of your friend.
What makes this game so unique and not like anything you have ever previously played is how the whole game is played in real time. The clock is always ticking on the Orient Express and you have both passengers and crew going about their own things no matter if you’re there to catch them in the act or not. By making it this way you never feel like the game is tailor made for you. Just sitting in the smoking car eavesdropping as the passengers babble on might give you important information or clues to your case or impertinent discussions about anything 1914 related topics or just ordinary daily life stuff - which is still very interesting mind you thanks to some of the most realistic and deepest characters I’ve ever seen in a video game.  Never have I played a game with this level of historical authenticity, you are immediately immersed in this game and convinced that you are a passenger on the Orient Express on the eve of World War 1.
Being in real time you will obviously miss tons clues, discussions, dialogue and events the first times playing it. Every time I come back to this game I always find new and undiscovered information. You are of course still able to rewind or fast forward the game at your leisure if you feel like experimenting with different routes. The game features a bunch of endings and only the most determined will make it all the way to Constantinople and find out the truth about the fate of his friend.
I highly recommend this game for any fans of point-and-click adventures who wants to try something different. It contains a compelling story, excellent characters and great voice acting who all speaks in their natural language; may it be Russian, English, German, Serbian, Arabian or French. The graphics are cartoony, but very stylish – I think it fits great for this game. All the characters are based off real actors who were mo-capped into the game so it still contains a very realistic look despite having cartoony colours.

TLDR: If you liked GalCiv 2 or you like 4X space games then you'll like GalCiv3.
For the more detail oriented folks:
I can understand how some critics can find the innovation lacking in GalCiv3. This game does just about everything GalCiv2 did, only better and shinier; a lot shinier. In my opinion the biggest innovations in the game currently come from the switch to 64-bit only. The massive map sizes, the huge number or players, even a lot of the shiny graphics are only truly possible because of that change. In part I feel that the number of possibilities left open to this game have yet to be realized due to the massive lack of restraints that 64-bit allows for. There are plenty of new things here, but sadly most of them were expected and thus undervalued. We have hex map tiles now, but that's now the status quo. We have adjacency bonuses, but that's also status quo. We have a pretty awesome, informative, and reasonably intuitive UI; which we must have or players will rage quit because they spent more than 30 seconds looking for a button. Aside from the new map sizes and high player count the newest and brightest feature is the freaking awesome ship builder. Sadly I think a lot of casual players may fail to see it as much of an improvement; however, ship builders know the difference, and it's amazing! The devs have talked a lot about things they wish they could have done for release and things being pushed off till later. Fortunately Stardock has a great reputation for continuing to work on games long after the initial release and as an elite founder I am very much looking forward to anything they come out with. I have yet to delve into modding and the steam workshop isn't up at this time so I cannot speak to that. All in all I am very pleased with GalCiv3 and look forward to many many more hours watching the Drengin run away from me. :)

My feelings about GalCiv III are kind of mixed. Pro: it is similar to GalCiv II. Con: some mechanics of GalCiv II are IMO not acceptable in 2015.
First of all, the UI. The fleet mechanics is clumsy. It may be me, but I always make wrong moves when I move ships in our out fleets. For example, you can only eject ships from a fleet. It would be much more natural to select that you want to move away of the fleet, and just move them.
Ship construction. I'm not really interested in making pretty ships. But during the design the ship view occupies 90% of the screen. Understanding what a component does requires to hover the very small icons of the components. And it gets hard understanding which components you are moving in and out the ship. I also didn't find easy to get around all the ship designs.
More serious issue, I'm worried that - an in GalCiv II - every single mission requires to get very close to the end of the tech tree. That is, destroying shipyards and space stations require a lot of firepower, that you get quite late in the game. That's the sensation I got after playing the tutorial, so I may be wrong. While in games like Civ V you can conquer other civilizations at every stage of the game.
The game also has bugs here and there at this moment. One annoying one is that you can't upgrade a ship that uses a strategic resource to a design that requires the same resource IF you have not any spare resource of that kind.
But for the rest the game seems very interesting and I'll spend more hours on the game, and for that reason I'll give it a thumbs up. However I really hope that Bradley & Co. decide to streamline ship design and improve fleet management.

Ah the last express! A masterpiece when it came out, hundred years ago... But it kind of still is a masterpiece, and now it looks like a real peace of antique art. It does have something great to offer though, if you can see past the technical aspects.
You are on the last voyage of the famous train the oriental express, just before the first world war breaks out. You arrive on the train just after the departure, finding out your friend has been murdered. Slowly you learn about the passengers and their complex stories and motivations, who all seem to intertwined. You really feel the tension of the situation and the looming war. It is a great murder mystery that you would snuggle up with in your sofa, but this time, you are really there, seeing and experience the train as the main hero.
Well, sort of. Due to restrictions of computers back then, scenes are more like gifs with few colors. I think the whole game was filmed, and then more than half of the frames had to be taken out in order to run well and save space.
But the style, and especially the colors work in favor of the game. It reminds of how commercial posters were designed at the time. The characters and writing is well done. It is particularly refreshing that people speak their languages, instead of everything being in English. Your character knows a few languages, and in those cases, subtitles are provided.
This is one of those games that made me interested in gaming: a chance to participate in a movie, an event that you have dreamed to be a part of. The whole idea of not just watching a murder mystery happening on this beautiful train, but to actually be the hero was what really drew me in.
What really makes this title even more special is that all passengers have a deeper story that happens with or without you. Instead of just running down a corridor, while a normal game would feed you events in specific order, in this game you can explore the train at your own leisure. You listen to people in order to understand their motivations and backgrounds. All the passengers have their own agenda and the game feels alive. Great AI considering when this game was developed (1997).  You have to behave, think and act like you were really on the train. You have to think: "What would they do now? Where are they now? How can I get to them?  What are the consequences?"  It is not about just finding objects and pulling levels. Also, you could argue there are multiple endings. In my mind there is only one good ending, but then you can end the game in other ways as well.
The game has a nice chapter system, and instead of saving, the story has "time". You can rewind the clock if you mess up.
The game is also not trying too hard to entertain you constantly with music and fantastic events. You are on a train, that behaves like a train. People behave like passengers from the time. But it is not boring at all, there is a real mystery going on of course. I for example love it how you can choose to interact with your romance interest. What would you do in real life?
So what is not so good about the game?
Well, the game is a sort of a port, because the original would not work on today's PCs. It is quite buggy. It crashed a few times, and the language files don't work as I write this. No matter what you select in the menus, the game will set the language to whatever your OS language is. There is a hint system included, which is both good and bad. It is good because the game does not behave like a normal game, and there is no hand holding, which can be confusing. Some help might be welcome. It is bad because you can just look at all the hints and the game offers no challenge what so ever. I recommend you don't use the hints, and just rewind the time if you mess up, it makes you interact more with the game like you are there. There are some quick time events. Not too many thank God, but they are not forgiving and some of them you end up doing 20 times before you win.
And, this title is not for everybody. This is a great old piece of art which really focuses on atmosphere, immersion and story. It is not a "gamey" game which feeds you constantly in fear of you being bored. You have to assume what to do yourself. It is more of an interactive story, and I think younger players are not going to dig it very much. It has nothing of what newer games provide (of course).
I'm not pushing the "older games were better" cliché, because it isn't true. But I miss these kinds of elements this game offer  in newer games. I would love it if someone did a reboot on this one, with today's technology. Or if there were more games like this where you are in a specific situation with developed NPCs, where the game assume you are not a complete idiot.
Recommended.

GALACTIC CIVILIZATION III is probably the ultimate space exploration world building strategy game available. Races are very different from one another with plenty of personality. There are those who will become trusted friends as you aid each other's growth in the cold reaches of space. Then there are others who truly are a menace to all and you will learn to despise utterly with furrowed brow and frothing mouth wishing to throw their entire race into a black hole though GALACTIC CIVILIZATIONS III gives you many choices not to and to be better then that.
Thanks to the amazing tutorial and tool tips GALACTIC CIVILIZATIONS III is extremely easy to get into with its layer upon layers of world building and space exploration depth. You can also just go through the mountain of options available on the screen pressing buttons to see what they do in a very intuitive way which rewards with plenty of easy to understand results. Its pretty incredible to see a strategy game with so much detail making everything feel realistic and alive be so easy to get into without insulting the intelligence of the player.
I love the environments in outer space with terrifying black holes which when you zoom in you can hear the eerie howl of some deep mysterious void. Gas clouds which can effect ship instruments in and outside of combat. Relics and space wreckage which hold useful salvage and important scientific discoveries from other races etc etc etc.
You can design and build ships once you have a ship yard constructed along with space stations which are very important playing multiple roles as planetary defense and a source of resources among many other commonsense purposes which i have not seen done in other games.  Commonsense that is the word i think of most when playing GALACTIC CIVILIZATIONS III from the design and purpose of ships and space stations to the way a world can evolve and grow along with interactions with other races it all seems to promote rational thinking instead of a bunch of psychotic races out to destroy everything and everyone. There is a certain calming reassuring quality about this as one does the best to live a happy life in space while dealing with warring races and space pirates which if you play your cards right you will have many an ally at your side to help keep the peace.
Graphics are excellent capturing a beautiful awe inspiring jaw dropping view of the universe and all it has to offer. User interface is a joy to use and i have yet to feel frustrated or confused interacting with it. Ships span a huge variety of styles from dashingly heroic to malevolently menacing. Combat which can can be viewed from a top down or cinematic camera angle is a thrilling and tense affair as you see battles play out before your eyes. Be sure though to repair your ships if they stay out too long in space eventually even small pirate encounters will leave it a hulking wreck which may never make it  home. Hmm i wonder if they have a derelict towing service :D
When discoveries are made or something of importance has been built or a major goal achieved the player is rewarded with intensely gorgeous videos just like the good old days of CIVILIZATION and ALPHA CENTAURI with all their eye candy when something important was achieved. I was in science fiction bliss seeing all this futuristic mysterious inspiring imagery play out before my eyes. Watch out BLIZZARD someone might just take your CGI video crown away when it comes to artistic quality and presentation.
Music and sound effects hit the spot with plenty of action packed rhythms along with relaxing soothing moments of meditative harmony of the sounds of the universe. It makes me question if Stardock Entertainment shot a satellite out into space to capture all the sounds of the universe for GALACTIC CIVILIZATIONS III.
If your a fan of space exploration and combat and such classic titles as the CIVILIZATION series, ALPHA CENTAURI, STAR DRIVE 2, GRATUITOUS SPACE BATTLES 1+2, SID MEIER'S CIVILIZATION BEYOND EARTH and SID MEIER'S STARSHIPS then GALACTIC CIVILIZATION III may very well be the game that satisfies in ways you never thought you could be satisfied by a video game.
Oh and did i mention GALACTIC CIVILIZATION III is also supporting modding :D

For the longest time, I thought turn based RPGs no longer had any value to them. Then I revisited FFVII and realized that though the gaming climate has changed a lot since 1997, traditional RPG's still have a lot to offer.
Gameplay wise, there is a decent amount of depth and variety, more than i remember. For the random encounters, consiter setting up gear between multiple characters, choosing between leveling up more materias or a safer HP bar, there is certainly a lot to consiter.
It's easy to criticize the character models being full of polygons, but looking past that, there is actually some phenominal art in this game. Particularly in the backgrounds that sometimes look beautifully hand painted. I haven't seen anything like it before or since, in games or not. It's obvioius that they put a ton of work and polish into the art despite having such limitations. It made the experience all the more enjoyable throughout the entire game.
The music also has plenty of limitations, so it's not much of a surprise that the tracks are hit and miss. But the hits are still quite impressive. Have a listen to "Cosmo Canyon" "Judgement Day" and of course "Those who Fight Further" If you're interested.
The characters themselves get a good amount of attention as far as the story is concerned, give or take one or two who seem a little archetypical. The game puts a lot of emphasis on Cloud and Sephiroth's writing in particular making them complex and admitidely pretty confusing at times. The story itself gets really gripping, so you shouldn't have to worry about not finishing the game once you start.

The story is pretty straight forward. Your the spiky haired protaganist. You start out as part of a group known as Avalanche. They are trying to take down a major corporation that is killing the planet for resources. The game takes  a sudden change when your second attempt at destruction goes wrong. Without spoiling to much for the handful of people that have not played this it goes from a simple take down this corporation to saving the world from a cataclysmic end. The story involves a non-standard love story that helps to drive the characters but each character holds their own reason for saving the world.
This was the Final Fantasy game that made the transition from 2D to 3D. At the time it was a revolution of sight and sound. The world is amazing and filled with a world worth exploring. The problem is this game has not aged well. While the style and gameplay hold dear to many peoples hearts the graphics have not stood the test of time. There is a lot of polygons that are reminisent of Quest 64. That being said the music, FMV's, and to an extent the gameplay graphics are still amazing and worth exploring. The world itself steps out of the normal realm of a final fantasy game of fantasy, castles, and chivalry instead it goes for a "real" world experience. That being said there is still magic, summons, and the impossible.
Gameplay is pretty standard of a Final Fantasy game. You have your main character with two support characters at any time. There are 7 characters you will get throughout the game and two that are optional. That being said both optional characters are easy to get and worth the work. Each character has its own style of fighting and there is no one right team. The battle system is a simple times battle. You start out with the ability to attack and use items but as you gather more materia you can add abilities and expand each characters worth.
You have an overworld that you traverse to go from town to town. Over time you gain different vehicles each having its own pros and cons.
You are able to use a controller with this game. I was able to use both a corded xbox 360 controller and a PS3 controller. It was more difficult to use the PS3 controller but it was well worth the effort. Of course you can use a keyboard but its not really advised.
The achievements in this game are bland. There was the ability to really make some interesting challenges however as I understand from the technical limitations it wasnt the easiest to add. That being said I have played about 70 hours of gameplay and the actual game took maybe 20 hours. The rest was grinding and working on the achievements. Its not an impossible task to complete but its not that amazing.
The game averages for about $12. On sale it has been as low as $5. Even for full price its worth picking up for some nostalgia but at the same time I would wait for the next sale to pick it up. The game is a lot of fun even though nothing has changed in 17 years but its worth picking up.

This game is definitely worth it on sale, if you like crime story games at all.
Great story(assuming you listen to the Hollow's radio broadcasts, and other sources too), great voice acting, amazing 1960's version of New Orleans that's fully driveable, and mostly explorable buildings.  Fun, but arcadey driving system.  If you're looking for an authentic driving sim, look elsewhere.
Average third person shooter gunplay, with an unfortunately limited inventory (only one pistol and one long arm at a time, plus grenades/equipment).  Silenced pistol is your friend.  .223 Auto is a beast.  It would have been a far better game with the ability to carry more weapons simultaneously.  Pistol, Shotgun, Auto, Rifle, Special... why not, devs? Just because Mafia 2 limited weapons is no reason to punish this game's audience.
Enemy and friendly AI is a bit on the weak side. Dead body, or eventually, PILE of dead bodies at a corner? Better walk over, alone, to investigate!  After awhile I started playing a lot more recklessly just to give the AI a chance. Stealth defeats the AI utterly.
Map Design is amazing. I'm not sure how much they copied from the actual New Orleans(if any!?) from 1968 to make this game, but it sure looks realistic and lived in, in game.
The music, all period correct, is amazing of course.  I  would have preferred a better radio tool, to just keep playing songs I loved, but they went for a more realistic radio than a user friendly 'radio' player.
Gameplay, either taking over the areas, clearing out enemy groups, putting wiretaps in, it all gets very repetitive. I kept playing just to see how the story turns out, to be honest.   Do not expect to be awed by the revolutionary gameplay.
Bugginess: I had a few bugs in cutscenes, which led to the game hanging. Exited out and restarted, got past the hangup. So it's not an error in the cutscene itself, but a memory leak possibly? I did not take the time to narrow it down further.  Had a couple of game-hang bugs in game as well, mostly where a needed NPC got bounced out of place or something.
Note to potential players: Don't ever use Markers to get rid of the cops. If you get into a gun battle in the middle of a public street with some mafia goons, and the cops show up and start going nuts, just let it happen, it'll be fun! You will either lay waste to dozens, steal a couple of cars and go on a mad chase, or go down in a glorious hail of gunfire.  Oh well, better luck next time.  I do wish the cop NPCs would drop ammo though, that gets annoying with the low ammo capacity on the player's character.
The game's engine overall is very impressive, in terms of level of detail and performance.   Windows  8.1, i7 6700k 4ghz, 32gig ram, SSD, GTX1070.
It runs wonderfully, has great graphical and control options and is a near-perfect co-op experience even with a single keyboard.
it is a good game, but it requires a good computer to run it smoothly

I have loved the series from the beginning (Gal Civ I), and am an Elite founder of Galactic Civilizations III (Which means I've been playing since the alpha). I might be a little biased, but when I think of turn-based-strategy games, this one is at the top of the pile! Here's a few things I love about Galactic Civilizations III:
- Being able to design your own ships and fleets
- Not just placing as many lasers as you can on one ship. There are many ship enhancing modules that require special resources
- Huge hulled ships that can fill space with glittering colors
- New resources make map positioning more exciting
- Resources can be incredibly powerful early game and lead to ship bonuses in late game
- New battle viewer makes watching massive fleet battles even more fun
- Relationships with other civs is in-depth and can change just by trading with the wrong civ
- In depth economic system based on morale, population, manufacturing, and research power
- Balancing your economy and turning a lifeless rock into a planet wide metropolis is pretty cool
- Fun dialogues, descriptions, and quips from other civ leaders
- Being able to design your own civ with their unique bonuses (both positive and negative)
- Massive research tree that allows you to enhance every faucet of your civ
- And last but not least MODDING
I love this game and would recommend it to anyone who loves strategy, space, Civilization Games, or sci-fy. It's a sandbox universe that will keep expanding!
The new Crusade update makes nearly everything about this game better. Check it out!

So I was both surprised and disappointed by this game.
For a Lego game I thought knew what I was getting into here, the standard, simplistic platformer, with a few chuckles here and there. Well, seeing how I don’t know much about The Clone Wars TV show I think it would be best if I stuck with the Pros-Cons list.
Pros.
-They add some puzzles to the levels.
-Lightsabers aren’t the “beat everything” weapon.
-Lots of characters and lots of slots for custom characters.
-Large main area that consists of two ships and their various parts
-“Battlefield Arena” style levels.
-Characters that can fill multiple roles, such as using multiple consoles and filling other character needs.
-You’re able to use your custom characters in the main area.
-Split screen co-op.
Cons.
-Bad camera angles.
-Some puzzles aren’t explained so you have no idea what you’re doing.
-Limited custom character parts, way less than the other games.
-Glitches with custom characters bodies that doubles the front on the back.
-Large main area can get tiresome to run around in.
-“Battlefield Arena” maps get used way too much.
-The reward for getting all the gold bricks is underwhelming.
I feel like there were a lot of things that were improved upon from the other Lego Star Wars games, but at the same time they messed up their own improvements in various ways. However, I think I can still recommend this game if you are interested in the Lego Star Wars games, but as with most games on Steam, wait till it’s on sale.

So I've finally picked the game back up, not sure if over time patches fixed it or what but the game is working now and it's great. I am changing my review to positive as it is working much better.

Development and managing your empire is intricate if not overwhelmingly so once you expand to a certain point but for someone that loves that level of detail it's great. Customization of ships, races, and other elements makes for a unique experience nearly every game.

I've resorted to setting the autosave feature to save every single turn, which keeps me from losing anything (aside from any major actions I take on a turn which I then have to redo), but I still have to go through the whole relaunching and loading the game and have to put up with even longer time between turns with the saving.
Overall, I like the game itself, it's a good addition to the series. But it would be nice if I could actually make it through a game. You can see I've put in 22 hours in the past 2 weeks and I've yet to finish a game, conquer a single empire, or even find all the civilizations on a large map. I'm about to shelf this game and give up on the $50 I spent until it's patched up some.

Sure, it's not Overwatch. Just like how Fatal Fury is not Streetfight 2, League of Legends is not DOTA, Quake is not Doom,  need I go on? Many many MANY concepts were lifted straight from Overwatch without careful consideration why those elements were put together in Overwatch in the first place (such as why Widowmaker's ultimate is a wallhack, as apposed to giving wallhack ultimate to a non-sniper in Paladins).  But Overwatch wasn't the original class based shooter and borrrowed plenty of elements from other games too (mostly TF2, but Reinhart's big shield is Overwatch's unique contribution to the genre).
Paladins isn't as polished as Overwatch, but it does have it's own spin on the genre. Time to kill is much higher. Healing is much more limited. Distances are much bigger. You cannot switch heroes. There are different ways to build your hero ala MOBAs. Some heroes are inspired from MMORPGS more than TF2.
Ultimately, when recommending a free-to-play game, the question becomes less of "Is it worth my money?" and more of "Is it worth my time to try it?". In this case, Paladins gets a  confident "YES.".  Give it a try if you like shooters and the type of gameplay TF2 and Overwatch has to offer, but want a bit of spice and variety. Perhaps you'll like it more than Overwatch.

After a long time of waiting and wondering what it is, ABZU finally appears. Was it worth the wait? Yes and no.
This is beautiful game in almost every respect. It jumps out from the opening with its incredible visual style, attention to detail, and has one of the most perfect soundtracks ever recorded for a video game. Its definitely worth a look.
The question most everyone is likely going to have is....is it worth it? My answer to that is entirely dependent on the gamer who's asking it. If you are looking for an experience that will have you audibly gasping at some of the environments and enjoy exploring and taking your time without a thought about a challenge or "goal" and are able to get something out of that, then yes, its a "cream of the crop" title for that vein of game. If you are a gamer who plays games purely and simply for the "win", then I would say no.  Make no mistake, this game is a "walking simulator" underwater. If that term turns you off, then you have your answer on whether or not you should play this at its current value.
PROS:
+ Stunning in literally every category. From things as simple as the sounds of a dolphin, to the music, to the vibrant world that you're in, it's at times breathtaking and full of vivid color and depth in the art.
+ Technologically sound. I was well above 60 FPS on Ultra the entire time.
+ An interesting way to learn about our ocean and the diversity of life that calls it home.
+ A meditative and relaxing experience.
CONS:
- Saddeningly short. It took me 1.7 hours according to Steam for my first playthrough. I likely could've extended this by exploring every nook and cranny, but I'm not that type of gamer.
- Vague "story" with very little explanation in respect to the point of the journey.
- Too high of an opening price point for what it provides.
- There is no challenge whatsoever. This game is very much like an interactive film in that you're controlling an avatar without a chance of dying/failing or being challenged by a puzzle.
Overall, I sincerely enjoyed my time during my playthrough. I cannot say that it's a must play or must own right now today though. If you are on the fence there is no harm in waiting. It will be there waiting for you when you are ready. Once it hits a price point you are comfortable with, jump on it and enjoy it.
Rating: 8/10 for the quality - 5/10 for the value

I'd been itching to play this throughout the Early Access, but just because of that, I waited till the release so I would be even more impressed. And heck, I was impressed. The more I play Crypt of the Necrodancer, the more things I find to appreciate. Ultimately simple using only four keys to play the game, but with a good amount of items, monsters, songs, bosses and characters to suit your disco of a dungeon crawl to make it both challenging and leave plenty to try as I continue exploring the crypt. Danny B's soundtrack is wonderful, it's fitting and mighty fine to slay monsters to, with the alternative soundtracks and the custom track option, even more opportunities open up. Monsters are both terrifying and downright adorable with their individual dances, and the bosses are simple in theory but perform so well. The inclusion of a daily challenge is entertaining and feeds the desire for so many players to just keep going, and something I was very glad to see included. I've noticed a few comments about the levels being timed, since when the beat drops, your heart stops. Personally I feel fine with this, not only do I feel the songs give you about the right time to explore everything, but it helps keep a pressure on your back that I would far rather have than not in keeping the drive of the crawl. It's not the Binding of Isaac, sure, but I don't want it to be. Absolutely I recommend this game as long as players jive and zombies thrive.

Update:
So I've finally picked the game back up, not sure if over time patches fixed it or what but the game is working now and it's great. I am changing my review to positive as it is working much better.
Additionally, since picking it back up I purchased a new computer, much faster than my old one. While it did start working on my old one, on the new one it runs amazingly.
It's a vast game with many interworking and intricate parts. The diplomacy is still pretty simple and straight forward as is often in these types of games, I would kill for a game that actually allows some real diplomacy other than just picking and choosing what items to trade and who to attack. But I recognize the difficulty in coding something like that up and not going to complain or change this review based on that.
Development and managing your empire is intricate if not overwhelmingly so once you expand to a certain point but for someone that loves that level of detail it's great. Customization of ships, races, and other elements makes for a unique experience nearly every game.
I fully recommend this game. Getting the DLC soon to try it out.
Would be a great game if it didn't crash every 5-20 turns. At one point I would open the game, play for 2 turns and it would crash, after restarting 5 times I gave up and didn't play for a few days. Now it lasts about 20 turns. Another review indicated that it happens if you try to do anything during the wait for turns, however, for me it just randomly crashes. And while it is software and waiting a few days shouldn't have any effect (not like it's an overheated computer or something waiting to cool down) it randomly started lasting longer after waiting. Makes me feel like it's saying "Oh, hey you've been playing too much, go do something else."
I've resorted to setting the autosave feature to save every single turn, which keeps me from losing anything (aside from any major actions I take on a turn which I then have to redo), but I still have to go through the whole relaunching and loading the game and have to put up with even longer time between turns with the saving.
Overall, I like the game itself, it's a good addition to the series. But it would be nice if I could actually make it through a game. You can see I've put in 22 hours in the past 2 weeks and I've yet to finish a game, conquer a single empire, or even find all the civilizations on a large map. I'm about to shelf this game and give up on the $50 I spent until it's patched up some.
It's fun.

Definitely underwhelmed by this game. I actually enjoyed the first one with all of its problems a lot more than the second.
Clunky controls, movement is painful and laggy and around openable doors (which you've just opened) the game often decides, no, you actually didn't want to go in, and if you press the forward movement key, instead of going in/out of the room, you'll make a U-turn and head the opposite direction.
This game is a resource hog often using 2+ GB RAM and runs slowly and stutters when it gets close to that size.
Numerous crashes and sometimes process won't end even after shutting the game down. Attempting to kill it via task manager or the command line sometimes doesn't work. Not to mention, often the game won't start up properly either. It'll spawn a witcher2.exe process that sits at 120MB big at 0% CPU usage and doesn't continue loading the game.
The arm wrestling and poker mini-games are monotonous and often frustrating. Though the poker less frustrating by far. I could go on and on...but, I'll leave it at that.
My recommendation: If you can get the game for less than $1.50, it's probably worth that. Anything above that, a waste of money. I would've been really irate had I paid full retail when this game first came out.

(Originally written 3/28/2011)
Star Wars has long been great fodder for video games, from the epic RPG Knights of the Old Republic (taking place 4,000 years before the first-released movie), to the RTS Empire at War (exploring rebel-versus-Empire skirmishes in detail from the movies and beyond), to the FPS Republic Commando (putting us in the armor of a Clone Commando and his unit, during the infamous Clone Wars).
The latter game is actually similar in time-frame to the latest Lego Crossover game with Star Wars, which previously saw all six of its movies fully Lego-fied (first in separate editions by trilogy set, then combined into the Complete Saga). This latest installment covers the events of the CG movie and first two seasons of the series which aired on Cartoon Network in 2009, The Clone Wars. The series starts parallel to the end of Episode II and continues to air; logically, it will end during the last third of Episode III.
While pretty much everyone knows what happened in the movies, it may a bit hard to follow a lot of the story of the action (or indeed, appreciate much of the now-famous Lego-based humor) if you haven’t kept up with the (decidedly less popular) series or seen the (somewhat critically panned) movie. But as with previous games (and in a departure from the war-newsreel presentation of the series), a short text scroll-up of the establishing events of the current chapter is run upon its selection.
As with the actual movie and series, the main heroic characters, Anakin and Obi-Wan Kenobi, are the most familiar from the live-action movies, but three main villain characters are (in one case) introduced and (in the others) given new facets, and indeed the game’s episodes are built around them. The Dark Jedi Asajj Ventress seeks to pervert Anakin into whom he will eventually become, Darth Vader; the Separatist Leader Count Dooku reels from his loss at Geonosis but continues his Sith training under the mysterious Darth Sidious, and robot army General Grievous continues the campaigns of the Clone Wars in other systems, striving to take them for the Separatists.
While it may indeed be a bit obscure for those who haven’t thoroughly seen the series, the slapstick nature of the previous games shows through quite strongly in the cutscenes here, and even if you don’t know why something is happening, you’re likely to laugh at it. The graphics have received a major overhaul, resulting in everything looking much more realistic, organic, metallic, what have you – except, of course, for the minifigures you’ll control, who are, as always, really just dressed-up Lego people with extra abilities. And there are over a hundred of them to unlock!
For added replay value, bring along a friend for co-op! And, when you want to take a break from the story, you can explore the massive Republic and Separatist capital ships for more bonuses and the invaluable Red Power Bricks.
For fast action, epic battles and more of that Lego-based humor, you can’t go wrong with Lego Star Wars III. I give it five out of five stars!

Sure, it's not Overwatch. Just like how Fatal Fury is not Streetfight 2, League of Legends is not DOTA, Quake is not Doom,  need I go on? Many many MANY concepts were lifted straight from Overwatch without careful consideration why those elements were put together in Overwatch in the first place (such as why Widowmaker's ultimate is a wallhack, as apposed to giving wallhack ultimate to a non-sniper in Paladins).  But Overwatch wasn't the original class based shooter and borrrowed plenty of elements from other games too (mostly TF2, but Reinhart's big shield is Overwatch's unique contribution to the genre).
Paladins isn't as polished as Overwatch, but it does have it's own spin on the genre. Time to kill is much higher. Healing is much more limited. Distances are much bigger. You cannot switch heroes. There are different ways to build your hero ala MOBAs. Some heroes are inspired from MMORPGS more than TF2.
Ultimately, when recommending a free-to-play game, the question becomes less of "Is it worth my money?" and more of "Is it worth my time to try it?". In this case, Paladins gets a  confident "YES.".  Give it a try if you like shooters and the type of gameplay TF2 and Overwatch has to offer, but want a bit of spice and variety. Perhaps you'll like it more than Overwatch.

I'd been itching to play this throughout the Early Access, but just because of that, I waited till the release so I would be even more impressed. And heck, I was impressed. The more I play Crypt of the Necrodancer, the more things I find to appreciate. Ultimately simple using only four keys to play the game, but with a good amount of items, monsters, songs, bosses and characters to suit your disco of a dungeon crawl to make it both challenging and leave plenty to try as I continue exploring the crypt. Danny B's soundtrack is wonderful, it's fitting and mighty fine to slay monsters to, with the alternative soundtracks and the custom track option, even more opportunities open up. Monsters are both terrifying and downright adorable with their individual dances, and the bosses are simple in theory but perform so well. The inclusion of a daily challenge is entertaining and feeds the desire for so many players to just keep going, and something I was very glad to see included. I've noticed a few comments about the levels being timed, since when the beat drops, your heart stops. It's not the Binding of Isaac, sure, but I don't want it to be. Absolutely I recommend this game as long as players jive and zombies thrive.

After a long time of waiting and wondering what it is, ABZU finally appears. Was it worth the wait? Yes and no.
This is beautiful game in almost every respect. It jumps out from the opening with its incredible visual style, attention to detail, and has one of the most perfect soundtracks ever recorded for a video game. Its definitely worth a look.
The question most everyone is likely going to have is....is it worth it? My answer to that is entirely dependent on the gamer who's asking it. If you are looking for an experience that will have you audibly gasping at some of the environments and enjoy exploring and taking your time without a thought about a challenge or "goal" and are able to get something out of that, then yes, its a "cream of the crop" title for that vein of game. If you are a gamer who plays games purely and simply for the "win", then I would say no.  Make no mistake, this game is a "walking simulator" underwater. If that term turns you off, then you have your answer on whether or not you should play this at its current value.
PROS:
+ Stunning in literally every category. From things as simple as the sounds of a dolphin, to the music, to the vibrant world that you're in, it's at times breathtaking and full of vivid color and depth in the art.
+ Technologically sound. I was well above 60 FPS on Ultra the entire time.
+ An interesting way to learn about our ocean and the diversity of life that calls it home.
+ A meditative and relaxing experience.
CONS:
- Saddeningly short. It took me 1.7 hours according to Steam for my first playthrough. I likely could've extended this by exploring every nook and cranny, but I'm not that type of gamer.
- Vague "story" with very little explanation in respect to the point of the journey.
- Too high of an opening price point for what it provides.
- There is no challenge whatsoever. This game is very much like an interactive film in that you're controlling an avatar without a chance of dying/failing or being challenged by a puzzle.
Overall, I sincerely enjoyed my time during my playthrough. I cannot say that it's a must play or must own right now today though. If you are on the fence there is no harm in waiting. It will be there waiting for you when you are ready. Once it hits a price point you are comfortable with, jump on it and enjoy it.
Rating: 8/10 for the quality - 5/10 for the value

The entire game is played like a rhythm game to the beat of either music native to the game, or your own music. Its fun, its fast, its challenging, and there's a good mix of RNG elements and player agency. The overall design is fantastic, packing tons of little details it doesnt need that bring the world to life, and making everything clear enough that failure is almost always the player's fault. Dont believe me? Try picking the Bard character that lets you move out of rhythm and the game becomes the easiest thing in the world. Thats honestly what makes this game so good. Its tight. The difficulty is right where it needs to be, in the rhythm elements and learning monster patterns.

There are more than a few games that bother me since their steam store page is filled with negative reveiws even though the game itself is actualy good. While some reveiws reflect a certain perspective that is negative and rightfully so based on people's entitlement of genuine opinions or opinions in general. Regardless, it's clear that once hating a game becomes a trend, gamers tend to treat revewing it as a mini-game where they compete with each other through negative and comicly bashful 'reviews'.
SO... Mafia III is one of these games, subject to mass ridicule by immature and ungrateful gamers.
Is Mafia III a perfect game?
No. However, it is a phenomenal game, with a vast, dense, and beautiful open world with an even better story and tight gameplay to match. Lincoln Clay is one of my favorite video game characters/ fictional characters. He's not just some crazy black man with ptsd seeking out revenge. He's composed, sympathetic, heroic, and in one word, just. The incredible voice acting and dialogue make this peroid piece all the more effective in doing what Mafia II did, transport the player back to a time that doesn't seem that exciting, but actualy turns out to be far more exciting and enjoyabale than any open world crime game set in modern time.
Sounds  perfect so far by the way i'm describing it but it's not.
The launch of this game was pretty awful, capped at 30 fps, some low res. textures, weird reflections, rain indoors (lol), and a ugly, very ugly sky box. Those are the main flaws that come to mind when recalling my day 1 & week 1 experience.
After leaving the game and returning a couple months after its release, almost all of these issues, if not all, had been resolved. As a result, making this game a masterpiece based on its own merits and not its ability to deliver an enthrawling Martin Scorsese style Mafia story like Mafia II's. Fans of Mafia II, myself included, would have asked for no more than that, another Scarface or Goodfellas ride where we loved every second and couldn't get enough. Nonetheless, Mafia III is a phenomenal period piece, and if I consider the prevelance of games that attempt to be period pieces, Assasin's Creed games are all that come to mind. Even though Mafia III's story is of a different style from Mafia II in that it is more reliant on the atmosphere, period, and city of New Orleans, it is just as effective in transporting the player to an exciting, beautiful, and brutally violent adventure set during some turbulent point of history.
All 3 DLCs are phenomenal and I would highly reccomend them.  Nonetheless, the main game's story itself is long and provides substantial closure to Lincoln Clay's story.
Mafia III is a special game that I will always remember and think fondly of. Thank you to Hangar 13 for continuing to truly support their game despite the epidemic/trend of mindless/simple-minded gamers that prefer hating on games and their developers for the sake of hating and competitive mockery. This game was not made for them, their attention spans are only substantial enough for hating on people such as the developers at Hangar 13 for being more talented than them, and for creating more than they ever will or could.

I am glad that I did NOT listen to the criticisms about this game from other people.
All I heard about the game was this:
-Bugs, glitches, performance issues
-Repetitive, boring, tedious
Ever since Dragon Age: Inquisition, I have taken it upon myself to try the game out for myself and not follow the herd. I then realized DA:I was amazing and poured hours into its massive world.
I bought this game for $20 and I have to say it is well worth the money.
I started playing it around June of 2017 and I have not:
-Suffered a crash or launch issues
-Had any gamebreaking glitches or bugs
-Gotten bored off the gameplay or content
This game has incredible attention to detail in its Presentation and Environment.
The locales, shops, warehouses, and districts all have it's "New Orleans" feel to it and to top it off, the graphics are DAMN good. I do recommend finding a sweetfx preset online because this game has the blur/muddy textures look like Dishonored 2 had as well.
The cutscenes, story, voice acting and music are ALSO top notch. I kid you not, all the attention went into this part of the game, NO DOUBT. I find myself playing 2 - 3 hour sessions just driving my Exotic Car while jamming out to Creedence when I am on the way to get a district settled to one of my underbosses. All 60's classics are in the game. Bravo, guys!
The gameplay is ALSO satisfying. You can upgrade Lincoln's weapons, health, ammo count, equipment load and more through the Arms Dealer which you can summon at any time in the game.
The budget of this game must have been huge IF you choose to pay attention to the small things and with that voiceacting alone, you can surely tell.
The missions and repetitive nature that some people call it, are the same you will find in any game such as Far Cry, Mad Max, Assassins Creed, and even Saint's Row; they include:
-Intimidating enemies
-Interrogating enemies
-Drug heists
-Liberating hideouts/districts
-Tailing someone (rarely)
-Random encounters where you must destroy a vehicle
-Invade hostile territory
You do these side-missions but the real Story Missions are really memorable.
The shooting and gunplay is also damn satisfying. Nothing like landing a well placed headshot with a Silenced Deacon in a warehouse and working your way through to remain undetected.

I've played some good games, and I've played some incredibly disappointing games. This is somehow both. This is also the first review I've ever felt inclined to write.
This game is like Civilization, Eve Online and the board game Twilight Imperium all rolled into one. Sounds like an awesome game. But a lot of the features feel largely incomplete. There are a lot of balance issues, and things like tourism and other money making things seem like they haven't really been fleshed out. Money seems almost superfluous. All great ideas, but even a rudimentary economy needs more attention than these have been given.
Early on in a level, my capital and starting planet have some level of importance. I care about what structures I build. But as the game winds on, planets and resources and even my territory and units just seem so pointless.
Maybe it's the lackluster battles involving an oddly large amount of micromanagement to prepare for, but no real control.
Maybe it's the constant spelling and grammar errors. Like, I'm the kind of person that notices spelling and grammar errors in basically every game I've ever played for the past 20 years. But this was insane.
And the stakes just seem so low when the game feels so unfinished. Awesome concept, and there is definitely a game somewhere in there! But this is not a finished game. This is what we come to expect from these pre-released games. Everyone buys into it, and they try to make these deadlines, but they've mostly moved on to the next project.
Again, I look forward to future updates, and I will keep my eye on this game. But as it stands, I don't feel it was worth my money, and it does not feel like the "V1.0" that the reputable companies of yesteryear would have produced. Hopefully that changes, because there are some really great games out there that rely on pre release funding, and if you don't finish your game, you bring the whole medium down a peg.

I remember playing FATE for the first time many years ago. It is one of my favorite games. Graphics don't even begin to compare to today's new games, but the game is so much fun that it doesn't even matter. I can spend hours scaling the dungeons. It never gets old. I highly recommend this game to anyone looking for hours of fun at a good price.
In the Steam version, the cheat console is missing, probably because the game includes achievements and the cheats would make getting all the achievements way too easy. This can cause a problem if one specific bug is encountered... I haven't seen it yet in this version, but in the past, when I played FATE, I remember getting caught in between two objects in such a way that there's no way to move. When closing this game, it saves EVERYTHING, including your EXACT position. That means if you encounter this bug and then try to close the game, your character is forever locked in a place where he/she will never be able to move from again. With the "cheat" console, you could type something in to relocate your character. In this version, your only option would be to use the task manager to close the game without saving and revert to your last save point.
As long as you don't make the fatal mistake of saving and closing the game in an effort to escape this bug (if it will ever even be encounted in the Steam version), this game is a brilliant, procedurally generated game that will never get old.

A great game that should have redefined the adventure game genre. The game largely plays out in real time, and your character can't be everywhere at once. Luckily, you're given the ability to rewind time to try to explore other parts of the train during times where you were otherwise occupied.

Personally, I found the original game to be a bit too difficult to fully complete without a walkthrough at points (since it can largely be trial and error figuring out which events happen at what time).
The only thing I really take issue is the system requirements. The game was originally released in 1997 and required 66 MHz CPU, 8 MB RAM, and 35 MB of hard drive space. This release has seemingly insane requirements for such an old game, and I was disappointed to find I couldn't run it on my laptop (which sports only a 1.6 GHz CPU - low for 'gaming', but should be adequate to run a game from 1997!).

The missions are broken into three different subcategories: adventure / platform, space combat, and real-time strategy. The adventure missions are the ones most closely related to those of past games of the series, but look and play better, with solid enemy AI and a ton more things to smash. The boss battles do a great job finishing levels with an epic struggle, but we expect no less from a Star Wars game. The space missions and RTS missions are where you see this game break from the standard. With literally hundreds of allies and enemies on the screen and no lag or drop in frame rate, the large scale battles are truly a spectacle to behold. The strategy missions feel like a light version of StarCraft with LEGOs, as you take out enemy buildings using a hefty variety of vehicles, then use blocks to create your own support buildings. But no matter which mission you're tackling, even when surrounded by a seemingly inescapable amount of enemies, the forgiving difficulty keeps you from breaking a sweat. You essentially have unlimited lives, and only lose a couple thousand studs (pocket change) when brought down to zero health. Despite having a varied group to control, you'll most likely keep to those wielding lightsabers, since continuous mashing of the attack button will thwart any attempts to do you harm. However, LEGO games have never been designed with challenging gameplay in mind, making the game approachable to a wider audience.
As touched on before, the graphics shine in this latest version. The venues are all perfectly molded and believable in the Star Wars universe, and the animations are fluid and varied. Each of the 114 characters is uniquely tailored with its own personality and combat style, so how Anakin swings his lightsaber is completely different than how Mace Windu or Obi-Wan does. Even small elements, like Yoda hobbling along on his cane when pressing the analog stick lightly, then quickly jumping into a double flip to decapitate a droid, all showcase the care given to each character's authenticity.
Little needs to be said about the music and sound. It's Star Wars; the music is world renowned, the sound effects iconic, and both are perfectly integrated into the game, period. The voice acting is an issue all on its own though. While I fully understand that voiced scripts have no more place in a LEGO game then they do in a Sims game, the lack of talking only accentuates the confusing direction and hint system.
LEGO Star Wars III: The Clone Wars is a pleasant break from the constant onslaught of first-person shooters, only made more satisfying by adding humor to the formula, a nearly extinct theme in modern video games. While the controls and difficulty are watered down, and you'll inevitably find yourself lost many times throughout, the game is just pure, addictive fun. And with so many things to collect and unlock, it's just that many more reasons to keep picking up the controller and redoing a level for the twelfth time.

The best in the series by far, with smooth animations and colorful backdrops, all which befit the Star Wars universe.

Although there are many different skills and attacks to use, button mashing seems to be the easiest way to get through a level. The lack of direction is also the game's biggest detriment.

From the great orchestrations penned decades ago, to the genuine blaster and lightsaber sound effect, this game showcases them beautifully. However, the lack of voice acting, and even subtitles, makes virgins of the animated series even more lost.

It's a rhythm-based top-down dungeon-crawl Spelunky-like that comes with a soundtrack from Danny Baranowski, and gives you the ability to add custom tracks as well. This coalesces as an experiences where you get incredibly focused and into the groove of the game, and you stop thinking and start making split-second decisions. It's fun to learn and fun to master. Really great mechanics and design.
The art is also delightful.
Necrodancer is a really fantastic game, and as far as Spelunky-likes go, Necrodancer is an amazing and unique entry in this growing genre that demonstrates the breadth of what kinds of games the genre can hold.
It may appear like a more traditional rogue-like, but as with all Spelunky-likes there's no random elements as far as it concerns your performance as a player. You are in complete control of your successes and failures. These are the types of randomized experiences I really enjoy. I have a really hard time enjoying games where a simple luck-of-the-die-roll determines my success or failure. Marrying zero-randomization game mechanics with completely randomized levels, loot and enemies is one of my favorite things and this game does it well.

First things first - yes, you CAN play entirely for free, though the game does take ages to unlock everything. But as long as you play survival and endless, it won't matter that much (sabotage, the third mode, is PvP, I'm not even touching that cause those people would annihilate me in seconds). I don't think there is a single person who has all of the traps and heroes maxed out, it's pretty much impossible. I also wouldn't touch it if you aren't planning on playing with friends, most maps CANNOT be completed solo, they're just too difficult. I'd advise new players to at least invest in a starter pack, it's gonna make your life a bit easier. After nearly 40 hours, my enjoyment of the game is still only increasing, I love the characters, the sense of humour, graphics, music, sounds, map design, the necessity to think and plan ahead and coordinate so that your traps complement one another. It really is a worthy successor to the series, if you're not discouraged by a VERY slow grind, then go for it.
Possibly the biggest downside is that you cannot simply purchase the entire game, only currency, which gives you access to mostly randomised chests (most of them will give you either new traps or slight upgrades to the ones you already have). I wish there was some 50-pound unlock-all version, but there ain't, if you wanted to get everything, you'd have to spend at least several THOUSAND pounds / dollars on currency, which means grinding is basically the only way to go.
Despite this, I'm easily giving it a 9/10 on count of the entertainment value.
Oh, and you might play with randoms, but I hear they often leave / go afk, so playing with your family / friends is much safer and ejoyable.

Pros:
-It's a rougelike, which means permanent death and constantly changing dungeon layouts. This game has tons of replayability because of this.
-Lots of unlockables, including items, spells, weapons and even characters that can drastically change how you play the game.
-The pixel animations are fantastic- not only do they look expressive and goofy, but they also help the player to know when to attack or dodge.
-The combat is incredibly simple to learn, but learning the attack patterns of enemies takes time and concentration. Mix this with managing your health and items as well as forcing the player to stick to the beat, and you have an incredibly tense yet fulfilling gameplay experience.
-The game is very difficult, but it is incredibly fair. All of the enemies can be beaten if you learn their patterns or know when to use the right items. Eventually, you end up getting into the zone and become a master dungeoneer.
-If an enemy is too confusing for you, there are rooms in which you can practice against all types of monsters, even bosses and mini bosses.
-Direct support for modding and even speedrunning. Neat.
-Local Co-op? Yes Please!
-Three equally awesome soundtracks of varying styles that can all be changed out on the fly? Count me the heck in!
-Singing merchants? Woo mama.
-You can play it with a DDR pad? BEST GAME EVER
Cons:
-Content wise, there isn't a whole lot to this game- there are only 4 zones with three stages and a boss each. However, the randomization completely makes up for this.
-While there are a lot of unlockables, I ran out of items to buy after about 8 hours of playing. There is, however, a system where you can trash unlocks, forcing you to get them back again. It essentially lets you play the game all over again if you want.
-The controls can sometimes be unresponsive, such as when you are trying to use an item or a spell. These inputs require hitting two keys at the same time, and I often would up missing a beat or getting in the way of enemies because the keys simply wouldn't register. This might be a problem with my computer.
Verdict:
This game is incredibly well put-together. It's compelling, challenging, and a heck of a lot of fun. Also, I will be really surprised if you don't get some of the songs from this game stuck in your head.

A Rhythm/Roguelike hybrid that follows most of the rules of a traditional, albeit streamlined Roguelike while forcing you to move to the beat of music. This combination is absolutely ingenious. The reason this works so well is because of the simple controls, consisting only of four buttons, the arrow keys. It feels extremely intuitive to move your fingers on the mini dance pad that is your keyboard. Speaking of dance pads, this game offers dance pad compatibility, which, although I have not personally tried, I would try in a heartbeat. The game only consists of four zones, each consisting of three floors and a boss, so the game isn't exceptionally long, however the fun in a Roguelike is replayability, and this game has plenty. Naturally, the game is procedurally generated, and it manages to be generated in a way that you never feel like you got screwed by luck. In fact, you can make it through the entire game from start to finish with the basic weapon without taking damage, and there is a game mode dedicated to just that. Now, all of these wouldn't mean anything if the sound track was bad, but it is exactly the opposite. The soundtrack is absolutely spectacular, so much so that I find myself listening to it even when I'm not playing the game. I wholeheartedly recommend this game if you're a fan of Roguelikes, Rhythm games, or simply a fan of well designed games, because this game has quickly become one of my favorites.

Once you finish the game you will be truly amazed and happy that you bought and played this amazing game.

This is the 4th installment in the LEGO Star Wars Franchise, after a 6 month delay on releasing the game (It was originally slated for a Late September 2010 release) those who have been a fan of Lego's Flag Ship Series Lego Star Wars you will not be disappointed. This new chapter in the Lego Star Wars starts off half way through "Attack of the Clones" were Ben, Anakin, and Padme' are to fight for their lives in Count Dooka's Arena against his assortment of savage beasts. This is more or less a revamp and redux of the original Lego Star Wars episode "Jedi Battle" that has been given a complete face lift (Take a Bow George) and is closer to the elements in the movie. From there you will continue to make your way thru a few more "redux" chapters of "Attack of the Clone's" into the "Clone Wars" T.V. Series.
Don't worry, The Game play is the same as in the previous Lego Star Wars Games with new features to include scenarios in which players can command large armies of clones to battle against droid armies, and Story Swap mode, in which players can switch between two characters in different areas whose stories run simultaneously. The game includes split screen combat. All new character features include lightsaber throwing, lightsaber slicing, picking up droids and stepping on certain pads in which Jedi do "combo moves" to destroy certain objects. Vehicle levels have been upgraded slightly: now, players can land their ship and begin fighting on foot. All the original elements in previous Lego Star Wars games have returned. The classic "hub" has also been changed, taking place in a Republic Cruiser named the Resolute, allowing the characters to explore all the parts of the Star Wars galaxy.
The Best way to describe the graphics is taking a standard Def DVD of the original Lego Star War Games and reprocessing them into Blu-Ray Hi-Def. The characters are amazingly clearer and smoothed out. The back ground elements are just astounding. The game engine used by the previous Lego Star Wars games has been upgraded. It can now hold more than 200 moving units/objects on-screen. The graphics are more detailed than before, and the lighting has been improved to enhance the feeling of depth.

If I were to give a real estimate, I would say it would take 5 hours at the most, but likely less if you can just sit and play without interruption. I would have loved seeing more, but the content it does have isn't bad for the price so it's not a big complaint.

Ok, so first of all I love this game, and after coming back to this game from a long break, I was looking forward to playing one of my favourite games, but I find I cannot play the game without it crashing after about 20 seconds.
At first I thought it was my PC, I uninstalled and reinstalled, I verified local files, I tried older versions, nothing..
So after spending literally hours trawling through forums and downloading and trying fix after fix after fix, I have found that there was some dispute with the creator or something, and he broke his own game.
There are pages and pages of forum posts from people claiming they have a fix but none of them actually do anything.
I even signed up on the Oovee website so I could download their "official" fixes, after trying numerous fix versions and tweaking config files and being sent to various web links that don't work.. in the end I decided I just cannot be bothered anymore, and frankly I shouldn't have to do any of it,  I paid good money for a working game, and frankly this is just plain theft!
So I gave up, and went to bed angry.
I came back the next day with a clear head, and decided to give it one more try.
I updated all my drivers and tried downgrading all visual effects in the game, still no joy.
But Then, I finally noticed that RivaTuner was running in the background..
I thought I would try turning it off.. Now the game works fine!..
So if there's a lesson to take from this, if you are having a similar problem, first thing you do is make sure you have no frame rate limiting software running in the background!

Writing this review after playing for about 8 hours straight right after install.
If you like NinjaKiwi's browser based or even mobile based BTD5 (Bloons Tower Defense 5), you'll love this game. There's a bit more strategy to this than BTD5 because you can only CHOOSE 3 towers per game, so you have to really learn the maps to decide how you want to attack it.
Pros:
Fun Tower Defence
Multiple game modes
Same mechanics and upgrades we've been used to
Neutrals
Very little pay to win, there is SOME, but it's 98% cosmetic and you CAN just grind to unlock the one tower that's mostly pay to win, which watching a few pros duel it out, nobody uses it anyways (it's more of a noob tower that helps early on)
Matching is FAIRLY even, I've never been someone with more than say 1 extra tier of upgrades I don't have
Pay to win mechanics are quite well balanced out to where they may have a TINY advantage like a few extra spikes per level, but it's capped to 5 per level so even if you do sink a whole paycheck into this game, skill can still easily triumph.
The learning curve is VERY steep. If you don't want your w/l ratio to go to♥♥♥♥♥♥ I reccomend you play every game mode very early on to at least get a basic grasp of how they are played.
The new card mode is very clash of clans-esque with the combat system as well
Cons
Matching system is a little slow in wierd hours of the day and from the ranks of 200-300
Still SOME pay to win aspects, balanced out or not
Would prefer to do it DOTA2 style and be able to ban a tower for play and vote on a map.
Also a cheesey way of winning I discovered pretty early is to sacrifice about 75 lives by not placing the first level, and then using what you've saved to immeadiately double your starting income. Very strategic, way more than I thought it would be initially.

I have played the game through once, without seeing/unlocking everything, and I'm 5 hours in (took my time), but will return to it.
Taking your time is key here: let yourself bathe (litterally:D) in Abzu's atmosphere, rather than racing toward the end.
Since I don't have a controller, I used keyb/mouse, and your character controls okay, not great. I hope the devs get a key mapping setup in a future patch, since I don't have the standard qwerty-keyboard but the azerty-kind.
Also, you need a DX11 or better compatible GPU.
Other than that, this game is gorgeous! Always wanted to go diving, but didn't make it past basic breathing through a breathing mask, so this is my best shot at experiencing underwater sea life. And in Abzu, it is abundant!
The puzzles are no big issue, and there is no survival element to it (other than some parts that don't kill you but incapacitate you temporarily).
You are essentially swimming with fish, and sometimes through meditation, following fish, and you can ride fish, dolphins, whales and more :D.
No shooting, and minimal interaction make this game one work of art to explore, enjoy, and interact with minimal pressure to advance. Yet the game nudges you toward its conlusion without forcing you.
This is one foolproof way to unwind after a stressful day :)
Technically, it's (I think) the first venture of the developers in the diverse PC-world (their former games were console-orientated), so they still have a couple of issues to solve.
Recommended, but waiting for a few patches should make it a better game to purchase.
That said, if the game works for you, dive in.

TL;DR
Short, but quite enjoyable RPG game, great for when you don't have a large amount of time to spend on a game, or need to be able to disengage easily. It has a nice little story (the game is mostly story telling, not much RPG action), and cute pixel graphics. Only thing that bothered me was the controls, (would have liked to use WASD instead of UpDownLeftRight).
I bought this because I was feeling brain fried from studying and needed a short break, but I had to be able to get off and go back to studying in a reasonable amount of time: this meant staying away from long or addictive games, and definitely staying away from Youtube and Netflix.
LiEat is actually three short games in one, each taking about 1.5 -  2 hours to complete, so I could play through an arc and get back to studying without a burning desire to get back to playing.
As far as gameplay goes, while there are some standard elements of a JRPG (turn based fighting, leveling up, items, and what not), these seem secondary to the story telling. Each arc, or game, revolves around some mystery that gradually reveals the history of the characters, and as such the bulk of the gameplay is running around talking to various NPCs or searching for clues, which is not bad if you enjoy a good story.
The only thing that really bothered me about this game was the control scheme. I would have liked to use WASD or a control pad for movement, but you are forced to use UpDownLeftRight.
Ultimately I would recommend this game to anyone who likes a good story, has little time/doesn't want to get too involved, or is a fan of cute pixel art.

I came to this game with a fondness for rhythm games but mixed experiences with roguelikes. Now I've put 50+ hours into it and am still having fun. What makes this work as a roguelike for me is that with enough skill, you can theoretically handle nearly any tough situation the game throws at you without taking any damage, even with only base equipment. To approach that level, you must develop considerable mechanical skill and tactical judgment. Thankfully, the game offers an approachable learning curve at every step of the journey.
Necrodancer isn't really a rhythm game as for the most part you are just holding a steady beat. But what I like about rhythm games is interactively engaging with great music, and Necrodancer is great for that. One great feature Necrodancer does import from rhythm games is offering a practice mode. Like in rhythm games, having a practice mode respects the time of the player by allowing practicing the hardest parts without needing to play through the easy parts every time.
I don't like permanent unlockable upgrade mechanics, so I'd like to note that while Necrodancer does offer some of these at first, it doesn't take long to unlock them all and they don't take effect in full-game playthroughs anyway, just in the single-zone modes which are mainly for practice.

Quick summary: Boring and slow. Most of the good parts are already in OMD2.
The big problem with OMD:C is that it follows OMD2 - what appears to have happened is a bunch of great ideas burdened with the terrible implementation of free-to-play.  OMD:C has lots more unique heroes + abilities along with the satisfying core gameplay of Orcs Must Die and great potential for online play. Unfortunately, this is balanced with an immense grind to get anything remotely interesting, also there is an feel like you definitely don't get to have all of the fun toys without paying money.
After 5 hours, I found myself using the basically same traps, fighting the same enemies, using the same three starter heroes.  That is when I quit: the game is simply too gated around paying money or grinding to get anything interesting. Every unlockable comes from chests that appear to be stingy when it comes to nice things: instead of new gear or traps, you acquire points to unlock/upgrade traps and gear in random(spiteful?) fashion. This leaves things that you may want unavailable until the gods of randomness bequeath it upon you, as opposed to OMD2 where you could spend your hard-earned skulls building a trap setup you wanted.  I never unlocked a second piece of gear despite opening maybe 30 chests - it tells me that is how I get it, but I don't feel like opening more chests to find out.
The trap upgrades appear to be a flawed system: normal upgrades to traps are uninspired: e.g. damage trap does X% more damage, snare trap does Y% more slow. The fun trap features appear to be gated behind "parts" you must get from chests, but even those seem boring compared to the skull unlocks from the previous game - minor alterations as opposed to the trap upgrades in earlier games which could even alter the core behavior (place flame traps on walls). However, a quick note: I only found 2 parts for traps (30 chests), and one of them buffed the physics traps which I didn't use because they are always too situational. Don't worry, there is gating for the normal upgrades as well, requiring a significant chunk of skulls to upgrade traps after the chests give you the points: maybe 1-2 games, or 25 minutes of gameplay for even the first upgrade for a single trap.
The heroes are fairly expensive for skulls - obtainable, but painful.  Maybe you could unlock the cheaper ones after 2-3 hours of straight grinding. It is probably for the best that I didn't unlock any more heroes, since the game's pacing seems to want you to play through each level multiple times with each hero for the optimal rewards - likely forcing you to go back and replay old maps when you do unlock a new hero.  Heroes can be unlocked directly with cash (not chests), but the amount to get all heroes piecemeal is truly absurd.
Pros:
Deep down, It is still Orcs Must Die with some fun new features.
Cons:
It is the bad free-to-play version with all that it entails: there is no story, slow unlocks for everything, and everything good only comes from random chance that may leave you running the same thing for hours.
