Set in 1968 you play as Lincoln Clay, born from a mixed-race relationship and raised in a orphanage, who just returned from his service in Vietnam. With his lack of roots and true family, he considers those that help and support him to be his family. But when he gets double-crossed by San Marcano and his son and sees his only family left being shot and killed in front of his eyes and barely surviving a bullet to the head himself he's out for revenge on the entire Marcano family.
He cannot do that alone and seeks the help of other organised crime who also carry a grudge against Marcano. He's joined by Cassandra, from the Haitian mob, Burke of the Irish, and Vito Scarletta (protagonist of Mafia 2) from the Italian mafia, who finds himself being discarded and seeks to settle for himself in New Bordeaux.
The game starts out really strong with a distinct sense of a documentary, as you see some characters talk about the happenings to have happened in the past. The mo-cap and the cut scenes are excellent and really drag you in. But once you get started and get things going, with the capture of your first racket, things start to slow down to a near crawl, which is really really sad.
The developers really set the bar high for themselves and built a lush city, but apart from the special racket locations it has little more in it. Furthermore the small underbosses that you encounter in these places all feel the same. The informants that help you tracking them down just stand there and talk. The developers really had some ambitious goals and set the bar too high, I get the feeling, which resulted that they had to cut some serious corners, resulting into a big chunk of the story gameplay feeling stale and almost lifeless this way. Only when you come to the key figures, the Marcano family members, when things are getting interesting. The rest in between is pretty much a grind to get to the next key part.
By comparison the cut scenes from The Witcher 3 were not from the same high mo-cap quality, but they were consistent throughout the entire game keeping you captivated. Here you have very high quality cut scenes mixed with some really dull two figures standing in front of each other talking with a static camera. These parts really take down the overall feeling of quality for the whole game. Here and there some if this had been remedied later on, but still too little.
Since the game is set in 1968 the game features a great soundtrack with some iconic tracks and some nice cars of that time period. Also the collectibles are interesting pieces of history for the most part. You will be able to collect a fairly big collection of Playboy magazines from the 60ies, of which the game only features the front cover page, the playmate centerfold and sometimes an article or interview (the one with the Beatles was fun to read!). Also some Vargas pin-up drawings, issues of the Hot Rod magazines (again: front cover and an article), and some made up issues of a religious magazine and made up Communist posters.
To those not unfamiliar with the American history of that time will know that the 60ies is also the time when racial segregation comes into question and various movements start stirring the pot, with the famous speech from Marthin Luther King Jr. whom was shot and killed in 1968. It was also the year of the Presidential elections in which none other than Richard Nixon won the vote.
However the developers only decided to take small portion of it all, the racism. But even that feels a little underwhelming. I was hoping to get a real sense of the hatred that was aimed at the afro-americans in that time,
in the south where this game is set. Instead, the whole thing had become just a backdrop for the main story: the revenge on San Marcano. Not even a glimpse of the elections either. Another missed oportunity, I'd say.
I personally found the game is enjoyable to play, especially now most of the glitches and crashes are fixed. I encountered
little of them, but some have had to struggle through a lot, so I've read. If you look passed the in-between grinds of the underbosses and can enjoy the world as far as it is given to you, then you will find yourself enjoy your time. The DLC will add some to that enjoyment as well.
I had an okay-ish deal when I purchased the whole package with the season pass, but the vanilla game sort of left me with a bit of a bitter taste in my mouth when I had started playing it. The DLC added some extra enjoyment back into the game, but it has taught me to be more careful a title like this from day 1. On a discount I could surely recommend picking it up, but at full price I cannot recommend it with a clear conscience.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a game that by this point in time really shouldn't need any introduction. The game has won multiple rewards, received much praise, and delighted many gamers, but how well does it hold up to all that hype?
In my opinion, very well, Admittedly the game does have its flaws, but when you stop to think about the fact that the vast majority of the game was made by one man, said flaws become much more forgivable. That said, the only note-worthy flaw with Dust: An Elysian Tail is the story, as it is rather generic. That's not to say that it's bad, but it's certainly nothing that you haven't heard before. However, that doesn't prevent Dust: An Elysian Tail from being a highly entertaining gaming experience. While the story may not be all that fresh, it does still manage to be entertaining, thanks mostly to Fidget, who will be your faithful companion throughout the game. You may have heard certain folks compare Fidget to Navi from The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, but I have no idea where they're drawing that comparison from. Fidget isn't some annoying creature with no purpose but to point out the painfully obvious and pester you every 5 minutes by reminding you of what you should be doing to advance the plot, but a fully realized and fleshed-out character with lots of humorous dialog. Without Fidget, Dust: An Elysian Tail would be far less entertaining in the story department, but thanks to her and her dialog/commentary, Dust's story becomes far more interesting.
Gameplay-wise, Dust: An Elysian Tail is more or less your standard "Metroidvania" fare, with side-scrolling action, lots of areas to explore, platforming, etc. However, Dust: An Elysian Tail also has RPG elements, such as stats, a Level Up System, Magic, loot, crafting, and items that will increase your stats. Granted that Castlevania: Symphony of the Night also had RPG elements, but Dust's feel a bit deeper than that, more in line with games like Muramasa: The Demon Blade than SotN, albeit the combat isn't quite as deep as Muramasa.
Graphics-wise, Dust: An Elysian Tail is beautiful game. All of the visuals were hand-drawn by Dean Dodril (the game's creator) himself, and they're gorgeous. However, words alone can't do it justice at all, so take a peek at the Screenshots and see for yourself.
Sound-wise, Dust: An Elysian Tail is beautiful as well. Hyperduck Studios did an excellent job on this game's soundtrack, and they really deserve more recognition for their work. Every bit of music in this game hits its mark, perfectly reflecting what's going on in the game around it.

Overall the graphics are okay, even though in some areas the games looks worse than Witcher 1. For example the children look like some sort of bug-eyed abominations straight out of Doctor Whos' CGI department pre Season 6. Whereas the model in Witcher 1 was at least passable.
Texture quality varies greatly with some things looking nice enough (Armors) and others looking like a blurry mess (Geralts skin), though all in all the textures get the job done. Settings were on High. I think.
Gameplay is kinda okay'ish,
you use a controller. KB+Mouse probably works once you get used to it, but there's really no need for the precision a mouse would net you and the movement felt a lot better and responsive with the controller/stick. Camera remains annoying regardless of what you use and it's positioned so close to Geralt, you can almost smell his crotchrot.
Combat is now more than just a glorified flashgame at least: You use light and heavy attacks, throw things at the enemy, dodge stuff, block and counter attacks. Simply all that typical third person action game stuff that you'd expect to do. Just don't expect it to feel or look fluid and "fast-paced" - better go watch a video about it.
Other than that the game consists of you running 20-30 meters down or up a road or path or sewer to the next cutscene, usually you kill around 10-15 things on your way to there.
The story sounds promising and it's the continuation of the first part, but it is done just as dull and boring as you should expect from a witcher game. Although that might just be the fault of the uninteresting and one-sided characters. The maincharacter is some 70 year old guy with alzheimer who travels around hunting ♥♥♥♥♥s and ♥♥♥♥ing boars. He's accompanied by his ♥♥♥♥♥y redhead concubine and some spy-dude who managed to break out of a Assassins Creeds Trailer. He probably wanted to see a woman at least once in his life.

There's also something about a dead king who was killed on a ship in the (badass) Intro, but then gets ganked and thuss double-killed later/sooner(the game loves to jump back and forth several months all the time) by the same rogue. Rage ensures and Geralt finds out he's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ tank. No idea what's up with that.
Sometimes the dialogue/banther between the NPCs is well done and voiced, but most of the time the voice acting and the writing is nothing special. Lipsyncing is near non-existent. I usually don't care much about voice acting though, so for someone who pays a lot of attention to it, it'll probably be a bigger minus.
Long story short...

Oh, and since you've read so far: Buy it if you liked the original Witcher and were able overlook/ignore all it's numerous weaknesses, because you will have to do the same in Witcher too, too. Don't buy it if you didn't. Also don't buy it if you didn't finish the original first.

OK so at the time of writing this short review GC3 has left early access and I believe is still in BETA, so I will just list a few things that need to be worked on just so whoever is reading this will know what they are getting.
Campaign:
I was surprised to see a campaign since leaving early access. Most 4X games I've played have not had proper story campaigns, so I was happy to see one here. However, there are 2 issues I have with the campaign (other than being very short. Maybe every major race will get one each???).
First off is the tech tree. In the first mission I advanced my kinetic weapons to near maximum however in the second mission I had to do it all again. Same can be said for nearly all techs. Now I'm not sure if they went to base levels again but that was practically the case. Personally I feel there should be some kind of system that carries tech into the next missions, even if it means limiting the max tech level per mission.
Secondly is the diplomacy. Simply put it is non-existant. Sure you can trade, declare war and ask for peace but thats it. I researched diplomacy to a high level and nothing changed. I could not form an alliance with the Thalians in mission  2, so I had to go to war with them because we were neighbours and my culture was taking them over. They ended up being angry at me and sending threats, then eventually declared war on me. Naturally they did so without fleets at my borders so I just overran them immediately. Maybe AI is an isue too!!!!
Open End Free Play:
Obviously the diplomacy has a problem here too, but at the moment if you play using the largest 3 galaxies then your game will more than likely crash as all the races get more numerous ships. I was in a game 700+ turns in over about 10 days when all of a sudden when I click on "turn", it froze. To say i was pi**ed was an understatement. It happened twice. The second being just over 400 turns in. But all in all that's my biggest issue with free play.
So in my opinion if the diplomacy and crashes are fixed this would be a great game. The tech tree is pretty minor since I will only play the campaign once since its not that interesting.

The Crypt of the Necrodancer is a fantastic rouge-like that is brutal, unforgiving and down right addictive.
The game works like all other rouge-likes out there, but you have to move your character to the music in the background. At first it is quite jarring, but within minutes you'll be dancing your way through all the darkest dungeons!
This game can be brutal in the final levels and it can be easy to be overrun with the many bosses and monsters this game can and will throw at you.
The music is catchy and works really well with the game and whenever the shopkeeper starts to sing...it's just a magical moment.
Here are some of the pros/cons of this game.
Pros
-----
* Punishing rouge-like
* Many items to discover and purchase
* Sooo many characters to unlock and gamemodes
* Catchy Soundtrack
* Custom Music and Maps
* Steam Workshop support
Cons
---
* Difficult can seem unfair in the later zones
* Some items are way too strong and remove the challenge
Put simply this is an incredible game that successfully blends the music genre and rouge-likes together to create something that is unique and will stand the tests of time.

LEGO Star Wars III: Clone Wars was the first LEGO game where I often gut stuck for not easily understanding what I was supposed to do next. Once I had a bug where a level couldn't be finished and I had to restart it, and I had the game crash a few times. Additionally we see weak design carried over from older LEGO games. Besides those problems this is still a LEGO game and you can expect about the same amount of fun offered by previous LEGO games. Plus, there are a few new though very lightly implemented features which I enjoyed, e.g. the pseudo RTS ground battles and sort-of capture-the-flag space fights.
+ Destroy and rebuild
+ Pseudo-RTS elements
+ Star system battles
0 Hide-and-seek missions
0 Still vanishing rewards but with acceptable time-outs
- Studs falling behind walls
- A few crashes
- Buggy levels
- No drop-shadows for coins, collectibles or characters
- Bad information density on overviews/menus
- Targeting of friendlies
- Uneasy access to unlocked characters
- Some confusing indicators
When referring to old weak design I mean problems like missing drop-shadows making it hard (for me) to get a clear idea of the positions of game elements - vehicles of all sorts have drop-shadows though. Menus and most screens that could easily display relevant information that information is hidden in sub-menus or altogether denied, e.g. the pause screen during missions should always display the level name.
There is a star map where each star has five data points, i.e. name, controlling faction and three completion states, only the first of which are available on the star map right away while the other three are hidden in each star's sub-menu. Admittedly they make sense in the sub-menus but should also be available outside.
The hide-and-seek missions are okay. Basically, they are nice as a new idea and manage to avoid becoming boring by virtue of being pretty short.
I like that collecting studs is easier here. Where in earlier LEGO games fighting often kept you from getting to your hard-earned studs in time, now you seem to have more time. Studs still fall behind walls or into the abyss though.
Newer LEGO games offer direct access to unlocked characters at least in free play. This game has you run to sparsely distributed consoles, get the character you need to progress a puzzle, then run back to get the next character to solve it.
Another old "feature" is the targeting of friendlies. I guess it's funny enough to punish your co-player from time to time but the concept makes absolutely no sense in single player mode. It feels almost as if the auto-aim - which in principle I agree is a sensible feature - prefers to aim at your sidekick rather than enemies or other sensible targets. This feeling may be due to my growing frustration with the effect and also the short distance your player 2 unnecessarily keeps.
As usual you'll be able to obtain indicators that help you find red bricks and minikits. But sometimes the indication is pretty far off, indicating where you find the minikit rather than where you need to get it.
Despite all the problems I still immensely enjoyed playing LEGO Star Wars III: Clone Wars and I recommend it without hesitation. If you had fun with other, specifically older LEGO games you should be sufficiently entertained by this one.

The Steam early access phenomenon, the roguelike with a twist, a unique combination of dungeon exploration mixed with Dance Dance Revolution style rhythm mechanics, this is Crypt of the NecroDancer.
In the game you take on the role of Cadence, a young adventurer searching the titular crypt for her missing father. On her adventure, Cadence will find new and powerful tools and weapons as well as unlocking new playable characters, all the while moving to the beat of the background music.
If you think this sounds a little bizarre, don’t worry, you’re not alone.
Mastering the rhythm mechanics is essential for your very survival as Cadence and her friends cannot move or attack outside of the beats of the soundtrack itself, precision timing will help you progress easily.
The great news is, the audio is superb. The electronic beats are great to listen to and even better to play along with, play Crypt of the NecroDancer for long enough and you’ll find yourself dancing along as you play (maybe that’s just me). The soundtrack is the very essence of the game, it’s the key ingredient and while the developer could have gone for something simple, purely for the purpose of the beat, what they’ve brought to the game is worthy of praise on its own.
If however, the in-game music isn’t to your liking, or you can’t quite hit the beat on a particular tune then don’t worry because Brace Yourself Games have you covered. The developers have opted to allow players to fully customise the music, giving you the ability to play along to the songs on your hard drive, the algorithm isn’t perfect, but it’s still a fun option.
There’s much more to Crypt of the NecroDancer then just a rhythm mechanic though, a dance game this is not. This is a dungeon-crawling roguelike with an array of things to keep you coming back for more. Top of the list is the randomized level structure, no two experiences are the same, no two levels contain the same bad guys. This certainly adds a level of difficulty to the game but once you’ve mastered the beats, this makes sure you don’t bore of the game easily.
The biggest issue is permadeath, die once and you’re heading back to the start of the game. This can be a little frustrating in the early days as you’re learning the game, but luckily Crypt of the NecroDancer does have a number of features to help you overcome the hindrance that is death.
Influenced by the likes of Rogue Legacy, there are plenty of options for weapon and magic upgrades, as well as permanent upgrade options to help with the inevitable restart or two you’ll face along the way.
The hidden gem in this game though, something that sets it apart from other roguelikes (not including the rhythm mechanics that is), is the ability to play local co-operative mode. Why head into the abyss alone when you can drag one of your good friends along for the ride as well?
Admittedly, I’ve only had a chance to play co-op with my seven-year-old daughter but after a bit of trial and error, this turned out to be incredibly funny, insanely frustrating at times but funny. The key here is for both players to stay in sync to survive, imagine how difficult that can be, it could ruin friendships along the way. If you’ve got more friends available locally than me then this mode can be a blessing given some of the tough bosses you’ll encounter in the game.
Controls are ridiculously simple with almost the entire gameplay using the four arrow keys, provided you’re in time with the beats of the music, killing bad guys is as simple as running into them using the directional controls. To be fair to Crypt of the NecroDancer though, there’s a bit more to it than that.
The levels are laid out on a square grid system, there’s no diagonal movement here I’m afraid. Despite that though, the game has a turn-based mechanic based around the beats of the music, it’s hard to fully explain but master this and you’ll have a lot more control over battle strategy.
Please don’t take the minimalist control scheme as a sign that this game is either basic or easy because it’s neither of the two, the simple controls just help you master the game quickly and it works well to get you into the action within seconds of your first load. Even the more advanced functions, such as bombs and spells can be accessed by pressing multiple arrow keys at once.
If the keyboard is not your thing then the developers have one more surprise in store, ready for this? Brace Yourself Games have made Crypt of the NecroDancer fully compatible with a dance pad, yep the dance pad is making a comeback people. If you imagine playing the game using the keyboard arrow buttons then it’s quite easy to translate that into the four arrows you can find on a dance pad, it’s a superb novelty if you happen to own a dance pad.
The one issue with this game is the fact that each levels music is static, meaning that if you find it incredibly difficult to master the rhythm-based gameplay, you’ll likely to hear the same 4 songs on repeat as to restart the game. This could have a significant impact on how long a player will stick with the game, the frustration of hearing the same music over and over can be anger-inducing.
Of course Brace Yourself Games have already thought of this and not only allowed you to add your own custom music into the mix but also made it possible for you to get help from a friend when the need arises.
Overall though, this is a game for those looking for a quick distraction, it’s a casual players game, fun in small bursts and fun with a friend but this isn’t going to be the game you sit down with for an all night session.
Crypt of the NecroDancer is a unique experience and one that is definitely recommended, it’s not quite perfect but surprisingly close. With a variety of gameplay options available despite such a simplistic control set-up, fun visuals and an awesome soundtrack, this game is a true testament to what great game design can create.

I really don’t know if i can recommend this game. :-/
Everything is more fun with friends, and that is so for this game too as usual.
And if you are willing to pay i have no doubt you will have a more fun time too, the more you pay the more the fun you have i imagine.
Even then rng may, i imagine, back stab you with the unlocks.
As a free to play person, so far, i can tell you the grind is real.
Currency to unlock traps and chars, and lvl up the traps with cards and currency.
And loot chest grind from other useful unlocks that i do not think you can actually pay for in the store for.
Like a amulet that makes traps and barricades takes less damage if you are close to them.
(if i heard and remember it right)
One of the both pro and cons of the game is the amount of traps and heroes.
If you are a free to play person i imagine you will never get any of the other cool ones (get perhaps one), and if you pay, you can get every hero for 30 euros.
But then you got the currency grind, and you can get it by playing, or paying, but the amount you get and the amount you need is silly large.
If you are free to play, hope for good daily deals to fill out your trap load out, and focus on a single few traps, as you will in NO way get enough currency, and cards to get em all far up the trap level tree.
Now the grind.
Almost all the maps have multiple entrances and with some few map exceptions they can not have one kill box.
Aggravating indeed if you try to single play em.
No doubt you can with good traps, right hero and youtube to help you out.
I can not say that it is fun tho.
With friends you will breeze thru the lower “challenge level” with 5 stars on all of em in no time.
There are also endless and weekly challenges that you can enjoy as a group.
Solo, not so much enjoyment.
Some maps revisits on the harder challenge levels, but have fun trying to guess a proper load out before you enter with the bare bones gray map as a guide.
And there after your memory to help you there, because we all love how we can not see stuff there, right?
Now for more cons.
Forget both breeze and proper load-out if you pub.
So far as i know, it is random which map you get when you wait for a game, but challenge level is set as you look for games under that window.
If you dare being slow, make a mistake or being inattentive you may get the usual, non friendly “banter” like “i am gonna report you, i am gonna sell all your traps, learn to play noob” and the rest we all come and love from pub games.
(thats after you have set up so your team mates can sell your traps if you made a mistakes, or if they have something better to place, trap lvls are a thing after all)
You don’t loose the credits, and you can place stuff else where you think?
Well, be prepared for the “helpful” person follow you around selling and putting up the cheapest thing he can till the 50 trap limit.
Other times you get nothing at all communicated, and it either goes great or not.
Some times there are actually helpful players who actually tell you their plans and what the team can do to make it awesome, but thats so rare i think i have only have it happened twice.
Or yet other times,  players may get disconnected or stand in spawn and do nothing whole game.
The chest rewards can be great, or for a mode you really should not play till you are max rank.
Same with the three daily quest, they can also have the same requirements.
Play sabotage for x reward, or kill this random boss that you have to google to see if you can find and beat.
Sabotage is a versus mode.
And apparently levels and unlocks matter allot, so good luck getting invited for one before lvl 50.
So keep re-rolling that one, or the other, with your one free daily re-roll of a quest.
Thankfully you get one free reward each day, so a bit of a passive slow help for everyone.
My advice, in the end?
Try it.
You may like it, and if so you perhaps can persuade your friends to play it with you.
Solo play tho?
Well, i dunno if i really can say its all that fun.
Either pay allot, or grind allot to sit and wait and hope some one else are playing what you are playing and the map you want will hopefully turn up.
And even then, are you really going to have fun with randoms?
If your tolerance is high for pupbs and solo play, and you are willing pay, or the grind is appealing.
Perhaps then i can recommend giving it a solo player try.

This is easily one of the worst zombie-themed games I've ever played.
Supposedly, developers tried to make something like a squad-based survival simulator. The final product is not a simulator, it's not about surviving (if we're not talking about user surviving through the UI), and squad-based part is just pontless.
Every aspect of the game represents raw incompetence of the developers -- game is bugged, UI is ridiculous, gameplay is extremely boring (if you'll last more than 1 hour, like I did, you're supposed to be awarded with a medal), fighting system is just plainly lame.
The game has active pause (you can prace Space to pause the game and give orders to your survivors). Presumably, this was implemented to introduce tactics to the game. Alas, this effort was fruitless -- fights are boring and repetitive. Most of the fights are ending up in user, luring enemies into some trap and then activating it. There's no tactics to it, honestly, it's just a waste of time.
There's a ton of useless mechanics. For example, your character can randomly start bleeding after he was wounded. You'll be bleeding for the whole duration of the level (it won't stop), yet you won't lose any HP for that. Why was that implemented? Because it attracts zombie in a bigger radius around you. But since you're walking faster then they do, they'll soon forget about you and would roam around their location aimlessly (pathfinding is awful here too, by the way).
The weapon system is plainly lame -- you can only hold 1 weapon, and if you want to turn on some switch, you first have to hide the weapon, then use the switch, then take out the weapon again. Developers couldn't care less about usability, I think.
One of the bugs that I've found in my short session was inability to launch game in windowed mode -- all my efforts lead to a point where my inventory disappeared alongside with all of the texts in the game. I was unable to fix it, so, obviously enough, I've decided to just uninstall.
Will I recommend this game? Never. I may recommend to try it to people with really low self-esteem that are enjoying UI masochism and poor gameplay.
I'd rate the game 2.0 out of 10.0, and would NOT recommend it to anyone.

I'm sure the people are nice and all, but after playing Spintires for a few hours I've decided I never want to go to Russia. The game shows us that Russian mud is thick, all-consuming, unrelenting; the nature is beautiful, yet deadly, capricious; the Soviet-era tenaments cold, unwelcoming. A hag beckons at the door. I stick to my vehicle to avoid being dragged into the muddy, murky abyss that my wheels defy. I can't get out to check my load in the rain. Hell, I'm afraid of leaving my vehicle in case an angry bear jumps in and steals the damn thing. After a dodgy turn over the underwater mire, my truck corkscrews in the river, flipping me over. I manage to gulp out a heathen prayer before the water covers my face, and the filthy, filmy desolation that extinguishes my lungs ensures that such a feeble whisper of defiance against unbridled nature goes unheard by living ears, smothered cruelly as my truck succumbs to the river's mighty furor at last.
Just lovely. And you know what? After Spintires, I feel safer here in Australia. AUSTRALIA.

Spin Tires is a log trucking game where you will have to overcome obstacles and rivers to get to your destination.  The game is mainly single player, although does have a multiplayer function. Personally multiplayer with friends is a much better mode as it can be a little bit boring completing scenarios on your own. Multiplayer is a great feature as you winch each other out of ruts and rivers and can be very challenging in an enjoyable way. If you lose internet connection you are kicked back to the main menu and all progress that you have completed is lost, it would be nice to save multiplayer progress. The camera views to see where you going and what you’re doing can be a little frustrating, this can be resolved by switching from 3rd person to 1st person views. The game is highly moddable which is great to play new maps and new vehicles, these mods can also be played online as long as all parties have the same mods applied. It is a shame that there are not many official game maps and it can be difficult to find high quality mod maps. One feature that I do like is a day/night cycle although I would like to see weather involved too. The game works with game controllers or steering wheels but when using manual gears is a little strange and sometimes stalls the truck.
The main menu is simple and can select where you want to go fairly easily. In-game menus can be a little confusing when trying to apply changes to your truck or trailer. It would be nice to see a slightly clearer design when changing modifications on the vehicles.
The graphics & physics are amazing even using medium graphical settings. The tire tracks leave groves in the terrain and can affect the physics on the truck including previous tire tracks. The suspension on the trucks moves extremely well, looking very realistic and sound effects also sounds great and changes on different surfaces.
No Australian servers, so all actions take a noticeable amount of time to complete after you click. Orcs must die 2 is better in every single way

This is easily one of the most beautiful games I ever played - eventhough it cannot rightfully be named a 'game'. So if you need points or a specific goal to feel satisfied, then don't play it. But if you can change your perspective and just enjoy this virtual experience, then go ahead!
To me this is interactive art, it's a symphony where so many things come together to create something utterly stunning. It's the graphics, the music, the incredibly naturally moving fish and also the freedom of movement you get as a player. It's quite similar to that feeling of joy when sliding down a sand-dune in Journey, of the same makers.
As mere humans we can only walk and crawl and run, we cannot fly or dive endlessly. The makers have in both games been really smart about crossing those human limits and a lot of the fun comes from being able to move freely in every single direction, twirl around and speed through the water. No need to refill the gasstank or resurface to breath.
As for the music, I think it sets a great deal of the atmosphere. It's the human voice that often surpasses other instruments, and here too. It is timed excellently to accentuate climaxes, speed runs and also the more murky waters.  The sacral humming and singing almost reminds of a church, and honestly that's what it is.
This is a natural church, the sacred underwaterworld. It's a hommage to the oceans and an ode to the fish. The graphics are absolutely beautiful, not super realistic but more in a painted kind of way. It reminds slightly of the game Subnautica, but then Abzu often times takes on a sudden surrealist appearance. For instance little fountains or streams of water, running as if they were above the surface. Love this detail!
While it might not be a real game in the classical sense of the word, there is a natural progression that keeps building this crescendo towards climax with several stages. Everything gets more and more intense, the music, the graphics, the size of the fish and the 'tasks' you have to perform - if they can really be called that.
It took me longer to finish it than most other players, because i lingered playing around with fish and simply twirling enveloped by all this beauty. And now that it's finished I want to go again! It's like a giant waterslide that you have to ride a couple of times to fully enjoy. It's a sacred space where you can almost fully disconnect from daily worries, especially when wearing headphones (and even moreso while stoned).
I recommend it to anyone who wants a beautiful experience and is not too bound on achievement. Consider it a virtual painting in which you get to play a part, accompanied by the most soothingly brilliant music. Go for it already :)
Sidenote: I didn't use a controller and it took me a few minutes to get used to the controls, but then it was completely fine.

Orion is a game worth playing, but is also likely never going to achieve the critical mass necessary to be as big as it deserves. The ambition of the developers is apparent in the massive, multi-level arenas, the scale and power of the larger dinos, and the range of abilities and equipment with which you can kit out your Tron-esk soldier. There's a tremendous variety of game modes as well, including multiple variants of PvE, PvP, and PvPvE. The three classes of soldier (Assault, Support, and Recon) each have their own tree of persistent skill unlocks, and a microtransaction shop gives you plenty of options for purely cosmetic customization. Orion is largely satisfactory in terms of the quality of its graphics, and even surprises with neat environmental effects and an excellent day/night cycle (the night is actually dark, and can add real tension to a match). In short, it is absolutely worth picking up at full price.
So why did I start my review with such ambivalent language, if I'm willing to recommend a purchase? Because I'm skeptical that Orion is going to live up to its potential; the variety of equipment and abilities I mentioned above is present, but in dire need of an overhaul in order to establish clear class roles (or roles, period, if you want to drop the A/S/R distinction entirely). Server caps are set at 10 total players, which means those massive, multi-level maps feel deserted. PvE modes will see you fight a T-Rex with a tank (or a tank with a T-Rex, in PvP), which is cool, but they'll also see you use the same tactics against the dinos over and over again because their behaviour is both predictable and exploitable, which is not.
I want to be wrong about this, but the game came out in 2012, and it still features what I feel are considerable design flaws. It is absolutely worth picking up - I've even bought several gift copies just to encourage people to try it out - but prepare to break out your disappointed father voice at some point while playing.

This feels like a reskin of GalCiv2, not a new version. Yes, there's some new bits and pieces to play with, but overall it's simply not different enough to really be compelling. There's a ton of issues that contribute to an overall lack of polish to the game. [edit] but given what happened to the X series, that's not necessarily a bad thing, it just means you may want to wait a bit[/edit]
Good are the ideologies. Now "good bad or neutral" reallllly means something in how you develop your race. The resources give you a nice boost, but be careful about including too many parts that require specific resources on ships as you'll end up burning through them quickly.
[edit]
Good is the construction of shipyards in space, rather than as planet bound (tile consuming) resources. Better is the ability to have multiple planets within range contribute resources.
[/edit]
Probably good for multiplayer: Technology Ages... basically, the tech tree controls one level of unlocking, but you also need a certain overall level of tech researched in order to get to each tier, or "age". WIthout the lock, multiplayer could quickly become "who can research [whatever ubertech] fastest".
Overall, there's just some really annoying issues (no particular order):
1) the starship editor is somewhat nicer looking, but it is a pain to use. Getting it to attach something to the anchor point you want is a pain. Too often, it seems to highlight a completely different anchor point than the one your mouse is directly over. Then, selecting it is a tricky click fest because most of the time it zeroes on the biggest thing. It's like it is preferring to highlight the thing most rearward instead of "closest" to the user. I never had this issue with prior versions.
2) For the fact that the game has a manual, it's still a lesson in mystery and trial and error with many options and commands. For example: what does Guard vs Sentry do? Guard doesn't guard at all apparently, it's more like "sleep" as far as I can tell. It's been a while, but I don't recall it working like that in GalCiv2.
3) It's already getting old seeing other civs building stations in your space and there's basically nothing you can do about it without just going and blowing them up (War) or spending a LOT of money in diplomacy. You can 'conquer' their planets through influence, but starbases are stuck unless you unlock the right ideology benefit(And that's one time). This isn't helped by the apparent lack of fog of war for the AI. The first time you see them, they're coming to occupy resources in your zone of influence. Resources you don't even know about yet.
4)[largely edited to elaborate] So far it seems like the difficulty levels need some tuning. Now it seems there's either "no room at all for error early" or "the AI is dumber than a stump and passive beyond belief" and "Normal" seems to be in the dumber than a stump category. Maybe that will go away over time, but it really can be discouraging to people who don't see potential for the game right away. It can also indicate that there's basically only one or two ways to reach each victory type. That stinks when you've got a nice custom race editor as it throws you into too much min/maxing. With further play, I've been able to mitigate this somewhat with custom races tuned for aggressiveness and expansion. It may be also mitigated by having more than one victory type active, but if you're going for the long haul conquest, that can be problematic too.
5) 4Xs have to balance speed of play vs the impression of scope of the universe. On default settings on a medium map, speed of play seems rather slow. Too, too many turns of nothing to do.
6) I'm not sure when "Real" diplomacy kicks in. The last option on the diplomacy menu has remained gray for me through two victories including one with a custom race where I put everything into research. I'll assume I've not researched the right techs. If so, diplomacy takes too much of a concerted effort to research.
Edits from here:
7) The map generator needs work. For instance... "abundant" really isn't and the way the configuration files work, it seems it can't be tuned it any higher for stars, asteroids seem to take up habitable planet slots rather than planet slots (tested that many times) , again messing with distributions, "tight clusters" isn't really reliable on the bigger maps as it often generates all the clusters right in a row and even on "abundant" still creates VAST areas of empty space. I mean sometimes well more than a 1/3 of the map is a single block of emptiness.
8) Money still needs tuning. For example: cost of upgrading ships is too high.
9) Repair? What's that? Until you unlock the techs that allow repair in combat, the best you can get is 5 points a turn without special faction abilities. No big deal for stub fighters, but it doesn't scale with larger vessel sizes. There really should at least be something that makes it a function of shipyard production.

Lego Star Wars 3 is the black sheep in the series. It seems like Traveller's Tales wanted to experiment a bit with this one. Many levels feel like Battlefront space battles (you get on and off your ship repeatedly), some levels are a simplified RTS game, the Hub is huge and expands as you explore it with new abilities... And that's not counting some new gameplay mechanics, such as the lightsaber throw.
You would think that with that many new features, it would be the most awesome game in the series. The thing is, it's not. The "Battlefront space battles" are quite amazing, but other than that everything feels off. The RTS parts are fun at first, but it feels quickly repetitive and not very clever (there are a too many levels like that to my taste). The Hub is just too big, and looking for a character you need to progress in it is a pain and can take a lot of time. Also, it's not always clear where you have to go or what you have to do. It's supposed to be a children game, but I often found myself stuck for a while. Walking in circles trying to find the next objective is really tedious and should not be a part of this game.
But the worst of all is that TT found a way to mess up with the coop part. Coop multiplayer is arguably the biggest selling point of the Lego games; ask anyone who love their game, and there's a big chance they'll tell you they love playing them with their partner, their friend or their kid. But in Lego Star Wars 3, their are phases where the two players are not even in the same room, and they have to do different tasks. It doesn't feel like they're playing together. And above that, one of the two players will often have less things to do than the other, so it's just a dull phase when they do nothing and have to wait for the other.
Why do I still recommend it, you ask? Well first thing, I'm sure that if you play it alone, it's a much better game. If so, I'm sure it's amazing. But even if you play with someone else like I did, the "classic" phases are as fun as ever (when you're not seperated, that is), the RTS ones are at least nice to discover, and in the case of the space battles they're quite fun the whole game. Also, the humor is enjoyable. It's not as great as the humor in Complete Saga, and some of the jokes are a bit too random, but it's good and certainly better than what you have in some of the most recent voiced games (looking at you, Lego Marvel).

Omfg, this game, this freakin' game. I got it in Early Access back in October 2014 because I saw that Danny Baranowsky (Super Meat Boy and Binding of Isaac) had composed the music. Installed, played, and all I could think was that this was the most genius game idea ever! Roguelike? Check. Turn based strategy? Check. Awesome music? Check...oh, you mean that the music determines the pace of the turns? Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥I just ♥♥♥♥ed a little.
But seriously, the game is incredibly fair, any time you so much as get hit, it's your own damn fault. Only one creature in the entire game (and the bosses, kinda) can be considered "random", and that's the bats which are quite easily managed by only moving at the right time.
If you want replayability, there are several characters each with unique styles. One has no weapon, unlimited bombs, and can kick bombs 3 units away. Another doesn't damage enemies and merely confuses them (they move in the opposite direction that they want) when she attacks. Another disregards the whole "rhythm game" thing and just moves whenever you want and the enemies will move at the same time you do, so you can pause for 5 minutes and think about the best course of action if you're so inclined (this was the first character I beat the game fully with, Zone 4 be hard yo). And then there are the characters that increase the beats per minute, or the ones that die if you so much as miss a single beat/get hit. And then there's the guy that combines both as well as dies if he picks up money...
There's also a local co-op mode if you're interested, and speedrun leaderboards.
There's something for everybody, the game is great and well worth the $15. You might not get as much replayability out of it as say Isaac purely because Isaac has like a billion items. But the game runs flawlessly on a potato, it's solid fun and you'll definitely get your fill, and there's no reason you can't replay it over and over, it's a roguelike, just play as much as you like.

For a free to play, this game is alright and you would rarely have to pay any cash for advancing your account in getting new characters or items since you have a good chance of acquiring them via chests and in-game rewards just for playing. Survival is the main highlight of this in terms of puzzle solving, though sabotage is sort of a backburner thing if you want a nonstandard challenge especially when it comes to going against players who may be a little bit on the sadistic side.
Opposed to others say, the progression is fairly steady, probably more so than other Free to play games and earning the nessecary skulls is fairly easy once you learn a few of the characters and nab some with your chest loot.  The game has a minor learning curve, but resetting traps is fairly easy and once you understand the maps along with some of the better places to set your traps, you are golden. Traps are also fairly easy to obtain and upgrade, especially with some daily deals, with the only potential drawback is the fact that traits are kind of  rarer thing but the game's Random item generation for chests is solid.
Overall, if I had the option of a star system, I would give it 7.5 stars out of 10.

I feel like the community on Steam can be unfairly harsh on some games that are free to play, and that includes OMDU. Unchained is really fun to play, and that's what matters. But there are many mistakes and errors in game design, and its very dissapointing.
I don't think that Robot Entertainment really unlocked the true potential of OMD. The decision to go Free to play is a mistake - but its all about the money as usual. Traps are no longer directly upgradable like OMD2....its the common, uncommon, rare, epic loot grade system straight out of your common RPG. Progression occurs as you "level up" and you get rewards after combat. But progression is slow. This is to encourage players to purchase chests. But get this - chests are too expensive as is. I dont think many players purchased them.
The other big mistake is the continual focus on mutliplayer gameplay. Players like me are perfectly content to play single player, and sometimes you want to, but you are practically forced into multiplayer by the nature of the game. Some things also suffer in multiplayer - the biggest being the fact that you lose some strategy involved with trap making. With powerful players, the maps become too easy with leveled up traps.
Tower defense was originally birthed in Warcraft 3. It required strategy and careful planning. In OMDU, the "Tower defense" aspect of it has been watered down. Theres not that much strategy involved, and spamming traps sometimes is good enough.
For those complaining about it being pay to win in PvP - thats not really the case, it just takes time to level up your traps. You can speed things up by purchasing chests, but they are absurdly expensive, so you'd might as well do what everyone else does and just play the game.
I think most players that loved OMD2 like me, will be content with slowly leveling up their traps. It's still fun, and the ease of multiplayer matchups is nice.
If only Robot Entertainment created a map editor tool and handed it off to the modding community, would we really have a great game. The modding community would have a blast creating new maps. Instead we get the Free to play model. F2P works for some games, but for a game like OMDU, I would have been much happier with a base game and then continual DLC's released.
Sometimes, KISS is the way to go. All that Robot had to do was expand OMD2. Thats ALL THEY HAD TO DO. Instead we get this mess. Is it fun? Yes. But its still a dissapointment.

The roguelike-like that I most enjoy getting frustrated at. Start off as a helpless child surrounded by horrible fleshbeasts, pray to the Random Number Gods, maybe become a destroyer of all who oppose you, likely die. A lot. Fun to play and discover the uses of every item on your own. Learn how to read enemies' tells and avoid damage! Fail anyway and get hit in the face! Have a lucky run and be friends with the RNG! Step on spikes and die anyway! Die constantly until you get better! And have fun the whole way!
The Wrath of Lamb adds more fun items, monsters, and death. More enemies, more items, more ways to die! More ways to win!
BoI isn't perfect, but there's both good and bad bugs. It's a good game and I highly recommend it, the WoL DLC, and the soundtrack.
[edit]
The Eternal Update. Well. While I'm glad that Florian decided to give us bonus DLC to a game that we all thought people were done with, it's not well implemented. It's got some great and unique ideas, but it's not balanced.
Eternal enemies follow the lazy route of "double it". Twice the health, attack two times per loop, twice as many projectiles or minion spawns. Boss battles take way too long and you're not even guaranteed an eternal heart drop.
And the bugs. Dear God, the bugs. Nothing is quite as infuriating as losing because the game breaks. Like when the framerate hiccups and then suddenly comes back and you got hit 5 times and you're dead. Or the items just stop working. Or a shop spawns in instead of the final boss.
TL;DR - hard mode, more like fake difficulty mode
[edit 2]
Patches have made Hard Mode more fair, but it's still tedious and frustrating. You need to be OP in order to even stand a chance of beating it, moreso than the original game. Still needs bug fixing and balancing, but it's getting there.

EDIT
I really should just revise this entire review, but that just begs to question where do I begin with what all is wrong with this game? Far too many words for not only the attention span of the average reader, but even more words than a Steam review can allow. So let me sum it up: Bad AI, unpredictable game bugs from minor to game breaking, plus everything mentioned below. Honestly, this game was at a: "Don't buy until on sale", but after putting more hours into it (and then rage quitting because of a daftly mind boggling stupid bug that made me uninstall the game in anger) I am now just saying: Avoid this game until it has plenty of patches. Don't trust this developer to deliver quality. I should have known from the beginning when they launched the early access at $99 that this game was a sham and a rip off. I'm still kicking myself - a week later - that I bought this game at $50. Terrible, terrible purchase.
Original review below:
I'm having a hard time getting into this game.
For most 4x games, particularly the Civ series, 2 hours is way more than enough for the game to sink it's hooks in and keep me going for "just one more turn!"
It's easy to draw similarities between the Civ franchise and Galactic Civilizations III, partly because "Civilizations" is in it's title, but it is also a 4x game with similar rulesets as the Civ franchise, which maybe is where I am having trouble getting in to it.
Civ5 made it easy to pick up and play. While it's not without it's bugs (especially at launch) some of the basic fundamentals seems refined.
GCIII, on the other hand, seems to have clunky controls which is the bare-bones basics of all games. The UI often provides too much unnecessary information at times, while at other times, it doesn't seem to give you enough feedback (like when building on a planet)
***EDIT***
below I mention using directional keys to move the camera bugs when selected on a ship. This isn't entirely true. After checking key-mapping, it turns out the W and the S key were mapped to 2 items, resulting in the seemingly weird bug. This comes back to my complaint about the UI not providing enough information. It would have been nice if the game informed me there was another function already mapped to those keys.
The camera - which I map to WASD - is picky. I can move it freely while I am NOT selected on any ship or planet, but should I select one, it locks my camera to the X axis, preventing any vertical scrolling. As for movement paths themselves - going back to the UI not providing enough feedback at times - when you tell a ship to auto move (either to your predefined location or just setting it to auto-explore) it seems like any action, big or small, while the unit is selected, will set the ship to idle and remove it's auto-path.
Race customization seems almost pointless. Aesthetically, there are very limited options to chose from - unless you want still images, which I find un-immersive. It does provide some RPG-esque stats to try and specialize your race in certain areas, but I found it to be so inconsequential. You only get 5 points to distribute, and since this is not an RPG - as far as I am aware - you do not get any more stat points to distribute.
While you could intentionally REMOVE points from existing areas to get more than the 5 stat points, it always feels like if you want to properly specialize your race you have to intentionally hinder your race. Honestly, It feels like it has the illusion of a deep stat system, but frankly, I think a basic "Choose 2 specializations and choose 1 weakness" from a small list of trees like, "Research, Commerce, Growth, Warfare, Politics" would have provided a more meaningful choice than the existing "specialization tree".
Ship building is a fine example of how clunky controls can be in this game. It feels like an almost direct copy-paste job of the ship building in GCII, and it has not aged well.
There is NO undo/redo option. There is NO copy-paste option. As far as I am aware, there is NO save and edit later function. When you have as many functions to control objects shape, size, appearance, and animation, the lack of the above listed utilities is a huge disappointment on Stardock. This makes repeating similar pieces for symmetry's sake tedious as hell with no copy paste. And if you use the gizmo's to control rotation, translation, and size, then it is very easy to accidentally click on a different piece than the one you are editing and wind up adjusting the wrong piece, which can result in screwing up the ship and without Ctrl-Z to undo, it can be astoundingly frustrating.
The use of snap-points for pieces also seems archaic, and often, getting the piece you want to snap to the points is a headache in it of itself, but more often than not, these snap points don't seem to want to work in your favor anyways. Often it seems like objects want to snap to the most illogical placement, such as clipping inside the object it snapped to, and usually with weird rotations.
I feel like a drag-and-drop system or a click-on system (without snap points) would have been more effective, but, without it, as a result, the ship-building is just a headache.
I came into this game hoping to experience a Sci-Fi equivilent to Civilizations with extensive customization, but I left feeling like I was burned by a bad game with poor, clunky controls, an uninfomative UI, and shallow, frustrating customization. DON'T BUY UNTIL IT HAS SEVERAL PATCHES!!!!

The Steam early access phenomenon, the roguelike with a twist, a unique combination of dungeon exploration mixed with Dance Dance Revolution style rhythm mechanics, this is Crypt of the NecroDancer.
In the game you take on the role of Cadence, a young adventurer searching the titular crypt for her missing father. On her adventure, Cadence will find new and powerful tools and weapons as well as unlocking new playable characters, all the while moving to the beat of the background music.
If you think this sounds a little bizarre, don’t worry, you’re not alone.
Mastering the rhythm mechanics is essential for your very survival as Cadence and her friends cannot move or attack outside of the beats of the soundtrack itself, precision timing will help you progress easily.
The great news is, the audio is superb. The electronic beats are great to listen to and even better to play along with, play Crypt of the NecroDancer for long enough and you’ll find yourself dancing along as you play (maybe that’s just me). The soundtrack is the very essence of the game, it’s the key ingredient and while the developer could have gone for something simple, purely for the purpose of the beat, what they’ve brought to the game is worthy of praise on its own.
If however, the in-game music isn’t to your liking, or you can’t quite hit the beat on a particular tune then don’t worry because Brace Yourself Games have you covered. The developers have opted to allow players to fully customise the music, giving you the ability to play along to the songs on your hard drive, the algorithm isn’t perfect, but it’s still a fun option.
There’s much more to Crypt of the NecroDancer then just a rhythm mechanic though, a dance game this is not. This is a dungeon-crawling roguelike with an array of things to keep you coming back for more. Top of the list is the randomized level structure, no two experiences are the same, no two levels contain the same bad guys. This certainly adds a level of difficulty to the game but once you’ve mastered the beats, this makes sure you don’t bore of the game easily.
The biggest issue is permadeath, die once and you’re heading back to the start of the game. This can be a little frustrating in the early days as you’re learning the game, but luckily Crypt of the NecroDancer does have a number of features to help you overcome the hindrance that is death.
Influenced by the likes of Rogue Legacy, there are plenty of options for weapon and magic upgrades, as well as permanent upgrade options to help with the inevitable restart or two you’ll face along the way.
The hidden gem in this game though, something that sets it apart from other roguelikes (not including the rhythm mechanics that is), is the ability to play local co-operative mode. Why head into the abyss alone when you can drag one of your good friends along for the ride as well?
Admittedly, I’ve only had a chance to play co-op with my seven-year-old daughter but after a bit of trial and error, this turned out to be incredibly funny, insanely frustrating at times but funny. The key here is for both players to stay in sync to survive, imagine how difficult that can be, it could ruin friendships along the way. If you’ve got more friends available locally than me then this mode can be a blessing given some of the tough bosses you’ll encounter in the game.
Controls are ridiculously simple with almost the entire gameplay using the four arrow keys, provided you’re in time with the beats of the music, killing bad guys is as simple as running into them using the directional controls. To be fair to Crypt of the NecroDancer though, there’s a bit more to it than that.
The levels are laid out on a square grid system, there’s no diagonal movement here I’m afraid. Despite that though, the game has a turn-based mechanic based around the beats of the music, it’s hard to fully explain but master this and you’ll have a lot more control over battle strategy.
Please don’t take the minimalist control scheme as a sign that this game is either basic or easy because it’s neither of the two, the simple controls just help you master the game quickly and it works well to get you into the action within seconds of your first load. Even the more advanced functions, such as bombs and spells can be accessed by pressing multiple arrow keys at once.
If the keyboard is not your thing then the developers have one more surprise in store, ready for this? Brace Yourself Games have made Crypt of the NecroDancer fully compatible with a dance pad, yep the dance pad is making a comeback people. If you imagine playing the game using the keyboard arrow buttons then it’s quite easy to translate that into the four arrows you can find on a dance pad, it’s a superb novelty if you happen to own a dance pad.
The one issue with this game is the fact that each levels music is static, meaning that if you find it incredibly difficult to master the rhythm-based gameplay, you’ll likely to hear the same 4 songs on repeat as to restart the game. This could have a significant impact on how long a player will stick with the game, the frustration of hearing the same music over and over can be anger-inducing.
Of course Brace Yourself Games have already thought of this and not only allowed you to add your own custom music into the mix but also made it possible for you to get help from a friend when the need arises.
Overall though, this is a game for those looking for a quick distraction, it’s a casual players game, fun in small bursts and fun with a friend but this isn’t going to be the game you sit down with for an all night session.
Crypt of the NecroDancer is a unique experience and one that is definitely recommended, it’s not quite perfect but surprisingly close. With a variety of gameplay options available despite such a simplistic control set-up, fun visuals and an awesome soundtrack, this game is a true testament to what great game design can create.

I picked this up, wanting a short narrative experience. Eight leisurely hours later I’d completed its three chapters and was satisfied.
I struggle to call this a game, it’s much more a choose-your-own adventure with RPG elements. Even then, there are a total of eight story branches, five are sudden death through different means, and the three ‘good’ endings at each of the chapters. So, really, you’re just along for the ride. Leveling, skills, equips are all but superfluous, and easy-mode weapons are easily obtainable.
It’s fluff. Enjoyable, but still fluff. It draws upon the type of clichés you’d expect, without being lost in the quagmire of tropes. The world is ambiguous enough in it fantastical bearings it doesn’t breach into ridiculousness, while being out there enough to suspend disbelief and take you along for the ride. Bonus points for not hating either of the protagonists, which is nice. By this, my criteria, it’s good fluff.
After you get all achievements, an easy enough task, there’s effectively zero replay value. Not a problem for the cost of entry. If price is a deterrent, for whatever reason, the developer has it free to download
(including English).
The character design/art is well done, understated, and grooves with the general atmosphere. The three-second animations fit both stylistically and thematically, leaving me wanting more. The soundtrack isn’t outstanding, but it works well enough, and satisfactorily fills the silence.
I have a lot of praise for the game, likely because I had very little expectation. I was delighted with what I was given, which is why I have no reserve in recommending it – so long as you’re in a mood for fluff.

I feel like the community on Steam can be unfairly harsh on some games that are free to play, and that includes OMDU. Unchained is really fun to play, and that's what matters. But there are many mistakes and errors in game design, and its very dissapointing.
I don't think that Robot Entertainment really unlocked the true potential of OMD. The decision to go Free to play is a mistake - but its all about the money as usual. Traps are no longer directly upgradable like OMD2....its the common, uncommon, rare, epic loot grade system straight out of your common RPG. Progression occurs as you "level up" and you get rewards after combat. But progression is slow. This is to encourage players to purchase chests. But get this - chests are too expensive as is. I dont think many players purchased them.
The other big mistake is the continual focus on mutliplayer gameplay. Players like me are perfectly content to play single player, and sometimes you want to, but you are practically forced into multiplayer by the nature of the game. Some things also suffer in multiplayer - the biggest being the fact that you lose some strategy involved with trap making. With powerful players, the maps become too easy with leveled up traps.
Tower defense was originally birthed in Warcraft 3. It required strategy and careful planning. In OMDU, the "Tower defense" aspect of it has been watered down. Theres not that much strategy involved, and spamming traps sometimes is good enough.
For those complaining about it being pay to win in PvP - thats not really the case, it just takes time to level up your traps. You can speed things up by purchasing chests, but they are absurdly expensive, so you'd might as well do what everyone else does and just play the game.
I think most players that loved OMD2 like me, will be content with slowly leveling up their traps. It's still fun, and the ease of multiplayer matchups is nice.
If only Robot Entertainment created a map editor tool and handed it off to the modding community, would we really have a great game. The modding community would have a blast creating new maps. Instead we get the Free to play model. F2P works for some games, but for a game like OMDU, I would have been much happier with a base game and then continual DLC's released.
Sometimes, KISS is the way to go. All that Robot had to do was expand OMD2. Thats ALL THEY HAD TO DO. Instead we get this mess. Is it fun? Yes. But its still a dissapointment.

I reviewed this when it was on early access and it was deemed helpful by a lot of people. For some reason when it launched I guess the review got removed. Anyway I'm just going to copy and paste my original review now.

I am loving and am addicted to this game. I'm a 100% free to play player as well. Yes I can tell buying packs would give you a benefit but honestly you still have to know how to use the cards correctly. This is something you cannot get until you've put some time into the game. By that point though you will have gotten enough credits for several booster packs and can probably make a decent deck for free.
Unlike Hearthstone decks can have anywhere from 25-40 cards. Each player starts with 25 life but for every card more then that in your deck you get another point. So if I have a 25 card deck and my opponent has a 40 card deck I'll start with 25 life and he will start with 40. This may seem bad but honestly it's not. With 25 card decks they are very focused and you have much higher chances of getting the cards you need. In fact I rarely lose to people with 40 card decks but lose to the people rolling 25 all the time lol.
The presentation for the game is top notch as far as I'm concerned. I mean there is only so much you can do with a ccg. I think it's one of the better looking/sounding card games out there.
Another HUGE plus are the devs. They are very active on the forums and respond to almost any question posted. They have even been known to give people boosters if they report bugs/problems with the game. They may seriously be the most open devs I've ever got a game from.
The one negative I have for the game though is it doesn't do a great job of explaining what different abilities are. I'm positive almost everyone says "wtf is firepower" their first few games. This isn't a big issue imo though b/c after a handful of games you'll have a good grasp.
In the end I cannot recomend this game enough. Yes it's very Hearthstone like but unless you're just in love with the Warcraft lore (hey nothing wrong with that!) I really feel as if this game has it beat. It also doesn't hurt that this is new and it does NOT require a significant investment to start if you want to be competitive, unlike Hearthstone.
END OF ORIGINAL REVIEW

ABZU is an extremely beautiful and immersive underwater adventure. The atmospheric detail and soul resonating composition carries you through one of the best audio-visual presentations seen in years. Although the short duration of the initial play-through may be a large concern for many, ABZU is truly a work of art deserving attention.
Awakening to a clear sky above crisp and crystal clear water, you control a scuba diver. That’s it. No instructions, no mini-map, no quest, guide, HUD or anything of that nature. Just open water filled with dense fauna and marine life. As you travel deeper and deeper down the rabbit hole, you will soon see areas devoid of such miraculous life. With the power to rejuvenate these barren abysses, one mystery is solved, as more seem to present themselves.
ABZU’s gameplay can be essentially described as a swimming simulator in 3rd person perspective. Although the travel is relatively linear, nodal areas in between connection points can be fairly expansive allowing a moderate amount of exploration. You are free to swim around, observe, ride or watch anything.
A very neat feature provided in this game is meditation. Unlocked by seeking meditation statues scattered throughout the game, meditation presents a new perspective mode that allows the player to watch marine life in their natural habitat from the fish’s perspective (3rd person).
Just looking at the various screenshots provided by the game, one should already get an idea of how pretty ABZU can be. The various wildlife, vibrant and diverse fauna, and masterful lighting effects help create one of the most breath-taking, jaw-dropping, awe-inspiring experiences imparted by a video game seen in quite a while. Seaweed part as you swim through them, carp flee from pursuing sharks, and clouds of sand appear upon stepping on the seabed. Such attention to detail is what makes the player feel one with the scuba diver.
What may be lost upon many people that throw a casual glance at this beautiful game, is ABZU’s equally fascinating musical composition and sound effects. Without the sounds of the seaweed parting, the fish scurrying, the sand lifting, or the water echoing, the experience would be much, much weaker. The orchestral soundtrack provides the monumental feeling needed to make ABZU seem daunting and imposing to explore, while satisfying to progress at the same time. The transitions between new areas seem epic, and the change in tempo while in the jetstreams are just some of the many audio-visual harmonies incorporated to help improve gameplay.
My first play-through of ABZU took a little under 2 hours to complete with semi-moderate exploration. Even with a more thorough search through each zone, there wouldn’t be that much game time added. Various features are incorporated to help provide the player with something to attain in a replay, such as: meditation statues, hidden sea shells, achievements, and secret areas. Users have reported getting 100% achievements within 4-7 hours. The deciding factor in how many miles you’ll get out of this game is dependent on if you are willing to just lose yourself in the world. From searching every nook and outcropping, to riding alongside manta rays or viewing the sharks exert their dominance.
Although the play time may be a major concern for many buyers, I personally feel that ABZU is a worthwhile experience. Mostly because a video game that is essentially a work of art is extremely rare to come by, and the impactful experiences that I gained throughout my journey in ABZU is something I will remember for years. Just make sure not to spoil yourself too much if you are still on the fence.
It is very difficult to describe how amazing ABZU is without experiencing it first-hand. Using so many positive adjectives in this review starts to diminish the effect of each, but that is just how great ABZU was for me. With such a grandiose display of audio-visual direction, ABZU is definitely recommended to those looking for an artistic, underwater adventure.

Main focus of this game is breeding based on DNA. This part is like a puzzle. Each monster has a DNA scheme consisting of up to 6 pairs of genes. Each pair (except cosmetic ones) has a best value and if you get that in your monster, it will gain certain percentage to it's stats. You can't farm for monster with best stats because they are not available in the wilds, so you have to solve the puzzle. When you solved it and make a team out of units with 100% bonus you can progress much further because monsters in the wilds will be much weaker than your own.
As soon as you get 2-3 monsters that have all the required genes that you need, you can make a plan and go for the 100% version of that monster. Each monster can only be used several times in the breeding, and also there is an item that costs only 1500 gold that restores the amount of times that monster can be bred. You get so many of those items from quests that if you have a certain plan that does not depend on probabilities with less than 10%, you will make required monster without running out of those.
On top of breeding part there is a combat that is rather simplistic. Each stage consists of 8-10 areas, when you enter each area you can be attacked or can find gold/healing/chest. Battle is automated between two teams. Each team consists of one leader that has a passive skill that affects all teammates and 3 other units. There is an elemental affinity system - fire>wind>water>fire. You can use potions to heal and resurrect units after the battle. Usually there are up to 4 battle areas on each stage. You get reward that you've collected if you make it to the end of the stage without wiping.
Overall I find the game rather fun. Main thing that I like is breeding - how you need to combine your units to get to certain combinations of genes. But if you just mix things randomly you will most likely not get anything good and it will be frustrating (I suppose that's why there are so many bad reviews for this game). Combat is very simplistic and it only depends on composition of your army, I started using Skip button from 2nd or 3rd stage. Shops contain only health/mana/resurrect/merge recover potions. You can also craft better health/mana potions and costumes for your assistant with resources that you farm.
Only thing that I miss is the filter for certain race when you start playing Merging. Usually you only need one race on that screen and default order is based on the order that you got units so it's kinda awkward to find units that you need.
Note: the review is based on the version that was available at June 30, 2016. That's when I was playing the game, but was not able to post a review due to some bug in Steam, so temporarily saved it in forum.
