"Star Crusade CCG" is a true archetype of our gaming age: the Neo-Bootleg.  For those who don't remember classic games such as the sixteen different versions of "Hangly-Man," a "bootleg" game was one that went beyond a cleared throat and an air-quoted "inspired by," past the bullet-riddled warning signs of "imitation of" and straight into the seedy, crack-scented chop shop of borderline counterfeiting.  Like it or hate it, one can't avoid the fact that it's a crass reskin of an existing product, muddied by free-to-play MMO clipart, an unappealing UI and a somewhat more exhausting monetization system.  The mechanics are the same.  The cards are the same. The heroes are the same.  The only difference between this and Hearthstone is that this is somehow the same thing but terrible.  If you could produce video games in a sweatshop, this is exactly the sort of game you would get.
If Hearthstone had a purchase price, I'd be giving SC:CCG a pragmatic, unsmiling thumbs up as the poor man's alternative. Since it doesn't, we have to concede that its only reason to exist is as a cynical, possibly even illegal cash grab typical of the modern mobile app market.  If you really, truly hate Blizzard and their smarmy high-fantasy IP, then by all means waste your time with THIS flavorless chunk of damp Chinese newspaper instead of THAT saccharine slice of carcinogenic angel cake.  But don't pretend you're having a good time, because you're not.

Now that the full release of this game has been out for awhile, I feel compelled to write a review of this game.
Crypt of the NecroDancer is a rogue like, rhythm based dungeon crawler that offers a unique challenge and experience, complete with multiple characters that have their own playing style that affects the gameplay greatly.
- Probably the most important aspect of a rhythm game is its music. Crypt does not disappoint in the slightest with its amazing tunes, composed by the one and only Danny Baranowsky as well as awesome remixes by FamilyJules7x and A_Rival.
- You can use your own music in the game, and this feature is implemented well.
- The game provides a hard but fair style of gameplay, something that is sure to keep people doing runs over and over again.
- Each of the characters adds an interesting twist (such as moving in cut time or being able to only use bombs) that provide an additional challenge for players to overcome.
- This game has high replayability as no two runs are exactly the same.
- A mix of items provides players with multiple ways to beatdown enemies to the beat.
- The devs constantly provide updates and work hard to fix any bugs that people encounter along the way.
- It can take awhile to get used to. You're probably not going to be able to get through Zone 1 on your first try. For some people, this may be a turnoff, though, if you're willing to put in the effort, you can really get a lot of enjoyment out of completing a run.
- If you're trying to 100% this game... think again. One of the achievements may be impossible to get, which may turn some people away.
- Pausing the game and regaining your pace can be rather difficult. While this may not sound like a big deal at first glance, there are some characters who will die if you miss a beat (Aria and Coda).
Some people may complain about the price, but you can find some 33% off coupons floating around on Steam. It's not much, but 10 bucks is less than 15.
If you like rogue likes, rhythm games, or dungeon crawlers, get this game. This game is an astounding combination of the three that works harmoniously. If the price seems like too much, go get a coupon from groups like Coupon Dumpster and that.

Paladins is only
like any other arena shooter being published today.
Despite what you may read or hear, this game is the evolution of game design and mechanics from Hi-Rez that started with Smite, their highly-popular DOTA competitor. They took League of Legends and, in my opinion, made it different and better. Not everyone agrees, but millions do. And so it is with Paladins.
You have to understand and, to some degree, like math to play Paladins. In that respect, it's more like Hearthstone than any other Blizzard game. From the instant your match selection starts, you have to gauge your opponent(s), figure out who they are choosing and why. Then you have cards and abilities that combine to suit your gameplay style, and enhance that Champion's kit. As a Casual player, the match can be won or lost just by making these decisions, and playing the Champion only adequately. The goal, then, is to find the best loadouts for different situations and become Competitive, as you continually improve your on-the-field gameplay.
Wins and losses are dependent on the objective, like in other games, but that is
influenced by the number of points each Champion accrues for performing their role well during the match. When a healer heals more (vs. doing damage or just staying alive), the Ultimate arrives quicker, their enhancement cards are available faster, and the Champion is more powerful - in just the way that suits your playstyle. So if I heal more with Pip, I can invest in the card that makes him run faster. But if I screw my team by being a flanker, contrary to Pip's class, I may have more fun, but I don't add to the team goal.
My point is that, unlike other games, it is not just a situation where you learn how a character does things, then you go do them. It's different, and a lot more complicated, if you want to be competitive. I'm not suggesting that it is better. It is only
in the sense that EVE Online is better than, say, Elite:Dangerous - it's just more complicated, with a higher learning curve, and less emphasis on the environments, lore, etc. that make up a title from a MUCH bigger ($$) publisher.
TL;DR - I prefer Paladins to other arena shooters because I enjoy its MOBA aspects. Your mileage may vary.

This is a rerelease of an old game so first I will cover the differences between this version and the original before entering an opinion about the original product.
If you have played the game before you will immediately notice the graphical difference. The textures have all been cleaned up and smoothed out. The first product of this is what I call 'Lego Face' where everyone has what looks like painted on faces and many of the characters are stuck with permanent 'O' mouths which are humorous. The second and larger problem is the screen backgrounds (Non-textured/interactive areas) have not been touched at all and have simply been stretched to fit the screen so they are horribly pixelated. Some screens are so bad it is hard to make out what the scenery is supposed to be and the characters look out of place. For this reason I have to fail the graphics even after giving a pass on the PSX-era graphics obviously.
As for the actual game it is of course a classic haralded for bringing this style of RPG back to the mainstream market. The music compositions as well as the character development and story progression have been raved about for decades. That being said, there is a nostalgia factor with most people that played the game during the PSX days and the game may not have aged well for new audiences.  First the game is buggy...to the point there are several Save-File-Corrupting bugs that no rerelease version has bothered to fix. As far as the gameplay difficulty is set to 'Idiot Proof'. To illustrate this there is a point in the game where on the screen before a major boss battle you are, in plain sight, given a chest containing an item that renders you invinicible in that boss battle and this is no isolated incident. You will find guides for the game that severely limit what upgrades and items you can use in an attempt to create difficulty.
At the time of it's release I can tell you the amount of character development was great. We grow with some characters and we start to see others in a different light. Sure the story was so-so and played up many tropes and cliche situations but at the time everything out was so flat that it stood out. I have to say it does feel dated though. Taking off the nostalgia glasses I really see the characters different than I did as a pre-teen and all of the 'deep' commentary about brooding angst, capitalism, religion, and the environment is really just eye-roll worthy.
All of that being said, when it is on sale (I got for $3 at the time of my purchase) it is worth it to play either simply for the nostalgia or to see where games came from to see where they got today.

As strange as overview of this game sounds, it is actually one of the best games in 3 categories: Roguelike, Rhythm Games and games that were in Early Access.
Pros:
Even with typical roguelike RNG involved, every battle is winnable. It can be walk in the park, or run on a thin edge of a blade, but still, there's always a way to win.
Every playthrough is different in terms of enemies you meet, map and items.
Most of the items have both good and bad side - what saves you in one situation can lead you to death in another.
Soundtrack - if you know Danny, there's nothing else to add, all of his works are brilliant, and this one isn't an exception.
Characters - each of them is actually unique, and will totally change the way you play.
Rhythm - you don't actually need to always follow it(with SOME secretly secret exception), but following the rhythm is rewarded in many different ways.
Cons:
Some characters are incredibly hard(think Blue Baby/Lost from BoI:Rebirth), but you knew it wasn't an easy game,right?
Learning enemies movesets is necessary for winning, and takes trial and error. Luckily, you can unlock special training grounds that let you kill them until you are sure you mastered all the ways of eliminating them.
Overall, the game is fantastic. Strongly recommended for people who are even barely interested in music games or roguelikes.

This is the "gateway" game that got me into the world of gaming. Hand's down the best RPG of it's time. It's not without bugs but it was well put together for what Hironobu Sakaguchi thought was his last leg in the industry, as were many of the renditions of Final Fantasy. VII was the first Final Fantasy to explore the limits of 3-dimensional role playing game play. The Materia system was a great idea and awesome to experience. Although there were limitations to the combinations available, you were still able to derive combinations of linked Materias that would give you an edge in battle. The battle system is on an 'Active Time Battle' which means you will be waiting for a short time before you can make an action with any one of your 3 active characters. There are plenty of entertaining encounters in which to utilize your epic equipment, magic, summons, and limit breaks.
The plot features a spikey blonde haired character with an unwieldy Buster Blade in which he flings around with ease. He suffers from amnesia and throughout the game, he relearns his past with some twists and turns along the way. Where would any RPG be without faithful party members to share in your journey. There are 9 characters in all, each with there own little side story and character development, some more developed than others. Last element to any RPG is the struggle or objective and in this story you learn of an individual who seeks to do harm to anything and everything and you guessed it, it is your duty to put a stop to it!
The story is interesting and entertaining and the game play was spot on for its time. This is about the 1000th time I've replayed/mastered the game. If you haven't played already and you like RPG's... this is a must!

There is a handfull of other characters you can play, some play difrent, but most are just plain harder to play, for those who want some aditional chalenge (and most of them are relatives of the main character Cadence and have music-pun names).
The enemies are unique and well designed, you can easily tell what kind of enemy is approaching you, and as you play, you wil get used to knowing what enemy is behind you just by their sound.
The shopkeeper is a retired badass like in most rougelikes, but also happens to be an opera (shopera) singer, which is really usefull as you can her him across the level, signaling how close to the shop you are. If you manage to kill him you get a bling crown that doubles all your coin drops, but his gost might come to avenge him in later levels.
If you like to play rougelikes to the beat this is the game for you (and if you don't want to be rushed, play as bard and play the turns as slowly as you want, while still enyoing the awesome music).

The game is a sequel to the cult games galactic civilization 1-2 and its easily described as a Civilization V set in space, where you move around in space and settle planets instead of ground. This game moves as Civilization V did to hex grids but it do allow stacking ships something Civ V did not allow. One other major difference is the way units are, instead of having this historical unit or set unit Galactic Civilization expands on the previous entries in its franchise and offer you to customize every single aspect of a ship. Its like having a Lego box with thousands of Lego parts, you want to build a boombox with a head like a unicorn that shoots lasers go ahead. You want to build the famous ships from other games or science fiction media in general go ahead. There is also some pre- built standard ships for each race that you can build if you don´t wanna design or build. There will also be a feature to download others creation trough steam workshop among mods of other things.
The game is regarded as a platform for Dlc and free patches with content so bear that in mind, it will be a lot of it, and it will be during a duration of its life cycle 5-7 years.
It is an improvement and refinement over Galactic Civilization 2. Various stuff like a perk system, vast tech tree that branches and the mod support is amazing. The game has a bit dated User Interface but it looks great, and the game looks very good. It also plays well and functions well, and can loose one many nights of sleep. It has that one more turn sickness the Civilization fans are so accustomed to at this point. Its a strong foundation of a strong game. And I would gladly recommend it to anyone new players as old timers.

Despite of all the hate surrounding this game I'm really enjoying it. It has some flaws, of course, but which game hasn't them?
Commands:
Commands are quite simple (but not simplistic) and respond pretty well. I don't really understand why people complain so much about the controls, mine always worked well. Maybe people were mistaking commands (ordering your party to walk into an enemy instead of fighting it - I did it a few times). Maybe devs released a patch or something, I don't know.
LMB to walk and RMB to fight. The guy you're directly controlling will keep hitting the enemy until you tell him to stop or until he runs out of stamina. Problem here are those guys you're not controlling - once you order them to attack, sometimes they keep attacking, sometimes they do it once and stop. I discovered that, most often, you give them a gun, you'll have to place an attack command for each shot; you give them a melee weapon, they'll do the job until stamina goes out
Camera can be controlled with mouse or keyboard. However, the mouse can only hover the camera throughout the scenario - if you want to turn the camera (and it does 360°, to the left and to the right), you have to use the keyboard, so controlling the camera can be a little tricky. I ended up preferring controlling the camera solely by the keyboard, which is not really difficult once you get used to it. Camera can also be freely moved when you pause the game
Mouse scroll zooms in and out is. Problem here is that the game didn't recognize the scroll on my wireless mouse (which didn't happen on my wired mouse) - so I had to rebind it to up/down. In the end, I didn't use it much because even though the zoom in is really "in", the zoom out is not that "out", it is pretty much the FOV you'll be using anyway, so it's not that useful.  Apart from that, both wired and wireless mouse work perfectly. Keys are rebindable, by the way.
The characters you are playing with can be selected either by mouse (clicking on the character or in the hud) or by pressing F1-F4 (I'll talk about the hud later on)
Graphics and sound:
Graphics are pretty good. The story is presented via cutscenes in such a comic book style which is pure eye candy, really well done. In-game graphics are also very good - there's blood and corpses everywhere, and the dead zombies (I mean, those you sent back to death) remain in the scenario
Overall sound is great - the zombies' moaning, the munching, even the doc's wheelchair makes noise when he moves. Voice acting, on the other hand…not so great. I don't know if they tried to parody old movies or if it was just bad choice, either way it didn't work. Thankfully, it only plays during cutscenes (and if you manage to blow a zombie's head off)
Gameplay
It's a strategy game, so run and gun will only get you eaten - which I soon discovered. There's a pause button ('space bar') so make use of it. Pausing and telling you're character what to do tends to work pretty well. Unfortunally you can't give commands in-a-row
Be advised not to bleed and be careful when running. Zombies will smell you if you're bleeding and will hear you if you run, so they will start to chase you. Besides, running burns stamina, and you may run out of it right before a fight - and you can't fight without stamina.
Problem is, zombies will not chase you forever. If you're on an open space, you can just keep walking. The zombies will start giving up on chasing you until there's only 2 or 3 left on your tail.
Talking about stamina, always keep an eye on it. If your guys run out of stamina while fighting, they'll stop the fight to take a break - meaning, they will just stand there taking hits until they eventually die. Trust me, you don't want to die on this game
Inventory management is neat - drag and drop all the way. Items can be rearranged, dropped on the floor or  given to another character and weapons take up to 3 spaces (each character has 12 inv spaces), no issues here
Game hud displays the characters you've met so far, the inventory (which you can hide by pressing 'I') and 4 buttons, each one representing walk, run, select group and camera mode. Select group means select the whole group and give them all the same order (the whole group can also be select via mouse). Camera mode 'on' means that the camera will follow the character you're controlling; 'off', that you'll have to control the camera yourself. Pretty good in my opinion
Avoid alt-tab at all costs. Sometimes, when you alt-tab back to the game, your inventory is gone. I mean, it's there but you can't see it, making the game unplayable. So, if you need to alt-tab, I highly advise you to do it right after saving
Micromanaging can became another issue - your party does not think for themselves, so you need to give your partners orders for every little thing, which may become a little tiring. Not an issue for me, actually, but some people just don't like it
Something I really missed is a bit more of exploration - you know, search locks, garbage cans, drawers, cabinets etc. Items are just dumped anywhere and they have a green glow - so you can't really miss them
The real problem in this game, the one that is most likely to make you stop playing it for good, is the saving system. The game doesn't allow manual save and: I) save points are oddly placed; II) can only be used once; and III) all your characters have to stand within the save radius in order to the game be saved. This, my friends, can be a pain, because if you die or if the games crashes you may easily lose one hour of gameplay
Here is how the save system works: save points are represented as closed manholes. Once the manhole is used, it opens and it can't be used anymore - so you know exactly which ones were used and which ones were not. Pretty cool if there were plenty of them. However, in some levels you'll desperate cry for save points, while in others you may even not use all of them. Besides, you have to have all your crew together at the same save point for it to work - sometimes it's nice because you can have the whole group to walk through the save point and keep it for later, but if you left someone behind due to the micromanaging thing, you'd better be sure that you left no zombie behind either
I don't play multiplayer games, so I can't talk about it, sorry. And I think it has any achievements, but as I don't care for them I'm not really sure
Conclusion:
This game is not, by no means, unplayable. Devs could had made a few things better, of course, and the saving system can be frustrating at times but the game does the job to keep you entertained. Zombies are slow as they should be and, for what it is, it is a good game
Even though I don't recommend it getting it at full price, if you can cope with the saving system just wait for a sale to grab it
All in all, I give it a 7 out of 10 - because I really liked it and I think it worth the money I paid for it

As someone who has not put a great amount of hours into the game, my review comes with some understandable questioning. However, I still feel as though I have a good feel of the game already, going through many different playthroughs until I finally reached the point where I had the power to beat the final boss and the second final boss in the second playthrough. With that in mind, I find myself going through spurts of loving this game to pieces, playing it bit by bit and getting better as time goes by, collecting more and more items as my personal list of achievements grows. With that in mind, The Binding of Issac more than delivers on its content for the price of 5 dollars (plus seven if you get the incredibly fun "Wrath of the Lamb" DLC). The game runs as an overhead shooter that drops you in the middle of a basement of horrors, pitting you against enemy after enemy as you struggle to survive against the different waves. At its very core the game is very simple: Kill the enemies with your weapon of choice while also avoiding the enemies with WASD at the same time. Once you are able to grasp the difficulty, it makes this game a very rewarding experience. But the true gold of the game shines through as you realize that there is a great deal of items available. In fact, there are so many items available that it makes for a different experience every time you play the game. Add the randomly generated dungeons and enemies throughout the game and you get to the point where you find yourself with an entirely different experience each time you play through the game. That being said, the game is not for those who are easily frustrated, as you will find yourself playing through it multiple times before you even get close to your desired goal. Despite that fact, I find the game well worth the seven dollars it is sold for.

The Witcher 2 is a narrative driven action RPG by Polish developers CD Projekt Red. To be reductive, it contains a lot of action-like RPG combat and deep mechanics common to Bethesda games, but is also extremely narrative driven to the tune of something Bioware might put out.  Over the course of the game, much of the Witcher's many turning gears become an immensely enjoyable machine, though it jumps to a rough start and could use a more enjoyable combat system.  I did play with the Combat Rebalance mod, which allegedly makes the combat better; truly I think it just made it more trivial, but those may be two sides of the same coin in this case.
I started Witcher 2 having never played the Witcher 1, and generally not knowing what the game was about or how it worked.  Let me be blunt -- that is the absolute worst way to start the Witcher 2.  The game does offer an overall useless tutorial (if you have the Enhanced Edition), but otherwise it throws you right into a pretty hot mess.  Very little is explained in the way of combat mechanics, the many systems at your control (things like potions, crafting, magic abilities), and the context of the warring monarchs and their mysterious assassin which are central to its plotline.  Overall, it’s a little daunting to start.  That said, I highly recommend you persevere; lying on the other side is a huge payoff.
What makes Witcher 2 shine is the well crafted, incredibly epic story of politicking and sorcery.  What’s even more impressive is the dynamic way in which it is presented to you; very few games give you the sense of control over the story the way Witcher does.  The game is divided into 3 acts, and the second act can be completely different based on decisions you make in the first act.  You will start in a different location, have different characters to interact with, and different quests.  Even more impressive is that Witcher 2 does a good job of staying away from the typical good/bad archetypes; characters usually feel complex and your decisions almost always fall into a gray area.  It never feels like the game is pushing you one direction or the other; sometimes being the bad guy pays off...other times, not so much.
The plot itself is very interesting, though you won’t find anything revolutionary about it.  Voice acting is typically well done, which is good because there is a LOT of it.  At least half the game can easily be spent talking to characters and fleshing out the world in which Witcher 2 takes place.  Cutscenes are serviceable, but nothing extraordinary.  Like many games of this scope, much of the Witcher 2 lacks a certain polish -- the game certainly looks beautiful, but animations are often clunky and transitions are not done well.
Lacking the most polish, certainly, is the combat.  Combat in Witcher 2 feels mostly like a buffer between unlocking more of the story.  With the Combat Rebalance mod, parrying is automatic and after some initial struggle, I quickly learned to spam the same ability over and over again, accented by mashing attack and rolling around.  I easily beat 95% of encounters this way.  While you have a lot of options in terms of equipment etc., the majority is useless or unnecessary and I would have liked a little more variety in loot and spells.  I wouldn’t say the combat is outright bad, but it is certainly mediocre and not the highlight here.
Overall, while there is a lot to nitpick about Witcher 2, I highly enjoyed it.  It’s a beautiful game which offers up one of the most interesting stories you can find in the medium.  Decisions are impactful and rewarding, even if combat is not.  If you like Skyrim, or Mass Effect, and wish there was a game which blended the two together into a great PC game, look no further than Witcher 2.

The most fun and engaging open-world crime game I've played in a while.
Pros:
1. Fantastic voice-acting with well-rounded characters, and a really interesting mockumentary-style exposition that makes you feel like you're living an alternate history. Nothing to make you feel like a badass than watching an FBI agent describe the lengths to which he had to go to uncover your victims' bodies.
2. Excellent gameplay that gives you a wide array of tools and options for any encounter, incredible setpieces (The Mardi-Gras heist and the extended gunfight in an abandonded theme park jump to mind as favorites), and a thrilling racing mini-game with pretty tight controls
3. A beautiful setting that feels fresh and inventive after a lifetime of playing in New-York-With-The-Serial-Numbers-Filed-Off, with varied vistas ranging from humid swamps to run-down slums to colorful tourist-trap party districts to rainy cobblestoned inner cities. Oh, and the BEST SOUNDTRACK I'VE HEARD IN YEARS. Seriously, when the opening screen slammed into All Along The Watchtower, I knew I was in for an audible treat, and it did not disappoint.
Cons
1. A little buggy, but nothing that did more than break my immersion somewhat, haven't run into anything game-breaking and I've logged almost a day's worth of play already.
2. The regular gameplay is solid enough that I didn't mind, but while a few of the setpieces stand out as absolutely excellent, a few of them could have used a bit more polish, resulting in moments of underwhelming frustration in an otherwise-amazing experience. However, it's worth it to note that, the two examples I can think of, a scene where you get ambushed by cops in the Mardi-Gras heist and have no choice but to flee as fast as possible, and the car chase against a prick who steals your ride where you pursue in a crappy four-door sedan, both, after several attempts, turned out awesome.
After getting gunned down four times in a row to the police, when I finally made it out, the ensuing stealth sequence was pure pulse-pounding enjoyment, and my solution to the car chase was to steal one of my attacker's armored cars, slam the guy who stole my ride off a bridge, whereupon he was satisfyingly eaten by an alligator, and escape the resulting squadron of police cars by off-ramping on the highway and blazing it out of town on an elevated train line. BAD.♥♥♥♥♥
Conclusion: If you aren't having fun in this game, it certainly aint the game's fault. I've grown a Louisiana accent and tripled the density of my spine just playing this beast.

A game designed by Tobias from this studio...
Love and hate are your two main protagonists in the game who you control. Love has a calling which draws objects towards him and hate has the opposite effect. Their objective is to simply hit a red button located somewhere on the level so that they can teleport themselves to the next level. The thing is, it doesn't matter which one hits it, as long as one of them does. Therefore the game especially at the start is quite easy, like a walk in the park. In fact, often I found I could solve certain area's ignoring many facets on the screen, probably due to oversights of the level designer and out of the box thinking by myself, as there were two or three ways to solve many of the problems.
There are 80 levels in total and as you traverse each level, over time you come across a couple more obstacles each with their own perks and introduction cut scene animation. The obstacles in reference are ...
'Lazy' - A block that travels in the direction of the call being made.
'Dead' - A block that refuses to respond.
'Blowing' - An upside down hat which causes an updraft of air that can be used as an elevator. It also has the ability of moving in the direction of a call being made.
'Afraid' - A block which flattens itself when called by 'hate' and goes back to normal to 'loves' call.
'Cold' - A block which exchanges its current position with the exact position of the caller.
'Magic' - A upside down hat which travels in the direction of the call made and makes obstacles disappear which are in its way.
All these quirky obstacles are known as the 'other ones' and a set amount of them are already in position on each level. Since each puzzle map fits on a single screen, no scrolling is required. Instead from the get go your goal is simply to locate the red button and to figure out what you will need in order to reach it, and then work a way of getting those obstacles/instruments there through the orchestration of 'Love' and 'Hates' calling.
In all truthfulness the game really felt like it had the park brake on from get go. It's really slow at the start and kind of just dawdles along. Then when you get to around level 70 before you know it, the park brake is off and you’ve flown over a guard rail and you just don't know what the hell you’re doing. From level 70 onward the difficulty is WAY INCREASED. It seriously goes from teeter totter brain dead place the shapes in the corresponding holes type of difficulty, to your now playing chess and have to declare checkmate within 30 moves level of difficulty.
The game tries to be cute, but never kind of reaches that plateau I wanted and my emotions never really became invested in their little welfare. Problem is that other than going forward through the levels, you’re not making a difference to any of the backgrounds. You’re not restoring the colourful kingdoms of the blobs and neither are you required to defeat any princess stealing nemesis by whizzing them through the air with their tail.
Still I enjoyed it and it did have me REALLY stumped a few times, but without achievements, involved storytelling and workshop your satisfaction will be rather short-lived. Still a worthy little puzzle to place in your library if you get a chance and if it goes on sale.
Now that I have given this a thumbs up and said 'I love you', hopefully black pants studio will move one step closer to their customers and give them what they need to hit that thumbs up button. Achievements, Work Shop, Better Story...

It's solid. Entertaining in short bursts. Played it for quite a bit and probably will play some more. I am a bit disappointed with it though.
You see, it describes itself as a roguelike rhythm game. There isn't much rhythm in there. Now, the problem might be, that I am a classicaly trained musician and the way I see rhythm is probably a bit different. My issues might not be revelant to other players.
How I would describe this game is a roguelike with simple mechanics but with a quite clever gimmick. Turns happen on their own in regular intervals, not when you move (as in classic rogue-likes). Enemies move in certain patterns (some move every turn, other every other turn etc.) The tricky part is to quickly evaluate your enemies and make right decisions in a short time given. To help you move in the right time turns are sincronized with music. That is really all there is to it. Also, the game is very forgiving when it comes to moving on time.
Occasionally, things get a bit more interesting. There are traps, which accelerate/slow down turns (and music.) There is one boss fight, where rhythm is irregular (one beat is skipped.) There is one miniboss, which disables the music until you kill it (never found it to be an issue... everyone can just tap a perfectly even rhythm, right?)
There are some choices in the design, which I am still not sure whenever I like or not. Do do have a choice of different characters but rather than offering alternative playstyles, they give you special challenges. I thought it to be a strange choice but I do like it more and more. The game core-mechanics are too basic to allow for different "playstyles" so just complicating things by creating special rules for all of the characters is a welcome addition. The weapons are very very unbalanced. However, the good ones seem to be difficult to get in the actual run. It work alright in the end.
Not a too big a fan of the soundtrack. I am usually a big fan of Danny B soundtracks, but this one is a bit dull. Probably the issue is the big focus on a regular beat, which I find to be snooze worthy. Comeon, rhythm is an importan part of music. You cant be THAT regular.
So lots of negative things. But it is still fun. Give it a bash. Probably none of my issues will be relevant to you.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is amazing game, especially for all the effort (apart from sound mixing and voice acting) one man put into it. Initally an entry to an XBLA contest, it won first prize and was placed onto XBLA possibly to the creator's surprise. The game was popular, so he began to create the Steam version you see before you to gain Linux, Mac and Windows user fans. I'm very glad he did.
Before I get onto the review, here's a disclaimer. I am not praising this game because I like "furries" (anthromorphic characters, you childish swine). I'm praising this game because it's an actual good game. It could have been full of normal humans and I would have loved it regardless. Anywho...
Dust is a Metroidvania game and it does the genre justice. It just does it so well. I was not bored at all throughout my playthrough, which took me perhaps a solid 6-8 hours to beat because I explored every bit of each level. There's a leveling system designed in a way that you get stronger, but you cannot pile something into one stat. You're restricted to having everything at least four points within each other (meaning you must fill out Health, Attack, Fidget, etc almost evenly). It was an attempt to making Dust not so overpowered too early. There are some special melee combos you could do, but all in all, they are not necessary. This isn't Mortal Kombat, so we don't need complex movesets in order to beat the enemies to a pulp. I do see many complaints about the combat system being shallow and to be honest I actually quite like it. It's simple and it's still hard as hell to get a 1,000 hit combo without knowing exactly what to do (this was the last quest  I completed).
My only gripes are that eventually, you become rather overpowered. This precaution with having the Skill Gems (aka Skill Points) within 4 points of each other doesn't offer much control when the items start having quite the state boots (such as +800 to Attack for your Weapon Augment, x3 to Fidget's power, etc). The aerial attack also can be somewhat exploited by knowing when you suddenly turn a light shade of red, you can let go of the button, wait a few seconds, then do it again (though it does reset your hit counter). The bosses are also not much of a challenge apart from Lady Tethys, who only ends up being a challenge because you're platforming while spamming Fidget's attack with Dust Storm.
TL;DR Version below.
Pros: Combat, story, visual style, the genre it picked is perfect, and it makes me want a Dust 2 or the man to finish the "An Elysian Tail" movie!
Cons: You can become overpowered toward the end of the game (perhaps 75% of the way through). The aerial attack despite never being able to hold it infinitely can still be easily used until you turn slightly red, let go and reset the timer and do it again. The bosses are also rather easy.

My first serious review.  This game has changed my opinion so much from the first time I played it I wanted to write this incase I can convince at least one other person who may have had similiar feelings as me when I first played it.
I tried playing this game a few times as Cadence when I first got it.
It was somewhat fun, although not enough to keep my attention.
Then I tried playing as the Bard.
It was fun not having to worry about the beat of music, and instead just learning enemy movement and attack patterns.
When you play as the Bard the whole game becomes turn-based.  Each move you make causes the enemies to do one movement.
A solid rogue-like.  You basically play over and over until you get familiar with all the enemies, each time you feel yourself getting better and better at this game.
I was in zone 2.  Just doing another run, when it hit me.  Even as the Bard I found myself moving to the beat of the music.  I was using my shovel to dig through dirt which added its own sound to the music playing.  I was realizing that some of the movements I was making when fighting a particular enemy was almost like doing dance moves.
It hit me.  This game is freaking genius.  Playing through a few times as the Bard is almost a necessity and I wish the game developers would have somehow made it more obvious that this should be a first step.
Binding of Isaac used to be my favorite Rogue-Like, now I can say without a doubt this is my new favorite.

I'm a big fan of Master of Orion 2, Gal Civ was never interesting, because it had no multiplayer.
But now, here it is! I bought this game in early access, last year around christmas.
The game was very rudimentary and not very polished, so i played a couple of hours and decided to wait till release.
And now, I'm looking at one of the best 4x space games that have come out in years! Serious, it has flaws, but overall it is the best 4x space game you can expect these days.
Here are my pros:
- The Tech-tree is gigantic and very diversified. You have often to choose which of three possible techs you want, the others are gone, till you are able to trade the techs with someone else.
- The building system on planets is unique and maybe you need a little practice before you are able to squeeze the last bit of efficiency out of it.
- Colonizing planets let you make ideologic decisions, because every planet comes along with some kind of speciality.
Maybe there are natives on the planet and you have now the possibility to decide what will happen to them.
Benevolent, would let them keep their lifestyle, which leads to an increment of your ideologic points and gets you a approval   bonus.
Pragmatic, would keep them in a reservat and make a tourist attraction of them. (Also getting ideologic points.)
Malevolent, would enslave them and use as a cheap labor force.
This system makes a lot of fun and seems to be thought through. (Maybe there are balancing issues, but we will see.)
- A lot of winning conditions, not just war.
- Customizing your race is nearly as good as in moo 2.
- Special resources for prototype weapons or buildings.
- Ship designer!
- A rich map generator, and last but not least...
- Multiplayer!
The cons:
-  Combat is automatic and the battle viewer has some issues getting the scene right and your spacecraft flying in strange circles around the enemy.
- No espionage!
- Stability issues.
(but i could solve mine, by increasing the swap file to at least 4 gb. No problems since. But my friend who wants to play the                                                             game with me, has a lot of problems, although he increased his swap file size too.)
- And there are maybe a lot of other minor things that can be personal preference.
As a conclusion I can say:
This game does a lot of things right and gives you a lot of freedom which you would expect, if you played games like Master of Orion 2 before. It goes even further by giving the community the possibility to mod the game.
You can spend dozens of hours in custom games or in multiplayer and every game could be a new experience.
There is also a new campaign, which i haven't played yet, but this is a big plus for the singleplayers.
Beside some features i would like to see and the bad stability, this game is (can be even better with some addons) the best experience 4x space gamers can get.

Galciv3 is a worthy sequel to its predecessor, and a good 4x game when compared to modern titles in the genre. This coupled with a developer with a proven reputation for supporting their games for a long time makes this a safe buy.
are very favorable as well. If you are in for the long haul this game has amazing potential for the future, and unlike most other games in the genre recently has the financial means to deliver.
-
: Perhaps the games most important feature, removing one of the genres biggest limitations: the 32bit 4gb memory limit. This allows the scale of the game to increase by a order of magnitude in terms of map size, amount of ships, planets and stars, and complexity of AI routines.
-
: The way you place planetary improvements matters. If you put 2 improvements of the same category next to each other, they will buff eachother. Combined with terrain bonuses native to the planet and clever terraforming means you can get factories or research labs with 6+ bonus levels on your high quality planets quite easily, massively boosting your production.
-
: The largest map in civilzation: Beyond earth and Endless Legend are
. Galciv3's biggest map size is
, appropriately named Insane. Keep in mind that a insane map requires at least 8gb ram to even start.
-
: A rarity in 4x games, this game offers a campaign. The main benefit this brings is that it allows newer players to jump straight into a game that in well in progress, giving them a chance to see the beauty of 4x games without having to struggle trough the learning curve to much, it starts of with a couple of large space battles to give players a taste of what is possible. A experienced 4x player can probably beat the campaign in one of two afternoons, while a new player might take a bit longer.
-
: A iconic feature of the series, the in game ship designer is a powerful tool that lets you build virtually any ship you can imagine, such as ships form popular TV series.  Chances are you can see a bunch of them in the
. The game comes with a bunch of pre-made designs and workshop integration will allow for easy downloading of other players ships if designing ships isn't your thing.
-
: Choose the stats and combat roles of your ships. Research ship components like enginers, weapons, shields and life support, then put them on your ships to create your own style. build anything from large capital ships, carriers that launch strike craft, bombers and interceptors to freighter hulls loaded with lazers. Customize your ships to be optimal against the enemy you are fighting. You can assign your ship combat roles that determine how they behave in fleet combat (ie interceptor, support ship, assault ship, etc) This part too is not mandatory, the game will dynamically generate ships for you as you research more parts, those ships will do the job but might not be exactly what you want.
-
: upload your own pictures and icons (or videos) to use for your faction, choose what positive and/or negative traits your faction gets, your ship style and looks, UI color, tech tree, etc. Set up how the AI should play your race if you want to fight against it by giving it personality traits and priorities.
-
: The devs went out of their way to make this game easy to mod, allowing virtually every aspect of the game to be changed. In June steam workshop support will arrive, allowing for players to easily share their mods, custom factions, ship designs and components, custom maps, balance changes, etc.
-
: The game supports up to 128 AI opponents for truly insane games, where entire factions will die out before you even meet them.
-
: Standard feature for any 4x worth it's salt.
-
: The tech tree is large enough that in a regular game you will only research certain parts of your choosing form it. Each race has a couple of unique techs, and gets certain techs earlier then others, each tech tree has its own full set of flavor text per race. Specialization techs offer you a choice between 3 techs of which you can only choose one, though you can get the others trough trade if you want.
-
: Colonizing planets and galactic events present you with ethical choices allowing you to choose a benevolent, pragmatic or malevolent path. Each choice might have pros and cons for the planet you are colonizing, and gives you ideology points to spend on perks. The perks become quite powerful in the higher tiers and each path offers strong options.
-
: Play with friends and stuff. 4 player multiplayer atm. At the time of writing there are still some stability issues to work out but that is slated to be fixed within the next weeks.

-
: Still a bit in it early shoes but is constantly being worked on. A common pitfall amongst 4x games is that this area lacks on launch, nevertheless the AI performs quite well compared to other games. The AI will regularly contact you with trade request, comment on your relationship (move ships out of my area, dont build up troops near my borders, your army is weak, i like that were trading, i dont like that your friends with the other guy, etc.). It's noteworthy that the AI doesn't cheat nearly as much as a lot of other games in the gerne, it can't see the entire map for example.

All in all, this game is a solid 8/10 for me.

I've not yet wrote a review of a game but I feel like this one deserves a review! When I saw this game I had to have it! The graphics are extemely beautiful and luring and the over all gameplay is really relaxing and fun! I streamed this live on Twitch and my audience really seemed to enjoy how peaceful it was, but not to an extent where they got bored! The game keeps the player active at all times but doesn't ask for complete and utter consentration (meaning I could sit and chat without missing a huge part of the story)
As you explore the depths of the ocean you get to learn a few sea creatures names, although I'd would enjoy it if there was a better system for this, because it pretty much goes through every single finish in an area (as in all of them - not just the types) so finding out what certian types where was a little difficult and after 5/10 mins trying to find out the name of one fish gets annoying and I just moved on. I'd also love if it included the coral but I think that's just me being nit-picky :P
One feature that I really didn't enjoy, but did not ruin the game is what we called during our stream 'Floppy Diver Syndrome'. I played this with a controller and my lord was it difficult to navigate! I tried inverted and normal and both where extremely difficult to use. I feel like the controls should have been neated up a little as sometimes it's just extremely difficult to control the main character, making things take way longer than they should - this is literally the only problem I had with the game.
As for the story line, I won't give anything away but I will say that it was really mind blowing and went in a direction that I honestly was not expecting! Really well done and very touching towards the end!
Also, just as a final note - a few people have said do not play if you are afraid of the ocean - I am terrified of being underwater and easily get anxiety when a game requires me to do so... but this game was different, I don't know whether it's the fact that the main character can happily breathe underwater or if it was just simply the breath-taking graphics but my anxiety was only spiked a little during certain parts of the game and not to an extent that I didn't want to continue playing (which is normally what happens). So I'd go into this game with an open mind, if it looks like something you'd like to play but are worried about how your fear might affect you.

Note: With The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings Enhanced Edition I entered the Witcher universe without playing the first title or knowing anything about the books let alone having read them. So here goes.
The first RPG I played where your choices actually DO matter (*cough* Mass Effect *cough*). Yes, I kid you not. Not only does the game split up after Act I depending on who you choose to side with, but the outcome of dialogues in the main quest and even the side quests offer multiple possibilites for the story to unfold. The complexity and ingenuity of the fantasy world this game is set in is comparable to the quality of GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire and can therefore be characterized as a so-called "low fantasy" story, as opposed to "high fantasy" settings such as The Elder Scrolls (just google the definitions if you don't know anything about them). Personally, I prefer low fantasy due to its focus on individual character development and their story/fate, as well as a "realistic" depiction of violence, language and society as a whole, but that's just my preference. So in a nutshell, I liked the story a lot, I think there's a lot of exciting things still to be told.
Now let's get to the technical aspects: Dialogue is great, offering many choices for convincing or intimidating and alike. Character customization is solid too (you can actually have your haircut changed to some very weird stuff throughout the game if you so desire), there's lots of item slots, but only two weapons, a fact I can however accept for story reasons. Then again, I always pick the sword in any fantasy RPG so having two different swords throughout the entire game was right down my alley.
Since we've arrived at the swords let's talk about the combat shall we. Yeah, I don't like it, why don't I like it you might say? It's basically a combo-based hack'n'slash system with a very console-y feeling (believe me or not, I liked Skyrim combat more, yes really). You just lock onto a target and smash LMB/RMB with the occasional blocking. I think this is simplistic and may be fun to watch, but it's not really immersive (on a side note: the combat is pretty hard and the boss fight require true skill and creativity and especially cunning use of magic abilities, I liked these a lot more). Speaking of immersive, the game looks gorgeous for a 2011 title, mostly good textures and effects. What struck me was the very high depth of field especially in the first act. I guess that's a way to make the lack of quality of distant objects unnoticable. Arguably, the biggest plus is the sound: ambient sound, voice acting and especially soundtrack are downright masterful, I loved it.
I can't think of anything else atm so let's jump to the conclusion. The game is great, with lots of replayability due to the many different paths you can go. The world sucks you in right from the start. If you're a fan of the combat then you've got absolutely nothing to fear, if you don't it's still worth it for the experience because mechanics are easy to get used to.
Performance notes: The game is Nvidia optimized. With my AMD card(s), it runs a solid 60fps though. Just tweak AA a bit and turn off Cinematic Depth of Field, it makes cutscene-fps drop by half, which is not cool. It supports CFX and probably also SLI. Oh yeah and the game is capped to 120fps, which is nice too.

The LiEat trilogy is a very short but sweet tale of Efina the Lie-Eating Dragon and her guardian, whose name and face change with each passing town.  Together, they work to... make money!  Naturally, though, in a world with dragons, that's hardly ever all they do.
Oftentimes, people's lies start to grow as they continue to tell them.  Ultimately, a person can become so lost in their lies that the lies take physical form, taking over the person in question and turning them into a monster.  Whether by fate or dumb luck, our heroes almost always end up having to solve these lies and uncover the truths of the people they meet.  However, even as they defeat the lies of others, the lies of a certain guardian start to grow all too apparent...
All in all, this is a really cute and enjoyable story.  It's very short, with each game taking roughly an hour to complete.  However, it's a very charming little game with a lovable cast and a beautiful ending.  ...Well, actually, there are multiple endings, most of which only appear if you fail.  But the good ending is beautiful!  If you're ever in need of a fun distraction, LiEat is definitely the game for you!

Though I initially bought this on Humble Bundle b/c of the XBLA demo, I got more than expected out of this Metroidvania. The story has some unexpected turns, and has several memorable side characters that left me smiling for days (SmoBop might be my favorite). The tale isn't too original, but that doesn't detract from the overall polish & cohesion, which is admirable for an indie. After seeing a bit of the early architecture and character design, I was hoping for more integration of Dodrill's Korean heritage throughout the story, though it's rich as it is.
Dust isn't shy about its roots, and pays homage to the games that inspired it via cameos. Bastion and Braid were perhaps my favorite nods. However, considering how much Dust borrows from Aquaria (eg projectile sprites, cooking), it's surprising that it wasn't numbered in the grand tribute.
In its transfer from XBLA, Dust does suffer a bit from consolitis, but a bit of seamless key rebinding helps a bit. Particularly useful for me was rebinding PgUp/Dwn to Q & E and having multiple mouse bindings.
Crafting was also a bit of a chore, but is easily alleviated by the inevitable gold surplus at later levels. The game can be a bit artificially grindy, esp the arenas, but the main game is beatable w/o those diversions. Characters could've been fleshed out a bit more, but in the vein of To the Moon, it'd be a bit much to ask for more from a mostly 1 man project.
The soundtrack was appropriate, esp in the later levels, but not too noteworthy. It def reaches its crescendo at the end.
In my brief trek through Falana, I found myself longing for more, even after a 2nd playthrough. Hope to see more from Dodrill.

It's solid. Entertaining in short bursts. Played it for quite a bit and probably will play some more. I am a bit disappointed with it though.
You see, it describes itself as a roguelike rhythm game. There isn't much rhythm in there. Now, the problem might be, that I am a classicaly trained musician and the way I see rhythm is probably a bit different. My issues might not be revelant to other players.
How I would describe this game is a roguelike with simple mechanics but with a quite clever gimmick. Turns happen on their own in regular intervals, not when you move (as in classic rogue-likes). Enemies move in certain patterns (some move every turn, other every other turn etc.) The tricky part is to quickly evaluate your enemies and make right decisions in a short time given. To help you move in the right time turns are sincronized with music. That is really all there is to it. Also, the game is very forgiving when it comes to moving on time.
Occasionally, things get a bit more interesting. There are traps, which accelerate/slow down turns (and music.) There is one boss fight, where rhythm is irregular (one beat is skipped.) There is one miniboss, which disables the music until you kill it (never found it to be an issue... everyone can just tap a perfectly even rhythm, right?)
There are some choices in the design, which I am still not sure whenever I like or not. Do do have a choice of different characters but rather than offering alternative playstyles, they give you special challenges. I thought it to be a strange choice but I do like it more and more. The game core-mechanics are too basic to allow for different "playstyles" so just complicating things by creating special rules for all of the characters is a welcome addition. The weapons are very very unbalanced. However, the good ones seem to be difficult to get in the actual run. It work alright in the end.
Not a too big a fan of the soundtrack. I am usually a big fan of Danny B soundtracks, but this one is a bit dull. Probably the issue is the big focus on a regular beat, which I find to be snooze worthy. Comeon, rhythm is an importan part of music. You cant be THAT regular.
So lots of negative things. But it is still fun. Give it a bash. Probably none of my issues will be relevant to you.

A LONG overdue review:
Long has there been a void in the gaming market for a truely outstanding Metroidvania style game. That is until "Dust: An Elysian Tail" was first released on Xbox Live.  Now it comes to PC; it's beautiful artistry made even more outstanding with higher resolution visuals.  Crafted by a single man over years of hard work, Dust shows just what the genre, and a single individual can be capable of.  The team gathered to finish off the game with it's music and voice acting round out this gem and help to truely make it stand out from it's contemporaries.  The painted scenery and landscapes, excellent voice work, outstanding musical score, and fluid animations all come together to make a game that big name publishers only wish they could produce.
Sadly it's artistic style may turn off many potential buyers due to it's use of anthropomorphic characters.  The character designs harken to a Disney style and help to lighten an otherwise dark-toned story.
Perhaps the only downside is it's difficulty, with the highest being the best to play on but having no challenge above it.  Playing on any lower setting just feels too easy and cheapens the gameplay.  Oh... and the sidekick can get a little annoying at times.
The best game I've played this year.

I LOVED this game. This is the first thing I've played since City of Heroes that I really, truly enjoyed. Not only is it gorgeous, but I found the story to be compelling, and I wanted to explore all the areas and find every last scrap of information I could about this world and the people in it. I love the crafting system (find an item, sell it to the merchant, and you never have to farm for it again!) and the combat, which I remapped for ease of use so that I wouldn't have to use the mouse. Did I mention how easy this game is to configure to your personal preferences? The music was okay, if occasionally annoying, and the voice acting was spot-on. The game is a mixture of combat, exploration, and puzzle-solving, and it's challenging but not frustratingly difficult. You do have to return to some areas in order to complete them, as there are sections that can't be reached without abilities gained later in the game, but I didn't find it problematic. The final battle felt epic enough to me to cap off the whole story, and while at first I was disappointed in the ending, my faith was rewarded after all. There are also easter eggs in the form of characters borrowed from other games, which you can encounter and free from captivity and then go hang out with, so that was cool. Overall, there's not much I didn't like about this one, and I'm going to be playing it again!

My first serious review.  This game has changed my opinion so much from the first time I played it I wanted to write this incase I can convince at least one other person who may have had similiar feelings as me when I first played it.
I tried playing this game a few times as Cadence when I first got it.
It was somewhat fun, although not enough to keep my attention.
Then I tried playing as the Bard.
It was fun not having to worry about the beat of music, and instead just learning enemy movement and attack patterns.
When you play as the Bard the whole game becomes turn-based.  Each move you make causes the enemies to do one movement.
A solid rogue-like.  You basically play over and over until you get familiar with all the enemies, each time you feel yourself getting better and better at this game.
I was in zone 2.  Just doing another run, when it hit me.  Even as the Bard I found myself moving to the beat of the music.  I was using my shovel to dig through dirt which added its own sound to the music playing.  I was realizing that some of the movements I was making when fighting a particular enemy was almost like doing dance moves.
It hit me.  This game is freaking genius.  Playing through a few times as the Bard is almost a necessity and I wish the game developers would have somehow made it more obvious that this should be a first step.
Binding of Isaac used to be my favorite Rogue-Like, now I can say without a doubt this is my new favorite.

The Lego games will always hold a very dear place in my heart. I love them. For me, they are my "relaxer" games.
So it is without hesitation that I recommend Lego Star Wars III: The Clone Wars to any and all Lego fans and Star Wars fans, as well as fans of goofy, exciting fun that isn't too much of a challenge.
Pros:
- Fun, colorful graphics.
- Loads of entertainment for anyone of any age.
- Hours and hours and hours of playability and replayability.
- Legitimately funny cutscenes and Lego antics.
- A HUGE central hub.
- A huge number of characters to unlock and play around with.
- As best I could tell (based mainly upon the fact that I am not quite caught up with TCW television series at the time of writing this review), the missions are faithful to the series.
Cons:
- Literally the worst Lego character creator I have seen yet. I LOVE to make my own characters in the Lego games and roleplay through the levels with them. I was, however, unable to create a cunning, bad-to-the-bone, bounty hunter or Magna Guard-turned-Dark Jedi to my liking. Shame on you, Tt Games, shame on you.
- Occasionally the graphics would hit a weird hitch where, during the cutscenes, the characters would be invisible.
But, despite these (very few) failings, I would absolutely, positively recommend this game. But do yourself a favor and get it on sale, like I did. The price is a tad steep for a game from 2011.
Cheers.

This game is an absolute blast. One of the most enjoyable games I've played in a long time. No artificial noise, no cut scenes, no dying over and over again. Just you and these badass trucks trudging through the mud. The sound of birds chirping as you make your way along tranquil dirt roads and beautiful lakes and forests. Loading up with logs and trying to navigate the terrain is intense. Weight and momentum are incredibly realistic. Will you tip over or do you have enough speed to make it up the hill? The physics of this game are easily the best I've ever seen. It's really satisfying to accomplish the objectives on each map. I've put in about 30 hours so far but I don't find myself wanting to move on from this game, which is rare for me. I honestly don't think this game could do anything better than it already does. Congratulations to the developers on this one. A true gem for anyone who enjoys driving simulators, problem solving or peace and quiet. Incredible game. 10/10!!!!!

I always liked the Galactic Civilizations games, but this game feels dumbed down from the second version, probably for appeal to a wider audience. It doesn't feel like the result of a lot of love, but rather like the outcome of a lot of compromises.
Race customization isn't very useful if your "new race" has the exact physical and technological features of the existing races.
Also, what made the earlier genres great was that space itself was connected by warp tunnles; this version just has a few habitable planets surrounded by many, many dead and useless planets.
The United Planets drudgery is bizarre and doesn't fit with the xenophobic tendencies I like to conquer with.
All in all, one of my favorite 4x games has just come out with a big meh and so I won't spend much time playing it.
